Management Plans help pull together an understanding of significance to evidence the conservation and management of heritage assets. From this informed basis, plans are then used to develop programmes of repair, restoration or to draw up proposals for change. Management Plans should be structured to meet the needs of the specific property/site and designed to be used for every day reference by staff managing the site. Management Plans not only pull together and analyse the history of a site or landscape, they can also be an important record in their own right.

The local heritage asset may provide evidence about past human activity in the locality, which may be in the form of buried remains, but may also be revealed in the structure of buildings or in a designed landscape, for instance. Heritage assets with archaeological interest are primary sources of evidence about the substance and evolution of places, and of the people and cultures that made them.

If heritage assets of archaeological interest are identified by stage 1 then for those parts of the site which have archaeological interest a stage 2 WSI shall be submitted to and approved by the local planning authority in writing. For land that is included within the stage 2 WSI, no demolition/development shall take place other than in accordance with the agreed stage 2 WSI which shall include: A. The statement of significance and research objectives, the programme and methodology of site investigation and recording and the nomination of a competent person(s) or organisation to undertake the agreed works B. Where appropriate, details of a programme for delivering related positive public benefits C. The programme for post-investigation assessment and subsequent analysis, publication & dissemination and deposition of resulting material. This part of the condition shall not be discharged until these elements have been fulfilled in accordance with the programme set out in the stage 2 WSI.

A significant historical association of local or national note, including links to important local figures, may enhance the significance of a heritage asset. Blue Plaque and similar schemes may be relevant. Social and communal interest may be regarded as a sub-set of historic interest but has special value in local listing. As noted in the PPG: ‘Heritage assets … can also provide meaning for communities derived from their collective experience of a place and can symbolise wider values such as faith and cultural identity’. It therefore relates to places perceived as a source of local identity, distinctiveness, social interaction and coherence, contributing to the ‘collective memory’ of a place.

In order to assess the impact that any development (including any ground works and archaeological mitigation) will have on the hydrology of a site the existing water environment at the site must be understood. This often involves looking beyond the red line of the site boundary to capture relevant aspects of river stream and drainage systems. Hydrology is a complex subject and the assessment should be carried out by a qualified specialist, usually part of the developer’s engineering team. The information gathered in a hydrological assessment is of use in identifying if the water pathways will change in a manner that could put waterlogged deposits at risk of drying out, it also informs the detailed design of foundations and a structures and in cases where preserving archaeological remains within/ under a new structure/ development it provides information on suitable redesign.

Fieldwalking is a rapid, cost-effective and relatively inexpensive technique which allows for ‘broad-brush’ archaeological prospection and landscape characterisation over large areas. It is most commonly employed as part of the archaeological evaluation stage of the planning process. It is particularly effective for locating Stone Age archaeology when undertaken at close-spaced intervals.

Coring can assist in a variety of situations to map stratigraphy (borehole surveys) and collect samples. It is mainly undertaken when the deposits of interest are too deep for conventional digging, or when large areas need to be mapped. In developer-funded evaluations, borehole surveys should not be seen as a replacement for conventional trench evaluation, but they can be used as a first phase where the results need to characterise the local sedimentary sequence and help pinpoint trench locations. This technique is also very helpful in establishing the presence of waterlogged deposits with potential for palaeoenvironmental evidence (see also Hydrological impact assessment).

A Heritage Statement (also commonly referred to as a Statement of Significance) is normally required to support all development proposals for planning permission, listed building consent or scheduled monument consent, when the proposal directly affects a heritage asset or its setting. It is an important practical tool to guide an applicant in developing their proposals.

The NPPF defines a heritage asset as ‘a building, monument, site, place, area or landscape identified as having a degree of significance meriting consideration in planning decisions, because of its heritage interest’. Designated heritage assets include listed buildings and conservation areas, which are legally protected under the Planning (Listed Buildings and Areas) Act 1990. Most works to listed buildings require listed building consent in addition to planning permission.

An archaeological field evaluation involves exploratory fieldwork to determine if significant remains are present on a site and if so to define their character, extent, quality and preservation. Field evaluation may involve one or more techniques depending on the nature of the site and its archaeological potential. It will normally include excavation of trial trenches. A field evaluation report will usually be used to inform a planning decision (pre-determination evaluation) but can also be required by condition to refine a mitigation strategy after permission has been granted.

The NPPF defines the setting of a heritage asset as ‘the surroundings in which a heritage asset is experienced. Its extent is not fixed and may change as the asset and it surroundings evolve. Elements of a setting may make a positive or negative contribution to the significance of an asset, may affect the ability to appreciate that significance or may be neutral’. An assessment of the contribution made by setting towards the significance of the affected heritage asset should be undertaken as part of a Heritage Statement and used to inform planning decisions. It uses existing baseline information such as views and surrounding spaces to assess the current setting of a heritage asset and how the proposed development would affect that setting.

A building or complex, housing powered machinery and employing a large workforce for manufacturing purposes. Use specific monument type where known.
Factory producing asbestos sheeting and or asbestos fibre.

Sites, buildings, structures & features related to the practice of rituals & religious beliefs, including funerary rites. Includes ancillary buildings, structures & features of uncertain use, which are thought to be ï¿½ritualï¿½ (eg. hill figures).
Religious establishment, founded in Somerset, where free love was practised.
A mutiple role hangar for aircraft and general storage, manufactured in the USA as a kit for on-site assembly during WWII and post-war. It comprises a steel box frame and a canvas covering.
A structure used for the housing and servicing of aircraft.
A panel, usually wooden or stone, painted or engraved with an illustration or inscription.
A defined portion of a surface, often a wall lining or door, usually rectangular, which may be recessed, level with or proud of its surrounding surface and may be framed by mouldings or channels.
A part of a building or structure that is an element of the construction.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production and use of steam power.
A building housing a turbine.
A factory or works engaged in the manufacture of the explosive guncotton. They may be found as separate factories or form part of a cordite factory.
A building or buildings where explosives are manufactured.
An end scraper which has a retouched end that is concave in form. (Source: SARC)
A flint blade or flake with retouch on one or both ends.
A flake or blade with retouch along one or more edges.
An end scraper that has a retouched end which is convex in form. (Source: SARC)

An end scraper which has a retouched end that is straight in form. If the tool blank is a blade or flake, and the retouch is abrupt retouch rather than scraper retouch then use either Truncated blade or Truncated flake. (Source: SARC)
An end scraper made on a flake that is wider than it is long. (Source: SARC)
A column base featuring a hollow, concave - or scotia - moulding between two tori, which are projecting, convex mouldings.
A classical order with an Attic base and fluted column. The cornice has dentils and the capital volutes.

skos:ConceptScheme.dcterms:title: FISH Maritime Fixtures and Fittings Thesaurus

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A craft or repair workshop in a boat yard, harbour or naval dockyard.
A wooden or metal structure covering a shipbuilding slip way.
A spiked, iron plate fixed to a boot for climbing on ice.
Items which are part of or added to footwear.
A cross channel telegraph office.
A building housing electrical or electronic equipment used for communicating over long distances. Use specific type where known.

The main office of a telegraph company containing rows of tables set with Morse sounders, keys, relays and pigeon holes from where MORSE coded messages were transmitted and received and telegrams dispatched.

A building temporarily requistioned for use as a hospital. Auxiliary hospitals treated the less seriously wounded and were less strict than military hospitals although they remained under military control.
A building temporarily requisitioned for use as an auxiliary hospital administered by members of the Voluntary Aid Detachment during the First World War.
An establishment providing medical or surgical treatment for the ill or wounded. Use narrower term where possible.
Armoured covering to protect the hand and wrist.
Armour designed to protect the chest, sometimes permanently attached to a backplate.
Armour designed to protect the leg or parts of the leg. For specific foot protection use FOOT GUARD
Piece of armour worn to protect the back, often permanently connected to the breastplate.
A piece of armour used to protect the armpit.
A specialised fitting for Roman armour. For a part of a garment use APRON.
A piece of armour worn to protect the throat.
Protective covering for the body.
A piece of armour designed to protect the arm or a part of the arm.
Armour designed to protect the torso, and consists of both back and breast plates.
A piece of plate armour designed to protect the shoulder.
Armour designed to protect the foot.
A cloth or leather tunic, usually worn underneath metal armour, although sometimes worn by itself.
A flexible armour designed to protect the torso.
A defensive or protective covering for the head.
The forms of armour used to protect various parts of the body.
A musical instrument which produces its sound by being scraped.
A primitive musical instrument.
Musical instruments by how the sound is produced by the instrument.
An instrument whirled to produce sound by a piece of flexible wood hitting against a ratchet wheel.
Any dome shaped metal bell struck either by an internal clapper or by a hammer.
A simple instrument where two pieces of material are manipulated to knock together.
A thin piece of metal which when struck vibrates to produce a sound, can be used in pairs.
A metal disk with a turned rim, giving a resonant note when struck.
A hollow instrument containing material that produces sound when shaken.
A triangle of metal which, when struck, produces a note.
An enclosed, round bell with a slit, sounded by a loose internal pellet.
An instrument consisting of a small lyre-shaped metal frame held between the teeth, with a steel tongue plucked with the finger.
A musical instrument producing sound from its own body.
The timber from genus Betula, found in Europe and North America, particularly in northern regions.
A hard, compact, unprocessed, fibrous cellulose substance. The roots, trunks and branches of trees and shrubs consist of this tissue.
Houses specifically of monks, canons or religious men but not friars.
A place of worship and residence for followers of Buddha.
The area directly in front of a fireplace or the floor of a firecplace itself.
A hearth, normally placed clear of the walls, without a chimney stack or hood above.
A room or building used as a store, usually for documents, works of art, books etc.
Component. Use wider site type where known.
A room or group of rooms usually below the ground level and usually under a building, often used for storing fuel, provisions or wines.
A communal dining room, especially in schools, colleges and monasteries.
A building or a room for accounts.
A structure with a roof to provide shelter from the weather for occupants or contents. Use specific type where known.
A place used to hide something or someone.
A structure which can be an area within a building, a separate building within a complex or a detached architectural component of a building
A vault or crypt under a church or chapel. Use wider site type where known.
Use for free standing column.
A place where material used for burning is stored.
An underground room or building with an arched roof, often used as a burial chamber. Use wider site type where known.
A self-service dining room, especially for workers/employees; also in institutions, such as schools, hospitals, etc.
A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of spirits.
A row of columns supporting an entablature.
A room or building housing the controls to a mechanized system, eg. in a power station, airport, etc.

A cylindrical bomb, designed by Barnes Wallis in 1941, containing hydrostatic pistols measuring water pressure for detonation at a depth of 30 feet. Dropped whilst fast revolving at a height of 60 feet at 240-250 mph to maximise the bouncing effect.
A hollow case containg explosive, incendiary, smoke-producing, poisonous or other offensive material, designed to be deposited, dropped, thrown or shot froma mortar.
Includes individual index cards
A building used to aid in the drying of goods, for example, by means of flowing air.
A building used to dry flax.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with railway transport.
A building in which railway wagons can unload local goods.
A plug for closing the neck of a container.
A stopper made of cork used to prevent liquid escaping from a container.
Two masted merchant vessel, rigged as a brig.
A vessel with a type of rigging where the main driving sails are fixed to yards which lie square to the mast.
The study of mollusca remains preserved within archaeological deposits and palaeoenvironmental archives.
The study of diatoms preserved in deposits.

The study of plant remains, typically seeds, fruits, wood, leaves etc, preserved within archaeological deposits and palaeoenvironmental archives. Use palynology when pollen and spores are being analysed as opposed to macroscopic plant remains.
The degree to which a material will become magnetised when placed in a magnetic field.
The microscopic analysis of thin sections of resin impregnated stratigraphy.
The study of biological remains preserved within deposits, including peat.
The study of foraminifera preserved in deposits.
A measure of the proportion of water within a sample.

The study of vertebrate remains, excluding human remains, preserved within archaeological deposits and palaeoenvironmental archives. Use archaeomalacology for the study of mollus remains and palaeoentomology for the study of insect remains.
The study of insect remains preserved within archaeological deposits and palaeoenvironmental archives.
The study of human remains preserved within archaeological deposits and palaeoenvironmental archives.
The study of minerals.
The analysis of the distribution and proportion of sand, silt and clay in a deposit.
The production of an image on a photographic plate as a result of X-rays (very short wavelength electromagnetic radiation) being passed through an object.
The examination of material by physical means, including detailed observation.
The identification and grouping of stone types in stratigraphy.
The study of pollen and non-pollen palyomorphs preserved within deposits, including peat.
The weight loss from low-temperature burning of material. It correlates well with organic matter (material derived from living things) content.
The careful observation and written description of the physical characteristics of stratigraphy. It will normally include information on texture, colour and the nature of the different components.
The use of magnifying equipment to examine materials not visible to the naked eye.
The use of annual incremental growth in temperate trees to investigate environmental, especially local, parameters and the history of individual trees.
A tower at the mouth of the harbour to defend the end of the harbour boom.
Sites, buildings and structures for the defence of the coastline from sea and air invasion.
Semi precious stone or glass engraved with a design and used to make an impression on wax or clay.
The object used to make impressions in wax as seals.
Equipment used to create a mark, image or character in an object.
A stamp, made of clay or stone, used to mark bars of eye ointment.
The tool used to create a mark on pottery by the potter.
An ancient Egyptian gem cut in the shape of a scarab beetle and engraved with symbols on its flat side.
A factory used for the processing of isinglass, a product obtained from the swim bladders of sturgeon and used in the brewing industry as part of the process for clearing wine and beer.
A works used for the production of parchment from animal skin.
A site used for the production of items derived from animal horns.
A building or site where the carcasses of whales were butchered and rendered into by products such as oil, fenk and whalebone.
A site used for the production of items derived from animal bones.
Sites, buildings, structures & features related to the extraction, processing & manufacture of finished goods. Includes structures associated with the supply, storage &/or transmission of power.
A slaughterhouse for horses.
A building or buildings where soap is manufactured.
A site which has produced evidence of in situ production of items derived from antler.
A site used for the butchery of animals.
A works producing gelatine from animal products for use as a culinary setting agent and in the photography, dyeing, brewing and glue industries. For explosives use GELATINE WORKS (EXPLOSIVE)
A factory where glue is produced.
A place where furs are made into finished products.
A building where tallow is produced, ie. solid animal fat that has been separated by heating, usually for making candles.
A building or complex where skins are prepared, with their hair still on, to make fur products.
A building or complex where animal hair is processed, using a variety of means, for use in products such as brushes, mattresses etc.
A mill for grinding or crushing bones, in the process of making bone china, for example.
Buildings or sites used in the preparation, treatment and working of raw animal hide into leather products such as gloves or saddles, etc.
Buildings or sites used in the production of items derived from the parts of animals not used for consumption.
A workshop, associated with a tannery, in which the fleece is removed from the skin prior to the tanning process.
Includes chemical and natural fertilizers and waste products. use more specific term.
Waste matter, usually liquid in form, consisting of the contents of sewers and cesspits.

An operations room, built to drawing number 367/41, to control the lighting arrays of the DREM type of bombing decoy in use during the Second World War. Unlike earlier designs it was surface built and then covered in earth to protect against flooding.
A decoy site designed to simulate the flarepath lighting of permanent RAF stations, to lure attacking night bombers away from legitimate targets.
A lock where the gates rise vertically. Rarely found on canals but common on navgable rivers in the Fens, particularly the river Nene.

A section of the water channel on a canal or river shut off above and below by lock gates provided with sluices to let the water out and in, and thus raise or lower boats from one level to another. Use more specific type where known.
A machine tool similar in general appearance to a shaping machine but in which the head or ram carrying the cutting tool moves in a vertical plane.
Apparatus using mechanical power for a particular function.
A site where all the processes for the production of glass and objects made from glass are carried out.
A building or complex, housing powered machinery and employing a large workforce for manufacturing purposes. Use specific monument type where known.
A factory used for the production of thick, flat glass used for shop window panes, etc. Plate glass is produced by rolling and casting rather than traditional blowing.
Romanesque overlapping arcades, producing a series of pointed arches.
A series of arches.
A building or site used in the production of enamelled goods.
Usually a complex of buildings for the processing of raw materials. Use specific type where known.
Any building designed or adapted to accommodate trades and manufacturing activity. Use more specific site where known.
A building or site used for the production of bricks and other items, from a clay with refractory properties.
A building or site used in the production of japanned goods. Japanning was the process of covering a material with a hard, black lacquer in imitation of Japanese lacquer work.
A site associated with the large scale construction of buildings or items manufactured by the building industry.
A manufacturing site producing weaving shuttles for the textile industry.
An engineering works that produces machinery specially for use in shoe making.
A site where concrete and concrete products are manufactured from a mixture of cement and aggregate.
A site where lime (calcium carbonate) is made.
An industrial manufacturing complex producing bricks.
A factory making baize for snooker and gaming tables.
A site incorporating all of the production processes for the manufacture of plaster.
Site used for the maintenance of aircraft.
A works, including an extractive site, producing a clay of high plasticity and firmness, used as a basic raw material for porcelain.
A site containing slipways and associated buildings used specifically for the repair of ships and larger ocean-going craft.
A site where tar is manufactured or combined with other substances to produce bitumen, for example.
An engineering works producing items for the railway other than rolling stock, such as signals, tracks, points, etc.
Recovery and removal of grease (lanolin) from raw wool.
A site where the process of combing, the preparatory process for long wools, takes place.
A building or site used for the manufacture of whiting either from crushed chalk, limestone, marble or through chemical preparation.
A site where clay pipes used for drainage are manufactured.
A site where metal springs are manufactured.
An industrial complex concerned with the manufacture of gas for domestic use from coal and oil.
An establishment used for the manufacture of jacquards and dobbys, which are textile loom components that control the weaving of complicated or figured patterns.
A site used for all the processes associated with the manufacture of roof, floor or decorative tiles.
A complex of buildings where barytes is processed for industrial use.
A place where telephones and their components are manufactured
A works using sealed retorts to produce charcoal. Wood distillates may be produced as byproducts of this process. They may be found at separate works or comprise part of a gunpowder works.
A building or site where boat sails are manufactured from processed cloth.
Works where yarn is prepared prior to spinning.
A large scale works for cloth finishing processes.
Works producing a refractory clay, kaolin. An essential raw material of porcelain and some types of papermaking.

An establishment used for the manufacture of reeds and healds, which are components of a textile loom with related functions, in that they move and control the threads, and similar wire-based construction.
Any factory or site using machine tools in a manufacturing or processing capacity.
A whole male figure used in place of a column to support an entablature.
A vertical, circular member, usually load-carrying. Where separate, use monument type.
Measurements or factual information which may occur in a manual catalogue system or database.
Forms used in the recording of archaeological or other site investigations.

Collective term for the Burlington (Silurian period) and Borrowdale (Ordovician period) groups of slates from the Lake District and parts of Cumbria, Lancashire. Hard, fine grained metamorphic rock, varying in colour from green/olive to black/blue black.
Collective term for the North and South Wales groups of slate. Hard, fine grained, metamorphic rock, with varying dark shades.

Collective term for a hard, fine grained, dark coloured metamorphic rock, which splits easily; hence its common use as a roofing and flooring material, and a functional description for any rectangular, sheet, roofing material.

Collective term for the Scottish Slates including the Aberdeen/Baniff and Ballachulish/Easdale groups. Fine grained, varying in colour from brown to dark grey/blue. Geologically different from Lake District, Welsh and West Country groups of slate.

Collective term for the slates from Devon and Cornwall. Hard, fine grained metamorphic rock. Varying in colour from dark grey/green to blueish/grey. West Country Slate is geologically different from both Lake District and Welsh Slate.
Rock of definite form and size, usually artificially shaped. See STONE CLass List for narrow terms.
Cornish miner's term for slates formed during the Carboniferous and Devonian periods.
The end of a timber post made wider than the rest of its length on one face to accomodate tiebeams, wall-plates etc..
A junction whereby two members or elements of an artificial structure or mechanism are joined or fitted together, whether rigidly or hinged.
A building, originally used as a shelter for the duty pilot or officer on watch on an airfield, and later used to direct air traffic. Use more specific type where known.

A two-storey, brick construction with a watch office and additional rooms given over to the meteorological section, including a forecast room and met store. A brick parapet on the roof differentiates it from 2328/39.

Based on the previous all-timber design 2423/39 and the temporary brick and timber design 518/40, the 8936/40 was built with pre-cast concrete slabs replacing the timber floors and staircases with only the balcony and watch office roof in timber.
An all timber constructed watch office with meterological section. Similar in design to 2328/39 and 5845/39. There were only two known examples built in the UK at Wick and St.Eval.
A watch office with additional rooms given over to the meteorological section, including a forecast room and met store.

A two-storey, all-concrete construction with a watch office and additional rooms given over to the meteorological section, including a forecast room and met store. A concrete parapet all around the roof differentiates it from 5845/39.
A temporary brick and timber watch office based on the all-timber 2423/39. Built after 1941 on many Operational Training Unit airfields the design was superseded by 8936/40.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Marshal of the Royal Air Force

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: Terms included here are for small scale agricultural production. See also FOOD AND DRINK INDUSTRY SITE grouping in INDUSTRIAL class.
A building or room for the storage of vegetables, particularly root vegetables, for human consumption.
A functioning clock designed to serve also as an ornamental feature or sculpture.
A 20th century feature found in public parks and seaside resorts. The face of the clock is planted with low-growing flowers and plants, while the moving hands are covered with small foliage.
Found in early churches this was a part of a church on the south side of the chancel where there were bookshelves and storage for vestments.
An area or space within a building.
A tunnel through which a tramway runs.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with tramway transport.
A long handled fork with two or three long curved tines for tossing straw or hay.
A tool used to impart heat in order to fuse two or more metal surfaces together.
Equipment used to compress or break through compression.
Knapped or ground stone/flint tool where the specific type is unknown. Use more specific type where known.
A hand held device with bristles or hairs used for cleaning or painting.
A tap inserted into a barrel to allow liquid to be drawn from it.
An object made of two verticals with rungs between for ascending or descending.
An object used to aid pouring a substance through a small opening.
A tool to apply material to the seams of a ship.
A weight hung on a piece of string or twine used to show the vertical.
A tool used for splitting straw. The straw splitter would be pushed down the hollow shaft of a piece of straw to produce six flat lengths of straw ready for plaiting. Used in straw hat making.
A flexible pipe, usually fixed to a pump or tap, for the conveying of water.
An object, usually wood or metal used to force open or keep open another object. Often used to split timber by striking the thick end and forcing the wood apart.
A pair of flat faced tools used to smooth iron.
A toothed, handled tool used to drag objects either to gather them together eg grass or hay, or to level them out eg sand or earth.
In the glass industry, a flat block of stone (idealy marble), cast iron, or a ceramic material, on which cylinder glass is flattened. Medieval and Post Medieval.
An iron bar used as a lever.
A block, usually of iron, upon which objects are shaped and hammered eg in smithing.
A tool, featuring a straight, horizontal handle from which extends a metal hook halfway along its length, used by a shearman (one who shears sheep) in the handling of wool.
Use for items of personal equipment used in a military context, eg AMMUNITION POUCH, PRIMING FLASK.
Equipment used to pierce or puncture other objects through the use of a point.
A tool used to filter solid material from liquid by means of a mesh, net or sheet with holes.
A monocular optical instrument possessing magnification for observing distant objects, especially in astronomy.
An object used in the sublimation process. It is pear shaped with both ends open.
Equipment used in the production of textiles.
Equipment used to scrape and smooth objects.
A flat object which is broad and rounded at one end and tapers to a handle at the other.
A stone used to test how genuine an object is by rubbing the object against the stone, particularly used for testing gold and silver.
A triangular sectioned rod probably used for making sparks.
Equipment used to create objects through the use of a pattern or matrix which shapes the object.
A container with a perforated bottom through which material is shaken or poured.
A rotating wheel, horizontal to the ground, on which pottery is made.
A clay cone, part of a furnace.
Equipment used to bore a hole in a solid object through the use of a twisting, drilling action.
The constituent parts of a kiln.
A rack to hold smoking pipes.
The windlass used to wind rope around to raise and lower the bucket in a well.
A tube, cyclinder or similar casing enclosing the mechanism of a pump.
A device for operating a lock.
A small cushion into which pins are pushed for storage.
An object used to create a blast of air.
An instrument to remove the seeds from flax.
A wheel with a groove in it for a rope or cord, used to raise heavy objects.
A device used to lock another object.
A wheeled open box for carrying loads.
A light plough used to break up the earth. It does not have a mouldboard to turn the earth.
A rod used to create repousee work on metal vessels. The rod is Z shaped.
Equipment used in the grinding of cereal to produce foodstuffs.
A tool which combines two or more different types of tool.
A board or slab, often with a thumb hole in it, used by an artist to hold and mix colours on.
A tool used to reduce the diameter of metal rods. Consists of a pair of semicylindrical surfaces.
A tool for scooping loose substances, usually with a handle and a curved blade partially covered at the handle end.
A tool used to examine or explore a cavity eg surgically for exploring the depth and direction of wounds.
A trough for containing moulding sand for use in casting metal artefacts.
A tool used in making pottery.
A tool used to twist fibres together to create yarn.
A frame shaped to fit around the neck and shoulders of a person for carrying buckets. Usually made of wood.

Tools and equipment with a specific function and those for which a function cannot be assigned with any degree of certainty. Where the function is known, the term is also included under the relevant Class.
Equipment used primarily to bring percussive force onto an object.
Equipment used to sharpen other objects.
A tool used to pull down burning structures.
A bar used to increase the force being brought to bear in order to move an object.
A tool with one or more serrated edges.
Equipment used in the making of tools.
A key for winding a clockwork mechanism.
A very small flint or other stone tool.
Implement with a shallow bowl at the end of a handle used to eat with or to stir food etc.
An object used in smithing to enlarge holes, consists of a tapered square rod.
Round object used to carry cable or wire
A machine for freeing the cotton from the plant.
A flat edged blade used in leatherworking
A bar or rod, usually of metal, used to push another object into place eg to push coals within a fire.
A device with hooks or claws attached to a rope and used for dragging or grasping.
A pillow or cushion for lace making.
A long handled scoop usually used with liquids.
A tool for holding or compressing objects together.
A knife used to rub grease into a hide and to force dirt out of it. The knife is symmetrical with a handle at each end.
A straight rod, made of glass, plastic or other materials, used to agitate or mix chemicals, pigments, beverages or other fluids or substances.
An instrument used to create and link loops of yarn to produce a garment.
A tool, possibly for cleaning mud from parts of a plough.
A device, often consisting of a cyclinder containing a piston or plunger, used to raise or move liquids or gasses by means of compression, lifting or suction.
A small blade for moving earth, applying liquids such as plaster, smoothing etc.
A long hollow tube used to blow molten glass into shapes.
Equipment for digging earth, etc.
A pair of round edged tools like chisels to make a groove in iron.
Equipment used to grip an object.
Equipment used primarily to cut, slice, chop etc, using an implement with one or more sharp edges.
A piece with one or more surfaces with either/both slightly convex shape appropriate for use in forming metal artefacts.
A large flake or blade blank thinned on both faces to form an approximate leaf shape. Precise function unknown.
A container for holding water in which to bathe.
Accessories used in furnishing and embellishing a building or structure.
A building used to store fertilizers.
Buildings, structures or sites used for the production of chemicals used in agriculture, such as fertilizers and weed killers.
The weapon end of an arrow, often shaped for particular uses.
An arrowhead which has a straight cutting edge.
A kiln principally used in brick making which gives a continuous operation.
A furnace or oven for burning, baking or drying. Use specific type where known.
A hospital providing medical, surgical or psychiatric testing and treatment for patients with specific illnesses or injuries.

Nowadays a hospital where patients suffering from psychiatric disorders receive medical care and treatment. Traditionally they were often places where psychiatric patients were kept confined away from society receiving minimal medical care or attention.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Hospital For People With Learning Difficulties
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A hospital where people with learning difficulties receive medical treatment.
An enclosed compartment within a building intended for a purpose other than as a thoroughfare.
A large, high-ceilinged room, usually in a great house or palace, serving as a principal reception room; also a room used by the public for a specific purpose; or a drawing room in a house.
Use for the remains of any part of an insect.
Remains of the animal group characterized by having jointed limbs and segmented bodies, including woodlice, spiders, insects etc. Note, crustaceans have been included in this category.
A factory or works which has been temporarily turned over to the manufacture of goods for the war effort.
An existing factory that was converted for use as aircraft works in the run up to or during the Second World War.
A strategically placed aperture in the wall of a fortification through which guns and cannon can fire upon an invading force.
A flat, horizontal piece of timber or masonry projecting from or recessed into a wall to hold objects.

Long-range, four-engine reconnaissance-bomber. Initially produced as a transport, converted and used against Allied convoys in the Channel and the Atlantic. Also served as a VIP transport, one of which was the Immelmann III: Hitler's personal aircraft.
A twin-engined development of the JU88, the JU188 had a higher service ceiling and greater maximum speed. JU188s operated over the UK from 1944 onwards as night intruders and reconnaissance aircraft.
Four-crew, twin-engined, general reconnaissance flying-boat. Entered service after World War One, becoming the RAF's standard flying-boat until replaced by the Supermarine Southampton in 1925.

Three-seat, twin-engined minelaying, torpedo-bombing and reconnaissance twin-float seaplane. First flown in 1936, in 1938 it set eight world speed records for its class in various range and payload categories.
A two-seat, reconnaissance biplane developed from the FK2 with a more powerful, but heavier, engine. Primarily used for training in the UK.

Interbellum, twin-engined, five-crew, biplane flying-boat with a characteristic triple tail-fin. Entered service in 1925 and used for general reconnaissance duties. The Mk.I had a wooden fuselage, whilst the Mk.II's was metal in construction.

Six-crew, medium-range, twin-engined reconnaissance flying-boat. Entered service with 209 Squadron in 1939 but, due to design and operation problems, saw little action and was not produced in large numbers.

Two-crew, twin-engined bomber. Entered production in 1934 and designed for dual use as a high-speed commercial transport. Technical problems hindered its use as a bomber and led to conversion to high-altitude reconnaissance.
Twin-engined, four-crew German seaplane. Entered service in 1932 as a torpedo bomber and naval reconnaisance aircraft, though by World War 2 those still serving were used mainly for air sea rescue.
A torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance biplane in service with the Fleet Air Arm 1935-1938. Rendered obsolete after 1938 by the Swordfish and withdrawn from service.
German single-engine, four-seat maritime patrol and reconnaissance flying-boat. In production between 1934 and 1940, the DO18 was replaced by the three engined DO24.

Twin-engined maritime-reconnaissance bomber adapted from pre-war American airliners, the A-28 and A-29, evident from the row of portholes along its fuselage. Entered service with RAF Coastal Command just before the outbreak of World War Two.

Three/four-crew, single-engine, shipboard observation and air/sea rescue amphibian seaplane. Entered RAF service in 1936. Also employed for gunnery spotting, anti-submarine and convoy protection duties.
Four-crew, twin-engined monoplane designed as a torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance aircraft for RAF Coastal Command. Withdrawn from operations in November 1940 and downgraded to a trainer.

Twin-engined, seven-crew, coastal reconnaissance, biplane flying-boat. Designed to the same specification as the Saro London, entered service in 1937. Also serving in an anti-submarine role, was replaced by the Consolidated Canso (Catalina) in 1943.
Single-engine, two-seat tractor bomber and reconnaissance aircraft. Entered service in 1916 and, during 1917 and 1918, equipped nine RFC squadrons in its reconnaissance role.
US Navy version of the four-engined, six-crew B24 heavy bomber. Modified for long-range reconnaissance duty and used as a patrol-bomber against shipping and submarines.

Twin-engined air/sea rescue and anti-submarine patrol aircraft. Originally developed from the Wellington and intended as a bomber, entered RAF Coastal Command service in 1943. Fitted with a Leigh Light and ASV radar.

Four-engine, ten-crew, long-range maritime reconnaissance and anti-submarine aircraft. Developed from the Short C-class Empire airliner. All metal in construction, entered RAF Coastal Command service in 1938.
A camera-equipped aircraft intended to fly over enemy territory and gather photographic evidence of strategic features and/or the position and strength of any military presence.
Single engine, two-crew shipboard reconnaissance and patrol seaplane. Entered service in 1939, this was the last combat floatplane built in Europe.
Large, three-engined, long range reconnaissance flying boat. Wooden hull and frame construction, with linen covering. Entered service in 1930.
Single-engine, three-crew torpedo-spotter, reconnaissance and anti-submarine biplane. Entered Naval service in 1936, designed for operation from aircraft carriers and equipped with folding wings.
American-built, twin-engined flying-boat designed for maritime patrol and reconnaissance. Entered US Naval service in 1936 as the PBY-1; christened the Catalina by the RAF, who used it from 1939 on.
Originally designed as a trainer but relegated to use by the RNAS in a Maritime Reconnaissance and anti-submarine role when the Avro 504 became the standard trainer.

Highly successful, two-seat, biplane fighter and reconnaissance aircraft with both forward and rear facing guns. Designed to replace the BE2, it entered service with the RFC in mid-1917 and remained in service until 1932.
A biplane, reconnaissance aircraft with a crew of 3 or 4 which equipped 3 and 22 squadrons RAF before passing to the Fleet Air Arm. Produced in two variants.
Twin-engined monoplane originally designed as a reconnaissance aircraft, but also widely used as a trainer. Entered RAF service in 1936.
An aircraft, often fitted with cameras, intended to fly over enemy territory to ascertain its strategic features and/or the position and strength of any military presence.

Originally designed as a wood and steel bomber-reconnaissance aircraft, subsequent variations served as special transports, glider tugs and paratroop carriers. Featured a tricycle-style undercarriage.

A bridge consisting of a lattice girder spanning the distance between the tops of two towers. Designed to transport vehicles across the gap in a container suspended at road level by ropes under a travelling crane on the girder.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with road transport.
A room intended for the pursuit of recreational activities.
A room set aside within a club, hotel, large residence etc. for the benefit of guests or individuals who wish to smoke.
A monument visible as a trace on marine survey equipment
A monument whose presence is inferred from verbally delivered information drawn from the speaker's personal knowledge.
Monument known only from primary documentary sources eg books, maps, legal records, where no physical evidence exists. Use also where a monument has been planned but never constructed.
An object in the sea bed recorded on the Hydrographic Office plot of objects snagged by nets during trawling.
Use where the presence or nature of a monument is inferred from placenames or placename elements.
Do not use
Monument type/interpretation is inferred, based on informed speculation eg by comparison with similar monuments, proximity to other monuments, topography, site character etc.
Not to be used for indexing. Broad term to assist retreival of all monuments where non-physical evidence is recorded.
A small merchant ship or warship with concealed weapons, intended as a trap for enemy submarines.
A vessel, usually a merchant vessel, altered to resemble a warship or another vessel.
A site where concrete and concrete products are manufactured from a mixture of cement and aggregate.
Large storage structure for powdered cement.
A kiln used to calcine the component parts of cement to remove excess water and other ingredients.

A mill which ground clinker in the cement production process. During cement production a mixture of lime and clay is burnt which forms a clinker which is then ground into powder. When mixed with water it solidifies to hard cement.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of cement.
Buildings and sites associated with the production of materials made from minerals.
A site where cement is manufactured for the building industry.
A tubular orifice to assist in pouring.
Objects which cannot be assigned to any one particular class, or the function of which is unknown.
A brush used to apply soap to the body when shaving.
Object used in shaving.
A sharp blade used for shaving.
An item used in caring for the body for appearance and cleanliness.
A bowl specifically used for shaving.
The principal church of a diocese in which the cathedra or bishop's throne is to be found.
The principal Eastern Orthodox church in an area.
Pictorial, painted or drawn material such as slides, drawings, photos, plans excluding cartographic.
Reproductive process for non-photographic media in which the image is created by transferring ink from a plate, block etc.
Photographic image produced using an ink-jet printer.
NB currently Includes ISOMETRIC though this has a separate term.
?what does this mean?
A building or buildings used for the production of whistles.
A monument consisting of parallel lines of banks, ditches, stones, timber posts or trees which appears to mark out an approach to another monument or monuments. Use specific type where known.
A monument consisting of parallel lines of spaced post- holes which appears to mark out an approach to another monument or monuments.
A form of thatching straw composed of stems that have been combed mechanically to remove grain and extraneous waste material without crushing the stem.

Composed of loose uncombed lengths of harvested wheat which are formed into bundles for laying. Distinctive appearance with both ears and butts visible on the surface traditionally using hazel spars which hold the straw in place.
Roofing material consisting of stems or stalks of wheat, rye, oats or barley separated from grain and laid flat in 'yealms' which form an overlapping surface which sheds water.
Any tree, shrub or herb of cellulose form, normally subsisting in soil and producing its food through photosynthesis.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the manufacture of products from metals.
A workshop or factory where bronze articles are made by casting molten metal into moulds.
A furnace or oven used for drying items or materials. Use specific type where possible.
A kiln used for the drying of wood.
Imported Italian marble varying in colour from green, blue, purple to white.
One of only three 'true' British marbles, pale green and white in colour.
White coloured marble. Imported from France.
One of only three 'true' British marbles, green and white in colour, predominantly used in large public buildings.
One of only three 'true' British marbles, white in colour, predominantly used for sculptures and statues.

Collective name for, in a true geological sense, a metamorphosed limestone, eg. Carrara marble, and, in the British sense any decorative stone that will take a polish, eg. Purbeck marble. In the latter's case index with specific stone type where given.

A site used primarily for domestic purposes on at least a semi-permanent or seasonal basis, and which has been surrounded by a bank and ditch, palisade, or some other form of enclosure. Use more specific type(s) where appropriate.
A small, Iron Age/Romano-British enclosed settlement found in South West England.
A metallic rod attached to a high point on a building and leading to the earth for the purpose of conducting lightning away from the main body of the building.
A strip of cloth used for binding a wound.
Objects used for the preparation of medicines or the diagnosis and treatment of ill health or disease.
A container for holding or pouring liquids, usually having a handle or lip.
A type of jug decorated with applied figures in the form of knights in armour. (Source: MPRG)
Use for a craft powered by a steam engine. Use also for a vessel employing a steam engine as its principle source of motive power.
Use for a craft powered by an engine. Use also for cases where the precise engine type is not known.
A heat engine where an (internal) working fluid is heated by combustion of an external source, through the engine wall or a heat exchanger.
Ramayana Week.
A group of coins deliberately deposited together.
A piece of metal, usually cast, struck or stamped, with a definite value.
An unofficial, usually local, substitute for coinage, which could be exchanged directly for goods or services in certain areas or with specified retailers.
Official currency printed or written onto paper which can be directly exchanged for goods, services or coins.
Silver rings believed to have been used in the Hebrides and Irish Sea regions during the Viking period, and derived from Hiberno-Viking arm rings.
Objects primarily intended to be used as a medium of exchange, eg coins.
A control tower designed for use on Very Heavy Bomber Station Airfields. Designed to Air Ministry drawing number 294/45 they were the first to be have a Visual Control Room
skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Very Heavy Bomber Station Control Tower (294/45)

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A central tower with a single-storey wing either side. The tower contained the watch office on the ground floor, observation room on the second with each wing containing an office for the Chief Flying Instructor or the officer commanding and their aides.
A high building at an airport from which air traffic is controlled by radio.

A control tower constructed on RNAS stations by the Royal Marine Engineers. Built to a common ground floor plan they could be built with one, two or three storeys above this depending on the requirements of the station.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Royal Naval Air Station Control Tower

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: Buildings, sites and structures associated with the control, accommodation, service and testing of aircraft.
The first standardized design for a building for the duty pilot. It took the form of a small bungalow with a bay window on the front elevation.
A building, originally used as a shelter for the duty pilot or officer on watch on an airfield, and later used to direct air traffic. Use more specific type where known.
A machine, powered by steam, gas, electricity or other energy source, which produces energy of movement. Use for stationary industrial engines rather than transport use.
A simple wind-driven machine used for a variety of purposes.
An establishment where beauty treatments and associated therapies are provided by professional practitioners.
A place where goods are sold in bulk, rather than by retail.
A store belonging to a cooperative society.
A large shop supplying many kinds of goods from various departments.
A place where perfume is sold, as well as manufactured.
A shop which sells vegetables and fruit.
A shop that sells men's clothes, either off the peg, bespoke or both.
A shop where meat is sold. Often includes large cold stores for the refrigeration and storage of carcasses and a butchery where the carcass is cut up prior to sale.
A place, often including a BAKERY, where sweetmeats and pastries are sold.

A supermarket for American military personnel, the National Guard and the Reserves and their immediate family, usually sited on a military installation throughout the world. Use term only in conjunction with an American military base.
A house or building where goods are made or prepared and displayed for sale and sold. Use more specific type where known.
A place where wigs, hair-pieces and hair extensions are made and sold.
A large self-service store selling foods and some household goods.
A building or other establishment used for the retail, making and repairing of jewellery.
A building where beer was sold or displayed.
A shop which dispenses medicinal drugs and other health-related items. Can include an area for the preparation and manufacture of medicines and other drugs.
A shop selling a variety of goods and merchandise.
A commercial premises where clocks are sold and repaired.
An establishment where people get their hair dressed and cut.
A hairdressing establishment for men.
A shop selling ironmonger's goods, household tools and utensils.
Sites, buildings, structures & features related to the sale, exchange &/or storage of goods or services. Includes commercially operated catering establishments & lodging premises.
A shop selling tea, butter, flour, sugar, spices, tinned foods and miscellaneous household stores.
A shop selling household furniture.
A shop where fish is sold.
A shop housing the business of a grindery dealer. Grindery are the tools and materials used by shoemakers and other leather-workers.
Traditionally the premises of a chandler, a maker and seller of candles. Now, a shop for the retail of groceries and other provisions.
A side scraper with a short concavity retouched into an edge. This may be achieved by a single blow. (Source: SARC)
A flake or blade tool with more than one notch on its edge.
A flake or blade with retouch along one or more edges.
A scraper with retouch at right angles to the bulb of percussion.
A building used for the daily administration of the Royal Air Force.
A building used as a headquarters and reporting centre for an Army, Navy or Air Force Group.
A building used for the daily administration of the Royal Navy.
A concrete structure designed to be the headquarters for the coordination of an airfield's defences. Constructed partially underground it was only intended to be occupied during an attack.
A building used as headquarters by the Territorial Army, the volunteer reserve of the British army.
A building used as the command centre of a military operation.
A building used for the daily administration of an army.
An underground bomb-proof structure used as a command centre for military operations.
A building or group of buildings, often surrounded by a system of fortifications, used as a residential and training site by members of an armed force.
A small structure providing cover and protected accommodation for a sentry.
General term describing any defence work where no more specific term is applicable.
A building or site used by the armed forces for the storage and issuing of military stores and materials.
A site or building associated with active or passive defence of the landing ground and buildings of an airfield.
A building, site or structure associated with the demonstration and testing of weapons and military equipment.
A gate leading to water, either a river or the sea. Used as a means of supplying castles, for example, with goods brought by water transport.
Site for the disposal of unexploded ordnance, possibly attached to a bombing range.
A fortress and dwelling, usually medieval in origin, and often consisting of a keep, curtain wall and towers etc.
A military building from which the guns of a battery were directed.
An underground vertical cylindrical structure for the storage and launching of ballistic missiles.
Sites, buildings and structures associated with the prevention of an invasion by a hostile force.

A site used primarily for domestic purposes on at least a semi-permanent or seasonal basis, and which has been surrounded by a bank and ditch, palisade, or some other form of enclosure. Use more specific type(s) where appropriate.
A 19th century structure of various shape or material for the protection of troops in an emergency.
An establishment from which food is distributed to the public during wartime or similar states of emergency.
Buildings, structures and sites for the detection of encroaching enemy forces.
The field or area of ground on which a battle or skirmish was fought.
Defensive fortifications such as ramparts, ditches and stone walls, built to defend a town or city.
A site equipped for passive or active defence against an airborne enemy assault.
Sites and structures, often un-manned, intended to impede or confuse enemy forces.
A major fortified place, often a town, capable of containing a large force. If Roman use LEGIONARY FORTRESS.
A building of unknown purpose found at a military site. Use more specific type where known.
Buildings, structures and sites for the training of military personnel.
A site for the storage, preparation and launching of missiles.
An armoured fighting vehicle. Often survive as commemorative monuments, targets and coastal wrecks.
A site on which rigs, towers and other associated structures and buildings used for the testing of helicopters and helicopter parts are located.

Land which has been temporarily taken over for use by the military or civilian authorities. During wartime land was requisitioned for various purposes, such as for argriculture or for military training/events etc.
A house which bears signs of fortification. These often include crenellated battlements and narrow slit-like windows.
A raised platform from which an officer can address or review his troops.
A site and associated buildings used by the military for various purposes. Use only where exact function is unknown otherwise use more specific term.

Sites, buildings, structures & features used in the defence of the civilian population. Includes civil defence sites, weapons stores, training sites, military signals & active defence structures such as anti-aircraft sites.
Buildings and structures used for sending and receiving signals.
Any church which bears signs of fortification. Churches on the Welsh and Scottish borders were often fortified, only allowing access to the tower from a single opening in the nave.
A building used to coordinate movement of railway engines and rolling stock in the event of war.
A site from which troops could be embarked onto transport vessels prior to the D-Day landings can also apply to muster/departure points from which troops embarked for their journey to the Front.

A building which has been temporarily taken over for use by the military or civilian authorities. During wartime buildings were requisitioned for various purposes, such as temporary hospitals or headquarters.
A building which has been fortified, often as a temporary measure rather than as part of the original design

A system of fortifications constructed along a national frontier to contain the local population, as well as keep out undesirable raiders eg. Offa's Dyke. Use with more specific monument type where known.
Sites and structures for the transport of military personnel, vehicles and armaments.
A permanently occupied position or building designed primarily for defence.
A site or structure associated with the activities of the Royal Observer Corps. The Corps was reformed on 1 January 1947 and disbanded in 1991.
A range marker allowing bombers to locate the bombing range.
A harbour constructed from floating pontoons or caissons connected end to end.
The rear part of a Roman fort, where barrack accommodation, stables and stores were situated. Use with wider site type where known.
Sites and buildings used in the coordination of the defence of the civilian population during times of war. Could also be used during times of national emergency.
A purpose built pit, usually below a gatehouse or barbican, into which the counterweight of a drawbridge could be lowered, thus enabling the bridge to be raised.
Sites, buildings and structures for the control and mounting of anti aircraft artillery. Also, structures for passive or indirect defence against enemy aircraft.

A missile or aircraft that obtain its thrust from a rocket engine. Some rockets will exist as monuments for example, in the form of gate guardians. Double index with the monument type where appropriate.
A usually temporary earthwork or fortification, the latter constructed by military forces operating in the field. Use more specific type where known.
A usually permanent defensive work. Use specific type where known.
An establishment for the storage of food for use during wartime or similar states of emergency.
A bridge which is fortified at one or both ends.
A site where guns, mortars or searchlights are mounted. Use specific type where known.
A garden in which a variety of plants are grown to encourage butterflies.
An enclosed piece of ground devoted to the cultivation of flowers, fruit or vegetables and/or recreational purposes. Use more specific type where known.
A crane which is driven by a petrol or diesel engine and travels on either crawler tracks or rubber tyres.
A crane mounted on wheels and/or rails, used for the unloading of ships' cargoes.
A large, metal or wooden structure, used for raising, lowering and moving heavy objects. Use more specific type where known.
Limestones formed during the Carboniferous period. Many are cut, polished and used as marble.
Sedimentary rock consisting mainly of calcium carbonate. Varying in grain size, colour and hardness, quarried and used throughout the country.

An enclosed structure of brick, stone or metal in which material is heated or burned, or, in a domestic context, food is cooked, through the continuous radiation of heat from its floor, walls or ceiling.
A flattened glass sphere used to give linen a gloss.
A long, wooden, metal or stone vessel holding drinking water for horses.
A narrow, open container, usually where food or water for animals is put. Use specific type where known.
A long stone or metal vessel for dogs to drink water from.

Sites, buildings, structures, features and areas of land associated with cultivation, the rearing of livestock, gathering, hunting & fishing. Includes farm based processing of foodstuffs & storage of agricultural produce.
A long metal or stone vessel for cattle to drink water from.

A type of large permanent military aircraft hangar with a curved steel frame and storage annexes on its side used in World War II. It was intended for storage purposes on Aircraft Storage Unit stations.
An object which is going to become a key. It has the shape but has not been cut to fit a lock.
An object that is to become a padlock key. It has the correct shape but has yet to be cut to fit the lock.
Parts of a building's fabric, structures and associated services, eg drain pipe. If the structure is complete use a monument type thesaurus.
A spout allowing water to spill away from a building. Usually carved in images of animals, people or grotesques.
A hospital which has been built either wholly, or partially, underground in order to protect it from attacks by enemy aircraft.
A working hospital, often near or associated with a university, where doctors and nurses are trained.
Usually a rural hospital with up to 25 beds. Can include small pre-Cranleigh institutions, eg: dispensaries with in-patients.
A hospital where patients can rest and recover after an operation or illness. Medical facilities for treatment are also available.
A hospital where people would pay a subscription in order to recieve treatment when ill.
Reformatory established under the Inebriates Acts 1879-1900 for repeat alcohol related offenders
A 19th century spa building, usually consisting of a hotel with baths used for water treatment.
A hospital which primarily cares for patients injured in accidents.
A hospital providing medical, surgical or psychiatric testing and treatment for patients with specific illnesses or injuries.
A hospital where Royal Naval personnel and their families receive medical and surgical treatment.
A non-specialist hospital dealing in general medical and surgical treatment.
A hospital for the care of patients with incurable illnesses.
A hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of military personnel and/or their families.

A building temporarily requistioned for use as a hospital. Auxiliary hospitals treated the less seriously wounded and were less strict than military hospitals although they remained under military control.
A hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of sailors and/or their families. For Royal Naval seamen use ROYAL NAVAL HOSPITAL.
A hospital for convalescents or consumptives.
A hospital where Air Force personnel and their families receive medical and surgical treatment.

Sites, buildings, structures & features associated with health (for example, treatment of the sick) &/or social welfare (for example, alleviation of poverty), including all charitable foundations & all forms of state defined social welfare.
A hospital where elderly people receive medical treatment, but not overnight accommodation.
A separate hospital building, or block of an asylum, where new arrivals were segregated from old inmates for a defined period. This system was developed from the mid-19th century onwards.
A medieval hospital for lepers, usually consisting of a church and individual shelters for the lepers.
An establishment providing medical or surgical treatment for the ill or wounded. Use narrower term where possible.
A series of long, raised ridges separated by ditches used to prepare the ground for arable cultivation. This was a technique, characteristic of the medieval period.
The subsoil traces of cultivation, presumed to have been caused by the use of a plough to till the soil.
A bank formed at the end of a field by soil which, loosened by the plough, gradually moves down slope through a combination of gravity and erosion.
Manmade marks or earthworks which provide evidence for agricultural cultivation.
Narrow ridges representing the surviving surface traces of later prehistoric cultivation.
A rafter of uniform size placed at regular intervals along the length of a roof.
An inclined member used to support laths under a roof covering. Normally one of a pair.
Stop-line against invading tanks in form of a ditch during the defence of Britain.
A man made ditch designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle. Ditches were often reveted with concrete or wood.
A natural ditch the depth and/or width of which has been increased so as to prevent the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle.
A building or group of buildings, often enclosed by a system of fortifications, used by an armed force for the storage and distribution of military equipment.
An inclined plane built to allow tanks to be loaded and unloaded between rolling stock on the railway network and vehicular low loaders.
A building or site used for the storage and distribution of the essential logistical requirements of an armed force.
A storage facility used for the accommodation and dispersal of vehicles. Often used by the military and emergency services.
A building or site used for the storage and distribution of the essential logistical requirements of the Royal Navy.
A building or site used by the armed forces for the storage and issuing of military stores and materials.
A building used to store military equipment and ammunition.
A military depot where horses were taken and trained for service in the army.
A building or site used for the storage and distribution lighter than air gases for use in barrage balloons.
An installation used to store ammunition and equipment ready for the mobilization of armed forces in the event of a war.
Any military base where the depot battalion of a regiment is based. Depot battalions maintain the stores and records of a regiment and train new recruits.
A building used for the storage of explosives of a non-military function, eg. mining explosives, signal explosivres etc.
A general term to describe a sediment or sample that contains a variety of different minerals.
A material composed of mineral grains derived from the breakdown of rocks by environmental processes.
A workshop for the manufacture of clothing, eg. tailor's workshop.
The dwelling and workshop of a framework knitter.
A small, finely-furnished room, traditionally where a lady could retire to be alone or entertain intimate friends.
A room used for sleeping or resting in. Use more specific term.
An area of land and associated buildings where vines are cultivated. The grapes produced are then used to make wine.
Areas of land used primarily for agriculture. See also GARDENS, PARKS AND URBAN SPACES.
A long piece of timber, thicker than a board.
Fragments of a structure, usually material that has been worked.
A vertical structure, sometimes made of steel, often used in the manufacture of cement. Material is loaded at the top, burnt in the middle and removed at the bottom.
A twin-shafted kiln, circular or oval in plan, consisting of a fire chamber, pre-heater and cooling chamber.
A furnace or oven for burning, baking or drying. Use specific type where known.

Fleet Air Arm fighter and torpedo-bomber, designed for operation from aircraft carriers. All-metal in construction, it entered service in 1944 and was rendered obsolete after the war by the advent of the jet aircraft.
Blackburn Aircraft, Ltd., founded by Robert Blackburn, who produced his first aircraft in 1910. Specialised in the production of torpedo-carrying aircraft.
Use for vessels believed to come from Europe but where the precise nationality is not known.
Use for vessels registered in Jersey, Guernsey or another of the other Channel Islands.
Any earthworks, walling, bastion or fortified outwork, or combination of these, generally with ditch or moat.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter biplane renowned for its high performance and manoeuvrability. Entered service in 1917.
A light, high-speed aircraft designed to engage in aerial combat.
A type of calcining kiln used in arsenic manufacture.
A calciner used in arsenic production from the 1820s to the 1950s featuring a distinctive, slowly rotating hearth.
A peg or upright object which is the target of a ball in skittles.
A flat, oblong gaming piece marked with spots used to play dominoes.
A toy designed to exercise the ingenuity.
A gaming implement usually used in conjunction with a ball.
A ring, often metal, which is used to be thrown as part of a game.
One of a pack, or deck, of cards used to play games, each distinguished from the others by markings on its face.
A heavy disc, usually thrown.
A metal spur fitted to the leg of a fighting cock as an aid in fighting.
A board marked up to play a game upon.
An item designed to be played with by children.
A small ball, usually of glass or porcelain, used in games.
A marker used in the playing of a game.
Objects used or associated with sport and games, eg gaming piece. This class includes toys.
A multi sided object usually used to obtain a unique value in games of chance.
A marker used to represent a gambling stake.
A round object used in games.
A container in which dice are shaken and from which dice are thrown.

The de Havilland Aircraft Co., Ltd., founded in 1920 by Sir Geoffrey de Havilland, C.B.E., A.F.C., F.R.Ae.S. Originally developers of commercial aircraft, were responsible for such notable wartime aircraft as the Mosquito and the Tiger Moth.

Impressed civil, twin-engined airliner converted to a military transport. Thirty were ordered for military use, though only eleven were actually built. Entered service in 1940, with the last being scrapped in 1950.
A workshop used by a craftsman who works in base or precious metals.
A building or room used for small scale manufacture. Use more specific term where possible.
A workshop used for the manufacture of items of jewellery and/or timepieces from precious metals and precious or semi-precious stones.
A terrace or row of dwellings, with a NAIL SHOP attached to each house.
A workshop with a forge for the melting and working of white metal, ie. low-melting alloys. Also used for a smith specializing in decorative or finely finished wrought iron work.
A place where metal knives and edge cutting tools were manufactured.
A place where an anti-corrosion coating of zinc is added to iron and steel products to prevent them from rusting.
Place where a smith works iron. May be for small scale local use or within a larger industrial complex.
A place where watches and timepieces are manufactured and mended.
A place where padlocks and rim locks for doors are made from iron and brass.
Four-seat, twin-engined medium bomber. Entered service in 1938. After serving Bomber Command from 1939-42, was converted to a torpedo-bomber and mine-layer with RAF Coastal Command.
Four-engined, five to seven crew, heavy bomber biplane. Entered service in 1918.

Four-engine, seven-crew heavy bomber. Entered service with RAF Bomber Command in 1940, becoming one of the twin sources of bomber strength along with the Lancaster. Also used for transport and glider tug duties.

A British medium-range biplane airliner designed and built by Handley Page in 1921. A twin-engined variant of the Handley Page W series (W8, W9), retired in 1931. Built for Imperial Airways (4 units built).
Twin-engined, four-seat medium bomber. A re-engined variant of the Hampden, less than 200 were built but never became operational due to engine unreliability. Some were converted to Hampdens.
Handley Page, Ltd.. Founded by Sir Frederick Handley Page, this was the first limited company to be incorporated in Great Britain for the purpose of aircraft manufacture.
A 1930s British short-haul biplane airliner for 6-8 passengers. It proved an economical and durable craft, despite its relatively primitive plywood construction. Primarily used by the RAF.
An aeroplane with two wings, or planes, placed one above the other either side of the fuselage.
Two-seat, single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer. Square-winged and fitted with dual controls, this popular trainer was used by British Commonwealth, as well as American and Canadian, air forces.
An aircraft with a single wing, or plane, either side of its fuselage.
The purpose of this object is unknown though it could be for surveying or it could be a charm.
A covered passageway projecting into or across a ditch of a fortified place to provide flanking fire to the ditch in which it stands or for the purpose of sheltering communication with outworks.
Buildings and structures associated with the use of animals to generate power.
A wheel rotated by the treading of persons or animals to power machinery to raise water, etc.
Sites and structures associated with the manufacture of bricks and tiles. Includes sites associated with earth extraction and preparation.
A building or site used for the production of bricks and other items, from a clay with refractory properties.
A building used to house peacocks.
Living quarters for animals, birds, etc, as pets or for observation, entertainment, etc.

Inshore craft used for carrying troops and military equipment used either for beach landings or as a ferry; as cargo smaller landing craft could be carried aboard larger craft in the D-Day operations, for example.
Vehicles owned or used by the armed forces. Includes tanks, armoured vehicles as well as civilian vehicles in use by the military eg. ambulances.
Equipment, including uniforms, small arms and field pieces, used by the armed forces.
Tracked, armoured fighting vehicles designed for front-line combat.

Sites, buildings, structures and features used for permanent, seasonal or temporary accommodation/habitation & related ancillary buildings. Includes commercial, military and religious sites used for residential purposes as well as industrial workplaces.

A mound of fire-cracked stones, normally accompanied by a trough or pit which may have been lined with wood, stone or clay. Assumed to be locations where heated stones were used to boil water primarily for cooking purposes.
Wind-blown sand.
A wind-blown deposit.
A form to record the details of a monument or site found during the course of a field survey or visit.
A paper form used to record specific information in a systematic way.
A small container for an aromatic substance, eg perfume.
A container for the storage and or use of cosmetics.
An area of ground or water containing explosive mines.
A large room for large numbers of people, eg for balls, meetings etc.
A chamber where discussions of issues take place, often found at universities.
A room where a committee meets to discuss matters put before them.
Originally a reception room where visitors come come to talk especially in a closed establishment such as a monastery or school. Later used to refer to any room used for entertaining guests.
A assembly room or rooms in which a collection of nominated persons meet to transact business of relevant purpose.
A room where the public can sit, often in hotels and airports.
A room where organizations and associations meet for the undertaking of presentations and consultation.

A room in the house of a Justice of the Peace in which cases were heard. Houses after 1848 contained these for prestige purposes since the practice of hearing cases at home was made illegal at that date.
The place, hall or chamber in which justice is administered.
A room to withdraw to from the dining room.
A communal living room.
A room in general use for persons to meet, often found at institutions such as colleges.
A meeting room intended specifically for the use of a board of directors or governors of an organization or company..
A room intended, and often furnished accordingly, as a venue for the holding of meetings.
A room where a monarch or similar would meet people, usually in a palace or similar building.
A room for general daily use, usually in a family dwelling.
The hard, close-grained wood of the Box or similar trees.
Wood, cut and seasoned for use as a constructional material.

A landscape which has been specifically designed or modified. Often indicated by proven below ground stratigraphy, revealed by deliberate investigation including geophysical survey, or other surface monuments or structures.
Not to be used for indexing. Broad term used to assist retreival of all monuments where physical evidence is recorded.
A modern building in which the load is carried by a metal girder framework and infilled with a light curtain wall.
Sites and structures associated with the disposal of waste water and waterborne refuse.
A pit for the reception of night-soil and refuse.
A toilet or toilets for public use.
