Sites, building, structures & features associated with the supply & drainage of water & the disposal of sewage and waste water. Includes bodies of water, waterways & associated ancillary structures.
A watertight reservoir or tank that receives sewage, and by sedimentation and bacterial action effects a process of partial purification.
A building housing filters for sewage. Usually associated with a sewage pumping station.
A waterworks pumping station.
A large drain or conduit for carrying away wastes.
A building containing apparatus for the removal of large pieces of detritus from a water supply.
A small latrine or toilet, usually built into the thickness of the wall of a castle or great house, with the waste dropping into a cess pit or straight to the outside.
A small room or building containing a lavatory and, in more recent times, washing facilities.
A tank or pond containing a layer of sand etc, for filtering large quantities of liquid.
A group of buildings in which local sewage is filtered and purified in large rectangular or circular tanks.
A small building housing a lavatory.
An inn, with an integral courtyard, for the lodging and entertainment of travellers. Often with open galleried wings overlooking the courtyard.
A public house offering lodgings to the passengers, and stabling for the horses of stage coaches.
An inn temporarily used for the performance of plays and other public entertainment.
A wayside inn for livestock traders.
A public house for the lodging and entertainment of travellers, etc.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Nitrate, used as a fertilizer or for use in the explosives industry.
A building or site where phosphorous-based fertilizers are produced by controlled chemical reactions.
A building or site used for the production of both chemical and organic fertilizer.
A building or site producing nitrogen-rich fertilizer.

A transonic jet fighter, first introduced by North American Aviation in 1947. Best known as the United States's first swept wing fighter. Total production at 9,860 units. Important fighter aircraft in the Korean War. Retired in 1994 (Bolivia).
A factory, incorporating power driven machinery from the late 18th century, where cloth was manufactured from threads interlaced at right angles to each other in a loom.
Includes bleaching, dressing, dyeing and printing.
A dam constructed across a stream to raise its water-level and make it available to power a mill wheel.
A barrier of concrete or earth, etc, built across a river to create a reservoir of water for domestic and/or industrial usage.
A building housing transformers to convert AC electricity supply to DC supply for use by tramcars.
A building housing transformers to convert AC electricity supply for domestic use.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of electricity.
A barn in which a central space is separated from side aisles by posts and braces.
A barn in which a central space is separated from a side aisle by posts and braces.
A costrel with a narrow-mouth and two opposed handles or lugs on the shoulder.
A costrel with a cylindrical body and a centrally placed neck. One end is usually domed and the other flat. Two opposed strap handles or lugs may join the rim or neck and shoulder. (Source: MPRG)
A container for the storage and/or transport of food and/or liquid.

A costrel with a flattened spherical form: the back is flat and the front domed or mammiform. The base may be slightly flattened or rounded. Two opposed strap handles or lugs join the rim or neck and shoulder. (Source: MPRG)
A costrel with a barrel-shaped body and a centrally placed neck. One end is usually flat and the other domed. Two opposed strap handles or lugs join the rim or neck and shoulder. (Source: MPRG)
A portable medieval container usually cylindrical or barrel shaped.

Planned &/or landscaped areas designed for aesthetic or recreational purposes. Includes all sites, buildings, structures & features normally associated with parks & urban spaces including street furniture.
A decorative or ornamental structure purposefully situated in a garden. Such as sculptures, sundials, bird baths, gnomes etc.
A garden ornament, usually of stone or metal, designed in the the form of a vase used to receive the ashes of the dead.
A stone, terracotta, wooden or metal receptacle used to grow flowers in.
A pedestal terminating in a head or bust of Hermes or some other deity.
Fixed instrument to measure altitude of stars and planets.

A glass sphere in a metal frame standing on a small pillar. A card is placed behind the sphere which focuses any sunlight, marking the card and thus indicating how many hours of sunlight there was on that day.
A figurative or abstract design in the round or in relief, made by chiselling stone, carving wood, modelling clay, casting metal, or similar processes.

A structure used to show the time of day by means of the sun shining on a 'gnomon', the shadow of which falls on the surface of the dial which is marked with a diagram showing the hours. Can be freestanding, usually on a pillar, or fixed to a building.
A tall, tapering pillar with a pyramidal top, generally square on plan. Used in England from the late 16th century as a public, funerary or garden monument.
A table found in a garden, often made of stone.
A large, decorative garden ornament resembling a vase.
A decorative garden ornament, usually of stone, in the form of a wide, shallow dish.
An ornamental receptacle to catch rainwater for birds to drink from and bathe in. Sometimes mounted on a column or plinth.
A sculptured, carved or moulded representation of an imaginary creature with a human head and breast combined with the body of a lion.
A type of GARDEN HOUSE, usually in the form of an open-fronted shelter with seat.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of shoe and leather polish, etc.
A tool for smoothing objects.
A large cargo vessel, either purpose-fitted or converted, for the transportation of slaves.
A craft used for the transportation of cargoes. Use specific type where known.
Buildings, structures and sites for regulating the flow of water.
A building in which apparatus measuring the amount of water supplied/used is housed.
Bases of this order are often referred to as spira and have a double astragal in the middle.
The lowest part of a structure, such as a pier, or the section of an order on which the shaft of a column sits.
A school in which elementary subjects are taught to young children.
A school for pre-Infant school children, usually 3-5 years old.
Containers used for cooking.
A form of frying pan, usually medieval.
A shaped or decorated raised panel below the sill of a window or a niche.

A specific type of hook used in textile production, also known as a sheer board hook. Harbicks were used in pairs to secure a cloth to a cropping board so that the nap (of the cloth) could be sheared.
Outerwear designed to protect the legs from weather.
Covering and accessories worn on the body.
A piece of cloth worn around the loins.
Outerwear covering the upperbody, including the arms. Covers to the waist.
An African cloth garment.
A garment worn by females.
An opaque, rigid sheath used to cover the penis. Not usually contraceptive and not for obvious visual display.
A loose piece of clothing about hip length worn over other clothes, not usually tucked in at the waist.
An appendage worn on the front of breeches.
Clothing worn on the upper body.
A sleeved garment worn on the upper body.
A piece of cloth or plastic worn especially by babies to protect clothes while eating.
A long loose fitting garment worn instead of a coat.
A garment used to wrap around a person.
A long outer garment reaching the ankles.
Pleated skirt, usua;;y of a tartan material, worn by men and women.
A piece of material worn over the head and or shoulders.
A voluminous garment worn over other clothing.
A garment covering from the waist to the knees, similar to trousers but stop at the knees.
Cloth or leather covering for the leg or ankle.
An outer garment worn on the legs.
Clothes worn so that they are visible, usually but not always worn over other clothes.
Sleeveless short jacket.
A shirt like garment.
A protective outer garment.
A sleeved outer garment.
An underskirt or dress with little shaping.
A garment worn from the waist down by women.
Barbed wire in the form of a coil which could be extended concertina-like to form a barrier to impede the movement of hostile troops.
One or more coils of barbed wire intended to impede the advance of hostile troops.
Rolls of barbed wire with supporting metal posts designed to impede enemy advance.
A range of techniques that use the build up of charge stored within a crystalline material to estimate its age

The light emitted from sedimentary minerals or mineral inclusions in bricks when stimulated in the laboratory by infrared light. Used to date samples up to 250,000 years old; especially appropriate for geological sediments containing feldspars
A building in which animals are housed. For non agricultural use see ANIMAL HOUSE and narrow terms in RECREATIONAL class.
A building used to house calves.

Simple organisms, mostly single celled, that move by means of two flagella (complex cellular projections). Most live as marine plankton, but some occur in fresh water. Members of the Kingdom Protista.

Animal, vegetable and mineral remains including edible materials, drink or residues and unworked imported objects which have been retrieved from archaeological contexts. Also soil samples taken for environmental analysis.

Amoebae which are partially enclosed in external shells, or tests. Found in wet soils, freshwater, decaying organic matter and on vegetation such as mosses. Used to examine environmental factors such as water acidity and moisture content.
Algae usually found as a silica skeleton. They obtain their food by photosynthesis and are used in ecological reconstruction.
Material derived from living things. Use more specific term where known.
Microscopic living things, usually unicellular, occasionally multi-cellular. They lack cell nuclei.
Use for the remains of any part of a plant.

Use for any soil or sediment. Sediments consist of mineral and/or organic material deposited by any process involving natural or human agencies. Soils are discrete bodies of altered mineral material (either sediment or in situ rock remains).
Kingdom of living things, lacking chlorophyll, that obtain their food from organic matter, usually by absorption. They include mushrooms, moulds and yeasts.
A specimen of material to represent the whole from which the sample was taken.

Single celled marine organisms. Some form calcareous tests (shells). They are used archaeologically to study the nature of marine environments or establish the presence of marine conditions or products (e.g. imported seaweed).
The remains of any part of any animal. Use specific term where possible.
Traces of food observed adhering to, or found within, an object or another material.
A site used for the extraction of metallic zinc by a variety of processes.
A complex of buildings used for the processing of metals. Use more specific type where known.
Stonemason's term for any easily worked sedimentary rock. Index with specific stone type where given.
A mill whose machinery is driven by water.
A water mill where the waterwheel directly drives a vertical shaft with grindstones on.
Any part of a maritime vessel. Use more specific term where known.
Objects used or associated with the movement of goods or people.
Parts which make up a maritime vessel.
A jettied house where the upper storey only overhangs the end elevation of the building.
Use where the intervening arcade is closed but timber-framed.
A house consisting of a single storey hall with two storey domestic ranges attached to either one or both ends.
A building for human habitation, especially a dwelling place. Use more specific type where known.
A house consisting of a public hall with private living accommodation attached. Built from the medieval period onwards.
A house consisting of a single storey open hall with a two storey domestic range attached to both ends forming an H shape.
A house with an open hall whose main span is separated by an arcade from the side aisles.

A high status building of the medieval period, consisting of a hall and attached room at first floor level with rooms below possibly for storage or living accommodation for a lower status family. The first floor was accessed by an external staircase.
A medieval house with central open hall and two storey bays, jettied at first floor level, on either side.
A house with a range at the end of it, at right angles to the main range.
A house consisting of a single storey open hall with a two storey domestic range attached at one end, forming a T shape.
A jug with a maximum diameter in the lower half of the vessel and with no discernible shoulder. (Source: MPRG)
A site where millstones have been cut to shape and/or fabricated from smaller pieces of stone.
A site used for the manufacture and finishing of querns.
A site where rough stone is processed, shaped, worked or formed into finished products.
A building or area where stone is stored for industrial or agricultural use.
A complex, comprising a workshop and a storage yard, used by a stonemason.
A site or building used for processing shale. Shale can be fashioned into goods or, if bituminous, distilled to produce oil, naphtha or tar.

A site which has produced evidence of in situ working of stone for the manufacture of tools, weapons or other objects. Such sites will usually, but not always, be of prehistoric date. Use object material where known.
A place where stone is dressed or shaped for use in building, etc.
A place where pieces of stone are crushed and ground.
Ceramic vessels made from potash, sand, feldspar and clay which is biscuit fired at a temperature of around 1000 degree Celsius. Usually glazed in order to become watertight.
Ceramic vessels produced out of wet clay which is shaped ad dried or fired to harden. In some cases other materials like sand are added to the clay.
An instrument for gauging the amount of rain which has fallen over a stated period.
A building, group of buildings or installation in which experiments and observations are undertaken to gather and record information about the weather.

A forcing house used for various types of fruit which first appeared in the 19th century. Lean-to houses were used for wall-grown fruit and free-standing houses for fruit grown in pots or for trees planted in the ground.
A glass-house or hot-house constructed for the cultivation of a grapevine.
A building made chiefly of glass, used to grow plants and fruit in. Use more specific type where possible.
A gallery or building in a garden, usually south facing, used for the growing of oranges and other fruit.
A garden building or greenhouse, containing pools in which Water Lilies are grown.
Includes some structures that are not strictly buildings. Use a more specific term where possible.
A glasshouse used for growing pineapples.
A building with a regulated moderate temperature for the cultivation of plants.
A glasshouse used for the cultivation of tropical plants.
A glasshouse used to grow and display tender decorative plants. May be either an extension to a house or freestanding.
A greenhouse used for growing palms and/or tropical plants.
A 19th century glasshouse built specifically for the fostering of camellias.
A glasshouse for the cultivation of ferns.
A greenhouse for the growing of figs.
Bank to let deer cross ditches, fences or roads, into, but not out of, a deer park.
A small area of managed woodland, created to provide cover for deer and other game.
An establishment or building where the breeding and training of birds of prey takes place.
A building used for the shelter and protection of deer, especially in winter.
A house or range of buildings in which dogs are kept, eg. hunting hounds.

An earthwork feature used by hunters to trap deer comprising a steep ditch into which the deer are chased with an enclosure to hold them at one end, known from the Isle of Rum and a debateable example in Cumbria.
A building used to shelter deer hunters.
Structure used for viewing deer hunt.
A large park for keeping deer. In medieval times the prime purpose was for hunting.
A building, site or structure associated with the hunting of animals.
Position often screened by earth, stone or wood from which game is shot.
A small area of managed woodland, created to provide cover for foxes.
An enclosure used for corralling deer.
A wooden stake fence, often associated with deer hunting.
A pond or pool with arms covered with nets into which wild birds, are lured and then caught. Monument type includes water feeder channels.
An area of land, heavily though not totally covered with trees, set aside for the royal hunt by Norman and Plantagenet kings.
A weekend retreat for Royal parties and others, when hunting in the Royal forests, or as a viewing station for the chase.
Sites, buildings, structures, features & areas of land associated with sport, leisure & entertainment. Includes sports grounds, hunting forests, cinemas, theatres etc.
A building used as a social venue by people interested in, and involved with, the sport of hunting.
A building for housing deer overnight.
A place where pheasants are reared and kept.
Shallow ditches and/or poles erected across open land to obstruct the landing of enemy aircraft and gliders.
Submerged obstacles to stop the landing of Seaplanes
A tube through which missiles are blown.
A weapon where an object is propelled away from its launcher by means of force. The launcher can be a weapon, eg a catapult, or a person. This term includes the projectiles themselves.
An industrial complex involved in the production of chemicals.
A chemical works producing mordants for the dying industry.
A twin-shafted kiln, circular or oval in plan, consisting of a fire chamber, pre-heater and cooling chamber.
A vertical structure, sometimes made of steel, often used in the manufacture of cement. Material is loaded at the top, burnt in the middle and removed at the bottom.
An entrance chamber from tide water to basin, with gates at each end and means of pumping up or lowering the level of water to suit.

A section of the water channel on a canal or river shut off above and below by lock gates provided with sluices to let the water out and in, and thus raise or lower boats from one level to another. Use more specific type where known.
Usually a row of bushes or small trees planted closely together to form a boundary between pieces of land or at the sides of a road.
An obstruction, usually manmade, which is used to restrict or prevent access to a settlement, building or area of land. Use more specific type where known.

A stone faced earth bank, usually with a concave batter, and with the base the same width as its height and the top half the width of the base. Vegetation usually grows out of the top. Found mainly in Cornwall, but also elsewhere in the Atlantic Arc.
Stop-line against invading tanks in form of a ditch during the defence of Britain.
A natural ditch the depth and/or width of which has been increased so as to prevent the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle.
A container used upon the altar.
A vase used on the altar.
The Festival of Lights.
The ridge formed at the intersection of two vaulted surfaces.
An engineering site where railway carriages are manufactured.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the construction and maintenance of railways and rolling stock.
An engineering workshop, often attached to an engine shed, for the running repairs of operational parts, etc.
Engineering works specializing in the production and maintenance of non-passenger carrying railway rolling stock.
An engineering works producing items for the railway other than rolling stock, such as signals, tracks, points, etc.
A large site specializing in the manufacture of locomotives.
Sites associated with the manufacture and engineering of vehicles.
A building used specifically for testing the boilers of railway engines, both hydraulically and with live steam.
An ancilliary workshop used for repairs, etc.
A type of seaplane, with one or more slender pontoons (known as "floats") mounted under the fuselage to provide buoyancy.
Single engine, two-crew shipboard reconnaissance and patrol seaplane. Entered service in 1939, this was the last combat floatplane built in Europe.
Building material made by combining gravel, cement, water and sand. When hard it forms a stonelike surface, used for paving and building.
Materials used for the construction of buildings, vehicles or other objects.
A site or building where silver was processed and/or worked and fashioned into objects.
A long building with a louvred roof in which silver is refined using the Pattinson Process, which had been developed in the 1830s.

Any building or site in which silver was refined and/or extracted by smelting, cupellation, liquation or by the Parkes Process. IA-C20. Don't use for lead or copper smelters at which silver has been extracted unless silver-related features survive.

A type of tower mill, either with turbine-type sails able to take wind from any direction, or with sails working with shrouds to direct wind from one direction. The sails directly drove millstones set beneath them.
A tower-like structure of wood or brick with a wooden cap and sails which are driven around by the wind producing power to work the internal machinery. Use with product type where known.
A knife handled at both ends used to shave wood.
A portable writing-case or surface, especially one for use on the lap. May contain compartments for storing writing materials and paper.
An object used in the transmission of the written word or drawn image.
Aircraft designed for the carrying and dropping of torpedoes.

A biplane torpedo-bomber designed to be flown from aircraft carriers. Equipped with foldable wings for ease of storage. Joined Fleet Air Arm service in 1940, intended as a replacement for the Swordfish.
A sailing vessel defined by a combination of such factors as hull design, locality and rig.
A decked sailing vessel of shallow draft.
Pictorial, painted or drawn material such as slides, drawings, photos, plans excluding cartographic.

A jar-shaped vessel with pierced apertures or cut-out on an open or closed pedestal base. Herbs, spices or scented woods would be placed in the pot and a burning coal placed underneath to warm the herbs so they would release their scent.
An object used to provide heat for various purposes eg to cook or to heat a room etc.
A long, narrow ditch designed to carry water away from a waterlogged area.
An artificial channel for draining water or carrying it off.
A clamp in which alum shale was burnt in the initial stage of processing.
A building or buildings used for the production of paints, varnishes, colours and distemper.
A site used for the production of dyes from natural ingredients.
A factory in which is ink is prepared from pigments and additives.
A works used for the production of copperas, a green iron sulphate which is used as a fixative in the dyeing process.
Grinding mill for producing dyes and pigments from natural materials.
A pit for the extraction of fullers earth (a hydrous silicate of alumina), which was used for cleansing, and finishing, cloth and wool.
A group of buildings or works where the evaporation and crystallization of sodium aluminium sulphate solution is performed.
A site where iron oxide and iron sulphates, used as brown pigments, are excavated.
Sites used for the manufacture of chemicals used as the basis for complex chemical processes or products.
A small dye works, often associated with a CALICO PRINTING WORKS.
Buildings and sites used for the production of inorganic and organic dyes, pigments and paints.
A mill for grinding ochre for the paint making process.
A pit from which marl, a mixture of clay and carbonate of lime, is excavated. Marl is used as a fertilizer.
Inshore craft used for carrying troops and military equipment used either for beach landings or as a ferry. Use specific type where known.
Small landing craft often armoured, designed to carry infantrymen and their equipment ashore from larger vessels offshore.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the commander of the Royal Engineers in Southern Area (Taunton Line).

An often squat building with thick, loopholed walls and a flat roof, designed to accommodate a variety of weapons, usually strategically positioned to cover a vulnerable point in a defensive system. Many were built to standardized designs.
A building used by an association of persons for social and recreational purposes or for the promotion of some common object.

A building with a range of facilities for the exclusive use of its all-male membership. Rooms were often provided as offices or short term accommodation, and the club could be used for business or social gatherings.
A military side-opening aircraft hangar originally designed for seaplanes and used RNAS bases from 1916. Steel framed with asbestos or corrugated iron cladding.
An aircraft hangar designed to house seaplanes.
Sites, buildings, structures, features & areas of land, both natural & man-made, which cannot be assigned to a particular class (for example, railings).
An artificially raised level of ground.
A site where coal is processed.
Includes terms for components of site. See also terms in MINING INDUSTRY SITE grouping.
Use for vessels registered in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
Use for vessels registered in Wales.
A structure of wood, stone, iron, brick or concrete, etc, with one or more intervals under it to span a river or other space. Use specific type where known.
A type of bridge which was designed for temporary use and then capable of being moved to another site. Use for temporary bridges which have remained in situ since erection.
A type of temporary bridge designed by Sir Donald C.Bailey during the Second World War.
A floating bridge, generally temporary, whose decks are supported on low flat-bottomed or hollow floats.
An object carried about the person for religious purposes.
A badge, usually of lead alloy, distributed at various religious shrines of the medieval period and worn on clothing as proof of a pilgrimage and as a talisman.
A site used for the production and/or working of glass.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of glass.
Mixed house of nuns and religious men.
A mixed house of Augustinian nuns, canonesses and canons.
A machine used for lifting materials.
A machine for hoisting or moving heavy weights, consisting of a spar or boom set up obliquely, with its head steadied by guys, and furnished with suitable tackle and purchases.
A small open container, usually with one handle, used for drinking.
A cup with a rounded body beneath a deep neck. There may be a marked junction between neck and body and the angle of the neck may be inward-sloping, upright or everted. (Source: MPRG)

A form of cup which incorporates a joke or conundrum, where cut-outs or holes in the body make conventional use impossible. The puzzle is how to drink from it without getting wet; usually achieved by sucking through a hollow rim or handle. (Source: MPRG)
A cup with a marked change of angle in the body wall, generally at the point of maximum girth. (Source: MPRG)

A vessel composed of three or more equally spaced lobes and usually, a waisted or pedestal base. The handles are vertical loops, generally of strap form. There may be two opposed handles, or one per lobe junction. (Source: MPRG)
A cup adapted by the addition of a pedestal base. (Source: MPRG)
A container from which liquid is drunk.
A cup with sides falring outwards from the base towards the rim, usually with a single handle.
A cup with convex body walls. (Source: MPRG)
A vessel composed of three or more separate compartments, joined together and pierced to allow liquid to flow from one to another. There may be one or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
Hard, compact, unprocessed, fibrous cellulose substance. The roots, trunks and branches of trees and shrubs consist of this tissue.
Durable wood from a non-native, evergreen conifer.
Includes interim, research, specialist reports on a specific topic.
Covering for the head, especially ornamental.
A pad of cloth or fur for keeping the ears warm.
A piece of strengthened material worn projecting over the forehead and eyes to provide shade for the eyes.
A form of hat, usually does not cover the forehead nor have a brim, and usually worn by women.
A fine net worn over the hair.
A head cover which can be attached to a piece of outerwear, eg a coat, or can be separate.
Headwear where a band of material is wound around a cap.
A covering for the head with a peak to shade the eyes.
A cloth or scarf worn over the head as a covering.
An object worn on the head.
A piece of cloth worn over the head.
An artifical head of hair worn to disguise baldness, for adornment, for ceremonial or theatrical use etc.
A head covering, usually with a brim.
A net worn over the hair to hold it in place.
A wig, toupee or section of extra hair designed to replace or enhance the wearer's real hair giving greater quantity, bulk or length.
Light material used to cover the face or head.
A band of cloth or other material worn around the head, not totally covering it.

A structure, often found in 18th century landscape gardens, that demonstrates eccentricity or excess rather than practical purpose. They can take many forms - ruins, sham castles, towers, hermits' cells or grottoes.
A house which bears signs of fortification. These often include crenellated battlements and narrow slit-like windows.
A manor house, which was granted a royal licence to crenellate.

A well or spring, possessing religious or otherwise ritualistic significance, around which a structure, such as a niche, wall or shelter, has been constructed. In the case of the water source being a natural spring, double-index with SPRING.
An establishment in which people, usually children, are taught.
19th century school administered by a school board.
A school run by a Christian church.
A school for pupils with physical or learning difficulties.
A school that is directly funded by central government (specifically, the Department for Education) and independent of direct control by local government in England.
A school serving or supported by a parish. Usually teaching religious as well as conventional education.
A school in which students are taught according to the beliefs of the muslim faith.
A school in which instruction is given on a Sunday, especially such a school for children connected with a parish or congregation.
A school that is established, run and supported by a private, non-governmental body.
Sites, buildings, structures & features relating to the provision of knowledge and skills.
A school built and/or supported by voluntary contributions.
A school where Jewish children are educated.
A school attended by children between the ages of eleven and sixteen.
An early to mid 20th century school designed to effect maximum ventilation and sunlight for its pupils.
A school conducted by members of a convent.
A school design consisting of single-storey buildings with classrooms entered from a verandah.
School built by the local Education Authority to provide residental schooling at the seaside for children from urban communities.
19th century school for the daughters of clergymen.
A school where specialist skills, relating to a particular subject, are taught. Use specific type where known.
A private school offering term time accommodation for pupils being taught there.
A school used by the children of settlers at a Chartist Colony.
Boarding school for children of Travellers and Romany Gypsies while their parents were away on agricultural work
A building or buildings used for the production of pens.
A large gearwheel which, together with a smaller gear called a pinion, connects two parrallel shafts and, in a corn mill, drives the stone nuts.
A row of balusters, usually made of stone, surmounted by a rail or coping.
A place where sails are manufactured.
A craft or repair workshop in a boat yard, harbour or naval dockyard.

An artificial aperture from which water springs. The water supply usually came from a lake or reservoir higher up in order to ensure the necessary flow and pressure. More recently fountains have been powered by pumps.
An automata or water device which surprises the unwary onlooker with water. A feature of 16th and 17th century gardens.
A vessel with heating apparatus beneath it, for cooking or keeping food warm at the table.
A decorative fitting of mid to late 11th century date, exclusively of copper alloy, and mostly zoomorphic. Arranged in pairs, on each stirrup either side of the footplate.
Objects associated with the care and use of animals.
A small building, often inhabited by a gatekeeper, gamekeeper or similar. Use specific type where known.
A pit used for the excavation of clay suitable for making bricks.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the extraction of clay.
A place from which clay is extracted.
Building housing apparatus for testing chain links.
A building in which wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
A site where wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
A marked path along which aircraft taxi to or from a parking area, runway, etc.
A rod to lift the odd numbered warp threads to enable the weft to be passed through.
An aircraft with a single wing, or plane, either side of its fuselage.
British twin-engined light/medium bomber developed from the model 142 civil transport. Noted for its speed, this three-crew monoplane had an all-metal, stressed skin structure and a 1000lb bomb load.
A kiln in which stone is burnt as it falls through a heated and slightly inclined steel tube.
A factory where cars are manufactured.
Buildings and sites associated with the manufacture of motor vehicles.
A structure for hanging criminals, often used to suspend criminals after execution, consisting of one upright post with an arm.
Objects relating to the punishment and restraint of humans.
A building to house waterwheels, attached to a WATERMILL or water-powered factory.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production and use of water power.

An area of land owned by a developer, whether a private entrepreneur or a public authority, and divided into plots for leasing or sale to manufacturing or commercial concerns which may share some common services.
Gun emplacement for static or mobile light anti aircraft artillery.
An anti aircraft battery usually mounting smaller, faster weapons such as Bofors guns or a single anti-aircraft machine gun, intended to engage fast low flying aircraft.
An anti aircraft battery usually mounting weapons with a larger calibre ammunition such as the QF 3.75 inch (94mm) gun.
A command post used to direct the guns of an anti aircraft battery.

Unspecified Second World War anti-aircraft battery. There were three types of battery. The U2P and U20P had different arrangements of DFW55373 projector sites for the 20-barrelled 3" projectors. The U9P mounted 12-barrelled projectors.
WW2 LAA battery consisting of two or four 40m guns or Bofors guns. Associated structures included tented accommodation, ammunition shelters, a 100 gallon water tank, latrines, wash-house and kitchen.
40mm gun emplacement created between 24th-26th June 1944 as part of the fourth deployment of Diver LAA guns to the Kentish Gun Belt. Each site had an extant searchlight battery.

Heavy anti aircraft battery used from June 1944-May 1945 to combat the V-bomb threat. They are distinct from normal HAA batteries, being laid out in a V-shape, and early on were mainly for mobile 3.7-inch guns.
A site containing one or more artillery pieces and/or rocket launchers for firing at enemy aircraft.
Natural inorganic substance possessing a definite chemical composition in a crystalline form. See MINERAL Class Listnfor narrow terms.
Hard, transparent, often coloured mineral. Can be found on its own as crystals and veins but also as a major constituent of rocks such as granite. Often used decoratively.
A trinket worn as a protection against evil.
An object, often including gems and ornamentation, used as an adornment, usually on a person.
An existing factory that was converted for use as aircraft works in the run up to or during the Second World War.
A factory or works which has been temporarily turned over to the manufacture of goods for the war effort.
A piston mounted horizontally supplying power via a valve gear directly to a crankshaft or flywheel.
An engine in which the mechanical force of steam is made available as a motive power for driving machinery.
A mill used for the mechanized processing of silk.
Any factory used for the manufacture of textiles.
A container used to hold, store, examine or create medicinal substances such as ointments, medicines, drugs, pills, tablets etc.
A medical container for collecting urine for study.
A castle without a motte.
A factory where metal wire is manufactured.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the extraction of metal ores.
A storehouse for ore, often found in conjunction with a BLAST FURNACE.
Residues from ore-processing operations; intact tips and deposits may preserve considerable evidence on the processes used. A high rpoportion have been destroyed by reprocessing.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the metal industry.
A site where metal is worked. Use specific type where known.
A floor area, covered in sand, onto which hot metal from a furnace is cast.
Building or structure covering a casting floor or pit.
A furnace used for melting metals for casting or for heating shot.
A mill with machinery used to cut slabs of metal into rods, or thin sections, for use in nail making or wire drawing.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the processing of non ferrous metal ores.
A mill in which sets of rollers were used to roll metal to set thicknesses or shapes such as rails, beams or rods.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the smelting of metals.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with sporting activities.

Feature, typically a ship, boat, aircraft or vehicle, deliberately sunk for recreational and diver educational purposes in inland bodies of water used as dive centres, such as lakes and water-filled quarries, or offshore as artificial reefs.
An object belonging to, used by, or related exclusively to one person and normally carried or kept privately by that person.
T shaped piece of bronze imitating a key and hung from a chatelaine.
Craft used to maintain, supply or assist larger vessels whilst in harbour.
A craft on which is a machine for the loading and unloading of grain to and from a warehouse.
A wall structure built to direct a current into the desired channel in a harbour, river etc.
A building on a river or canal in which the water levels are controlled.
A vertical shaft, usually with an internal ladder, allowing access to a sewer or underground counduit for inspection and maintenance.
A pit filled with rubble, etc., into which rain or waste water flows in order to disperse into the surrounding soil.
An open area of water, usually artificial and enclosed by dock gates or locks, lined with wharves, warehouses and berths to enable vessels to load and unload.
A dam which can be raised or lowered to regulate the flow of water.
A small building built over the end of a water conduit or spring.
An instrument for measuring and indicating the height of tide.
The masonry beneath a lock gate, sometimes projecting several feet from the gate.

A section of the water channel on a canal or river shut off above and below by lock gates provided with sluices to let the water out and in, and thus raise or lower boats from one level to another. Use more specific type where known.
A building containing machinery for operating sluices.
A small building housing a valve which controls the flow within a water regulation system.
A double lock placed between tidal water and a canal, etc..
A building in which apparatus measuring the amount of water supplied/used is housed.
The horizontal beam on a lock gate.
Buildings, structures and sites for regulating the flow of water.
A balance engine used to replenish the water levels of a river by transferring water from a reservoir or other supply.
A system of artificial or natural drains and ditches used to drain off surplus water.
A waterworks pumping station.
Manmade constructions used to prevent rivers breaking their banks and flooding the surrounding area with water. Often taking the form of a bank or wall.
A gate which allows water to pass into a dock, etc, at flood tide, and by which it is retained during the ebb tide.
The space enclosed between the gates and side-walls of a lock.
A gate used to seal the entrance to a dock to prevent water escaping from a wet dock or entering a dry dock.
Two or more adjacent locks where the upper gates of one lock serve as the lower gates of the next.
Wind or water-powered mill for land drainage in fens or marshlands.
A pipe, usually of reinforced concrete or metal, which delivers pressurized water from a dam to hydraulic turbines.
A chamber attached to the sewer of a building to facilitate the removal of any blockage.
The gate of a sluice which can be opened or shut to let out or retain the water.
A head of water raised in a conduit system.
A drainage structure that extends across and beneath roadways, canals or embankments.
A large wooden gate, positioned at either end of a canal or river lock, equipped with sluices to let water through.
A barrier of concrete or earth, etc, built across a river to create a reservoir of water for domestic and/or industrial usage.
A channel carrying overflow water past a dam. Early 19th century onwards.
Manmade constructions used to prevent water flooding the surrounding area. Often taking the form of a bank or wall but may be more elaborate e.g. the Thames Barrier.
An iron, stone or concrete tower built up from the bed of a reservoir. From it the control valves of the pipes which draw off water at different levels are operated.
A basin or harbour, which is open to the tides. Vessels can only enter and leave at high tide and are stranded at low tide.
Buildings used as non-permanent homes.
A residential establishment for retired armed servicemen and women.
An artificial navigable waterway used for the transportation of goods. Nowadays also used for recreational purposes.
A canal that can accommodate ocean-going ships, usually built across an isthmus or to give access to a river port e.g. Manchester ship canal
A canal built as a military obstacle, but also used for the transport of military stores, equipment and personnel.
Buildings and structures associated with canal transport.
Objects used to secure buildings, furniture or objects or used in the finishing and (non-structural) decoration of buildings, equipment and furniture.
A hole or opening in a ship's hull to allow light and air to enter the vessel, or to aim a weapon through.
Not a round barrow ploughed out at one end, but a specific type, the flat edge being additionally defined by stone slabs.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within an earthen mound. Use more precise term where known.
A burial monument, usually of Iron age date, comprising a small square ditched enclosure surrounding a central interment, which may also have been covered by a mound.
Site types normally or frequently associated with burials which in some instances may have had solely religious or ritual functions.

Hemispherical mound surrounded by a ditch (or occasionally two or more concentric ditches), often accompanied by an external (or occasionally internal) bank. Mound and ditch may sometimes be separated by a berm. Use specific type where known.
A monument featuring an artificial circular shallow depression surrounded by a bank which runs around the rim of the depression.
A circular bank surrounding an area where burials were placed.
Artificial mound of earth, turf and/or stone, normally constructed to contain or conceal burials. Use specific type where known.

A poorly understood Neolithic monument comprising a very long, narrow earthen mound. They may be of single-phase construction, or represent the addition of a linear extension to the bank of an existing Long Barrow.

A rectangular or trapezoidal earthen mound of Neolithic date, usually accompanied by flanking or encircling ditches, and normally associated with human remains. Mound construction and associated features vary considerably in type and complexity.
A landing and taking-off area for military aircraft. Often includes ancilliary structures and buildings for the maintenance and storage of aircraft, etc.
A landing circle marked out in white used as the airfield symbol.
For example allergic contact dermatitis, Barlows Syndrome, cutaneous melanoma, irritant contact dermatitis, MRSA infection, mummification and other related illnesses.
Small ornamental pyramid or cone, often decorated, crowning a spire, turret, buttress etc.
A component part that is designed deliberately for decorative purposes.
The use of knapped flint applied to a wall to form a decorative pattern.
Circular or almond-shaped halo surrounding the figure of Christ, the Virgin or a saint.
A decorative feature, or non-heraldic badge, representing the name of a person connected with a building, often in the form of a graphic pun on the name.

A decorative, repeating geometric pattern, utilizing motifs such as lozenges, leaves etc., applied to a wall or panel, or incorporated into brickwork by laying different coloured bricks in a series of squares, diamonds.
An inscription or illustration carved into the surface of a stone wall or other architectural element.

A decorative feature of wood, plaster or carved masonry, often used in low relief on ceilings, panels or screens and resembling interlacing leather straps. Popular in the late 16th and early 17th centuries.

An arrangement by which panels, screens, vaults or windows are divided into parts of different shapes or sizes by means of moulded stone bars or ribs, called form-pieces or forms in the Medieval period.
Decorative ornamentation in the form of interlacing ribbons or cords, usually in an intricate pattern.
A case or border, usually wood or metal, enclosing a picture, painting or photograph.
One of a series of small, rectangular blocks arranged like a row of teeth, projecting from the lower part of a cornice in many classical orders.
Decorative ornamentation in the form of a horn filled with fruit etc.
Classical decorative motif of interlocking right-angled and vertical lines, usually applied as a continuous pattern.
A decorative feature in the style of a flower or plant. Use more specific term.
Paper, often decorated with a printed pattern, painted or embossed design, and usually provided in rolls and used to line the interior walls of a building for decorative purposes.
A series of panels, usually of wood, combined to line a room.
A series of concentric mouldings decorating the curved face of an arch.
Fine art depiction in oil, watercolour or other media on wood panels, canvas or paper
A two dimensional image using paint applied to the surface of a wall.
The shaped projection on the top of a newel post or at the apex of a gable.
A sculptural or decorative representation of an animal. Includes mythical and fantastical animals such as dragons, centaurs etc.
An area or series of tiles applied, usually to an interior floor or wall's surface, for practical or decorative effect.
A figurative or abstract design in the round or in relief and can be of various materials. For freestanding sculptures see also Monument Types Thesaurus.
A decorative, framed tablet, usually bearing an inscription or coat of arms, in the form of a scroll or curving piece of parchment.
An inscription on illustration applied to a wall by carving into its plaster to reveal a different colour beneath.
A surface formed by cutting off a square edge, usually at 45 degrees. Use more specific type where known.
A decorative form consisting of two upright S-shaped curves positioned opposite one another with their concave sections placed at the top.
A sculptural or decorative representation of a human figure. Includes mythical and fantastical figures such as Cupid, Atlas etc.
An ornamental contour given to the angles or features of a building, whether a projection or a cavity, such as a cornice, an architrave or an astragal.
An ornamental panel or decorative structure situated above a mantelpiece
A decorative feature, usually Norman, in which fluting takes a spiral rather than vertical form.
A display or depiction of authorised armorial bearings, such as the elements of a coat of arms, livery and personal badges and flags, mottoes etc..
The application of colour and other materials to a structure to either conceal it from identification or to make it look like something else.
A flat oval or circular ornamental feature decorated in relief, often with flutes or floral motifs.
A decorative, spiral scroll form, thought to have been based upon the shape of a ram's horn, employed in consoles, modillions, the capitals of orders such as the Ionic, Composite and Corinthian etc..
An area of plasterwork modelled or incised with ornamental designs or motifs.
Small 'drops' or conic projections under the mutules (a repeating block motif) and triglyphs (rectangular blocks embellished with vertical grooves) in a Doric entablature.
A decorative tile on the end of the cornice or eaves of a building to conceal the ends of tiles.
A two dimensional image using paint applied to the surface of a ceiling.
A panel of often decorated wrought-ironwork forming the arch between two gate-piers or standards or above a gate. Also used for an arched support for a lamp-holder between two standards.
An oval or circular decorative feature often bearing an illustration or portrait in light relief.
Decorative ornamentation consisting of alternating oval and V-shaped motifs, used to enrich ovolo mouldings.
A full written presentation of the details of a particular event or investigative technique, often including illustrations and appendices.
A report on the archaeology of an area, based primarily on existing records and resources.
A projecting stud which fastens into a socket.
A projection used to clip clothing together.
An object designed to float in water and to support a net.
An object that supports another in water, eg float on a fishing line or net.
A tool, piece of equipment, container or other object used for or in fishing.

Staircase whose moving steps are driven mechanically whilst remaining permanently in a horizontal plane allowing users or objects to be moved effortlessly from one level to another, within or outside a building.
A flight of steps leading from one level to another.
A building in which purified charcoal was produced by distillation of wood in sealed cast-iron retorts heated in fire-boxes. Tarry by-products were sometimes recovered by condensation flues.
A works using sealed retorts to produce charcoal. Wood distillates may be produced as byproducts of this process. They may be found at separate works or comprise part of a gunpowder works.
Blackburn Aircraft, Ltd., founded by Robert Blackburn, who produced his first aircraft in 1910. Specialised in the production of torpedo-carrying aircraft.
A torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance biplane in service with the Fleet Air Arm 1935-1938. Rendered obsolete after 1938 by the Swordfish and withdrawn from service.
An artificial watercourse for the conveyance of water.
A channel or pipe providing water to a canal or other body of water.
A jug with a sinuous profile where the rim, girth and base are of roughly equal diameter, and the neck and lower body are narrower.(Source: MPRG)
A container for holding or pouring liquids, usually having a handle or lip.
A small house built out of rough logs.
Places of residence.
Aircraft grouped according to their manufacturer.

A civil passenger transport biplane produced by the Farman Aviation Works from 1919. Instrumental in the creation of early airlines and commercial routes in Europe after World War I. Initially designed in 1918 as a heavy bomber. Some 60 units built.

Farman Aviation Works was an aircraft company founded and run by the brothers Richard, Henri, and Maurice Farman in 1908. The firm made pusher biplane aircraft for military and training purposes, it was eventually dissolved in 1956.
A cup with convex body walls. (Source: MPRG)
A small open container, usually with one handle, used for drinking.
A body of still water often artificially formed for a specific purpose. Use specifc type where known.
An ornamental garden feature, sometimes with an associated bath house.
A building or part of a building used for the storage of goods or merchandise. Use more specific type where known.
A building or part of a building used specifically to store items of hardware and ironmongery.

A place of worship for members of the Congregational Church. These churches, the first of which was founded in 1616 in Southwark, practised self government. Most of them were merged to form the United Reformed Church in 1972.

A place of worship for members of the United Reformed Church, a group formed in 1972 by the amalgamation of most of the Congregational Churches in England and Wales with the Presbyterian Church in England.
Buildings and structures associated with the creation and use of hydraulic power.
An engine house used to pump water to the top of an ACCUMULATOR TOWER.
Oil obtained from the flesh of the coconut and used in ointments, soaps etc.
An uncrystallized syrup, produced as part of the sugar refining process. Used as a food additive and in the production of rum.
A fluid substance. Use for unspecified liquids only, where known use more specific type.
Oil manufactured from fish.
Drinks containing alcohol, an intoxicating substance found in fermented or distilled liquids.
Oil derived from palms, used for a variety of purposes.
A sour tasting liquid, produced from wine and other liquors, used as a preservative, in pickling, or as a flavouring for food.
Oil produced from the pulp of olives.
A clear liquid that forms oceans, rivers etc.
Includes raw and processed.
A sweet fluid substance, the nectar of flowers, gathered and worked up for food by insects such as bees.
A building for human habitation, especially a dwelling place. Use more specific type where known.
The residence of a verger, typically a layperson who assists in the ordering of religious services within the Anglican church.

A service is a system that provides one or more functions of value to the end-user. Examples include: a photocopying service, a banking service, an authentication service, inter-library loans, a Z39.50 or Web server. [DC]
A database stored on a computer linked to the internet, which can be queried and browsed by remote users using the internet.
A series of locks usually with short reaches between them allowing boats to travel up and down a steep incline.
Deposits that accumulate at the bottom of a slope, at a break in a slope, or where a barrier is encountered.
The cutting part of a drill. Often bits are interchangeable.
A factory for the manufacture of vehicles
A building where motor cycles are assembled.

Noorduyn Aviation Limited. Formed in 1934 by Mr R.B.C. Noorduyn as a successor to Noorduyn Aircraft Limited, which was formed in 1933. The company's most notable production aircraft was the Norseman transport.

Canadian-built, single-engine, high-wing transport and communications aircraft converted from a civilian model. Metal-framed with fabric covering, saw service in 1944-5. Was capable of being equipped with wheels, floats or skis.
Structure used for viewing deer hunt.
A building, site or structure associated with the hunting of animals.
Open-air area often terraced on which a range of ore processing operations are carried out.
An aircraft used for the training of pilots, sometimes fitted with dual controls for use by the instructor.
Miles M.14 Magister. Single-engine, two-crew training and communications aircraft. Spruce and plywood in construction, with open cockpits and a fixed landing gear, served between 1937 and 1945.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by one or more substantial banks, ramparts and ditches. Use more specific type where known.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by a single rampart, usually accompanied by a ditch.
A residence for a member of a religious community eg. Abbot, Prior, Manciple etc. For multiple occupancy use more specific term eg. DORMITORY.
Living and working quarters for the cellarer who was in charge of provisions and the running of the cellar.
A feature which forms part of a building and has a specific functional usage or decorative form.
A small structure, often polygonal or circular, on top of a roof, dome, tower etc. featuring apertures to light or ventilate the building it adorns.
An RAF Base, used specifically for the storage and maintenance of barrage balloons.
Shallow draft vessel used to carry ammunition.
Shallow draft cargo vessel, often broad beamed and flat bottomed, powered by engine and or sail.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the process of distilling.
A brewery building where malt is mixed with hot water to form wort.
All-weather fighter/interceptor first flow in 1951, introduced into service in 1956 and retired from the RAF in 1968.
A knife used for sacrifices.
An object for making an offering to a deity. It includes objects concerned with curses, sacrifices, and prayers and their related objects.
A type of steam engine in which the steam cylinders are placed above the crankshaft supported on a robust frame.

A power source deriving its energy from solid fuel, which is used to boil water in an almost closed vessel, producing steam which moves one or more pistons in tight fitting cylinders, the energy being transmitted by a piston rod to a diversity of devices
Use specific type where known.
A building, on an airfield or military base, used for the maintenance and storage of motor vehicles.
A building, on a military airfield or base, in which motor vehicles are housed.
A semi circular jewelled headdress for formal occasions.
Decorative ornamentation worn on the head.

Developed as a long range, heavy day-fighter, the ME110 found its niche as a night fighter. It saw service over Southern and Eastern England during the Battle of Britain but lost out in the daytime to the faster British fighters.
A light, high speed aircraft equipped specifically to engage in night combat.
A major horizontal timber spanning a roof space to connect a pair of principal rafters and prevent them spreading.
A tiebeam whose central section is omitted to increase head room; its inner ends are held by a slip-braces or struts rising from a dropped tiebeam and can be used in end frames.
Pieces of metal money usually small in size and circular in design. Manufacture from a variety of metals including gold and silver but more recently manufactured from base metals and alloys.
Metal, usually gold and silver, in the form of ingots prior to being minted into coinage.
Metal, either precious or base, in the form of bars and coins. Use more specific type.
Any material, including gold, silver, copper, tin etc. which is ductile, malleable, usually lustrous and a good conductor of heat and electricity.
A hospital for convalescents or consumptives.
A house by a toll gate or toll bridge where tolls are collected.
The residences of people involved in transport work.

Two-seat, twin-engined light/medium bomber celebrated for its speed and versatility. Entering service in 1941, was also adapted for duties as a fighter-bomber, Pathfinder, mine-layer, transport, trainer and photo-reconnaissance aircraft.
A mill for beating and cleaning cloth, using soap or fullers earth.
Gun battery built specifically to mount short range weapons to defend a beach against an attempted landing.
A small vessel used to carry supplies and personnel to lighthouses.
A vessel used to maintain supply or assist larger vessels. Use more specific term.
A waterwheel in which the incoming water is directed onto the periphery below the top of the wheel.
A waterwheel where the water enters below the top of the wheel but above the axle.
A raised platform, especially in a theatre or auditorium, for the use of performers or speakers etc.
Distinctive clerestory-roofed building, used for the drying and storage of military parachutes.
A distinctive, clerestory-roofed building of five 10ft bays, used for the drying, storage and packing of military parachutes and built to Air Ministry drawing number 11137/41.
An object to sit upon. Use narrower terms where known.
A long seat for reclining on.
A brick built railway signal box, usually with a reinforced correct roof, designed to minimize the effects of blast damage from aerial bombardment and thus protect the signalling equipment.
A purpose-built or adapted structure intended as a headquarters for an air raid precautions warden.
A site used by the Air Raid Precautions network. Use more specific term.
A centre used by the Air Raid Precautions network to co-ordinate reports of air raids in an area.
A building used as a control centre for the Air Raid Precautions network, responsible for issuing air raid warnings and coordinating fire and rescue services.
An observation post used by Air Raid Precautions wardens to watch for aircraft and bomb strikes.

A building or structure used to provide protection to an Air Raid Warden or firewatcher during an air raid, thus enabling the identification of the locations of fires caused by incendiary bombs in comparative safety.
A centre used to train Air Raid Precautions wardens.
A siren used to warn of an impending attack by enemy aircraft.
A specialized lantern, with a reduced glare, for use in air raids.
A building used for the storage and distribution of civilian respirators and Air Raid Precautions equipment.
A sign used by the Air Raid Precautions network to assist in identifying vital equipment and resources in the event of an air raid or to aid movement during blackouts.
A building used in the Second World War to co-ordinate action against enemy air raids.
A vertical cladding consisting of tiles hung in overlapping rows.
A non-structural covering, such as tile, slate, wood etc., applied to an exterior wall.
An ornamental moulding whose curved, segmented form resembles that of a scallop shell.
A container in which the Sacrament is carried.
Objects used or associated with religious, ritual or funerary activities.
A private room or parlour usually at the same level as the hall.
A room for personal rather than public use.
A site, often in a woodland clearing, used for the production of pure carbon by the controlled burning of wood and other organic materials.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of charcoal.
A vessel used to carry essential supplies, such as food and armaments, to naval ships in order to keep them replenished whilst on patrol. Use more specific term.
A vessel containing equipment for reducing the magnetic structure of a ship's hull making it immune to magnetic mines.
Use for completed, accuarately surveyed maps

skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: National Mapping Programme Morph Number Sheet

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: Maps or charts.
Not subdivided
A rescue tug equipped to care for survivors from torpedoed vessels and also available for towing to port ships damaged by enemy action.
A specially equipped ship designed to care for survivors of stricken vessels and offshore drilling platforms. These ships were often converted naval trawlers or minesweepers.

A stand by set house similar to 13244/41 and designed to drawing number 16302/41 and comprising of 4 rooms; a fuel storage room, a transformer chamber, a switchgear chamber and the main engine room with 3 diesel engines.
A building housing the stand-by generator set and associated equipment which could supply electricity to all essential services in the event of a power cut.
A building containing mechanically powered ore crushers or rollers.

Component part of a Flint Mill where flint is calcined before it is brittle enough to be ground in the mill. Ground, burnt flint is used in the production of earthenware pottery, which whitens and strenghens the body.
A mill for crushing flint. Crushed flint was used in the manufacture of pottery in order to whiten and strengthen the body of earthenware pottery.
Building housing machinery used in the production of wooden pulley blocks for the rigging of sailing ships.
A steeply pitched spire whose base is significantly narrower than the tower on which it sits.
A tall, circular, polygonal or square structure rising from a roof, tower, turret etc., tapering to a slender point.
A fan used to create an air current to separate grain from chaff.
Objects used to thresh and winnow crops.
A type of calcining kiln used in arsenic manufacture.
A calciner dating from the early 17th to early 20th centuries, usually made of brick and without moving parts, consisting of a reverberatory furnace, and used for the extraction of arsenic.
A covering for the leg which fits closely.
Clothes worn against the skin and beneath other clothes.
An object which supports or is attached to a curtain.
The residence of a coastguard.
The residence of a lifeboatman.
The residence of a Royal Navy or Merchant Navy officer.
The residence of an admiral of a port.
The residence of a master ropemaker.
The residence of a piermaster.
The residence of a sailor.
The residence of a dock worker.
A purpose-built fisherman's house, eg. a house with a first floor dwelling and ground floor fish store, or a house with a watch tower for spotting shoals.
The residence of a lightkeeper.
The residence of a storekeeper of naval ordnance.
The residence of a master shipwright.
The residences of people associated with the sea.
A dwelling for the keeper of a canal wharf.
Buildings and structures associated with lifting and winding at the site of a mine.
A steam driven winding engine house for raising coal to the surface.
Gothauer Waggonfabrik A.G., based in Gotha, Thuringia (Germany). During World War 2 produced mostly training and light commercial aircraft and troop and freight-carrying gliders.

A World War One German three-crew, twin-engined, long range heavy bomber biplane manufactured by Gothaer Waggonfabrik A.G.. Entering service in 1917, this aircraft incorporated a ventral tunnel allowing the gunner to shoot downwards and to the rear.
Machine readable files suitable for use in a geographic information system (GIS).
Information encoded in a defined structure (for example, lists, tables, and databases), intended to be useful for direct machine processing. [DC] For manual data use index, gazetteer etc.
A craft employed to harpoon whales and bring them in to be processed.
Any vessel involved in the catching or transportation of whales.
A place where money is coined under public authority.
An industrial complex involved in the production of chemicals.
A chemical works producing mordants for the dying industry.
A large building where fish are stored before sale.
A crane used for the refueling of coal-powered vessels.
A school where no fees were charged.
A school for the teaching of poor children, often the recipients of Poor Law relief.
A report written as a result of archaeological monitoring during development work.
A purpose built covered market hall, usually 19th century, although earlier examples do exist, eg. that at Abingdon, Oxfordshire c.1680.
An open space or covered building in which cattle, goods, etc, are displayed for sale.
A market hall where cloth merchants can show their wares and conduct business.
Buildings and structures associated with the process of brewing and malting.
A building, or room within a brewery, where beer or cider undergoes fermentation in vats or tuns.
Use where decoration is present.
Material with evidence of the application of a pigment or dye.
Aspects of a material which result from the modification or use of the material by humans.
Use where evidence of tool marks is present
Use for any material that shows evidence of modification by humans.
An inclined course on top of a projecting sill, cornice etc., designed to throw off rainwater.
An area of a barn, paved or boarded, on which corn was threshed by hand flailing. Use broader site type where known.
A workshop or factory for casting metals.
A workshop or factory where the barrels of cannon are cast.
An excavation used as a means of concealment, protection or both.
Usually a small, two or three man trench, dug as an isolated fieldwork rather than as part of a defensive system. A WWI and WWII feature.
A hospital devoted to the curing or correcting of physical deformities.

Noorduyn Aviation Limited. Formed in 1934 by Mr R.B.C. Noorduyn as a successor to Noorduyn Aircraft Limited, which was formed in 1933. The company's most notable production aircraft was the Norseman transport.

Canadian-built, single-engine, high-wing transport and communications aircraft converted from a civilian model. Metal-framed with fabric covering, saw service in 1944-5. Was capable of being equipped with wheels, floats or skis.
This period follows on from the Bronze Age and is characterized by the use of iron for making tools and monuments such as hillforts and oppida. The Iron Age is taken to end with the Roman invasion.
The earliest subdivision of the Iron Age.
A specialist hospital treating patients with chest disorders and diseases, can be pre sanatoria.
The main vertical beam standing at the centre of a post mill carrying the bearing upon which the body of the mill rotates.
A commercial premises supplying ships with provisions.
A tunnel through which a tramway runs.
Sites and structures used for the transportation of goods and people under roads and rivers, or through hills, etc.
Jewish New Year.
Engineering works specializing in the production and maintenance of non-passenger carrying railway rolling stock.
A flat band carrying a motto.
A continuous series of ornaments within a horizontal moulding.
A complex maze incorporating tall hedges. A popular feature of 16th and 17th century gardens.

A confusing and baffling network of winding and intercommunicating paths, often bordered by high hedges or walls. Some early examples are believed to have had ritual uses. Use more specific type where known.
A structure used for the roasting or drying of chicory.
A structure used for the drying of food using an indirect source of heat.

A family of jet fighters capable of vertical/short takeoff and landing. A subsonic aircraft, later designs adapted for use from aircraft carriers. Built between 1967-2003. Used by the RAF and the Royal Navy.
The flat slab at the top of a capital.
The top part of a column, often decorated.
Organised and documented collection of the records made during the course of a project.
A resource comprising of a group of items the parts of which may be separately described and navigated. [DC]
Use for vessels registered in England
A long stone or metal vessel for dogs to drink water from.
A narrow, open container, usually where food or water for animals is put. Use specific type where known.
An extant settlement which shows evidence of a shift in focus, eg. towards a new road, generally in the form of abandoned buildings or earthworks on the margin furthest from the new focus.
A collection of dwelling-houses and other buildings, usually larger than a hamlet but smaller than a town with a simpler organisation and administration than the latter.

A well concealed structure, usually constructed undergound, intended for use by members of the Special Duties section of the Auxiliary Units (or British Resistance Organization) in the event of invasion.
A hideout containing radio equipment to be used by the Special Duties sections of the Auxiliary Units to send information to the control station for relaying to headquarters.
An engineering works that produces tufting machinery especially for use in the manufacturing of carpets.
A board, wall painting or other structure displaying advice, giving information or directions
A plaque attached onto, or a line incised into, a wall face or other surface to indicate the height of flood water inundation.
A joist that has its end resting in a recess in a transverse beam.
Horizontal timbers laid parallel to each other on which flooring is laid and to which a ceiling is fixed.
Single-engine fighter/dive-bomber. The Fleet Air Arm's first operational monoplane, and its first aircraft to shoot down an enemy during the war.

Two-seat, twin-engined fighter/fighter-bomber designed as a replacement for the Bf110. Of the 600 or so produced, only 258 reached the Luftwaffe due to serious design faults. The ME210 was superseded by the ME410 Hornisse.

Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber: Curtiss P40 Warhawk, known to the RAF as the Tomahawk, later renamed Kittyhawk. Serving from 1941 to 1942, control difficulties in dive attacks impeded bombing accuracy, resulting in use for larger targets only.
A large, powerful aircraft, usually with two or more engines, designed to carry a payload of bombs.

An American turbojet fighter-bomber aircraft. The F-84 was the first production fighter aircraft to utilize in-flight refuelling and the first fighter capable of carrying a nuclear weapon. Designed by Alexander Kartveli, 1946.
A light, high speed aircraft designed to engage in aerial combat and also equipped to carry bombs.
A fighter-bomber designed to deploy its bombs during the latter stage of a diving manoeuvre, thus increasing the accuracy of its targetting.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter-bomber developed from the Typhoon and the abandoned Tornado. Entered service in 1944 with its greatest success being in destroying V.1. flying bombs. One of the fastest World War 2 aircraft, with a top speed of 436 mph.
Twin-engined, single-seat fighter-bomber. Flown by USAAF fighter groups from 1942, excelled as a ground-support fighter. Could carry two 1600 lb bombs or rocket projectiles.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber and ground-attack aircraft. Entered service with the Luftwaffe in mid-1941. Approximately 20,000 were constructed between 1941 and the end of the war.
Single-engine, single-seat fighter-bomber. Designed to replace the Hurricane as an interceptor, excelled as a rocket-projectile-firing ground-attack fighter. Entered RAF service in 1941.
Twin-engined fighter-bomber. All metal in construction, entered service in 1940. Supported bombing operations and participated in attacks on France, but not widely used due to engine faults.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber. Fitted with eight fixed forward-firing machine guns in the wings, plus two 1000lb bombs or six rocket projectiles.
Single-seat fighter-bomber with a single, midships engine and tricycle landing gear. After proving a failure as an air-combat fighter, was used mainly in the ground attack role.
Mark 7 or the seventh variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
Used to identify the variations of an aircraft. Index with Manufacturer, Form and Function.
Fine grained, iron rich, liassic limestone, found in Dorset, Somerset, Oxfordshire, Northamptonshire, Leicestershire and Rutland.
Collective term for the building limestones formed during the Lower Jurassic period.
A round hut, similar to a CHARCOAL BURNERS HUT, associated with forest industry. The bark was later used in the tanning process.

A building of basic construction, usually smaller in size than a house and constructed from a variety of materials such as mud, turf, branches, wood, brick, concrete or metal. Use more specific type where known.
A pattern used to create a consistent shape for an object, often hollow and reusable.
A mould in which an ingot is made.
A container for holding or pouring liquids, usually having a handle or lip.
A jug with little or no discernible neck and an even, convex profile form rim to base, which are roughly equal in diameter. (Source: MPRG)
A round container open at the top, usually to hold liquids.
A bowl adapted by the addition of a short tubular spout applied just below the rim.
A container with a religious, ritual or funerary use.
A container for holy relics.
A room before a larger room which is often used as a waiting room.

Includes the processes for investigating and recording historic buildings. Differences in terminology may apply to the recording of buildings due to the approach taken. As such, concepts in this hierarchy may be country specific.
The process of investigating and recording historic buildings for the purposes of historical understanding.

A comprehensive written report drawing together the evidence from the recording programme, archive research and consideration of the historical and landscape context supported by measured plans and elevations and a thorough photographic survey.

A preliminary assessment of a building or structure, often carried out as pre-application work, including an archive assessment, a general description of the structure, photographs and an annotated ground plan.
A descriptive account of the building supported by detailed archive research, annotated measured plans and elevations and a detailed photographic record.
A written description of the structure including archive assessment supported by drawn and photographic evidence including a ground plan.
A written, drawn and photographic record, including a ground plan and elevations to produce an adequate record of the structure.
A reinforced concrete block designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle. Use more specific type where known.

Blocks of solid concrete, in the form of cylinders usually 2 feet across x 2 feet 6 inches or 3 feet high. Cylinders were mainly used in road blocks intended to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion.
A building in which hoops (for masts) were heated.
A wooden or metal structure covering a shipbuilding slip way.
Building housing machinery used in the production of wooden pulley blocks for the rigging of sailing ships.
A building for the storage, repair and maintenance of chains for lighthouses, lightships and lightbouys.
A craft or repair workshop in a boat yard, harbour or naval dockyard.
Used for the laying out and marking of the smaller parts of a ship prior to construction.
A workshop with equipment for the making and repair of ships' rigging.
A light, mostly wooden errected structure serving as workshop for the building, storage, repair and maintenance of boats.
A building where masts are made and stored.
A place where sails are manufactured.
A naval dockyard building used for the manufacture of flags.
A place where dockyard craftsmen both design and build ships.
A roughly hemispherical mound constructed primarily of stones, normally containing or covering one or more human burials. The mound may be surrounded and partly retained by a low stone kerb.
A circle of spaced upright boulders emerging from a low, hemispherical, stony mound. The boulders may lean outwards due to pressure from the cairn material.
A building or wing of a large house in which the servants would live and carry out some of their duties.
A workshop where wooden brushes are manufactured on a small scale.
A workshop in which products are made using wood and timber.
A container used in the preparartion of food.
A shallow tray or dish used for baking food.
