Objects used to measure time, distance, weight, number or natural forces.

A device used to slow the fall of a person or an object from a great height. When open it consists of a large umberella like sheet with wires or ropes converging from the edge to a harness attached to the lower end.
A calculating table or frame, specifically one in which balls slide upon wires. Used for the mechanical solution of arithmetical problems.
A building used for the administration of a squadron.
An administrative building used to organize and co-ordinate the activities of members of the armed forces.
A hoist suspended from a girder within the roof of a building or workshop.
A crane suspended from running rails in the roof of an engineering workshop or similar establishment.
A crane suspended from running rails in the roof of an engineering workshop or similar establishment.
A hoist suspended from a girder within the roof of a building or workshop.
Mark 6 or the sixth variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
Second World War allied patrol-bomber built by Lockheed Vega, a Lockheed subsidiary. This aircraft was a military development of the Lodestar, USAF designation B-34.
A short blade set at an angle in a slot between two handles.
A farmstead where the main range of working buildings are attached in-line and form a long row often facing a series of yards.
A farmstead where the buildings and yards are loosely arranged, with no focal yard. Use more specific type where known.
A farmstead where the working buildings are arranged around a yard.
A farmstead where the farmhouse and working buildings are attached and in-line. They can comprise the extension of linear farmsteads.
A farmstead, often of linear plan, where the working buildings are placed opposite and parallel to the house and attached working buildings with a relatively narrow space between.
A medieval high status farmstead, acting as the centre of the estate, directly controlled by the lord and used for the benefit of his household and dependents.
A farmstead where the house and working buildings are attached and in-line. Can include Bastles, Longhouses and Laithe houses.
The homestead of a farm consisting of a farmhouse and working farm buildings, with yards, other working areas and usually a garden to the house.
A rectangular pillbox with an enclosed square plan section for three light machine guns and an adjacent open area housing a mounting for a light anti-aircraft weapon. Designed by DFW branch 3.
Pictorial, painted or drawn material such as slides, drawings, photos, plans excluding cartographic.
A round container open at the top, usually to hold liquids.
A bowl with straight sides which are at an approximate right angle to the base, i.e. a roughly cylindrical shape. (Source: MPRG)
A hall licensed for musical performances, singing, dancing and other entertainments, exclusive of dramatic performance.
Buildings and structures associated with the performance of musical, oratory and dance events.
An end scraper made on a flake that is wider than it is long. (Source: SARC)
An end scraper which has a retouched end that is concave in form. (Source: SARC)
A flint blade or flake with retouch on one or both ends.

An end scraper which has a retouched end that is straight in form. If the tool blank is a blade or flake, and the retouch is abrupt retouch rather than scraper retouch then use either Truncated blade or Truncated flake. (Source: SARC)
An end scraper that has a retouched end which is convex in form. (Source: SARC)
A building housing an engine. Use specific type where known.
Steam engine, usually, driving a centrifugal fan to provide an air blast for a blast furnace.
A stone or platform on which lumps of ore are manually broken up.
A two dimensional image using paint applied to the surface of a ceiling.
A floor composed of small cubes (tesserae) of variously coloured materials (eg tile, stone, marble). In the Roman period, mosaics often depict a religious theme or symbol.
A painting executed directly onto a wall.
Objects forming fragments or parts of a building's fabric, structures and associated services, eg drain pipes. Where an object is a fixture or fitting use the separate class.
Northern hemisphere mean summer intertropical convergence zone; note this is prepended with the last 300 years of IntCal13
Southern hemisphere mean summer intertropical convergence zone; note this is prepended with the last 300 years of SHCal13
Between 40¡N and mean summer intertropical convergence zone; note this is prepended with the last 300 years of IntCal13
Between 40¡N and mean summer intertropical convergence zone; note this is prepended with the last 300 years of IntCal04
North of 40¡N; note this is prepended with the last 300 years of IntCal13
Southern hemisphere; note this is prepended with the last 300 years of SHCal04
Southern hemisphere (not in mean summer intertropical convergence zone); note this is prepended with the last 300 years of SHCal13
Northern hemisphere mean summer intertropical convergence zone; note this is prepended with the last 300 years of IntCal04
North of 40¡N; note this is prepended with the last 300 years of IntCal04
A hospital where patients would bathe daily in the sea or in indoor salt-water swimming baths.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter. Entered service in 1943 as a land-based fighter. Converted to a carrierborne fighter in 1944 for use by US Navy and Fleet Air Arm. Mostly saw action in the Pacific and Far East.
A protected building used for the storage of explosives and other pyrotechnic equipment and designed to Air Ministry drawing number 2647/37.
A building used for the storage of explosives of a non-military function, eg. mining explosives, signal explosivres etc.
A place in which gunpowder and other explosives are stored in large quantities.
A metal collar or cap to strengthen the end of tubes, sticks, shafts, etc. Use with specific object name where known eg spear and ferrule.
Grassland fertilized by allowing floodwater to cover it in winter.
A group or complex of fields which appear to form a coherent whole. Use more specific type where known.
A specialist hospital where medical and surgical dental treatment takes place.
A metal spur fitted to the leg of a fighting cock as an aid in fighting.
Flat bottomed, two-masted Dutch coastal vessel of the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries. Sometimes used as an English term for fluit, also a flat-bottomed vessel.
Goods, usually foodstuffs, which have been sealed inside canisters, usually made of tin or steel, to preserve them.
General merchandise and saleable commodities. Use more specific type where known.
Meat precooked and then sealed in cans made from steel, tin or aluminium plate to preserve it.
Use for vessels registered in Belgium.
A building or group of buildings, incorporating radio masts, built to intercept radio transmissions from enemy vessels and aircraft during WWI and WWII.
Specially designed/fitted carriers of crew and/or supplies to offshore oil platforms.
A vessel used for transporting passengers or goods.

A place of worship for Presbyterians, a movement who started off attempting to reform Anglicanism before breaking away in 1660. Sometimes referred to as moderate puritans, they joined with the Congregationalists to form the United Reformed church in 1972.
A place of worship for Welsh Presbyterians. Formerly known as Calvinistic Methodists, the Presbyterian Church of Wales separated from the established church in 1811.
Ore that has been burnt.
An unprocessed mineral, collected for the extraction of metals or other substances contained within the mineral.
A round container, open and wide at the top with sides sloping inwards toward the bottom.

Any object, often made of ceramic or 'porcelain' used for the purposes of personal cleansing, especially fittings such as toilets, baths and basins. May survive as fragments in the archaeological record. Use more specific term where known.
A building with malt kilns for the malting of grains and with other similar equipment for brewing work.
A gap which allows air to circulate.
A container used to serve drinks and liquids.
Container with a handle, spout and narrow neck.
Programmes of research that seek to identify the archaeological and/or architectural significance of a site or landscape.

An overview of the historical and architectural development, character and heritage assets of a settlement or area. An HAA may result in the creation, at varying levels of intensity, of individual site-based records informed by area context.
An inlet in the banks of a navigable river, often lined with brick and gated, into which boats can be drawn for repair etc.
A floating structure consisting of two walls standing on pontoon tanks, the latter of which can be flooded to receive a vessel and then pumped out until the pontoon deck and the ship are dry.
An artificial area of open water, enclosed by masonry and fitted with dock gates in which ships can be repaired, loaded/unloaded or berthed.
An artificial area of open water, situated on a river, enclosed by masonry and fitted with dock gates in which ships can be repaired, loaded/unloaded or berthed.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with water transport.
An artificial area of open water, situated on a canal, enclosed by masonry and fitted with dock gates in which ships can be repaired, loaded/unloaded or berthed.
A large, watertight enclosure in which the water is maintained at the high-tide level so that vessels remain constantly afloat in them.
Traditionally a dock where cambering, the bending of beams for shipbuilding, took place. Now used for a small dock.
A dock with gates which open for access for some hours before and after high water.
A stone-faced enclosure, with entrance closed by a floatable caisson or by gates, which can be pumped dry for inspection, maintenance, or repair of the hull or underwater fittings of a ship or ships.
The residence of a coastguard.
The residences of people associated with the sea.
A holding tank/pen on a river or seashore for raising and preserving fish and/or for catching them easily.
An area where fish are naturally present, eg. part of a river.
Scotland
Scotland
Scotland
Scotland
Scotland
A large, luxuriously appointed hotel.
A large building used for the accommodation of paying travellers and guests.
A specialist hospital for the medical treatment of patients suffering from epilepsy. Originally epilepsy was seen as a mental illness.
Boulton Paul Aircraft, Ltd., formed in 1934 to take over the Aircraft Department of Boulton & Paul, Ltd.
British single-engine, two-seat night fighter. Originally intended as a day fighter, but withdrawn and converted in August 1940, this was the first fighter to incorporate a power-driven gun turret.
An iron rod with both ends sharpened and turned down, used for holding timbers together.
An object to fasten, bind or join one item to another.
A three sided or U-shaped metal fastener on which the ends are pointed.
A type of staple used to hold two object together.
Any brooch with the pin sprung or hinged at one end and the catchplate at the other end of a curved or flat bow. Can be one or two piece construction.
A mid-1st century AD brooch influenced by the Thistle type, commonly with projections on the upper bow and widening to a triangular plate, often described as a fantail, below.
A building owned by a constituency political party which provides a meeting place for local political activities and also provides entertainment facilities for its members and guests.

A French airliner produced in 1925. A four-engined biplane developed from the Bleriot 115 and 135 but larger than these. Two were built for Air Union (the Paris-London route). Both crashed with fatalaties in 1926 (Kent).
An aircraft used for the transportation of troops, supplies, vehicles or passengers.
Use as an external architectural feature only.
Use more specific term where known.
Transport vessel, usually a hired vessel of mercantile origin, used for the exchange of prisoners-of-war; sometimes, specifically a hospital ship with such prisoners.
A library where books may be consulted but not taken away.
A building, room or suite of rooms where books, or other materials, are classified by subject and stored for use by the library's members.

Originally ordered as land based dive-bombers, with 950 being delivered to the RAF, none are known to have flown operationally, instead apparently serving as target tugs. Bermuda was the name given to the Brewster SB2A Buccaneer in RAF service.
An aircraft used for the towing of targets.
An instrument where vibrating air is confined by a tube. Use narrower terms where known.
An instrument which creates a buzzing noise.
A piece of wood attached to a thong that makes a roaring sound when the thong is whirled.
A musical instrument producing sound by air vibrating.
A carved head of Iron Age or Roman date, with uncertain use.
A three dimensional representation usually done in wood, ivory or stone.
A three dimensional representation of an object, person or animal.
A by-product created through a manufacturing process. This does not include the production of tools, for this use tool by product.
A by-product usually from the smelting process.
A public house for the lodging and entertainment of travellers, etc.
An inn, with an integral courtyard, for the lodging and entertainment of travellers. Often with open galleried wings overlooking the courtyard.
Unspecified. Use specific type where known.
Platform or structure used for viewing performances.
A levelled area of ground, circular in shape, used as the base on which a monument was built.Sometimes raised, a platform is often the sole surviving evidence for a monument.

A site where a building once stood as identified by a level area of ground, often compacted or made from man-made materials. Use only where specific function is unknown, otherwise use more specific term.
A raised platform or stage for public speaking or conducting an orchestra. Also a platform for supporting cameras during filming.
A shady cavern built as a garden feature. In the 18th century it usually took the form of an artificial rocky cave or apartment decorated with stalactites and shells in a wild part of the grounds.
A grotto decorated with shells, sometimes a room in a house, sometimes a detached building.

A bladed wheel attached to the rear, and at right angles to the main sails, of a windmill. Connected to winding gear, the fantail would catch the wind when it changed direction, allowing the mill to move automatically into the wind.
A plot of land longer than it is wide, can include any structures on it. Typical of medieval towns.
Muslim funeral mosque.
A Muslim temple or place of worship.

skos:Concept.skos:definition: 100 links, 4 rods or 1⁄10 of a furlong. The distance between the two wickets on a cricket pitch.

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: Twin-engined monoplane that served the RAF as an advanced trainer and flying ambulance. Mk. I featured a gun turret and served for gunnery and bombing-crew training. Subsequent versions used for pilot, radio and navigation training.
Photomechanical or photolithographical reproduction process representing a photographic image as a series of dots or lines.
Pasture to which animals were driven for grazing, with associated temporary huts for domestic or agricultural use.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of crucibles.
Goods and equipment used to supply a navy.
An object placed to mark the site of a grave.
Use for structural objects within or connected to a place of worship, eg font. For structures, use a monuments thesaurus.

An anti aircraft battery armed with 3 inch rockets with a ceiling of 22,000 feet. Both single and multiple launchers were designed. Single launchers being used to defend vulnerable points such as coastal batteries with multiple launchers defending town.
A vessel comprising two or more dishes, generally of small size, joined together. There may be one or more handles of varying forms. (Source: MPRG)
A dish with straight or convex sides that turn inwards, forming an acute basal angle. (Source: MPRG)
A dish comprising three or more lobes, usually equally spaced. There may be one or more animal or other figures inside the base and two or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
A container used to serve food from.

A wide, shallow, straight-sided, circular DISH, with concentric divisions, formed by vertical partitions, or by concentric grooving around the base. The use is uncertain but the name implies it was designed to hold feed for domestic fowl. (Source: MPRG)

A type of dish specifically designed to catch the juices from roasting meat. The dish may be oval, semi-circular, rectangular or wedge-shaped. Usually has one or two handles located on one long side and a lip at one or both short sides. (Source: MPRG)
A dish adapted by the addition of a pedestal base. (Source: MPRG)
A container used for holding or serving food, especially an open shallow container.
A round, oval or rectangular straight-sided dish, divided into two or more units or compartments of varying sizes by vertical slab partitions. (Source: MPRG)
Clothing worn on the foot.
Type of footwear which covers a minimum of the foot and ankle.
An aircraft used for the transportation of troops, supplies, vehicles or passengers.

American troop and supply-glider constructed from steel tube and fabric-covered wood, with a hinged nose to allow loading and unloading of troops or light vehicles. Also known as the Haig, this was the only US glider to see combat service.
A mill for the removal by mechanical means of the dried wood and seeds of the flax and cotton plants after retting. The resulting 'tow' is then spun into linen and cotton respectively.
The Douglas Aircraft Company, Inc., established in 1920, reorganized in 1928. Produced such notable aircraft as the Dakota.
Three-seat tactical support aircraft. Entering service with the US 9th Air Force in 1944, the Invader had a bomb load of 4,000 lbs and was later used as a conventional medium bomber.
The dwelling and workshop of a framework knitter.
Three storey house with a topshop; machinery powered by shafting through the upper floor.
A lodging house for apprentices learning a trade or profession. This accommodation was often provided in lieu of wages.
The residence of a miller, often attached to a mill.
The residence of a clothier.
The residence and small-scale workshop of a hosier.
Industrial worker's house which has been purpose built by an employer, as opposed to the workshop houses used by artisans.
The residence of a lacemaker.
The residence of a cloth cutter.
The residence and sometimes workplace of industrial workers.
A type of clothier's house, consisting of TOPSHOP and dwelling, used for hand-weaving of textiles.
A purpose-built dwelling for the supervisor of a factory, mine or other industrial complex.
The residence of a glover.
The dwelling of a blacksmith, nailer, sword cutler, etc, often adjacent to, or containing, a BLACKSMITHS WORKSHOP.
A crude, stone-built shelter for persons involved in lime production and the processing of lime burning.
Based on a typical 18ft span, 40ft long temporary brick hut but with two bay windows in the front elevation, one for the watch office and one for the chief instructor.

Sites, buildings, structures etc associated with the civil administration of settlements & enforcement of the laws of the land. Includes local & central government, settlements granted by the crown or ruling administration does not manorial settlements.
A building or building complex where municipal offices and other public buildings are situated.
A light, high speed aircraft equipped specifically to engage in night combat.
Developed from the ill-fated ME210, the ME410 Hornisse entered service in May 1943. Although underpowered as a day fighter the ME410 saw service over the UK as a night fighter from 1943-45.
A site where clay is mined from the ground.
A factory or site for the manufacture of food stuffs from raw ingredients.
A site where products containing sugar or honey, such as cakes, sweets, crystallized fruits or jam, were manufactured.

Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of pottery. Use only for sites where there is evidence of pottery manufacture but no specific monument, otherwise use more specific term.
An 18th century cottage with a pottery kiln attached.
A knife with a hinged blade which folds into a slot in the handle.
A stone tool, often only polished on the edge.
A discoidal flint tool often has a ground edge.
A leather working tool.
Includes equipment for the consumption of food.
A tool used in the separation of fibres from the bark in flax working.
A cutting blade with handle used for food preparation and consumption.
A small knife used in surgery.
A knife that is used for circumcision.
A small, sharp bladed knife for sharpening pens, originally sheathed, now the blades fold.
A knife designed to be used for pruning plants.
A flint tool with a convex top and flat base.
Ore containing high levels of lead, eg. galena.
A place where processed wood is sold.
An enclosed piece of land adjoining a house.

A decorative design or illustration, often an anthropomorphic or geometrical image, carved into a stone surface, such as a cave wall or free-standing stone. Usually, though not always, of Prehistoric date.
Refers to art, whether carving or painting, applied to free -standing stones or cave walls.
Art applied in pigment to rock wether in the form of a free-standing stone or the walls of a cave.
An object used in lighting a fire, lamp, oven, candle etc.
A staff with a fork at one end which would be used to hold a lighted slow match which was used to fire a canon.
An aeroplane with two wings, or planes, placed one above the other either side of the fuselage.
A single-seat, biplane fighter. One of the last open cockpit types to see widespread service with the RAF, equipping 10 squadrons and, at one point, 70% of the Home Defence fighter force.
A pit filled with rocks and metal, designed to be fired with an explosive charge.
A tool used to pound, crush or beat an object.
A pouch for containing tobacco.
Containers identified by function rather than by form.
A container for the storage of tobacco.
An industrial complex involved in the production of chemicals.
A chemical works engaged in the production of the coal tar derivative phenol, a chemical used for the manufacture of explosives during WWI.
The open space surrounded by a cloister.
A factory where aircraft are assembled.
A factory where aircraft engines are assembled.
A structure used to test the aerodynamics of aircraft or vehicles.
A factory for the manufacture of rocket motors, both for civil and military use.
A site specializing in the manufacture of parts for the Aerospace industry.
A site used for the functional testing of aircraft and their components.
A building used for fabricating balloon and airship envelopes.
Construction works for the production of rigid or dirigible airships.
Sites used for the manufacture of aircraft.
A roof with a bow-shaped, segmental timber truss which has the space between its members filled by a lattice of crossing diagonal rods.
A roof constructed of horizontal tiebeams and curved trusses.
The exterior upper covering, and its supporting structure, of a building.
Including ground in current use for burials and legally consecrated ground, e.g. graveyard, chapel-ground etc.
A large tank used for soaking alumina-bearing shale in water and chemicals, the initial stage in the alum-making process.
A large mounted gun, now disused and placed in a prominent position as a piece of street furniture or as a "feature".
Structures erected on or near a public highway.
A building used for the storage of fish.
A whole male figure used in place of a column to support an entablature.
The part of the wall that supports a pitched roof at the end of the roof.
A gable without a roof behind it.
A temporary fence of boards, often enclosing a building on which posters and bills are attached.
A container filled with musket balls, metal fragments, nails etc. Designed to kill or maim the enemy at a close range.
Articles used in charging guns and ordnance.
Cube-shaped shot.
An instrument, usually consisting of a disc and pointer, formerly used to make astronomical measurements, especially of the altitudes of celestial bodies and as an aid in navigation.
An instrument for viewing or measuring information on heavenly bodies.
A weekend retreat for Royal parties and others, when hunting in the Royal forests, or as a viewing station for the chase.
A type of guildhall belonging primarily to the London livery companies, but also found elsewhere in the country, so called because of the livery worn by members of the guild.
A box used for storage or shipping.
This does not include food or liquid storage.
A stone with a cross carved into the surface.
An aircraft, often fitted with cameras, intended to fly over enemy territory to ascertain its strategic features and/or the position and strength of any military presence.

Six-crew, medium-range, twin-engined reconnaissance flying-boat. Entered service with 209 Squadron in 1939 but, due to design and operation problems, saw little action and was not produced in large numbers.
A factory manufacturing electrical cables.
A factory or plant used for the manufacture of electrical machinery or components.
A small building housing pilot's and locker rooms with flight offices and a watch office. The only known example was built at Tangmere.

A bomber designed to operate with medium bombloads over medium distances.The medium bomber was generally considered to be any design that delivered about 4,000 lb (1.8 t) over ranges of about 1,500 to 2,000 miles (2,400 to 3,200 km).

A jet-powered tailless delta wing high-altitude strategic bomber plane, operated by the RAF from 1956 until 1984. Typically armed with nuclear weapons but capable of conventional bombing missions. Used as a nuclear deterrent in the Cold War.
A progressive development of the DO17, the twin-engined DO217 entered service in 1941. The DO217 saw service as a bomber over the UK and took part in the 'Baedecker' raids of 1942.
High speed, short to medium-range bomber, usually powered by two engines.

Originally designed as a wood and steel bomber-reconnaissance aircraft, subsequent variations served as special transports, glider tugs and paratroop carriers. Featured a tricycle-style undercarriage.
A light, high speed aircraft designed to engage in aerial combat and also equipped to carry bombs.

Long-range, four-engine reconnaissance-bomber. Initially produced as a transport, converted and used against Allied convoys in the Channel and the Atlantic. Also served as a VIP transport, one of which was the Immelmann III: Hitler's personal aircraft.

A two-seat, single-engine bomber. Fast, versatile and well armed, but with a fuel tank poorly placed between pilot and gunner, was considered to be the best day bomber of the First World War. Later entered civil service.
American A-20 twin-engined, light, day bomber. Some supplied to the RAF and known as the Boston I. Subsequent variations adapted to night flying and re-christened the Havoc.
Second World War allied patrol-bomber built by Lockheed Vega, a Lockheed subsidiary. This aircraft was a military development of the Lodestar, USAF designation B-34.
Developed from the DH4, featured the pilot and gunner cockpits in closer proximity, but suffered from engine reliability problems. Also known as the Ninak, saw service from 1918 to 1931.
A single-engine, two-crew biplane day bomber and general purpose aircraft, developed from the IIIF (some of which were converted into Gordons) and first flown in 1931.

A single-engine dive-bomber, the JU87 was very successful during the invasions of Poland and France but suffered heavy losses during the Battle of Britain. Withdrawn from NW Europe in 1941 for use in the Mediterranean and on the Eastern Front.
Single-engine, two-seat tractor bomber and reconnaissance aircraft. Entered service in 1916 and, during 1917 and 1918, equipped nine RFC squadrons in its reconnaissance role.
A single-engine, heavy, long range, three to five-crew day bomber. Served only with 99 Squadron RAF, 1924-5.

Twin-engined maritime-reconnaissance bomber adapted from pre-war American airliners, the A-28 and A-29, evident from the row of portholes along its fuselage. Entered service with RAF Coastal Command just before the outbreak of World War Two.

A streamlined, twin-engined bomber, the DO17 entered service in 1937 with the Condor Legion, having started life as a high-speed mail and passenger transport aircraft, a role for which it was ill-suited due to the narrowness of the fuselage.
A large, powerful aircraft, usually with two or more engines, designed to carry a payload of bombs.
Twin-engined, four-crew bomber. Wooden framed, with linen covering, entered service in 1924, equipping several RAF squadrons.
Long-range, usually four-engined, bomber designed to carry a large bomb payload.
Aircraft grouped according to their function.
A workshop in which saggars - fire clay boxes to protect ware from direct action of flame and gases during firing - were manufactured.
An image of a deity used as a focus for worship, usually used for non Christian images.
An alcoholic beverage distilled from grain or malt and usually flavoured with juniper berries.
Usually distilled alcohollic drink but also used for liquids where a substance is in solution with alcohol.
A steam engine that uses the same steam successively to drive pistons in high and then low pressure cylinders.
A high speed, single acting compound steam engine with centrally placed piston valves controlling the distribution of steam.
A place of worship for Methodists, a movement founded by John Wesley. Following his death in 1791 there were many secessions.

A place of worship for members of the United Methodist Free Church. Formed in 1857 by the amalgamation of the Methodist Reform Church and the Wesleyan Association they later became part of the United Methodist Church in 1907.
A group of buildings or works where the evaporation and crystallization of sodium aluminium sulphate solution is performed.
A large tank used for soaking alumina-bearing shale in water and chemicals, the initial stage in the alum-making process.
Fine grained, yellow/buff to grey/black coloured sedimentary rock.
Single-engine, spruce and plywood, fabric-covered training and communications low-wing monoplane. Served from 1939 to 1950.
A factory where aircraft are assembled.
A factory where seaplanes are manufactured.
A specialist unit within a hospital complex. It may be a separate building or sometimes linked by a corridor or covered walkway to a main building.
An area within a hospital used for the isolation of patients. Patients were isolated if they had an infectious disease or suffered from a psychiatric illness.
Use with other minerals extracted and MINE where relevant, eg. ZINC MINE.
An excavation made in the earth for the purpose of digging out metallic ores, coal, salt, or precious stones etc. Use specific type where known.
A hole occupied by a timber post or the void remaining after its removal, usually with packing.
The space occupied by or left where a post has been.
A protected building used for the storage of explosives and other pyrotechnic equipment and designed to Air Ministry drawing number 2647/37.

A room where surgical operations are performed. Originally in the form of a room with a raised table surrounded by tiered seating from where students could watch an operation or disection be performed.
A circular frame or disc arranged to revolve on an axle and used to facilitate the motion of a vehicle.
Parts which make up a vehicle.
Any of the plants of the grass family, Graminae, cultivated for their edible seeds, especially corn, wheat etc.
The seed of a cereal plant used in the manufacture of foodstuffs.
A jug with straight vertical sides and roughly equal rim and base diameters. (Source: MPRG)
A hard, igneous rock formed from the cooling of molten volcanic magma.
Coarse basaltic rock.

Geologically sandstone consists of particles of quartz naturally cemented together by either silica, calcium or iron. It is this geological composition that accounts for the varying colours and grain sizes found in the many building sandstones.
A coarse grained metamorphic rock that is composed maily of green, brown or black amphibole minerals and plagioclase feldspar. Amphiboles are usually members of the hornblende group.
Natural inorganic substance possessing a definite chemical composition in a crystalline form. See MINERAL Class List for narrow terms.
Medium to coarse grained metamorphic rock, colour being determined by its dominant mineral. Often used for floor and wall cladding.
A brownish-red mineral commonly used as a semi-precious gemstone. A variety of the silica mineral chalcedony coloured by impurities of iron oxide.
Soft, white, porous sedimentary rock, a form of limestone composed of the mineral calcite.
A sedimantary rock composed of fine grained clay particles. Flaky mudstone is called shale.
A hard, translucent variety of jade which is rarer than the other varieties of nephrite as a result considered to be the best and very desirable.
Rock of definite form and size, usually artificially shaped.
Geologist's term for any dark coloured, slightly metamorphosed igneous rock. Index with specific stone type where given.
An ornamental green stone of the mineral nephrite.
Conglomerate consisting of rounded flint pebbles held together in a natural silica and sand cement.
A sedimentary rock primarily composed of silt sized particles.

Collective term for a hard, fine grained, dark coloured metamorphic rock, which splits easily; hence its common use as a roofing and flooring material, and a functional description for any rectangular, sheet, roofing material.
Sedimentary rock consisting mainly of calcium carbonate. Varying in grain size, colour and hardness, quarried and used throughout the country.
A hard, coarse grained, durable igneous rock. Can be used decoratively or as a main material. Found throughout the country.

Collective name for, in a true geological sense, a metamorphosed limestone, eg. Carrara marble, and, in the British sense any decorative stone that will take a polish, eg. Purbeck marble. In the latter's case index with specific stone type where given
Soft, very fine grained, dark coloured, sedimentary rock which splits easily.
Originally designed as a light bomber but diverted for use as a high speed target tug to replace out-dated biplanes.
Hawker Aircraft, Ltd., established 1933 to succeed the H. G. Hawker Engineering Co., Ltd., which had been formed in 1920 as the result of the voluntary liquidation of the renowned Sopwith concern.
Report prepared by a specialist in a particular field, often as a contribution to a wider project.
Includes interim, research, specialist reports on a specific topic.
Unpublished written work such as manuscripts, dissertations etc. not disseminated to the public.

Controlled intrusive fieldwork which examines, records and interprets archaeological deposits, features and structures and, as appropriate, retrieves artefacts and ecofact remains within a specified area or site on land or within the inter-tidal zone.

Controlled investigation, recording and removal of archaeological deposits according to the principles of strategraphic excavation. The size of an open area can range from holes to examine pile foundations to extensive trenches of 100 square meters.
An oil-fuelled internal combustion engine, developed in the late 19th century, and usually made as a stationary, horizontal unit.

An engine or prime mover, in which a mixture of air and fuel is ignited inside a closed cylinder, and the resulting explosion drives a piston to the opposite end of the cylinder, its movement turning a crankshaft via suitable mechanical parts.
German single-engine, four-seat maritime patrol and reconnaissance flying-boat. In production between 1934 and 1940, the DO18 was replaced by the three engined DO24.
Ornament often with a hinged pin and catch, worn fastened to clothing.

A highly decorated Anglo-Saxon Long Brooch, often made of silver or bronze, worn by women. Contemporary with the Cruciform Brooch, it features a large, square head plate and usually three rounded foot-terminals.
An Anglo-Saxon cruciform Long Brooch, often ornamented with knobs across and terminating its crossbar and head, and frequently with its foot shaped into a zoomorphic motif.
A small, often of about two inches or less in length, version of the Long Brooch usually made of less expensive materials than other brooch types and frequently worn in pairs.
An Anglo-Saxon brooch type dating from the 5th to 7th centuries AD and influenced by the Crossbow brooch, featuring a sprung pin and a head plate.
A tool used in etching which is the use of acid to breakdown parts of a metal plate in order to create an image.
A barge with a spritsail rig commonly found on the River Thames.
Flat-bottomed barge with shallow draft adapted for carrying bulk cargoes among the shoals of the Thames Estuary; usually spritsail-rigged, though other rigs were permissible.
A wooden, metal or stone strip attached to the floor between the door posts in a doorway covering the joint between two floor surfaces.
A magistrates court sitting for the purpose of holding trials for children and young people. Replaced the juvenile court, following legislation, in 1991.
A place, hall or chamber in which justice is administered.
A raised carving.
A large ship's boat powered by oars and or an engine.
A barge with a lugsail rig commonly found on the River Thames in the late 19th century. Also a general term applied to the family of Deal luggers.
Craft intended for recreation and not intended for any commercial use.
A vessel with equipment for processing dead marine life whilst still at sea.
A steam vessel propelled by a pair of paddle wheels amidships or a single wheel astern, driven by a reciprocating engine.
Any vessel operated by Trinity house masters and brethren in the maintenance of lighthouses, lightships, buoys and other navigation aids.
A vessel fitted with a catapult for launching an aircraft.
A boat used as private or domestic living accomodation.

Generic name for a vessel used for work rather than for recreation, transportation, or military purposes. The vessels include tugs, barges, landing craft, dredgers and standby safety vessels. Use only were the exact type of vessel is unknown.
The class term, use more specific terms.
Vessel fitted with broadcasting equipment and used for off-shore radio programme transmission.
Cargo vessel or warship captured by a warship or privateer of a hostile nation in time of war, usually taken into that nation�s mercantile, privateering or naval service.
Generic name for a small steam or power boat often carried on board a larger vessel.
The characteristics of a sailing vessel where her type is determined by her masts and sails.
A craft which is equipped for and performs hydrographic surveys.

An artificial harbour, constructed using prefabricated, concrete caissons, floating breakwaters and blockships, which were towed across the channel and assembled off the coast of Normandy to assist the allied forces after the D-Day landings in June 1944.
A hulk or obsolete vessel filled with cement or similar material and scuttled to block an entrance to a port or anchorage, usually as a defensive measure.
A steam vessel propelled by rotating propellers called screws.
Vehicle either adapted, or purpose-built, to operate on both land and sea, for example a tank or DUKW.
A vessel or craft used for catching or harvesting marine life by a variety of methods, use specific method where known.

Any boat used to transfer crew from shore to an offlying vessel. May also carry the catch from a fishing boat to shore. Used as special boats by the Royal National Lifeboat Institution for conveying crew from the beach to a moored lifeboat.
An old ship converted for a variety of uses for which it is not required to move under its own power.
A vessel equipped with sealed tanks for transporting sewage and dumping it in deep water.

Small, light, fast, all-purpose craft designed primarily for inland use. Generally flat-bottomed, often with rocker; sharp bow, sharp or transom stern, lapstrake or carvel planking. Propelled by oars, sails or motor. Used for fishing and leisure.
A ship that is built and primarily intended for war.
A vessel, purpose-built or requisitioned, used for patrolling inland or coastal waters, e.g. Coastguard and Customs vessels.
A craft used to deepen shipping channels, harbours and other water courses.
A relatively small and heavily built vessel equipped with large engines. Used for towing ships at sea or manouevring them in tight spaces.
A flat bottomed boat or hollow float of which a number are used to support a temporary bridge over a river.
Oared fighting ship with ancillary sails.
A craft built with the intention of demonstrating or advertising a novel design feature.

A freelance boat used off the south and east coasts of England to provide passing ships with pilots, supplies, new anchors and other gear. Some helped sailing ships and barges get underway. Generally lug-rigged. Also used for fishing. Half decked.
A flat floating framework of planks or other materials used for supporting or carrying persons or goods.

Any vessel in the service of one of the historical or modern agencies concerned with the prevention of inbound or outbound smuggling: namely the Preventive Service, the Coastguard, or the Customs and Excise. Use more specific term.
The largest boat belonging to a sailing vessel, and usually the means of escape from a sinking ship; powered by oars.
A ship used for laying cables (often telephone cables) along the sea bed.
A buoy with a compartment into which shipwrecked mariners could climb to await rescue.
All vessels, use more specific type where known.
A private fighting ship under a letter of marque or financed by subscribers, shareholders or individuals.
Vessels of various types used specifically for providing an initial training in seamanship.
A hospital for the treatment of venereal disease.

Medieval Fenland ditched field system where the land is divided into strips for agricultural production. The strips are separated by hand-dug wide shallow drainage ditches with the spoil thrown up to create a dryer ridge.

An Iron Age round defended house, found mainly in the north and west of Scotland. Brochs have a tapering profile and thick, usually hollow dry stone walls which contain galleries, cells and a stairway, with guard cells at the entrance.
Naturally occuring substances eg. coal and salt, obtained by mining.
A fibrous silicate mineral used to manufacture incombustible items.
A hall, often associated with a synagogue, used for studying the Torah and other religious texts.
The skirting or projecting base of a wall.
A structure, usually of brick, stone or timber, that encloses or defines a space or room.
A warship used to provide an escort to other warships or merchant ships against attack.
A medium speed anti submarine escort vessel built from World War II
A prepared slope with rails on which boats can be transferred from one canal to another at a higher or lower level. The boats can either be floated in a caisson or carried in a cradle or sling.
A prepared slope on which rails are laid to enable early tramroads and railways to negotiate a steep gradient.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Gilbertine order.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Augustinian order.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Bridgettine order.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Poor Knights of Christ and the Temple of Solomon, commonly known as the Knights Templars

An outlying farm or estate, usually belonging to a religious order or feudal lord. Specifically related to core buildings and structures associated with monastic land holding. Use specific term where known.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Order of Tiron.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Benedictine order.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Cluniac order.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Cistercian order.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Premonstratensian order.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Carthusian order.
Modelled ocean average
Modelled ocean average
Modelled ocean average

A limited programme of intrusive fieldwork which determines the presence or absence of archaeological features, structures, deposits, artefacts or ecofacts within a specified area or site on land or within the inter-tidal zone.
A limited programme of intrusive fieldwork which determines the presence or absence of archaeological features, structures, deposits, artefacts or ecofacts within a specified underwater area.
A building for the housing of trams.

Includes all stages of production process of textiles, eg. wool, cotton, linen, etc, and textile products. Use only for sites where there is evidence of textile manufacture but no specific monument type, otherwise use more specific term.
A building housing a number of power looms.

Two-seat, twin-engined fighter/fighter-bomber designed as a replacement for the Bf110. Of the 600 or so produced, only 258 reached the Luftwaffe due to serious design faults. The ME210 was superseded by the ME410 Hornisse.

Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber: Curtiss P40 Warhawk, known to the RAF as the Tomahawk, later renamed Kittyhawk. Serving from 1941 to 1942, control difficulties in dive attacks impeded bombing accuracy, resulting in use for larger targets only.
A light, high speed aircraft designed to engage in aerial combat and also equipped to carry bombs.
Single-engine, single-seat fighter-bomber. Designed to replace the Hurricane as an interceptor, excelled as a rocket-projectile-firing ground-attack fighter. Entered RAF service in 1941.
Single-engine fighter/dive-bomber. The Fleet Air Arm's first operational monoplane, and its first aircraft to shoot down an enemy during the war.
Twin-engined fighter-bomber. All metal in construction, entered service in 1940. Supported bombing operations and participated in attacks on France, but not widely used due to engine faults.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber and ground-attack aircraft. Entered service with the Luftwaffe in mid-1941. Approximately 20,000 were constructed between 1941 and the end of the war.
Twin-engined, single-seat fighter-bomber. Flown by USAAF fighter groups from 1942, excelled as a ground-support fighter. Could carry two 1600 lb bombs or rocket projectiles.
Single-seat fighter-bomber with a single, midships engine and tricycle landing gear. After proving a failure as an air-combat fighter, was used mainly in the ground attack role.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter-bomber developed from the Typhoon and the abandoned Tornado. Entered service in 1944 with its greatest success being in destroying V.1. flying bombs. One of the fastest World War 2 aircraft, with a top speed of 436 mph.

An American turbojet fighter-bomber aircraft. The F-84 was the first production fighter aircraft to utilize in-flight refuelling and the first fighter capable of carrying a nuclear weapon. Designed by Alexander Kartveli, 1946.
A light, high-speed aircraft designed to engage in aerial combat.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber. Fitted with eight fixed forward-firing machine guns in the wings, plus two 1000lb bombs or six rocket projectiles.
A fighter-bomber designed to deploy its bombs during the latter stage of a diving manoeuvre, thus increasing the accuracy of its targetting.
A type of shield, usually wooden and circular.
A protective piece of armour carried in the hand to protect the bearer from weapons.
A vessel or aircraft lost at sea, cause unknown.
Acts of vandalism, or deliberate damage by owner or other parties, which result in the `Constructive Total Lossï¿½ (CTL) of vessel, or contributes to CTL of an abandoned vessel.
Loss due to action of self propelled submerged missile.
A vessel or aircraft lost due to an accidental explosion. Do not use for losses caused by deliberate action.
A vessel which runs aground and does not get off.
Use only for fragmentary wreckage washed up at the time of loss or subsequently: but not for complete hulls for which STRANDED or another appropriate manner of loss should be used.
Loss due to action of free floating or tethered explosive device set to explode on contact with or in proximity to a vessel.
A vessel which has been dismantled for the purpose of removal from the shore after stranding.
A vessel which comes ashore and breaks up immediately due to severe weather.
The loss of a craft due to structural or engine failure. In the case of loss resulting from the malfunction of navigational or operational apparatus, use INSTRUMENT FAILURE.

Damaged, usually by weather or warfare, to such an extent that the vessel is in severe or imminent danger of being lost; i.e. a pre-existing condition of the vessel which contributes to the final wrecking event.
An aircraft which has been damaged beyond repair due to a collision with the ground or sea.
A vessel which has been deliberately scuttled using explosive charges.
Loss of a vessel due to bombardment from ship, shore or submarine. For Aircraft use SHOT DOWN.
An aircraft lost due to offensive action. Includes air-to-air and ground-to-air combat. For Vessels use GUN ACTION.
Deliberate sinking of a vessel, e.g. to prevent capture or to act as a blockship.
Refers to the abandonment of a vessel at sea due to its becoming unseaworthy. Do not use for vessels abandoned having run aground. For aircraft use DITCHED.
A vessel lost due to aerial bombardment.
Loss of a vessel or aircraft through accidental contact with another or a structure. Do not use when contact is with natural feature or rocky shore.
Loss of a vessel or aircraft primarily due to fire.
Loss of a vessel due to running aground and subsequently refloating before final loss.

Loss of a craft, especially aircraft, resulting from the malfunction of registering or measuring apparatus vital to its navigation or operation. In the case of structural or engine failure use MECHANICAL FAILURE.

Use where an entire, wrecked or incapacitated, craft has been recovered or salvaged, possibly leaving debris or other evidence of its presence at the wreck or crash site. If part of the wreck remains on the seabed use PARTIALLY RECOVERED.
Stoving in or fracturing of lowest part of vessel's hull.
A vessel lost having overturned due to severe weather or shifting cargo.
A vessel that has sunk at sea: Double-index with background cause were known, e.g. LEAKED, COLLISION.

Use where a section of the vessel has been recovered from where she lies, either at the time or subsequently, leaving behind substantial remains (unlike RECOVERED, where the entire vessel has been removed from the site).
Use for 'constructive total loss' (CTL) or where a vessel is abandoned because she is beyond repair or has become so after abandonment, which may include acts of vandalism.
Loss of a vessel or aircraft due to an explosion caused by its own armament or cargo.
Reuse of timbers or hull of a vessel in construction. For example sinking of hulks as harbour foundations or recycling of timbers in domestic contexts.
A vessel withdrawn from active use and awaiting disposal or reuse. Vessel subsequently becomes derelict.

Use when the vessel splits in two due to stresses on her frame where she lies unsupported either amidships or at the ends, typically after stranding, although this may also happen in similar conditions on the seabed after foundering.
Deliberate collision with another vessel in order to inflict damage.
An aircraft which has been forced to land on the sea in an emergency.
For use when a vessel, already lost through other causes, is dismantled or dispersed by means of explosives to render it harmless to other shipping.

Loss due to cumulative damage sustained during acts of warfare, capture, piracy, privateering etc. Use in instances where a more specific manner of loss (e.g. SCUTTLED, GUN ACTION) cannot be assigned.
Ignition from within rather than through external forces; frequently associated with cargoes of organic material such as manure, owing to an internal rise in temperature of the cargo itself.
A vessel that is deliberately run or dragged up the beach to save cargo and or crew. Do not use if the vessel is refloated.
A vessel which has damaged by a lightning strike and subsequently lost.
Loss of vessel due to deployment of explosive charges set to detonate at a predetermined depth.

Judged as irreparable or no longer seaworthy following a wrecking incident (from which the vessel may have been recovered) or a difficult voyage: a term with legal force indicating that the vessel is unfit for service.
Ingress of water through damage or defects in the hull. Double-index with any cause, were known, e.g. COLLISION, and consequence, were known, e.g. BEACHED, FOUNDERED.

Three-seat, twin-engined minelaying, torpedo-bombing and reconnaissance twin-float seaplane. First flown in 1936, in 1938 it set eight world speed records for its class in various range and payload categories.

Twin-engined, six-crew, heavy bomber. Conceived as a rival to the Lancaster and Flying Fortress, the HE177 was dogged by mechanical and structural problems. Of a thousand produced, only about two hundred saw action.
Ernst Heinkel A.G.. Formed in 1922 by Dr. Ernst Heinkel, previously Chief Designer with Hansa-Brandenburgische Flugzeugwerke, where he produced many notable seaplanes during World War One.
Twin-engined, four-crew German seaplane. Entered service in 1932 as a torpedo bomber and naval reconnaisance aircraft, though by World War 2 those still serving were used mainly for air sea rescue.

The main German, medium bomber of the war, the HE111 first saw action during the Spanish Civil War. HE111s took part in the Battle of Britain and from 1944 onwards were used to launch airborne flying bombs against London.
A projectile discharged from a weapon, usually a firearm.
A type of kiln, usually built into banking, with a stone lining that was used to produce white coal which was used as fuel in the lead smelting process.
A rough shelter or dwelling, sometimes used to house cattle.
Wood, cut and seasoned so forming or capable of forming any part of a structure. May be treated with preservative before use.
Wooden roof tile (traditionally oak) which is riven or sawn from good quality timber to a regular size and used as a roof and/or wall covering. Index with type of wood if known.

A British medium-range biplane airliner designed and built by Handley Page in 1921. A twin-engined variant of the Handley Page W series (W8, W9), retired in 1931. Built for Imperial Airways (4 units built).
Handley Page, Ltd.. Founded by Sir Frederick Handley Page, this was the first limited company to be incorporated in Great Britain for the purpose of aircraft manufacture.
A group of buildings, or part of a works, housing apparatus used in the process of distilling.
A tool used to produce a polish on an object.
An iron plate connecting two or more timbers together.
When secondary product use with major product and MINE, eg. COPPER MINE.
A form of granite found in Cornwall
A granular, crystalline, hard rock often used as a building material.
An abbey or priory for nuns ofthe Benedictine order.
Houses specifically of nuns/canonesses or religious women.
A waterside depot for coals brought from the collieries for shipment, furnished with staging and chutes for loading vessels.
A military camp providing training facilities.
Includes sites associated with extraction.
A structure erected for the processing of shale, to extract oil through heating.
An underground structure for the storage of mineral oil.
A site where petroleum is drawn.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the retrieval, refining, processing and storage of petroleum oil.
A supporting structure for drilling machinery used in the extraction of or prospecting for mineral oils.
A piece of machinery used to raise oil from a well.
A site used for the separation of oil into its constituent parts by heating in an enclosed vessel(s).
A works where crude oil is distilled into its fractions or cuts.
A charity school, usually housed in an almshouse.
A light, high speed aircraft designed to engage in aerial combat and also equipped to carry bombs.
Single-engine fighter/dive-bomber. The Fleet Air Arm's first operational monoplane, and its first aircraft to shoot down an enemy during the war.
A triangle of cloth worn by ladies to cover the shoulders, neck and throat.
A covering for the arm, usually attached to or part of another garment.
Long piece of silk etc worn around waist or over one shoulder often as a symbol of rank.
A band of material worn around the neck, waist or shoulder.
A cylinder of fur or cloth into which the hands are placed to keep warm.
A conspicuous ornament usually a feather or of horse hair worn attached to headwear.
A band worn around the wrist as a bracelet.
The bottom part of a sleeve, can be ornamental.
A band of leather, cloth etc worn usually around the waist to support clothing, carry weapons, pouches, tools etc or as a decoration.
A piece of material worn as a band around the arm.
A sash or belt worn over the shoulder to the hip for carrying a sword.
A belt worn around the waist from which a sword is hung. Where worn over the shoulder use baldric.
A neck band or necklace worn tightly around the throat.
A decorative panel worn over the chest and stomach by both men and women in the 16th century and later only by women.
A piece of material worn around the neck. Where it is a collar for an animal use animal collar.
Woman's fur cape for the shoulders.
A square of fabric tied around the neck.
An object worn, or carried, to cover the face.
A covering for the hand.
A projecting starched frill worn around the neck, especially 16th century.
A long scarf or shawl.
A piece of fabric worn tied or knotted around the neck.
An item worn as clothing or in addition to clothes.
A form of belt or sash worn to hold in garments.
A pipe in which a substance is smoked.
A pipe designed for smoking opium.
Engineering works specializing in the production and maintenance of non-passenger carrying railway rolling stock.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the engineering industry.
A large site specializing in the manufacture of locomotives.
A building or works in which carriages were built. Use RAILWAY CARRIAGE WORKS for sites making railway carriages.
Engineering works dedicated solely to the manufacture and repair of boilers.
Small engineering works specialising in the production of items such as ploughs and threshing machinery.
A group of buildings where consumer goods, such as small machines and electrical components, are manufactured.
Any factory or site using machine tools in a manufacturing or processing capacity.

Traditionally a building or site where stage coaches were built. Nowadays the term is applied to buildings used for the manufacturing of the body work and furnishings of motor vehicles and railway carriages.
An engineering site where railway carriages are manufactured.
Specialized engineering workshop particularly for the production of marine engines or other large components of ships.
A container for holding ink.
A pot for ink usually housed in a hole in a desk.
A container for sand which was used to stop ink from spreading.
A container holding materials used in writing.
A pot for fine powder.

Twin-engined, seven-crew, coastal reconnaissance, biplane flying-boat. Designed to the same specification as the Saro London, entered service in 1937. Also serving in an anti-submarine role, was replaced by the Consolidated Canso (Catalina) in 1943.
A part of a coffin that is removable eg handle, mount etc.
An object related to deaths, burials or funerals.
A factory where preserved food is canned.
A factory or site for the manufacture of food stuffs from raw ingredients.

Developed as a long range, heavy day-fighter, the ME110 found its niche as a night fighter. It saw service over Southern and Eastern England during the Battle of Britain but lost out in the daytime to the faster British fighters.
A factory where glue is produced.
A controlled point with warning lights and gates or barriers where a road crosses a railway line.
A level crossing designed to allow the passage of aircraft to and from a runway which has a railway or road running through it.
A place where people meet for entertainment, discussion or assembly. Use more specific type where known.
A large building used for the transaction of the public business of a town, the holding of courts of justice, entertainments and other activities.
A school attended by children between the ages of seven and eleven.

A French aeroplane company that primarily built racing aircraft before World War I and fighter aircraft during World War I and between the wars. First set up in 1902 as manufacturer of engine components, then aircraft in 1911 as Nieuport et Deplante.

A French airliner which entered service in 1920. A conventional biplane design with enclosed cabin for four passengers and open cockpit for the pilot. Fitted with an early audible guidance system. Withdrawn from service in 1921.
Cloth finishing process using machinery to raise the nap of the cloth before shearing.
A jug with a constriction between the upper and lower body sections. (Source: MPRG)
Animal skins which have the outer pelt of fur on them.
Animal skins, either raw or dressed which are used in the tanning industry to produce leather.
Products derived from the carcasses or hides of animals. Includes bone and ivory products, blubber and grease but not meat.
The hides of animals, either untreated or tanned.
Hawker Aircraft, Ltd., established 1933 to succeed the H. G. Hawker Engineering Co., Ltd., which had been formed in 1920 as the result of the voluntary liquidation of the renowned Sopwith concern.

A British two-seater army co-operation aircraft manufactured by Hawker Aircraft for the Royal Air Force. A Hart variant biplane that first flew in 1931, becoming a prominent British aircraft in the inter-war period with over 700 units built.
An iron cover for a manhole
A subterranean feature entered from a hillside, cliff face, etc. A cave may have been used for occupation, storage, burial, refuse, or as a hide-away. Index with site type or objects where known.
Use only for natural features mistakenly assumed to be archaeological or natural features with archaeological significance.
Deposits laid down as the result of river action.
Based on a typical 18ft span, 40ft long temporary brick hut but with two bay windows in the front elevation, one for the watch office and one for the chief instructor.
A single seat with back and arms and usually upholstered.
A single seat with a back, sometimes also arms.
Hard, black, carbonized plant matter, usually found in seams below the earth's surface and used as a fuel and for the manufacture of gas.
Coal dust or slack, especially that of anthracite.
Powdered coal.
A building used by the church to promote Christianity through lectures, study, etc.
An institute provided by a regiment for the improvement of the soldiers and to reduce excessive drinking.
An establishment where deaf people receive education, training and social support.
A building used by members of the Womens Institute, an organization which meets regularly and engages in various social and cultural activities.
A building used by an organization or society instituted to promote the study of mathematics through lectures, research, etc.
A subscription club, usually with a library and newspaper room, established from c.1815-1860, their educational function gradually taken over by the public libraries in the later 19th century.
A place where working men could educate themselves through lectures and the use of a reading room with newspapers, etc.
A building where miners could improve their knowledge by attending lectures and using the reading room facilities.
A building used by an organization instituted to promote the needs and rights of the blind.
A building in which an organization or society is instituted to promote foreign languages in England such as French and German, etc.
A building used by organizations or societies for the promotion of a particular profession through lectures, research, etc.
A building in which a society or organization is instituted to promote science, art, literature, education, etc. Use more specific type where known.
A building used by an organization or society instituted to promote technology through lectures, research, etc.
A building for a society formed for the promotion of some branch of learning or science.
A building used by an organization or society to promote the study of oriental languages and history through lectures, research, etc.
A building where artisans could learn more about their craft, and the scientific and theoretical principles behind it, by attending lectures and the use of the reading room facilities.
An building, often including recreational facilities, provided for the relaxation of serving Royal Air Force Personnel.
A building used by an organization or society instituted to promote research.
An engine in which the power is provided by electricity either in the form of batteries or direct from the mains supply.
Bordering the continents of Africa, Antarctica, Europe, North and South America the Atlantic is the second largest of the oceans, covering 31,736,000 square miles.
That portion of the Atlantic Ocean which stretches from the Equator in the north to Antarctica.
Thick material, usually woven, used as a covering for the floor.
An article laid over the floor or ground as a protcetive and or decorative covering.
A bridge in which the load is carried by a single beam, or beams, spanning the space between two supports.
A simple form of stone slab bridge, particularly associated with South West England.
Scotland
Angus, Scotland
A bed of low-growing foliage plants, all of an even height, arranged in patterns that resemble a carpet both in the intricacy of their design and in the uniformity of surface.
A flower bed, usually circular and convex in form, edged with wicker basketwork, iron hoops or terracotta.
A bed raised above the level of the surrounding walks. A common feature of medieval and Renaissance gardens.
A plot of earth used for the raising of plants.
A plot of earth used for the raising of flowers and shrubs.
Use for vessels registered in Slovakia. See also Czechoslovakian (for vessels registered between 1918-1992)
An indoor or outdoor market where leather and untreated animal hides are sold.
Buildings and structures associated with good health and recreation.
A building used by visitors at a health resort.
A building, usually part of a textile mill complex, where warp yarn is sized prior to weaving. Sizing is the application of a starch solution to warp threads to add strength and protection.
Movable, usually functional, articles in a room. Use only for objects believed to be furniture where more specific term is not identifiable.
A set of shelves.
A column whose shaft is scuplted to give it a contorted or twisted appearance, sometimes referred to as a barley-sugar column.
Reproductive process for non-photographic media in which the image is created by transferring ink from a plate, block etc.
A mill where flax fibres were woven into linen cloth.
Any factory used for the manufacture of textiles.
A stone-faced enclosure, with entrance closed by a floatable caisson or by gates, which can be pumped dry for inspection, maintenance, or repair of the hull or underwater fittings of a ship or ships.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the construction and repair of ships and boats.
A building or settlement enclosure with a thick drystone wall, generally circular or oval in plan, usually sited in an elevated position.
A passageway within a building providing access to rooms.
A workshop used by a craftsman who works in base or precious metals.
A terrace or row of dwellings, with a NAIL SHOP attached to each house.
An area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or other similar barrier. Use specific type where known.
A small circular enclosure defined by a turf or earthern bank.
Pieces of leather connected to a bridle designed to direct a horse's vision straight forward only.
The arrangement of straps used to control an animal and/or to attach the animal to a vehicle.
Cubes of solid concrete, usually with sides of 3 feet 6 inches or 5 feet which when placed in rows were intended to form a substantial barrier to enemy armoured divisions in the event of invasion.
A reinforced concrete block designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle. Use more specific type where known.
A paddle blade, typically of wood, from a horizontal or vertical mill wheel.
Objects associated with cultivation, the rearing of livestock, gathering, hunting, fishing, horticulture and the primary processing of foodstuffs.
Small crustaceans ranging in size from 0.2mm to 30mm and possessing a bivalve carapace or 'shell'.
Group of fresh water crustaceans which include the water fleas (Daphnia ssp.) the egg cases (ephippia) of which are found in archaeological deposits.
Remains of the animal group Crustacea: hard-shelled arthropods which are largely aquatic. Use for the remains of shrimps, prawns, crabs and lobsters, and also woodlice.
A circular or sub circular brooch with an attached pin. There is a gap in the circular part of the brooch.
A club where predominantly rhythm and blues style music is played, analagous to a jazz club.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 17658/40.
A small single storey structure with just one room containing a pyrotechnic cupboard and built of rendered brick with a flat reinforced concrete roof
A musical instrument with a toothed cylinder.
A framed instrument, in which strings are plucked or hit, operated from a keyboard.
An instrument in which strings are vibrated by an internal wheel cranked by a handle.
Instruments of psaltery and dulcimer type.
An musical instrument where the strings are played by plucking or bowing. Use more specific term where known.
A musical instrument producing sound by the use of strings.
A miniature lead phial worn around the neck as a religious pilgrim sign, generally medieval.

A device for telling the time by the sun, using the shadow cast by a gnomon, or sometimes a spot of light through a small hole. They were often used for checking the accuracy of clocks. They range from panels on the sides of churches to pocket watch size.
An instrument used to measure the passing of time.
A library for use of the public.
A building, room or suite of rooms where books, or other materials, are classified by subject and stored for use by the library's members.
A library where books may be consulted but not taken away.
A library which lends books (and sometimes other materials) to its members.
Buildings and structures associated with educational and artistic recreational activities.
Tongs used with incense.
Penannular objects of late Bronze Age, usually gold and too small to be worn on arms.
A fighter-bomber designed to deploy its bombs during the latter stage of a diving manoeuvre, thus increasing the accuracy of its targetting.
A stone with a concave upper surface on which grain was ground by using a rubbing stone.
A stone for grinding grain.
A large building, situated by or near a canal, used for the temporary storage of goods or merchandise awaiting transportation to or from the canal.
A large building, situated by or near a dock, canal, road or railway and used for the temporary storage of goods or merchandise awaiting transportation.
Position often screened by earth, stone or wood from which game is shot.
An unengaged, or free-standing, column.
A resource whose content is primarily words for reading. For example - books, letters, dissertations, poems, newspapers, articles, archives of mailing lists. [DC]
This class of documents confers statutory designation on the monuments listed within them. It usually is restricted to legally defined national or local notifications of designation.
The contents of these documents do not confer any statutory designation on the monuments listed, they are purely advisory notifications for use within preserving the historic environment.

This term is appropriate to official notifications of a monument or area whether they are statutory or purely advisory. Where possible the specific document type should be indexed for example Scheduled Monument Notification.
A building or site producing nitrogen-rich fertilizer.
A building or site used for the production of both chemical and organic fertilizer.
An abbey or priory of Cluniac monks.
Aircraft hangars designed by T. Bedford Consulting Engineers to meet the requirement to repair damaged heavy bombers in situ on their airfields.

A large type of military repair hangar mainly used on WWII bomber bases, constructed using steel stanchions and clad in corrugated iron. B 1 hangars were part of a series of prefabricated buildings intended to supplement existing hangars on bases.
A mill used for the production of wadding, as opposed to yarn or cloth. Often associated with steam or water power.

Twin-engined monoplane that served the RAF as an advanced trainer and flying ambulance. Mk. I featured a gun turret and served for gunnery and bombing-crew training. Subsequent versions used for pilot, radio and navigation training.
A building used for an agricultural and/or subsistence purpose. Use more specific type where known.
A room with special ventilation used for the slow drying of foodstuffs.
Unbaked clays and/or soil material often mixed with, or performing the function of an aggregate or binder. See EARTH MIX Class List for narrow terms.
Wet soil, sand or other earthy matter combined with ballast and bonded with straw or other binding material. Walls are built in the absence of shuttering by the simple process of pitching in layers.
Buildings and sites associated with the manufacture of clothing.
A factory where buttons are manufactured.
An establishment used for the custody of money received from, or on behalf, of its customers.
A bank which specializes in accepting savings deposits. Originally established to help the poor.
Small port on River Trent, North Lincs.
Various flavoured aromatic and savoury substances, such as herbs, salt etc, used to impart flavour to food.
The stigmas of the crocus, Crocus sativus, used as a flavouring and for colouring food.
A mineral, Sodium Chloride, obtained by mining or the evaporation of brine used as a seasoning and for preserving food.
A pungent condiment manufactured from the dried berries of the plant Piper Nigrum. Use for cargoes of peppercorns or ground pepper.
Savoury ingredients, such as herbs, used to add flavour to food.

A calciner commonly used between 1870 and circa 1900 for extracting arsenic from mined ores and featuring a slightly inclined rotating iron tube with a firebox at the bottom and an ore feed at the top.
A place used to clean the fleece of sheep before shearing. This could be a watercourse temporarily dammed in order to wash sheep.
A place or building where animals can be washed. Often in the form of a pool with a walled funnel-like structure enabling animals to be guided into the pool.

High speed craft developed in the 20th Century which employ a wing-like structure mounted on struts below the hull which lift the vessel above the water line during forward motion, reducing drag and increasing speed.
Aromatic vegetable substances, either in their natural form or ground, used to add flavour or scent to food.
A hard aromatic seed, obtained from the fruit of an East Indian evergreen tree and used as a spice.
A dam constructed across a stream to raise its water-level and make it available to power a mill wheel.
A bit for an auger to scoop out material.
A tool with a cross handle at one end and a spoon shaped or gouge cutter at the other, used for drilling holes.
An auger bit which creates its hole by drilling into the material.
A gun emplacement associated with a coastal battery.
A fortified site in which a gun, mortar or cannon is positioned.
Festival of Lights
A house for storing or drying saddles.
Use where the material presents debris or waste from manufacturing.
Specialist hospital treating patients with physical disabilities.
A type of pottery kiln in which air rises up inside the oven to be forced back down and out through the base of the oven.
A structure, composed of oven and hovel, used for the firing of pottery ware.
A place of burial. Use more specific type where known.
A grave which has been formed by cutting into the bedrock of a site.
A grave lined with slabs of stone or slate and covered by a large slab of stone. Commonly found on the Isle of Man.
Graves known to be of shipwreck victims buried close to their site of discovery, as was customary until the 19th century, rather than in consecrated ground.
An intrusive feature cut for the purpose of containing a cremation burial within it.
A small Anglo-Saxon cross-slab buried on the breast or beneath the head of a corpse.
Saxon rectangular burial chamber comprising a large sunken 'room' lined with wood. 6th and 7th century AD.
US Navy version of the four-engined, six-crew B24 heavy bomber. Modified for long-range reconnaissance duty and used as a patrol-bomber against shipping and submarines.
Long-range, usually four-engined, bomber designed to carry a large bomb payload.
A house consisting of a public hall with private living accommodation attached. Built from the medieval period onwards.
A house consisting of a single storey hall with two storey domestic ranges attached to either one or both ends.
A cruck which is set in solid masonry above floor level but stretching a long way down the wall.

A pair of timbers, or blades, usually curved, rising from a place at or near ground level to a point at or near the apex of a roof, forming an approximately triangular frame on which the subsidiary structure rests.
A small warship (often adapted from a trawler or drifter) used to hunt enemy submarines.
A place of worship and residence for Anglican nuns.
A structure, building or site housing equipment for transmitting radio or television signals.
A site, including buildings and structures, from which communication signals are transmitted.
A store for undressed meat, usually for keeping grouse, partridge, pheasant or rabbit in a cool environment.
A room in which food, usually meat, is kept.
Photographic negative using nitrate process on a film base material.
A piece of sculpture usually representing the head, shoulders and breast of a person.
A ladle used for the making of drugs and medicines.
A building or site for watching specific military activities or the movement of enemy forces, etc.
An observation post used by members of the Home Guard.
A building with small observation ports used for plotting mines dropped by parachute.
Buildings and structures used to monitor the accuracy of bombs dropped on a bombing range
A building, situated on the coast, used for observing the movements of enemy shipping.
A plate used in the Eucharist.
An object used in the Eucharist.
