A small enclosure containing cold frames, often of brick and glass construction, usually situated against the exterior of a walled garden's south-facing garden.
The residences of people involved in transport work.
A house for the keeper of a level crossing on a railway.
A secondary or incidental product of a process.
A collective name for the pans and fire bars used in the making of salt through evaporation.
Aland Islands, Finland
Headgear for a horse, usually consisting of a series of buckled straps and a mouthpiece, bridle bit, by which the horse is controlled.
A path that is roofed over.
A bowl adapted by the addition of two handles, generally opposed. (Source: MPRG)
A small, double-handled bowl with horizontal loop handles decorated with a cockerel motif. (Source: MPRG)
A three-dimensional decorative ornamentation composed of a series of Vs forming a zigzag.
A structure inclined towards the water on which a ship may be built or lowered into the water.

A pillbox design, assigned a drawing number by DFW branch 3. Although originally believed to be a distinct type, FW3/45 has recently been found to be a design for modifications to existing types. Double index with specific type where known.
A maritime monument where the remains of a vessel are known to exist but where no detailed information is available.
A maritime monument where the hull of a vessel is mostly in one piece, with large pieces of the superstructure intact.

A man-made construction or object (such as a gravestone) which has been moved from its original site either through active human intervention or natural processes such as erosion. For buildings which have been moved use MOVED BUILDING.

A building which has been moved from its original site either through active human intervention or natural processes such as erosion. For structures or objects such as gravestones use MOVED STRUCTURE.
An artificial mound of earth outside a ditch or wall intended to deflect or absorb cannon fire.
A large, convex moulding, sometimes ornamented, set at the base of a column and above its plinth.
A bridge constructed using rockwork to create a craggy, naturalistic appearance. A feature of 18th century rococo gardens and parks.
A bridge built to enhance or compliment the surrounding landscape. Mainly found on estates or in parkland and usually 18th and 19th century.

The name given by the Allies during the Second World War to the German motor torpedo boat. E Boats carried two torpedo tubes and anti aircraft guns. They had a maximum speed of 39 knots and were considered superior to their Allied counterparts.
A small warship powered by petrol or diesel engines and armed with torpedo tubes and small guns. Used for coastal anti shipping patrols and warfare in coastal waters.

A short, tapered, vertical stone supporting a rough stone disc so resembling a toadstool, often forming one of several uprights on which a timber structure, such as a granary rests, protecting the building from damp and vermin.
A fitting specifically functioning as the strengthener and support for the end of a strap of leather or fabric.
The fittings or parts on a strap.
An item used to join together clothing (includes footwear).
A pointed spout attachment.
The Sopwith Aviation Co., Ltd.. Established in 1911 by the noted aviator Mr T. O. M. Sopwith. Produced many notable aircraft, including the Camel and a Schneider Cup-winning seaplane.
Single-engined fighter, developed from the Camel. Entered service in 1918 and became the RAF's first mainstay peacetime fighter.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter biplane renowned for its high performance and manoeuvrability. Entered service in 1917.
A strut with a reflecting counterpart that forms the letter A on either side of a king post.
A short timber set diagonally in the spandrel of an arch brace, between the brace and the corner of the main frame.
A room, usually at ground level or below, housing the tank in which water is heated as part of a building's heating system.
A structure comprising two upright spars, joined at the top to form a triangle, with a hoisting tackle suspended from the apex. Used to lift cargo or other weights.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the construction and repair of ships and boats.
The principal longitudinal member or spine of a windmill sail, extending from the stock and supporting the sailbars.
A bridge, usually resting on raised arches, carrying a railway across low-lying land or water.

A machine for weaving cloth. A traditional loom comprises a framework with a horizontal back roller, the warp beam or warp roller, around which closely spaced warp threads have been wound parallel to each other, stretched horizontally onto a front roller.
A power driven cloth-weaving machine.
A machine used for combing wool. Use more specific term where known.
A machine for combing out wool, cleaning out extraneous matter and short fibres and laying the combed long fibres more or less parallel to each other as required for Worsted spinning.
A threshing barn which also houses farm animals and is somethimes used to stotre grain, house carts and other functions.
A building for the storage and processing of grain crops and for housing straw, farm equipment and occasionally livestock and their fodder. Use more specific type where known.

A room, particularly in a house or theatre, intended for dressing or changing one's clothes and furnished with wardrobes, dressing tables and other facilities for the application of make-up, styling of hair etc.
Continent.
A cheap eating establishment traditionally serving jellied eels, pies and mash.
For commercial or non commercial use. See narrow terms in each class.
A factory where preserved food is canned.
A pit used to bury a large number of people who have died, or been killed, either as a result of warfare, epidemics or natural disasters.
A place where dead animals are buried.

A pit used for the re-burial of disarticulated human remains from many individuals, occasionally displaying sorting of remains, eg. grouping of skulls or long bones. Distinct from mass burials which contain articulated skeletal remains.
A place where dead bodies are buried together. Often unconsecrated ground.
A deep pit used for the burial of plague victims.
A pit over which a corpse has been cremated on a pyre into which the remains and debris, and sometime grave goods, collapse and are buried. Generally confined to the Roman period.

A farmstead with multiple yards which are grouped together and regularly arranged (other than the defined E, F, H, T or Z plans). The yards may relate to one or more buildings or ranges which may be of either loose courtyard or regular courtyard form.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the working buildings are carefully planned as linked ranges and are focused around one or more working yards. They often result from a single phase of building.
A non-profit making restaurant administered by a Local Food Committee which provided customers with good quality and wholesome food which could be purchased without ration coupons.
For commercial or non commercial use. See narrow terms in each class.
A place where refreshments or meals may be obtained.
Any structure or object, used for the purpose of practice bombing.
An area of land, with associated buildings and targets, used for practicing the dropping of bombs and other aspects of air warfare.
Use where the intervening arcade is closed but timber-framed.
A house with no row of posts between the central space and the aisles.
Founded by Professor Willy Messerschmitt as the Bayerische Flugzeugwerke. Reconstituted in 1938 as the Messerschmitt A.G..

Developed as a long range, heavy day-fighter, the ME110 found its niche as a night fighter. It saw service over Southern and Eastern England during the Battle of Britain but lost out in the daytime to the faster British fighters.
A factory or complex where chamois leather is produced using fish oils as the tanning agent.
A factory for the manufacture of leather goods, such as shoes, saddles, etc. Use TANNERY for the manufacture of leather.
A workshop used for the manufacture of items of jewellery and/or timepieces from precious metals and precious or semi-precious stones.
A place where silverware is manufactured.
A specialized form of truss bridge that extends or cantilevers from both sides of the pier, the inner 'arms' usually supporting a central span.
A structure of wood, stone, iron, brick or concrete, etc, with one or more intervals under it to span a river or other space. Use specific type where known.
A bridge made up of many relatively small members joined together in a series of interconnecting triangles.

Bordering the five continents of Antarctica, Asia, Australasia, North and South America, the Pacific is the largest of the world's oceans, and covers more area (63,838,000 square miles) than that of the combined seven continents.
That portion of the Pacific which stretches from the Arctic Ocean in the north to the equator.
Horn is a hollow, bone-like projection consisting mainly of keratin, found on certain animals (sheep, cows, goats etc.)
Pertaining to or deriving from a living organism. See ANIMAL Class list for narrow terms.
The sill beam of the jettied upper floor resting on projecting ends of joists or on jetty brackets.
A projecting part of a building that overhangs the wall below it.

A large twin-engined airliner produced by the Dutch aircraft manufacturer Fokker in the 1920s. First flight March 1927. Designed by Reinhold Platz. Mixed construction, fuselage/ tail in steel covered with plywood, canvas and duralumin (11 units built).

Dutch aircraft manufacturer named after its founder, Anthony Fokker. Set up in 1912 in Schwerin, Germany, moving to the Netherlands in 1919. The world's largest aircraft manufacturer in the late 1920s.
Man-made building, edifice or construction of assembled material parts.

A monument consisting of a built structure, but which has been demolished so that only a ground plan and foundations, or similar, are thought to remain. Where all below ground traces have also been removed use DESTROYED MONUMENT.
Man-made, roofless edifice or construction visible as substantial above-ground remains retaining evidence of architecture and materials, but which has been substantially destroyed.
Man-made roofless edifice or construction which is intact or substantially intact, with significant survival of original features, even if no longer serving original intended function.
A vessel with heating apparatus beneath it, for cooking or keeping food warm at the table.
A structure providing protection against the weather at bus stops.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the processing of foodstuffs.
A site where sugar beet was processed before being washed and dried to form granulated sugar.
A machine for spinning cotton yarn.
An 18th century hand-operated machine capable of spinning several yarns at once, invented in circa 1767.
A machine used for drawing out and twisting together short fibres to make a yarn or thread. Use more specific term where known.
A machine used for spinning cotton powered by water.
The grounds of an institution for higher education eg. a university, including the educational buildings, entertainment and sports facilities and student's halls of residence.
Aspects associated with the genetic make up and/or factors that affected the organism from which the material is derived during its life
A cover for an object, usually designed to fit the object.
A lid comprising a shallow flared dish with an integral knob rising from the centre. (Source: MPRG)
A string of beads used to aid the memory in reciting a set of devotions.
An enclosed cage used in a mine shaft to transport miners from the surface to the mine workings.
A seperate wing of a large house provide accommodation for guests.
A place or path for walking in a park or garden. Use more specific type where possible.
A garden walk lined with yew trees and hedges.

A large twin-engined airliner produced by the Dutch aircraft manufacturer Fokker in the 1920s. First flight March 1927. Designed by Reinhold Platz. Mixed construction, fuselage/ tail in steel covered with plywood, canvas and duralumin (11 units built).

Dutch aircraft manufacturer named after its founder, Anthony Fokker. Set up in 1912 in Schwerin, Germany, moving to the Netherlands in 1919. The world's largest aircraft manufacturer in the late 1920s.
The principal storey of a building, containing the main reception rooms, when not situated on ground level.
Plans of structures, particularly ground plans, and divisions or elements of structures that form part of these plans.
The element or elements that make up the different parts of a structural plan.
The main body of a structure not including wings etc.
A regular structural subdivision or compartment within a building, defined by dividing walls or the positions of the principal supporting members.
A part of a building joined to the core of the structure and at an angle to it.
A site where methane gas, released by coal mining, is collected and processed.
Buildings and structures associated with the mining industry.

A British medium-range biplane airliner designed and built by Handley Page in 1921. A twin-engined variant of the Handley Page W series (W8, W9), retired in 1931. Built for Imperial Airways (4 units built).
A roof whose ends are partly gabled and partly sloped.
A mill used to process raw timber.
A mill used to process logwood, the inner red wood of a South American tree used widely in dyeing. Imported in the form of logs and cut and ground into dye by a mechanical process.
A sample taken from waterlogged conditions.
Generic term for the oolitic limestones quarried in Northamptonshire, Lincolnshire and Rutland. Varying in grain size from medium to coarse, and colour from cream to pale brown.
Limestone formed during the Jurassic period. Composed of ooliths, literally small rock particles with the appearance of fish roe.
Even grained, poorly fossiliferous, light brown/cream coloured, oolitic limestone. Quarried in the Bath area.
Sandy, light brown (cream to golden) coloured limestone, easily worked and readily available.
Fine to coarse grained, cream to green/grey coloured oolitic limestone. Quarried since Roman times, it is one of Britain's best building stones, hence its use throughout the country.
Limestone formed during the Jurassic period. Provides many widely used building stones.
A dwelling for the keeper of a canal wharf.
Warship or trading vessel, three masted with a low forecastle.
A room in which music is performed.

Traditionally, dating from the medieval period, this was an area on the north bank of the Thames where the Merchants of the Hanse conducted their business. Now includes a similar establishment in a provincial town.

A patented manmade rock invented by James Pulham and Son of Broxbourne. Pulhamite was used to join natural rocks together or crafted to simulate natural stone features. It is an artificial form of sandstone.

A material or combination of materials manufactured by human effort, or fashioned into shape by man or a man made industrial process (excluding metal). See MAN MADE MATERIAL Class List for narrow terms.

Synthetically manufactured stone made from natural stone aggregate or reconstituted ceramics or clay, and made to appear natural. Used as solid stone for masonry or for sculptural and architectural ornament.
Durable artificial stone consisting of china clay, sand and finely ground stoneware cast from moulds and fired in a kiln. Commonly used for architectural ornament and facings.

The British designation for any German submarine built for military purposes. U-Boat is an anglicization of the German U-Boot, an abbreviation for Unterseeboot (Undersea Boat). In German U-Boot refers to any submarine.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War. The U Boat had 5 torpedo tubes (4 bow/1 stern) and carried 10 torpedoes as well as an 88mm (or in some cases 105mm) deck gun.
A small dwelling providing living accommodation for a tin miner.
Industrial worker's house which has been purpose built by an employer, as opposed to the workshop houses used by artisans.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of heart disorders and diseases.
Microscopic mineral body (usually silica) found in many plants.
A classical order having a bell shaped capital that is decorated with laurel, olive or acanthus leaves from which CAULICOLI emerge. The shaft is usually fluted and the base is often an Attic base.
A column base featuring a hollow, concave - or scotia - moulding between two tori, which are projecting, convex mouldings.
Living and working quarters for the cellarer who was in charge of provisions and the running of the cellar.
A residence for a member of a religious community eg. Abbot, Prior, Manciple etc. For multiple occupancy use more specific term eg. DORMITORY.
A tower, consisting of one or several testing shafts, for testing lifts and for training personnel.

A site used for the placing of an explosive, demolition charge. Many types of structures were prepared for demolition in the event of an invasion in order to cause the maximum disruption to the advance of hostile forces. Use more specifc type where known.
A bridge which has had mines placed within its structure to enable it to be destroyed in the event of an invasion.
An ovolo moulding below the abacus of a Doric or Ionic Capital.
Mine for the extraction of bismuth, which usually occurs in small quantities in the ores of other metal ores, particularly lead, and some copper ores.
A flat nail of the same thickness that tapers in width to a point.
A nail used for roofing.
A metal spike for fixing one object to another.
A nail adapted so that the end of the nail can be turned over and driven back into the substance through which it has passed.

Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber: Curtiss P40 Warhawk, known to the RAF as the Tomahawk, later renamed Kittyhawk. Serving from 1941 to 1942, control difficulties in dive attacks impeded bombing accuracy, resulting in use for larger targets only.
A building containing mechanically powered ore crushers or rollers.
A mill in which barytes concentrates were ground to fine white powder, normally by use of flat millstones similar to those of a corn mill.
Four-seat, twin-engined medium bomber. Entered service in 1938. After serving Bomber Command from 1939-42, was converted to a torpedo-bomber and mine-layer with RAF Coastal Command.

Short Bros. (Rochester & Bedford), Ltd. founded by Eustace and Oswald Short in 1898, originally manufacturing spherical balloons. In 1936 became Short & Harland Ltd. in collaboration with Belfast shipbuilders Harland and Wolff.

Seven/eight-crew, heavy night-bomber. The first four-engine bomber to join the RAF, with a bomb load of 14000 lb, entered service in 1940. Superseded as a bomber by the Lancaster and Halifax, later versions served as transports and tugs.
A visual representation of a physical object, place or person. [DC] Use a more specific term where appropriate.
Broad term for all types of animated or live action images.
Recording of a complete broadcast television programme, for instance a documentary. For extracts such as items from news broadcasts use VIDEO CLIP.
An extract from a longer video film, used as an illustration.
Victoria, Australia
A small flake or blade with a series of notches along the edge.
A flake or blade tool with more than one notch on its edge.
British two-seat, twin-engined night fighter. Also used for roles such as long-range escort fighter, ground-attack and anti-shipping strike aircraft, bomber, torpedo-carrier and rocket fighter.
A room within a building, such as a shop or leisure complex,sometimes equipped with cubicles or screens to allow a degree of privacy, where clothing can be tried on or changed.
American-built, twin-engined flying-boat designed for maritime patrol and reconnaissance. Entered US Naval service in 1936 as the PBY-1; christened the Catalina by the RAF, who used it from 1939 on.

A small clinker-built craft, dating primarily from the 19th and early 20th centuries, fitted with oars and often a sail, usually found on the north-east coast of England and used for fishing or pilotage.
Small, heavily built coble, usually fitted with lugsail and oars, used on the north-east coast of England to assist, tow, pilot, provision or otherwise attend ships.
A building containing machinery for the spinning of yarn.
Factory where yarn is made from paper.

Three/four-crew, single-engine, shipboard observation and air/sea rescue amphibian seaplane. Entered RAF service in 1936. Also employed for gunnery spotting, anti-submarine and convoy protection duties.
Westland Aircraft Ltd., formed in 1935 to take over the aircraft branch of Petters Ltd., previously known as the Westland Aircraft Works.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Fifth Rate Ship Of The Line

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A sailing ship with a sufficient numerically large gun armament to stand in the line of battle.
A sailing frigate mounting 32 to 44 guns with the main battery on a single deck.
Use for Insectivores (hedgehogs, shrews, moles), Chiroptera (bats) and rodents (squirrels, rats, voles, mice, dormice).
Use for the remains of any part of a mammal, except for humans.
Magnetic tape used to record sound. Includes both cassette and reel tapes.
The storage of material (text, images, files etc) in an electromagnetic format.
A cupboard set into the eastern wall of a synagogue, facing Jerusalem. The Torah scrolls are kept in the Ark.
Components within a religious, ritual or funerary site directly connected to the sacred practices involved at the site.
A building, usually housing electrical or electronic equipment, used for gathering and disseminating information. Use specific type where known.
A building or group of buildings in which communications signals, usually intercepted fro military purposes, are analysed.
A simple, flat or nearly flat lid. In ceramic forms, often made by rolling out clay rather than by throwing on a wheel. (Source: MPRG)
Single-engine, single-seat fighter-bomber. Designed to replace the Hurricane as an interceptor, excelled as a rocket-projectile-firing ground-attack fighter. Entered RAF service in 1941.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the enactment and enforcement of public law.
A building or complex used for the temporary detention of people with no legal right to be in the UK who have refused to leave voluntarily.
A small paved area attached to a building.
An object used in washing or cleaning the body.
An object made of sponge used to wash or clean with.
Argyll and Bute
Scotland
A long wooden shafted weapon tipped with a metal point.
A long spear used on horseback.
A long shafted weapon with a pointed head used for thrusting or as a missile.
A long shafted weapon with a head that can be edged and/or pointed.
A long spear designed to be thrown in order to injure or kill a given target.
A residential establishment for the care and accommodation of children and young people.
A public institution for the care and protection of children without parents.

skos:Concept.skos:definition: 1⁄100 of a chain and 1⁄1000 of a furlong.

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: Two-crew, twin-engined bomber. Entered production in 1934 and designed for dual use as a high-speed commercial transport. Technical problems hindered its use as a bomber and led to conversion to high-altitude reconnaissance.

A single-engine dive-bomber, the JU87 was very successful during the invasions of Poland and France but suffered heavy losses during the Battle of Britain. Withdrawn from NW Europe in 1941 for use in the Mediterranean and on the Eastern Front.

Junkers Flugzeug und Motorenwerke, A.G.. Formed in 1910 with Professor Junkers being granted a patent for an all-wing aeroplane. Produced first successful all-metal aeroplane, the Junkers J1, in 1915.
A twin-engined development of the JU88, the JU188 had a higher service ceiling and greater maximum speed. JU188s operated over the UK from 1944 onwards as night intruders and reconnaissance aircraft.

A twin-engined, multi-role aircraft built by Junkers. Originally designed as a medium bomber with the speed of a fighter, but its adaptability allowed it to fulfil the roles of night fighter, torpedo-bomber, anti-tank aircraft and photo-reconnaissance.
A wall built to give shelter to sheep.
An embankment of earth alongside a tramway.
A church built within the bounds of a parish for the attendance of those who cannot reach the parish church conveniently.
A freestanding building, or a room or recess serving as a place of Christian worship in a church or other building. Use more specific type where known.
A house for the keeper of a level crossing on a railway.
A tool for extracting nails, tacks, pins etc from objects.
A processing house or room in a brewery.
A building from where marine operations are directed.
A building used for a variety of administrative purposes, usually at a naval dockyard.
A duct or channel for hot air to travel through.
A metal girder, usually of iron or steel, embedded in the ground designed to obstruct the progress of hostile tanks or armoured vehicles.
Obstacles like concrete cubes, cylinders or pimples erected in the defence of Britain.
Record of events.
A type of temporary bridge designed by Sir Donald C.Bailey during the Second World War.
A bridge manufactured from prefabricated sections.
From 1822, any vessel in the service of HM Coastguard, principally deployed on Customs and Revenue duties, i.e. anti-smuggling operations. Superseded the Preventive Service Vessel.
A single masted cutter built specifically for the prevention of smuggling and the enforcement of customs regulations.
A vessel for carrying messages between warships.

Archaeologically excavated trench, either hand of machine dug, as part of a sampling programme to evaluate the presence/absence, nature, preservation, age and extent of any buried archaeological features.
Any small rigged warship below the sailing classification of frigate.
Place where a smith works iron. May be for small scale local use or within a larger industrial complex.
Equipment and parts used in the manufacture of railway tracks, locomotives and rolling stock.
Carriages, locomotives and other vehicles used on a railway.
An establishment where offenders are confined. Use more specific type where known.
An institution for the imprisonment of military personnel convicted under military law by a military court.
Use for vessels registered in the Czech Republic. See also Czechoslovakian (for vessels registered between 1918-1992)
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of women and children.
The residence of a person employed in the textile industry.
A piece of ground over which small arms or large artillery may be fired at targets. For rocket and missile firing use ROCKET TEST FACILITY.
An earthwork or structure on a rifle range used to mark a set distance from the rifle butts (usually at 50 or 100 yard intervals).
That portion of the Atlantic Ocean which stretches from the Arctic Ocean in the north to the Equator.

There are certain units, which are accepted for use with the SI. It includes units which are in continuous everyday use, in particular the traditional units of time and of angle, together with a few other units which have assumed increasing technical importance. There are also units which are currently accepted for use with the SI to satisfy the needs of commercial, legal and specialist scientific interests or are important for the interpretation of older texts.
A building made chiefly of glass, used to grow plants and fruit in. Use more specific type where possible.
A greenhouse used for growing palms and/or tropical plants.
Hollow cylinders or tubes of ceramic, wood, plastic or metal used to convey liquids, gases etc. Used in a variety of industries.
Pipes manufactured from iron and used for a variety of purposes.
Pipes manufactured from cast iron and used for a variety of purposes.
A horizontal tunnel dug specifically for draining, for example, a mine.
An artificial channel for draining water or carrying it off.
A medieval house with central open hall and two storey bays, jettied at first floor level, on either side.
A wealden house with only one end being jettied.
A small shovel for adding or placing coals onto a fire.
Tools used to maintain a fire.
Originally designed as a trainer but relegated to use by the RNAS in a Maritime Reconnaissance and anti-submarine role when the Avro 504 became the standard trainer.
A settlement built to a pre-determined plan, including housing, infrastructure and associated amenities.
A village laid out systematically with spacious and garden-like surroundings.
A settlement carefully planned from its inception and usually constructed in an area which was previously undeveloped. Many new towns were developed following the New Towns Act 1946.
A planned, self-contained, community incorporating green open spaces and containing housing, industrial and agricultural zones.
A town laid out systematically with spacious and garden-like surroundings.
A small concentration of dwellings.
A type of malt house.
A basement or cellar, usually within a house, leased as a separate dwelling.
A structure used for the drying of food using an indirect source of heat.
A kiln where gypsum was dried to a state where it could be used as plaster of Paris or for the production of cement.
A kiln used for the drying of wood.
A building found in conjunction with a WATERMILL, used for the drying of corn after harvesting, with a slatted drying floor set above a kiln.
A furnace or oven used for drying items or materials. Use specific type where possible.

A dwarf shrub of the heath family used as an alternative to straw as a roof covering in moorland regions. Cut while in bloom and laid with the roots carefully entwined. The covering turns a characteristic black colour with age.
A wall structure built to direct a current into the desired channel in a harbour, river etc.
A glasshouse used to grow and display tender decorative plants. May be either an extension to a house or freestanding.
An enclosure for the containment of a bull.
Cubicles for housing rams, resembling pigsties with their own yard but slightly larger.
An enclosure where ewes are kept at the time of lambing.
An enclosure or pen for confining geese.
A pen to separate the boar from the other pigs.
A small enclosure for cattle, sheep, swine, poultry, etc. Use more specific type where known.
An enclosure for cattle.
Mushroom-shaped stones used to raise the floor of barns, granaries etc. above ground level, to prevent vermin gaining access to stored grain and fodder.
A holder for weapons, explosives and ammunition.
A container for loose gun powder. Sometimes with a regulator to release enough powder for one shot.
A working tunnel or gallery in a mine used for the extraction of ironstone.
A site where iron ore is extracted.
Narrow, rough tracks often over upland routes used by packhorse trains to carry goods.
A way between different places, used by horses, travellers on foot and vehicles.
A room that serves as a combined living-room, kitchen and workshop.

A large communal room often occupying the full height of the building, used for functions such as meetings, entertainments etc. Traditionally found in medieval buildings but also found in later buildings emulating medieval architecture.
The principal room in early houses, which occupies the entire height of the building.
Protective covering for personal defence, objects designed to kill, injure or overwhelm an opponent or quarry, and ancillary equipment.
Four iron spikes joined together so that when the caltrop is on the ground a spike is always pointing upwards. Used to disable infantry and cavalry.
An object used in combat to attack or cause damage to an opponent.
A shaped flint used in flintlocks to create the spark to fire the gun.
A curving metal band attached to the underside of the stock of a firearm, vertically enclosing the trigger to prevent accidental discharge.
A kiln in which lime is made by calcining limestone or in some areas chalk.
A lime kiln where the fuel is not mixed with the limestone but burnt below it.
A castle surrounded by two or more lines of walled fortifications.
A fortress and dwelling, usually medieval in origin, and often consisting of a keep, curtain wall and towers etc.
Mill for producing a smooth surface and edges on newly sawn timber.
A landing and taking-off area for military aircraft. Often includes ancilliary structures and buildings for the maintenance and storage of aircraft, etc.
An airfield with associated hangars and control buildings used for the storage, maintenance and deployment of military aircraft and airships flown by the Royal Naval Air Service.
A site used for the separation of oil into its constituent parts by heating in an enclosed vessel(s).
Buildings and plant used for the refining of oil or the production of chemicals using oil.
A manmade barrier built across a river in order to increase the depth of water.
Long parallel soil ridges in excess of 5 metres across separated by furrows, formed by using a heavy plough capable of turning the soil.
Watch Office with operations room designed to Air Ministry drawing number (7345/41
Watch Office with operations room designed to Air Ministry drawing number (13079/41)
A building, originally used as a shelter for the duty pilot or officer on watch on an airfield, incorporating an operations room.
Site underlying building or structure.
A construction trench dug to receive a line of posts for a wall, with associated packing.
A trench dug in order to receive the foundations of a structure such as a stone wall etc.
A building or site for the industrial manufacture of locks.
A building or site where bloom iron or cast iron is forged into wrought iron.
A building used for the decarburizing of pig iron to produce wrought iron.
Reheating of iron from a finery, for rolling or slitting.
A symbol with secular signifigance, particularly implying authority.
A staff used for ceremonial purposes, often highly decorated.
A tunnel carrying a railway beneath the surface of the ground.
Place where ships and boats are dismantled.
A British aero- and marine-engineering company based on the Isle of Wight specializing in the construction of flying boats.

Six-crew, medium-range, twin-engined reconnaissance flying-boat. Entered service with 209 Squadron in 1939 but, due to design and operation problems, saw little action and was not produced in large numbers.
The tall, straight stalks or stems formed by plants found in the wetland areas, particularly The Fens. Used as a roofing material, the reed is laid with the ends forming the exposed covering surface.
A defensive structure or site where an anti-tank gun is emplaced.

A square pillbox with walls up to 48in thick, designed to emplace a 2 pounder anti-tank gun. A large opening in the back allowed the gun to be wheeled into position at the large embrasure in the front wall. Designed by DFW branch 3.
A container for ointments or perfume.
A container used to hold, store, examine or create medicinal substances such as ointments, medicines, drugs, pills, tablets etc.
A factory where china products are manufactured.
Any of large class of polymers based on synthetic resins or modified natural polymers which may be moulded, extruded or cast while soft or liquid, which then set rigidly or slightly elastic in form.
An early thermosetting plastic commonly used for its properties of electrical insulation.
A graduated post or pole adjacent to an area at risk of flooding to indicate the depth of water during a flood.
A post, made of wood, metal or other material, erected to mark a particular spot in the landscape. Can be used for various reasons such as measurement, calibration etc.
The hard material, consisting mainly of calcium compounds, which makes up the skeleton of vertebrates. Used for ornaments or ground for use in the manufacture of bone china.
Ground and crushed bones used as a fertilizer.
A farm building in which cattle are housed before slaughter.
A mechanical testing machine used to carry out pioneering tests on various materials, particularly cast-iron beams, to determine practical data on their strength and other properties.
A pump used for moving brine (salt water).
A hand operated mechanism used to raise and move water, liquids, compressed gases etc.
A wind-powered pump for land drainage.
A water pump situated at the side of a road or track for use by travellers and their animals.
A machine used to raise and move water and other liquids, compress gases, etc. Use more specific type where known.
Site and structures associated with the supply of clean water.
A point of public water supply, including conduits, fountains, wells, pumps and standpipes.
The lowest part, usually projecting, of a pedestal or the base of a column.
The area between the base and the cornice of a plinth.
A base on which a statue, column etc. stands.
A plinth or pedestal, sometimes decorated, and sometimes supporting statuary, placed at the apex and lower extremity of a pediment.
North Yorkshire
North Yorkshire
A coastal battery designed for use in short range engagements with enemy vessels, minelayers, blockships ad torpedo craft.
A coastal battery containing one or more artillery pieces for to defend the coast against hostile motor torpedo boats.
A coastal battery used for delivering fire at long distance thus forcing a warship threatening or bombarding shore installations to withdraw out of range.
A defensive gun battery positioned to face out to sea to fire on enemy ships and amphibious craft.
A coastal battery constructed at short notice usually mounting a variety of artillery pieces.
A defensive battery positioned facing out to sea enabling the guns to be brought to bear on enemy shipping and amphibious craft.
A long tapered flexible pole used with a fishing line and usually with a fishing reel.
A site or building used for the manufacture of goods made from pewter, an alloy of tin and lead.
A mill or factory in which raw cotton, wool, nylon or other material is spun into yarn or thread.
A lap joint which has a notch cut in one side.
A joint with a notch cut into its invisible inner face.
Use for vessels registered in Denmark
Use only where stone is natural or where there is no indication of function.
A stone, of unidentified function, showing evidence of great heating at some point in the past, leading to vitrification.
Wooden boxes or cases for carrying fruit and other similar goods.
Receptacles, including boxes, barrels etc., designed to contain something.
An ornamental grove, thicket or shrubbery pierced by walks.
A plantation of shrubs.
Medium to coarse grained metamorphic rock, colour being determined by its dominant mineral. Often used for floor and wall cladding.
A small apse.
A polygonal or semicircular recess projecting from an external wall, often with a rounded vault.

A crane consisting of a lattice girder carried on a lattice tower forming a T-shaped structure. A hoist is carried along the girder by a 'crab', enabling the crane to perform a variety of tasks eg loading/unloading of ships.
A large, metal or wooden structure, used for raising, lowering and moving heavy objects. Use more specific type where known.
Term applied to both the pit trap itself, and the walled enclosure containing pit trap(s).
An aircraft equipped to deploy explosive mines.

Three-seat, twin-engined minelaying, torpedo-bombing and reconnaissance twin-float seaplane. First flown in 1936, in 1938 it set eight world speed records for its class in various range and payload categories.
Equipment used in the preparation and maintenance of ground, and in the planting and maintenance of crops.
A tool used for digging the ground.
German three-engined air/sea rescue and transport flying boat. Entered service in 1940 as a replacement for the DO18.
German single-engine, four-seat maritime patrol and reconnaissance flying-boat. In production between 1934 and 1940, the DO18 was replaced by the three engined DO24.

Twin-engined, seven-crew, coastal reconnaissance, biplane flying-boat. Designed to the same specification as the Saro London, entered service in 1937. Also serving in an anti-submarine role, was replaced by the Consolidated Canso (Catalina) in 1943.
Large, three-engined, long range reconnaissance flying boat. Wooden hull and frame construction, with linen covering. Entered service in 1930.
Four-crew, twin-engined, general reconnaissance flying-boat. Entered service after World War One, becoming the RAF's standard flying-boat until replaced by the Supermarine Southampton in 1925.

Four-engine, ten-crew, long-range maritime reconnaissance and anti-submarine aircraft. Developed from the Short C-class Empire airliner. All metal in construction, entered RAF Coastal Command service in 1938.

Three/four-crew, single-engine, shipboard observation and air/sea rescue amphibian seaplane. Entered RAF service in 1936. Also employed for gunnery spotting, anti-submarine and convoy protection duties.

Six-crew, medium-range, twin-engined reconnaissance flying-boat. Entered service with 209 Squadron in 1939 but, due to design and operation problems, saw little action and was not produced in large numbers.
An aeroplane with the capability to land at sea, the underside of its fuselage shaped like the hull of a sea-going vessel and designed to make contact with the water.

Interbellum, twin-engined, five-crew, biplane flying-boat with a characteristic triple tail-fin. Entered service in 1925 and used for general reconnaissance duties. The Mk.I had a wooden fuselage, whilst the Mk.II's was metal in construction.

An aircraft designed to land on water. They can be divided into 2 types: Flying boats (designed with a hull allowing the aircraft to land directly on water) and Floatplanes (where the undercarriage was replaced by fixed floats).
American-built, twin-engined flying-boat designed for maritime patrol and reconnaissance. Entered US Naval service in 1936 as the PBY-1; christened the Catalina by the RAF, who used it from 1939 on.
A figurative or abstract design in the round or in relief, made by chiselling stone, carving wood, modelling clay, casting metal, or similar processes.
A representation in the round of a living being, allegorical personage, eminent person or animal, etc, sculptured, moulded or cast in marble, metal, plaster, etc.
An external wall cladding consisting of overlapping horizontal boards.

The controlled measurement of natural and artificial landscape features to produce a measured plan or a 3D data set reading as a plan. Features are depicted by either hachures, symbols or contour lines.
The accurate survey and analytical depiction of earthworks and their relative chronological relationships by means of hachures and related symbols.
The collection of information relating to the location, distribution and organisation of past humna activities involving field or site-based investigation of a certain geographic area.
The systematic survey and recording of graveyards and burial spaces recording the position of individual grave markers and the detail of any inscriptions.
Field survey undertaken to investigate land formation processes often carried out in association with, or in the vicinity of, an archaeological site, or as part of a wider landscape project.

Structured & carefully executed scanning of the ground surface with a metal detecting device in order to recover surface scatters of metal objects & plot them spatially within the study area as part of an archaeological survey or metal detecting rally.
A subsurface detection method performed by striking the ground with a heavy wooden mallet or a lead-filled container on a long handle.
The recording of a surface, or surfaces, using scanning technologies, to create a 3D model of the target structure/object.

The assessment of the age of a hedge based on its nature, condition and the number and type of woody plant species present. Most surveys make use of Hooper's hypothesis which states that for every 27m a new woody species invades a hedge every 100 years.

Ground-based or marine subsurface mapping of archaeological features using different sensing technologies. Most commonly applied are magnetometers, electrical resistance meters, ground penetrating radar, side scan sonar, and electromagnetic conductivity.

Detailed survey using photographic images to record archaeological and architectural sites or features of interest. Record photography is an important aspect of recording such features before they are destroyed.
The taking of photographs during informal site visits, which may be undertaken by amateur archaeologists or architectural students. More formal, detailed surveys should be termed Photographic Survey.

The supposed detection of subsurface features by employing a twig, copper rod, pendulum, or other instrument. Discontinuous movements in these instruments are believed by some to record the existence of buried features.
A planned programme of investigation conducted within a defined area aimed at identifying and surveying previously unrecorded sites and checking the condition of known sites.

The non intrusive processes by which information is collected about the location, distribution and organisation of past human activities that are now submerged by water. The approaches can be either extensive or intensive depending on the objectives.

The non intrusive processes by which information is collected about the location, distribution and organisation of past human activities. The approaches can be either extensive or intensive depending the objectivies that need to be addressed.
A dimensional check on a building or site giving detailed measurements.

A descriptive survey involving the systematic measurement and recording of the dimensions or features of a building. Where the survey is accompanied by systematic investigation and analysis, use Architectural Survey.

Recording and analysis of built structures utilising close observation as well as manual or electronic survey equipment such as GPS and REDM (Reflectorless Electromagnetic Distance Measurement). Includes research, fieldwork and a report.
Coarse grained, metamorphic rock in which the colour is dependent upon the predominant mineral.
An engineering works producing items for the railway other than rolling stock, such as signals, tracks, points, etc.
A broad, flat-bottomed boat.
A stone placed across a grave.
Small seeds of the leguminous plant Lens culinaris, eaten in stews and soups.
Seeds of any of the various related plants of the leguminous plant Vicia faba.
The fruit of certain varieties of the plant Capsicum Annum eaten as vegetables.
The plant, Allium cepa, whose bulb is used, usually for culinary purposes.
Any plants which are grown to be eaten. Includes parts of plants, especially roots and leaves.
The edible tubers of plants of the family Ipomoea Batatas eaten as a vegetable.
The plant, Allium sativum, whose bulb is used for culinary purposes.
The round seeds of the plant Pisum sativum which grow in pods and are eaten as a vegetable.
A cottage erected over a short period of time, by people who had no legal right to the land. Squatters were often tolerated by the landlord as they provided cheap labour.

Twin-engined, medium bomber with a 1200 mile range and a bomb load in excess of 10,000 lb. Entered service in 1940, but engine faults resulted in retirement in 1942 with its design later modified into the acclaimed four-engine Lancaster bomber.
A photo- reconnaissance variant of the Boeing Superfortress, used from 1944, initally deployed in the Pacific war, later for Cold war duties over Europe.
A Jewish graveyard headstone.
A stone placed over or at the head or foot of a grave, or at the entrance of a tomb.
A matzevah from the Sephardi group of Jews descended from medieval Jewish communities of the Iberian Peninsular and Northern Africa. Characterised by flat slabs with Hebrew Inscriptions
A matzevah from the Ashkenazi group of Jews descended from medieval Jewish communities of the Rhineland and Eastern Europe. Characterised by upright headstones with Hebrew Inscriptions
Aquatic invertebrate animals whose outer covering is a shell, often 'farmed' to be eaten. Includes molluscs and crustaceans.
A mollusc usually used as a foodstuff.
A place where gardening tools, plants, etc, are sold.
A round container open at the top, usually to hold liquids.
A bowl whose form resembles two cones joined together at their widest points, forming a carination.
An area of a site or building providing a stable base for the firing of artillery pieces.
A wealden house with only one end being jettied.
State.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production, testing and storage of gunpowder.
A building containing equipment used for the polishing of grains of gunpowder and extraction of the resulting dust.
A building in which works of art are displayed, permanently or temporarily.
A site containing plant and machinery for the manufacture of steel.
A site used for the manufacturing of steel. Use more specific type where known.
A hydraulic engine patented in 1830 comprising a large specially shaped cast-iron outer casing enclosing a close-fitting but separate solid globe.
An engine, introduced in Germany 1748 for use in mines, worked by high pressure water.
A piece of machinery used to convert energy of one sort (for instance steam) into motive energy.
An item designed to cover, decorate or enhance a wall.
Material hung from walls, excluding paper.
Large wall hung tapestries only.
A burial ground for followers of the Jewish faith.

An area used for the deposition of human remains where the principal funeral rite is the burial of the corpse complete. Generally indicated by the discovery of articulated human skeletal remains, occasionally with evidence of coffins and/or grave goods.
A house consisting of a single storey open hall with a two storey domestic range attached at one end, forming a T shape.

The Republic Aviation Corporation. Developed from the Seversky Aircraft Corporation, founded by Alexander P. de Seversky in 1931 after the collapse of his previous company, the Seversky Aero Corporation, in the 1929 stock market crash.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber. Fitted with eight fixed forward-firing machine guns in the wings, plus two 1000lb bombs or six rocket projectiles.
A form of armour made up of overlapping squares of protective material.
Armour formed from thin pieces of metal fastened together or on leather or some strong woven material.
Armour made up segmentally, usually of bands of material.
Armour made up of interlaced metal rings.
Use for the construction style of the armour, eg plate armour.
A flask with a hollow ring-shaped form. (Source: MPRG)
A bottle with a narrow neck used for wine, oil etc.
A type of stock exchange for tin which replaced the stannary courts in the mid 19th century.
A stock exchange dealing in the prices for coal and shares in coal production.
A commercial building used primarily as a trading place for breweries and hop merchants.
A commercial building used primarily as a trading place for wool merchants.
A building where samples of corn were sold or auctioned during the early to mid 19th century. When not in use, between market days, the buildings were used as public halls.
A building in which the buying of raw cotton and finished goods took place.
A building which provides the centralized market for trading in stocks and shares and for raising capital for industry.
A multi-purpose commercial building, used primarily as a trading place for merchants, but also incorporating shops, public offices, guildhalls, etc.
Materials or goods which have been produced wholly or in part from oil, e.g. petroleum.
A thick, viscous, black liquid obtained by the destructive distillation of coal or other organic substances used for preserving wood or rope and for covering road surfaces.
A member whose purpose is to keep two other members apart, so acting in a state of compression.
An upright timber similar to a crown post, but not supporting a plate.
A tunnel carrying a railway beneath the surface of the ground.
A tunnel running under a river or a hillside through which a railway line runs.
The wood from trees of the type Quercus.
A building containing a flight siumlator used to provide safe training for pilots.
A building housing a flight simulator designed to air ministry drawing number 10040/41.

skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Asylum For Aged And Decayed Freemasons
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A house devoted to the shelter of the poor and endowed by a benefactor for this use.
A Roman wine cup with a shallow bowl and a circular foot.
An aircraft used for towing gliders aloft.
An aircraft used for towing another aircraft or object, such as a glider or target.
An imprecise term used to describe large Iron Age settlements of town-like proportions.
A site with one or more defensive earthworks, often at a river crossing incorporating natural features which define parts of the curtilage.
German single-engine, four-seat maritime patrol and reconnaissance flying-boat. In production between 1934 and 1940, the DO18 was replaced by the three engined DO24.
An aeroplane with the capability to land at sea, the underside of its fuselage shaped like the hull of a sea-going vessel and designed to make contact with the water.
A factory where tweed, a twilled woollen fabric with an unfinished surface, is manufactured.
A single-seat, pusher prop, escort and patrol-fighter. Used in the UK in a Home Defence role until superseded in 1917.
The Consolidated Aircraft Corporation. In 1943 merged with Vultee Aircraft, Inc. to form the Consolidated Vultee Aircraft Corporation.
US Navy version of the four-engined, six-crew B24 heavy bomber. Modified for long-range reconnaissance duty and used as a patrol-bomber against shipping and submarines.
Four-crew, twin-engined, general reconnaissance flying-boat. Entered service after World War One, becoming the RAF's standard flying-boat until replaced by the Supermarine Southampton in 1925.
Marine Aircraft Experimental Establishment, RAF Felixstowe. Developed seaplanes and flying boats until World War Two, when the establishment moved to Helensburg, Scotland.
A pipe through which water is conducted.

The room housing the looms in a domestic handloom weavers cottage. In general, wool loomshops were above the living quarters, whereas cotton loomshops were often below in a cellar, since the floor was usually kept damp to aid the weaving of the cotton.
A band of material, often leather, or a chain or similar worn around the neck of an animal for identification and or restraint. Where this is part of harness use the specific harness term.
An early Medieval commemorative monument in the form of a stone which has been inscribed with symbols.
American-built, twin-engined flying-boat designed for maritime patrol and reconnaissance. Entered US Naval service in 1936 as the PBY-1; christened the Catalina by the RAF, who used it from 1939 on.
A book containing prayers.
A bound collection of paper or other materials.
A pin used to hold meat together whilst cooking.
Areas and spaces within a monument or site.
A pavilion ward in a workhouse, used to accommodate inmates
The class or material that a photograph is produced upon. [AAT] Use a specific term or terms as appropriate.
A photographic slide of a black and white (monochromatic) image.

A building or part of a building, sometimes attached to a religious community, where religious activities such as worshipping, meetings, teaching about the faith and conferences take place. It can also provide accommodation.
A type of retort used for distillation.
Containers used for industrial or scientific purposes.
The Fairey Aviation Co. Ltd., established 1916 by Sir Richard Fairey. During WW2 formed a group production scheme with Blackburn Aircraft, Ltd. and Boulton Paul Aircraft, Ltd..
A single-engine, two-crew biplane day bomber and general purpose aircraft, developed from the IIIF (some of which were converted into Gordons) and first flown in 1931.
A system of petrol burners, pipework and pump houses on an airfield used to 'burn' away fog so that aircraft may take off and land safely.
A bowl adapted by the addition of a single handle
A bowl adapted by the addition of one or more handles. The handles may be vertical or horizontal loops, or straight, or may comprise vertical or horizontal lugs. (Source: MPRG)

Sites, building, structures & features associated with the construction, maintenance & supply of maritime craft. Includes associated ancillary structures such as navigation aids, dockyards, wharves, etc; does not include vessels.
A site where the magnetic signature of ships was lowered thereby making them less susceptible to magnetic mines.
A small roofed shelter for cattle without tethering point or stalls, but with a small yard attached. It is often detached from the main range of farm buildings.
A piece of metal or wood with a hole through which a bolt can be screwed.
An area, often consisting of widened streets or a town square, where booths and stalls may be erected for public sales.

A type of goose pen with stone-clad compartments, built into the base of a Cornish hedge near the periphery of a farmstead. Aspect is often towards entrance track or driveway since geese were used in similar role to guard dogs. Particular to Cornwall.
A factory or complex containing machinery for the manufacture of printed materials.
A factory complex consisting of PRINTING SHOPS, COLOUR HOUSES, DYE HOUSES, etc, in which patterns are printed onto calico.
A building, site or structure associated with the playing of ball sports.
An area of grass, marked out for use in the game of cricket.
A twin-engined development of the JU88, the JU188 had a higher service ceiling and greater maximum speed. JU188s operated over the UK from 1944 onwards as night intruders and reconnaissance aircraft.
A type of fabric often used to trim clothing.
A small pierced disc which glitters, used as ornamentation on clothing
A piece of material, eg metal, cloth, leather etc, added to a button to enhance or embellish it.
Clothes, items of attire and ornament and objects for personal use by individuals, including toiletries.
A narrow strip of fine material, used for trimming or tying.
A woven fabric used to trim clothes.
Items which are used in clothing but which are not necessarily a separate item of clothing.
A walkway on the top of a defensive wall, providing access to the parapets and towers.
A wide mouthed container, usually cylindrical without handles.
A jar with a roughly cylindrical or slightly flaring lower body and a rounded, inward sloping shoulder. (Source: MPRG)
Thin rods or threads of metal formed by rolling or wire-drawing and used for a variety of purposes including electrical circuitry.
Thick ropes and rigging.
The framing of a door or window with two columns piers or pilasters which support a lintel,entablature etc.

The Stinson Division of The Consolidated Vultee Aircraft Corporation. Originally the Stinson Aircraft Division of the Aviation Manufacturing Corpn., who were taken over by Vultee Aircraft Inc., who merged with the Consolidated Aircraft Corpn. in 1943.

Single-engine navigation trainer and communications aircraft. Constructed of tubular steel and duralumin frame, with a duralumin and canvas covering, 500 were delivered to the FAA, serving from 1944-5.

Aircraft Manufacturing Co., Ltd. Established in 1912 by Mr G. Holt Thomas. In 1914 secured the services of Capt. Geoffrey de Havilland as designer-in-chief, who went on to lend his initials to a number of highly successful machines.
A single-seat fighter which began service with the RFC's fighter squadron in 1916. Some short-term success in dealing with new Fokkers but was withdrawn from service in mid-1917.
A group of buildings or rooms equipped with apparatus for scientific experiments or other research, testing and investigations.
A scientific laboratory where marine life is studied and researched.
A plan form of a structure or building.
A plan in which a chimney containing back-to-back fireplaces heats two rooms simultaneously by being placed within the dividing wall.
A place of entry into a site, monument or building.
A form of entrance closed by a gate.
The residence of the head or president of a chapter, or community of religious persons.
Residences of religious people and members of the clergy.
A residence for all clergy having the sole or subordinate charge of a living.
A place from which chalk is extracted.
A pit from which sand is excavated.
Surface workings including shallow shafts, lode workings, open-pit methods and quarrying including some mines of stone, clays, compounds, etc. See also MINERAL EXTRACTION SITE.
A site where copper ore is extracted directly from the surface of the ground.
A steep-sided pit formed by, and for, the extraction of gravel.

A pit dug to extract Sarsen stones from the superficial geology in which they occur. They range in size from one dug for the extraction of a single boulder to pits from which multiple boulders are extracted & date from the Neolitic to the mid 20th century
An extractive pit or pits, usually 2.5m square by 2m deep dug to extract tin ore in areas where streamworking is not possible. Usually dug along a vein rather than across it.
A pit from which marl, a mixture of clay and carbonate of lime, is excavated. Marl is used as a fertilizer.
A site where iron ore is extracted.
A site where iron oxide and iron sulphates, used as brown pigments, are excavated.
A pit in the ground from where minerals are dug.
The name of a class of excavations, found in chalk formations in England, consisting of a shaft sunk to the chalk, and there widening out into one or more chambers.
A site where jet is extracted from the surface of the ground.
A place where lead ore is extracted from an open cast mine.
A pit for the extraction of fullers earth (a hydrous silicate of alumina), which was used for cleansing, and finishing, cloth and wool.

A trench dug through topsoil in an arable field in order to extract underlying clay which was then spread on the field and ploughed in to improve soil fertility. Usually found in peaty soil areas such as the Lincolnshire and Cambridgeshire fenlands.
A large, powerful, hand-drawn bow, usually 6 ft (1.8m) in length and traditionally made of wood.
A weapon for shooting arrows.
Equipment for the hunting and capture of animals.
A building where students study theatre and the dramatic arts.
A small port town on the coast of northern Lolland.
An enclosure surrounded by a wooden stockade. A rare site type of Neolithic date.
A measure for dry substances. A quarter of a bushel.
A container which holds a set quantity of a substance, can be graduated to show quantities.
A kiln that is octagonal in plan. Use with functional kiln type where known.
A site where gypsum and anhydrate is mined.
A bridge with two or more decks allowing it to carry various modes of transport at the same time.
Single-engine, single-seat fighter-bomber. Designed to replace the Hurricane as an interceptor, excelled as a rocket-projectile-firing ground-attack fighter. Entered RAF service in 1941.

A Dutch barge-like sailing vessel whose shallow draught enables it to navigate in shallow water not accessible by other vessels. Used for fishing or carriage of cargo in the 19th century this type of vessel was adapted for use as a type of leisure craft.
A site where a body of troops is temporarily or permanently lodged, with or without entrenchments and fortifications.
A site where an army or body of troops is, temporarily or permanently, lodged, with or without entrenchments and fortifications.
A gun designed to be held in one hand. It has a short barrel length compared to long guns.
A handheld weapon that fires missiles by means of explosives.
A hand held long barrelled gun.
A smooth bore weapon usually for firing shot as opposed to bullets.
Buildings, engineering constructions and machinery, used for the purpose of supplying a town, etc, with water distributed through pipes.

Twin-engine, three-crew, long-range heavy bomber biplane. Entered service in 1917. Of wooden construction with a fabric covering, the Vimy was fitted with a skid under the nose of its fuselage to prevent tipping forward upon landing.
A type of pavilion sometimes found in public parks or country house estates.
A tall, usually steel, structure used to receive and transmit radio telegraphy signals.
Written communication, generally in the form of letters.
Originally designed as a trainer but relegated to use by the RNAS in a Maritime Reconnaissance and anti-submarine role when the Avro 504 became the standard trainer.
An opening in a wall, roof, door, etc to allow light to enter. Usually used to include all component parts.
A window set within a curved projection from the face of a wall.
A maritime monument where the fabric of a vessel has collapsed, leaving the hull structure flat on the sea bed but not widely dispersed.
A temporary support placed under a vault or arch to support them during construction.
Military provisions, traditionally of all types but now used specifically for projectiles and propellants such eg. bullets and gunpowder.
Manufactured goods, including shells, dynamite etc., containing substances which can be made to explode.
Weapons used for cutting and thrusting, consisting of a blade and a hilt.
Military weapons, amunition and stores.
Weapons including portable firearms and large artillery pieces.
A road used primarily, but not exclusively, for the rapid transport of military vehicles, equipment and personnel.
A short squat gun or cannon used to test the strength of coarser blasting powders. Mainly 18th-19th centuries.
A gun designed to fire shells, etc at a high angle.
An area of hardstanding to allow movement of farm transport in all weathers.
A type of temporary bridge designed by Sir Donald C.Bailey during the Second World War.
A type of bridge which was designed for temporary use and then capable of being moved to another site. Use for temporary bridges which have remained in situ since erection.
Concrete or steel pontoons that supported the Whale piers. They were moored in position using wires attsched to Kite anchors.

A floating pier, comprised of a floating pierhead (SPUD) and a roadway resting on pontoons (BEETLES). The pierhead and roadway were capable of rising and falling with the tide enabling unloading of troops and equipment to occur at any state of the tide.
Includes worsted and other wool-related textiles.
A factory where worsted, a well-twisted woollen yarn made from long staple wool and used in the manufacture of suits and other garments, was produced.

A boat specifically designed for saving lives at sea, they can be either: a boat carried on a larger vessel for use in emergency evacuation of crew and passengers in the event of shipwreck or a boat built for the purpose of shore-to-sea rescue missions.
Items of crockery and cutlery which are used whilst dining, either to eat with or for table decoration.
Tableware manufactured from any kind of ceramic and either carried as an export cargo or for the benefit of crew and/or passengers on board ship.
Metal knives, forks and spoons, carried either as an export cargo or for crew and/or passengers.
Goods, including portable objects and furniture, commonly found in the home.
A malleable, ductile ferromagnetic metal widely used for structural and decorative purposes.
Iron coated in zinc, giving good protection against weathering.
A building specifically built to house life saving apparatus used when conditions prevented the lifeboat from deploying.
Buildings, sites and structures used by mariners for purposes of navigation.
A building designed to house a lifeboat, usually with a stone ramp to launch the boat into the sea.
A plain stone course, sometimes projecting, above a cornice and counterbalancing the cantilevered sections of stone, or at the base of a building.
One of a pair of crossing braces halved or lapped across each other, tying a pair of rafters together.
An inclined timber used to support and provide rigidity to roofs, partitions etc.
A type of jug decorated with applied figures in the form of knights in armour. (Source: MPRG)

Originally denoting a Byzantine vessel, powered by oars, from the 6th century onwards, this developed into a large Mediterranean ship with oars and a single mast, used for trade or for war transport, (e.g. during the Crusades) until the 15th century.
A channel or pipe providing water to a canal or other body of water.
A deep gutter, drain or sink.
Artificial water channel, usually leading to a mill.
A channel used for or formed by the conveyance of water. Can be natural, eg. a river or artificial eg. an aqueduct. Use more specific type where known.
An artificial watercourse for the conveyance of water.
A tool for boring holes.
A drill where the bit is twisted by means of a bow with the string wound around the shaft of the drill.
Short publication used to disseminate information about a particular project or organisation, issued on a regular basis.
General term for documents that have been produced in large numbers for public sale or distribution.

Also known as the C-47 Skytrain, this twin-engined, military transport was developed from the DC-3 twenty-eight-seat commercial airliner and was the most extensively employed transport of the Second World War.
A temporary fieldwork, usually a few feet in height, constructed for defence against enemy forces.
Railway constructed specifically for the movement of coal around the pithead of a coal mine.
A tunnel with a canal running through it.
A canal tunnel built with one or more integral towpaths
The cutting or chopping part of an adze; bifacially worked, longitudinal section symmetrical, cutting edge parallel to the direction of the hafted tool as swung.
A factory in which logs are converted to timber by running them through a series of saws.
North American Aviation, Inc., incorporated in Delaware in 1928.
Two-seat, single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer. Square-winged and fitted with dual controls, this popular trainer was used by British Commonwealth, as well as American and Canadian, air forces.
A semi-circular opening or window divided, by two mullions, into three sections, the central section being wider than those either side of it.
A window divided into lights by mullions.
An object which has been bent and angled from which something else can be caught or suspended.
A hook with a spiked tang which allows it to be driven into a vertical surface.
A hook from which a lamp could be hung.
A residence for military personnel.
Purpose built accommodation for members of the armed forces and their families.
A building where military officers are accommodated.
A hut used for the accommodation of members of the armed forces.
A building used to house members of the armed forces.
A building where non-commissioned aircrew are housed.
A large drain or conduit for carrying away wastes.
The outlet or mouth of a sewer where it dispenses into the sea, lake, etc.
Buildings, structures and sites directly associated with the operation of military airfields. See also AIR TRANSPORT SITE in the TRANSPORT Class.
A modified Nissen hut, based on drawing number (2900/43), used for the repair packing and storage of inflatable liferafts.
A sweet, crystalline subtance obtained from sugar beet or sugar cane and used in cooking, brewing etc.
A horn containing gun powder used for priming a firearm.
Vickers (Aviation) Ltd. formed in 1911, as the aviation division of Vickers Ltd., and took control of Supermarine Aviation Works Ltd. the same year. Taken over by Vickers-Armstrongs Ltd. in 1938.
Twin-engined, four-crew bomber. Wooden framed, with linen covering, entered service in 1924, equipping several RAF squadrons.
An object used within a divinational process.
A staff used in divination.
A chamber for the incarceration of one or more prisoners.
A hidden dungeon entered through a trap door from the room above it. Also a similarly concealed pit into which prisoners would be cast.
A large shed for the housing of aircraft, etc.
Vertical screens made of wood or steel framing mounted on concrete blocks were built to protect airships from cross winds when entering or leaving the airship sheds.
A hangar for the storage and maintenance of dirigible motor-driven balloons.
A passage providing access to utility services or a larger tunnel for the purposes of monitoring and maintenance. May also provide be used as an evacuation route.
A narrow means of access, often internal.
A canal tunnel built with one or more integral towpaths
A tunnel with a canal running through it.

Also known as the C-47 Skytrain, this twin-engined, military transport was developed from the DC-3 twenty-eight-seat commercial airliner and was the most extensively employed transport of the Second World War.
The main administrative building and headquarters of a regiment
A prepared area of ground used to play the game of golf on.
A golf course, usually situated on or near the coast, consisting of sand dunes with few trees or water obstacles.
An obstacle on a golf course constituting a hazard. Usually taking the form of a sand trap or dirt mound.

A prime mover in which a central wheel with curved vanes, enclosed in a chamber, receives water directed onto the curved vanes by a ring of fixed guide vanes, causing the wheel to rotate about its axis.
An impulse water turbine comprising a wheel with hemispherical cups arranged around the circumference using high water pressure to revolve the wheel.
Originally a light day-bomber, the Boston II, re-christened the Havoc, was adapted for night-flying in the fighter-intruder role. Was capable of a top speed in excess of 300 mph.
High speed, short to medium-range bomber, usually powered by two engines.
British, single-engined, light day bomber biplane. Built in 1923, this was the RAF's first interbellum designed day bomber.
British three-seat, single-engine light bomber. All metal in construction, this monoplane had a 1000 lb bomb load.
Twin-engined, four-crew German seaplane. Entered service in 1932 as a torpedo bomber and naval reconnaisance aircraft, though by World War 2 those still serving were used mainly for air sea rescue.
A managed small wood or thicket of underwood grown to be periodically cut to encourage new growth providing smaller timber.
An area of cultivated, managed woodland producing wood which is used for a variety of purposes.
A container holding a set quantity used specifically for measuring grains or cereal.
A measure for dry substances. A quarter of a bushel.
A container to provide a set amount of gun powder.
A container used to measure liquids.
A container which holds a set quantity of a substance, can be graduated to show quantities.
A measuring container to measure dry goods.
A joint in which the tenon passes completely through the receiving timber.
A space or area that is outside a building.
An open roofed structure on which climbing plants are grown in order to provide a shaded walkway or seating area.
A slender and elegant base usually of Attic type with two tori, two scotiae and two astragals.
A building on a river or canal in which the water levels are controlled.
A small gate swinging in a U or V-shaped enclosure, which allows only one person to pass through at a time.
An early plastic formed from a condensation reaction of phenol with formaldehyde which was developed by Leo Baekeland in 1907.
Materials used in the manufacture of objects.
A protected chamber for investigating the controlled detonation and burning of explosive compounds, typically associated with a protected control room and high speed visual recording facilities.
A stone used to cover a grave.
A North country memorial imitating a wattled hut decorated with formalized bears or snakes.
A stone, slate, iron or wooden structure used to mark the site of a grave. Use only where evidence of the form is uncertain otherwise use more specific type.
Wooden board marking a grave.
A grave marker in the form of a casket.
An oblong mass of hardened clay or mud, used in building.
A brick made of clay which is difficult to fuse, used in boilers and fireplaces.

Fleet Air Arm fighter and torpedo-bomber, designed for operation from aircraft carriers. All-metal in construction, it entered service in 1944 and was rendered obsolete after the war by the advent of the jet aircraft.
Aircraft designed for the carrying and dropping of torpedoes.
A set of steps or a framework of bars and steps for crossing over a fence or wall.
Sites and structures associated with pedestrian transport.
The external face or elevation of a building, especially the principal front.
Describes a Classical interior, exterior or facade without pilasters or columns.
A place where hops are stored.
A heavy framework of parallel beams used to support a ship in dock.
A storage rack for sections of steel plate used in the construction of ships.
A building or site used for the production of anchors.
An open metalwork structure supporting either a fabrication shed or the runners for an overhead crane.
Specialized engineering workshop particularly for the production of marine engines or other large components of ships.
Covered area for making large engineered constructions such as sections of ships or bridges.
Large covered spaces where the steel plate used for ship construction was cut and marked out, prior to being craned onto the hull, etc.
A command post used to direct the guns of a coastal battery.
A device in the form of a loop with a flat base hung on either side of a saddle to support the rider's foot.
Twin-engined, four-crew German seaplane. Entered service in 1932 as a torpedo bomber and naval reconnaisance aircraft, though by World War 2 those still serving were used mainly for air sea rescue.
A factory where jute (plant fibres), was used to make products such as hessian, sacking, cordage and backing materials for carpet and linoleum.
Buildings, sites or structures used for the manufacture of linen and/or flax.
A large, level structure, usually of stone or timber, built alongside water to allow warships to moor for the loading and unloading of guns.
A large wooden structure built alongside the water's edge where ships may lie for unloading.
A trumpet type of instrument made from or in imitation of an animal horn.
An instrument which has a cupped mouthpiece and may have a straight, bent or curved tube. It includes slide trumpets like the trombone.
A war trumpet, usually Iron Age.
An instrument in which air is made to vibrate by the player vibrating their lips and blowing into a mouthpiece.
A horn used in hunting to give signals.
A Roman market hall principally selling meat and poultry but also other provisions.
A place where meat is displayed for sale.
A place of worship for members of the Romanian Orthodox Church, the national church of Romania.
A place of worship for followers of the Eastern Orthodox churches. This family of churches separated from the Western church in the 11th century and recognizes the Patriarch of Constantinople.
Room within a building or complex used by a porter.
An arch produced by two curves, usually each with a radius equal to the span, which meet at a point.
A curved construction, spanning an opening, formed from wedge-shaped blocks supported by mutual pressure; they can also be formed from moulded concrete and cast metal.
