A pointed arch in which the arcs comprising it are centred on points both outside and inside the arch so that the point takes the form of a double S, or ogee.
A pointed, two-centred, arch whose height is much greater than its span.
A pointed, two centred, arch whose span is greater than its height.
Includes interim, research, specialist reports on a specific topic.
Report prepared by a specialist in a particular field, often as a contribution to a wider project.
A manor house, which was granted a royal licence to crenellate.
A man made ditch designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle. Ditches were often reveted with concrete or wood.
A natural ditch the depth and/or width of which has been increased so as to prevent the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle.
Obstacles like concrete cubes, cylinders or pimples erected in the defence of Britain.
Stop-line against invading tanks in form of a ditch during the defence of Britain.
A bridge carrying a road over land or water.
Photographic image produced on transparent medium suitable for use in projection equipment. Use specific term where known.
Photographic transparency on an acetate base material.
Threads of material used to form cloth.
A strong unbleached cloth manuifactured from hemp, flax or similarly coarse yarn. Used mainly in the manufacture of sails, tents and for painting on.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around three sides of an open cattle yard.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around one or more sides of an open cattle yard.
A farmstead where the working buildings are arranged around a yard.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around four sides of an open cattle yard.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around one side of an open cattle yard.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around two sides of an open cattle yard.
A stone or stone platform in a fire upon which cooking vessels are placed.

The fertilized ovules of a plant, often occurring in an archaeological context, in the form of small roundish bodies or grains. Seeds are dispersed naturally or collected for sowing to produce a new generation of plants.
Remains of the endocarp (stone) of a member of the genus Prunus which includes sloes, plums, cherries, apricots and peaches.
An object which has words inscribed, engraved carved or written upon it.
An inscribed marker stone found on Hadrian's Wall.
A chamber for heating or baking objects.
Diesel engined submarine designed for long ocean voyages in search of enemy shipping.
A vessel designed to operate below the surface of the sea.
Containers identified by the form they take rather than by function.
A vessel consisting of three small pots joined, often on a hollow ring, at the base.
Flat, rectangular piece of material, traditionally of wood but now of any material, used in the construction industries.

A French airliner produced in 1925. A four-engined biplane developed from the Bleriot 115 and 135 but larger than these. Two were built for Air Union (the Paris-London route). Both crashed with fatalaties in 1926 (Kent).

A French aircraft manufacturer founded by Louis Bleriot and Gabriel Voisin, both aviators and inventors, in 1903, dissolved in 1906. After World War I Bleriot founded Bleriot Aeronautique developing commercial aircraft.
The Middle Stone Age, falling between the Palaeolithic and the Neolithic; marks the beginning of a move from a hunter gatherer society towards food producing society.
The latest subdivision of the Mesolithic, or Middle Stone Age.

Troop and general transport glider. Almost entirely wooden in construction, many were manufactured by the furniture industry. Mk I featured a a door-ramp on the port side whilst the Mk II was fitted with a hinged nose.
An engineless aeroplane, designed to be towed aloft, that travels suspended by upward air currents.
Principal glider-pilot training glider fitted with tandem seats. Spruce and plywood in construction, the Hotspur served with the Glider Pilot Regiment between 1941 and 1945.

Wood and fabric transport glider, twenty of which were produced with twin Bristol Mercury engines. Fitted with a hinged nose for loading and unloading, this was the largest glider used by the RAF and could accomodate a 7-ton tank.
Aircraft grouped according to their physical form.

American troop and supply-glider constructed from steel tube and fabric-covered wood, with a hinged nose to allow loading and unloading of troops or light vehicles. Also known as the Haig, this was the only US glider to see combat service.

Six-crew, medium-range, twin-engined reconnaissance flying-boat. Entered service with 209 Squadron in 1939 but, due to design and operation problems, saw little action and was not produced in large numbers.
A British aero- and marine-engineering company based on the Isle of Wight specializing in the construction of flying boats.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
The Consolidated Vultee Aircraft Corporation. Formed in 1943 with the merging of The Consolidated Aircraft Corporation and Vultee Aircraft, Inc..
Single-engine aircraft designed as a dive-bomber. Found to be inadequate in this role, a number of those delivered to the RAF were used as target tugs. Entered service in 1941.
Vultee Aircraft, Inc.. In 1943 merged with The Consolidated Aircraft Corporation to form The Consolidated Vultee Aircraft Corporation.
The entrance to a building, apartment or any enclosure consisting of a movable barrier, usually lockable, of wood or other materials.
A priest's private entrance into a church, usually found on the south side of the chancel.
A single-seat, pusher prop, escort and patrol-fighter. Used in the UK in a Home Defence role until superseded in 1917.
A bridge carrying a railway track across a river, valley, road etc.
A waterwheel where the inflow of water strikes the paddles, or floatboards, below the axis of the wheel.
An undershot waterwheel, developed by General Jean Victor Poncelet (1788-1867) in France, which improved efficiency through the replacement of flat, wooden paddles with curved, metal vanes.
Circular structure, normally indicated by one or more rings of post holes and/or a circular gulley, and usually interpreted as being of domestic function.
A sea within a sea, the Andaman Sea consists of that part of the Indian Ocean bordered by Myanmar, Thailand, Malaysia, Sumatra and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
An area of the northern Indian Ocean bordered by India, Bangladesh and Myanmar.
A sea within a sea, the Arabian Sea consists of the northern part of the Indian Ocean bordered by India, Pakistan, Iran, Oman and Yemen.
Bordering the continents of Africa, Antarctica, Asia and Australasia, the Indian Ocean covers 28,364,000 square miles.
A piece of forest land converted into arable.
An area of cultivated, managed woodland producing wood which is used for a variety of purposes.
A staircase divided into two parallel flights joined by a landing with no well between the outer strings.
An object used for counting, keeping count or marking the position of a player in a game, usually in the form of a small circular-shaped piece of bone, metal, wood, plastic or other material.
A single line, or pair of roughly parallel lines, of pits set at intervals along a common axis or series of axes. The pits are not thought to have held posts.
A pit alignment accompanied by a linear bank (or banks) running parallel and adjacent to the line(s) of pits.

A stone, either in situ or part of a monument, bearing one or more small, roughly hemispherical depressions surrounded by a concentric arrangement of annular or pennanular grooves. More complex designs may also occur.
A public ground with facilities for games and other activities.
A sports pitch usually with a synthetic surface (ie. not grass).
Soft coverings and associated objects used within buildings.
All linen used at the table, including tablecloths.
A building in a garden or park designed to provide a shady retreat from the heat of the sun.
The residence and sometimes workplace of industrial workers.
A type of clothier's house, consisting of TOPSHOP and dwelling, used for hand-weaving of textiles.
A place where paper, frequently printed in ornamental designs, used for covering the interior walls of buildings, is manufactured.
A machine producing mechanical power by the internal combustion of gas.
A substantial area of ground surrounded by slight univallate earthwork often interpreted as stock enclosures or as sites where agricultural produce was stored.

A small, defended settlement dating to the Early Iron Age, located on spurs, promontories or hilltops. The defences are marked by single or double trenches which originally held substantial palisades.
Use for vessels registered in Romania.
A tippler, a machine for loading wagons at a pithead, operated by hydraulic power.
Loading machinery tipping coal into railway wagons usually at a pithead.
A general term given to all horizontal timbers laid on walls or posts in order to support other timbers.
A timber running above vertical posts, in the place of a wall-plate, within a timber-framed building.
American, four-engined, long range, medium/heavy day bomber. Produced in greater numbers than any other American aircraft during the war.
A deep, rectangular or oval, straight-sided vessel with an everted, crenellated rim, used to hold either wax for dipping candles or molten sulphur for dipping matches. (Source: MPRG)
"Looking glasses", up to and including the medieval period made of polished steel or other reflective metals; later a piece of glass with a reflective coating, e.g. silver or aluminium.
An opening in the ridge of a roof intended to provide ventilation or an outlet for smoke; also the hood on such an opening that prevents rain entering.
An opening normally in a door or window filled with diagonally set slats to provide ventilation.
A square, concrete pillbox-like structure with 36in thick walls and a single large embrasure used to emplace a Vickers Medium Machine Gun. The entrance was protected by an external blast wall.
A structure, usually or concrete or sandbags, in which a machine gun was emplaced.
An aerial lift in which cabins are suspended from a continuous cable between two towers which hold the winding mechanism. The cable may be supported by towers or pylons.
A means of transportation where cars, chairs or cabins are carried above the ground by means of one or more cables suspended between towers or pylons.
Structures used for the lifting or hoisting of goods, machinery, vehicles, people and livestock.
A building used to dry teazle heads in. Teazles were used to raise the nap on cloth in teazle shops.
Use for vessels believed to come from Asia but where the precise nationality is not known.
Use for vessels registered in Pakistan.
A place where public sales of goods are made by competitive bidding.
A searchlight battery used to light a beach.
North Yorkshire
A jar adapted by the addition of a single handle. Profiles vary and should be double indexed with the appropriate JAR type. (Source: MPRG)
A jar adapted by the addition of one or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
A factory where shirts are manufactured.
A factory or works housing machinery used to produce stockings and socks, using mechanized knitting processes.
A factory where collars, for shirts and other garments, are manufactured.
A factory where hats are manufactured.
A large factory or series of workshops for the manufacture of clothing.
A factory where knitted fabrics are manufacterd using knitting machines.
A factory where gloves are manufactured.
A factory or site where wooden clogs are manufactured.
A factory where boots and shoes are manufactured.
A German coastal minelaying submarine in use during the First World War.
Covered area for making large engineered constructions such as sections of ships or bridges.
Large covered spaces where the steel plate used for ship construction was cut and marked out, prior to being craned onto the hull, etc.
A building or site used for the production of anchors.
Specialized engineering workshop particularly for the production of marine engines or other large components of ships.
An open metalwork structure supporting either a fabrication shed or the runners for an overhead crane.
A heavy framework of parallel beams used to support a ship in dock.
A storage rack for sections of steel plate used in the construction of ships.
The principal house of a manor or village.
Netherlands
Zeeland
A religious receptacle, especially Jewish where it contains four Hebrew texts worn during morning prayers.
A single-seat, biplane fighter. One of the last open cockpit types to see widespread service with the RAF, equipping 10 squadrons and, at one point, 70% of the Home Defence fighter force.
British two-seat, twin-engined night fighter. Also used for roles such as long-range escort fighter, ground-attack and anti-shipping strike aircraft, bomber, torpedo-carrier and rocket fighter.
The Bristol Aeroplane Co., Ltd.. Founded in 1910 by Sir George White, a pioneer of electric tramways. The company had previously been The British and Colonial Aeroplane Co., Ltd..

Highly successful, two-seat, biplane fighter and reconnaissance aircraft with both forward and rear facing guns. Designed to replace the BE2, it entered service with the RFC in mid-1917 and remained in service until 1932.

Twin-engined, four-seat torpedo-bomber designed to replace the Vildebeest. Entered service with RAF Coastal Command in 1939. Later versions incorporated a remote-controlled machine gun with periscope sight.
British twin-engined light/medium bomber developed from the model 142 civil transport. Noted for its speed, this three-crew monoplane had an all-metal, stressed skin structure and a 1000lb bomb load.
The area surrounding a monastic house including conventual buildings, outbuildings, cemetery, fishponds, etc, usually marked out by a bank and/or ditch or precinct wall.
Shallow ditches and/or poles erected across open land to obstruct the landing of enemy aircraft and gliders.
Submerged obstacles to stop the landing of Seaplanes
A tool with an edged head and a wooden shaft, used for a variety of purposes. Where the function is known use the more specific terms of AXE (TOOL) or AXE (WEAPON).
A tool with an edged head and a wooden shaft, used for a variety of purposes.
For chemical processes making nylon, rayon, etc.
A jar with vertical concave body walls. (Source: MPRG)
A concave sided jar made in tin-glazed earthenware. (Source: MPRG)
A building with a range of educational and recreational facilities for the exclusive use of its all-female membership.
Positive image on continuous film strip suitable for projection of moving images.
Any material that records, holds and communicates information in a primarily visual manner.
A single-engine, heavy, long range, three to five-crew day bomber. Served only with 99 Squadron RAF, 1924-5.

A. V. Roe & Co., Ltd. formed in 1909. A subsidiary of the Hawker Siddeley Aircraft Co., Ltd. from 1935, having formerly been a member of the Siddeley group. Produced such notable aircraft as the Lancaster, the York and the Anson.
A small, flat band or fillet around a shaft or column.
A stone erected to mark a particular spot in the landscape. Can be used for various reasons.
A marker stone used to demarcate the boundaries of peat cutting grounds and indicate who held the rights for each particular parcel of land.
A marker stone showing the extent of a measure of land containing a vein of ore.
A marker stone erected to indicate a claim to the rights, usually mineral, of an area.

Twin-engined bomber. The Whitley was the first 'heavy' bomber to be built in quantity for the RAF and made the first bombing attack on Germany in May 1940. It was later used for convoy protection and reconnaissance.
A chamber in which minerals, metals, etc, are subjected to the continuous action of intense heat. Use specific type where known.
For reheating of worked metal or glass to make it malleable or to harden it after use for toolmaking, etc.
An engine in which the mechanical force of steam is made available as a motive power for driving machinery.
Small mobile steam engine.
A freestanding structure commemorating nations, actions, soldiers and/or civilians that served or died as a result of conflict.
A structure, building or site commemorating soldiers and civilians killed in war.

A site, complex or building which has been converted for use as the headquarters for the civilian authorities in the event of a nuclear attack or major natural disaster destroying the seat of government.
A building used to coordinate civil defence in times of war. Can also be utilized as aid centres in times of national emergency.
A building used for the daily administration of Civil Defence activities.
A pump used to move water.
A type of water pump used in the Wigan coalfields in the late 18th and 19th centuries.
A container used for holding or serving food, especially an open shallow container.
A dish adapted by the addition of a pedestal base. (Source: MPRG)
Space used for storage in the roof.
An apartment contained, wholly or partially, within the roof space of a house.
An area partly or fully within the roof space of a building.
One of a building's horizontal divisions, being the space between two floors, or a floor and the roof structure.
A roof made up of common and principal rafters.
A tall, usually steel, structure used to receive and transmit radio signals in order to determine the height, distance and number of aircraft approaching.
A large drainage channel used for improving the land.
Twin-engined, single-seat fighter-bomber. Flown by USAAF fighter groups from 1942, excelled as a ground-support fighter. Could carry two 1600 lb bombs or rocket projectiles.
A large wooden structure built alongside the water's edge where ships may lie for unloading.
A large wooden structure built alongside the edge of a river where boats may lie for the loading and unloading of goods and passengers.

American, single-engine fighter designed for operation from US Naval aircraft carriers. The Hellcat was a more powerful version of the Wildcat, a total of 1000 being provided to the Fleet Air Arm under Lend-Lease.
Residential development, including housing, flats, tower blocks etc. For single houses use: building construction

Formed in 1935 by Lawrence D. Bell, Ray P. Whitman and Robert J. Woods, who left the Consolidated Aircraft Corporation when it moved its factory from Buffalo to San Diego. Sub-contracted work before its first original design, the XFM-1, in 1937.
Single-seat fighter-bomber with a single, midships engine and tricycle landing gear. After proving a failure as an air-combat fighter, was used mainly in the ground attack role.
Soft, medium grained, green/grey coloured, highly calcareous, cretaceous sandstone. Mined (more frequently than quarried) since pre-Norman times from the Reigate area of Surrey.

Geologically sandstone consists of particles of quartz naturally cemented together by either silica, calcium or iron. It is this geological composition that accounts for the varying colours and grain sizes found in the many building sandstones.
A hall in which public assemblies and meetings can be held.
Generic term for all vessels used to supply warships with any type of fuel.
Evidence of past environmental conditions, eg insect, seed, pollen remains
A building or room where items of pottery are manufactured. Includes handcrafted and machine made pottery.
Small settlement with no ecclesiastical or lay administrative function.
Engagement between any combination of warship, privateer, or commercial vessel in a time of war but not itself a battle. Such skirmishes may precede or follow naval battles.

Raid or assault by ships upon a terrestrial location, typically a settlement or town, which may involve a terrestrial incursion and damage to buildings and/or capture of people. It is distinct from a battle or naval skirmish.
Seaborne assault landing troops ashore with resultant fighting on land, examples being the Battle of Maldon, 991, the Normandy landings of WWII and so on.
Movements of men, munitions, and supplies in support either of naval manoeuvres and engagements or of terrestrial troop movements at home and abroad.
A lodging house for apprentices learning a trade or profession. This accommodation was often provided in lieu of wages.
A broad class of drawing that is produced following precise conventions of scale and projection. [AAT]
General term for images used to represent a particular place or item, or convey information.
A representation of a monument or landscape based on historical or archaeological information.
A plan of a feature or small area generally done in the field to quickly record the main features.
A manually produced image for illustration or record purposes.
A drawn representation of an archaeological 'find' or other cultural object.

Buildings used for the accommodation, welfare and recreation of servicemen, especially those serving in the Royal Air Force. Use only for buildings associated with military installations. For non-military, use DOMESTIC class and its narrower terms.
A hostel used to accommodate members of the Womens Land Army who undertook essential agricultural work during the Second World War.
A container for the storage of rice.
A storage container designed to contain corn.
A container for the storing of substances.
A factory where general hardware, fittings, items of ironmongery are produced.
A wooden bench with a back and ends, usually fixed and found in churches. The bench ends are often decorated.
An enclosed, high-sided seat, sometimes entered through a door, usually found in churches as one of a series of box-like compartments.
A specialist hospital where medical and surgical dental treatment takes place.
A fence or row of stakes, often with nets attached forming an enclosure within a river or harbour and used for catching, or holding, fish.

A structure comprising of two walls of stone or wood with nets or fish traps attached. Located in coastal waters, on shelving coastlines or in river estuaries they form large enclosures with a V or L shaped plan. The narrow point on the seaward side.
A device for catching fish, may be a portable or permanent structure, often a fence or row stakes made in a river, harbour, etc
A bridge, often over a canal or road, allowing access between two parcels of land.
A container for ointments or perfume.
A building or site incorporating equipment used for detecting the presence of enemy aircraft or ships. Radar Stations can also be used to aid aircraft navigation in dark or poor conditions.

Part of the WWII air defence radar system, whereby in 1939 a chain of radar stations were established along the south and east coast of Britain. The equipment was based upon apparatus developed for ionospheric research.
A forester's cottage.
A two-seat trainer chosen to replace the Avro 504. 380 entered RAF service with many finding their way onto the civilian market at the end of their careers.
A site used for the manufacture of lasts, shoemaker's models of the foot for shaping and repairing footwear. Lasts can be from a variety of materials, such as wood or iron.
A large factory or series of workshops for the manufacture of clothing.
A factory for the manufacture of heels for the shoe making trade.
Factory making slippers.
A factory where boots and shoes are manufactured.
Animal remains bearing evidence, such as knife marks on bones, that they were slaughtered and used for food.
A smooth bore weapon usually for firing shot as opposed to bullets.
A handheld weapon that fires missiles by means of explosives.
A heavy, smooth bore, long barrelled weapon, fired from the shoulder.
A long barrelled firearm. The barrel is spirally grooved on the interior, which gives the bullet a spinning motion leading to greater accuracy over a longer range.
A hand held long barrelled gun.
A fully automatic mounted or portable firearm, usually designed to fire bullets in quick succession from an ammunition belt or magazine.
An area of the floor, wall or ceiling of a building, which has been painted, carved, sculpted or decorated.
A carved figure or design.
A building from which the administration of a county is carried out by the County Council. It is also, historically, the site where the county quarter sessions and assizes were held.
The offices of a Government Department responsible for the administration of the country.
A building which houses the administrative functions of a local authority.
Forms used in the recording of archaeological or other site investigations.
Record of an individual context (ie layer or feature) from an archaeological excavation.
A tall structure of any form, high in proportion to its lateral dimensions, often rising in stages, freestanding or part of another building, often used in fortifications and churches.
A tall structure, high in proportion to its lateral dimensions, often rising in stages, free standing or part of another building, surmounted by a clock.
A small fast warship developed in the late nineteenth century. Armed principally with quick firing guns to destroy enemy torpedo boats.
A very fast small warship, armed with small calibre guns and torpedoes. Used for attacking enemy vessels, escort duties and anti submarine duties.
A row of houses attached to and adjoining one another and planned and built as one unit.
A purpose-built tenement. Use specific monument type where possible.
A multi-storey building in which individual blocks of flats cluster around a central service core.
A place where a group of people live together sharing accomodation and goods, forming their own community based upon common ideals.

A group of four houses in quadruplex form within a single block, of approximately square plan and set in a spacious garden. Such houses were usually provided for supervisory or skilled workers within a textile factory.
A row of buildings built during different periods, as opposed to a TERRACE.
Originally built as a family house. Converted into flats during the 19th or 20th century.

Traditionally a mew was a building housing hawks when they were moulting, however since the C16th the term has been used for a series of stables grouped around an open yard or alley, often with rooms above. Use only for stables otherwise use FALCONRY.
Residence for retired people, often in the form of an apartment complex, differing from a nursing home as the residents live independently.
Buildings designed for the accommodation of large numbers of people, rather than single families, etc.
Use for speculatively built 19th century "model dwellings", rather than those built by a philanthropic society.
A building manufacturing bandages.
A tool with a curved blade used for pruning.
A place where people meet for entertainment, discussion or assembly. Use more specific type where known.
A meeting place for freemasons.
A jug form characterized by the addition of three applied feet. The feet are usually short and stubby. Double index with the appropriate profile type. (Source: MPRG)
A waterworks pumping station.
A building used to pump sewage from the sewers to the filter beds of a sewage works.
A flight of stairs, situated on a building's exterior, extending to an upper storey.
An enclosed area of ground immediately surrounding a cathedral.
The white, fibrous substance surrounding the seeds of plants of the genus Gossypium, which can be spun and used in the manufacture of thread and cloth or used in its raw form as wadding or packing.
Goods manufactured from processed cotton.
A textile mill where thread undergoes the processes of twisting and doubling to provide material strong enough to be spun and woven.

Twin-engined maritime-reconnaissance bomber adapted from pre-war American airliners, the A-28 and A-29, evident from the row of portholes along its fuselage. Entered service with RAF Coastal Command just before the outbreak of World War Two.
Use for vessels registered in Turkey or the Ottoman Empire.
When secondary product use with major product and MINE, eg. COPPER MINE.

The de Havilland Aircraft Co., Ltd., founded in 1920 by Sir Geoffrey de Havilland, C.B.E., A.F.C., F.R.Ae.S. Originally developers of commercial aircraft, were responsible for such notable wartime aircraft as the Mosquito and the Tiger Moth.
Three-seat, single engine, high wing braced monoplane designed for civil use and first flown in 1929. Saw military service in World War 2 in an Army co-operation and communications role.
Writing implements; formerly quill pens made of bird feathers, and in more modern times fountain pens made of various materials with metal nibs, both used with ink to write.
A house or shelter used by drovers, herders or shepherds during the seasonal moving of livestock from the highlands to the lowlands. Use more specific type where known.
The residence of a drover.
A largely residential area on the outskirts of a town or city.
A building which has been altered to increase its defensive characteristics. Use more specific term where known.
A large pillbox-like structure, often L-shaped or angular, with numerous loopholes used as a defensive position.
Blocks cut from marble.
Rock or hard minerals used as a building material and for carving etc.
Collective name, in a true geological sense, for a metamorphosed limestone eg. Carrara marble. In British sense, any decorative stone that will take a polish, eg. Purbeck marble.
Used for the laying out and marking of the smaller parts of a ship prior to construction.
Scotland
A cup with a rounded body beneath a deep neck. There may be a marked junction between neck and body and the angle of the neck may be inward-sloping, upright or everted. (Source: MPRG)
A weight used to sink a fishing net in water.
A weight used to sink a fishing line or a net in water.
A weight attached to a fishing line in order to help it sink towards the bottom.
A group of aluminosilicate minerals with varying compositions. The most common mineral in igneous rocks, and common in other rocks and sediments.
A sole held onto the foot by straps or thongs.
A fully automatic mounted or portable firearm, usually designed to fire bullets in quick succession from an ammunition belt or magazine.
A building on a railway system housing levers used to regulate trains on the tracks using signals and to change the points to enable a train to transfer from one track to another.
Buildings and structures associated with signal communication.
A circular shaped area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
An area of land, in the shape of a D, enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.

A site consisting of, usually two, sub-circular enclosures linked by a linear ditch running tangentially to the enclosure boundaries. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period in the Wessex region.
A monument consisting of an area of land enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the boundary follows an irregular curving course.
An oval shaped area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
A monument consisting of an area enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the barrier follows a circular course, but is not regularly laid out.
Early Bronze Age assumed to be a neck ornament, crescent moon shaped, often gold and elaborately decorated.
A place of worship specifically for mariners and their families.
A building used for public Christian worship. Use more specific type where known.
A small chamber or private room.
A 'through' BACK TO BACK HOUSE - an interlocking L-shaped plan gave each house two street frontages, thus providing better lighting/ventilation.
A house in a line of houses attached to and adjoining one another and planned and built as one unit.
A house in a terrace consisting of a double row of houses sharing a common back wall, characteristic of industrial cities in the North of England.
A small port town on the coast of northern Lolland.
A type of slender support carried on a corbel.
A mass of stone or brick built against or as part of a wall to provide additional strength to it.
A separate functional unit of a hospital not necessarily on the same site.
A hospital department for the medical treatment of eye disorders and diseases.
A large wheel, often of timber construction, rotated by the walking action of people or animals placed within it usually to provide a power source for another machine or device.
A factory where tobacco was ground to form snuff.

A mill used for the production of mortar; a combination of sand, lime and water, used to make the joints between courses of bricks in buildings. In more recent times cement has replaced lime to create a quicker drying mortar.
A factory where paper is made. Use with power type where known.
A mill used to process raw timber.
A mill used for the preparation of Barilla, an ash of burnt seaweed that was used for the production of soda.
A factory containing machinery for processing clay for the manufacture of bricks, tiles or pottery.
A mill for the processing of rice for use in food products.
A plant used for the manufacture of tubes and tubing, from wrought iron or steel.

A mill for the processes of grinding, balling, couching, drying and packing of woad. The mill can be demountable, enabling it being located close to the fields, as woad crop has to be rotated and move to new fields as soon as the ground is exhausted.
A mill with machinery used to cut slabs of metal into rods, or thin sections, for use in nail making or wire drawing.
A steam-powered factory.
A mill in which sets of rollers were used to roll metal to set thicknesses or shapes such as rails, beams or rods.
A mill used for the preparation and production of Calamine.
A factory where pencils are manufactured.
A building containing a machine tool for boring out large cylindrical holes in items such as steam engine cylinders, pump barrels, etc.
A mill for grinding ochre for the paint making process.
A stone edge-runner grinding machine or mill used for mechanically grinding and mixing the ingredients of gunpowder.
A mill used to dress ore by means of a jigging machine.
A factory where rock gypsum is ground into a powder used in the production of plaster.
Machine, frequently horse powered, for mixing raw clay into brick earth.
A mill for producing abravive papers and cloths such as glass paper or emery cloth.
A mill used for the processing of tin ore by crazing, stamping or smelting.
A factory used for processing raw materials. Use more specific mill type where known. See also TEXTILE MILL, for more narrow terms.
A mill where mustard is produced.
A mill for grinding or crushing bones, in the process of making bone china, for example.
A factory where metal wire is manufactured.
A factory where flour was produced for use in food products.
A building or site for the manufacture of livestock fodder.
A building housing machinery for crushing chalk for whiting. Whiting was used in toothpaste, paint, tablets, putty and other products.
A mill manufacturing bobbins for the textile industry.
A mill where china stone is grinded.
A factory where putty, used as a means of securing windows and for setting plumbing fixtures, is produced from a combination of whiting and oil.
A mill used for the extraction and processing of starch.
A mill which contains machinery for separating grain from the chaff.
A mill used for the manufacture of walking sticks.
Mill incorporating water-powered hammers for beating brass sheet, etc. into vessels, pots, etc.
A manufacturing complex incorporating furnaces, calciner and condenser flues. Use SMELTERY for more modern type of plant.
A mill for grinding corn. Use with power type where known.
A factory where fruit and seed oil is produced by an oil machine.
An mill in which manganese was ground to a powder between two horizontal millstones.
A factory used for the manufacture of scythes.
A type of WATERMILL, powered by retaining seawater at high tide and then releasing it at low tide via the water wheel.
A mill or works where needles were manufactured.
A factory used for the manufacture of screws.
An axe designed and weighted to be thrown.
An axe used by the Saxons and Franks for throwing.
A weapon featuring a single or double edged head attached to a wooden shaft.
A building where official archives are kept for public inspection.
A building or group of buildings owned and operated by a governing body and often occupied by a government agency. Use specific type of building where known.
A hall built as a memorial to a particular person or event.
A building or set of rooms, primarily of the 18th century, in which social gatherings and balls were held.
A market building, pre-19th century, incorporating other function rooms, eg. theatres, courtrooms, schoolrooms.
A large factory or series of workshops for the manufacture of clothing.
A factory where collars, for shirts and other garments, are manufactured.
A building used to dry flax.
Ketch or yawl rigged vessel with a large mizzen sail used in the west country.
Gates that can be opened or closed, to admit or exclude water, especially flood water.
A low stool for resting feet upon.

Component part of a mungo and shoddy mill, where non-wool fibres from shredded material are destroyed by either soaking rags in an acid solution or rotating them in drums in a hot acidic gas followed by heat. The result is an all-wool product.
A mill for the manufacture of low grade cloth made from ground-up heavy woollen rags.
Large concrete letters representing the ground-to-air airfield code. It has been used to show pilots in WWII the name of the airfield they were above e.g. DW for Dunkeswell.
Use for the remains of any part of a mollusc. Use more specific term if known.
Molluscs found in dry to damp habitats rather than fully aquatic or marine habitats. Use more specific term where known.
Molluscs found in terrestrial habitats as opposed to fresh or brackish water.
Molluscs found in fresh or brackish water habitats.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Fresh And Brackish Water Mollusca Remains

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: Single engine, two-crew shipboard reconnaissance and patrol seaplane. Entered service in 1939, this was the last combat floatplane built in Europe.
A type of seaplane, with one or more slender pontoons (known as "floats") mounted under the fuselage to provide buoyancy.
Collective name for a series of rocks (granite, syenite, porphry and slate) found in the Charnwood Forest of Leicestershire. Index with specific stone type where given.
An area of a church, often a free-standing building, in which baptism is administered
A toy in the image of a human being.

A circular pillbox designed by the Engineering and Metals Company using 'Armco' corrugated iron sheets as the inner and outer skins into which concrete was poured, giving a 12in wall thickness. The design was taken up by DFW and assigned a drawing number.
A long spear with a double barb where one barb is longer than the other.
A long shafted weapon with a pointed head used for thrusting or as a missile.
A long spear designed to be thrown in order to injure or kill a given target.
A site where weapons and/or explosives are tested experimentally, or are routinely tested as part of a manufacturing quality control process.

Objects used in, or which are created as part of, a manufacturing or production process, including the by-products of such processes. This does not include finished items, these will appear in other appropriate classes.
Piece of work to test eventual pattern, sometimes small and used as a demonstration of crafter's skill.
A structure, often concrete or brick, used as a shelter by members of the British citizen army during watch or patrol duties, or air raids, in wartime.
A red dye made from the dried bodies of the insect Dactylopius coccus.
Colour or dye, often in powder form, from natural mineral or vegetable sources (e.g. ochre) or created through chemical process (e.g. lamp black).
Sites and structures associated with the cutting and processing of peat.
A structure used to dry peat on.
Single-engine, single-seat biplane seaplane built for the 1924 Schneider Cup Race.
A factory manufacturing billiard tables.
A factory manufacturing sports equipment.
The official residence of a dean.
A residence for all clergy having the sole or subordinate charge of a living.
Includes dissertations
Unpublished written work such as manuscripts, dissertations etc. not disseminated to the public.
A diagonal brace running from an end of a cross tree to the vertical post to support this.
A temporary, steel-framed transportable hangar developed by Teesside Bridge and Engineering Company to replace the obsolete Bellman hangars.
A steel framed transportable hangar similar in construction to Type T2 but about half the size. Designed in 1941 and 1942.

A type of steel framed transportable British military aircraft hangar developed from 1941onwards. The hangar had a steel frame, some versions used commercially available sheeting for cladding. It was similar to but smaller than the arcraft hangar type T2.
An aircraft hangar designed to be moved from site to site as necessary.

A type of temporary military aircraft hangar introduced in 1940; of steel welded and bolted construction typically clad in galvanized corrugated iron sheets. The T2 became the standard temporary hangar for the RAF in World War Two.
A schematic diagram showing the relationships of the composition and strata of layers identified during excavation or intervention.
A factory where jute (plant fibres), was used to make products such as hessian, sacking, cordage and backing materials for carpet and linoleum.
A rectangular dripstone.
A moulding that projects from a wall above an exterior opening and is shaped to channel rainwater away from it.
An ornamental building, usually decorated with or displaying shells.
A metal girder, usually of iron or steel, embedded in the ground designed to obstruct the progress of hostile tanks or armoured vehicles.
A building, room or area, often within or attached to a church or other building, serving as a place of worship. Where a monument, use the Thesaurus of Monument Types.
A chapel that radiates from an apsidal end of a cathedral or church.
One of a series of chapels which project symmetrically from an apse or ambulatory at the east end of a church.
A lobby or chapel at the western entrance of a church. Sometimes a place of burial, an area reserved for women, or a place where monks could meet female relatives.
A chapel, often attached to or screened off inside a church, endowed for the celebration of masses principally for the repose of the founder?s soul.
A chapel dedicated to the Virgin, usually east of the chancel.
Measurements or factual information which may occur in a manual catalogue system or database.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Nitrate, used as a fertilizer or for use in the explosives industry.
A building or site used for the production of both chemical and organic fertilizer.
The court or enclosed space at the front of a building or structure.
Roman coastal forts fortified with large walls and a ditch, introduced to cope with raids from across the English Channel and North Sea.

Nowadays a hospital block where patients suffering from psychiatric disorders receive medical and surgical treatment. Formerly a place where psychiatric patients were primarily segregated from other patients in a hospital.
Specify in Description using: hedge, fence, wall etc.
A pillow-shaped, flat topped rectangular mound often surrounded by a shallow ditch used to farm rabbits.
A natural or artificial elevation of earth or stones, such as the earth heaped upon a grave. Use more specific type where known.

Twin-engine, three-crew, long-range heavy bomber biplane. Entered service in 1917. Of wooden construction with a fabric covering, the Vimy was fitted with a skid under the nose of its fuselage to prevent tipping forward upon landing.
Machinery for lifting pieces of stone or loaded trucks out of a quarry.
A hospital which primarily cares for patients injured in accidents.
A pan with a perforated bottom for straining or rinsing food.

Controlled investigation, recording and removal of archaeological deposits in targeted areas in order to answer specific questions relating to a particular archaeological site or landscape. Usually undertaken by university departments or amateur groups.

Long-range, four-engine reconnaissance-bomber. Initially produced as a transport, converted and used against Allied convoys in the Channel and the Atlantic. Also served as a VIP transport, one of which was the Immelmann III: Hitler's personal aircraft.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber and ground-attack aircraft. Entered service with the Luftwaffe in mid-1941. Approximately 20,000 were constructed between 1941 and the end of the war.
Focke-Wulf Flugzeugbau G.m.b.H.. Founded in 1924 and amalgamated in 1931 with the Albatross-Flugzeugwerke G.m.b.H.. Converted to a G.m.b.H. in 1937.
Poles of timber, metal etc. used as masts, booms or yards on a vessel.
Materials used to equip and fit out a ship. Includes masts, spars, rigging etc. Use only where evidence is less specific, otherwise use most relevant term.
A large division of a building which lies across, and at right angles to, its main axis, such as the arms either side of the crossing in a cruciform church.
The transverse portion of a cruciform church, or the arms on either side of the crossing, often with chapels at the east sides and possibly with aisles as well.
Products manufactured from plant materials.
The seeds of the palm Phytelephas macrocarpa, the albumen of which, hardens resembling ivory in colour, texture and toughness and is used to make ornamental buttons etc.
A power house built to Air Ministry drawing number 1380/24.

A building housing the permanent electricity generator supply for domestic use or small scale unspecified power generation on an airfield. Unlike stand by set houses, power houses had to cope with both essential and non-essential loads.
Fishing smack specialised both for working shoal water and for trawling for shrimp, predominantly in and around Morecambe Bay.
Includes individual index cards
An extension to a building usually made primarily of glass, for growing plants.
A tool with a handle and curved blade designed to cut through grass sods.
The flue or channel that funnels smoke from a fire.
A masonry or brickwork structure projecting above a roof and containing several flues.
A tower built to display a large clock.

A tall building, either round, square or polygonal in plan, used for a variety of purposes, including defence, as a landmark, for the hanging of bells, industrial functions, etc. Use more specific type where known.
A plan featuring a doorless entry to a lobby in front of an axial chimney-stack.

Aircraft as cargo carried whole or crated ready for assembly on arrival at the destination port. Do not use where the vessel is an aircraft carrier and the aircraft is carried as part of the vessel's armament.
Machinery and equipment used in the manufacture of aircraft.
A burial vault built to contain the remains of members of a single family, household or dynasty.

A built structure, generally below ground, designed for the interment of several burials over a period of time. Usually constructed with a door or sealed entrance to allow reopening for further burials.
A library which lends books (and sometimes other materials) to its members.
An enclosed settlement surrounded by a single or double row of close-set timbers embedded in a foundation trench, without ditches or banks.

A small, defended settlement dating to the Early Iron Age, located on spurs, promontories or hilltops. The defences are marked by single or double trenches which originally held substantial palisades.
A field system which appears to have developed in an organic, or piecemeal, fashion over time.
Large wooden hammer beams pounding cloth in a fulling solution.
A building, sometimes polygonal in plan, attached to a cathedral, church, abbey etc. and used for the assembly of chapter or brethren, often to address official business.

A type of prefabricated house erected, to 11 approved designs, as part of the Temporary Housing Programme, between 1944 and 1948. This scheme was devised to relieve the post-war housing shortage at a time when conventional materials were unavailable.
A building constructed from prefabricated sections. Use more specific type where known.
A place where goods and merchandise are temporarily stored before being transported to or from somewhere by road.
A crude, stone-built shelter for persons involved in lime production and the processing of lime burning.
Originally a light day-bomber, the Boston II, re-christened the Havoc, was adapted for night-flying in the fighter-intruder role. Was capable of a top speed in excess of 300 mph.
A machine in which a heavy block of metal is used for beating, breaking or driving something.
Early form of powered hammer, usually wooden, used primarily in the iron industry.
A flush decked sailing warship with a single tier of guns.
A heavy framework of parallel beams used to support a ship in dock.
British two-seat, twin-engined night fighter. Also used for roles such as long-range escort fighter, ground-attack and anti-shipping strike aircraft, bomber, torpedo-carrier and rocket fighter.
A joint with a loose tenon morticed into two touching pieces of timber
Dating to the reign of Elizabeth 1st of England.
Dating to the reign of the Tudor monarchs.
The Medieval period or Middle Ages begins with the Norman invasion and ends with the dissolution of the monasteries.
A curfew consisting of a half section of an inverted bowl. The form has been adapted for use against a wall. (Source: MPRG)
A metal or ceramic cover for an open fire or hearth.
Softwood obtained from trees of the genus Pinus, often used for the manufacture of furniture.
A building, usually open to the public, containing a number of areas for bathing. In the case of such a complex containing baths for swimming, also index with INDOOR or OUTDOOR SWIMMING POOL.
Originally partially covered baths shaped somewhat like a slipper, now usually a number of single baths of the modern domestic style installed for hire at public baths.
A purpose-built hall (usually 19th century) which was available for public hire and could be used for a variety of activities, eg. lectures, meetings, balls and concerts.
A soft, grey to white coloured, sandstone formed during the Cretaceous period, whose sand grains are cemented together with lime.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged around three sides of a yard which is open to one side.

Four-engined heavy bomber, developed by Avro from the twin-engined Manchester. Entered service in 1942 as the RAF's principal night bomber and took part in the 1,000 bomber raids as well as the famous Dam Busters raid.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the manufacture of silk.
A building wherein silk worm cocoons are boiled to release the silk fibres.
A training ship to which boys who had committed petty crimes were sentenced for 4 to 5 years to be reformed and trained as sailors.
A mill for beating and cleaning cloth, using soap or fullers earth.
A thin scoop used for cleaning the ear.
The dwelling place of a farm worker.
An instrument used for surgery, which is the treatment of injuries by instruments and manually.
An instrument in the form of a pair of pincers used to grip and pull objects, usually used in surgery.
A factory where biscuits are manufactured.

A small, defended settlement dating to the Early Iron Age, located on spurs, promontories or hilltops. The defences are marked by single or double trenches which originally held substantial palisades.
An enclosed settlement surrounded by a single or double row of close-set timbers embedded in a foundation trench, without ditches or banks.
The heartwood of a leguminous tree from which an extract is obtained. The extract being used for dyeing.
Wood used to produce a dye.
Products manufactured from timber.

A building as part of a workhouse, prison or hospital, often including porter's lodge, baths, clothes store, washrooms, casual cells, rooms etc, for receiving inmates/patients. Use term from Components thesaurus if it is part of a building complex.
A slab of stone, either standing or recumbent, inscribed with a cross. Usually found in association with burials.
A container used to hold and or pour out liquid in honour of a deity.
A container used to hold and or pour a liquid in honour of a deity.

American, single-engine fighter designed for operation from US Naval aircraft carriers. The Hellcat was a more powerful version of the Wildcat, a total of 1000 being provided to the Fleet Air Arm under Lend-Lease.
The Grumman Aircraft Engineering Corporation founded by Leroy R Grumman and incorporated in 1929.
A bowl with a sharp change of angle in the vessel wall, generally at the point of maximum diameter. the carination may be in the upper or lower half of the vessel. (Source: MPRG)
A specialist hospital where water treatment is given to patients suffering from muscular-skeletal complaints, etc.
The measurement of the decay of radioactive uranium (U) isotopes. Particularly useful for dating calcite and sometimes bone, tooth and shell up to 70,000 years old.
Techniques applied to a material in order to date it or material associated with it. Use more specific terms.

A metal, wooden or concrete box containing a telephone for use by the public, limited accommodation for use as a temporary cell, and a lamp on top that could be used to attract the attention of a passing patrol.
A barge fitted with a large tank in its hull for carried liquid cargoes.
A building or group of buildings, incorporating radio masts, built to intercept radio transmissions from enemy vessels and aircraft during WWI and WWII.
An axehead of early Bronze Age date, made of copper or bronze, which is flat on both sides and generally lacks side flanges or other hafting aids.

A form of axehead where the body is hollow allowing for insertion of the haft. Usually bronze or iron and of late Bronze Age or Iron Age date. Most examples feature a side loop to further assist hafting.

A stone axe in which the surface is fully covered by negative removals. Core axes may be made on flakes and have part of the flake's original surface but this cannot be part of the edge otherwise use FLAKED AXE. (Source: SARC)
A chisel ended flaked axehead common in the Mesolithic.
The cutting or chopping part of an axe; bifacially worked, longitudinal section symmetrical, cutting edge parallel to the direction of the hafted tool as swung.
An axehead of flint or other stone, commonly used for Neolithic types.

A bronze axehead of earlier Bronze Age date the sides of which are raised, either by casting or hammering, to form flanges on both faces which aid hafting. Some types also feature a raised bar or stop between the flanges.

A bronze axehead of middle or late Bronze Age date in which the side flanges and the bar/stop on both faces are connected, forming a single hafting aid. For palstaves with side loops use looped palstave.

A form of bronze axehead of middle or late Bronze Age date in which narrow, high flanges on both faces are hammered over to enclose the axe haft. Some types feature a side loop to further assist hafting.
An axehead of flint or other stone commonly used for Neolithic types.
A 1930s British short-haul biplane airliner for 6-8 passengers. It proved an economical and durable craft, despite its relatively primitive plywood construction. Primarily used by the RAF.
A building where animals are slaughtered.
A metal safe built in to wall
The impost, or point at which a vault rests upon its support, and from which it seems to spring. Hence the term describes the bottom stone of a vault, which lies on the impost.
Buildings and structures associated with the production, processing and storage of coal gas.
An industrial complex concerned with the manufacture of gas for domestic use from coal and oil.
A place where ceramic tiles are manufactured.
Site of small scale industrial production often involving hand work and craft skills.
A factory where ribbons are manufactured.
England
South Yorkshire
South Yorkshire
A monastery governed by a prior or prioress. Use with narrow terms of DOUBLE HOUSE, FRIARY, MONASTERY or NUNNERY.
Use only for a monastic house of unknown status, religious order and uncertain authenticity.
A priory dependent on a foreign mother house. Use with narrow terms of DOUBLE HOUSE, MONASTERY or NUNNERY.
An inward radial-flow reaction turbine developed by James Thomson.
An inwards, radial flow reaction water turbine developed by Jean Victor Poncelet (1788-1867) in France in 1826.
An outward radial flow reaction water turbine.
A mixed-flow reaction water turbine, developed in the USA in 1840 by James Bichino Francis, in which water enters the runner radially and leaves axially.
A motor in which rotary motion is produced by motive power, usually of water, steam or gas, impinging directly on a series of vanes upon the circumference of a revolving cylinder or disc.

A prime mover in which a central wheel with curved vanes, enclosed in a chamber, receives water directed onto the curved vanes by a ring of fixed guide vanes, causing the wheel to rotate about its axis.
A parallel or axial-flow reaction water turbine invented in France in 1843, in which water descends through fixed curved guide vanes which direct the flow sideways onto curved vanes on the runner.
A place of worship for Protestant Methodists, a group who broke away from the Methodists to form their church in Leeds in 1828.
Tablet of a uniform shape. Used as finishing or covering materials which fit together in a regular format.

A large rectangle roof tile in the form of an upstand on one side followed by three rolls, the last of which fits over the upstand of the adjacent tile. The name does not denote a relationship with the Roman period.
A comb made up of riveting together sections between connecting plates.
A toothed strip of material used to disentangle hair. Can be either single or double sided.
Single-seat carrierborne jet fighter. Originally conceived as an RAF land-fighter, entered Fleet Air Arm service in 1951 and was the first jet fighter to be standardised in first-line squadrons.
The Supermarine Company was formed in 1912 and specialised in producing sea-going aircraft, including several Schneider Trophy winners. Taken over by Vickers-Armstrongs Ltd., in 1938.
A building, on an airfield, used to house a fire engine designed to Air Ministry drawing number 5342/42.
A building, on an airfield, used to house a fire engine.
The carriage house or garage for a fire engine - especially those built by insurance companies or industrial concerns.
A building, on an airfield, used to house a fire engine designed to Air Ministry drawing number 12563/40.
A hall used for the promotion and selling of agricultural produce and practice.
A meeting hall, or sale room in a town, for manufacturers and traders.
A hall used for housing public displays.
A hall used for the promotion and selling of horticultural produce and practice.
The hood used to completely cover a hawk's head.
Straps fastened around the legs of a hawk.
A belt used to confine a hawk's wings.
A small spherical bell for fastening onto the leg of a hawk.
A metal ring which joins the jess to the leash. The owner's name is often on the vervel.
Equipment used on a bird of prey for hawking.
Medium grained, hard, white/grey coloured stone consisting of quartz and often silica, produced by the metamorphosis of sandstone.
A track inlaid into a surface, on which tram cars run for the conveyance of passengers and/or goods or raw materials.
A track consisting of flanged strips used in early colliery railways.
A radio-controlled target tug version of the Tiger Moth used for target practice. 380 were built for the RAF.
An aircraft used for the towing of targets.
A building or works in which carriages were built. Use RAILWAY CARRIAGE WORKS for sites making railway carriages.
A hut provided as accommodation for hop pickers and may also be know as a Hop Pickers' Hut
A single-span aircraft hangar designed by Boulton & Paul of London and Norwich (drawing number 4178/44). Mainly used on aircraft factory sites and at Armament Training Schools.
A barn which is constructed with a timber framework; between the members are panels which are infilled with timber, wattle and daub, plaster, brickwork, stone or other materials.
A barn in which a pair of curved timbers form a bowed A-frame which supports the roof independently of the walls.
A pillbox constructed for use in training exercises forming part of a simulated defensive position
A site in which one or more searchlights and their accompanying structures were positioned to locate enemy aircraft or surface vessels for the benefit of batteries and night fighter aircraft.
An emplacement mounting a small, portable electrically-powered searchlight.
A site in which one or more searchlights were positioned to locate enemy aircraft or surface vessels for the benefit of batteries and night fighter aircraft.
Containers used for cooking.
A container for cooking.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Perchlorate, a product used in the explosives industry.
A pool of water and associated ancillary buildings designed to accommodate sea lions.
A stone coffin.
A building adjacent to a monastery where alms were distributed to the poor.
A medical container for collecting urine for study.
A needle for making and mending nets, often forked at both ends.
A thin, pointed implement used for sewing with a hole at the blunt end for threading the sewing material.
A needle used to sew together thatch.
A treadwheel using a donkey as motive power. Usually found operating wells.
A hall used for the promotion and selling of agricultural produce and practice.
A hall used for housing public displays.
A meeting hall, or sale room in a town, for manufacturers and traders.
A hall used for the promotion and selling of horticultural produce and practice.
A large-scale site where medicinal drugs are maufactured.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of chlorophyll for medical purposes.
A concealed passage or room for the purpose of hiding and protecting a (Roman Catholic) priest during times of religious persecution.

A permanent military RAF aircraft hangar type, designed in 1924. It features a steel frame (with longitudinal ridge and valley trusses for the roof) reinforced concrete and brick infilling for the walls. Typically 122 foot span by 249 foot in length.
An aircraft hangar built to Air Ministry design number 454/43. Mainly constructed on aircraft factory aerodromes
An aircraft hangar built to Air Ministry design. Mainly constructed on aircraft factory aerodromes.
Spice from the bark of an East Indian tree
Objects designed to be played with, often a model or miniature replica of something and especially for a child.

Single-engine, two-crew fighter, also used for convoy escort and reconnaissance. Designed to operate from aircraft carriers. Entered service with the Fleet Air Arm in 1940 and remained in use until 1945.
A building where timber was allowed to dry and harden, to render it fit for use as a working material.
An open yard or place where timber is stacked or stored.
A place where tree trunks were sawn into planks by hand.
Includes processing and manufacturing of all forms of wood.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the processing of timber.
Building containing transformers to reduce the high voltage of the National Grid to the lower voltage of domestic supply.
A rectangular pillbox with an enclosed square plan section for three light machine guns and an adjacent open area housing a mounting for a light anti-aircraft weapon. Designed by DFW branch 3.
An artificial water channel for carrying water over long distances. Use also for bridge-like structures that carry the channel or canal across a valley, river or other obstacle.
A barn in which a central space is separated from a side aisle by posts and braces.

Twin-engine, three-crew, long-range heavy bomber biplane. Entered service in 1917. Of wooden construction with a fabric covering, the Vimy was fitted with a skid under the nose of its fuselage to prevent tipping forward upon landing.
The limit to an area as defined on a map or by a marker of some form, eg. BOUNDARY WALL. Use specific type where known.
The limit line of a field.
A form of tumbler lock key which pushes the bolt.
An anti aircraft battery usually mounting smaller, faster weapons such as Bofors guns or a single anti-aircraft machine gun, intended to engage fast low flying aircraft.

A large octagonal pillbox, with a projecting entrance, equipped with loopholes for eight light machine guns and a light anti-aircraft mounting sited in a central well which was accessed from inside the pillbox. Designed by DFW branch 3.
Soft limestone consisting almost entirely of calcite.
A glass vessel with a long tapering neck that is bent down. Used for distillation.
The base to a door or window frame or of a wall.
Cotton which has not been processed.
A vessel used as a platform for flying a barrage balloon from.
A jug with more or less straight sides that flare out from a narrow rim or neck to a wider base. (Source: MPRG)
A large building used to store tea.
A moveable section of light fence, traditionally made from wattle and used for herding livestock, to separate land or to act as river bank revetments.
An extractive pit or pits, usually 2.5m square by 2m deep dug to extract tin ore in areas where streamworking is not possible. Usually dug along a vein rather than across it.
An ore works at which gold was separated from the ore by the addition of mercury.
A stone or timber lined channel for conveying ore out of a working.
A site or building where ore is processed to obtain metal.
A mill used to dress ore by means of a jigging machine.
A 19th century ore processing works which processed the waste material from a mine.
A factory used to make packaging.
A command post used to direct the guns of an anti aircraft battery.
A site containing one or more artillery pieces and/or rocket launchers for firing at enemy aircraft.
A metal grid, usually iron, used to support pots over a fire.

Single-engine, testbed monoplane built to Air Ministry Specification 43/37. Only twelve were produced, the first of which tested the Sabre I engine in 1940, and were used throughout the war. The cockpit could seat two observers behind the pilot.
Second World War allied patrol-bomber built by Lockheed Vega, a Lockheed subsidiary. This aircraft was a military development of the Lodestar, USAF designation B-34.
A subsidiary of Lockheed.

The upper parts of walls carried on arcades or colonnades in the nave, choir or transepts of a church or hall, rising higher than the lean-to roofs of the aisles and pierced with windows to allow light to penetrate.
A crane powered by a treadwheel and used for lifting and lowering, dating from the Roman period. Also used in later periods to assist on building sites, at mines and in ports.
Graves known to be of shipwreck victims buried close to their site of discovery, as was customary until the 19th century, rather than in consecrated ground.
A bridge that incorporates one or two spans that tilt at the abutments, to move up and out of the way of shipping. The most famous example of which is Tower Bridge, London.
A piece of wax, lead, paper etc, with a stamped design, attached to a document as a guarantee of authenticity.
A lead seal marking newly woven cloth which served as a quality control method in medieval and post medieval periods.
A building or set of buildings and structures where power, especially electrical or mechanical, is generated. Use more specific type where known.
Power station using domestic refuse as its principal fuel.
A group of buildings where consumer goods, such as small machines and electrical components, are manufactured.
A factory manufacturing timepieces, including clocks and watches.
A site where scientific and technical instruments such as microscopes are assembled.
A report depicting the results generated from an intensive survey of a large area of land including field recording, measured site surveys and land history.
A lime kiln where the fuel is not mixed with the limestone but burnt below it.
A lime kiln built into a low hillside or slope to facilitate top loading of the limestone.
A kiln in which lime is made by calcining limestone or in some areas chalk.

A kiln in which lime is made by calcining limestone. This type of kiln usually consists of a circular bowl surrounded by pennanular banks with a funnel exit on the lower side. They normally survive as an earthwork. Superseded by Flare Kilns.
A detached block within a hospital complex used as sleeping accommodation for patients.
A ceramic made from clay and fired in a kiln or oven. This term has been used interchangeably with EARTHENWARE and with TERRACOTTA

A clay-based ceramic fired at low kiln temperatures (c.800-1200 degrees). Essentially, earthenwares are porous and require glazing for most applications. This term has been used interchangeably with TERRACOTTA and with POTTERY
A building or group of buildings used for the raising of mink, a semi-aquatic mammal which is farmed for its fur.
A tract of land, often including a farmhouse and ancillary buildings, used for the purpose of cultivation and the rearing of livestock, etc. Use more specific type where known.

Four-engine, long range heavy bomber. Developed from the Lancaster, and originally designated the Lancaster Mk. IV, it was larger in size, bombload and fuel capacity. Never used operationally in World War Two.
A light porous cellular rock, consisting of consolidated volcanic ash ejected from vents during a volcanic eruption.
A structure consisting of a large plastic pipe attached to a high tower and sloping down to a swimming pool. Water flows down the inside allowing people to slide down into the pool below.
A telephone exchange housing one end of an underwater cable and used to send messages overseas.
An office or central station of a local telephone system where the various lines are brought to a central switchboard and communication between subscribers is achieved.
A building where documents such as title-deeds, charters, etc, were kept as evidence of rights or privileges.
A stable associated with a horse-drawn tramway system.
A factory complex consisting of PRINTING SHOPS, COLOUR HOUSES, DYE HOUSES, etc, in which patterns are printed onto calico.
A factory complex consisting of PRINTING SHOPS, COLOUR HOUSES, DYE HOUSES, etc, in which patterns are printed onto textiles.
A stick for digging up roots etc. Sometimes a stone weight is attached.
A prototype semi-underground silo based launch system specifically designed to hold and fire the Blue Streak Missile. The silo was constructed at RAF Spadeadam in c1959 and abandoned in April 1960.

Where the land on which the monument stands is dedicated to the monument itself: this may include Guardianship sites displayed, also sites which exclude any other Land Classification e.g. Cross, Commemorative Monument etc.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Other 8 (Dedicated to the display of a monument)

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A car park on the roof of a building.
A place where cars and other road vehicles may be parked and left.
A car park, on two or more levels.
A car park situated beneath the surface of the ground.
The term scrub includes invasive woodland characterised by the presence of birch, willow, alder, ash, sycamore, conifers as low trees, with shrubs.
US Navy version of the four-engined, six-crew B24 heavy bomber. Modified for long-range reconnaissance duty and used as a patrol-bomber against shipping and submarines.
Use to record the names and parts of names of people and organizations.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a rectangular or trapezoidal earthen mound.
A terrace with windows and doors on one side only, often built facing inwards onto a burgage plot, or sometimes on a steep slope, with no apertures on the uphill side.
Plain, white, cotton cloth often unbleached.
Documents relating to the planning, inception and management of a project.
A boundary post for the payment of tax or duty.
A boundary marker for the payment of tax or duty.
An enclosure surrounded by a wooden stockade. A rare site type of Neolithic date.
A church attached to or founded by a college.
Previously recorded as 'Modern'. Covers the period from 1901-2000.
The mid third of the 20th Century.

Used to record resources dating to, and associated with, the Second World War. For other types of resource not directly associated with the war, (such as houses, built during this period) use MID 20TH CENTURY.

The period of political and military opposition between the major Superpowers (USA and USSR) and their allies. Known as the Cold War as there were no direct military conflicts between the two main protagonists.
A factory used for the production of acetate.
A place where scrap metal is collected.
Series of rooms within a workhouse where elderly men were housed.
A house in a terrace consisting of a double row of houses sharing a common back wall, characteristic of industrial cities in the North of England.
A 'through' BACK TO BACK HOUSE - an interlocking L-shaped plan gave each house two street frontages, thus providing better lighting/ventilation.
Containers of cylindrical form, traditionally made of curved wooden staves bound together by hoops of metal. Also includes modern plastic and metal barrels.
Metal hoops used to hold the staves of barrels in position.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the manufacture of plaster.
A factory where rock gypsum is ground into a powder used in the production of plaster.
A section of a hospital specializing in the treatment of patients with serious mental disorders.

A large room, similar to a dormitory, within a hospital, and used for the temporary or permanent accommodation of patients, either waiting for or recovering from operations or undergoing long term treatment.

A fastener made of a metal circle connected to a metal loop fixed to an object and used to fasten to another object by means of a button or a loop. The usage of these items is unclear, could include use for animals or for dress.
A loft over a stable or barn used for storing hay.
A building or structure of unknown function found on a farm. Use more specific type where known.
A thin wooden slab or tile used in quantity as a roof or wall covering.
Transport version of the four-engined Lancaster bomber. Serving from 1943 to 1951, and all metal in construction, this aircraft was used extensively during the Berlin airlift.
A relatively small and heavily built vessel equipped with large engines. Used for towing ships at sea or manouevring them in tight spaces.
A small and powerful vessel used to assist vessels that are sinking or disabled at sea.
Thick, viscid liquid, obtained by the distillation of wood, coal or other organic substances, chemically a mixture of hydrocarbons with resins.
Road or paving material combining crushed stone, rolled and mixed with bitumen type mixer.
Solid or viscous bituminous pitch of natural occurrence,or produced from petroleum mixed with sand or other aggregate filler, for use in roads or as a covering material
A semi solid mixture of complex hydrocarbons derived from coal or petroleum. Used as a waterproof binder or protective coating.
A residence used during short visits by an official and attendants of the Knights Templars for administrative purposes on their estates.
A subsidiary form of preceptory provided with a chapel. Use specific type where known.
Aluminium oxide.
A sulphate of aluminium and potassium used in the dyeing process as a mordant to increase the intake of dye into a cloth.
A light, ductile metal, used in the manufacture of aircraft etc.
A defensive battery positioned facing out to sea enabling the guns to be brought to bear on enemy shipping and amphibious craft.
A coastal battery constructed at short notice usually mounting a variety of artillery pieces.
A large shallow bowl for letting liquids stand.
Maps or charts.

skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: National Mapping Programme Morph Number Sheet

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A mixture of paraffins distilled from petroleum and used as a fuel and solvent.
Documents relating to the planning, inception and management of a project.
A site showing some signs of occupation but evidence is insufficient to imply permanent settlement.
Unclassifiable site with minimal information. Specify site type wherever possible.
Works producing a refractory clay, kaolin. An essential raw material of porcelain and some types of papermaking.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter biplane renowned for its high performance and manoeuvrability. Entered service in 1917.
Specify in Description using: cave, cliff etc.
A house provided for the treasurer of a cathedral, palace or similar.
An object which surrounds or makes up a keyhole.
A small cargo craft, usually with two masts and a lateen rig.

A structure consisting of three stretches of tramline joined by points. The tram is able to go forward, reverse and then go forward again changing line each time until it has turned around completely.
An optical instrument for making distant objects appear nearer and larger, often found on the promenade or pleasure pier at a seaside resort or at a site of scenic beauty.
A telegraph pole, tree trunk or similar erected on the side of a road, or in an open space, to prevent the landing of hostile aircraft
A purpose built trench designed to prevent the successful landing of enemy glider-borne and airborne forces.
A cable, usually erected between posts, used to prevent the landing or hostile aircraft.
Obstacles placed in open spaces and alongside roads designed to prevent the successful landing of enemy airborne forces.
A room in a monastery used by monks or nuns as a day room.
An educational establishment where dentistry is taught.
An arch made up of part of a circle, the centre of which is below its springing line.

A jar with a single handle attached to the rim edge and looped over the top of the vessel. There may be a lip. Profiles can vary and should be double indexed with the appropriate JAR type. (Source: MPRG)
A series of water or engine-driven crushing machines used in ore dressing.
An aeroplane featuring three wings, or planes, placed one above the other either side of its fuselage.
A recess, often containing shelves and usually fitted with a door or doors, used for the storage of items.
A room or cupboard usually used for the storage of garments.
A recess or cupboard within a church, usually positioned near the altar, used for the storage of sacred vessels.
A stone-lined pit or tank, sometimes circular, for concentrating ores by sedimentation.
A transportable hangar designed by A & J Main of Glasgow.
An aircraft hangar designed to be moved from site to site as necessary.
A room containing a boiler, used to provide heating.
A building housing a boiler, often connected to a steam engine house.
