A musical instrument that produces sound through the passage of air through a number of pipes controlled by stops, pedals and keyboards.
A building where carpets and other floor furnishings were woven.
A handloom weavers workshop where the weaver received yarn from a clothier and manufactured a woven piece of cloth from it.
A type of pavilion sometimes found in public parks or country house estates.
A container for one or more candles.

A candlestick in which the socket is above a drip tray or grease tray, placed on a pedestal base which is generally hollow. There may be a vertical loop handle and one or more secondary drip trays. (Source: MPRG)
A place where graphite is extracted.
Sites where minerals are extracted from the ground.
Daily record of events or appointments.
Particulars of a property for sale.
Includes dissertations
An article, but published as a separate item.
Loose notes
Includes excavation, research and general notes.
Mechanical reproductive process using photographic, electrostatic and dry powder techniques.
Record of events.
Unpublished written work such as manuscripts, dissertations etc. not disseminated to the public.
A structure in a garden used to house gardening implements, etc.
A naval base that builds, repairs, docks or converts warships, and is manned by civilian engineers and workers and administered by engineer duty officers.
An enclosure in which ships are built and repaired, and all sorts of ships' stores are brought together.
An area of a port, dock or harbour, often including buildings for passport control and customs, where passengers of ocean liners can embark/disembark and where supplies can be taken on board.
A port, dock or harbour where ferries, hovercraft, ocean liners and cargo vessels can load and unload. May include road and/or rail terminals for transportation to the port.
A small, double-handled bowl with horizontal loop handles decorated with a cockerel motif. (Source: MPRG)
A bowl adapted by the addition of two handles, generally opposed. (Source: MPRG)
A slope, usually with rails, along which a vehicle can be moved between two relatively flat stretches of railway.
A slope, usually with rails, along which a vehicle can be moved between two relatively flat stretches of railway, or by which a boat can be transferred from one level of waterway to another.
A slope, usually with rails, by which a boat can be transferred from one level of waterway to another.
Unable to identify actual place from documentary sources alone.
A small workshop, employing up to 10 men, working on hand-operated carding engines and hand jennies, spinning yarn for handloom weavers.
A textile mill where crepe is manufactured.Crepe is a fine cloth particularly silk or mixture of silk and cotton.
An establishment, often forming part of a university, for higher or tertiary education.
A training college where workers can attend classes in vocational subjects. The classes are often day-release and sanctioned by the employer.
A container to receive milk during the milking process.
Containers in which food and or drink is gathered or processed.
A pipe used for smoking where the smoke passes through water.
A site or building used to co-ordinate Air-Sea Rescue operations.

A site, usually with an airfield, hangars and control buildings, used for the storage and deployment of military aircraft or the administration of the Royal Air Force. May also include accommodation buildings for personnel.
A hard, white, fine-grained substance forming the main part of the tusks of elephants, walruses, hippos and narwhals.
A hard, bone-like material obtained from animal teeth.
Permanently moored historic maritime craft preserved and converted into a museum and open to the public.
A building, group of buildings or space within a building, where objects of value such as works of art, antiquities, scientific specimens, or other artefacts are housed and displayed.
A recess or chamber near the altar which holds a relic. A feature of medieval churches.
A room in which food is prepared.
A room in which food is prepared.
A coin-operated meter receiving fees for parking a vehicle in a street, and indicating time allowed.
A double lock placed between tidal water and a canal, etc..
An engineering workshop for the manufacture and repair of springs.

A classical ornamentation featuring foliage, fruits and, unlike Arabesque, human and animal figures, sometimes fantastic or mythological in nature. The term may have originated from the fact that many examples of such ornamentation were found in grottoes.
A settlement without any obvious evidence for a boundary. Use specific type where known.

A settlement with evidence for several hut circles but clearly lacking an obvious boundary. Where it is not certain whether a boundary existed or not, use HUT CIRCLE SETTLEMENT. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period.
An area used for crushing mineral ore or stone. Often includes mechanically powered ore crushers.
Textile mill producing calico, ie. coarse, unbleached cotton cloth.
Usually a cotton spinning factory, although some mills have weaving sheds attached, in which case the end product is completed cloth, not yarn only.
Photographic colour print developed using wet process.
Photographic image with normal polarity.
Colour positive print developed using a dry process.
Photographic format.
Aquatic invertebrate animals whose outer covering is a shell, often 'farmed' to be eaten. Includes molluscs and crustaceans.
Small, marine crustaceans are used as food.
A bridge, usually resting on raised arches, carrying a road across low-lying land or water.
A bridge, usually resting on a series of arches, carrying roadways or railways over low-lying areas.
A garden incorporating features of traditional Japanese gardens - a pool, an island, stepping stones or a bridge, cherry trees and other shrubs and flowering plants grown with the emphasis on line.
A tool with adjustable jaws for gripping and turning objects.
A factory where china products are manufactured.
A site containing plant and machinery for the manufacture of steel.
Production of high quality steel by reheating cementation steel in a refractory crucible.
A tool used to cut or split wood.
A shafthole adze with additional hammer knob, normally polished stone.
1st World War end-opening aeroplane hangar.
For example Binge eating, Anorexia Nervosa and Bullemia.
A garden incorporating features of Moorish-influenced Spanish gardens - water features, patios, benches, walls and compartments, evergreens, etc.

A surface technique of spectroscopic analysis which relies on the interaction of primary X-rays with the sample to generate a range of secondary X-rays. These have energies characteristic of the elements present in the sample.

A surface technique that uses the diffraction of X-rays to examine the mineral composition of a sample. Useful for identifying corrosion products, pigments etc. but of little use with organic compounds which consist largely of carbon, oxygen and hydrogen.
Techniques investigating more than one element at a time.
Examination of a material using chemical means.
Dating to or characteristic of the reigns of any of the first four kings of Great Britain called George.
Dating to the reign of the Hanoverian kings and queens.
Scotland
East Lothian, Scotland
A short published document, often a single sheet, describing a particular place, feature or service to assist visitors and users.
A garden or park, with ancilliary buildings, in which wild animals are kept and reared for public exhibition.

A garden or park, with ancilliary buildings, in which young and domesticated animals are kept for public exhibition, especially for children. Children are given the opportunity to come into close contact and handle animals.
A cylindrical container, usually bulging outward in the middle and usually held together by metal hoops.
A lever lock key.
A object fitted to an item or garment for the purpose of display or decoration.
Hard, fossil rich, white to deep red coloured limestone, laid down during the Tertiary period. Used since Roman times because of its good durability and weathering properties.
Generic name for the hard, white/cream coloured, freshwater limestone. Quarried on the Isle of Wight.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: First Rate Ship Of The Line
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A ship of the line mounting 100 guns or more on three gundecks.
A mill in which poor quality woollen cloth was made from fibres produced by grinding light woollen rags.

Component part of a mungo and shoddy mill, where non-wool fibres from shredded material are destroyed by either soaking rags in an acid solution or rotating them in drums in a hot acidic gas followed by heat. The result is an all-wool product.
A human-powered, pedal-driven, single-track vehicle, having two wheels attached to a frame, one behind the other.
A self-propelled wheeled vehicle that does not operate on rails, such as trains or trolleys.
A means of transportation.
Any vehicle/craft used for transportation on water.
A machine that can be flown in the air, now specifically an aeroplane or helicopter.
Any vehicle for transportation on land.
A mill used for grinding textile rags.
A medieval house with central open hall and two storey bays, jettied at first floor level, on either side.
A house where the upper storeys rest on projecting floor joists and so create the effect of an overhang.
A jettied house where the upper storey only overhangs the end elevation of the building.
A house constructed with a basic timber framework; between the members are panels which can be infilled with timber, wattle and daub, plaster, brick or other materials.
A jettied house where the overhanging upper storey runs along the entire length of one side.
A weapon with a sharp edge or point.
A tool with an edged head and a wooden shaft, used for a variety of purposes. Where the function is known use the more specific terms of AXE (TOOL) or AXE (WEAPON).
A short stabbing weapon with a pointed blade. In Medieval period daggers served a dual function being also used as knives.
A short stabbing weapon, designed to be fixed to the muzzle of a musket or rifle, even in some cases to pistols. Some were designed to be used both fixed to long guns and independent of them.
An axe designed and weighted to be thrown.

A cutting and thrusting weapon consisting of a blade and a hilt. The blade varies in length and width and the cutting edge can vary from being purely the point to being one or both sides or a combination of these.
Smelting furnace into which compressed hot air is driven.
A furnace where metal is manufactured from ore.
A building or buildings where electronic components or devices are designed, developed, manufactured and assembled.
An object that commemorates an animal, person, location or event.
A stone which bears an inscription commemorating an event or person.
Sites, buildings or stuctures associated with the entire process of salt production.
A site, building or factory used for the production of salt.
A site, building or factory where seawater is used in the production of salt.
A site, building or factory where geologically-derived brine is used for the production of salt.
A vault, often located under a chancel or chancel aisle, containing an altar and usually used for burial.
A type of temporary bridge designed by Sir Donald C.Bailey during the Second World War.
A bridge manufactured from prefabricated sections.
A vertical or inclined excavation giving access to an underground mine.
Horizontal tunnel opening from the surface used for haulage or access to a mine. It can also be used for drainage.
An area of several rooms in a medieval house or building. Probably for domestic use.
A mill where mustard is produced.
A base of the Roman Doric order with a torus, an astragal and a fillet.
A container used to hold and or pour a liquid in honour of a deity.
A container used to hold and or pour out liquid in honour of a deity.
A container used to hold and or pour a liquid in honour of a deity.
A container used to hold and or pour a liquid in honour of a deity.
A container to hold a liquid in honour of a deity.
A container to hold and or pour a liquid in honour of a deity.
A building used to shelter deer hunters.
A tool for gripping with, often used to pinch objects together.
A type of temporary transportable aircraft hangar designed in 1936 by N.S. Bellman. It was designed for ease of installation, and was composed of light rolled steel sections.
Two linked quadrangular open areas surrounded by walls or buildings.
A plan of a house where the buildings are around at least three sides of a quadrilateral courtyard.
Fixed or hardened installation for machine guns. Temporary soft installations are possible as well.
Replacement of organic material by minerals, including calcium carbonate and calcium phosphate.
An engine that extracts thermal energy from pressurized steam, and converts it into rotary motion.
A construction designed to look like a pillbox in order to deceive or confuse the enemy.
A path across a road marked with black and white stripes where pedestrians may cross.
A path across a road, usually marked as a crossing for pedestrians.

An element such as a window, door or wall decoration, usually associated with a larger monument but which may be found in isolation. For example a stained glass window or panelling saved from a demolished building.
A tool used in processing the fibres from coconuts.
An tool used to separate flax fibres from the wood and bark following retting.
A general tool used to beat objects with.
A tool used to hit fabric, eg to remove dust or dirt.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of eye disorders and diseases.
Residences of religious people and members of the clergy.
The residence of the head or president of a chapter, or community of religious persons.
A collective term embracing a church tower's entire structure, including its spire.
A steeple in which the spire resembles a crown.
A sharp blade used for shaving.
A factory where tobacco pipes made of clay are manufactured.
A single-seat, biplane fighter. One of the last open cockpit types to see widespread service with the RAF, equipping 10 squadrons and, at one point, 70% of the Home Defence fighter force.
Photographic negative using nitrate process on a film base material.
Fat from an animal used to lubricate objects.
An arched or vaulted recess, within a tomb or catacomb, intended to contain a coffin or sarcophagus.
A wholly or partially underground chamber, often beneath a chancel, equipped for religious services and usually containing tombs.
A semicircular crypt below the apse of a church.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as an H-shaped plan, commonly with cattle housing to two or more cattle yards.
An object which is propelled by force away from a launcher, which can include from a human.
A pointed projectile fired from a crossbow designed to injure or kill a given target.
A tool with an edged head and a wooden shaft, used for a variety of purposes.
A site, usually including hardstandings and associated buildings, used for the storage of military vehicles.
A nursery for infants, where they are taken care of while their mothers are at work.
A room or a building set aside for infants and young children.
A communal residence of secular priests and/or other clerics sometimes with the condition of learning and education attached.
A communal residence of secular vicars whose duties included the education of choristers attached to cathedrals and collegiate churches.
An ornamental chain, worn around the ankle.
A hall or chamber in which justice is administered.

A building or tower used to communicate information to shipping or other stations using signals such as flags, fires or lights. Roman signal stations took the form of a stone tower surrounded by a ditched enclosure and were used to warn of Saxon raids.
The residence of health workers. Includes single dwellings of doctors, nurses etc. but not multiple dwellings eg.NURSES HOSTEL
A rudimentary roofed building found in school playgrounds, open at the side. Used as a shelter from bad weather.
A depot used for the unloading of coal.
The main gear wheel, which is engaged by a brake to halt or slow the machinery, mounted on the windshaft of a windmill.
A factory for processing rubber or manufacturing rubber goods, such as tyres.
Mud walled building found on the Solway Plain.
A temporary settlement established as a public protest against an aspect of government policy or more specifically the development of a site.
An informal encampment, usually near a military establishment, set up as a public protest against that establishment or against some aspect of military policy.
A tablet used for divination.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged around all four sides of the yard.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the working buildings are carefully planned as linked ranges and are focused around one or more working yards. They often result from a single phase of building.

A flour mill which uses one or more pairs of horizontal millstones to grind wheat into flour which millers call a ï¿½sudden deathï¿½ process; within not more than 90 seconds complete wheat grain becomes wholemeal flour.
A factory where flour was produced for use in food products.
Single-engine, two-seat tractor bomber and reconnaissance aircraft. Entered service in 1916 and, during 1917 and 1918, equipped nine RFC squadrons in its reconnaissance role.
Use with form of extraction where known. Also use MINE and other ores extracted where relevant, eg. SILVER MINE.
Four-seat, twin-engined medium bomber. Entered service in 1938. After serving Bomber Command from 1939-42, was converted to a torpedo-bomber and mine-layer with RAF Coastal Command.
A room in a monastery used by monks or nuns as a day room.
The excrement of seabirds and bats used as a fertilizer.
Previously arable, usually part of Countryside Stewardship Scheme.
A booth, cubicle or recess, often enclosed, in which a priest, usually screened from view, hears confessions.

skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: City Of London Coal Duties Boundary Marker

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A boundary marker for the payment of tax or duty.
A cast-iron or stone boundary post, obelisk or plate found on roads, railways, canals etc around London marking the boundary within which a duty was payable on coal.
A garden designed to display sculpture, publicly or privately.
A joint in which the tenon retains one or more of the original sides of the timber.
A temporary earthwork or fortification constructed by forces laying siege to a castle or town, etc.
A rampart or other defensive entrenchment.
A covered trench, often in a zig zag form, made for the purpose of approaching a beseiged place under fire of the garrison.
An object used in the harvesting or mowing of crops etc.
A machine for cutting down cereal crops.
A power station used to produce electricity, fired by coal gas.
A site where cementstone nodules are extracted under ground.
A small, pierced, often spherical or cylindrical, piece of glass, wood,etc, which may be strung together with others to form a necklace.
A melon shaped bead.
Dating to the reign of the Tudor monarchs.
Begins with the dissolution of the monasteries and ends with the death of Queen Victoria. Use more specific period where known.
Dating to the reign of Elizabeth 1st of England.
The residence of a person entrusted with the management of a great house or castle.
The residence and sometimes workplace of industrial workers.
The residence and small-scale workshop of a hosier.
A small round shield.
A key for a padlock.
Remains of any of the groups of animals characterized by having a bony or cartilaginous spinal column (backbone) and a well developed brain.
Use for the remains of an egg whether from a bird, reptile or amphibian.
A structure, often ornamental, in a garden, park or area of recreation, designed to reflect the style of Indian architecture. The most famous example of which is the Royal Pavilion in Brighton.
An often light and airy garden building in the Moorish style used for recreational purposes.
A type of GARDEN HOUSE situated on an island in a garden lake or canal or, more generally, by any waterside.
A light, sometimes ornamental structure in a garden, park or place of recreation, used for entertainment or shelter. Use specific type where known.
A waterside building from which one could fish.
A building, usually at a sports ground, with facilities for players and spectators.
A type of pavilion sometimes found in public parks or country house estates.
A light, ornamental structure in a garden, park or place of recreation built in the Chinese style.
A house by a toll gate or toll bridge where tolls are collected.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as an H-shaped plan, commonly with cattle housing to two or more cattle yards.
A pipe allowing the passage of water through it and designed only for this.
A tube for the transport of liquids and gases eg for drainage purposes.
A pipe designed to act as a drain or within a drain.
The apse at the west end of the nave in a double-ended church.
The residence of a teacher, often on the site of a school.
A twin engined advanced trainer aircraft developed for the military by the US firm of Cessna
Sedimentary rock consisting of rounded pebbles naturally cemented together.
Conglomerate consisting of rounded flint pebbles held together in a natural silica and sand cement.
Conglomerate consisting of nodules of calcium rich clay (marl). Used as a building stone from Roman times and as a key ingredient in Parker's Roman Cement, between 1796 and circa 1850.
A defensive bank and ditch, circular or oval in plan, surrounding one or more buildings.
A hinged, sliding or rolling door placed over a window's exterior or interior.
A pit used for containing manure.
A building in which a supply of arms, ammunition and provisions for an army is stored.
A place in which gunpowder and other explosives are stored in large quantities.
A mechanism used for lifting and lowering weights, operated by hand.
The premises of an agricultural merchant where agricultural equipment, animal feed and fertilizers can be bought.
Small fish, Sardina pilchardus, common to European waters and eaten as a food fish.
Any of a large group of cold blooded vertebrates who live exclusively in water. Also can refer to the flesh of fish which is eaten.

Any activity, undertaken by professional archaeologists or experienced amateurs, that has a physical impact, actual or potential, upon the archaeological resource, substituting the physical resource with recorded information.
Type of survey involving the drilling of deep and narrow shafts in the ground used to describe deposits, understand stratigraphy and collect cores amples.
Man made structure to contain tidal waters, often part of a LIDO, bathing or swimming complex at the sea edge.
Man made structure, usually sub-terranean, built to contain water for the purpose of immersion of people for sport and leisure.
An inhumation, usually Roman, which has been covered by tiles to form a tent-like structure over the body; the apex is covered by ridge tiles.
An interment of human or animal remains. Use specific type where known. If component use with wider site type. Use FUNERARY SITE for optimum retrieval in searches.
A large stone used to grind grain or similar.
Use for bone remodelling, new growth, loss or destruction caused by age, activity, disease or trauma during life.
A vertical partition used to separate one area from another.
A timber screen, often richly decorated, placed in front of a chancel to support a rood loft.
A gun emplacement which conforms to Department of Fortification and Works drawing number 55483.
A house with a pitched or gabled roof with a double slope and gables on two or more sides.
A house with a pitched roof with a double slope and gables on the side elevations of the building.
A barrel-making workshop or factory, found in conjunction with a number of industries.
A pit from which sand is excavated.
A site associated with the extraction, from the ground, of sand and gravel. Use more specific type where known.

An aircraft lifted by gas bags, containing hydrogen or helium, but propelled by engines. Also known as a dirigible balloon, firm and streamlined in shape and incapable of high speeds. Used extensively during World War One.
A rigid frame type of airship pioneered by Count Zeppelin and used by the Germans in WWI for military purposes: do not use asa generic name for airships
A building used for drilling out the bores of cannon and other military pieces.
A building or site used for the manufacture of small arms and artillery pieces, etc.
A building used for the testing of weapons for quality, accuracy and explosive power.
A workshop or factory where the barrels of cannon are cast.
A building or large scale site for the manufacture and/or storage of weapons, ammunition and equipment.
A building or site used for the manufacture, assembly and testing of weapons, explosives and associated military hardware.
A workshop for testing guns, incorporating louvred sheds to serve as firing ranges.
A tower in which shot is made from molten lead poured through sieves at top and falling into water at bottom.
A building or site used for the manufacture of weapons, ammunition and military supplies. Use more specific type where known.
A path or area for exercise, usually taken in the form of walking. Can be partially or totally covered.
A covered ambulatory, usually arcaded, arranged around three or four sides of a quadrangle in a monastic or collegiate establishment.
Drawing of the vertical face of an excavated feature or features depicting the vertical extent and stratigraphic relationship between identified layers or deposits.
A schematic depiction of the results of an archaeological excavation.
A building used to store fodder for deer.
A building used to prepare and store dry food such as hay and straw for the feeding of cattle.
Characteristic waste flakes struck off in the production of axes.
Waste flakes and cores produced in the manufacture of stone implements.
A construction material made by the firing or baking of clay.
A hard, unglazed earthenware, characteristically reddish-brown in colour, used in decoration and construction.
The oil rich seed of the plant Bracchus napus.
A key, usually with a long stem, its terminal is generally hooked or looped, and bit set at angle to stem with radiating or looped wards.
German single-engine, four-seat maritime patrol and reconnaissance flying-boat. In production between 1934 and 1940, the DO18 was replaced by the three engined DO24.
Originally the Zeppelin Werk Lindau G.m.b.H., developed metal aircraft from World War One under the guidance of Dr. Ing. Claude Dornier, changing its name to Dornier-Werke G.m.b.H. in 1922.

A streamlined, twin-engined bomber, the DO17 entered service in 1937 with the Condor Legion, having started life as a high-speed mail and passenger transport aircraft, a role for which it was ill-suited due to the narrowness of the fuselage.
German three-engined air/sea rescue and transport flying boat. Entered service in 1940 as a replacement for the DO18.
A progressive development of the DO17, the twin-engined DO217 entered service in 1941. The DO217 saw service as a bomber over the UK and took part in the 'Baedecker' raids of 1942.
Rough, unhewn, undressed building stones with irregular faces, generally not laid in regular courses. Index with type of stone if specified.
A raw material determined by its form or a finished product material characterised by its end shape or form. See MATERIAL <BY FORM> Class List for narrow terms.

A perforated stone basin usually built into the wall of a church on the south side of the altar. Used for carrying away the ablutions (wine and water used to rinse the chalice, and wash the priests hands after communion).
A mound used to elevate buildings associated with a fishery e.g. smoke houses, above the level of a flood plain.
A lock, often containing a fish ladder, which allows fish to swim upstream bypassing a weir or other obstacle.
A holding tank/pen on a river or seashore for raising and preserving fish and/or for catching them easily.
An area where fish are naturally present, eg. part of a river.
A series of steps designed to enable fish to ascend a fall of water or a dam.
The residence of a lightkeeper.
A dwelling for the keeper of a canal wharf.

A vessel composed of three or more equally spaced lobes and usually, a waisted or pedestal base. The handles are vertical loops, generally of strap form. There may be two opposed handles, or one per lobe junction. (Source: MPRG)

Twin-engined, four-seat torpedo-bomber designed to replace the Vildebeest. Entered service with RAF Coastal Command in 1939. Later versions incorporated a remote-controlled machine gun with periscope sight.

Traditionally a mew was a building housing hawks when they were moulting, however since the C16th the term has been used for a series of stables grouped around an open yard or alley, often with rooms above. Use only for stables otherwise use FALCONRY.
Metalwork attaching or attached to a harness.
The part of the bridle that fits around the horses head.
Production of steel by reheating wrought iron in charcoal filled containers.

Circular or near circular ditches, usually seen as cropmarks. Use the term where the function is unknown. Ring ditches may be the remains of ploughed out round barrows, round houses, or of modern features such as searchlight emplacements.
An aisle divided into chapels. This term is sometimes applied to the screens dividing the aisle, or the chapels themselves.

The side compartment of a building, usually a church, hall or barn, separated from the main body of the building by an arcade; or a passage allowing access to rows of seats in an auditorium or church.
An enclosure, usually within a zoo, designed to represent the natural environment for bears, including shelter. For bear baiting enclosures use BEAR PIT.

Inhumation rite in which charcoal is included with the buried corpse, possibly in an attempt to preserve the body. Thought to be associated with high status burials of the early medieval and medieval period.
A house with an aisle on one side only.
Photographic transparency mounted for use in projection equipment.
A building housing a turbine.
Ornamentation fixed to a horse's harness.
A factory producing drabbet, a type of linen cloth.
A site where the baiting of animals took place. Use more specific site type where known.
An arena for bull-baiting, not a tethering ring.
Prehistoric structure consisting of three or more standing stones in close proximity to each other, forming an unroofed approximately rectangular structure open in one direction.
Two masted vessel with a square rig on both masts.
A building used for meetings and worship by a religious community trying to propogate its faith in an area.
A building, usually associated with a port or dock, where seamen could get a meal and a cheap room. Often established by religious groups for the moral betterment of seamen.

A commercial building, or buildings, used for the production of beer and other alcoholic drinks. Size may range from a single room such as a microbrewery in a public house to a complex of buildings including production line machinery for bottling.
A plsce were herbal beers are brewed.
A building equipped with facilities for bathing, and occasionally public baths.
The upper part of a column or pier.
A place where injured or endangered animals are kept and looked after.
A building, range of buildings or site, for the accommodation, rearing and/or treatment of animals, birds and fish, both wild and domestic.

A site where flint seams within chalk have been exploited by digging deep vertical shafts, often with horizontal galleries radiating out from the base. Use for Neolithic examples and for Post Medieval gunflint industry.
A bridge decorated with shells forming an ornamental feature.
A mill in which oilcloth (a heavy cotton or linen cloth with a linseed oil coating) was produced.

A flask holding gunpowder used to prime a firearm, ie to provide a small quantity of gunpowder to be put in the pan which would be lit to set off the main charge in the barrel. The powder would often be a finer grade than that used for the charge.

The hobby of using a metal detector to hunt for buried coins or artefacts; alternatively the use of a metal detector to locate metal artefacts on an archaeological excavation that otherwise would go unnoticed.
A two-storey watch office, built to Air Ministry drawing number 1959/34. It became the standard design for watch offices with a large, almost square, ground plan with a central observation tower.
A small warship with a shallow draught. Used for patrol duties and shore bombardment on major rivers.
A small warship built to operate close to the shore or in river estuaries. Used for shore bombardment and patrol duties.
A strip of ground forming a fringe to a garden. Use more specific type where known.
A bed or border in which different species and colours are mixed.

A temporary structure used for the firing of bricks or tiles. Unfired bricks or tiles were stacked upon a layer of fuel (usually wood) and then surrounded by a wall of old bricks and covered by a layer of mud or clay. The clamp was then fired.
A tunnel running under a river or through a hill along which vehicles may travel.
Decorative fitting hung from harness.
A metal pillar with a flashable lamp on top containing an emergency telephone for use by members of the public and by officers of the local police force.
A freestanding public call box, containing a telephone and usually operated by inserting coins.
A room or building used for recording and broadcasting radio programmes.
A building or series of rooms specially designed for the recording and transmission of live or taped television programmes.
A place where radio programmes are produced and broadcast.
A structure consisting of a large, metal framework holding a skyward facing dish. Used for transmitting and receiving signals which are relayed by satellite.
A large dish-like structure designed to observe the invisible outerspace phenomena detected by radio waves, eg. Jodrell Bank.
A tall wooden pole used to support telegraph wires.

Sites, buildings, structures & features associated with the transmission & receiving of information. Includes signalling, broadcasting & telecommunications; does not include transport except where there is a specific connection with communication.

A metal, wooden or concrete box containing a telephone for use by the public, limited accommodation for use as a temporary cell, and a lamp on top that could be used to attract the attention of a passing patrol.
Structures associated with telecommunications.
A curving, upright timber brace used in roof construction, found in pairs, forming an arch.
A place where gold ore is extracted.
An interior or projecting shelter surrounding an entrance to a building.
A porch which is sufficiently large enough to allow a vehicle beneath it.
Water channel leading to water wheel.
A water channel leading from a water wheel.
The channel of water that provides a current of water to drive a millwheel.
A single decked cargo vessel carrying the majority of its cargo on deck.
A piece of land, sometimes man-made, completely surrounded by water.
A small island, especially within a river.
Oven for roasting coal to drive off chemical constituents and reduce it to almost pure carbon, ie. coke.
The large main axle on which a waterwheel, which turns the shaft, and a pitwheel are mounted.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a mound of earth or stone. Use more specific type where known.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a rectangular or trapezoidal earthen mound.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a circular or sub-circular earthen mound. See RELIGIOUS, RITUAL AND FUNERARY Class List for context.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within an earthen mound. Use more precise term where known.
A miniature lead phial worn around the neck as a religious pilgrim sign, generally medieval.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a mound of stones. Use more precise term where known.

A Neolithic burial monument comprising a rectangular or trapezoidal stony mound which contains either a passage at one end with or without lateral chambers, or one or more smaller chambers entered from the side of the mound.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising an approximately circular stony mound which contains a stone-built chamber, with or without additional lateral chambers.
A container to hold and/or apply grease.

A settlement consisting of several hut circles, either grouped together or dispersed. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period. Use specific forms where supported by the available evidence. For isolated hut circles use HUT CIRCLE.

A settlement with evidence for several hut circles but clearly lacking an obvious boundary. Where it is not certain whether a boundary existed or not, use HUT CIRCLE SETTLEMENT. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period.
A site, usually consisting of a bowling green and pavilion, frequented by lawn bowlers.
An administrative building used to organize and co-ordinate the activities of members of the armed forces.
A building used for the administration of a squadron.
A device for winding and casting a fishing line, consisting of a revolving spool with a handle attached to a fishing rod.
A structure providing protection against the weather at tram stops.
Ornamentation worn specifically for formalised dancing.
A building used by an organization or society instituted to promote science through lectures, research, etc.
The taking of photographs from above using photographic equipment mounted on, or used from an aircraft or other airborne vehicle.

Light detection and ranging is a type of aircraft based remote sensing which records reflected laser pulses. The data can be used to produce very accurate digital elevation models. For ground-based work use LASER SCANNING SURVEY.
Airborne survey to discover, record and monitor archaeological sites and other heritage assets. Sites will usually be recorded by aerial photography.
Survey using photographic or other recording equipment mounted on or used from either an aircraft or other airborne vehicle or a maritime vessel/submersible craft.
A vehicle containing a couch shut in by curtains and carried by men or beasts of burden.
An observation post for a naval officer in charge of a marine minefield.
For example mine, quarry etc.
A small house, usually on the estate of a country house, forming part of a widow's dower and intended as her residence.
Late nineteenth and early twentieth century warship armed with guns and torpedoes.
Use for vessels registered in Norway.
The wedge shaped end of a bridge pier designed to break the current of water.

Device for extracting juice from apples, usually crab apples, for use in cooking and medicine. Consists of a stone base carved with channels in the upper surface which was used with an upper weight, often secured with a wooden beam wedged into position.
The administrative office of a commercial concern.
A room or building occupied by a person employed to keep accounts of workers' hours of labour.
An area of shallow linear cuts made by the removal of turf for fuel or building material.
A pair of tongs used for placing coals onto a fire.
Twin bars riveted together which can open and close allowing it to grip objects, usually to lift and move them.

A building complex, usually including kennels and cages and built close to a port or airport, in which animals can be securely held, for a designated period, to ensure that they are not carrying any infectious diseases which could be spread to others.

A World War One German three-crew, twin-engined, long range heavy bomber biplane manufactured by Gothaer Waggonfabrik A.G.. Entering service in 1917, this aircraft incorporated a ventral tunnel allowing the gunner to shoot downwards and to the rear.
Gothauer Waggonfabrik A.G., based in Gotha, Thuringia (Germany). During World War 2 produced mostly training and light commercial aircraft and troop and freight-carrying gliders.
A mill for the removal by mechanical means of the dried wood and seeds of the flax and cotton plants after retting. The resulting 'tow' is then spun into linen and cotton respectively.
A long narrow two edged sword with a guarded hilt, used as a thrusting weapon.
Open decked vessel used for sight seeing or pleasure voyages.
A vessel designed principally for the carriage of fare paying passengers.
Term used to indicate the basic unit of accommodation in the plan of a building. It does not necessarily relate to the structural divisions within a building.
A projection on the under side of a hinged choir stall seat providing support during long periods of standing.
A watch office designed for bomber satellite station comprising a long, temporary brick hut with a watch office, operations room and crew briefing room.

A detached building without an operations block and crew briefing room designed on modern lines similar to, but smaller than WATCH OFFICE (12779/41). Began appearing on new stations from September 1941.
A kiln with a pyramid roof and capped vent in which barley is dried. Found on the site of a malt house.
A monument composed of plants or trees which are still extant. Especially relevant for park and garden features. For example tree avenue, orchard, rose garden and lawn.
A single piece of apparatus that uses mechanical power for a particular function.
A crane with a projecting arm, usually one that can be raised and lowered.
A dockside crane with a solid curving jib made out of rivetted iron plates.
Establishments authorized to sell or allow the consumption of alcoholic liquors on their premises.
The public house was a 19th century development, distinctive from the earlier BEER HOUSE by its decorative treatment and fittings.
A public house licensed for the sale of wine and other alcoholic drinks.
Garden area next to public house used for the comsumption of alcoholic beverages.
An area of land, usually planted with creeping plants and turf, laid out in a woodland landscape to produce the natural effect of a clearing.
An educational establishment, often privately funded, for young women.
A bayonet designed to plug into the muzzle of a musket or rifle.
Establishments authorized to sell or allow the consumption of alcoholic liquors on their premises.
A licenced establishment where wine and other alcoholic drinks are sold for drinking on the premises.
Wooden roof tile (traditionally oak) which is riven or sawn from good quality timber to a regular size and used as a roof and/or wall covering. Index with type of wood if known.
External decorative plasterwork often incised or modelled with ornamental patterns. Usually applied to timber-framed houses, especially during 16th and 17th centuries.
Ornate or patterned decoration, carved into or moulded from plaster.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the defence of the coastline from foreign invasion.
A coastal gun/watch tower built as part of the anti-invasion defences during the Napoleonic Wars.

An astronomical instrument for telling the time at night. The date is set on the nocturnal then its pointers lined up with the Pole Star and the two primary stars in the Great Bear, thus allowing an approximate time to be read off.
The analysis of the amount of phosphorus (P) present in a soil.
The analysis of the amount of phosphorus (P) (liable fraction) available to plants.
The analysis of organic plus inorganic phosphorus (P).
The analysis of inorganic phosphorus (P).
The residence of a marsh keeper.
Buildings and structures inhabited by agricultural workers.
Bordered by the continents of Africa, Asia and Europe, the Mediterranean covers some 967,000 sq miles. It is linked to the Atlantic Ocean by the Straits of Gibraltar.
Equipment used on or with water craft.
A heavy weight used to moor a ship.
A building or site used for the production of acids by a range of chemical processes.
A lock or a dam in a river.
A narrow, open container, usually where food or water for animals is put. Use specific type where known.
A long, wooden, metal or stone vessel holding drinking water for horses.
A large store for the temporary accommodation of goods awaiting transportation to or from the sea.
A crane mounted on a large metal gantry, used for the lifting of large-scale building materials, etc.
A factory or works principally engaged in the refining or manufacture of TNT.
Second World War allied patrol-bomber built by Lockheed Vega, a Lockheed subsidiary. This aircraft was a military development of the Lodestar, USAF designation B-34.
A straight-grained, durable and often resinous timber obtained from trees of the genus Pinus.
A piece of openwork fabric made from twine or cord, either natural fibre or artificial, forming a mesh used for catching birds, animals or fish or for holding other inanimate objects.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as two ranges at right angles to each other.
A collar, usually metal, used to signify slavery and to inhibit freedom, usually with a chain attached.
Chests connected with the burial of a body.
A site used for the extraction of metallic zinc by a variety of processes.
A processed used to increase the thickness of the natural oxide layer on the surface of metal parts. The part being treated forms the anode of an electrolytic cell.
A mill, including a forge and powered hammers where hot metal is shaped by hammering and rolling.
A site or building used for the manufacture of goods made from pewter, an alloy of tin and lead.
A site where iron is smelted or iron goods made.
A complex of buildings used for the processing of metals. Use more specific type where known.
A site or establishment for the casting and refining of metallic copper.
A factory used for the production of red lead used in glass manufacture, or white lead used as the pigment in white paint.
A site where large sheets of thin metal are manufactured.
A place for sharpening metal objects like tools and weapons.
An alloy of tin, antimony and copper used as a replacement for pewter.
A brass manufacturing complex incorporating battery mill furnaces, hammers, etc.
A factory or group of buildings used for the production of plated goods. Plating is the process whereby one metal object is coated with a thin layer of another metal.
A pontoon element of a Mulberry Harbour that sits between the Spud Pontoons that allow oit to rise and fall with the tide.
Very fine particles of gold.
A yellowish, tarnish-resistant precious metal used to make jewellery and coins.
A staircase, usually leading from a dormitory, used by monks to enter the transept of a monastic church.
A line or track consisting of iron or steel rails, on which passenger carriages or goods wagons are moved, usually by a locomotive engine.

A railway, usually by the sea, linking the beach with the cliff top. Various mechanisms were used the most common being that the cars were attached to a cable and winding drum and were balanced so that one travelled up, as the other came down.
A measuring rule graduated in feet.
A graduated length of material used for measuring distances.
A mug with roughly vertical body walls. (Source: MPRG)
A mug with straight sides flaring outwards from the base towards the rim. (Source: MPRG)
A mug with a rounded body profile below a deep neck. There may be a marked junction between the neck and the body. The neck may be inward-sloping, upright or everted. (Source: MPRG)
A mug with little or no discernible neck and an even, convex profile from rim to base, which have roughly equal diameters. (Source: MPRG)
A mug with more-or-less straight side which flare out from the rim to the wider base. (Source: MPRG)
A container from which liquid is drunk.
A drinking vessel with a handle.
A building housing a flight simulator designed to air ministry drawing number 7790/40.
A nonconformist church for the followers of Edward Irving.
A place of worship for members of Protestant sects dissenting from the established Church.

Originally designed as a wood and steel bomber-reconnaissance aircraft, subsequent variations served as special transports, glider tugs and paratroop carriers. Featured a tricycle-style undercarriage.

Sir W. G. Armstrong Whitworth Aircraft, Ltd. formed in 1921. Controlled by the Armstrong Siddeley Development Co., Ltd., a subsidiary of the Hawker Siddeley Aircraft Co., Ltd. from 1935. Pioneers in the development of all-metal aircraft.
A WWII structure designed to project sheets of flame across an area such as a beach, the sea or a road, to hinder attacking forces.
A site, usually including fuel tanks, pipe works and control buildings, where flaming petroleum was intended to be used as a weapon against a hostile invasion.
A place where manganese ore is extracted. Use with other ores extracted and MINE where relevant.
A compact, free standing steam engine introduced circa 1810 and built mainly in small sizes.
Small square rigged ship with a narrow overhanging stern.
The powdery residue of burnt bones.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by a double line of ramparts.
A feature found during an archaeological investigation which implies the presence of a monument, building, structure or human activity.
A small hole filled or vacated by a stake, normally driven into the ground.
A piece of land used for the cultivation of hops.
A room in which board and table games are usually played.
A room intended for the placement and use of a billiard table.
A road block formed by placing rails or girders in an upright position in sockets in the road surface, forming a moveable barrier.
A hard, lustrous metallic element obtained from various ores, including sphalerite, and used in roofing, alloys and for galvanizing iron.
Zinc, now mainly used for smelted zinc but has been used to include zinc ores.
Solid bars made from pure zinc.
A vessel for the storage and transport of wine.
A container, typically cylindrical with a narrow neck, usually for containing liquids.
A bowl adapted by the addition of a short tubular spout applied just below the rim.
A building plan in which a passage crosses the axis of the building, often at one end of a hall, with an external door at each end.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the Air Ministry. Usually found on or near airfields.
A horizontal, moulded band, usually projecting, running across a wall, often indicating the position of a building's interior floor.
The public house was a 19th century development, distinctive from the earlier BEER HOUSE by its decorative treatment and fittings.
Garden area next to public house used for the comsumption of alcoholic beverages.
A site where acts of corporal and capital punishment were carried out.
A chair fixed to the end of a plank, in which scolds or dishonest people were tied and ducked in water as a punishment.
Norfolk
A settlement showing evidence for one or more hut circles, enclosed by a distinct boundary ditch, wall, earth rampart or similar barrier. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period.
A bridge used for carrying liquids, usually water, although sometimes oil, in a pipeline over a river. Mid 19th century onwards.
A container used to hold substances for dying or painting.
A building, site or container used to store the bones of the dead after they have been removed from graves to allow new burials.
A container holding items associated with the period of burial. Often buried to commemorate a certain event, such as the foundation of a building.
An instrument in which air is made to vibrate by a cane reed.
An instrument in which air is made to vibrate by a cane reed, which may be single or double, and may or may not be contained in a reed cap.
A building used in the preparation of manure.
A site where household rubbish and other waste products can be disposed of. May take the form of a pit, rubbish tip, landfill site or incineration plant.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the disposal of domestic and industrial waste.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Cluniac order.

An outlying farm or estate, usually belonging to a religious order or feudal lord. Specifically related to core buildings and structures associated with monastic land holding. Use specific term where known.
A single-seat, pusher prop, escort and patrol-fighter. Used in the UK in a Home Defence role until superseded in 1917.
The main dwelling-house of a farm, it can be either detached from or attached to the working buildings.
A house in which a member of the Royal Court lives.
A hanging frame with branches which act as candle holders or to which lights are attached.
An object in which a candle is put in order to provide light.
A large, branched candle holder.
A holder for a candle, usually fitted to another object.
An object used in the lighting of an area.
A tall holder for candles which stands on the floor.
A small shallow cup used in assaying gold or silver.
A furnace in which the flame is turned back over the substance to be heated.
An enclosed furnace used for the continuous casting of plate glass.
A place, where a corpse could be laid whilst being carried on its way to a burial, to allow the bearers to rest.
A quarry for the extraction of Soapstone (also known as steatite or soaprock), a metamorphic rock largely composed of the mineral talc and rich in magnesium.
An excavation from which stone for building and other functions, is obtained by cutting, blasting, etc.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Order of Tiron.

A prefabricated temporary structure made of lightweight timber framed panels clad externally with corrugated iron sheets. Used during WWII as officers quarters. Possibly manufactured by Boulton and Paul Limited.
An indented parapet consisting of raised parts, called merlons, separated by gaps, or crenelles.
A barrier, usually in the form of a small wall, set to prevent people falling over the side of a bridge, balcony, roof etc.
A gutter running behind a parapet wall, the water channelled by it being discharged from holes in the wall.
A mug with little or no discernible neck and an even, convex profile from rim to base, which have roughly equal diameters. (Source: MPRG)
A drinking vessel with a handle.
A grave or sepulchre including a monument. Use specific type where known.
A burial site for an animal, usually commemorated by a gravestone or other structure.
Developed from the DH4, featured the pilot and gunner cockpits in closer proximity, but suffered from engine reliability problems. Also known as the Ninak, saw service from 1918 to 1931.
A decorative feature in the style of a formalized rose.
Pieces of bone used in a game, the pieces are thrown and then picked up between bounces of a small ball or throws of another piece.
A barn belonging to, or associated with, a grange.
Use for completed, accuarately surveyed maps
A house with no row of posts between the central space and the aisles.
Use where the intervening arcade is closed but timber-framed.
An alloy, traditionally of tin and lead but now of tin, antimony and copper, used for domestic utensils.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of firelighters.
Photographic print using silver gelatine.

A small rectangular or sub circular area or areas bounded by an earthwork, ditch or similar boundary, where one side is formed by an existing linear boundary, forming a pattern reminiscent of clothes hanging from a washing line.
A public house where no alcohol is sold.
Unfermented wine.
An alcoholic drink made from fermented grape juice (or occasionally other fruits).
Use for vessels believed to come from North America but where the precise nationality is not known.
Used for the island of Jamaica which gained independence from Britain in 1958.
A two-seat, reconnaissance biplane developed from the FK2 with a more powerful, but heavier, engine. Primarily used for training in the UK.
A woollen mill in which the cloth was passed over rollers covered in short spikes to raise the nap in one direction only.
A factory where short wool was spun into woollen yarn to produce cloth.
An ancillary building in a factory or other industrial complex where manufactured goods are packaged.
The entrance to a tunnel. Use more specific type where known.
An often stately or ornate entrance to a railway tunnel.
A place where knitted fabrics and legware garments were manufactured.
A room or building for hand knitting garments on simple hand frames.
A hearth used for the reheating of metal slag to extract further metal.
Unable to identify actual place from documentary sources alone.
Canal docks where the freeboard of a boat was marked. By placing increasing ton weights at 4 points around the boat, its displacement could be marked for toll purposes.
A garden with one or more platforms with walks, often on different levels, usually close to the house.
A dedicated room for housing the organ feeder bellows, can be an underground chamber or a free-standing building.
A weapon featuring a single or double edged head attached to a wooden shaft.
An axe designed and weighted to be thrown.
An axe designed for fighting could be single or double headed and used with one or two hands. Where use is thought to be ceremonial multiple index with ceremonial object.
A long shaft topped by an axe head. Differs from a battleaxe by the length of the shaft.
A building in which horses are accommodated.
A stable where horses are kept at livery, or are let out for hire.
A stable used for riding horses or those used to pull coaches, gigs, etc.
A stable found at a coaching inn where horses are housed.
A stable associated with a horse-drawn tramway system.
A stable located at a railway station or goods yard. Horses were necessary both for freight and passengers to continue their journey beyond the railway.
A stable, on two or more levels.
An aircraft used for the training of pilots, sometimes fitted with dual controls for use by the instructor.
Single-engine, spruce and plywood, fabric-covered training and communications low-wing monoplane. Served from 1939 to 1950.
A wing in a workhouse to accommodate vagrants overnight.
Fruit native to the countries bordering the Mediterranean Sea.
The edible product of a plant, usually consisting of the seed and its sweet, juicy envelope.
A place of worship for members of the Greek Orthodox Church, the national church of Greece.
A single-seat fighter which began service with the RFC's fighter squadron in 1916. Some short-term success in dealing with new Fokkers but was withdrawn from service in mid-1917.
A container used to serve drinks and liquids.
A small round dish on which a drinking vessel is set.
A mark erected on or near danger or on shore as an aid to pilotage.
A stopping place on an underground railway system where passengers can board and disembark from a train.
A place where railway trains regularly stop for taking up and setting down passengers or for receiving goods for transport.
An object used to weigh something down or to measure the weight of another object.
Weight used for weighing specific quantities and qualities of gold.
A small building used as a shelter by a shepherd.
The retrieval of samples for laboratory analysis from buried features that have been sampled using boring equipment.

A maritime coring technique which penetrates the ground due to the force of gravity. Since the speed of penetration is the same as the sampling speed, it barely disrupts the sedimentary layers. A cable attached to the ship is used to recover the core.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the preserving of food.

A building where fish are stored. Often taking the form of a single storey building with one room, but also may provide living accommodation for a fisherman above. Found mainly in the South West of England.
A room for higher-ranking servants.

A French aeroplane company that primarily built racing aircraft before World War I and fighter aircraft during World War I and between the wars. First set up in 1902 as manufacturer of engine components, then aircraft in 1911 as Nieuport et Deplante.

A French airliner which entered service in 1920. A conventional biplane design with enclosed cabin for four passengers and open cockpit for the pilot. Fitted with an early audible guidance system. Withdrawn from service in 1921.
A school founded by the British and Foreign Society to provide non-denominational education. Usually built and supported by voluntary contributions.
Three-dimensional artwork usually created out of stone, e.g. marble; metal, e.g. bronze; ceramics, e.g. terracotta, or other suitable materials.

Any unspecified items without utility or function and prized for personal or domestic decorative value. Examples might be unspecified metal objects from the Bronze Age or Victorian Staffordshire china dogs.
A style of decorative design consisting of intertwined, geommetrical patterns of leaves, branches, tendrils etc. Often defined as being devoid of human or animal figures.
A wheel with a series of teeth on its outside which interlock with similar teeth on another cogwheel to receive or give motion.
A building designed to house insects.
A factory where general hardware, fittings, items of ironmongery are produced.
Fine grained, whitish, granular variety of Gypsum. Suitable for carving.
A factory used for the manufacture of serge, a heavy woollen cloth.
A building offering accommodation to people who are visiting a town or locality renowned for its mineral springs.
A large building used for the accommodation of paying travellers and guests.
A system of long, continuous banks and/or ditches dividing land into well defined areas. Possibly used for controlling livestock
A forest killed by rising sea-level. Nowadays only tree stumps survive.
Former terrestrial landscape of any kind now submerged through erosion, as at Dunwich, or historical inundation processes, eg. post-glacial submersion of the North Sea landscape ("Doggerland").
A plate used during circumcision.
Equipment used to perform circumcision.
A small coastal fishing vessel peculiar to Kent, cutter rigged.
An establishment for the theoretical and practical training of nurses.
A malleable, ductile ferromagnetic metal widely used for structural and decorative purposes.
A metallic substance made by combining two or more elements at least one of which is a metal. Use more specific terms where known.
Metal used primarily for roof coverings and window fittings. It is easy to work, can be worked cold and does not rust which makes it suitable for holding or repelling water.
A precious metal of lustrous white colour with great malleability and ductility.
A soft, lustrous low-melting crystalline metallic element that is malleable and ductile at ordinary temperatures and that is used as a protective coating, in tinfoil, and in soft solders and alloys.
A white ductile metal used, for example, in alloys, for instruments, and in aircraft construction.
Metal used primarily for roofing and ornamental purposes, being lighter and stronger than lead.
Blue-white metal, obtained from ore, and used commercially for roofing, galvanizing iron, or in alloys. Also used in the 19th century as sheathing for ship's hulls.
A metallic element often used in alloys and historically used in pottery and glass-making, paints, enamelling, and in cosmetics and medicine. Often derived from its sulphite ore, stibnite.

Class of elements and alloys that are characteristically lustrous,ductile, fusible and malleable. These are extracted from ore minerals originally existing in nature and processed before becoming a recognisable metal. See METAL Class List for narrow terms
A precious metal characterized by its yellow colour and resistance to tarnishing.
A road surface made out of wooden blocks or planks. It was much used in English cities before 1940, but the cost of wooden blocks eventually made it uneconomical.
A room used for storing food.
A small earthenware container used for liquids.
A component of reciprocating engines - the moving component that is contained by a cylinder.
A former ground surface buried beneath an earthwork or other sequence of deposits. (includes palaeosoils, turf lines)
Use only for features assumed to be archaeological but which cannot be identified more precisely without further investigation .Use more specific term where known
A place of worship for members of the Seventh Day Adventists Church. This was formed in 1843 by followers believing in the imminent second coming of Christ.
A post to which ropes are attached to secure vessels at a landing place.

Canadian-built, single-engine, high-wing transport and communications aircraft converted from a civilian model. Metal-framed with fabric covering, saw service in 1944-5. Was capable of being equipped with wheels, floats or skis.

A long, thin cane of glass made by layering glass of various colours in a mould and pulling the soft glass until the cane was of the desired thickness. When cut and viewed in section the cane has a mosaic like appearance.
A watch office with additional rooms given over to the meteorological section, including a forecast room and met store.

A two-storey, brick construction with a watch office and additional rooms given over to the meteorological section, including a forecast room and met store. A brick parapet on the roof differentiates it from 2328/39.
Bomb series based on growth season
A building situated next to a horse racing course with facilities for participants and spectators.
A place where the game of skittles is played.
The principal stand at a sporting ground, eg. at a racecourse.
A building, usually at a sports ground, with facilities for players and spectators.
An area, often including a platform, used for boxing competitions.
A 16th century tower for observing tournaments, eg. at royal palaces.
A building in which a sport is played. Use more specific type where known.
A building with facilities for playing snooker.
A large structure, found at sports stadiums, from where television or radio broadcasts are made of the sporting events.
An indoor alley for playing bowls or skittles.
A small garden building used to store equipment used in the game of croquet.
A building or room, originally equipped for gymnastics or indoor sports but also, more recently, equipped with cross-training machines and free-weights for members to improve their physical fitness.
An establishment where the art of sword fencing is taught.
A venue, with a boxing ring and associated facilities, which is used to train for and undertake amateur or professional boxing.
A specially built building where facilities exist for the playing of a variety of sports.
A wall used in the game of handball.
A Hall where billiards was played.
A piece of ice or a floor, often within a building, used for skating.

One of two or three bands on a classical architrave, each projecting slightly beyiond the one below, often separated by enriched mouldings. Also a vertical band or board, such as that over a shop front on which its name is painted.

The lowest of the three main parts of an entablature. Also the lintels, jambs and mouldings surrounding a door, window, panels or niche; or the ornamental mouldings around the exterior curve of an arch.
Photographic image produced using an ink-jet printer.
A port on the sea, rather than on river or estuary.
A port situated on a river, often associated with a town or overland goods transport facilities.
An inland settlement such as Runcorn, Ellesmere Port or Stourport, that combines docks and terminal facilities at the interface between land and canal transportation systems.
A settlement area that combines a harbour and terminal facilities at the interface between land and water transportation systems.

Single-engine, two-seat, light, biplane, elementary-flying trainer. Adapted from a civilian design, and constructed from tubular steel and spruce with plywood and fabric covering, entered service in 1931 and was available in land-plane or seaplane forms.
Synthetic fibres and reconstituted materials imitating, or in the form of, timber created by a man-made process. Use carefully - do not confuse with mock and sham timber work.
A gun emplacement which conforms to Department of Fortification and Works drawing number 55415.
A playing piece for draughts
A Mark 2 aircraft which has undergone slight modifications to enhance performance or armament.
A fighter version of the SKUA fitted with a four-gun turret. The majority were converted to target tugs for use by the RAF and Fleet Air Arm.
A sculpture on top of a tomb etc.
Sites and buildings used for the storage or equipment, ordnance or vehicles. Use more specific term.

A site used for the safe storage of the art held in the national collections. During the Second World War many paintings, sculptures and works of art were moved to modified mines for safe keeping to protect them against bomb damage.
A door, gate, doorway or gateway of grand or elaborate construction. Use specific type where possible.
Pasture to which animals were driven for grazing, with associated temporary huts for domestic or agricultural use.
A large, rectangular open space at the centre of a Roman town, incorporating public spaces and a market area.
Pond, created specifically for providing power to water-powered forges, blast furnaces, helve or other hammers.
A triangular arrowhead retouched to form a central tang and lateral barbs. The sides may be straight or concave.
A three-cornered arrowhead.
Building housing apparatus for testing chain links.
A site where wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.

A family of jet fighters capable of vertical/short takeoff and landing. A subsonic aircraft, later designs adapted for use from aircraft carriers. Built between 1967-2003. Used by the RAF and the Royal Navy.
A building, structure or landscape created to commemorate a person or event.
One of 12 roadside crosses erected by Edward I in memory of his wife, Eleanor of Castile, the most famous being Charing Cross in London.
Urn with a heavy rim or collar which may be vertical or slightly inverted. This may carry incised or impressed decoration, particularly herring-bone, encircling lines, hurdling or chevron decoration.
A vase-like receptacle, especially a large bulbous one with a foot.
A site where terracotta, made from weathered clay and grog, was manufactured.
A store for keeping undressed meat.
A small building in which game is hung up and kept cool.
An open area used for drying products manufactured using an industrial process.
Field or area of ground where washed new cloth is stretched out to dry.
A pipe used for smoking tobacco.
A stone-faced enclosure, with entrance closed by a floatable caisson or by gates, which can be pumped dry for inspection, maintenance, or repair of the hull or underwater fittings of a ship or ships.
A decorative S-shaped moulding, usually placed at the top of a cornice, with a convex lower half and a concave upper half.
Not subdivided
A special school to train personnel for employment in Air Traffic Control and operation duties.
A house or range of buildings in which dogs are kept, eg. hunting hounds.
A defensive gun battery positioned to face out to sea to fire on enemy ships and amphibious craft.
A command post used to direct the guns of a coastal battery.
Machinery including tractors, ploughs, harrows etc, which are used on farms.
Apparatus used for applying a mechanical force, or to perform a particular function. Use more specific type where known.
Machinery, e.g. drive wheels, used in powering and excavating mines, i.e. mines for the extraction of minerals such as coal, lead or tin.

Machines for mechanical sewing, as opposed to sewing by hand. Victoriran and early 20th century examples are usually constructed of metal and operated by a hand wheel or treadle. Later examples may be electrically operated and/or have a plastic shell.
Originally a light day-bomber, the Boston II, re-christened the Havoc, was adapted for night-flying in the fighter-intruder role. Was capable of a top speed in excess of 300 mph.
Onyx is a cryptocrystalline form of quartz. It is a semi-precious stone that is usually cut as a cabochon, or into beads, and is also used for intaglios and cameos.
Hard, transparent, often coloured mineral. Can be found on its own as crystals and veins but also as a major constituent of rocks such as granite. Often used decoratively.

A purple or violet variety of quartz often used in jewelry. Amethyst is a semi-precious stone which owes its violet colour to irridation, iron impurities, and the presence of trace elements, which result in complex crystal lattice substitutions.
A purpose built section of path linking two sections of a canal enabling a horse to be led over or around an obstacle such as a hill. Horse paths predate towpath tunnels.
A complex or ornate lid which cannot be easily classified according to the main forms of lid. (Source: MPRG)
A civil vessel disguised as a warship.
A submarine built or adapted to carry mines and lay minefields.
A German coastal minelaying submarine in use during the First World War.
A dense, high strength, low absorption brick of uniform size, employed predominantly in industrial structures such as railway viaducts.

Standard rectangular block or tablet bonded on mortar joints in a regular arrangement or pattern for strength or decoration. Made from clay or brick earth which may contain varying quantities of chalk, lime or iron oxide which effect colour or density.
A base embellished with horizontal reeds and other mouldings.
A slot, usually in a wall, into which a beam was placed.
Terms covering features of a monument or building which imply the previous presence of a component or structure. Use for negative evidence of a component or structure.
A decorative moulding featuring a geometric pattern suggesting the crenelles and merlons of a battlement.

A lid with a distinct flange, projecting upwards, horizontally or downwards, and an integral knob. Complex examples can include a simple locking device: lugs on the lower flange can be twisted into matching cut-outs in the rim to lock it. (Source: MPRG)

A type of flanged lid where the lower flange is partly cut away to leave two projections or lugs, which can be fitted into corresponding cut-outs in the rim of the vessel beneath and secure the lid when it is rotated. (Source: MPRG)
A mill where mustard is produced.
A type of Red Wine from Bordeaux in France.
A small, double-handled bowl with horizontal loop handles decorated with a cockerel motif. (Source: MPRG)
A bowl adapted by the addition of two handles, generally opposed. (Source: MPRG)
A container for pills or tablets.
A container used to hold and or pour a liquid in honour of a deity.

A shallow ceramic or metal libation bowl, usually with no handles or feet. The Greeks called it a phiale, the Romans a patera. Used in religious practice. Could contain mixed wine and water but also unmixed wine, honey, oil, water, or milk.
Narrow necked containers, originally of leather but now usually made of glass or plastic. Used for storing liquids.
Land use involving no operations likely to be damaging to archaeological remains.
A shelter for the storage of bicycles.
A by-product of the production of microliths.
A by-product created during the manufacture of a tool.
A cantilevered block projecting from the face of a wall and supporting a structure such as a parapet, beam or arch.
A stone edge-runner grinding machine or mill used for mechanically grinding and mixing the ingredients of gunpowder.
A site where copper or copper based alloys are produced by smelting copper ore.
Photographic negative on film. Use for all acetate material types.
Length of timber boarding (usually elm, now pine) fixed horizontally or vertically to the exterior of a structure which may be 'tongue and grooved' or 'feathered' to provide external protection.
A pond with protection for nesting ducks and other wild fowl
A structure providing accommodation for poultry.
An uncovered area, surrounded or partially surrounded by buildings.
A natural compound used as in the building and medical industies.
Substances, including acids, alkalis etc. obtained by or used in a chemical process.
A dome shaped building, housing training apparatus, including a projector, for training ground gunners in the art of airfield defence. (WWII).
A hall built for the use of people living within a parish boundary.
A training college for the instruction of military trainees in the theory and practice of warfare.
A chemical works engaged in the production of the coal tar derivative phenol, a chemical used for the manufacture of explosives during WWI.
A jar with an evenly rounded profile. (Source: MPRG)
A specific type of small rounded jar. (Source: MPRG)
A building complex with hangars and slipways built adjacent to a body of water where seaplanes can be stored and maintained.
Studding in which the studs are at an inclined angle to the posts.
A stud on the outside of a cruck blade and attached to it.
In timber framed buildings this is the division of a wall into narrow panels by vertical studs.
A subsidiary member, usually vertical, in a framed wall or partition.
A crane used for moving coal during the refuelling of coal-powered vessels or locomotives.
The wall plate of the lower storey on which the joists of a jetty rest.
A small artificial pond of water often found in parks and gardens, for decorative purposes.
A fence that indicates the limit of an area or a piece of land.
A place where stained glass is manufactured, traditionally for church windows.

An establishment originally providing terminals to allow the public to access the internet, usually for a fee. They originally provided snacks and drinks to customers although now this is not always the case.
A cheap eating and drinking establishment usually serving snacks and non-alcoholic drinks.
A small pond, usually circular and serving as a feature at the centre of a walled garden, used for the purpose of filling watering cans.

Monument visible as a mark in standing crops or parchmarks, but where no subsurface deposits have been proven eg by excavation or other ground disturbance, in which case SUB SURFACE DEPOSIT should be used.
A hinged or looped clasp that fits over a staple and is secured by a pin, bolt or padlock.
A farmstead where the buildings and yards are loosely arranged, with no focal yard. Use more specific type where known.
A dispersed farmstead where buildings and yards (regular or loose courtyard in their form) are sited alongside a routeway.
A dispersed farmstead where buildings are arranged around scattered yards which can be loose or regular in their form.
A dispersed farmstead where the farm buildings and farmhouse are loosely grouped together within the boundary of the farmstead.
The homestead of a farm consisting of a farmhouse and working farm buildings, with yards, other working areas and usually a garden to the house.
The Consolidated Vultee Aircraft Corporation. Formed in 1943 with the merging of The Consolidated Aircraft Corporation and Vultee Aircraft, Inc..
Vultee Aircraft, Inc.. In 1943 merged with The Consolidated Aircraft Corporation to form The Consolidated Vultee Aircraft Corporation.
