Single-engine aircraft designed as a dive-bomber. Found to be inadequate in this role, a number of those delivered to the RAF were used as target tugs. Entered service in 1941.
A two dimensional image using paint applied to plasterwork whilst the plaster is still damp.
A place of worship specifically for mariners and their families.
A bridge crossing under railway property.
A dock with gates which open for access for some hours before and after high water.
A building adjacent to a monastery where alms were distributed to the poor.
A craft used to deepen shipping channels, harbours and other water courses.
A self propelled vessel for deepening harbours using a continuous chain of buckets
A hand held device for mashing food, usually with a flat holed base attached to a handle.
Dress designed to be worn for theatrical purposes.
Clothing worn specifically for formalised dancing.
A style of dressing including all the clothes, accessories etc worn at one time, as in a particular country or period.
A tool used to provide grip and mechanical advantage in applying torque to tighten or loosen objects such as nuts and bolts.
A pipe in which air is made to vibrate by blowing across an edge, including transverse flutes and recorders.
An instrument where the note is made by air being blown over an edge.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber. Fitted with eight fixed forward-firing machine guns in the wings, plus two 1000lb bombs or six rocket projectiles.
Deliberate interment of a complete, or substantially complete, animal. Use the object type thesaurus term ANIMAL REMAINS where skeleton is fragmentary.
A column joined to another by a band or ring.
A cord or handle which rings a bell when pulled.
A mortar used specifically for grinding cosmetics.
An object used with cosmetics.
A ring fixed to a vehicle through which the reins were passed.
A beaker with convex body walls. (Source: MPRG)
A straight sided drinking vessel, usually with a wide mouth and without handles.
Canvas or similar fabric used for the manufacture of sails.
The engine housed within the fuselage of an aircraft that powers its flight.
Any part of an aircraft. Use more specific term where known.
Single-engined fighter, developed from the Camel. Entered service in 1918 and became the RAF's first mainstay peacetime fighter.
The Sopwith Aviation Co., Ltd.. Established in 1911 by the noted aviator Mr T. O. M. Sopwith. Produced many notable aircraft, including the Camel and a Schneider Cup-winning seaplane.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter biplane renowned for its high performance and manoeuvrability. Entered service in 1917.
Mark 4 or the fourth variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of candles.
A horizontal pierced metal object upon which to hold the coals of a fire.

A short wide-beamed Dutch craft, often used as a fishing vessel or, in the 17th and 18th centuries, a privateer due to its manoeuvrability. Fitted with a ketch rig or variations thereof. Used extensively in the North Sea.
A vessel with two masts, rigged as a ketch, used for coastal trading.
A long, narrow yard used for jousting.
A container used for holding or serving food, especially an open shallow container.

A wide, shallow, straight-sided, circular DISH, with concentric divisions, formed by vertical partitions, or by concentric grooving around the base. The use is uncertain but the name implies it was designed to hold feed for domestic fowl. (Source: MPRG)

Aircraft Manufacturing Co., Ltd. Established in 1912 by Mr G. Holt Thomas. In 1914 secured the services of Capt. Geoffrey de Havilland as designer-in-chief, who went on to lend his initials to a number of highly successful machines.
The DH5 was an attempt to give a tractor-type fighter a good forward view. However it suffered from unpleasant flying characteristics and, as a result, had a short service career.
An office, particularly at a seaport, at which customs are collected.
A structure, usually well concealed, used to store explosives intended for use by the Auxiliary Units (or British Resistance Organization) in the event of an invasion.
A site intended for use by the Auxiliary Units (or British Resistance Organisation) in the event of an invasion. Use more specific term.
For chemical processes making nylon, rayon, etc.

Two-crew, twin-engined bomber. Entered production in 1934 and designed for dual use as a high-speed commercial transport. Technical problems hindered its use as a bomber and led to conversion to high-altitude reconnaissance.
A wall constructed for the purpose of confining or supporting a mass of earth or water.
A wall or masonry construction built for the purpose of retaining or supporting a bank of earth, wall, rampart etc.
A large bolt or arrow fired from a ballista.
British three-seat, single-engine light bomber. All metal in construction, this monoplane had a 1000 lb bomb load.
Originally designed as a trainer but relegated to use by the RNAS in a Maritime Reconnaissance and anti-submarine role when the Avro 504 became the standard trainer.
Particulars of a property for sale.
A cottage for workers on a country house estate.
Gloster Aircraft Co., Ltd. formed in 1917, later became part of the Hawker Siddeley Group. First British or American company to design, build and fly a jet-propelled aircraft.

Single-seat, single-engine biplane fighter. In operational service from 1939 to 1941, this was the last, and believed to be the best, biplane to be flown in the RAF. All-metal in construction with fabric and aluminium covering.

The Gloster Grebe was the Royal Air Force's first post WWI fighter aircraft, entering service in 1923. Designed by Henry Folland, a single-seat, single-engined biplane of fabric-covered wood construction with two Vickers machine guns (133 planes built).

The RAF's first jet fighter, flown operationally during 1944-5, with later versions serving for a further ten years after the war. The Meteor's first active operations were in the interception and destruction of V.1. flying bombs.
Single-engine, single-seat biplane seaplane built for the 1924 Schneider Cup Race.
All-weather fighter/interceptor first flow in 1951, introduced into service in 1956 and retired from the RAF in 1968.
Use for vessels registered in the Isle of Man.
A building or site used for the production of acids by a range of chemical processes.

Twin-engined, seven-crew, coastal reconnaissance, biplane flying-boat. Designed to the same specification as the Saro London, entered service in 1937. Also serving in an anti-submarine role, was replaced by the Consolidated Canso (Catalina) in 1943.
A large house dating from the 16th century onwards, built as a symbol of the wealth and status of the owner but not intended to be defensible unlike the castles and manor houses it replaced.
A place where tin ore is washed using a stream as the water source.
A site where tin ore is extracted from suspended fire waste in tin mine spoil heaps.
An office at which the registration of marriages, births and deaths are recorded, and in which marriage ceremonies may take place.
Waste material resulting from industrial manufacturing processes.
A system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used during WWII to provide a counterfeit target for enemy aircraft.
Dummy construction in the form of a battery used during WWII to provide a counterfeit target for enemy aircraft.
A bridge whose upkeep and repair was financed by the exaction of a toll.

The Gloster Grebe was the Royal Air Force's first post WWI fighter aircraft, entering service in 1923. Designed by Henry Folland, a single-seat, single-engined biplane of fabric-covered wood construction with two Vickers machine guns (133 planes built).
The rural residence of a country gentleman.
Documents relating to the planning, inception and management of a project.
A number of small iron balls, each about the size of a cricket ball, often numbering nine, wired together and bound in a canvas bag.
A pair of cannon balls joined by a solid bar.
A solid, spherical projectile, originally made of stone but later iron.
A projectile or group of projectiles fired from a weapon, usually solid rather than explosive.
A pair of cannon balls joined by a chain.
A reinforced concrete structure, usually sited underground, from where it was intended to conduct the business of government in the event of nuclear war. Date specific late 1950's to early 1970's.

A structure, often sited underground, from where it was intended to conduct the business of government in the event of nuclear war. Sub RSGs were introduced between the RSGs and local authorities to allow the RSGs to focus on strategic direction.
An area of land used for camping. Often includes facilities for washing, catering and entertainment.
A long room for recreation, often on an upper floor.
A room within a house or building used to exhibit artworks, often decorated and lit accordingly.
A long, high-ceilinged room, usually extending the full length of an Elizabethan or Jacobean house and often occupying an upper floor, used as a promenade, place of entertainment etc..
A loft, balcony or gallery, in a hall or church, for the use of musicians.
An excavation from which stone for building is obtained by cutting, blasting etc.
A place where shale, a laminated clay or silt which has been compressed by the weight of the rocks over it, is extracted from the ground.
A building or site used for the production of naphtha, a volatile petroleum-derived product used in the manufacture of solvents, cleaning fluids etc.
A mine yielding rock salt.
A small metal bar for the cleaning of dirty footwear before entering a house, etc.

A jar adapted by the addition of three or more vertical loop handles. They may be equally spaced, or confined to one section of the circumference. Profile vary and should be double indexed with the appropriate JAR type. (Source: MPRG)
A jar adapted by the addition of one or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
A vehicle used in warfare, racing or to carry passengers.
The premises of a builders merchant where building materials such as stone, cement, bricks, tiles and timber could be bought.
An outdoor theatre for the staging of dramatic productions.
An object that carries the weft in a loom without the need to be passed from hand to hand. The thread is wound into the shuttle and can be used in hand or machine looms
Fife, Scotland
Engineering workshop housing specialized machinery such as lathes, presses, etc., for making machines.
An employment exchange for unemployed labourers, servicemen, etc.
The residence of a teacher, often on the site of a school.
A simple machine, worked by horses, to provide a power take-off for driving agricultural machinery.
A place where umber or oxide of iron and manganese, is extracted from an open cast mine.
An establishment where the art of sword fencing is taught.
Items worn or carried as an adjunct to clothing, for example, headdresses, sashes, fans, masks etc.
A works where cotton waste is stored or processed.

Monument whose existence is inferred from the traces of architectural features. Eg include shadow marks on building walls or beams, pillars, floors incorporated into a later structure, suggesting the existence of an earlier building.
Seed of the cotton plant from which edible oil is extracted.
The white, fibrous substance surrounding the seeds of plants of the genus Gossypium, which can be spun and used in the manufacture of thread and cloth or used in its raw form as wadding or packing.

An object such as an organ, display case or piece of furniture such as a pew, usually associated with a larger monument but which may be found in isolation. For example a war memorial roll of honour in its display case.
A tomb with a raised canopy over it.
The residence and small-scale workshop of a hosier.
Large covered spaces where the steel plate used for ship construction was cut and marked out, prior to being craned onto the hull, etc.
A widening in a canal to allow boats to turn around.
A factory where aircraft are assembled.
A factory where seaplanes are manufactured.
A room intended for the purpose of teaching a group or class of students simultaneously.
A room within a school, private house or institution used for lessons.
A hall, apartment or large room, designed or used primarily for festive or state functions.
A jug with an evenly rounded profile and a discernible basal angle; the maximum diameter is near the mid point and in the upper half of the vessel. (Source: MPRG)

A specific form of rounded jug with a wide mouth, a large parrot-beak spout and three handles in the form of wide straps that spring from the rim to the girth.The spout may have a lug applied to the outside. (Source: MPRG)
A type of tomb in the form of a slab raised on freestanding legs.
A specially marked ground used by children for the game of hopscotch.
A building used by an organization instituted to promote the needs and rights of the blind.
A workshop used by a joiner; a craftsman working with wood and producing more ornate work than that of a carpenter.
A workshop in which products are made using wood and timber.
In use for fruit growing. Includes former orchard retaining trees etc.
Purpose built area, incorporating water supply, for the cleaning of carriages, carts, etc.
British twin-engined light/medium bomber developed from the model 142 civil transport. Noted for its speed, this three-crew monoplane had an all-metal, stressed skin structure and a 1000lb bomb load.
The Bristol Aeroplane Co., Ltd.. Founded in 1910 by Sir George White, a pioneer of electric tramways. The company had previously been The British and Colonial Aeroplane Co., Ltd..
An isolation hospital for infectious diseases and leprosy, sometimes known as a Pest House; commonly situated on the edge of a town.
A small fast warship powered by diesel or petrol engines. Built during World War II for coastal patrol work and anti shipping missions close in shore

A prefabricated structure consisting of sectional timber framed units that were bolted together. The structure was clad with Canadian Cedar weatherboarding and had a roof of corrugated asbestos. They were used as temporary accommodation on airfields.
The structure consisting of a series of balusters supporting a rail or coping, and sometimes a base and pedestal, on a parapet, balcony or staircase.
A half or whole baluster applied to a wall or pedestal, thus described as engaged.
A spirally turned baluster.
An upright member supporting a coping or handrail in a balustrade or staircase.
A baluster, circular in plan, turned and cut on a lathe.
A window with a single mullion and a single transom.

A wide, shallow, straight-sided, circular DISH, with concentric divisions, formed by vertical partitions, or by concentric grooving around the base. The use is uncertain but the name implies it was designed to hold feed for domestic fowl. (Source: MPRG)
An enclosure created by constructing one or more lines of ramparts across a promontory which projects into the sea.
A defensive enclosure created by constructing one or more lines of ramparts across a neck of land, in order to defend, or restrict access to, a spur or promontory, either inland or on the coast.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Augustinian order.
Hand held instruments which assist in the holding, cutting and eating of food.
Implement with a shallow bowl at the end of a handle used to eat with or to stir food etc.
Building or structure housing a form of ore crushing device associated with tin mines.
A hall used for housing public displays.
A hall used for the promotion and selling of horticultural produce and practice.
Wood that has been burnt and largely reduced to carbon as a result of burning in a reducing atmosphere below 500 degress C (Celsius).
Microscopic charcoal fragments that are concentrated and counted as part of standard pollen preparation techniques.
British, single-engined, light day bomber biplane. Built in 1923, this was the RAF's first interbellum designed day bomber.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up the chief engineer of Scottish Command
A church, the plan of which is based on that of a Roman basilica.
A tool used to examine or explore a cavity eg surgically for exploring the depth and direction of wounds.
A shade for a window.
An item hung over a window, usually can be open or shut to allow light in.
A building housing a beam engine.
A building housing a steam engine.
Equipment for turning wood, metal, bone etc.
Pipes manufactured from concrete used in the construction industry for drainage etc.
Hematological disorders such as chronic anemia, hemophilia and acute leukemia.
A microlith retouched to a thomboid shape. (Source: SARC)
A wayside inn for livestock traders.
A field and desk based assessment of heritage asset condition and vulnerability so that informed decisions can be made regarding how best to manage the resource.
A place where gold is worked into articles or products.
A building or site used for the production of bricks and other items, from a clay with refractory properties.
A crane, located in an engineering workshop or similar establishment, which can be moved on rails and thus used anywhere within the workshop.
A crane suspended from running rails in the roof of an engineering workshop or similar establishment.
A beacon used for coastal navigation. Many date from the Medieval period.
The area beneath a natural overhang at the base of a cliff or crag. This may have been used for occupation, burial, etc. Index with site type where known.
Area in a brewery used for the production of beer by the Burton Union method.
A tall, thin pillar of wood, stone or metal on which a lamp could be fixed.
A device for holding a lamp in a fixed position. These could take many forms from a simple bracket fixed to a wall to an onrate candelabra.
Twin-engined monoplane originally designed as a reconnaissance aircraft, but also widely used as a trainer. Entered RAF service in 1936.
A kiln with a pyramid roof and capped vent in which barley is dried. Found on the site of a malt house.
A knife that is used for circumcision.
The residence of a marsh keeper.
A room set aside for the storage of goods or valuables. Use more specific term where known.
A room or cupboard usually used for the storage of garments.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter, also adapted as a night-fighter, fighter-bomber, rocket-projectile fighter and tank-buster. The first monoplane to enter RAF service with 14,000 being produced between 1937 and 1944.
A building or buildings where soap is manufactured.
Sites where controlled chemical reactions are employed to help manufacture domestic products.
A commercial premises supplying ships with provisions.
A housing for one or more bells, usually gabled or roofed.
A furnace for the calcining and roasting of a mixture of sand and fluxes as a preparatory stage in glass-making.
A furnace for the manufacture of glass. Includes glass cones, open hearth and oil-fired furnaces.
A long spear with a double barb where one barb is longer than the other.
A long spear designed to be thrown in order to injure or kill a given target.
A large portable container used for carrying items such as clothes, papers etc.
A container, capable of being carried by hand, often for carrying such items as clothes, keys, money, etc.
A building in which the lay sisters resided. Lay sisters were not nuns and as such weren't bound by any vows. They could leave the convent and even marry if they wished.
A house or shelter used by drovers, herders or shepherds during the seasonal moving of livestock from the highlands to the lowlands. Use more specific type where known.
A small building used as a shelter by a shepherd.
The fine, keratinized, flexible filaments that grow from follicles beneath the surface of the skin in mammals.
Cut human hair, usually intended for wig-making.
A capital with an abacus, ovolo, neck and astragal.
A slim piece of wood used to ignite fires, lamps, ovens etc.
A jug with straight vertical sides and roughly equal rim and base diameters. (Source: MPRG)
A positive colour image on film which can be projected onto a screen when light is shone through it.
A building within a transport terminal, often associated with the registration and clearing of incoming and outgoing passengers or freight.
Accommodation, often in private houses or lodgings, provided for military personnel.
Accommodation in hired rooms or a lodging house.

The Stinson Division of The Consolidated Vultee Aircraft Corporation. Originally the Stinson Aircraft Division of the Aviation Manufacturing Corpn., who were taken over by Vultee Aircraft Inc., who merged with the Consolidated Aircraft Corpn. in 1943.

Single-engine navigation trainer and communications aircraft. Constructed of tubular steel and duralumin frame, with a duralumin and canvas covering, 500 were delivered to the FAA, serving from 1944-5.
Any by-product which cannot be reused.
All-weather fighter/interceptor first flow in 1951, introduced into service in 1956 and retired from the RAF in 1968.
An exotic hardwood with great strength and durability.
Arlingham civil parish, River Severn, Gloucestershire

A bomber designed to operate with medium bombloads over medium distances.The medium bomber was generally considered to be any design that delivered about 4,000 lb (1.8 t) over ranges of about 1,500 to 2,000 miles (2,400 to 3,200 km).
American twin-engined medium bomber. Entered service with the US 22nd Bombardment Group at Langley Field in February 1941. Also served with the 14th and 39th RAF squadrons.
Norfolk
A kiln that is octagonal in plan. Use with functional kiln type where known.
An object designed to hold food for birds.

A wide, shallow, straight-sided, circular DISH, with concentric divisions, formed by vertical partitions, or by concentric grooving around the base. The use is uncertain but the name implies it was designed to hold feed for domestic fowl. (Source: MPRG)
A long bed planted with mixed shrubs, usually found near the house.
Loose notes
A large building used for the transaction of the public business of a town, the holding of courts of justice, entertainments and other activities.
A building or site used as a storage and distribution centre.
A building or site used for the storage and distribution of fuel.
A system of lights to aid aircraft when landing at night. When viewed from above the runway lights form an outline of the runway.
Remains of the wood seeds of fruits such as apples, pears, grapes or citrus.
Use for the function that the armour is intended for, eg parades, field use, decorative etc.
The front piece of horse armour.
Armour used to protect a horse.
An open space or area, usually square in plan, in a town or city, enclosed by residential and/or commercial buildings, frequently containing a garden or laid out with trees.
An open area, often paved or cobbled, surrounded by privately owned buildings and inaccessible to the public.

A jar-shaped vessel with pierced apertures or cut-out on an open or closed pedestal base. Herbs, spices or scented woods would be placed in the pot and a burning coal placed underneath to warm the herbs so they would release their scent.
A small outer courtyard, or service-yard.
An enclosed area, often surrounded by walls or buildings.
A metal counter used in calculation of financial sums but not itself directly exchangeable for coins, goods or services.
Item in a format suitable for normal reading or viewing, without a computer or other device. For digital files or disks use MACHINE READABLE STORAGE MEDIUM or specific terms.
A translucent paper, which when laid over an existing image, permits the image to be seen and/or traced.

The Fi 103 is the more technical nomenclature for the Second World War German V1 flying bomb, produced by Fieseler. Multiple index together with Fieseler and flying bomb for maximum chance of retrieval for users.
Jet-propelled, pilotless aircraft carrying a one-ton explosive warhead. Also known as the Fieseler FI-103, the V1 was nicknamed the doodlebug, or buzz bomb.
A type of small boat that was often carried, or towed by a larger vessel and used as a ship's boat. Dinghies can also be used recreationally as independent sailing vessels.

A kiln in which lime is made by calcining limestone. This type of kiln usually consists of a circular bowl surrounded by pennanular banks with a funnel exit on the lower side. They normally survive as an earthwork. Superseded by Flare Kilns.
A free-standing building or a room used as a storage place for valuable objects.
The month of pilgrimage to Mecca.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter-bomber developed from the Typhoon and the abandoned Tornado. Entered service in 1944 with its greatest success being in destroying V.1. flying bombs. One of the fastest World War 2 aircraft, with a top speed of 436 mph.
A flat board with short spikes used to comb out the staple of wool to remove tangles before spinning. Usually used in pairs.
A metal sphere, usually lead, fired from a musket. Often bound into a cartridge.
A small hut, dwelling or cave, usually in a secluded spot, in which a hermit lived. Hermits chose to live solitary lives often due to religious motives.
A sailing warship armed with one or more heavy howitzers or mortars and used for bombarding shore positions. The modern equivalent is the MONITOR.
A late Neolithic/Early Bronze Age earthwork enclosure distinguished from a henge primarily by its larger size, irregular shape, and greater complexity of internal features.

Circular or sub-circular enclosure defined by a bank and (usually internal) ditch, with one or two (rarely more) entrances. Of ceremonial/ritual function, they contain a variety of internal features including timber or stone circles.

A small, circular Late Neolithic/Early Bronze Age enclosure which bears a morphological resemblance to henges, but may belong to another category of circular earthwork-defined monuments, or is enclosed by something other than a bank and ditch.
A fixed object to sit upon. Use narrower terms where known.
Set of three seats for the clergy found in the chancel
A sensing technique that consists of measuring minute variations in the gravitational pull of the Earth in order to detect gravity anomalies arising from voids and cavities within the earth.
A site or structure on which a signal, especially a fire, could be placed as a warning or means of communication. Use for beacon sites or surviving beacon structures.
A structure which allows aircraft fitted with radar equipment to 'home' in on an airfield in the dark or in poor visibility, and land safely. Radar beacons can also be used as navigation aids.
A building, factory or works which was engaged in the manufacture of refining saltpetre. Often part of a gunpowder works.
An electric fan used for the ventilation of mines.
A building housing an electric powered mine ventilation fan.
A building housing a fan used for the ventilation of mines
A building housing an electric powered ventilation fan for use in deep mine shafts
A ventilating fan house with an expanding chimney.
A building housing a steam driven ventilation fan used in mines
A building housing a double inlet fan that was used for the ventillation of mine shafts
A building forming part of a colliery ventilation system exhausting stale air from shafts and headings.
Photographic negative on polyester base material.

A control tower constructed on RNAS stations by the Royal Marine Engineers. Built to a common ground floor plan they could be built with one, two or three storeys above this depending on the requirements of the station.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Royal Naval Air Station Control Tower

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: Central two-storeyed tower surmounted by an octagonal glazed control room giving a 360 degree view. Flanked by single-storey wings.
The main dwelling-house of a farm, it can be either detached from or attached to the working buildings.
A piece of machinery for lifting stone, or containers loaded with stone, from a quarry.
A written journal, often of a personal nature.
Bordering the continents of Asia, Europe and North America the Arctic Ocean covers 5,426,000 square miles. Situated over the North Pole, much of the ocean remains frozen year round.
Arlingham civil parish, River Severn, Gloucestershire
A barge with a lugsail rig commonly found on the River Thames in the late 19th century. Also a general term applied to the family of Deal luggers.
A planned village or settlement, usually developed by a philanthropic industrialist , to house workers. Most include facilities for the education and betterment of the workers and their families.
A model village built in association with a factory, mill, railway, or any other industrial complex; usually built by the employer.
A crosspiece fastened over the necks of two or more animals, often oxen, and attached to the plough or cart to be drawn.
A pair of tongs used for placing coals onto a fire.
Building used for field studies and outdoor pursuits in the countryside and in an urban context.
A kiln with a pyramid roof and capped vent in which barley is dried. Found on the site of a malt house.
40mm gun emplacement created between 24th-26th June 1944 as part of the fourth deployment of Diver LAA guns to the Kentish Gun Belt. Each site had an extant searchlight battery.
A bowl with a sharp change of angle in the vessel wall, generally at the point of maximum diameter. the carination may be in the upper or lower half of the vessel. (Source: MPRG)
An area within a building open to the public where light meals and drinks can be purchased and consumed.
A form of lock on a river, which increased the depth upstream and had a gated opening.
South Yorkshire
England
South Yorkshire
A lintel over a door.
A horizontal member spanning an opening and providing support to the wall above the opening.
A container used upon the altar.
A vase used on the altar.
Baths containing water impregnated with mineral substances in which patients bathe for medicinal purposes.
A tool with a sharp, concave edge for shaping wood, stone or metal.
A type of cast chisel with a sharp, concave edge for shaping wood, stone or metal. A particular type of British Bronze Age tool.
A depot for the storage of various minerals.
An artificial paved bank or solid landing place built parallel to, or projecting out from, the shoreline to serve in the loading and unloading of vessels.
A place where a ship lies at a wharf. Use specific type where known.
A house to receive boat landings.
A platform, sometimes floating, for the landing of passengers and goods from vessels.
A mole or pier-like structure situated at the entrance of a harbour, or running out into a lake or the sea, usually used for the landing of craft.
A waterside depot for coals brought from the collieries for shipment, furnished with staging and chutes for loading vessels.
A place where vessels can land passengers and goods.
Steps found at a landing point.
A structure of iron or wood, open below, running out into the sea and used as a promenade and landing stage.
A firm beach or foreshore used for landing and loading of ships and other vessels. In more recent times hards have been reinforced with concrete.
A place of worship for the believers of spiritualism: The belief that the spirits of the dead can somehow manifest themselves and speak with the living.
A place where worship is offered or devotions are paid to a deity or saint.
A form of volcanic glass with similar properties to FLINT and often used in the manufacture of sharp-edged tools.
A crane whose winding mechanism was operated by hydraulic jiggers.
A hydraulically-powered crane where the jib and windlass are mounted on a central pillar.

A civil passenger transport biplane produced by the Farman Aviation Works from 1919. Instrumental in the creation of early airlines and commercial routes in Europe after World War I. Initially designed in 1918 as a heavy bomber. Some 60 units built.
A room or building for hand knitting garments on simple hand frames.
A place where knitted fabrics and legware garments were manufactured.
A workshop for the manufacture of clothing, eg. tailor's workshop.
World War II naval support vessel usually converted from a mercantile or other warship type and used for the distillation of water by both the Royal Navy and the American Navy.
The residence of a well keeper.
Transportation, usually wheeled or tracked, used for the conveyance of goods or people.
Heavy caterpillar tractors fitted with broad blades to the front for moving or levelling earth and obstacles.
US Navy version of the four-engined, six-crew B24 heavy bomber. Modified for long-range reconnaissance duty and used as a patrol-bomber against shipping and submarines.
A dispersed farmstead where buildings and yards (regular or loose courtyard in their form) are sited alongside a routeway.
An engine house which used air pressure to power trains on the experimental atmospheric railways of the 1840s.
A place where padlocks and rim locks for doors are made from iron and brass.
Any type of jug with decoration representing the form of a human face or figure. The shape of the vessel often forms the outline of the human face or figure. (Source: MPRG)

A tunnel built alongside a canal tunnel to enable a horse to be unhitched and led through the hillside to meet the barge when it emerged from the tunnel. Mainly built prior to the development of the towpath tunnel.
Fine grained, buff, brown to green coloured Cretaceous sandstone. Quarried at various locations in Sussex. Not to be confused with Sussex marble which is a cretaceous limestone.
Fine grained, brown/yellow to dark grey coloured cretaceous sandstone. It is a particularly good freestone and was often used for ashlar finishes.
Hard, fissile sandstone which weathers to a dark brown colour. Mainly used as a stone roofing material (stone slate) throughout Sussex and Surrey.
A building, factory or works which was engaged in the manufacture of refining saltpetre. Often part of a gunpowder works.
A hard, black form of lignite that takes a brilliant polish. It is used in jewellery and for ornamentation.
A dark, viscous liquid, obtained from the ground, which is refined for use as a fuel for motor vehicles and in generators to produce light and heat, and as a solvent.
An oil based derivative used as a fuel in diesel engines.
This is the top term for the thesaurus.
A liquid distilled from petroleum.
An airlike, fluid hydrocarbon suitable for burning to produce light, heat or power.
Materials or substances, including petrol, firewood etc., used as a source of heat or power.
A solid material which is combustible distilled from petroleum.
Vegetable matter decomposed in water and partially carbonized to form bogs, whence slabs are cut out to use as fuel.
Photographic print on glass, using a wet process.
Explosive devices which produce spectacular visual effects when ignited.
A decorative clasp to fix sleeve cuffs together.
A floating, fixed marker used to indicate to a navigator a sea area to approach or avoid.
A castle surrounded by two or more lines of walled fortifications.
A trough or watercourse constructed to collect rainwater from a roof and channel it towards a drain or pipe.
A V-shaped gutter.
A gutter running behind a parapet wall, the water channelled by it being discharged from holes in the wall.
A map generally produced manually to indicate main features of an area quickly, for example to assist location of a particular place.
A depiction of land, coastal or sea areas intended to aid navigation, usually using latitude and longitude co-ordinates.
A pictoral depiction of an area of landscape.

A building within a complex, such as a leisure centre, school, industrial site etc, often containing toilet and washing facilities, where individuals can change their clothes. For a changing room within a larger building, see Components.
A place in which turpentine is produced.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the farming of fish.
A pond used for the rearing, breeding, sorting and storing of fish.
A mill where long-staple hair, often from llamas, is made into yarn.
Fish of any kind preserved by salting, for example salted cod such as bacalhau or bacalao.
Mackerel which has been salted to preserve it.
Permanently moored historic maritime craft preserved and converted into a museum and open to the public.
A building where artefacts, scientific specimens, antiquities and similar objects of interest could be examined through microscopes by members of the public.
A building, group of buildings or space within a building, where objects of value such as works of art, antiquities, scientific specimens, or other artefacts are housed and displayed.
A factory used for the manufacture of screws.

Flexible, synthetic, polymeric organic material formed by chemical synthesis usually in imitation of a natural substance. It can be moulded to shape, extruded or formed into a sheet from solid or foam material.

A type of temporary military aircraft hangar introduced in 1940; of steel welded and bolted construction typically clad in galvanized corrugated iron sheets. The T2 became the standard temporary hangar for the RAF in World War Two.

A type of steel framed transportable British military aircraft hangar developed from 1941onwards. The hangar had a steel frame, some versions used commercially available sheeting for cladding. It was similar to but smaller than the arcraft hangar type T2.
A temporary, steel-framed transportable hangar developed by Teesside Bridge and Engineering Company to replace the obsolete Bellman hangars.
A steel framed transportable hangar similar in construction to Type T2 but about half the size. Designed in 1941 and 1942.
Feature visible following archaeological excavation

Standard dwelling of the non-ruling classes of Japan until the mid twentieth century. Minkas are timber-framed houses with mud-plastered panels and thatched roofs. The design varies from region to region. Minkas served as home as well as workplace.
An area of the sea or coastline where vessels have been abandoned.
Post-World War Two, single-engine, high-wing utility transport. Manufactured by De Havilland Canada, was also produced in a seaplane version. Known as the U6A from 1962.
A site, containing installations and machinery, used for measuring the power of explosives.
A building where mineral jelly was stored. Mineral jelly was used as a stabilizer in the manufacture of the explosive, cordite.
A building at the entrance to an factory manufacturing explosives where a person was searched for matches, prior to entering the workplace.

A structure or building used in the manufacture of the explosive cordite. After the cordite had been pressed to extract moisture it was placed on racks within the stove prior to being taken to the reeling house for winding.
A building in which the ingredients of an explosive charge are weighed into their correct proportions and mixed prior to incorporation.
A building in which cordite dough is stored before extrusion.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production, testing and storage of explosives.
Workshop, as part of a gunpowder works complex, in which explosive is loaded into shells. Also used for expense magazine, where powder was stored between work processes.
A building in which cordite paste is blended with the solvent acetone and Vaseline to form a cordite dough.
A component building of an explosives works where cartridges were filled with explosives with the aid of cartridging machines.
A building in which moist guncotton is dried by warm air for use in nitroglycerine manufacture.
A building, or part of a building, for the milling and pressing of cider apples to produce cider (or pears for perry) and for storing the drink in barrels.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production of wine and cider.
A small detached building used to accommodate patients with tuberculosis.
A cup with sides falring outwards from the base towards the rim, usually with a single handle.
A cup adapted by the addition of a pedestal base. (Source: MPRG)
A cup with a marked change of angle in the body wall, generally at the point of maximum girth. (Source: MPRG)
A vessel composed of three or more separate compartments, joined together and pierced to allow liquid to flow from one to another. There may be one or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
A cup with a rounded body beneath a deep neck. There may be a marked junction between neck and body and the angle of the neck may be inward-sloping, upright or everted. (Source: MPRG)
A cup with convex body walls. (Source: MPRG)

A vessel composed of three or more equally spaced lobes and usually, a waisted or pedestal base. The handles are vertical loops, generally of strap form. There may be two opposed handles, or one per lobe junction. (Source: MPRG)

A form of cup which incorporates a joke or conundrum, where cut-outs or holes in the body make conventional use impossible. The puzzle is how to drink from it without getting wet; usually achieved by sucking through a hollow rim or handle. (Source: MPRG)
A small open container, usually with one handle, used for drinking.
A meeting place for freemasons.
An interment of unburnt, articulated human remains. Use specific type where known.
A form of inhumation in which the skeleton is interred, usually on its side, with hip and knee joints bent through an angle of more than 90 degrees.
A form of inhumation in which the skeleton is interred, usually on its side, with hip and knee joints bent through an angle of less than 90 degrees.
A form of inhumation in which the skeleton is interred, usually on its side, with the knees brought up against the chest. This is a more extreme form of crouched inhumation.
A form of inhumation in which the skeleton is laid out in an approximately straight line, whether face up, face down, or on its side.
Twin-engined, four-crew bomber. Wooden framed, with linen covering, entered service in 1924, equipping several RAF squadrons.

Three/four-crew, single-engine, shipboard observation and air/sea rescue amphibian seaplane. Entered RAF service in 1936. Also employed for gunnery spotting, anti-submarine and convoy protection duties.
A single-seat fighter which began service with the RFC's fighter squadron in 1916. Some short-term success in dealing with new Fokkers but was withdrawn from service in mid-1917.
A tool used to pound, crush or beat an object.
A flat based stone used in conjunction with a grinding stone
Equipment used in the grinding of cereal to produce foodstuffs.
A stone for grinding grain.
A tool for pounding or grinding.
A shaped stone, which could be hand held, used in combination with a saddle quern to grind or rub grain.
A large stone used to grind grain or similar.
A channel which feeds water from a reservoir into a canal when the water level gets low.
Steps found at a landing point.
A workshop or foundry where iron articles are made by casting molten material into moulds.
A very small flint or other stone tool.
A microlith retouched to a rectangular shape. (Source: SARC)
A railway station or platform built specifically for the loading and unloading of goods.
A place of worship for members of the United Methodists Church, a group formed in 1907 by the amalgamation of the United Methodist Free Church, the Methodist New Connection and the Bible Christians.
A series of billet mouldings forming a decorative band of small, regularly placed squared or rounded blocks.
An ornamental moulding consisting of a series of small, regularly placed squared or rounded blocks.

A loom developed by Joseph Jacquard in 1801 which used a series of punched cards to control the movement of the warp threads thereby allowing complex patterns to be created without the intervention of the weaver
A container within which a body is placed for burial, usually made of lead or wood.
An axe designed and weighted to be thrown.
An axe used by the Saxons and Franks for throwing.
Porous black residue of partly burnt wood, bones etc. used as fuel or, in the form of charcoal pencils, as a tool for drawing.
Containers used to serve food and drink. Use appropriate term.
Objects used for the preparation of food and drink,for cooking and consumption.
A building where milk is deposited and stored before it is despatched to the consumer.
A building in which horses are accommodated.
A tower used for surveying, especially in civil engineering projects such as bridges.
A facility used for the storage and distribution of fuel for transportation. Often associated with dockyards and railways.
A platform which moves laterally on wheels, by which boats, railway carriages and engines may be moved from one place to another, eg. from one slipway to another parallel to it.
An early form of railway for the transportation of freight by sleds.
A room used by those who have to wait at railway or bus stations, etc.
A depot for the storage of various minerals.
A path, or marked lane, designated for use by cyclists.
A building containing a weighing machine for weighing goods; sometimes found in markets, ports, etc.
A post or pillar set up alongside a road to mark the miles from or to a place.
Emergency deceleration lane.

Sites, buildings, structures & features related to the conveyance of goods &/or passengers. Includes man-made routeways, mechanical structures & some vehicle types where it is deemed necessary to record such as monuments.
A building used to coordinate movement of railway engines and rolling stock in the event of war.
A small shelter used by a man employed to carry links (torches) to light people along a street.
A depot used for the unloading of coal.
Pens for housing cattle awaiting transportation.
Use for distinct structure on a large scale.
A component part of a treadmill crane, the shed is used to enclose the treadwheel.
A building housing the brakes for an incline railway or tramway.
A road or pathway raised above surrounding low, wet or uneven ground.
A plate, usually of wood or metal, set up on a road, canal or railway to mark the miles from or to a place.
An inclined plane with a cradle designed to lift a ship from the water onto a slip.
A stone set up on a road or path to mark the miles from or to a place.
A small building housing a mechanism used for winding a cable.
The administrative office of a transport company who provide a service for the conveyance and transportation of either goods or people.
A platform scale, flush with the road, for weighing vehicles, cattle, etc.
A depot for the transfer of town refuse to river barges before transportation to the REFUSE DEPOT.
The SI derviced unit for wavenumber
An ancilliary building within a larger works, as distinct from a SMELT MILL.
A site where ores are smelted. Use more specific site type where known.
Any building, group of buildings, or site in which antimony was smelted. Mainly 18th century.
A factory producing metallic aluminium by an electrolysis process.
A building or site where lead is obtained from ore.
A factory manufacturing electrical cables.
A factory or plant used for the manufacture of electrical machinery or components.
A stall where animals are kept individually.
A stall, often within a cow house, where cattle are kept individually.
A representation of the crucifixion of Christ or related scenes as a sculpture, etc.
A site where terracotta, made from weathered clay and grog, was manufactured.
A complex of buildings used for the manufacture of pottery.
A land based establishment armed with torpedoes and used to defend the coast from enemy shipping.

A land based installation armed with wire -guided and powered "Brennan torpedoes" which were in operation beween 1890 and 1906. These torpedoes were invented by Louis Philip Brennan. The stations were used to defend the coast from enemy shipping.
A residence of two or three monks dependent on a foreign mother house sent to exploit a distant estate. Alien houses were officially suppressed in 1414.
A residence of two or three monks of the Benedictine order dependent on a foreign mother house.

Stonemason's name for granite found lying upon the moorland surface, as opposed to having been quarried, in the West Country and the Lake District. Used, as found, since prehistoric times, in later years was often dressed and shaped.
Medium grained, dark bluish-grey stone. Quarried mainly from the Rubislaw Quarry.
Hard, coarse grained, grey to red/brown coloured granite. Used predominantly for tombstones becasuse of its ability to take a polish, but it is also in demand for underwater construction.
A hard, coarse grained, durable igneous rock. Can be used decoratively or as a main material. Found throughout the country.
Coarse grained, dark coloured granite, quarried in the Peterhead and Cairngall areas of Scotland, but used throughout the North.
Very hard, rough medium/coarse grained, pink to grey coloured granite. Usually found and quarried in Leicestershire.
A seaside pier used as a promenade and amusement park.
A wheeled passenger vehicle, especially one with four wheels and pulled by horses.
A room or hall designed for an audience to listen and view, as in a theatre, concert hall, lecture hall etc..
A large room with fixed seating, often including audio-visual facilites, in which lectures are given.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber. Fitted with eight fixed forward-firing machine guns in the wings, plus two 1000lb bombs or six rocket projectiles.
A factory, works or structure used for the manufacture and purification of gas.
The SI derived unit of volume.
A joint with each timber ending in a cut slanted across its length.
A subsidiary tower or projection attached to the front of a keep containing access to its first floor entrance.

The RAF's first jet fighter, flown operationally during 1944-5, with later versions serving for a further ten years after the war. The Meteor's first active operations were in the interception and destruction of V.1. flying bombs.
A stone/cobble/boulder with worn/smooth wear traces left by grinding/polishing axes/adzes.
A pool and ancilliary buildings used for the housing of dolphins.
A substantial house in a town or the country (particularly associated with medieval London). Use more specific monument types where known.
A large, luxuriously appointed building used as an official residence by a member of royalty.
An official residence of an abbot during the summer months.
The official residence of a bishop.
The official residence of an archbishop, eg. Lambeth Palace.
The official residence of an abbot.
A site containing a forge for the manufacture of cutlery.
A sample consisting of minerals, stones etc.
A waterwheel where water enters below the axle but above the bottom of the wheel.

A curved dam usually built of concrete and designed with the curve upstream so that the force of the water compresses the structure and strengthens it as it pushes it into its foundations. Arch dams are best suited to narrow gorges
A barrier of concrete or earth, etc, built across a river to create a reservoir of water for domestic and/or industrial usage.
Photographic image produced on transparent medium suitable for use in projection equipment. Use specific term where known.
Lantern slide developed using a dry process.
Lantern slide developed using a wet process.
A place of worship for members of Protestant sects dissenting from the established Church.
A place of worship for Protestant followers of Hussite doctrines which accept the Bible as the only source of faith.
A plate in a crown post roof, supported on crown posts and bearing the collars.
A pond used for dissipating heat by evaporation from steam engine condensate. Mid 19th century to mid 20th century.
A heavy grade, water proof plastic film used for the preparation of technical drawings.
A house with an aisle on one side only.
A self-contained establishment (out-patients) where pregnant women receive check-ups, counselling and medical treatment.
An institution, sometimes attached to a hospital, where patients may receive treatment or health checks.
A drainage structure that extends across and beneath roadways, canals or embankments.

A musket where a wheel on the lock is wound back and when the trigger is pulled the wheel moves dragging pieces of iron pyrites over the lock tocreate sparks and set powder in the pan off and so firing the main charge.

A musket fired by use of a flintlock. A gunflint is held in the lock which on pulling the trigger pushes back the pan cover creating sparks which set off the powder in the pan causing a flame to go through and set off the charge in the barrel.
A musket fired by a piece of burning match being held in the lock which, when the trigger was pulled, would contact with powder in the pan to set off the charge.
A musket with a snaphance lock. This lock consisted of a flint and steel but the pan cover was separate to the steel unlike the flintlock.
A heavy, smooth bore, long barrelled weapon, fired from the shoulder.
Use for deposits formed in estuaries.
A farmyard or enclosure containing regularly built stacks of hay, corn, peas etc.
Optical discs on which programs, data, or music are digitally encoded for a laser beam to scan, decode and transmit to a playback system, computer monitor or television set. [AAT]
Storage medium for information (text, images, files etc) in an encoded digital format.
Single-engine, three-crew torpedo-spotter, reconnaissance and anti-submarine biplane. Entered Naval service in 1936, designed for operation from aircraft carriers and equipped with folding wings.
A bridge which takes the towpath across the canal.
Originally designed as a light bomber but diverted for use as a high speed target tug to replace out-dated biplanes.
A type of carriage house, usually in a churchyard, for storing a hearse.
A building associated with funerary rites and burials.

A multi-storey, fortified hall house with one of the crosswings being raised in the form of a crenellated tower. Permanently occupied, they date from the mid 14th to the 17th century and are found mainly in the border counties of the North of England.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of urinary disorders and diseases.
A perforated strip of metal for shoeing the bifurcated hoof of an ox.
A shoe fixed to an animal, either permanently or temporarily, to protect the hoof and provide improved grip.
A platform, usually in concrete, on which radar equipment was mounted to assist the targetting of artillery guns. The platform is often the only evidence surviving in the landscape.
An anti aircraft battery usually mounting weapons with a larger calibre ammunition such as the QF 3.75 inch (94mm) gun.
The first court which is before the principal court.

The period once referred to as the Old Stone Age. It is defined by the practice of hunting and gathering and the use of chipped flint tools. This period is usually divided up into the Lower, Middle and Upper Palaeolithic.

The earliest subdivision of the Palaeolithic, or Old Stone Age; when the earliest use of flint tools appears in the current archaeological record. A hunter gatherer society is a defining characteristic.
A large room with fixed seating, designed for lectures.
A building in which a judicial court is held.
A building for the storage and drying of hops, often including a hop drying kiln. Usually built as part of a farm.
A movable bridge that swings or rotates around a central pier, or one that is pivoted only at one end, to provide a passageway for navigation.
The surface of a room which conceals overhead structural members.
A ceiling that is curved or vaulted, sometimes employed to give a space the appearance of a vault.
The residence of a dock worker.

A wall within a lead mine surrounding a dressing floor, where waste from mining and smelting is deposited, to protect livestock from entering and consuming contaminated material and becoming poisoned, or 'bellanded'.

The Republic Aviation Corporation. Developed from the Seversky Aircraft Corporation, founded by Alexander P. de Seversky in 1931 after the collapse of his previous company, the Seversky Aero Corporation, in the 1929 stock market crash.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber. Fitted with eight fixed forward-firing machine guns in the wings, plus two 1000lb bombs or six rocket projectiles.
British three-seat, single-engine light bomber. All metal in construction, this monoplane had a 1000 lb bomb load.

Single-engine, two-crew fighter, also used for convoy escort and reconnaissance. Designed to operate from aircraft carriers. Entered service with the Fleet Air Arm in 1940 and remained in use until 1945.
A single-engine, two-crew biplane day bomber and general purpose aircraft, developed from the IIIF (some of which were converted into Gordons) and first flown in 1931.

A biplane torpedo-bomber designed to be flown from aircraft carriers. Equipped with foldable wings for ease of storage. Joined Fleet Air Arm service in 1940, intended as a replacement for the Swordfish.
British, single-engined, light day bomber biplane. Built in 1923, this was the RAF's first interbellum designed day bomber.

Single-engine, two or three-crew pre-World War 2 biplane fighter and general purpose aircraft. First flown in 1931, the Seal was a Naval variant on the Fairey Gordon and a forerunner of the Swordfish.
A single-engine, photo-reconnaissance fighter designed for operation from aircraft carriers. Later adapted as a night fighter, it entered service in 1943 and remained in production until 1956.
The Fairey Aviation Co. Ltd., established 1916 by Sir Richard Fairey. During WW2 formed a group production scheme with Blackburn Aircraft, Ltd. and Boulton Paul Aircraft, Ltd..
British multi-purpose, single-engined monoplane that served as a torpedo-bomber, dive-bomber, reconnaissance aircraft and in other roles. Equipped with folding wings for use aboard aircraft carriers.
Single-engine, three-crew torpedo-spotter, reconnaissance and anti-submarine biplane. Entered Naval service in 1936, designed for operation from aircraft carriers and equipped with folding wings.
Photographic transparency on nitrate base material.
A long handled scoop usually used with liquids.
Unable to identify actual place from documentary sources alone.

A concrete arched military hut constructed by pouring concrete over hessian cloth that had been stretched over a temporary steel framework. Semi circular in section usually with end walls of brick. Designed by the Waller Housing Corp in 1943.
An apartment or suite of rooms usually occupying the top floor of a building.
An open area of water, usually artificial and enclosed by dock gates or locks, lined with wharves, warehouses and berths to enable vessels to load and unload.
An area of a building or complex, such as a workhouse, hospital or prison used to house infirm inmates suffering from fever.
An area of a building or complex, such as a workhouse or hospital, for isolating new residents before admission into main building, used to prevent spread of disease
A ward in a workhouse for vagrants
A room, usually in a hospital, in which a number of beds are located.
A sleeping apartment usually containing a number of beds and sometimes partitioned into cubicles.A room for sleeping in, usually for a number of beds.
A ward for receiving new paupers upon entry to a workhouse. They had to remain there until checked by medical officer.
A prison for the confinement of people who owe money.
The negative trace left by an object type or material (eg. animal, plant or textile) on another object type or material, often on ceramics or metal corrosion products.
A building where the administrative functions of a Trade Union are carried on.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of firelighters.
Small discreet rural settlements which do not provide the commercial, legal or ecclesiastical services typically found within medieval urban areas.
A piece of prepared ground on which the game of polo is played.
A channel for conveying vegetables.
Views across or along the sea and seafront, lakes and rivers.
A building, or first-floor room in a building, for the dry and secure storage of grain after it has been threshed and winnowed.
A cage specifically designed to hold insects.
A portable confining enclosure or framework.
A cage for containing birds.
A container designed to be difficult to get into or out of, thus ensuring the safety of objects inside the container.
A tall wooden pole used to support telegraph wires.
A microlith retouched to a triangular shape. They can be sub-divided into scalene and isosceles triangles. (Source: SARC)
A building where the upper storeys rest on projecting floor joists and so create the effect of an overhang.

A light timber framed building usually with brick panels which rests on a timber frame with jacking points; should ground subsidence occur the structure could be jacked to a level position. Usually found in the Cheshire Salt Field.
A building constructed with a basic timber framework; between the members are panels which can be infilled with timber, wattle and daub, plaster, brick or other materials.
Not subdivided
Maps or charts.

skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: National Mapping Programme Morph Number Sheet

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: Use for completed, accuarately surveyed maps

A single engine, jet propelled twin boom aircraft which came into service in 1945 in a variety of roles including night fighter, trainer, the carrier-borne Sea Vampire, and the MK5 version, a fighter bomber. Produced by De Havilland.
Removal of a sample from a vertical section generally using a U sectioned tin to extract an intact column of the observed stratigraphy. Used in the study of pollen, diatoms etc.
Intervention into the archaeological resource intended to gather information about past ecologies and economies, formation processes, and to retrieve material for scientific dating purposes.
Removal of samples from insitu deposits for dating analysis by studying the remnant magnetism contained within the deposit.

Removal of samples from deposits, including archaeological contexts to recover information about past environments and economies, retrieve material for scientific dating and for the investigation of the deposits themselves e.g. formation processes.
A floating structure designed to resist the force of waves.
A structure which protects a beach or harbour by breaking the force of the waves.
Non-military maritime flood and erosion defences.
A heated iron used to label, burn or mark animals, slaves, criminals etc.
An air-cushioned vehicle capable of travelling over land or water.
The final third of the 20th century.

The period of political and military opposition between the major Superpowers (USA and USSR) and their allies. Known as the Cold War as there were no direct military conflicts between the two main protagonists.
A two storey building with a watch office on the ground floor and a control room above. Originally based on drawing number 12096/4.
A night fighter station watch office based on the standard design dor Bomber Satellite Station watch offices

A large octagonal pillbox, with a projecting entrance, equipped with loopholes for eight light machine guns and a light anti-aircraft mounting sited in a central well which was accessed from inside the pillbox. Designed by DFW branch 3.
An establishment where tea and other non-alcoholic refreshments and light meals are served.
A workshop used by a craftsman who works in base or precious metals.
A workshop with a forge for the melting and working of white metal, ie. low-melting alloys. Also used for a smith specializing in decorative or finely finished wrought iron work.
A castle erected without permission, ie. without a royal licence to crenellate.
A rafter set at the corner of a hipped roof, to take the upper end of a common rafter.
A room containing one or more thrones.
Entry to a hall through opposing doors with a partition screening the hall and forming a passageway.
Transect or area-based arrangements of drilled auger-holes used to describe deposits and collect samples.
A small garden enclosure within a BOSQUET or surrounded by clipped hedges.
Outer casing of an explosive cartridge fired from a cannon or mortar.
A screen to intercept the heat from a fire.
A transept in which the two wings that extend beyond the walls of the nave are lower than the nave and the crossing of the church.
A Cornish Medieval amphitheatre used for the performance of mystery plays and sports.
NB currently Includes ISOMETRIC though this has a separate term.
A place where students live, sometimes on a college campus.
A university or college building set apart for residence or instruction of students. They can be located either on or off campus.
Use for vessels registered in the Republic of Ireland (Eire).
A house where the upper storeys rest on projecting floor joists and so create the effect of an overhang.
A jettied house where the overhanging upper storey runs along the entire length of one side.
A place at a school where children receive medical advice, health checks and treatment.
Persons captured in land or naval engagements either being transported to prison out of their native country, sent for exchange, or being returned home.
People who serve as members of an army.
People who have paid to travel on a vessel without having to work their passage.
Personnel serving with one of the three armed forces - army, navy or air force.
A path or road for pedestrians, laid or beaten in with stones or other materials.
A pavement walkway for pedestrian use, often raised above the level of a road or path.
Originally used to describe very strong, often thick, rope made of metal or hemp. Now can be used for protective flexible tubing encasing wires such as telephone wire.
A cable laid under the surface of the sea, often on the seabed, for various purposes including telecommunications.
A stone or metal head on a wooden shaft. Where the use is thought to be ceremonial multiple index with ceremonial object.
A Mesolithic type of mace head made of stone.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of foot disorders and diseases.
A bridge which takes the towpath across the canal.
An intially worked object, prepared to be made into a final product.
An unfinished, roughly shaped axehead.
A building for the storage and drying of hops, often including a hop drying kiln. Usually built as part of a farm.
Unpowered flat bottomed vessel, used for carrying cargo from ship to shore or as a working platform.
A machine used to raise and move water and other liquids, compress gases etc. and powered by a steam engine.
Man made shallow pool, usually made for children to play in rather than swim.

A building designed specifically for handling tobacco. This may be a bonded warehouse containing facilities for removing tobacco leaves from the hogsheads in which they were imported, and pressing them.
A machine used to burn and desiccate rubbish.
An enclosure used for corralling deer.
A pen, often circular and stone-walled, for rounding up livestock.
A small pumping station.
A room or building where a pump is worked.
A radio-controlled target tug version of the Tiger Moth used for target practice. 380 were built for the RAF.
A tree-lined way or approach where the trees have been cut into various forms and shapes.
A single-seat fighter which began service with the RFC's fighter squadron in 1916. Some short-term success in dealing with new Fokkers but was withdrawn from service in mid-1917.
A building used as emergency accommodation and food distribution centre for people displaced by a natural disaster or conflict.
A small room communicating with one or more apartments.
A house provided for the treasurer of a cathedral, palace or similar.
A building where nurses live.
A stone circle featuring a stone which lies lengthways between two of the upright standing stones.

A stone circle featuring four upright stones standing at the corners of an irregular quadrilateral. The monument may feature more than 4 stones, overall, but the corner stones are often the most prominent.
A circular arrangement of spaced stone uprights set within a high bank, often interrupted by a formal entrance gap.
An approximately circular or oval setting of spaced, usually freestanding, upright stones. More than one circle may be present, arranged concentrically.
A type of pottery oven in which the air passes from the base of the kiln out through the top.
A structure, composed of oven and hovel, used for the firing of pottery ware.
Elastic polymeric substance made from the latex of a tropical plant or synthetically
Stone, brick or wooden steps or stairs found in a garden.
Garden steps covered in turf.
A container made of interwoven strips of pliable materials, such as cane or reed, often carried by a handle.
A site where lime (calcium carbonate) is made.
Developed from the ill-fated ME210, the ME410 Hornisse entered service in May 1943. Although underpowered as a day fighter the ME410 saw service over the UK as a night fighter from 1943-45.
A early match made of a piece of wood and an inflammable substance, lit by friction between the inflammable substance and a rough surface.
A plan in which a four-sided figure has all its angles at right angles and its opposite sides equal and parallel.
Clothing, cloth and woven fabric manufactured from either natural or artificial fibres.
An ornate, openwork fabric made by twisting, knotting or looping threads. Originally made by hand but more recently manufactured mechanically.
In churches a niche, or shelf, within or beside a piscina, or a table for the sacramental elements and vessels. (Source: Pevsner Glossary)
A semicircular niche in the wall of a mosque used to indicate the Qiblah - the direction to be faced during prayers. Qiblah is set as the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca.
An enclosure or niche in a library or cloister used for study.
A shallow, ornamental recess, often arched and semicircular in plan, set in a wall or pier and usually containing a statue or ornament.
A semicircular niche or recess in a wall.
A niche in the corner of a structure.

Single-engine, two or three-crew pre-World War 2 biplane fighter and general purpose aircraft. First flown in 1931, the Seal was a Naval variant on the Fairey Gordon and a forerunner of the Swordfish.
An architectural ornament usually surmounting the apex of a gable, canopy or roof.
An ornament at the top of a roof or spire.
A chamfer with a convex bead-like moulding projecting from the chamfer.

A fairly regular system of small rectangular fields. Examples may date from the middle Bronze Age to the Roman period. The word 'Celtic' carries no chronological or cultural connotations in this context.
A female figure used instead of a column, usually supporting an entablature.
Objects used for, or associated with, the production of heat and light.
An iron striking plate used to create sparks to ignite a fire.
This includes cosmetic containers.
A bowl specifically used for shaving.
An enclosing structure composed of bricks, stones or similar materials, laid in courses. Use specific type where known.
A wall used in the game of handball.
An aircraft hangar designed to Air Ministry specifications (drawing number 2243/41). Constructed from prefabricated A-frames and clad in corrugated iron.
A structure used for the housing and servicing of aircraft.
Remains of barley (Hordeum sp.) grain (caryopyses). These grains are sometimes itemised separately.
The fruit or seed of a cereal plant such as wheat, corn etc.
A residence of two or three monks of the Premonstratensian order dependent on a foreign mother house.
Use for vessels believed to come from South America but where the precise nationality is not known.
Use for vessels registered in Peru.
Accommodation for the warrener(s) usually located within the boundary of the Rabbit Warren. They also provided a place to store nets, traps and other necessary equipment.
A building, usually containing several dormitories, used as a cheap, short term residence. Use more specific term if known.
A building, usually associated with a hospital, where doctors live. Include blocks of self-contained flats.
A place where pheasants are reared and kept.

A single engine, jet propelled twin boom aircraft which came into service in 1945 in a variety of roles including night fighter, trainer, the carrier-borne Sea Vampire, and the MK5 version, a fighter bomber. Produced by De Havilland.
A piece of ground over which small arms or large artillery may be fired at targets. For rocket and missile firing use ROCKET TEST FACILITY.
A designated area of land, usually closed to the public, used for military exercises and training purposes.
An area of ground where training in the use of grenades can be carried out.
A mechanism within a windmill, attached to the striking rod, allowing the opening and closing of the shutters or vanes of patent sails.
A small body of water, either natural or artificial.
A small cold water bath, often known as a natatio when part of a Roman bath complex.
A large, manmade pool, usually lined with tiles, rubber or similar. Can be placed in the open air, eg. a LIDO, or built as part of a covered sports centre.
One or more arches built across an angle between two walls to support a polygonal or circular structure.
Garden associated with a crematorium where the ashes of the deceased are scattered or buried.
A garden associated with a crematorium where the ashes of deceased infants are scattered or buried.
A 19th century Tudor revival garden.

A stone core with a conical form and a core platform which may or may not be prepared. Blades are removed around the circumference of the platform. The end of the core opposite the platform usually tapers to a point. (Source: SARC)
The piece of stone or flint remaining after blades have been produced.
A building and open area from which buses, usually those working local or regional services, begin or end their journeys.
The limit line of a medieval local administrative unit of a hundred.
A crane powered by a steam engine.
A straight sided drinking vessel, usually with a wide mouth and without handles.
A beaker adapted by having a pedestal base. The upper part of the pedestal is solid and may be thrown as an integral part of the vessel, or added as a separate element.(Source: MPRG)
A garden maintained by, and for the benefit of, a community.
Large, three-engined, long range reconnaissance flying boat. Wooden hull and frame construction, with linen covering. Entered service in 1930.
A pit dug in the prospect of finding valuable minerals, coal, metal ores, etc, beneath the ground surface.
By-product or waste, resulting from an industrial process.

Calcium Oxide obtained by heating limestone in a kiln. Used as a constituent of modern mortar, or as slaked (non-hydraulic) lime in lime putty, daub, limewash and traditional lime plaster, mortar and renders.
A bridge which takes a towing path over a branch canal, basin, etc.
Use for material that has been burnt.
Material that has been burnt and at least in part reduced to carbon as a result of burning in a reducing atmosphere below 500 degrees Celsius.

Blocks of concrete with four protruding arms so that, whichever way up the caltrop is placed, one arm will always point upward. Used in imitation of the iron caltrops thrown on the ground to impede cavalry.
An object on which thread or yarn is wound or hooked.
A small bobbin used in lace making.
Specify in Description using: pond, lake, artificial lake, canal (if wet) etc.
Photomechanical or photolithographical reproduction process representing a photographic image as a series of dots or lines.
The opening at the base of a chimney stack.
The heat-resistant wall, or sometimes decorative cast iron panel, at the back of a fireplace.
Pit for the depostion of ore sediment from waste water collected from ore washing.
A long handled shallow pan used for frying.
Obstacles such as scaffolding, barbed wire and concrete blocks or cylinders placed on a beach to impede the progress of enemy soldiers, vehicles or watercraft landing from the sea.
Obstacles, including scaffolding and anti tank blocks designed to impede an enemy's attempts to land forces onto open beaches.
American, all-metal-construction, fighter. Entered service in 1941. 209 were delivered to RAF/FAA, most of which were used in the Far East.
Use for coastal cliffs; for inland features use OTHER 9.
A yard for pigs.
A civil and administrative area incorporating a town of medieval origin.
A jug with a constriction between the upper and lower body sections. (Source: MPRG)
A recess, usually situated in the north wall of a chancel, often canopied, containing a decorated tomb chest representing the burial and resurrection of Christ.
Glass used within a window, usually to protect from the elements, can permit a view through it or can be for decorative purposes.
Glass that has been coloured by fusing glass with a metallic oxide film or by burning pigment into the surface.
A factory where nails are manufactured.
A room in a church to receive the congregation's offerings.
A building where lace was laid out to dry.
A flat surface supported by legs used for many purposes.
A flat surface often with drawers used for working upon.
Use where the motive power behind the turbine is unknown. Use DIesel Turbine Engine or Steam Turbine Engine where appropriate
A site comprising a system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used during WWII to provide a counterfeit target for enemy aircraft. Use more specific type where known.
A decoy fire positioned close to a legitimate target which would be lit in the event of an incendiary attack in the hope that subsequent bombs would be drawn to the area of the decoy.
School built by the local Education Authority to provide residental schooling at the seaside for children from urban communities.
Oven for roasting coal to drive off chemical constituents and reduce it to almost pure carbon, ie. coke.
An addition to the west end of a church which is similar to a porch or narthex but usually consists of a nave and aisles.
An antechurch which is transverse to the axis of the church and is covered or enclosed.
An instrument of punishment, in which the offender was placed in a sitting position in a timber frame, with holes to confine the ankles and wrists between two planks.
Photographic print using silver gelatine.

Farman Aviation Works was an aircraft company founded and run by the brothers Richard, Henri, and Maurice Farman in 1908. The firm made pusher biplane aircraft for military and training purposes, it was eventually dissolved in 1956.

A civil passenger transport biplane produced by the Farman Aviation Works from 1919. Instrumental in the creation of early airlines and commercial routes in Europe after World War I. Initially designed in 1918 as a heavy bomber. Some 60 units built.
Old ship with a hull stripped to the water line and used as a platform for mounting the sheers used to lift masts into and out of sailing ships.
The entrance to a road tunnel, sometimes of a grand construction.
A tall, polygonal structure with ornamental roofs at each storey which is associated with Buddhist temples; the style was adapted for secular eyecatchers and pavilions in the 18th century in England.

Single-engine, two-seat, light, biplane, elementary-flying trainer. Adapted from a civilian design, and constructed from tubular steel and spruce with plywood and fabric covering, entered service in 1931 and was available in land-plane or seaplane forms.
A building in which a parliament meets and conducts the business of government.
