A shelf that is behind an altar.
A shelter for the parson during the burial service.
Workshop for producing crates, particularly for the packing of pottery.
A pound for the accommodation of livestock.
A lock at the end of one company's canal where it joins another company's canal.

Twin-engined maritime-reconnaissance bomber adapted from pre-war American airliners, the A-28 and A-29, evident from the row of portholes along its fuselage. Entered service with RAF Coastal Command just before the outbreak of World War Two.
A licenced establishment where wine and other alcoholic drinks are sold for drinking on the premises.
A beam that has been applied to a wall face.
A ceiling beam aligned with the length of a building.
A beam the end of which is fixed beyond the upright it passes through.
A beam which is half the width of a main beam, usually supporting joists.
A beam that is part of a frame in a wall.
A composite beam of timber strengthened by an iron plate, or plates, used in the construction of 18th and 19th century timber framed mills and warehouses.
A horizontal member cutting through the corner formed by two walls to act as a support to a hip rafter to support jetties on two adjacent sides of an upper floor.
A main load-bearing horizontal member.
A major horizontal timber spanning a roof space to connect a pair of principal rafters and prevent them spreading.
A decorated beam, above the dais or high table, attached to the partition at the upper end of a hall.
A beam often situated above, and spanning the width of, the west end of a chancel and supporting a cross or crucifix.
A beam that runs the width of a building.
A horizontal, supporting beam set above an opening in an external wall, a fireplace opening or in timber framed construction set forward from the lower part of a building to support a jettied wall.
A short beam that projects into a roof space from the foot of a principal rafter to receive a hammer post and, often, an arched brace.
A transverse timber in aisled construction, joining aisle posts below tiebeam level, to allow rearing of pairs of posts.
A transverse timber resembling a hammer beam but without a hammer post above, being braced to a principal or collar instead.
Any church which bears signs of fortification. Churches on the Welsh and Scottish borders were often fortified, only allowing access to the tower from a single opening in the nave.
Lightweight, strong metal with good corrosive resistance, normally used as an alloy.
A precious metal characterised by its yellow colour and resistance to tarnishing.
Easily formed metal alloy composed of copper and zinc.
Malleable metal used for roofing and for alloys such as bronze.
Metal used primarily for roofing and ornamental purposes, being lighter and stronger than lead.
Metal used primarily for roof coverings and window fittings. It is easy to work, can be worked cold and does not rust which makes it suitable for holding or repelling water.
A precious metal of lustrous white colour with great malleability and ductility.
A hard and lustrous metallic element, used for roofing, galvanising iron and a component of alloys such as brass.
Hard, corrosive resistant alloy of copper and tin.
An alloy of iron and carbon, its strength makes it suitable for load bearing purposes. It is primarily used in structural steelwork and concrete reinforcement.

Class of elements and alloys that are characteristically lustrous,ductile, fusible and malleable. These are extracted from ore minerals originally existing in nature and processed before becoming a recognisable metal. See METAL Class List for narrow terms
A vessel to contain wine or water used in the Eucharist.
Compact grained, brown/yellow/green/grey blue, coloured liassic limestone.
North European medieval merchant vessel.
A mine used for the extraction of uranium bearing ores.

The unplanned observation of archaeological features or the recovery of artefacts of interest, for example either random finds by members of the public or the unplanned observation of archaeological features during the course of unmonitored developments.
Any activities, that have a physical impact upon the archaeological resource where the purpose is not primarily archaeological research.
A slight structure built for shelter or storage, or for use as a workshop, either attached as a lean-to to a permanent building or separate. Use more specific type where known.
A slight structure built on an allotment for shelter or storage, or for use as a workshop, by the allotment holder.
An area of land, usually on a slope, which has been built up to provide a flat surface for the cultivation of crops.
A chest made of stone, wood or lead, used to enclose a dead body.
A prehistoric coffin made out of a hollow tree trunk.
A stone coffin embellished with sculpture.
Central functional building of a gas works. Coal is roasted in retorts producing gas and coke.
An octagonal spire atop a square tower, the transition between structures effected by partially pyramidical masonry forms called broaches.
Photomechanical or photolithographical reproduction process representing a photographic image as a series of dots or lines.
A vertical faced projection in the cornice.
The upper part of the classical entablature. Also a moulded projection crowning a door, wall, window etc.
A building or room where business, administrative or professional activities are conducted. Use specific type where known.
Second World War allied patrol-bomber built by Lockheed Vega, a Lockheed subsidiary. This aircraft was a military development of the Lodestar, USAF designation B-34.

The Lockheed Aircraft Corporation. Founded in 1916 by Allen and Malcolm Loughead. In 1926 the company moved to Burbank and changed its name to The Lockheed Aircraft Company, and was then incorporated in 1932.
A subsidiary of Lockheed.
A semi-circular or pointed vault uninterrupted by cross vaults, the ceiling bearing a resemblence to a tunnel or the inside of a barrel.
A room or space with an arched ceiling or roof, the depth of which exceeds its span.
A horizontal member along the length of an aisle wall to receive the ends of rafters.
A longitudinal timber set on top of a timber frame, brick or masonry wall on which roof-trusses or rafters rest.
A structural member that supports a purlin and is also a common rafter.
A principal rafter below a hip rafter that supports the ends of purlins under a hip.

Two-seat, twin-engined fighter/fighter-bomber designed as a replacement for the Bf110. Of the 600 or so produced, only 258 reached the Luftwaffe due to serious design faults. The ME210 was superseded by the ME410 Hornisse.
Founded by Professor Willy Messerschmitt as the Bayerische Flugzeugwerke. Reconstituted in 1938 as the Messerschmitt A.G..
Any vessel propelled by sail or power and used for pleasure and not plying for hire.
A specialist veterinary hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of horses.
A hospital for the medical or surgical treatment of domestic or wild animals.
A small single storey structure with just one room containing a pyrotechnic cupboard and built of rendered brick with a flat reinforced concrete roof
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 3156/41.
A place where coal is mined.
A medium containing microphotographic images, usually reproduced on film, requiring magnification to render them readable.
A film strip or roll containing reduced images.

A biplane torpedo-bomber designed to be flown from aircraft carriers. Equipped with foldable wings for ease of storage. Joined Fleet Air Arm service in 1940, intended as a replacement for the Swordfish.
A soft, porous, white to light grey coloured limestone.
Coarse, hard Chalkstone, light grey to white coloured, containing shell fragments.
A hard, gritty, grey/green coloured form of chalk.
Limestone formed during the Cretaceous period.

A World War One German three-crew, twin-engined, long range heavy bomber biplane manufactured by Gothaer Waggonfabrik A.G.. Entering service in 1917, this aircraft incorporated a ventral tunnel allowing the gunner to shoot downwards and to the rear.
A deeply concaved moulding, with a projecting lower edge, that sits at the base of a column between two torus mouldings.
Photographic transparency on an acetate base material.
Traditional term for any fine to medium grained igneous rock, containing large crystal fragments.
Miner's term for fine grained, often light grey/fawn coloured porphyritic rocks. Commonly found in Devon and Cornwall.
American, four-engined, long range, medium/heavy day bomber. Produced in greater numbers than any other American aircraft during the war.
A double lock placed between tidal water and a canal, etc..
An unpublished document.
Products, such as cheese and butter, manufactured from milk.
Dairy produce formed from the curds of milk, coagulated by rennet and pressed into a solid mass.

A kiln in which lime is made by calcining limestone. This type of kiln usually consists of a circular bowl surrounded by pennanular banks with a funnel exit on the lower side. They normally survive as an earthwork. Superseded by Flare Kilns.
A kiln in which lime is made by calcining limestone or in some areas chalk.
Hydrocarbon secretion of a tree or bush, either naturally exuded or deliberately tapped from the tree, valued for its varied uses in chemicals and perfumery.
An amber like substance derived from pine or turpentine.
A capital at the corner of a colonade or portico in the Ionic Order in which the volutes are splayed outwards at 45 degrees.
A Capital with a rolled up cushion-like form on either side creating distinctive volutes.
A religious house governed by an abbot or abbess. Use with narrow terms of DOUBLE HOUSE, MONASTERY or NUNNERY.
Silver fashioned into coin for use as currency.
A shallow dish or plate used to serve main meals off or to serve sweetmeats, these usually being painted with devices and riddles.
A mechanism used to transport minerals or granulated materials.
A device used to remove pollutants from gas or smoke produced during industrial processes such as burning high-sulphur fuels.
An apparatus used for the process of condensing: the conversion of vapour into a liquid.
A mechanism through which crude coal gas is passed to remove any impurities eg Ammonia and Sulphur.
A machine used in a mill to remove bran scales and flour from grits or middlings.
Apparatus used for applying a mechanical force, or to perform a particular function. Use more specific type where known.
A photo- reconnaissance variant of the Boeing Superfortress, used from 1944, initally deployed in the Pacific war, later for Cold war duties over Europe.
A sunken arena used by the Romans for training cavalry horses and recruits.
A site where machine tools, machines designed to remove surplus material from a work piece by accurately guided cutting tools, are manufactured.
Material comprising entrie or partial transverse sections of stems. Bark may be present or not. Can include complete sections of tree trunk but generally comprises smaller (<20cm diameter) material.
An alloy, principally of copper or tin, but which may also include zinc and/or lead.
The residence of a bridge keeper.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the manufacture of timber products.
A workshop used by a joiner; a craftsman working with wood and producing more ornate work than that of a carpenter.
The middle section, between the architrave and the cornice, of an entablature.
A frieze that has a convex section.
Twin-engined, four-crew bomber. Wooden framed, with linen covering, entered service in 1924, equipping several RAF squadrons.
A series of connecting metal links.
An enclosed chair for carrying a person, usually carried by two people.
A hinge composed of two parts: a u-shaped hinge attached to a door which slotted over an L-shaped staple in the door jamb.
Movable joint attached to fixtures and fittings to enable opening and closure of eg a door.
Three-seat, single engine, high wing braced monoplane designed for civil use and first flown in 1929. Saw military service in World War 2 in an Army co-operation and communications role.
A mechanism through which crude coal gas is passed to remove any impurities eg Ammonia and Sulphur.
An outline of the circumstances to be addressed, with an indication of the scope of work which will be required (Scottish term)
A purpose built quay for supplying ships with fuel.
A factory for the production of missiles
A hospital which has been built either wholly, or partially, underground in order to protect it from attacks by enemy aircraft.
A house where the upper storeys rest on projecting floor joists and so create the effect of an overhang.
A jettied house where the upper storey only overhangs the end elevation of the building.
A site where gypsum and anhydrate is mined.
An endowed school providing a liberal education for such as can afford it.

Rectangular slabs of concrete with a sloping top usually with sides of 5 feet by 3 feet and 3 feet high which when placed in rows were intended to form a substantial barrier to enemy armoured divisions in the event of invasion.
A hangar for the storage and maintenance of dirigible motor-driven balloons.
A large shed for the housing of aircraft, etc.
A building or site where aircraft can be stored and maintained.
A naval dockyard building used for the manufacture of flags.
A workshop where baskets were manufactured.
Fife, Scotland
A booth, shed or stall erected at the side of a road, canal, bridge or gate where a toll must be paid.
A military base normally between 20 and 30 acres in size, containing legionary and auxiliary battle units, which served as stores depots and winter quarters during campaigns.
A flail used for the mortification of the flesh.
A building found at the site of a mine. Use specific type where known.
A small hut erected over a mine shaft.
A structure used for the secure storage of bicycles.
A building in which sheep are sheared.
A site where alum (hydrous sulphate or salt and alumina) is quarried.
A place where photographs are displayed for sale.
A works or factory where shells or projectiles were machined before they were dispatched to a filling factory to be filled with explosives.
A building or site used for the manufacture of weapons, ammunition and military supplies. Use more specific type where known.
A large storehouse where wholesale goods are stored.
A place where trams are maintained and refitted, etc.
A large, level structure, usually of stone or timber, built alongside water to allow warships to moor for the loading and unloading of guns.
A building used for drilling out the bores of cannon and other military pieces.
A building containing a machine tool for boring out large cylindrical holes in items such as steam engine cylinders, pump barrels, etc.

An American turbojet fighter-bomber aircraft. The F-84 was the first production fighter aircraft to utilize in-flight refuelling and the first fighter capable of carrying a nuclear weapon. Designed by Alexander Kartveli, 1946.
A hall, apartment or large room, designed or used primarily for festive or state functions.

A northern term for water reservoirs at steam powered industrial sites that are part of the steam raising plant and are used for recirculating condenser cooling water. The lodge had to be large enough to supply the condenser with cool water for a day.
Sites and structures associated with the storage of water and waste water. Use only where the exact form or function is unknown otherwise use more specific term.
A large natural or artificial body of water, sometimes covered, used to collect and store water for a particular function, eg. industrial or public use.
A supply of water used to keep canals that were vulnerable to water shortage topped up.
A wide-mouthed, narrow based flared bowl associated with dairying activities. (Source: MPRG)
A flared bowl of medium to deep depth, with wide horizontal everted rim. These vessels may have a single handle. (Source: MPRG)
A bowl with straight sides which turn outwards, forming an obtuse angle with the base, i.e. and inverted, truncated, conical shape. (Source: MPRG)
A place where osiers (willows) are grown for basket-making.

A civil passenger transport biplane produced by the Farman Aviation Works from 1919. Instrumental in the creation of early airlines and commercial routes in Europe after World War I. Initially designed in 1918 as a heavy bomber. Some 60 units built.

Twin-engined air/sea rescue and anti-submarine patrol aircraft. Originally developed from the Wellington and intended as a bomber, entered RAF Coastal Command service in 1943. Fitted with a Leigh Light and ASV radar.

A building or tower used to communicate information to shipping or other stations using signals such as flags, fires or lights. Roman signal stations took the form of a stone tower surrounded by a ditched enclosure and were used to warn of Saxon raids.

A communication system in which cylindrical containers are propelled through a network of tubes either by compressed air or partial vacuum. They are used for transporting solid objects, as opposed to conventional pipelines, which transport fluids.
Garden or open-air enclosure, usually connected to commercial premises, where tea and other refreshments are served to the public.
A ridge and furrow produced by a plough drawn between two steam engined vehicles, or a steam engined vehicle and a moveable windlass, standing on opposite headlands.
A hall, or main living-room in a medieval house, open to the roof.
Single-engine, single-seat biplane seaplane built for the 1924 Schneider Cup Race.
The core of a capital.
A device which automatically controls a particular funtion within a machine or mechanism, such as regulating the gap between millstones in a windmill.
A building or room where railway tickets may be bought and administrative duties associated with a railway are conducted.
Three-crew, single-engine carrierborne torpedo-bomber. Entered service in 1942, first seeing action during the Battle of Midway. Served with the US Navy until 1956.

A stone wall, often of considerable length, built to divide an area of land. Most occur as part of extensive walled field systems. This is a regional term specific to Dartmoor and should not be used in other parts of the country.
Brewery which produces lager
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
A meeting hall, sometimes equivalent to a GUILDHALL, but also associated with some early mining industries.
A wooden nail, round or square in section, used to fix a joint.
Manufacture and use of wood side products, ie. unprocessed wood rather than processed timber.
A hut used by a person who makes items from wood. Often found in a woodland setting.
A flammable liquid that occurs naturally and is also now distilled.
The process of investigating and recording historic buildings for the purposes of historical understanding.
Visual record of a building, usually exterior only. Equivalent to Historic England Level 1.
A ship designed or modified to carry large numbers of mines and be able to lay them as a minefield.
Buildings incorporating a high degree of protection against damp for the bulk storage of salt.
Sites for the manufacture of substances or items by controlled chemical reactions.
A light, mostly wooden errected structure serving as workshop for the building, storage, repair and maintenance of boats.
A factory manufacturing timepieces, including clocks and watches.

Ditches interrupted by wide, regular causeways. Each section of ditch is about 30-40m long, and each causeway is 10-15m wide. In some cases, a network of fields has been created. Found mainly in the South East of England.

A collared urn with a heavy rim or collar on top of a concave neck or cavetto zone, which may or may not be decorated, and this in turn leads down to a straight-sided but narrowing body. Decoration may extend below this cavetto zone, but this is rare.
Originally a light day-bomber, the Boston II, re-christened the Havoc, was adapted for night-flying in the fighter-intruder role. Was capable of a top speed in excess of 300 mph.
Houses specifically for men and of chiefly mendicant religious orders. The status of priory is represented in several friaries. Use with PRIORY if required.
A house of friars of the order of St Dominic. Also known as Friars Preachers or 'Black Friars'.
A hotel adjacent to a railway terminus. Railway hotels were often owned by a railway company.
An object designed to be the end of a lace or simimlar to aid the insertion of the lace through a loop or eyelet.
The ending for a lace.
A site used for the production of sodium bicarbonate, soda ash or caustic soda.
A town for citizens of Roman or Latin status with a constitution governed by charter, which if possessing only Latin rights could be promoted to the status of a colonia.
A planned administrative capital for local government which provided amenities for the Roman and peregrine (non-Roman) inhabitants of the town.
A town founded as an act of government by charter to house Roman or Latin citizens, usually retired legionaires who had been granted land within a territorium.
An assemblage of public and private buildings, larger than a village and having more complete and independent local government.
A civilian settlement outside a Roman fort.
A mould used to cast coins.
A hut 51ft long by 20ft wide used to dry, store and pack parachutes.Similar in design to the 2355/25, but constructed in timber instead of brick.
A method of grinding cereals where one stone is rotated on another by hand.
An expansion period stand by set house designed to drawing number 607/36 and containing a single generator set and switch board. Constructed in reinforced concrete.
A die used in divination.
An educational establishment primarily for children aged 16-18 years old but can provide education for more mature students.
A factory in which varnish is manufactured.
Material that has been altered as a result of chemical action.
A site visit to ascertain the nature and extent of the site and its surrounding environs by means of a visual inspection from which a written and/or photographic record is made.

A two-storey, structure with a brick ground floor and a reinforced concrete upper floor with balcony and large windows to the watch office and control room. This became the most common building design for air traffic control in the Second World War.
Use for complexes where services (eg. restaurants, shops) are provided in addition to facilities for buying petrol.
An axe with a cutting edge and a hammer head.
A device for separating grain from chaff by means of a wind or current of air.
A native hardwood of the Beech family with hard and durable characteristics which traditionally made it appropriate for structural work.
A small timber fixed to a wall to support items such as cladding. Also a strip of timber fixed across two or more parallel boards to join them together or conceal their join.
A place where current and former members of the armed services meet for social and recreational activities.
A maze used for the act of penitence.

A confusing and baffling network of winding and intercommunicating paths, often bordered by high hedges or walls. Some early examples are believed to have had ritual uses. Use more specific type where known.
A ravine formed by using water to reveal or exploit a vein.
A factory used to manufacture fibreglass.
A hall normally reserved for holding feasts on special occasions.
A room, furnished with tables and chairs, where meals and refreshments are served and consumed.

An establishment originally providing terminals to allow the public to access the internet, usually for a fee. They originally provided snacks and drinks to customers although now this is not always the case.
A cheap eating and drinking establishment usually serving snacks and non-alcoholic drinks.
The front piece of horse armour.
Armour used to protect a horse.
The Supermarine Company was formed in 1912 and specialised in producing sea-going aircraft, including several Schneider Trophy winners. Taken over by Vickers-Armstrongs Ltd., in 1938.

Interbellum, twin-engined, five-crew, biplane flying-boat with a characteristic triple tail-fin. Entered service in 1925 and used for general reconnaissance duties. The Mk.I had a wooden fuselage, whilst the Mk.II's was metal in construction.

Land which has been temporarily taken over for use by the military or civilian authorities. During wartime land was requisitioned for various purposes, such as for argriculture or for military training/events etc.
Hanging drapery used to cover an opening eg a window, often decorative.
A building in which goods were kept prior to being cleared by customs officers.
A structure inclined towards the water on which a ship may be built or lowered into the water.
A factory where pianos are manufactured.
A factory where musical organs are manufactured.
A building where violins are manufactured and the art of violin making is taught.
A factory where musical instruments are manufactured.
A machine tool capable of creating a variety of forms and surfaces in materials by way of a spinning cutter positioned over a movable table.

A curfew consisting of a half-bell shape with a raised flange around the cut-away side. A vertical loop handle joins the flange and body. The form is adapted for use against a wall and some are highly decorated. (Source: MPRG)

An early warning structure built during and after WWI along the south and east coasts of England. Sound detecting acoustic dishes and walls could detect the sound of approaching enemy aircraft at a distance of 8 to 15 miles.
A concrete, circular concave dish 30 feet in diameter used as an acoustic listening device to detect approaching enemy aircraft.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Fishing Industry Protocal for Archaeological Discoveries (FIPAD)

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: An initial synthesis of the data collected from an excavation.
A curved structural span which is supported at the sides or ends. May vary in shape from the horizontal flat arch through semicircular and semielliptical forms.
A public building where regular dances were held.
A shaft sunk into the ground to reach the water level.
An often ornately decorated theatre for the performance of opera.
Place where a smith works iron. May be for small scale local use or within a larger industrial complex.
An observation post used by members of the Home Guard.

Use to identify a feature, previously thought to be a monument but now disproved, or to avoid erroneous identification as a monument in future. Where a feature is regarded as an antiquity, but is unclassified, use SITE.
A bound written work.
An indoor or outdoor market where hay and straw is sold.
A place where boats or ships are built or repaired.
A working hospital, often near or associated with a university, where doctors and nurses are trained.

A register which including sites retaining any evidence of pre-1750 layouts; significant evidence of pre-1820 layouts; good examples of the best gardens from 1820 to 1880; are good examples of the best gardens laid out after 1880 but before 1970.
A horizontal tunnel dug specifically for draining, for example, a mine.

Accommodation used as an alternative to the workhouse following several Poor Law Acts. Modelled on continental examples and first erected at the end of the 1860s, it is based on the idea of a "village" of small houses accommodating a small group.
A residential establishment for the care and accommodation of children and young people.
A tower containing a curfew bell. The bell was rung in the evening, as a signal that fires were to be extinguished.
A tower or turret in which bells are hung.
A flat tile with raised or flanged edges, used with imbrex for roofing.
A thin slab of hard material, such as baked clay, shaped and used in quantity as a roofing material.
A room where meals, particularly breakfast are partaken.
A site where iron oxide and iron sulphate is extracted.
The hall before a great hall.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber and ground-attack aircraft. Entered service with the Luftwaffe in mid-1941. Approximately 20,000 were constructed between 1941 and the end of the war.
Focke-Wulf Flugzeugbau G.m.b.H.. Founded in 1924 and amalgamated in 1931 with the Albatross-Flugzeugwerke G.m.b.H.. Converted to a G.m.b.H. in 1937.

Long-range, four-engine reconnaissance-bomber. Initially produced as a transport, converted and used against Allied convoys in the Channel and the Atlantic. Also served as a VIP transport, one of which was the Immelmann III: Hitler's personal aircraft.

A curved dam usually built of concrete and designed with the curve upstream so that the force of the water compresses the structure and strengthens it as it pushes it into its foundations. Arch dams are best suited to narrow gorges
A garden in which bees are kept.
A room or building used for the storage of fleeces.
A building associated with the legal administration of a forest, eg. Forest of Dean.
A device for raising miners individually from a shaft consisting of two rods, raised and lowered alternately, fitted with small platforms and powered by a waterwheel or steam engine.
A defensive construction situated in the sea, designed to protect the land from seabourne attack. The term applies mainly to those monuments built from around 1860 onwards.

Twin-engined maritime-reconnaissance bomber adapted from pre-war American airliners, the A-28 and A-29, evident from the row of portholes along its fuselage. Entered service with RAF Coastal Command just before the outbreak of World War Two.

Monument whose existence is indicated by the discovery of isolated artefacts or an artefact scatter. Eg a scatter of roofing tiles indicating the presence of a building. Use narrow terms where circumstances of discovery are known.
A Monument whose presence is inferred from artefacts found in stratified below ground deposits, as distinct from surface collection or chance find.
A distribution of artefacts indicating the presence, or former presence, of a monument.
Monument whose presence is inferred by discovery of unstratified artefacts, for instance in plough soil.
Vickers (Aviation) Ltd. formed in 1911, as the aviation division of Vickers Ltd., and took control of Supermarine Aviation Works Ltd. the same year. Taken over by Vickers-Armstrongs Ltd. in 1938.
Twin-engined, four-crew bomber. Wooden framed, with linen covering, entered service in 1924, equipping several RAF squadrons.
A textile mill where felt is produced.
A crane or hoist within a building found mainly in the North of England. Can also refer to a projecting crane located above a loading slot.
A mechanical lift or elevator, used to lift goods, etc.
A layer of stone, brick or boards, etc, on which people tread. Use broader site type where known.
Floor cover in Roman time, where small cubes (tesserea) of one or more colours were laid in a geometric pattern.
A cutting tool for shaping and carving materials, often used in conjunction with a hammer or mallet.
A specially designed chisel for producing ornamental mouldings.
A residence of two or three monks of the Cluniac order dependent on an English mother house.
A monastic enclave dependent on a mother house.
A crude shelter for persons engaged in the production of pure carbon by the controlled burning of wood and other organic materials.
A stone on which Runes have been inscribed. Often used as memorials though not always associated with a burial.
A site where tar is manufactured or combined with other substances to produce bitumen, for example.
A hearth constructed specifically for the manufacture of pitch.
The area of a military base where engineering and maintenance functions are grouped.
Arado Flugzeugwerke. Formed in 1931 in Germany when the aircraft manufacturer Albatros Flugzeugwerke was declared bankrupt and part of it merged with Arado Handells-Gessellschaft.
Single engine, two-crew shipboard reconnaissance and patrol seaplane. Entered service in 1939, this was the last combat floatplane built in Europe.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Listed Building Certificate of Lawfulness proposed

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: Small building in which labourers, such as miners and tin workers. They are also associated with gardens where they provide on-site accommodation for gardeners and estate workers.
A platform for storing winter fodder.
A bell mounted on an anchored vessel, buoy, headland, rock etc and rung as a warning to mariners in foggy weather.
A place where boats are built and stored.
A coloured fluid used for writing, drawing and printing.

An enclosed feature, usually sub-terranean, constructed to contain water for public or private recreation and sporting activities. Often a component of a larger SPORTS CENTRE. Use OUTDOOR SWIMMING POOL for unenclosed pools.

A unenclosed feature, usually sub-terranean, constructed to contain water for public or private recreation and sporting activities. Sometimes part of a LIDO complex. Use INDOOR SWIMMING POOL for pools within a covering structure.
A swimming pool restricted to the use of females only.
Man made structure, usually sub-terranean, built to contain water for the purpose of immersion of people for sport and leisure.
Man made structure to contain tidal waters, often part of a LIDO, bathing or swimming complex at the sea edge.
Swimming pool, usually part of a larger LIDO or SPORTS CENTRE complex. Medium size pool, between large pool and paddling pool, used primarily for learners.
A swimmin pool restricted to the use of men only.
An instrument for establishing the horizontal line of sight and used in surveying. It usually has an eyepiece and an air bubble in a glass tube or dome.
Factory where yarn is made from paper.
A building containing machinery for the spinning of yarn.
Human beings. Use more specific type where known.
People who have been convicted of criminal offences. Traditionally criminals, even those convicted of petty offences, were transported from Europe to penal colonies in the Americas and Australia.
A public house where no alcohol is sold.
A prison used for temporary detention. The typical village lock-up was a one-storeyed, one-celled building, sometimes of round or polygonal plan.

A secure, bomb-proof, undergound complex designed to be used by the government in the event of a national emergency such as nuclear war. Usually equipped with communications equipment, emergency rations and water and air filtering plants.
A succession of arches on shafts with no openings, attached to and used to enliven a wall.
A mug with a rounded body profile below a deep neck. There may be a marked junction between the neck and the body. The neck may be inward-sloping, upright or everted. (Source: MPRG)
A specific German Stoneware form of rounded mug. (Source: MPRG)
Timber or metal structure consisting of upright and cross members designed to support climbing plants.

A type of transportable aircraft hangar patented by Miskins and Sons in 1939. The arched hangar was constructed of steel or wooden ribs and generally clad in steel sheets. The hangar did not require any foundations and could be anchored by iron stakes.
Use for microscropic remains.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the generation and transmission of power.
Buildings and structures associated with the processing and storage of natural gas.

A facility where natural gas is made smaller in volume, to facilitate its distribution through the National Transmission System. Term can also be used for a station, which recompresses the gas to the required pressure.
An alcoholic spirit distilled from sugar products, especially molasses.
A site where granite is excavated.
Fish which has been preserved by drying.
A residential home for adults with learning difficulties and/or physical disabilities.
One of a set, used as standards for specific coins, often bearing stamps and other marks of authenticity.
Glazed and decorated, patterned earthenware tile combining different coloured clays which are inlaid and burnt in. Mainly used for flooring and external decoration.
An accessory vessel to a cremation.
A sacred area of a building or a consecrated piece of land.
A room or suite of rooms used as dwellings, eg. in private houses, hotels or tenement houses.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War. The U Boat had 5 torpedo tubes (4 bow/1 stern) and carried 10 torpedoes as well as an 88mm (or in some cases 105mm) deck gun.
A figurative representation used in divination.
An often highly elaborate water fountain, usually found in parks, gardens or urban spaces.
A fortified house of two or three storeys, the lower floor being used to house animals and the upper for domestic use.
A garden for the cultivation of herbs used for medicinal or culinary purposes.
Specify in Descriprion whether currently managed, neglected, unmanaged or management not determined.
A mobile crane which floats on water.
A mill for shredding cloth, for use in flock paper, etc.
An ornament for the ear, usually clipped to the lobe or fastened through a hole pierced in the lobe.
Examination, recording and plotting of variations in the electrical resistivity of soils in order to locate and define buried features.
A fine grained earth which becomes more plastic when water is added and can be moulded and dried to make bricks, tile, pottery, etc.
A site where barytes (barium sulphate) is mined. Barytes is also commonly worked from the waste tips of lead mines.
Buoys used to direct craft on water along the correct route or away from a hazard. Usually used in coastal areas.
A long ridge of earth, rocks or gravel primarily constructed to carry a roadway.
An H-sectioned strip of lead used to hold panes of glass in position in stained-glass windows or other leaded lights.
A dredger which can act as its own hopper and can thus transport the mud which it picks up to dump it at the desired place.
A restraining ring usually linked to another.
A shackle for the feet.
An abbey or priory of Carthusian monks.
An ancilliary building or structure associated with a military base. Use only where exact function is unknown otherwise use more specific term.
A building used for the accommodation of sick and wounded members of the armed forces.
A structure for visually communicating the exact time to ships in anchorage. A ball slides down a mast at the top of the tower, usually at noon or one o'clock exactly.
Residue resulting from the presence of sewage. While you can have a cesspit, it contains sewage not cess.
Material of unknown origin observed adhering to, or found within, an object of another material.
Plaster which has been painted either for decorative purposes or to protect it.
Lime plaster, consisting of lime and sand, is the oldest type of render. Applied externally to walls or onto laths for infill panels and usually limewashed.
A farm with a pond, river, lake or tanks where fish are kept and bred for commercial purposes.
Where several minerals produced, use with other products and MINE, eg. ARSENIC MINE.

A jug that incorporates a practical joke or conundrum into its construction. A combination of cut-outs in the body and hollow handles and tubes render conventional use impossible. The puzzle being to work out how to empty it. (Source: MPRG)
The rural residence of a country gentleman.
A kiln or furnace for the firing of bricks.
A circular kiln or oven used in the manufacture of bricks. Common in Staffordshire in the 18th century.

An engine which operates machinery via a pivoted, horizontal beam with a piston located at one end and a reciprocating pump beneath the other, resulting in a rocking, seesaw-like motion. Variations featured the steam piston placed above the beam.
A form of tandem compounding of early beam engines, with a high pressure steam cylinder mounted on top of a low pressure one, introduced in Cornwall the 1840s by James Sims.
A two-seat, reconnaissance biplane developed from the FK2 with a more powerful, but heavier, engine. Primarily used for training in the UK.

Waste material from the digestive tract of animals. The term coprolite comes from the Greek 'kopros' meaning dung and 'lithos' meaning stone, and is used for faecal matter that has been preserved by mineral replacement or dessication.
A stick used as an aid or accessory when walking.
Earthworks and buildings added around a bastion to enhance protection of the bastion.
A defence work, either a detached fieldwork or an outwork built as part of a fortification as a last defensive position.
A machine gun post designed by James Ruck constructed from hollow blocks and prefabricated concrete sheeting with loopholes allowing for a garrison of eight.
The quasi-triangular area between, and defined by, the upper sections of a pair of adjacent arches, or between the curve of an arch and the angle of a surrounding frame or structure.
A spandrel that is sunk below the surface of the arch.

A propulsion system for ships which need a maximum speed that is considerably faster than their cruise speed, particularly warships. It consists of diesel engines for cruising and gas turbines for high-speed transits.
A propulsion system for ships using a combination of steam turbines and gas turbines to power the shafts.
A heat engine prime mover in which hot gases or hot air expand as they pass through and rotate vanes attached to a central shaft, enclosed in a chamber.
A vessel for the storage and transport of wine.
A bottle for the storage and transportation of milk.
A container, typically cylindrical with a narrow neck, usually for containing liquids.
Garden area next to public house used for the comsumption of alcoholic beverages.
The public house was a 19th century development, distinctive from the earlier BEER HOUSE by its decorative treatment and fittings.
A kiln where gypsum was dried to a state where it could be used as plaster of Paris or for the production of cement.

A house within a row. At first floor level a gallery which runs through the front of the building. Access to the gallery was gained by steps set at intervals along the row. Commonly found in the city of Chester.
A terrace house sharing a common wall with its neighbours.
A centre for the teaching of crafts.
A road or street covered with small, rounded cobble stones.

skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Asylum For Aged And Decayed Freemasons
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A house devoted to the shelter of the poor and endowed by a benefactor for this use.
A place of worship for Primitive Methodists, a group founded in Manchester who broke away from the Methodists in 1806.
A small vessel used to carry fresh water to ships at anchor or in harbour.
A usually shallow cut linear feature often used for drainage.
A mobile crane usually found on a marine or inland quay.
A crane usually found at a marine or inland quay.
A crane that is fixed to a quay and used for the loading and unloading of cargo.
A photographic frame of developed black and white film from which a positive print can be produced.
A single-seat, pusher prop, escort and patrol-fighter. Used in the UK in a Home Defence role until superseded in 1917.
Purpose built or modified structure used for scenery in a film.
A building or complex of buildings where cinematographic films are produced.
Small hand-held firearms.
A free school for poor children.
A shallow tray or dish used for baking food.

An institution for the imprisonment of prisoners who can be trusted to serve their sentence without likelihood of escape and of being a threat to the public. There is no physical barrier designed to prevent absconding.
A labyrinthine garden feature, common during the 16th and 17th centuries, created by cutting shallow pathways into deep lawns.
A building housing an economizer, a machine designed to preheat water for boilers.
A large, rectangular pillbox based on the FW3/28 with the addition of a small infantry chamber to one side of the main gun chamber.

An acoustic method which involves the creation of a shock wave through the ground. By recording the time interval between the initial shock and the reflected or refracted shock waves it is possible to define subsurface deposits.

A term for a type of house, with varying definitions according to period. Roman villas were high-status and usually associated with a rural estate, whereas Georgian and later period villas were often semi-detached, town houses.
Factory or workshop making bits, spurs and other small metal objects associated with horse harness.
A living thing that is not an animal. Use for unspecified plants only. Use a more specific type where known.
Includes all trees, flowers, vegetables etc. and any products manufactured from them.
A plant incorporating a range of ore processing operations such as buddles.
A man-made passageway, which is built through a sea- or riverbed.
A missile consisting of a number of weights joined together by cord. The bolas entangles the legs of a target causing it to fall.
A high explosive, manufactured by absorbing unstable nitroglycerine in a material such as kieselguhr, a soft, earthy material.
A fragment of the base of a vessel, or hollow object, usually of ceramic or glass. If known, use specific vessel type.
A fragment of a vessel, or hollow object, usually of ceramic or glass. If known, use specific vessel type.
An S-shaped ornamental bracket with a greater height than projection.
A bracket that is shaped to form an angle.
A small support designed to help support a weight, such as that of a projecting member.
A small moulded bracket found on the Corinthian and Composite orders, and in plain form in the Ionic.
An interior wall, usually not load bearing, that divides a space.
A leather working tool.
A knife that is used for circumcision.
A cutting blade with handle used for food preparation and consumption.
A tool used in the separation of fibres from the bark in flax working.
A stone tool, often only polished on the edge.
A knife with a hinged blade which folds into a slot in the handle.
A small, sharp bladed knife for sharpening pens, originally sheathed, now the blades fold.
A flint tool with a convex top and flat base.
A knife designed to be used for pruning plants.
A small knife used in surgery.
A discoidal flint tool often has a ground edge.
A structure, composed of oven and hovel, used for the firing of pottery ware.
A type of pottery oven in which the air passes from the base of the kiln out through the top.
Monument with roof or walls intact or substantially intact, significant survival of original features, even if building no longer in use for original function.
Monument with a roof and walls or evidence of these.
A dedicated room for housing the organ feeder bellows, can be an underground chamber or a free-standing building.

A building, similar in style to a telephone exchange but smaller. They were used to compensate for the inadequacies of 1920's and 30's equipment over long distances, by repeating the signal every 200 miles.

A cable repeater station for the undersea telephone and telegraph cables. Repeater stations compensated for the inadequacies of 1920's and 30's equipment over long distances, by repeating the signal every 200 miles.
Mark, usually consisting of a horizontal line above an arrow, cut by the Ordnance Survey as part of the survey of Britain and referenced to a known height above mean sea level.
A steam engine, often used in the 18th century, which drove a pump to return water back to a waterwheel so that it could be used over and over again.
A struck piece of flint or other stone where the length is at least twice the width.

A flint blade with negative impressions of removals on one side of the dorsal surface, creating a crest. These constitute part of a previously worked striking platfom or result from preparing the flaked surface on a core before detaching flakes or blades.
A complex of buildings where electricity is produced using steam-powered turbines.
Photographic plate, on glass, developed using a wet process.
A case for the transportation and protection of musical instruments.
An engine in which a vertical piston rod supplies energy via a crankshaft directly to the flywheel suspended above the cylinder. Extensively used as mine winding engines.
Twin-engined, single-seat fighter-bomber. Flown by USAAF fighter groups from 1942, excelled as a ground-support fighter. Could carry two 1600 lb bombs or rocket projectiles.
A building used for the accommodation of a military guard and/or the detainment of prisoners.
A type of windlass for drawing up ore.
A place where processed cloth is cut for use as garments or soft furnishings, etc.

Protective equipment, usually made of metal, to protect parts of the body, e.g. helmets, breastplates, or full suits of armour, to protect troops or individuals in warfare. Most examples date from the Middle Ages, obsolete from the 17th century.
Temporary settlement relating to the construction of railways, viaducts, dams, etc.
Originally a room in a house where a family would gather, usually in the evening, to sit and read, write, sew, play music etc. This term has become commonly used as an alternative to living room.
A sitting room fitted with large windows for the purpose of admitting the maximum amount of sunlight.
A lighted pillar or LIGHTHOUSE, eg. Dunston Pillar, Lincs., erected in 1751 to guide travellers over the heath.

A tower or structure, with a powerful light or lights at the top, usually erected at an important or dangerous point on or near the sea-coast for the warning and guidance of mariners, but can also be erected inland for the guidance of travellers.
An object which supports or is attached to a blind.
A place in which turpentine is produced.
A kiln used for the slow burning of vegetable matter to produce potassium carbonate.

The first transportable aircraft hangar developed by the RFC/RAF, which comprised a kit of timber and canvas that could be assembled in 48 hours. The canvas doors open one end only. Also known as Type H hangar.
A sheet of glass coated in a light sensitive substance on which a photgraphic image can be developed.
Pairs of canal gates (also called Brindley gates) designed to rapidly shut off a section of a canal to prevent flooding
A castle without a motte.
A building or site incorporating sonar equipment used for detecting the presence of enemy ships or submarines.
An object originally created to communicate a particular personal belief, achievement, status or membership. It includes articles of adornment or clothing worn primarily for their symbolism.
An heraldic design depicting armorial bearings.
An institution for the detention of prisoners considered to be a major threat to public safety and/or to the security of the nation.

The light emitted from sedimentary minerals or mineral inclusions in bricks when stimulated in the laboratory by infrared light. Used to date samples up to 250,000 years old; especially appropriate for geological sediments containing feldspars

The light emitted from sedimentary minerals or mineral inclusions in bricks when stimulated in the laboratory by light of a different wavelength. Used to date samples up to 250,000 years old; especially appropriate for geological sediments.
A range of techniques that use the build up of charge stored within a crystalline material to estimate its age

The measurement of the light emitted from sedimentary minerals, mineral inclusions in bricks, burnt flint or unburnt calcite when they are heated. The signal relates to their prior exposure to radioactivity. Used to date samples up to 500,000 years old.
American twin-engined medium bomber and ground-attack aircraft that entered service in 1941. A small number were delivered to the RAF under the British designation Mitchell I.
The edge of a roof that hangs over the wall.
A board on the lower edge of a sloping roof which protects the top of the external wall.
A dedicated room for housing the organ feeder bellows, can be an underground chamber or a free-standing building.

Fleet Air Arm fighter and torpedo-bomber, designed for operation from aircraft carriers. All-metal in construction, it entered service in 1944 and was rendered obsolete after the war by the advent of the jet aircraft.
A material made of felted fibres bonded by bitumen. Often used as a roofing material.

A single engine two seat cabin monoplane tourer, first flown in 1933 as a successor to the Puss Moth. Impressed into military sevice in WWII by the RAF and the Fleet Air Arm as a liaison and communications aircraft, also used by training units.
A building or room containing a collection of preserved plants (usually pressed and dried specimens).
Swimming pool, usually part of a larger LIDO or SPORTS CENTRE complex. Medium size pool, between large pool and paddling pool, used primarily for learners.
A prepared area used for the game of baseball.
Photographic negative on polyester base material.

A first century AD one-piece bow brooch, one end of which is drawn out to form a spring and pin, characterized by its long, narrow, tapering bow, a small crossbar in front of the spring and a forward hook which holds the spring chord.

Derived from the Colchester in the mid to late 1st century, particularly in south and east Britain. Characterized by the attachment of the separate spring and pin through two holes in a lug behind the head, which projects to form a crest atop the bow.

Capturing visible spectrum photographs or images of monument features or character using still or motion cameras from an aircraft or other airborne vehicle or apparatus. Covers both digital and film-based cameras.

A calciner commonly used between 1870 and circa 1900 for extracting arsenic from mined ores and featuring a slightly inclined rotating iron tube with a firebox at the bottom and an ore feed at the top.
A college where specialist skills, relating to a particular subject, are taught. Use specific type where known.
A college where subjects relating to trade and commerce are taught.
A grooved block placed in series, alternating with the metopes, in a Doric frieze.
Bleach works or bleach house for bleaching of textiles, etc.
Use for vessels registered in Greece.
The fibrous stalks of the plant, Linum usitatissimum, which can be processed and used to manufacture linen.
Hard iron ores
Ore containing high proportions of Iron.
A circular window containing tracery.
A long spear used on horseback.
A building, or part of a building, used to house doves and pigeons, usually placed at a height above the ground, with openings and provision inside for roosting and breeding.
Gun battery built specifically to mount short range weapons to defend a beach against an attempted landing.
A conduit or pipes, used primarily for conveying petroleum from oil wells to a refinery, or for supplying water to a town or district, etc.
A joint used to secure the end of a joist
A deep, square or rectangular, flat slab of clay, the upper surface of which has two or more cup-shaped holders cut into it. (Source: MPRG)

A small bowl on a pedestal base above a drip-tray or saucer. It may have a wick lip at the rim. May have pierced lugs projecting form the rim for suspension of a handle, spout or vertical loop handle linking bowl and saucer. (Source: MPRG)
A small hemispherical or flared bowl with a solid pointed base or spike. May include a wick lip at the rim and one or two pierced lugs for suspension. (Source: MPRG)
An appliance that produces light by means of a liquid fuel and a wick.
A small bowl on a pedestal base, which may be solid or at least partly hollow. It may have a wick lip at the rim or a lug handle. (Source: MPRG)

A pedestal lamp with a drip-tray below the bowl. There may be a vertical loop handle linking bowl and drip-tray. Some variants have a more enclosed bowl form with a small tubular spout projecting from the bowl. (Source: MPRG)
An open lamp which was filled with oil then a wick floated on the oil.
A lamp designed to be hung rather than to stand.
A small hemispherical bowl with a pinched or pulled wick lip. (Source: MPRG)
A light porous acid volcanic rock used for scouring and, in powdered form, as an abrasive and for polishing. Also used to make lightweight concrete.
A factory where knitted fabrics are manufacterd using knitting machines.
Prefabricated small building that is designed and built to be movable rather than permanently located.
A crane which is driven by a petrol or diesel engine and travels on either crawler tracks or rubber tyres.
A crane mounted on wheels and/or rails, used for the unloading of ships' cargoes.
Three-crew, single-engine carrierborne torpedo-bomber. Entered service in 1942, first seeing action during the Battle of Midway. Served with the US Navy until 1956.
A machine for making paper in a continuous length.
A large container for milk.
A form of Neolithic burial monument comprising a large circular stone or earthen mound, with a low and narrow entrance passage leading to a wider and higher stone built chamber.
A bookbinding workshop.
A complex or network of earthwork or cropmark linear ditches, banks or other features. Use specific type where known.
A bow, fixed to a stock, with a mechanism to fire the bow.
A jar adapted by the addition of a straight handle and three feet. Profiles vary and should be double indexed with the appropriate JAR type. (Source: MPRG)

A jar adapted by the addition of one straight handle, attached to either rim or body, and usually with a lip at right angles to the handle. The body is generally rounded, with a short neck and an everted rim. (Source: MPRG)
A building, or part of a building for the boiling and preparation of animal feed, usually attached to pigsties.
An engine in which the oscillating motion of the beam is translated via gearing to a rotative motion.
A small self-contained rotative Beam Steam Engine.
A room in which a judge sits to hear cases and undertake other official proceedings which are not of a sufficient importance to be brought into court.
A device for rotating a spit.
The part of a column between the capital and the base.
A moulded ring around a shaft.
A place where processed cloth is cut for use as garments or soft furnishings, etc.
A place where members of the British Legion meet.
A place where an anti-corrosion coating of zinc is added to iron and steel products to prevent them from rusting.
Single-seat carrierborne jet fighter. Originally conceived as an RAF land-fighter, entered Fleet Air Arm service in 1951 and was the first jet fighter to be standardised in first-line squadrons.
A building, department or shop where postal business is carried on.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the collection, distribution, sending and reception of mail.
A site or building used for the manufacture of goods made from pewter, an alloy of tin and lead.
A complex of buildings used for the processing of metals. Use more specific type where known.
A purpose-built firing platform on which an anti-aircraft battery could be emplaced.
An obsolete vessel used as a weapons target.
A waterwheel where the water enters at the same level as the axle.
A general term for the weatherproof coat on the external walls of a building.
A render with small washed stones added as aggregate. Popular in the early 20th century.
A decorative building in the form of a dairy, used for recreation.
A small carved figure, usually female in appearance, probably representing fertility charms, found on Romanesque churches in the West of England, eg. Kilpeck.
The residence of a telegraph keeper, associated with a telegraph station.
An underground cell, or group of cells, used for imprisonment.
An underground cell, usually hidden and accessed only through a trapdoor, in which a prisoner was confined and then allegedly forgotten about.
The degree of acidity or alkalinity of a material.
A horizontal member connecting rafters or cruck blades at a point between their feet and the apex of the roof.

A complex of buildings, often within an enclosure, housing a pre-Benedictine Reform secular religious community. Now commonly used to describe the main church within such a complex, which over time attained higher status.
A building used for services by a nonconformist protestant sect, especially by Quakers and Presbyterians.
A hall, often associated with a synagogue, used for studying the Torah and other religious texts.
Use for places of worship. For later landscape features use, eg. GARDEN TEMPLE.
A large, circular hollow, often with a platform and seating built into the sides, used for preaching.
A place of worship for the followers of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints
An ancillary building to a synagogue, used as a place of worship at the feast of the tabernacle.
A place where appropriate acts, rites and ceremonies are performed to honour or revere a supernatural being, power or holy entity. Use specific type where known.
A place of worship for Jewish people.
A stone or brick wall enclosing a park.
A mixing or grinding vessel.
A circular toy which spins on a point. Can be kept spinning by whipping with a lash.
A circular toy which spins on a point.
A purpose-built dwelling for the supervisor of a factory, mine or other industrial complex.
A garage for the storage and maintenance of motor vehicles, such as ambluances and fire engines, used for civil defence purposes.
This includes all articles created to be used for personal care, hygiene, grooming and cosmetic activities.
A C20th military building used to test the efficiency of gas protection equipment provided for drivers of all forms of vehicles.
A site containing a forge for the manufacture of cutlery.

A tandem two-seat, twin-engined, all-weather, long-range supersonic jet interceptor fighter/fighter-bomber originally developed for the United States Navy by McDonnell Aircraft.It first entered service in 1960 with the U.S. Navy.
McDonnell Douglas was a major American aerospace manufacturer and defense contractor, producing a number of famous commercial and military aircraft.
A complex of buildings with the purpose of providing and storing food and drink supplies (esp. for the navy).
A container used to assist in cooling water.
A container used to assist in cooling wine.
A container designed to assist in cooling foodstuffs or liquids. Use specific type where known.
A light, open structure for the sale of newspapers, tickets, etc.
A thin opaque, slightly absorbent material, generally made from processing of plant or other fibres, for use as a medium for writing, drawing and printing.

A pass, vulnerable to attack from the enemy but essential for the movement of troops and which, if captured, could divide a defending force. As a result such passes are defended with anti invasion defences such as pillboxes.
A textile-weaving factory housing powerlooms; commonly a one-storeyed shed with wide, north-light roof carried on iron columns.
A barrier used to close an opening, usually hinged and often hung within a supporting frame.
A large, usually unroofed building with tiers of seats for spectators built in various shapes and enclosing a field used for sports events.
The residence of a marsh keeper.
Obstacles such as scaffolding, barbed wire and concrete blocks or cylinders placed on a beach to impede the progress of enemy soldiers, vehicles or watercraft landing from the sea.
Obstacles, including scaffolding and anti tank blocks designed to impede an enemy's attempts to land forces onto open beaches.
Vickers-Armstrongs Ltd.. In 1938 took over Vickers (Aviation) Ltd., which itself had taken control of Supermarine Aviation Works Ltd. in 1928.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter. Entered service in 1943 as a land-based fighter. Converted to a carrierborne fighter in 1944 for use by US Navy and Fleet Air Arm. Mostly saw action in the Pacific and Far East.
A boat roofed over and fitted up as a home for living in permanently or temporarily.
Jet-propelled, pilotless aircraft carrying a one-ton explosive warhead. Also known as the Fieseler FI-103, the V1 was nicknamed the doodlebug, or buzz bomb.
A pilotless aircraft armed with explosives and fuelled to stall over its intended target.
A capital at the corner of a colonade or portico in the Ionic Order in which the volutes are splayed outwards at 45 degrees.
A Capital with a rolled up cushion-like form on either side creating distinctive volutes.
A house having four rooms of equal height on each of two floors; in larger houses there are often two parallel and equal roofs.
Four-crew, twin-engined monoplane designed as a torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance aircraft for RAF Coastal Command. Withdrawn from operations in November 1940 and downgraded to a trainer.
A straight mine entrance, driven on a constant downwards slope.
A loft, balcony or gallery, in a hall or church, for the use of musicians.
A gallery or platform within a place of worship housing the organ.
An upper story in a chapel, church or cathedral, situated above the aisle and below the clerestory, often arcaded and sometime called a Tribune.
A moulding which is small, convex and circular.
Decorative ornamentation consisting of alternating bead shapes with small, elliptical forms resembling reels
A frame containing glass tiles or bricks set into a pavement to allow the lighting of basement areas.

A distinctive form of jar being a flat-based, straight-sided or slightly rounded jar with two opposed, upright, rounded, tongue-shaped lugs raised from above the rim and bridged by added, internal struts used to suspend the pot over a fire. (Source: MPRG)
A kind of stone used in making ink.
An assemblage of public and private buildings, larger than a village and having more complete and independent local government.
A town founded as an act of government by charter to house Roman or Latin citizens, usually retired legionaires who had been granted land within a territorium.
A small shaft or column.
A colonnette set in a corner or angle, such as the meeting of two walls or the place at which a doorframe meets the wall it is set in.

Twin-engined bomber. The Whitley was the first 'heavy' bomber to be built in quantity for the RAF and made the first bombing attack on Germany in May 1940. It was later used for convoy protection and reconnaissance.
A garden featrue where several allees radiate from a single point (usually the house). French for 'Goose Foot'
Unspecified landscape feature. Use more specific type where known.
An open circular area where avenues converge.
A series of arches, linked together, often made out of clipped hedges or trees with the trunks forming the uprights
A slate situated at the end of a terrace for a coal company employee to wake the miners for their shift. The slate had the time of the shifts written on it.
A stone set up on a road or path to mark the miles from or to a place.
A chequered board used to play chess.
A brick, stone or iron receptacle for baking bread or other food in.
A single-engine, photo-reconnaissance fighter designed for operation from aircraft carriers. Later adapted as a night fighter, it entered service in 1943 and remained in production until 1956.
A factory or works principally engaged in the production of a single base propellant, using nitrocellulose without the addition of nitroglycerine.
Factory where yarn is made from paper.
A building containing machinery for the spinning of yarn.
Use for a craft powered by an internal combustion engine powered by petrol fuel.
An ornamental garden feature, sometimes with an associated bath house.
A box crane which uses hydraulic power
A crane using hydraulic power.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Carthusian order.
A building where clothes are washed.
A laundry built in conjunction with a PUBLIC BATHS.
Mark 14 or the fourteenth variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
A coin-operated meter receiving fees for parking a vehicle in a street, and indicating time allowed.
A tool with a pointed head for breaking ground.
A winding path in a garden or park, common in the late 17th and early 18th centuries.
A place of worship for members of the French Protestant church of the 16th and 17th centuries.
A factory where china products are manufactured.
An area of either natural or artificial stone arranged to resemble a rocky outcrop or cliff face within animal cages/enclosures of a Zoo.
A piece of wood of square or rectangular section driven through a scarf joint to tighten it
An item used to fasten, bind or join one item to another.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a rectangular or trapezoidal earthen mound.
An alcoholic drink made by the fermentation of malt and flavoured with hops or other bitters.
A bitter beer brewed using charred or browned malt.

Protective equipment, usually made of metal, to protect parts of the body, e.g. helmets, breastplates, or full suits of armour, to protect troops or individuals in warfare. Most examples date from the Middle Ages, obsolete from the 17th century.
A pit used for the prolonged steeping of the flax plant in water to separate the fibres from the wood.

A large communal room often occupying the full height of the building, used for functions such as meetings, entertainments etc. Traditionally found in medieval buildings but also found in later buildings emulating medieval architecture.

A place of worship for General Baptists, a movement established by John Smyth in 1603 and which grew out of the original Baptist church. They believed in free will and are often referred to simply as Baptists.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: New Connexion Of General Baptists Chapel
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A place of worship for members of the New Connexion of General Baptists,an orthodox Baptist church which broke away from the General Baptists in 1770 when the latter became influenced by Unitarianism.
A place of worship for Baptists. The first Baptist church was formed by Thomas Helws in 1611 and gave rise to the General Baptist Movement.
A factory for processing rubber or manufacturing rubber goods, such as tyres.
A factory for the manufacture of heels for the shoe making trade.
A factory where boots and shoes are manufactured.
Fish which has been preserved by drying.
Any of a large group of cold blooded vertebrates who live exclusively in water. Also can refer to the flesh of fish which is eaten.
A building, often located in a park, where players can change and store equipment and from where spectators can watch the game.
A disc capable of holding more data than a conventional CD or CD-Rom. Commonly used as storage medium for film and interactive products.
Record colour in appropriate field.

Six-crew, twin-engined medium night-bomber. Entered service in 1938 and was the RAF's principal bomber until 1943, participating in the first bombing raid of the war. Later versions served as torpedo and reconnaissance-bombers, transports and trainers.
A small artificial pond of water often found in parks and gardens, for decorative purposes.
A ground used for the performance testing of motor vehicles, for example prototype vehicles.
Cottage provided for guests to a country house.
A massive structure designed to transfer canal boats between different canal or river navigations, eg. Anderton boat lift.
Twin-engined, four-seat medium bomber. A re-engined variant of the Hampden, less than 200 were built but never became operational due to engine unreliability. Some were converted to Hampdens.
A photograph taken from the air.
A photograph usually of a standing structure that has been manipulated to allow the creation of a measured drawing of the facade or elevation.

An image created by controlled exposure of light sensitive film. Usually a static image in time and space. For digital photographs double index with an appropriate term under MACHINE READABLE STORAGE MEDIUM.

Recording using specialist equipment that allows discrete wavelengths in the visible spectrum and beyond to be recorded. The combination of different spectral bands allows features to be identified that would not be visible to the naked eye.
Aerial photography using infrared sensitive film or sensors to reveal soil and vegetation characteristics not apparent in photographs derived from conventional aerial photography.
The residence of a coachman.
Miles Aircraft, Ltd., originally known as Phillips & Powis Aircraft Ltd.. Formed in 1935 as a public company to take over aircraft manufacture from Phillips & Powis Aircraft (Reading) Ltd.
Single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer. Spruce and plywood in construction, entered service in 1939, continuing to serve as a trainer, and also a target tug, until 1950.
Miles M.14 Magister. Single-engine, two-crew training and communications aircraft. Spruce and plywood in construction, with open cockpits and a fixed landing gear, served between 1937 and 1945.
Single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer used in secondary flying training schools. Serving from 1939-50, was also used as a target tug for gunnery practice.
A water-filled structure for experimental research.
A room where usually materials or consumables are processed into tools or meal, for example in a workshop or mill.
An enclosure where the boundary consists of a line of discrete pits, as opposed to a continuous ditch. Use with a term that describes the shape of the monument.

Bow Brooch derived from the Colchester type in the mid to late 1st and 2nd centuries AD. Typically the spring is held in a semi-cylindrical crossbar with closed ends and holding the axial bar and a hook or lug on the head to hold the chord.
An abbey or priory of Augustinian canonesses.
The weight attached to a spindle used for handspinning.

skos:Concept.skos:definition: Traditionally 3 miles. No longer an official unit in any nation.

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: Hard, coarse grained, calcareous sandstone, coloured by iron oxide. Quarried in the Guildford and Godalming area of the South East.
A chain, band or cord, often bearing beads, pearls, jewels etc worn around the neck.
A heavy chain, usually of gold, worn as insignia of office or a mark of fealty or other association from the Middle Ages onwards.
A transverse ceiling beam set below wall-plate level in order to increase head room within the roof space; it carries knee principals, or the struts or braces of an interrupted tiebeam truss.
A bridge, often over a canal or road, allowing access between two parcels of land.
A building in which raw pottery is finished by dipping it in glaze.
Use for vessels registered in Slovenia.

A lighthouse whose lantern is sufficiently low to be seen below low lying cloud. In locations where varying weather conditions occur a Low Light is usually accompanied by a HIGH LIGHT built alongside or nearby.
A portable timepiece capable of being worn on the wrist or carried in a pocket.
A building or group of buildings used for the storage and issuing of rations and equipment to an army unit.
A large area, usually open-air, used for permanent, seasonal or regular shows, events or exhibitions.
An Egyptian container for holding the entrails of a mummy.

A Roman under-floor heating system in which hot air heated by a stoked furnace, flowed through channels, created by either raising the floor on pillars of brick and tile or cutting channels into the concrete floor and tiling over them.
An indicator of the extent of an area of land.
An indicator of the extent and or ownership of a property.
A factory or plant for the manufacture of ice using mechanized refrigeration techniques.
A fishing vessel specially designed to operate and trawl for the catching of bottom lying fish. Use with power where known.
A long shaft topped by an axe head. Differs from a battleaxe by the length of the shaft.
A photo- reconnaissance variant of the Boeing Superfortress, used from 1944, initally deployed in the Pacific war, later for Cold war duties over Europe.
A single-engine, photo-reconnaissance fighter designed for operation from aircraft carriers. Later adapted as a night fighter, it entered service in 1943 and remained in production until 1956.
A camera-equipped aircraft intended to fly over enemy territory and gather photographic evidence of strategic features and/or the position and strength of any military presence.
The bottom of a dock.
A pillbox which has been modified from a standard Directorate of Fortifications and Works design. Double index with specific type where known.
A pit, sometimes found close to a church or cathedral, where bells were cast in medieval times.
An object used to fill up a hole.
A plug to keep out dust, moisture etc.
Water spraying tower for cooling coke after it emerges from the furnace.
A steam engine from which the spent exhaust steam either passes out to the atmosphere and is lost, or in some cases is used as process steam in a factory.

Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as an E-shaped plan around two cattle yards. Cattle housing and stabling typically extend as three ranges from the longer main range which includes a barn or mixing house.

Troop and general transport glider. Almost entirely wooden in construction, many were manufactured by the furniture industry. Mk I featured a a door-ramp on the port side whilst the Mk II was fitted with a hinged nose.
An engineless aeroplane, designed to be towed aloft, that travels suspended by upward air currents.
A metal container for liquids and foodstuffs, often sealed.
A place providing social, recreational, and educational facilities for a neighbourhood.

A prefabricated structure of reinforced concrete posts and beams with infillings of pre stressed concrete planks and felted slabs. Initially used for military barracks in WWII and later for civilian housing. Manufactured by the Orlit Company.
The black, lightweight and porous residue of partly burnt wood.
A structure or building, often within a secluded area of a garden, where people could go for quiet reflection.
A lattice work bower or shady retreat covered with climbing plants.
A shallow, usually circular, dish on which food is served or eaten from.
A slab which can be decorated, shaped, hollow etc. Used for a variety of purposes in construction.
One of the component tiles used in the construction of a tile hearth, being the floor of, or area in front of, a fireplace.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Benedictine order.
An arch consisting of a segment of a circle connected to other segments with smaller radii.

Single-engine, single-seat interceptor fighter developed from the race-winning Schneider Trophy seaplanes. One of the most famous of all combat aircraft, entered RAF service in 1938 and was still in use in the 1950s.
A kiln in which the contents are protected from the fire, usually by a lining of tiles or refractory bricks.

A large twin-engined airliner produced by the Dutch aircraft manufacturer Fokker in the 1920s. First flight March 1927. Designed by Reinhold Platz. Mixed construction, fuselage/ tail in steel covered with plywood, canvas and duralumin (11 units built).

Dutch aircraft manufacturer named after its founder, Anthony Fokker. Set up in 1912 in Schwerin, Germany, moving to the Netherlands in 1919. The world's largest aircraft manufacturer in the late 1920s.
A group of buildings or rooms equipped with apparatus for scientific experiments or other research, testing and investigations.
A scientific laboratory where marine life is studied and researched.
Mechanical reproductive process using photographic, electrostatic and dry powder techniques.
Early form of photographic print.
A building or site where phosphorous-based fertilizers are produced by controlled chemical reactions.
