A building or site used for the production of both chemical and organic fertilizer.
A building or site producing nitrogen-rich fertilizer.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Nitrate, used as a fertilizer or for use in the explosives industry.
A form of blast furnace. Steel is smelted in an open hearth while the waste gases are used to preheat the air blast.
A building housing a flight simulator designed to air ministry drawing number 1762/39.
An open area within an exchange building (e.g. cotton exchange, corn exchange, stock exchange) where goods are traded.
A kiln with a pyramid roof and capped vent in which barley is dried. Found on the site of a malt house.
An attached plaque, inscription, mural or display commemorating nations, actions, soldiers and/or civilians that served or died as a result of conflict.
A gallery or building in a garden, usually south facing, used for the growing of oranges and other fruit.
A moulded bar or baton dividing the panes of glass within a window light.
A building equipped with instruments and a flight simulator used to teach members of bomber crews how to correctly identify targets for bombing.
A long seat usually without a back.
A brass manufacturing complex incorporating battery mill furnaces, hammers, etc.
A workshop or factory where brass articles are made by casting molten material into a mould.
A channel which carried processed alum as liquid from the alum quarry/works to the alum house
A large, deep, manmade pool, usually with accompanying diving boards/platforms and forming part of a swimming pool complex.
A dwelling house forming part of a Chartist Land Colony.
An area for the testing of guided missiles.
A post to which ropes are attached to secure vessels at a landing place.

Survey using a magnetometer, a device capable of detecting variations in magnetic susceptibility between topsoils, subsoils and rocks, can also be used in a maritime context to detect variations in the magnetic field of seabed sediments.
Solid bars made from pure iron.
A magnetic metal found abundantly in certain ores and widely used for the manufacture of tools, machinery etc. Iron is also a chief component of steel.
Factory or workshop making bits, spurs and other small metal objects associated with horse harness.
Obstacles, often semi permanent, which are placed on railway lines to prevent the enemy from using them. Set up during the defence of Britain.
A tool for removing the core from an apple.
A device for removing the core from fruit.
A site occupied by people who have no legal right to the land or buildings on it.
An artificial paved bank or solid landing place built parallel to, or projecting out from, the shoreline to serve in the loading and unloading of vessels.
An area of a port, dock or harbour where cargo vessels can load and unload large storage containers. May include a rail terminal for containers which have been transported to the port by rail.
A long much indented leaf usually curled over at the tip which is a standard form of foliage in classical decoration.
A dry ditch or sunken fence which divided the formal garden from the landscaped park without interrupting the view.
Shaped material used for covering buildings, usually as a roofing material though can be used on walls or floors. Often of fired clay they can be of other materials particularly stone.
A linear open working along a lode vein, worked directy from the surface. Survives as a gully or ravine, normally with closed ends.
A material in a granular form that is smaller than gravel and created by the erosion of rocks.
Sand consisting of a mineral common in igneous rocks.
Observations made by an archaeologist or architectural historian as the result of a field visit to a site or monument.
A factory that manufactures toys.
A factory or building where furniture is upholstered.
Use for the remains of any part of a fish.
Objects used for looking after hair.
A brush used to disentangle hair.
A site or building where barrage balloons are manufactured. Consider double-indexing with the term WAR PRODUCTION FACTORY if appropriate.
A stone inscribed or marked with ogham letters used for a memorial
When a secondary mineral, use term for product type, eg. LEAD MINE.
An instrument with curved arms for measuring difficult or awkward shapes.
Instruments used within geometry, geometrical drawing and navigational mapping.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter manufactured by Messerschmitt. First used as part of Germany's Condor legion during the Spanish Civil War, the 'one-o-nine' was the Luftwaffe's most widely used fighter seeing service throughout World War II.
A box to contain the dowry which is a gift or endowment given to or on behalf of the wife.
A dredger that works by the use of suction.
An office where the administrative duties of a university are performed.
Outdoor site for domestic washing, etc.
A building housing washing facilities and toilets. The term occurs mainly in a military context.
A military base for the training of SOE operatives in the skills and techniques required to survive in enemy-occupied territory.

A round house indicated by the presence of a low, roughly circular bank of turf, earth or stone, which formed the base of the walls. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period. Where several occur together use HUT CIRCLE SETTLEMENT.
An engine used for directly winding up coal from deep mines, dating from the 18th century.
A site incorporating all of the production processes for the manufacture of plaster.
In which a range of conifers may be planted e.g. spruce, larch, pine.
Traditionally a place where meat and fish were sold.
A hard level roadway or other surface from which aircraft take off and land.
Levelled or terraced area of ground presumed to have been the site of a house or hut.
A specialist hospital where the elderly receive medical treatment.
A large jug, usually rounded with a narrow neck, used for holding liquids.
A vault used for the storage of cider.
A two-piece Bow Brooch, derived from the Colchester Brooch, dating from the later first and second centuries AD and so called due to the decorative stud on the upper bow.

A two-seat, single-engine bomber. Fast, versatile and well armed, but with a fuel tank poorly placed between pilot and gunner, was considered to be the best day bomber of the First World War. Later entered civil service.
A kiln for drying hops in a brewery or maltings complex, as distinct from the OASTHOUSES found on farms.
A garden surrounded by a substantial wall.
A large kitchen garden enclosed by a substantial wall, not usually adjacent to its associated house.
The DH5 was an attempt to give a tractor-type fighter a good forward view. However it suffered from unpleasant flying characteristics and, as a result, had a short service career.
A small dwelling for the solitary confinement of a pious reclusive religious man or monk, often attached to the north wall of a church. A squint enabled the occupant to witness the Mass.
A detachable lock with hinged loop used for attachment operated by a key.
A security device attached to objects.
A form of padlock with a cylindrical case and bolts and springs attached to spines.
A fountain decorated with shells forming an ornamental feature.
A container used to hold an offering.
A bowl in which an offering is made.
Building or buildings used for the production of Gas Masks. Consider double-indexing with the term WAR PRODUCTION FACTORY if appropriate.

Active sonar systems are based on the behaviour of sound waves in water; acoustic energy is transmitted and the time for the returning echo is measured to allow submerged seabed features to be mapped. Use specific type where known.
An underwater technique that records bathymetric (depth) data by generating point depths in a line directly beneath the transducer mounted on a vessel as it progresses along the acquisition line.
The dwelling of a blacksmith, nailer, sword cutler, etc, often adjacent to, or containing, a BLACKSMITHS WORKSHOP.
A small cutting hook on a long handle.
A shaft, separate to the main working shaft, used to pump water out of the mine workings.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the drainage and/or ventilation of mines.
A building within a transport terminal, often associated with the registration and clearing of incoming and outgoing passengers or freight.
A building at an airport from where passengers embark and disembark from an aircraft.
A barn used for the storage and drying of wool.
The residence of a sailor.
Coastal base for the docking, launch and maintenance of submarines.
A mineral salt consisting of potassium chloride and mangensium sulphate, used as a fertilizer.
A chemical fertilizer made by treating powdered phosphate rock with sulphuric acid.
A fertilizer containing nitrogen.
Substances, either natural or man-made, used to make soil more fertile.
Dung or compost, carried either as an export cargo or as waste to be dumped out at sea.
Fossilized animal dung, often ground into powder and used as fertilizer.
A joint in which the end of one timber is shaped to fit around the moulding on another.
A light made by dipping a rush in grease.
A torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance biplane in service with the Fleet Air Arm 1935-1938. Rendered obsolete after 1938 by the Swordfish and withdrawn from service.
An open market where cloth and other textiles can be traded.
A pumping station used as part of a clean water supply system.
Transport version of the four-engined Lancaster bomber. Serving from 1943 to 1951, and all metal in construction, this aircraft was used extensively during the Berlin airlift.
A vessel used for the transport of troops, either during wartime or for garrison duties in peacetime.
Site used for the maintenance of aircraft.
A 19th century spa building, usually consisting of a hotel with baths used for water treatment.
The passage, area, lobby, room or vestibule into which a building's main entrance opens.
Movable, usually functional, articles normally found in the home.
An office which administers the affairs of the church.
An object in the shape of an Egyptian dung beetle, used to symbolise the motive power of the sun. Use specific term where known.
An artificial stretch of water, usually rectangular in shape, used decoratively, particularly in formal gardens, eg. Long Water, Hampton Court. Occasionally used to supply water to cascades.
A body of water, building or structure found in a park or garden used as a water supply or ornament. Use more specific type where known.
A hall used by the members of a trade union for meetings and social functions.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of crucibles.
A machine for combing the fibres of cotton, worsted, flax etc to remove short fibres, clean out extraneous matter, and lay the fibres more or less parallel to each other.

A multipurpose hut constructed from stone and turf, covering a square or polygonal plan. It has drystone walls and a slightly corbelled roof, usually topped with slabs. Can be either free-standing or embedded in a Cornish hedge. Particular to Cornwall.

A convex, usually round, piece of metal or other material mounted at the centre of a shield. Originally serving a practical purpose in deflecting blows and providing a mounting for the grip, it later developed into an ornamental feature.
A carved or moulded decorative projection adorning an object or, in the case of architectural features, the termination of a moulding or the intersection of ribs or beams.
A plate on which an offering is made.
A factory, where preserves such as jam and marmalade, are manufactured.
A factory or site for the manufacture of food stuffs from raw ingredients.
A factory, or group of buildings, containing apparatus used to extract specific properties, e.g flavour or scent, from natural ingredients.
A factory where security safes are manufactured.
The rigging mast of a sailing ship erected as a monument. Used for naval displays.
A pillbox with walls that have been thickened to protect against shells. Double index with specific type where known.
Modified or damaged by an animal.
A prison site for the containment of servicemen captured in war.
A container for ointments or perfume.
A large jug or pitcher with a wide mouth.

The main German, medium bomber of the war, the HE111 first saw action during the Spanish Civil War. HE111s took part in the Battle of Britain and from 1944 onwards were used to launch airborne flying bombs against London.

Three-seat, twin-engined minelaying, torpedo-bombing and reconnaissance twin-float seaplane. First flown in 1936, in 1938 it set eight world speed records for its class in various range and payload categories.
Twin-engined, four-crew German seaplane. Entered service in 1932 as a torpedo bomber and naval reconnaisance aircraft, though by World War 2 those still serving were used mainly for air sea rescue.

Twin-engined, six-crew, heavy bomber. Conceived as a rival to the Lancaster and Flying Fortress, the HE177 was dogged by mechanical and structural problems. Of a thousand produced, only about two hundred saw action.
Ernst Heinkel A.G.. Formed in 1922 by Dr. Ernst Heinkel, previously Chief Designer with Hansa-Brandenburgische Flugzeugwerke, where he produced many notable seaplanes during World War One.

skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Preceptory Of The Knights Of St Lazarus
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A manor or estate owned and run by an order of knights and governed by a preceptor.
An estate or manor of a subordinate community of the Knights of the Order of the Hospital of St John of Jerusalem. Includes the mother house, the Priory of St. John, Clerkenwell.

The residence of a preceptor, officials and servants, etc, supervising the estates of the Knights Templars military order. Includes the mother house styled the Temple, London. The Order was suppressed in 1312.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production and use of wind power.
A simple wind-driven machine used for a variety of purposes.
A type of factory building, often single-storey, designed so that windows incorporated into the vertical faces of its saw-tooth roof can allow the maximum amount of natural light into its interior.
Any vessel which has been hired or impressed for use by the Admiralty.
Moorings for a seaplane not part of a seaplane base.
A room in a library or institution providing periodicals, newspapers, etc.
An area of a building providing reading materials for the benefit of colliery workers.
A dam constructed on the reaches of a canal or river designed to retain the water and to regulate its flow.
An outfall from a canal, river or reservoir.
A dock or basin, often inland, used for mooring yachts and other small pleasure craft.
Single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer. Spruce and plywood in construction, entered service in 1939, continuing to serve as a trainer, and also a target tug, until 1950.
A place of worship within the grounds of a cemetery.

Twin-engined, seven-crew, coastal reconnaissance, biplane flying-boat. Designed to the same specification as the Saro London, entered service in 1937. Also serving in an anti-submarine role, was replaced by the Consolidated Canso (Catalina) in 1943.
A terrace, balcony or room exposed to the rays of the sun which were thought to be beneficial to recovering from an illness.
North Carolina, USA

Originally designed as a wood and steel bomber-reconnaissance aircraft, subsequent variations served as special transports, glider tugs and paratroop carriers. Featured a tricycle-style undercarriage.

Sir W. G. Armstrong Whitworth Aircraft, Ltd. formed in 1921. Controlled by the Armstrong Siddeley Development Co., Ltd., a subsidiary of the Hawker Siddeley Aircraft Co., Ltd. from 1935. Pioneers in the development of all-metal aircraft.

Component part of a mungo and shoddy mill, where non-wool fibres from shredded material are destroyed by either soaking rags in an acid solution or rotating them in drums in a hot acidic gas followed by heat. The result is an all-wool product.
A mill for the manufacture of low grade cloth made from ground-up heavy woollen rags.
Essex
An appliance for producing motion by the stepping of men on movable steps on a revolving cylinder. Used as a form of punishment in prisons.
A structure for producing power through a rotary motion achieved by the weight of men or animals treading on a succession of moving steps or a belt that forms a kind of continuous path.
A small boat of wickerwork covered by a watertight material.
A spa building to which water was pumped from springs or wells; usually also serving a social function as an ASSEMBLY ROOM, eg. as at Bath.
An establishment used to serve ice cream to the general public.
An object that contains bones. Use a monuments thesaurus where this is a site type.
A cairn used to indicate the limit of an area or a piece of land.
A marker of some form used to indicate the limit of an area or a piece of land.
A hospital where Royal Naval personnel and their families receive medical and surgical treatment.
A tower built on a prominent part of an estate to provide panoramic views of the surrounding countryside.

Twin-engined, medium bomber with a 1200 mile range and a bomb load in excess of 10,000 lb. Entered service in 1940, but engine faults resulted in retirement in 1942 with its design later modified into the acclaimed four-engine Lancaster bomber.
A factory manufacturing personal hygiene and beauty products
An encircling ornament for the head, usually denoting sovereignty.

Blocks of solid concrete, in the form of cylinders usually 2 feet across x 2 feet 6 inches or 3 feet high. Cylinders were mainly used in road blocks intended to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion.

A list of buildings of special architectural or historic interest. This list confers a statutory level of protection status to the buildings contained within it and usually includes a description of each building.
Part of a musical instrument.
The peg of a stringed instrument which, when tightened or loosened, tunes the string of the instrument.
A beaker with convex body walls. (Source: MPRG)
A round hut, similar to a CHARCOAL BURNERS HUT, associated with forest industry. The bark was later used in the tanning process.
An inclined concrete ramp on which cars can move from one level to another.
An inclined plane connecting two different levels, used to accomodate the movement of vehicles, wheeled apparatus,livestock etc.
A very high chimney, though more often a chimney stack containing only one flue.
The space between the high altar and the east wall or chapel in a large church, and often the area west of a Monks' choir.

A Roman Bow Brooch, dating from the later 1st and 2nd centuries often worn in pairs with a linking chain. Characterized by its distinctive head, sometimes enamelled, and resembling the mouth of a trumpet.
An internal combustion turbine engine powered by diesel, in use during WWII, for example.
Internal combustion engine powered by diesel fuel.
Also known as a half-beam engine, named for the characteristic nodding action of the overhead beam which is supposed to resemble the action of the rear legs of the grasshopper.
A purpose built indoor cricket facility for training and playing matches
A bridge over a canal.
A case designed to hold a fan.
A dish in which an offering is made.
A chamfer which does not extend the whole length of the surface it is ornamenting. The stop is the end of the feature and can be simple or ornamented.
A cottage for workers on a country house estate.
Bank to let deer cross ditches, fences or roads, into, but not out of, a deer park.
A building used to dry wool in.
A small dish, often with a handle, for soup, porridge etc.
A jar with an evenly rounded profile. (Source: MPRG)
A wide mouthed container, usually cylindrical without handles.
A specific type of small rounded jar. (Source: MPRG)
A portable shelter, usually of fabric or leather.
A tent especially one made of bark, rushes or skins spread over a set of arched poles that are lashed together.
A freestanding staff upon which a flag is hung.
An ornamental shoulder piece, usually a badge of military office.
Gates that can be opened or closed, to admit or exclude water, especially flood water.
A canal built as a military obstacle, but also used for the transport of military stores, equipment and personnel.
A canal that can accommodate ocean-going ships, usually built across an isthmus or to give access to a river port e.g. Manchester ship canal
An artificial navigable waterway used for the transportation of goods. Nowadays also used for recreational purposes.
A garden building or greenhouse, containing pools in which Water Lilies are grown.
A house with an aisle on one side only.

Limestone formed during the Devonian period, and found predominantly between the Exe and Tamar rivers in Devon. Varying in colour from black/grey to pink/white it was often polished to imitate, and be used as, marble.
A tool for cutting substances eg wood, metal etc. Its blade has teeth down one edge.
Twin-engined, four-crew German seaplane. Entered service in 1932 as a torpedo bomber and naval reconnaisance aircraft, though by World War 2 those still serving were used mainly for air sea rescue.
A workshop or factory unit where small or light goods are manufacture without the need for large-scale industrial machinery.
A building used by labourers who clean and pump the docks, and in general, assist shipwrights.
A small container used to fill a lamp with fuel.
A mine from which potash is obtained. Potash is a deposit of potassium carbonate: the only example of a potash mine in the country is at Boulby in Cleveland.
Southern Hemisphere

A streamlined, twin-engined bomber, the DO17 entered service in 1937 with the Condor Legion, having started life as a high-speed mail and passenger transport aircraft, a role for which it was ill-suited due to the narrowness of the fuselage.
Originally the Zeppelin Werk Lindau G.m.b.H., developed metal aircraft from World War One under the guidance of Dr. Ing. Claude Dornier, changing its name to Dornier-Werke G.m.b.H. in 1922.
Similar in design to the FROMSON HANGAR but designed to drawing number 3752/43 and used for storing aircraft with small wingspans.
A small arched hangar built by the Canadian company Fromson of Byfleet to drawing number 3971/43. Used only as storage sheds on RNASs.
A group of buildings containing machinery for the production in bulk of butter or related dairy products.
A modern piece imitating an ancient coin in an attempt to deceive, usually for financial gain.
Large, moulded, unburnt blocks of clay type soil laid in a similar way to brick, but bedded in lime and clay 'mortar'. The walls produced are characteristically thinner than those of cob and pise.
A place where (young) holiday-makers and hikers can be put up cheaply for the night.
A bead used to create a space or interval within a necklace.
A small barrel.
Flats or houses first built by 19th century philanthropic societies as a model to encourage the development of approved working class housing.
A building, usually one-storeyed, for dyeing cloth.
A camp used for the accommodation of members of the Womens Auxiliary Air Force who undertook a variety of essential roles within the RAF to enable their male counterparts to fight more effectively.

Fleet Air Arm fighter and torpedo-bomber, designed for operation from aircraft carriers. All-metal in construction, it entered service in 1944 and was rendered obsolete after the war by the advent of the jet aircraft.
A depot for the depositing, storage and dispatch of plant or other resources associated with the delivery of local government public services.
North Carolina
Visual and descriptive record of a building, usually interior and exterior. Equivalent to Historic England Level 2.
Twin-engined, four-seat medium bomber. A re-engined variant of the Hampden, less than 200 were built but never became operational due to engine unreliability. Some were converted to Hampdens.
A precious or semi precious stone used within jewellery.
Part of a piece of jewellery.

A maritime technique which involves the simple process of bringing up surface sediments from the seafloor for analysis usually using mechanical apparatus. As the process recovers a mixture of sediments it cannot be used to characterise stratigraphy.
A roofed structure, open on one side, usually attached to a building, providing a seating area and its occupants with an uninterrupted exterior view.
A pillbox constructed of prefabricated concrete panels. Double index with specific type where known.
Curved, interlocking roof tile of S-shaped section usually made of clay or concrete.
A piece of equipment fastened on an animal for carrying loads, including riders, or for assisting in traction.
A burial ground for victims of cholera.
A residence of the Bonhommes brethren, who followed the Augustinian rule.
A type of clothier's house, consisting of TOPSHOP and dwelling, used for hand-weaving of textiles.
A marker stone showing the extent of a measure of land containing a vein of ore.
A hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of patients with cancer or related illnesses.

Interbellum, twin-engined, five-crew, biplane flying-boat with a characteristic triple tail-fin. Entered service in 1925 and used for general reconnaissance duties. The Mk.I had a wooden fuselage, whilst the Mk.II's was metal in construction.
Ground-covering herbage, some varieties of which can be used, especially when dried and in large quantities, as a construction material.
A form of floating, moveable pier designed for use in open water.
A site, including buildings and hardstandings, used for the storage and distribution of ammunition.

A 19th century establishment for the provision of work for the unemployed poor of a parish; later an institution administered by Guardians of the Poor, in which paupers are lodged and the able-bodied set to work.
For the production of clay tobacco pipes.
An instrument for writing or drawing, which usually consists of a thin rod of graphite surrounded by a wooden cylinder.
Part of a church in front of the choir and usually enclosed by tombs, screens etc.
Name given to a vessel of the East India Company. Usually large, well built and magnificently decorated.
Objects denoting membership and/or authority. Including objects associated with ceremonial rites or symbolising secular power.
A flag or object depicting a symbolic representation carried as part of a religious ceremony.

A piece of metal or wood, or other material used in the manufacture of an item, intended for further fabrication and therefore representing an unfinished object. Usually relates to objects manufactured in quantity such as coins, knives etc.
A metal disc before it is stamped to become a coin.
A knife prior to undergoing the processes of sharpening or finishing, consisting of a single piece of metal from which the blade and tang have been shaped.
A vertical structure usually with an Attic base or spira with slender and elegant design, with a capital decorated with acanthus leaves and an entablature rich in carved ornament.
Workshop for the painting of vehicles, machines, etc.
A container used in growing plants, either to contain or for use in their cultivation eg watering cans.
A container, usually metal, used to water plants.
A container, usually ceramic, used to water plants.
A container in which plants are grown.
A wealden house with only one end being jettied.
A medieval house with central open hall and two storey bays, jettied at first floor level, on either side.
A purpose-built factory for more than one occupier (eg. for several different workshops).
Stone composed mainly of calcium carbonate, used as a building material and in the production of cement.
An object used to preserve fish by immersing the fish in smoke.
Linear earthwork boundary denoting furlongs
A stone inscribed or marked with runes.
A building plan in the shape of a cross.
A zoo building containing artificial ponds or tanks in which aquatic plants and animals are kept alive for purposes of observation and study.
A defensive cattle enclosure added to fortified towers.
Material that has been damaged by fungal growth or secretions.
A circular flask with one or two flattened faces. (Source: MPRG)
A bottle with a narrow neck used for wine, oil etc.
A cemetery comprising exclusively cremated human remains, some or all of which may be contained within pottery vessels.

A cemetery of later prehistoric date comprising exclusively cremated human remains, some or all of which may be contained within pottery vessels. The cemetery area is partly or wholly surrounded by an earthwork bank and/or ditch.
A torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance biplane in service with the Fleet Air Arm 1935-1938. Rendered obsolete after 1938 by the Swordfish and withdrawn from service.
An isolation hospital for infectious diseases and leprosy, sometimes known as a Pest House; commonly situated on the edge of a town.
A workshop used in the manufacture and preparation of textiles.
A workshop used in the manufacture and preparation of cotton

Twin-engined, seven-crew, coastal reconnaissance, biplane flying-boat. Designed to the same specification as the Saro London, entered service in 1937. Also serving in an anti-submarine role, was replaced by the Consolidated Canso (Catalina) in 1943.
A bridge whose deck is directly supported from pylons by straight cables without vertical suspenders.

A building or site used to train civilians and members of the services in the skills designed to protect the civilian population during times of war. Could also be used during times of national emergency.

Originally ordered as land based dive-bombers, with 950 being delivered to the RAF, none are known to have flown operationally, instead apparently serving as target tugs. Bermuda was the name given to the Brewster SB2A Buccaneer in RAF service.
A building where advice and aid appertaining to physical and economic wellbeing of disadvantaged members of a community are made available.
A building, either purpose-built or modified, used for the co-ordination of the Fire Service.
A twin engine advanced trainer developed by Beech/ Beechcraft , a US firm, used in WWII
A military storage aircraft hangar built in the late 1930s. It comprises a semicircular concrete structure with reinforced concrete columns, featuring a curved roof and straight walls.
A bridge over a canal.
A pond with underwater arches where the poles for masts were stored to prevent them from drying and splitting.
A plain area situated between the top of the shaft and the capital of a Renaissance Tuscan or Doric Order column.

Two-seat, twin-engined fighter/fighter-bomber designed as a replacement for the Bf110. Of the 600 or so produced, only 258 reached the Luftwaffe due to serious design faults. The ME210 was superseded by the ME410 Hornisse.

Heavy anti aircraft battery used from June 1944-May 1945 to combat the V-bomb threat. They are distinct from normal HAA batteries, being laid out in a V-shape, and early on were mainly for mobile 3.7-inch guns.
A large building or structure where coal is washed, sized and graded before being sold.
Fabric of fibrous materials consolidated by heat and mechanical action so that the fibres are matted together.
A woven or bonded fabric or cloth. See TEXTILE Class List for narrow terms.
A binder combined with various aggregates which sets and holds together into a mass which then hardens and gains strength.
Cement/water mix often used as covering. Use this for entries including slurrying and slurried.
An aircraft hangar designed to house seaplanes.
A side-opening steel framed shed. A smaller version of the SEAPLANE SHED (TYPE F) they were built from 1916 on RNAS seaplane bases
A ring shaped brooch, commonly Anglo-Saxon and medieval.

Privateer operating under government licence to act against enemy merchant shipping. The term is closely associated with North African privateers which operated off the Barbary coast prior to the mid-1800's.

Twin-engined air/sea rescue and anti-submarine patrol aircraft. Originally developed from the Wellington and intended as a bomber, entered RAF Coastal Command service in 1943. Fitted with a Leigh Light and ASV radar.
A bridge that incorporates one or two spans that tilt at the abutments, to move up and out of the way of shipping. The most famous example of which is Tower Bridge, London.
Small fish, Sardina pilchardus, common to European waters and eaten as a food fish.
A building, often close to a churchyard, used for the entertainment of poor people on their wedding day.
Three storey house with a topshop; machinery powered by shafting through the upper floor.
A fighter version of the SKUA fitted with a four-gun turret. The majority were converted to target tugs for use by the RAF and Fleet Air Arm.
A megalithic tomb of Neolithic date comprising a chamber bounded by large upright orthostats, often only three or four in number, which support a large capstone.
An administrative building used by the official in charge of a dock or harbour.
Unenclosed wasteland, forest and pasture used in common by the community.
A woollen mill in which the cloth was passed over rollers covered in short spikes to raise the nap in one direction only.
A factory where short wool was spun into woollen yarn to produce cloth.
A wealden house with only one end being jettied.
A medieval house with central open hall and two storey bays, jettied at first floor level, on either side.
Current recorded information does not give the evidence for a monument, or the information is regarded as unreliable.

skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Royal Flying Corps Side Opening Aircraft Hangar

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: The earliest side-opening standard type of aircraft hangar designed in 1913 and used in WWI. Originally constructed from wooden trusses and struts, some examples have steel frames. It comprised a single or coupled shed with rear workshops.

The earliest side-opening standard type of aircraft hangar designed in 1913 and used in WWI. Originally constructed from wooden trusses and struts, one example has steel frames. It comprised a single or coupled shed with rear workshops.
An area, with fixed defences, designed to act as a focal point for a defending force.
A fortifed position, often including fieldworks or defensive structures, designed to keep enemy forces engaged to allow reinforcements to be mobilized.
A muzzle loaded explosive projectile fired from a mortar. Typically they are short range and low velocity with a high arcing trajectory.
A building or range of buildings used to accommodate race horses.
A specially prepared track used for fast motorcycle racing.
A building, site or structure associated with various racing sports.
A building situated next to a horse racing course with facilities for participants and spectators.
A piece of ground used for motor racing.
A flat slab of stone used to provide a level surface from which to measure the height of racehorses at a meeting, as part of the handicapping and anti fraud systems.
A piece of ground on which athletes race.
A running track used for athletic practice and competition.
An area or route marked out for the site of a race.
A gate or mechanism designed to allow animals which are being raced to start at the same time.
A racing track, often within a permanent stadium, for racing dogs, usually greyhounds and whippets.
Stadium housing a track and associated buildings and structures for the public racing of greyhounds.
A sulphide of copper and iron, reddish brown in colour.
Measurements or factual information which may occur in a manual catalogue system or database.
A factory where brushes are manufactured. Use for all types of brush.
A custodial institution for offenders below the legal age of responsibility.
A place in which gunpowder and other explosives are stored in large quantities.
A factory where matresses are made.
A narrow timber board or moulding lining the base of an interior wall as a finish between it and and the floor.
A hostel for packhorse teamsters.
A pin or bolt, especially one on which some other object turns.
A long usually cylindrical object usually made of wood.
A horse-powered winding engine used at mining sites.
A stamp used to emboss paper.
A tool used to impart an image, impression or mark onto a surface.
Optical and/or navigational instruments with powerful lenses for observing remote objects or used in astronomy.
In Orthodox churches, the screen that divides off the sanctuary, usually decorated with sacred images (icons). (Source: Pevsner Glossary)
A board used in divination.
North American wood, the name being applied either to the American Larch; or to the Black or Ridge-pole Pine of inland areas; and the Scrub Pine of maritime regions.
A screen used to decorate or protect an opening.
Stone for holding ox yokes.
A building providing business premises to companies or individuals, sometimes for short periods, in exchange for a membership fee.
A platform scale set within, and flush with the surface of, a roadway, for weighing vehicles, cattle etc.
A machine used for weighing objects.
An Anglo-Saxon fortified town or other defended site, not necessarily urban.

A structure to which a net filled with mail bags is attached. Situated next to railway lines, it allows mail to be collected by a train without it stopping, the bag being 'caught' by the train as it passed. Can also be used to 'catch' mail.

Two-crew, twin-engined bomber. Entered production in 1934 and designed for dual use as a high-speed commercial transport. Technical problems hindered its use as a bomber and led to conversion to high-altitude reconnaissance.
Scenes of snowfall or lying snow.
A model village built in association with a factory, mill, railway, or any other industrial complex; usually built by the employer.
A heated room or building used to dry yarn after it has been washed.
An alluvial deposit laid down in an estuary.
A glass-house or hot-house constructed for the cultivation of a grapevine.
A thin piece of wood used as a roofing material.
A site where tin ore is extracted from suspended fire waste in tin mine spoil heaps.
A place where tin ore is washed using a stream as the water source.
A mounting or fixture attached to a cart.
Any non structural fitting on a vehicle.
A mounting or fitting attached to a chariot.
The method of retrieving animal remains, artefacts and other remains by dry or wet-sieving whole earth samples, typically over 100 litres, sieved through a 2mm or larger mesh.
A room or building used for curing fish or meat.
A kiln or furnace for the firing of bricks.
A circular kiln or oven used in the manufacture of bricks. Common in Staffordshire in the 18th century.
A factory where chocolate products are produced.
A projection which can be used to lift or suspend an object, often used as a handle.
A canopy suspended, or on pillars, over a throne or altar.
A recording of voice, music or other sounds.
Works producing a refractory clay, kaolin. An essential raw material of porcelain and some types of papermaking.
A free-standing cross made of stone in the form of a cross with a ring surrounding the intersection. Often used as a grave marker
One of 12 roadside crosses erected by Edward I in memory of his wife, Eleanor of Castile, the most famous being Charing Cross in London.
A rural cross erected to show the way.
A churchyard or memorial cross set on a long shaft.
A sculpted cross, or a cross incised into stone or trees, to mark a parish boundary.
A cross found in a market place.
A cross, erected on a highway or in an open place, at which monks and others used to preach.
A cross erected in a village.
A free-standing structure, in the form of a cross (+), symbolizing the structure on which Jesus Christ was crucified and sacred to the Christian faith. Use specific type where known.
A cross erected by the side of the road.
A cross erected within a town, usually funded by the inhabitants.
A dockyard crane permanently mounted on a lighter.
A rectangular multi-storey block of flats, greater in width than height.
A tall, multi storeyed building either used as business premises or, more usually, as residential accomodation.
Block of flats incorporating broad, street-width balconies to give access to dwellings and connect to other blocks.
The DH5 was an attempt to give a tractor-type fighter a good forward view. However it suffered from unpleasant flying characteristics and, as a result, had a short service career.
Programmes of research or investigation involving the examination of primary documentary material to inform the understanding of heritage assets.

Formed in 1935 by Lawrence D. Bell, Ray P. Whitman and Robert J. Woods, who left the Consolidated Aircraft Corporation when it moved its factory from Buffalo to San Diego. Sub-contracted work before its first original design, the XFM-1, in 1937.
Single-seat fighter-bomber with a single, midships engine and tricycle landing gear. After proving a failure as an air-combat fighter, was used mainly in the ground attack role.
A device used to throw projectiles, can vary from a small forked stick for hurling stones to a large engine of war to hurl large projectiles.

A camp providing accommodation for members of the Canadian Forestry Corps along with facilities such as saw mills for the sawing and squaring of timber to create pit props, shoring, crates etc for the war effort.
A fitting of unknown function. Use more specific type where known.
A ring, flange or short piece of pipe, made of iron, clay or other materials, used to join and seal two sections of water pipe.
An aircraft used to facilitate communications, for example in a military context.

A single engine two seat cabin monoplane tourer, first flown in 1933 as a successor to the Puss Moth. Impressed into military sevice in WWII by the RAF and the Fleet Air Arm as a liaison and communications aircraft, also used by training units.
A device to hold and rotate food against a heat source during cooking.
A tall chimney terminating a CONDENSING FLUE, used to extract metal from the smoke produced by a lead smelter.
Chimney used on an industrial or commercial site.
The hard, black, heavy wood of various tropical trees native to Africa and Asia, used in furniture manufacture and for making ornaments.
A vessel used for the underwater recovery of a ship and/or her contents or to assist vessels that are sinking.

A freelance boat used off the south and east coasts of England to provide passing ships with pilots, supplies, new anchors and other gear. Some helped sailing ships and barges get underway. Generally lug-rigged. Also used for fishing. Half decked.
Developed from the ill-fated ME210, the ME410 Hornisse entered service in May 1943. Although underpowered as a day fighter the ME410 saw service over the UK as a night fighter from 1943-45.
Large fish, native to the North Atlantic and adjacents seas which has been fished since the Middle Ages.

The measurement of the ratio of the radioactive Carbon 14 (C-14) isotope and non-radioactive carbon isotopes. Useful for dating organic materials such as wood and bone between 500 and 45,000 years old.
A site used for the production of sodium bicarbonate, soda ash or caustic soda.
A factory or works used for the forging and sharpening of a variety of tools including scythes, spades, etc.
A factory used for the manufacture of scythes.
A marine survey in which a multi-element transducer provides many (30-150) individual soundings of the water depth and echo strength for each ping.
Soft, damp soil.
A wood or metal dowel for joining objects together eg for securing roofing slates.
A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of wine.
A metal or stone plate or tablet, usually inscribed, set into a wall, pedestal, floor etc., often serving as a memorial.
A wall in a flower or kitchen garden, containing conduits or pipes for heating the wall.
Use for vessels registered in Uruguay.
Small fish, common in European waters, caught for food.
A barrier consisting of a horizontal rail supported by uprights.

Use for pollen and diaspores. Pollen consists of pollen grains which are the male gametes of flowering plants. Diaspores are the dispersive units of mosses, ferns, fern allies and some plants. To describe the actual object use PLANT REMAINS.
A place where silicate rock was extracted to be shaped for use as whetstones. Examples can be found in Derbyshire and the Blackdown Hills in Devon.
A hand held instrument for producing a current of air for cooling the user. It is both a practical and a fashion item.
A double-span aircraft hangar designed by Boulton & Paul of London and Norwich. Mainly used on aircraft factory sites and at Armament Training Schools.
The residence of a miller, often attached to a mill.
A hall used for the promotion and selling of agricultural produce and practice.
A factory where floorcloths are manufactured.
Includes any textile floor covering.
A structure composed of two large upright stone supporting a third, lintel stone.
A stone or boulder which has been deliberately set upright in the ground. Use only for isolated stones. Otherwise use specific type where known.
A fountain decorated with shells forming an ornamental feature.

An artificial aperture from which water springs. The water supply usually came from a lake or reservoir higher up in order to ensure the necessary flow and pressure. More recently fountains have been powered by pumps.
A single-seat fighter which began service with the RFC's fighter squadron in 1916. Some short-term success in dealing with new Fokkers but was withdrawn from service in mid-1917.
The meeting hall of a secular or ethical society.
A Palaeolithic or Mesolithic temporary site where there is evidence to suggest animal butchery. Evidence may include animal remains and a specialized tool assemblage.
A truss with paired vertical posts set on the tie-beam and supporting collar purlins or plates.
A combination of timbers to form a frame placed at intervals and carrying the purlins.
Hard, durable, dark grey stone, the purest native form of silica, which can either be used decoratively or as a main material. Predominantly found in East Anglia and the South East.
A hard, silica rich rock, black or brown coloured, commonly found in nodular form.
A room intended for the taking of refreshments, usually containing a counter from which they are served.
A purpose-built dwelling for the supervisor of a factory, mine or other industrial complex.
A building associated with a spinning mill in which raw material is mechanically spun into yarn or thread.
A tool used to incise or ipress images.
An open-sided building known to have been used for sheltering animals other than cattle.
A road or way for riding on horseback within a park or estate.
A shed used for the maintenance and repair of aircraft.
Defences or an external wall surrounding a castle's motte or keep. Also a castle's outer court, or a court within a castle's walls.
A large defensive area that usually has to be crossed before entering the inner bailey of a castle.
A hook to join parts of clothing together.
A pan for cooking fish.

The main German, medium bomber of the war, the HE111 first saw action during the Spanish Civil War. HE111s took part in the Battle of Britain and from 1944 onwards were used to launch airborne flying bombs against London.
A small tool which pierces material. It has a flat cutting edge.
Gun emplacement for static or mobile light anti aircraft artillery.
Northumberland

A row of houses linked at first floor level by an open continuous gallery which runs through the front of the buildings. Access to the gallery was gained by flights of steps. Commonly found in the city of Chester.
A building providing lodgings for members of the police force.
Gates that can be opened or closed, to admit or exclude water, especially flood water.
An encircling ornament for the head, usually denoting sovereignty.

The tower, generally attached to a church or other building but sometimes separate, where bells are hung and from which sound is emitted. Also applied to the upper chamber where bells are hung, or the wooden structure supporting them.
Mark 8 or the eighth variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
A vertical member standing without support.
A factory or works used for the forging and sharpening of a variety of tools including scythes, spades, etc.
A factory used for the manufacture of scythes.
A barge with a lugsail rig commonly found on the River Thames in the late 19th century. Also a general term applied to the family of Deal luggers.
One or more ropes or straps attached to an animal's head to provide guidance and control.

The first transportable aircraft hangar developed by the RFC/RAF, which comprised a kit of timber and canvas that could be assembled in 48 hours. The canvas doors open one end only. Also known as Type H hangar.
A medieval hospital for lepers, usually consisting of a church and individual shelters for the lepers.
The residence of a miller, often attached to a mill.
A mine used for the extraction of the mineral Witherite. When secondary mineral, use with term for product, eg. LEAD MINE.

Dark and dense hardwood timber which may be sourced from various species of true ebony from southern Asia and Africa, but the name may also be given to dark hardwoods from elsewhere, e.g. the Americas.
A place where an anti-corrosion coating of zinc is added to iron and steel products to prevent them from rusting.

Fish which have been caught and kept alive. Fish were kept alive on ships in earlier centuries to ensure they reached their destination as fresh as possible. In more recent times exotic fish have been kept alive to sell as pets.
A place where people were put to death. Use narrower monument type where known.
An upright post with projecting arm from which the body of a criminal would be hung in chains after execution.
Of Somalia
The nationality of a vessel according to its registration.
Use for vessels registered in Egypt.
Use for vessels registered in Morocco.
Use for vessels registered in Liberia. Often used as a flag of convenience.
Use for vessels registered in Algeria.
Use for vessels registered in South Africa.
Use for vessels believed to come from Africa but where the precise nationality is not known.
A mine for the extraction of iron ore.
Room in a building or complex in which the master of an establishment, such as a workhouse or a school, is accommodated.
Residence of a leading land-holding family within the district.
A light, usually encased and mounted upon brackets, often used outdoors. It may be powered by gas, electricity or house a candle.
A bridge supported by large beams or girders, originally of wood or iron, now usually of steel or reinforced concrete.
An oven used in the coal industry for the recovery of gas, tar and other by-products of the coking process. Late 19th century-20th century.
A site containing a tennis court, changing facilities and a club house.
The limit line of a township.
A small knife used in surgery.

A small dispersal WWII military aircraft hangar featuring an "A" shaped steel frame clad with corrugated iron; end doors were supported by outriggers when open.Typically used on aircraft storage units or satellite landing grounds. Variations in size.
A charcoal fired shaft furnace used for the direct reduction of iron ore to produce wrought iron.
A furnace constructed as a shaft with the fire at the bottom and the fuel and ore added from the top.
A long metal or stone vessel for cattle to drink water from.
A kiln principally used in brick making which gives a continuous operation.
A circular kiln or oven used in the manufacture of bricks. Common in Staffordshire in the 18th century.
A kiln or furnace for the firing of bricks.
A crane operated by a treadmill turned by the walking action of men placed within it.
A lock at the end of one company's canal where it joins another company's canal.
The residence of a Royal Navy or Merchant Navy officer.
An attic workshop for textile manufacture, usually weaving.
A large body of water surrounded by land.
An artificial lake, often made by damming a stream. A common feature of landscape parks.
A house or shelter for the storage and/or launching of boats.
British single-engine, two-seat night fighter. Originally intended as a day fighter, but withdrawn and converted in August 1940, this was the first fighter to incorporate a power-driven gun turret.
A metal, stone or wooden projection with a flat upper surface to support a shelf, arch, statue etc.
Items made from cloth, wool etc used as a covering for the human body.

Clothes which are distinctive in cut, colour and fabric and worn by members of the armed forces, emergency services or civilian organizations to help to distinguish their members form other organizations.
Single-engine, spruce and plywood, fabric-covered training and communications low-wing monoplane. Served from 1939 to 1950.
A flared bowl of medium to deep depth, with wide horizontal everted rim. These vessels may have a single handle. (Source: MPRG)
A bowl with straight sides which turn outwards, forming an obtuse angle with the base, i.e. and inverted, truncated, conical shape. (Source: MPRG)
A wide-mouthed, narrow based flared bowl associated with dairying activities. (Source: MPRG)
A building used to pump sewage from the sewers to the filter beds of a sewage works.
A waterworks pumping station.
A coal-burning power station where domestic electricity for an area is produced, eg. Battersea Power Station, London.

A building designed specifically for handling tobacco. This may be a bonded warehouse containing facilities for removing tobacco leaves from the hogsheads in which they were imported, and pressing them.
A warehouse, usually under the charge of CUSTOM HOUSE officials, in which goods were stored before the duty had been paid. Often found in dockyards, harbours, etc.
A small park or enclosure where animals are kept.
A container, in the form of an urn, for keeping the ashes of the dead after cremation.
A vessel for keeping the ashes of the dead after cremation.
A hospital where people with learning disabilities receive medical treatment.

A multi-storey, fortified hall house with one of the crosswings being raised in the form of a crenellated tower. Permanently occupied, they date from the mid 14th to the 17th century and are found mainly in the border counties of the North of England.
A house which bears signs of fortification. These often include crenellated battlements and narrow slit-like windows.
Four-crew, twin-engined, general reconnaissance flying-boat. Entered service after World War One, becoming the RAF's standard flying-boat until replaced by the Supermarine Southampton in 1925.
A purlin that is threaded through a hole in the principal rafter.
A purlin that passes a principal rafter
A dockyard crane permanently mounted on a lighter.
A funnel-like container from which grain or other material is fed to a grinding mechanism below.
A capital featuring stylised, often projecting, three-lobed leaves.
An iron, stone or concrete tower built up from the bed of a reservoir. From it the control valves of the pipes which draw off water at different levels are operated.
Small square rigged ship with a narrow overhanging stern.
A vessel with a type of rigging where the main driving sails are fixed to yards which lie square to the mast.
Building or structure housing a form of ore crushing device associated with tin mines.
A mill used for the processing of tin ore by crazing, stamping or smelting.
A free standing small turf and timber fortlet, situated every Roman mile along Hadrian's Wall.
A fortified Roman site, usually under 1 hectare in area, strategically situated, housing small military patrols, often defended by a rampart, one or two ditches and a gate.
A pendant in the shape of a cross.
Accommodation in a monastery for new monks.

skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Guild Of The Holy Cross Chapel
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A place of worship for members of a guild.
A nail of distinctive form, specifically used in the shoeing of animals, eg horses, donkeys, oxen.
A jug with an evenly rounded profile and a discernible basal angle; the maximum diameter is near the mid point and in the upper half of the vessel. (Source: MPRG)

A specific form of rounded jug with a wide mouth, a large parrot-beak spout and three handles in the form of wide straps that spring from the rim to the girth.The spout may have a lug applied to the outside. (Source: MPRG)
A vessel used for medical purposes.
A revolving stone used to sharpen or polish by grinding.
A battery mounted in the flank of a bastion from which flanking fire is directed across a curtain wall.
A small form of spire.
A room in which actions are checked, verified and approved.
A place provided for leisure-time activities of young people.
A metal basket, mounted on a pole, in which oil or pitch was burned for illumination.
A depot for the transfer of town refuse to river barges before transportation to the REFUSE DEPOT.
A place where domestic refuse is collected for disposal.

A French airliner which entered service in 1920. A conventional biplane design with enclosed cabin for four passengers and open cockpit for the pilot. Fitted with an early audible guidance system. Withdrawn from service in 1921.
A place of worship for followers of the Wesleyan Reform Union, a movement formed in 1859 by those members of the Methodist Reform Church who did not join the Wesleyan Association.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Cistercian order.
A small hinged opening within a large door.
Trading premises of a carter.
A floatable concrete vessel, numbers of which made up the main breakwater of the Mulberry Harbours used to secure beachheads during the allied invasion of Europe in June 1944.
A shackle for the hand.
A pipe or channel for conveying water or other liquids.
An object assumed to be to pick limpets out of their shells.
A stick or rod with an attached lash.

The common design of steam engine, where steam enters the cylinder at one end, and after it has pushed the piston to the other end, its direction of flow is reversed as the piston returns, the steam leaving the cylinder through the exhaust ports.
A building or site used for the manufacture of pins.
Sacred Jewish texts and appurtenances buried within a Jewish cemetery.
Building or buildings housing equipment for generating heat for a building complex.

Usually dating from the early 20th century these cabinets, sited alongside public highways, were used for the distribution of electricity for street lighting control and later for domestic use. In Wolverhampton these boxes also serviced the tram system.
Signs or badges of office, honour, membership, occupation etc.
The residence of a person employed in the textile industry.
A building or site conducting research into communication techniques for use in the Royal Navy.

A civil passenger transport biplane produced by the Farman Aviation Works from 1919. Instrumental in the creation of early airlines and commercial routes in Europe after World War I. Initially designed in 1918 as a heavy bomber. Some 60 units built.

Traditionally a building or site where stage coaches were built. Nowadays the term is applied to buildings used for the manufacturing of the body work and furnishings of motor vehicles and railway carriages.
An emplacement mounting a small, portable electrically-powered searchlight.
A site in which one or more searchlights and their accompanying structures were positioned to locate enemy aircraft or surface vessels for the benefit of batteries and night fighter aircraft.
A site in which one or more searchlights were positioned to locate enemy aircraft or surface vessels for the benefit of batteries and night fighter aircraft.
An educational establishment where the art and theory of building and construction is taught.
An institution for convicted prisoners held under a regime which strove to reform by means of silent isolation and labour.
A dark, viscous liquid, obtained from the ground, which is refined for use as a fuel for motor vehicles and in generators to produce light and heat, and as a solvent.
Waste material.
An enclosure created by constructing one or more lines of ramparts across a promontory which projects into the sea.
A defensive enclosure created by constructing one or more lines of ramparts across a neck of land, in order to defend, or restrict access to, a spur or promontory, either inland or on the coast.
A prepared area of cleared ground on which an aircraft could make an emergency landing.
An area or site used for the landing and take-off of aircraft, often including associated buildings, equipment and other installations.
Originally designed as a light bomber but diverted for use as a high speed target tug to replace out-dated biplanes.
A place of accommodation at a college for staff and students.
A house of Roman Catholic nuns or canonesses.
A brace which is cut to a double curve.
A place where (young) holiday-makers and hikers can be put up cheaply for the night.
A building used as a temporary form of accommodation during a holiday, which includes self-catering.
Publication on a specific topic, or limited scope of subject matter. Complete in itself, though may form part of a series.
A type of small boat that was often carried, or towed by a larger vessel and used as a ship's boat. Dinghies can also be used recreationally as independent sailing vessels.

Satellite craft belonging to a larger vessel, usually a rowing vessel; used to pick up or set down passengers or crew when lying offshore, or stowed on board as the "long boat" or "jolly boat" for lifesaving purposes.

A tandem two-seat, twin-engined, all-weather, long-range supersonic jet interceptor fighter/fighter-bomber originally developed for the United States Navy by McDonnell Aircraft.It first entered service in 1960 with the U.S. Navy.
The standard RFC power house built to Air Ministry drawing number 476/18 and comprising an engine room with a small workshop and driver's room.
A mill where flax is processed to make linen, thread and yarn.
A finishing process for cloth involving the pounding of the cloth with heavy weights.
A mould which is used to provide the shape of a piece of footwear.
A Palaeolithic or Mesolithic occupation site, excluding occupations of caves and rock shelters. Evidence for occupation may include traces of hearths and other structures.
Where secondary product use with major product and MINE, eg. LEAD MINE.
Used to detach flakes from cores or tools.
A reinforced wall designed to reflect the blast from an explosion. Often found associated with powder magazines, pillboxes and air raid shelters.
The masonry beneath a lock gate, sometimes projecting several feet from the gate.
A low-temperature oven for the firing of metallic-based colour onto pottery after glazing.
The office of the body controlling a harbour and docks.
A depressed arch formed around three arcs: two struck from the springing line with one centrally placed arc struck from below it.
A place of meeting and worship for Jehovahs Witnesses.
A building or room used for the exhibition of upholstery for sale.
A room used for the display of merchandise for sale.
A building or room where motor vehicles are exhibited for sale.
A room to display various items of hardware and ironmongery.
A room specifically used for the display of furniture and other related materials
A building plan where space is unconstrained by partitions.
A small building housing a valve which controls the flow within a water regulation system.
A building where pins are manufactured.
The chemical breakdown of a material by water.
Workshop for the construction and maintenance of boilers within an industrial complex.
A room used for directing military operations and exercises.
A small vessel used as transport for customs officers.
A glasshouse used for the cultivation of tropical plants.
A stone that indicates the limit of an area or piece of land.
A movable joint, usually consisting of two plates joined by a pin, that fastens a door, gate, window etc. to its frame and allows it to open and shut.
A simple type of hinge used for large gates.
A tool for splitting and chopping.

A shallow ceramic or metal libation bowl, usually with no handles or feet. The Greeks called it a phiale, the Romans a patera. Used in religious practice. Could contain mixed wine and water but also unmixed wine, honey, oil, water, or milk.
A bowl with straight sides which turn outwards, forming an obtuse angle with the base, i.e. and inverted, truncated, conical shape. (Source: MPRG)
A wide-mouthed, narrow based flared bowl associated with dairying activities. (Source: MPRG)
A flared bowl of medium to deep depth, with wide horizontal everted rim. These vessels may have a single handle. (Source: MPRG)
A vessel designed for the transport of persons and goods from one place to another an a regular schedule of sailings. Use specific type were known.
A small ferry powered by steam or diesel engine, which pull vessel from one side of a river crossing along submerged chains.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the commander of the Royal Engineers for the Colchester Garrison.
A structure in which pottery tiles were baked.
A container in which dice are shaken and from which dice are thrown.
A building or group of buildings designed for the breeding and rearing of animals, including fish and birds. Often include incubators and heated rooms.
US Navy version of the four-engined, six-crew B24 heavy bomber. Modified for long-range reconnaissance duty and used as a patrol-bomber against shipping and submarines.
Single-engine, two-seat tractor bomber and reconnaissance aircraft. Entered service in 1916 and, during 1917 and 1918, equipped nine RFC squadrons in its reconnaissance role.
A twin cylinder compound steam engine introduced in the 1870's which combined a horizontal and vertical configuration in the same machine.
German single-engine, four-seat maritime patrol and reconnaissance flying-boat. In production between 1934 and 1940, the DO18 was replaced by the three engined DO24.
Engine driving a continuous wire rope for the haulage of tubs in a mine and at the heapstead.
A council-owned single apartment.

Seven/eight-crew, heavy night-bomber. The first four-engine bomber to join the RAF, with a bomb load of 14000 lb, entered service in 1940. Superseded as a bomber by the Lancaster and Halifax, later versions served as transports and tugs.

Short Bros. (Rochester & Bedford), Ltd. founded by Eustace and Oswald Short in 1898, originally manufacturing spherical balloons. In 1936 became Short & Harland Ltd. in collaboration with Belfast shipbuilders Harland and Wolff.
A fan designed to fan the coals of a fire to increase the oxygen around the coals and thus to help the fire burn.
A building where a stallion is kept.
Chests connected with the burial of a body.
Metal alloy with lead as the principal component.
A jug with a rounded profile and a rounded base, i.e. with no discernible basal angle. (Source: MPRG)
The residence of a ferrykeeper.
A fatty substance rendered from animal fat and used in the manufacture of soap, candles and for dressing leather.
An object to point at words whilst reading, eg the Alfred jewel.

A small dispersal WWII military aircraft hangar featuring an "A" shaped steel frame clad with corrugated iron; end doors were supported by outriggers when open.Typically used on aircraft storage units or satellite landing grounds. Variations in size.

Single-engine, testbed monoplane built to Air Ministry Specification 43/37. Only twelve were produced, the first of which tested the Sabre I engine in 1940, and were used throughout the war. The cockpit could seat two observers behind the pilot.

Formed in 1936 as British Marine Aircraft Ltd. to construct civil flying-boats. In 1937, with the arrival of H P Folland, formerly Chief designer for Gloster Aircraft Co., became Folland Aircraft, Ltd..
A drainage structure that extends across and beneath roadways, canals or embankments.
A fitting incorporating a series of overlapping flaps providing ventilation or transmission of sound.
A vessel to contain holy water located near the entrance of a church.
The solid, upright part of a battlement separating the openings, or crenelles.

Twin-engine, three-crew, long-range heavy bomber biplane. Entered service in 1917. Of wooden construction with a fabric covering, the Vimy was fitted with a skid under the nose of its fuselage to prevent tipping forward upon landing.
A type of jug decorated with applied figures in the form of knights in armour. (Source: MPRG)

A prefabricated structure of cellular hollow plywood 'aero' beams and columns clad with timber framed units of flat asbestos facing sheets and a felt roof. Designed as airfield accommodation that could be reused as post WWII emergency housing.
Citrus fruit of a distinctive yellow colour.
A residence of two or three monks of the Gilbertine order dependent on an English mother house.
A large block of wood used to support the roof of a mine.
Port in Somalia, one of largest in East Africa

American, four-engine, long range, heavy strategic bomber. Entered service in 1943 and used exclusively against Japanese forces. The B29s Enola Gay and Bock's Car were used to drop atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945.
The residence of a coachman.
Textile mill producing calico, ie. coarse, unbleached cotton cloth.
A works where cotton waste is stored or processed.
Usually a cotton spinning factory, although some mills have weaving sheds attached, in which case the end product is completed cloth, not yarn only.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as two ranges at right angles to each other.
An outline of the circumstances to be addressed, with an indication of the scope of work which will be required (English term)
The SI derived unit of specific volume.
Includes all forms of paper and any products manufactured from it.

A German coastal minelaying submarine in use during the First World War. In addition to 18 mines, the U BOAT also carried 7 torpedoes in 3 tubes (2 bow/1 stern) and and 88mm or 105mm deck gun. A very successful design, UCIIs sank more than 1800 vessels.
A factory where carpets are manufactured.
A hoop or band of material put around a wheel to protect it and, when filled with air, to provide a more comfortable ride.
A row of columns that carry arches or an entablature.
A colonnade where it is exposed to the air on two sides.
A building licensed for the sale of beer.
A free-standing building with enough space to hang and dry nets.

A building as part of a workhouse, prison or hospital, often including porter's lodge, baths, clothes store, washrooms, casual cells, rooms etc, for receiving inmates/patients. Use term from Components thesaurus if it is part of a building complex.
A track inlaid into the road surface of a street or road, on which tram cars run for the conveyance of passengers.
The oldest form of iron, it is a tough, pure form of iron that can be fashioned into decorative items or shapes by hammering, squeezing or rolling.
A flake or blade tool with more than one notch on its edge.
A small flake or blade with a series of notches along the edge.
A scraper with retouch at right angles to the bulb of percussion.
German port on the River Ems.
Material preserved by the exclusion of oxygen usually due to saturation with water which inhibits decay by micro-organisms.
A covered pit into which raw sewage is discharged.
A building or room for the distribution of medicines, eg. in a hospital or clinic.
Compact, grey/green/brown/white-speckled coloured igneous rock, peculiar to Cornwall. It is easy to carve and readily takes a polish, hence its similarity to British marbles.
A deep gutter, drain or sink.
A rustic building of picturesque design.
A sheltered port for ships.
A harbour constructed from floating pontoons or caissons connected end to end.
A simple, single cylinder vertical steam engine with its cylinder mounted directly on a baseplate, driving an overhead crankshaft which is supported by two A-shaped frames
Castles constructed between 1481 and 1561 for defence using heavy guns.
A concrete marker placed to indicate the direction of a target on a bombing range to aircraft.
A vessel with a lid, handle and spout used particularly for boiling water.
A steam powered winding gear used at a colliery or other mine.
A farrier's tool for paring a horse's hoof.
Equipment used in the care and upkeep of animals, usually used directly on the animal.
A coastal site producing salt by boiling of unconcentrated seawater in a PANHOUSE, normally using coal fuel. Foreshore BRINE TANKS may also be present
Stiff hairs used in the manufacture of brushes.
Hair taken from animals and used in a variety of manufacturing processes.
Hair from the Angora goat
A factory where explosives and the components of munitions of all types are brought together for assembly.
A group of buildings, or part of a works, housing apparatus used in the process of fermentation.
A place where furs are made into finished products.
Use for vessels registered in Yugoslavia between 1918 and 1992.
A site associated with Operation PLUTO (Pipe Line Under The Ocean) the operation to supply the allies with fuel following the invasion of Normandy.
A projecting, sometimes decorated, finish to a moulding, chamfer, label, hood-mould or string-course.
The process of transcribing the features on an aerial photograph onto a map or plan.

A four-storey RNAS control tower. The first floor contained offices for the commander flying and meteorological offices and the upper two floors, in the form of a central tower, provided offices for air traffic control.
Developed from the ill-fated ME210, the ME410 Hornisse entered service in May 1943. Although underpowered as a day fighter the ME410 saw service over the UK as a night fighter from 1943-45.
A long wooden shafted weapon tipped with a metal point.
A long shafted weapon with a pointed head used for thrusting or as a missile.
A long spear used on horseback.
A Roman wine cup with a shallow bowl and a circular foot.
A complex of buildings used for the manufacture of radio valves or similar electronic components.
Large keyboard, percussion instruments in which strings are struck by hammers to produce notes.
Bells used either as a percussion instrument or for other purposes such as calling attention, marking time periods etc.
Use for unspecified musical instruments.
Missiles, such as cannon balls and musket balls, designed to be discharged from a gun or cannon using an explosive propellant.

Single-engine, single-seat, long range fighter originally designed in 1940 to a British requirement. Outstanding low-level speed and range resulted in its assignment to the ground support (Army co-operation) role.
A site including a pitch, stands and other ancillary buildings associated with the game of rugby.
An area of prepared ground on which a sport is played. Use more specific type where known.
The residence of an employee with the duty of maintaining a section of a railway or road.
An early form of castle consisting of a flat-top steep-sided earthen mound, supporting a wooden tower, and a bailey.
The residence of a vicar, parson or rector.
Soft, porous objects used in bathing and for cleaning. Originally made from the dried skeletons of marine sponges but now more commonly manufactured from synthetic foam.
A market where cattle, pigs, sheep and poultry are bought and sold.

An earthwork feature used by hunters to trap deer comprising a steep ditch into which the deer are chased with an enclosure to hold them at one end, known from the Isle of Rum and a debateable example in Cumbria.
A building in which people are held in a state of imprisonment or confinement as punishment. Usually associated with military and political offenders.
A workroom or apartment, often with a north-light, used for the creation of artwork by painters, sculptors etc.
This is the top term for the class. This class includes terms with very broad definitions which could be assigned to three or more classes. See UNASSIGNED Class List for narrow terms.
The pit in which human or animal remains are placed for interment,which may be either an inhumation or cremation.
An archaeological unit of soil in a horizontal plane which may seal features or be cut through by other features.
An archaeological component which cuts, overlies or abuts other features such as ditches, pits and building foundations.
Large, three-engined, long range reconnaissance flying boat. Wooden hull and frame construction, with linen covering. Entered service in 1930.
American twin-engined medium bomber. Entered service with the US 22nd Bombardment Group at Langley Field in February 1941. Also served with the 14th and 39th RAF squadrons.
A bowl with convex body walls. (Source: MPRG)
Westland Aircraft Ltd., formed in 1935 to take over the aircraft branch of Petters Ltd., previously known as the Westland Aircraft Works.

Three/four-crew, single-engine, shipboard observation and air/sea rescue amphibian seaplane. Entered RAF service in 1936. Also employed for gunnery spotting, anti-submarine and convoy protection duties.
A workshop where tapestries were made.
A handloom weavers workshop where the weaver received yarn from a clothier and manufactured a woven piece of cloth from it.
A volatile, colourless distillate of petroleum used as a solvent and paint thinner.
A system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used to simulate a dockyard and thus confuse enemy aircraft into bombing these counterfeit targets.
A semi-precious, fossilised resin usually used for ornamentation and jewellery.
Engineering works dedicated solely to the manufacture and repair of boilers.

Developed as a long range, heavy day-fighter, the ME110 found its niche as a night fighter. It saw service over Southern and Eastern England during the Battle of Britain but lost out in the daytime to the faster British fighters.
A service building to a country house, farm, etc, used for baking. If commercial premises use BAKERY.
A bakehouse built in association with a group of dwellings who shared the baking facilities. Often found in model settlements.

Single-engine, single-seat interceptor fighter developed from the race-winning Schneider Trophy seaplanes. One of the most famous of all combat aircraft, entered RAF service in 1938 and was still in use in the 1950s.
A type of bridge which has machinery and movable elements, eg. to allow vessels to pass.
A bridge that incorporates one or two spans that tilt at the abutments, to move up and out of the way of shipping. The most famous example of which is Tower Bridge, London.
The bracket under a jetty bressumer.
Pipes used to carry water or hydraulic fluid for power transmission within a hydraulic system.
A comparatively thick, roughly shaped piece of stone, usually square or rectangular, used to roof structures.
A vessel carrying square sails on all masts and having three or more masts.
A container packed with explosives, with a detonator triggered by contact or a timer, for the purpose of destroying enemy craft, personnel etc.
A weapon which causes damage through exploding.
A small explosive device, usually hand thrown.
A holder for arrows.
A room where organizations and associations meet for the undertaking of presentations and consultation.
A pond storing water to supply a HAMMER POND.
Timber manufactured from fir or spruce trees.
A factory where lengths of soft, woollen cloth, loosely woven to retain heat, used as a bed covering, were manufactured.
