The residence of a lightkeeper.
Twin-engined, single-seat fighter-bomber. Flown by USAAF fighter groups from 1942, excelled as a ground-support fighter. Could carry two 1600 lb bombs or rocket projectiles.
A pawnbrokers shop or place of business.
A municipal pawnshop.
An axe designed for fighting could be single or double headed and used with one or two hands. Where use is thought to be ceremonial multiple index with ceremonial object.
A raised platform for the unloading of coal from waggons or other containers.
A mole or pier-like structure situated at the entrance of a harbour, or running out into a lake or the sea, usually used for the landing of craft.
A strong vehicle with four wheels for carrying loads, usually horse or ox drawn.
Remains of the group of animals characterized as being radially symmetrical in form, such as sea urchins, sea cucumbers and starfish.
Remains of Bryozoa, which are small animals, usually marine, that form colonies producing coral-like skeletons or jelly-like masses.

Remains of animals characterized as having bodies made up of annular segments, such as worms and leeches. Earthworm eggs and granule comonly occur. Bristle worms are found associated with marine molluscs.
Remains of parasitic or free-living worms of the phylum Nematoda, characterized as having slender, cylindrical unsegmented bodies. Cysts of Heterodera commonly occur archaeologically
Remains of one of the groups of animals characterized as lacking any form of backbone or spinal column.
A place of meeting and worship for Brethren, a fundamentalist puritan sect founded in Ireland in the late 1820s and established in England in Plymouth in the 1830s.
A place of meeting and worship for Exclusive Brethren, an exclusive fundamentalist puritan sect which was created when the Brethren split in 1847.
A vessel used for carrying cargoes, fitted with defensive weapons. Use with specific type and form where known.
Support or 'mother ship' used for the repair, maintenance and refuelling of submarines, specifically 20th century submarines.
A site with one or more defensive earthworks, often at a river crossing incorporating natural features which define parts of the curtilage.
An imprecise term used to describe large Iron Age settlements of town-like proportions.
The outer layer of tissue on a tree or woody plant, often used in the dyeing and tanning industries.

A biggest and plainest of the classical architectural orders, based upon a simplified version of the Doric Order. Sometimes called the Gigantic order, though not to be confused with the Colossal or Giant Order.
An entablature of the Tuscan Order consisting of a plain architrave, frieze and cornice without decoration or enrichments..
A form that records the details of a project, for example, an excavation index form.
A purpose-built model village for the workers on a country house estate.
A site where cement is manufactured for the building industry.
Production of high quality steel by reheating cementation steel in a refractory crucible.
A fuel store for the storage of dried peat.

The RAF's first jet fighter, flown operationally during 1944-5, with later versions serving for a further ten years after the war. The Meteor's first active operations were in the interception and destruction of V.1. flying bombs.
Gloster Aircraft Co., Ltd. formed in 1917, later became part of the Hawker Siddeley Group. First British or American company to design, build and fly a jet-propelled aircraft.
All-weather fighter/interceptor first flow in 1951, introduced into service in 1956 and retired from the RAF in 1968.

The Gloster Grebe was the Royal Air Force's first post WWI fighter aircraft, entering service in 1923. Designed by Henry Folland, a single-seat, single-engined biplane of fabric-covered wood construction with two Vickers machine guns (133 planes built).

Single-seat, single-engine biplane fighter. In operational service from 1939 to 1941, this was the last, and believed to be the best, biplane to be flown in the RAF. All-metal in construction with fabric and aluminium covering.
Single-engine, single-seat biplane seaplane built for the 1924 Schneider Cup Race.
Country bordering the Black Sea.

Single-engine, two-crew fighter, also used for convoy escort and reconnaissance. Designed to operate from aircraft carriers. Entered service with the Fleet Air Arm in 1940 and remained in use until 1945.
A room dedicated to the drawing or letting of blood, a procedure once thought to possess medicinal properties.
A fall of water. Use for artificial waterfalls if naturalistic in form, otherwise use CASCADE.
A large one handled drinking vessel, sometimes fitted with a hinged lid.
A machine for mechanically separating the grain from the straw and husks.
A beaker with a construction above the base to form a waisted profile. (Source: MPRG)
A paved area, generally found at the back of a house.
A covered area of ground attached to a building.
A staircase, circular in plan, that winds around a central newel.
Sedimentary rock consisting of angular fragments naturally cemented together.
Beaches used for the departure of troops and equipment for the D-day landings.
A place from which chalk is extracted.
A place where sheep are washed in a chemical bath to control the parasites of sheep. To conserve the poisonous chemicals the bath is usually small and are not allowed to enter any watercourse.
A site where all the processes for the production of glass and objects made from glass are carried out.
A factory used for the production of thick, flat glass used for shop window panes, etc. Plate glass is produced by rolling and casting rather than traditional blowing.
A large pit formed by, and for, the extraction of iron ore.
A strip of lead holding small pieces of glass (quarries) in a window.
A portable writing-case or surface, especially one for use on the lap. May contain compartments for storing writing materials and paper.
An elevated platform on which a criminal is executed.
A small and powerful vessel used to assist vessels that are sinking or disabled at sea.
A flexible holder for a bladed tool or weapon.
A shop where fish and chips are sold.
A stable used for riding horses or those used to pull coaches, gigs, etc.
A house with an open hall whose main span is separated by an arcade from the side aisles.
A common type of lock in the form of a chamber with gates on either side.
Specialized engineering workshop particularly for the production of marine engines or other large components of ships.
A building or site used for the production of anchors.
A jug with a roughly cylindrical or slightly flaring lower body, a pronounced inward-sloping shoulder and a marked neck/body angle. (Source: MPRG)
A purse, sometimes of bronze, usually worn on the forearm.
A container, capable of being carried by hand, often for carrying such items as clothes, keys, money, etc.
A small bag or pouch for carrying money, especially coins.

The measurement of a surface, either in elevation or plan, determined from measurements derived from two or more photographic images taken from different positions; this allows three dimensional viewing of the surface to be mapped.
A factory, incorporating power driven machinery from the late 18th century, where cloth was manufactured from threads interlaced at right angles to each other in a loom.
A curved structural span which is supported at the sides or ends. May vary in shape from the horizontal flat arch through semicircular and semielliptical forms.
A house with windows and doors on one side only; often built facing inwards onto a burgage plot, or sometimes on a steep slope, with no apertures on the uphill side.
Previous name for Mumbai.
Purpose built workers' accommodation comprising single rooms with communal eating and washing facilities. Usually for short stay accommodation only.
Post-World War Two, single-engine, high-wing utility transport. Manufactured by De Havilland Canada, was also produced in a seaplane version. Known as the U6A from 1962.
A building where the study and practice of preparing, preserving, compounding and dispensing drugs is performed.
Fruit which has been preserved by drying.
Dried seedless grapes used in cookery.
A building or site from which a watch can be kept to prevent the illegal import/export of goods.
A flexible container with an opening at one end.
A form of dagger.
A substantial area of ground surrounded by slight univallate earthwork often interpreted as stock enclosures or as sites where agricultural produce was stored.

A small, defended settlement dating to the Early Iron Age, located on spurs, promontories or hilltops. The defences are marked by single or double trenches which originally held substantial palisades.
An ornate public house that developed in the 1830s after the passing of a law to encourage the drinking of beer in alehouses licensed for the sale of beer only.
An object worked on a lathe, usually the bi-product of such work.
A place where money is coined under public authority.
A school which combines the functions of both Infant and Junior Schools, teaching children up to the age of eleven. Use specific type where known.
Civil building in Cornwall and Devon for assay and sale of tin ingots.

Single-engine navigation trainer and communications aircraft. Constructed of tubular steel and duralumin frame, with a duralumin and canvas covering, 500 were delivered to the FAA, serving from 1944-5.
An extended arbour, eg. the beech arbour at Hampton Court, Middlesex.
A set of small pincers used for gripping and plucking.

Impressed civil, twin-engined airliner converted to a military transport. Thirty were ordered for military use, though only eleven were actually built. Entered service in 1940, with the last being scrapped in 1950.
A building used for the education of, and as a residence for, chantry priests.
A lake, often artifical, in a park or open space, used for the recreational rowing and sailing of boats.

Three-seat, twin-engined minelaying, torpedo-bombing and reconnaissance twin-float seaplane. First flown in 1936, in 1938 it set eight world speed records for its class in various range and payload categories.
A facility for the kitting out and induction of recruits before being sent on for training.
A stone grooved on one face thought to have been used to straighten and smooth arrow shafts.
An arrowhead with its base hollowed to allow it to fit onto the shaft of an arrow rather than having a tang that fits into the shaft.
A rustic building of picturesque design.
A large discharge pipe with a valve for drawing water from a water main. Used to help extinguish fires.

Single-engine, two-seat, light, biplane, elementary-flying trainer. Adapted from a civilian design, and constructed from tubular steel and spruce with plywood and fabric covering, entered service in 1931 and was available in land-plane or seaplane forms.
A house used to accommodate Llamas at a zoo or wildlife park.
A post set up alongside a canal to mark the miles to and from a place.
A coastal battery designed for use in short range engagements with enemy vessels, minelayers, blockships ad torpedo craft.
An Anglo-Saxon fortified town or other defended site, not necessarily urban.
A water-tight cover that closes and opening in a vessel's deck used for the ingress and egress of persons and cargo.
An object which is attached to or connected with a door.
A pile of rough stones and soil used for the growing of ferns and other plants.

A type of dish specifically designed to catch the juices from roasting meat. The dish may be oval, semi-circular, rectangular or wedge-shaped. Usually has one or two handles located on one long side and a lip at one or both short sides. (Source: MPRG)
A necklace holding charms or being itself a charm.
An opening in a wall that is usually narrow on the outside but widens internally to allow a defender to stand and shoot through the loophole.
A flat bottomed drinking vessel with no handle or stem.
Manmade constructions used to prevent rivers breaking their banks and flooding the surrounding area with water. Often taking the form of a bank or wall.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the large-scale production, processing and preserving of food and drink.

A strategic food store, directly operated by, or on behalf of, the government. The stores were used to store a variety of foodstuffs. They were in operation from the end of the Second World War until the early 1990's.
A container used to serve food from.
A narrow container, especially one in which food or water for animals is put.
A small and powerful vessel used to assist vessels that are sinking or disabled at sea.
A building where onions are laid out to dry.
Large board used for covering the internal surfaces of a building, ie. floors, walls and ceilings. Some forms can be used as external cladding.

Thin layers of wood, bonded together to form a structural board. The grain of the adjacent layers lie across one another to give structural strength. Produced since mid 19th century for use in interior joinery, since 1930's for exterior use.
A hole or cavity in the ground, either natural or the result of excavation. Use more specific type where known.
A pit containing burnt ashes.
A machine used for the loading and unloading of grain to and from a warehouse
A place for keeping vestments and sacred vessels.
A building used to accommodate ducks.
A block on which objects are chopped or cut.
A series of columns in a straight line supporting an entablature with no openings or glazing.
A room for the storage of bread, biscuits, flour etc. Often part of a buttery in medieval times.
A meeting hall, or sale room in a town, for manufacturers and traders.
A flat, circular stone, usually made of sandstone, used in pairs for grinding corn and other meal.
A trench dug to contain a sill beam, a horizontal timber beam used as a foundation for the wall of a building. Use wider site type where known.
Large, three-engined, long range reconnaissance flying boat. Wooden hull and frame construction, with linen covering. Entered service in 1930.
A factory or group of buildings used for the production of plated goods. Plating is the process whereby one metal object is coated with a thin layer of another metal.
Deposits formed by the mass downward movement of surface deposits over underlying frozen ground under periglacial conditions.
Deposits formed under conditions present adjacent to ice masses during glacial periods.
A building housing the generator set and associated equipment supplying electricity to a radar station.
An arch which is formed by keystones but is flat like a lintel
A building, site or structure associated with the playing of racket sports.
A plain four walled court used to play the game of racquets on.

A single engine, jet propelled twin boom aircraft which came into service in 1945 in a variety of roles including night fighter, trainer, the carrier-borne Sea Vampire, and the MK5 version, a fighter bomber. Produced by De Havilland.
A house in which a passage runs across the building, usually adjacent to a hall, between front and back entrance doors.
Earthworks of uncertain date and purpose, consisting of cross-shaped banks sometimes with an accompanying ditch. Their distribution is largely confined to North Yorkshire.
A bank or mound of earth used as a rampart or fortification.
An educational establishment where law is taught.
A building where people could bathe in salt water. Salt water was believed to have medicinal properties.
The post at the centre of a winding staircase from which the steps radiate; or the post, supporting the handrail and string, at the angle of a square staircase.
A craft available for public hire for short journeys.
Single-engine, single-seat biplane day fighter developed by Siddeley. Variations included an all-metal, fabric-covered Mk.III, which became the RAF's main fighter in the 1920s.
Single-engined fighter, developed from the Camel. Entered service in 1918 and became the RAF's first mainstay peacetime fighter.
A laithe with an attached house.
A marker of some form used to delineate a route, especially ones associated with pilgrimages.
The SI derived unit of Area
A plan in which entry is directly into a room without being situated opposite a fireplace.
Redcar and Cleveland
Block of flats within which the individual dwellings are accessed by narrow external balconies.
The lower area of a interior wall between the skirting board and the dado rail
A centre attached to a prison where families and friends can visit with the inmates.
A spatially discrete group of pits usually containing artefactual material with little or no accompanying evidence for structural features.
A hopper for the storage of ash.
A biplane, reconnaissance aircraft with a crew of 3 or 4 which equipped 3 and 22 squadrons RAF before passing to the Fleet Air Arm. Produced in two variants.
A roof consisting of trusses that have a pair of brackets supporting the hammer posts that in turn support the rafters.
A natural flow or current of water issuing from a source.
A drinking vessel, usually curved in shape, fashioned out of animal tusk or horn and sometimes with bands of decoration.
A type of back to back house built on a hillside, of four storeys and with entrances at different levels.
A house with windows and doors on one side only; often built facing inwards onto a burgage plot, or sometimes on a steep slope, with no apertures on the uphill side.
A house in a line of houses attached to and adjoining one another and planned and built as one unit.
A house in a terrace built on top of another, with access at high and low level to either side.
A tall chimney terminating a CONDENSING FLUE, used to extract metal from the smoke produced by a lead smelter.
A spoil heap consisting mainly of slag, pieces of refuse material separated from a metal during the smelting process.
Three storey house with a topshop; machinery powered by shafting through the upper floor.
An open metalwork structure supporting either a fabrication shed or the runners for an overhead crane.
A training school where ballet is taught.
A purpose built trench designed to prevent the successful landing of enemy glider-borne and airborne forces.
Obstacles placed in open spaces and alongside roads designed to prevent the successful landing of enemy airborne forces.
A cable, usually erected between posts, used to prevent the landing or hostile aircraft.
A telegraph pole, tree trunk or similar erected on the side of a road, or in an open space, to prevent the landing of hostile aircraft
A bowl adapted by having a pedestal base. (Source: MPRG)
An outwork joined to the mainwork by two parallel wings.
Ornamental band or chain worn around the arm or wrist.
A ditch which is not continuous but instead is made up of segments which may vary in length and width.
A long and narrow hollow or trench dug in the ground, often used to carry water though it may be dry for much of the year.
A ditch that indicates the limit of an area or a piece of land.
A ditch associated with a palisade.

A two-seat, single-engine bomber. Fast, versatile and well armed, but with a fuel tank poorly placed between pilot and gunner, was considered to be the best day bomber of the First World War. Later entered civil service.
A building complex with hangars and slipways built adjacent to a body of water where seaplanes can be stored and maintained.
A shaft constructed to allow the circulation of fresh air, into a mine, building etc.
A long, wooden, metal or stone vessel holding drinking water for horses.
A resource which requires interaction from the user to be understood, executed, or experienced. [DC]
Materials selected and organised to be of use to teachers for use in education.

Medium to coarse grained, green to dark red/black coloured igneous rock, mainly found on The Lizard, South West Cornwall. Due to its fragmentary structure, Serpentine is mainly used for decorative and ornamental purposes.
A compact design of engine in which a connecting rod is dispensed with, giving a short baseplate.
A house devoted to the shelter of the poor and endowed by a benefactor for this use.
skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Asylum For Aged And Decayed Freemasons

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: Engineering workshop intended either for final adjustments of new machinery or the fitting of replacement parts to machinery under repair.
A building or room used for any type of engineering work. Use more specific type where known.
A system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used to simulate a domestic site such as a city and thus confuse enemy aircraft into bombing counterfeit targets.
A radio station set up to broadcast signals aimed at 'bending' or altering German navigation transmissions.
A building or group of buildings containing equipment capable of transmitting and receiving radio signals. Use BROADCASTING RADIO STATION for broadcasting establishments e.g. BBC Radio stations.
Metal spikes used for fixing one object to another.
A kiln used for the drying of wood.
A man made terrace, often constructed in concrete, built to allow spectators a view of organized outdoor events or activities.
The unsystematic study of ground surfaces and collection of visible archaeological material.
A quadrangle or courtyard, often grassed or planted, surrounded by cloisters

A vessel used as the lower part of a distillation unit consisting of a round-bottomed vessel with walls sloping inwards towards the rim. Some examples may have an external flange to support the upper unit (ALEMBIC). (Source: MPRG)
A musical instrument that produces sound through the passage of air through a number of pipes controlled by stops, pedals and keyboards.
A factory where chocolate products are produced.
A container with three legs.

A building, with adjacent open areas, in which buses are maintained, usually having an extensive area free from upright columns or stanchions to permit overnight storage, repair bays, stores and an office.
A group of buildings and satellite dishes used to transmit and receive signals relayed by satellites.
A route across a river, or lake. Use only for small inland ferries and index with LANDING POINT/STAGE/STEPS or PIER where known.
A labyrinthine garden feature, common during the 16th and 17th centuries, created by cutting shallow pathways into deep lawns.
A jar adapted by the addition of a straight handle and three feet. Profiles vary and should be double indexed with the appropriate JAR type. (Source: MPRG)

A jar adapted by the addition of one straight handle, attached to either rim or body, and usually with a lip at right angles to the handle. The body is generally rounded, with a short neck and an everted rim. (Source: MPRG)
A large, vertical revolving wheel with passenger cars or pods on the periphery used to give a bird's eye view of the surrounding area.
A stable found at a coaching inn where horses are housed.
A kiln used for extracting salt through the evaporation of salt water.
An area of arable land with common rights after harvest or while fallow. Usually without internal divisions (hedges, walls or fences).
Use for feathers, an epidermal growth found in birds consisting of a quill, shaft and two vanes of barbs.
A bowl used in magical ceremonies.
A measuring container to measure dry goods.
Salmon which has been pickled in vinegar or brine to preserve it.
Fish of the Salmonidae family, caught for food.

The Fi 103 is the more technical nomenclature for the Second World War German V1 flying bomb, produced by Fieseler. Multiple index together with Fieseler and flying bomb for maximum chance of retrieval for users.

A German aircraft manufacturer of the 1930s and 1940s, pre-war the company were noted for making sailplanes and sports planes; during the Second World War they made military aircraft including flying bombs.
Forms used in the recording of archaeological or other site investigations.
Record of an individual context (ie layer or feature) from an archaeological excavation.
An area of a carriageway, usually delimited by road markings, for the sole use of bicycles.
The part of a road intended for vehicular traffic.
A concrete, cylindrical pedestal on which a spigot mortar was mounted. The pedestal is often the only evidence for a Spigot Mortar emplacement to survive.
A pit or emplacement surrounding a concrete pedestal, or 'thimble', which was used to mount a spigot mortar. Deployed by the Home Guard during WWII as an anti invasion measure.

A term for a type of house, with varying definitions according to period. Roman villas were high-status and usually associated with a rural estate, whereas Georgian and later period villas were often semi-detached, town houses.
An object with a broad enough blade which catches the wind and so is pushed until it shows the direction the wind is blowing in.
A building used for the preparation of animal skins and hides prior to the tanning process.
A building occupied by a club or commonly used for club activities.
The dwelling place of a farm worker.
A pipe or channel for conveying water or other liquids.
A glass-like compound first made in ancient Egypt. It involves coating a core material of powdered quartz with a vitreous alkaline glaze. Also the name given to a tin-glazed earthenware.
A mill used for the preparation of Barilla, an ash of burnt seaweed that was used for the production of soda.
Salt in its natural state
A measuring rule used for cloth, with the imperial yard divided into quarters and nails (sixteenths), or using the now obsolete ell of 45 inches.
A detached, sometimes monolithic vertical structural element usually circular, square or polygonal bearing an ornate eight-voluted Ionic Capital.
A clip for marking or holding down pages in a book.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of kidney disorders and diseases.
A single-engine, photo-reconnaissance fighter designed for operation from aircraft carriers. Later adapted as a night fighter, it entered service in 1943 and remained in production until 1956.
A landing circle marked out in white used as the airfield symbol.
Mill for fine grinding of tin ore between millstones.
A vessel used for carrying weapons and ammunition to warships.
A sloop used for carrying weapons and ammunition to warships.
A winding walk, common in early 18th century Rococo gardens and parks.

American troop and supply-glider constructed from steel tube and fabric-covered wood, with a hinged nose to allow loading and unloading of troops or light vehicles. Also known as the Haig, this was the only US glider to see combat service.

The Waco Aircraft Company, established in 1921. One of the largest pre-war producers of civil aircraft in America, Waco specialised in the production of troop and cargo carrying gliders during World War Two.
A building used by a group of people who meet socially to participate in activities, usually related to a particular interest or occupation.
A photographic print of a mononchrome image (composed of grey, black and white tones).
A dry ditch or sunken fence which divided the formal garden from the landscaped park without interrupting the view.
A box used for storage or shipping.
Commercially manufactured sodium carbonate used in glass and soap making.
A playing area for the game of hockey. May be a grass or artificial surface.
Any structure or object, used for the purpose of practice shooting by aerial, seaborne or land mounted weapons.
A place where marble is extracted from the ground.
A building or room in which wood is stored.
No longer used. Traditionally used for resources that could only be identified to a date range from the Palaeolithic to Iron Age. Included here to aid migration.
No longer used. Traditionally use for resources that could only be identified to a date range from Neolithic to Iron Age. Included here to aid migration.
A cutting through a wood to open up a view or establish an allee.
A factory where short wool was spun into woollen yarn to produce cloth.
A woollen mill in which the cloth was passed over rollers covered in short spikes to raise the nap in one direction only.
A type of pottery kiln in which air rises up inside the oven to be forced back down and out through the base of the oven.
A ship designed specifically for the carriage of liquid cargoes, particularly oil.
Transect or area-based arrangements of drilled auger-holes used to describe deposits and collect samples.
A garden where yew and other coniferous trees are grown.
Reproduced image derived by mechanical printing from an image engraved or carved on a suitable surface.
An image produced by creating marks on a hard material from which a print is then taken.
A relief process in which the design is cut into and printed from the plank side of a wood block [AAT].
A room for washing and cleaning linen.
A substantial piece of timber which is part of, and integral to, the structure of a building.
An engineering workshop for the manufacture and repair of springs.

Composite substance of plaster formed by gypsum, sand and lime and coloured with pigments, fixed under heat and highly polished. Used to imitate marble and popular in the 17th and 18th centuries for architectural features.
Ornate or patterned decoration, carved into or moulded from plaster.
External decorative plasterwork often incised or modelled with ornamental patterns. Usually applied to timber-framed houses, especially during 16th and 17th centuries.
Used for holding water and washing hands, usually in the shape of an animal.
Two or more adjacent locks where the upper gates of one lock serve as the lower gates of the next.
A stone used to cover a grave.
A tray used in divination.
A military storage aircraft hangar designed in 1937. It has a curved profile and is constructed from steel ribs supporting a concrete skin. The roof is covered with earth and turf.
A settlement, usually enclosed, on a sloping hillside containing a number of oval or circular scopped house floors separated by walls or unexcavated ridges.
An object used to prick holes on each side of a manuscript page to mark the postion of the horizontal lines.
Photographic print using silver gelatine.

A specific form of rounded jug with a wide mouth, a large parrot-beak spout and three handles in the form of wide straps that spring from the rim to the girth.The spout may have a lug applied to the outside. (Source: MPRG)
A jug with an evenly rounded profile and a discernible basal angle; the maximum diameter is near the mid point and in the upper half of the vessel. (Source: MPRG)
A leaf or diamond-shaped arrowhead with shallow retouching at the edges.
Use for vessels registered in Canada.

A prefabricated structure of reinforced concrete posts supporting a pitched roof frame with an infilling of concrete panels. Produced by during WWII as barrack accommodation and as emergency housing. Similar in style to Maycrete huts.
An aircraft maintenance workshop deriving from the use of weather proofing varnish to aircraft canvas called "dope" in order to keep the canvas taut and airtight. From 1912 onwards.
A single-engine, heavy, long range, three to five-crew day bomber. Served only with 99 Squadron RAF, 1924-5.
A school for instruction in the art of horsemanship.
A column of the Ionic Order, set upon a base and characterized by its slender form.
A device inserted in the ear canal to protect the wearer from loud noises or the intrusion of water, foreign bodies, dust or excessive wind.

A factory used for the production of artificial limbs. They were often located within the precincts of a hospital, to enable fittings to take place and help the amputee to get used to wearing the limb.
An amulet containing a charm in the shape of a scarab.
A mug with straight sides flaring outwards from the base towards the rim. (Source: MPRG)
A drinking vessel with a handle.
A public institution for the care and protection of children without parents.

American troop and supply-glider constructed from steel tube and fabric-covered wood, with a hinged nose to allow loading and unloading of troops or light vehicles. Also known as the Haig, this was the only US glider to see combat service.
A large trough or vessel commonly created from a hollowed out tree trunk for the storage of brine prior to processing for salt.
A support projecting from a wall.
Transport version of the four-engined Lancaster bomber. Serving from 1943 to 1951, and all metal in construction, this aircraft was used extensively during the Berlin airlift.
An ore containing sufficient quantities of a mineral as to make its extraction profitable.
Calcium sulphate used as a fertilizer and for making plaster of Paris.
Ore containing a high proportion of sulphur.
An ore containing a high proportion of manganese.
An enclosed area in front of a structure.
Moored barge providing a refuge for shipwrecked sailors or downed airmen, for example the air-sea rescue Cuckoo barges of WWII.
A factory for the production of plastics by chemical processes.
Northern Hemisphere
West Yorkshire
A small container used for dispensing table salt for seasoning purposes.
Previous name for Chennai.
A non-conformist minister's house.
A bridge whose upkeep and repair was financed by the exaction of a toll.
Pit for mixing raw materials with water in the preparation of a clay body.
A house or range of buildings in which dogs are kept, eg. hunting hounds.

A musket where a wheel on the lock is wound back and when the trigger is pulled the wheel moves dragging pieces of iron pyrites over the lock tocreate sparks and set powder in the pan off and so firing the main charge.
Hillslope forts with wide spaced ramparts.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by one or more substantial banks, ramparts and ditches. Use more specific type where known.
A wheel, usually steam driven, used for raising water by means of buckets attached to its circumference.
A hospital department concerned with the reconstruction or repair of parts of the human body using transferred tissue, either in the treatment of injury or for cosmetic reasons.
A purpose-built dwelling for the manager of a factory, works, textile mill, etc, often found within the complex itself.
An instrument for breaking open hard shelled nuts.
Model village built as a holiday resort.
Originally designed as a trainer but relegated to use by the RNAS in a Maritime Reconnaissance and anti-submarine role when the Avro 504 became the standard trainer.
A stoppered bottle, for serving drinks.
A floatable concrete vessel, numbers of which made up the main breakwater of the Mulberry Harbours used to secure beachheads during the allied invasion of Europe in June 1944.
A hospital where more 'natural' means of treatment are used rather than conventional methods.
Single engine, two-crew shipboard reconnaissance and patrol seaplane. Entered service in 1939, this was the last combat floatplane built in Europe.
A ship belonging to a shipping company which carries passengers on a scheduled route usually applied to steam ships only.
Narrow strips of wood which can form the groundwork for slates, panels or plaster work.
A mixed house of nuns and religious men of the Benedictine order.
A toothed comb used to beat the weft against the cloth in weaving.

A large circular defence work surrounded by a brick revetted ditch and sunken below a glacis. Usually built out of brick with the embrasures lined with granite blocks. Armed with ten or elven guns. Early 19th century as part of coastline defence.
A necklace or armband made of metal.
A bracelet or necklace formed by hammering gold onto a triangular-sectioned bar and twisting the metal to form a spiral pattern.
Cotton which has not been processed.
A form of handgun.

A pistol fired by use of a flintlock.A gunflint is held in the lock which on pulling the trigger pushes back the pan cover creating sparks which set off the powder in the pan causing a flame to go through and set off the charge in the barrel.
A ring used in the marriage ceremony.
Objects concerned with marriage and weddings.
Photographic print on self-developing photographic paper in a format developed by Polaroid in the 1970's
The lesser stalks springing from the principal stalks, or caules, within the decoration on a Corinthian capital.
Clothing designed to protect the wearer from physical hazards.
A reinforced and padded item of clothing designed to protect the upper body in sports associated with physical contact or possible injury from sporting equipment. For military uses use BREASPLATE.
A kiln used for the production of any of the soda group of alkalis by the heating of plant remains or salt.
A short bay, usually in a hall, commonly as a smoke bay or for a cross-entry.
A brush for applying paint.
The residence of a cloth cutter.
A jug with a roughly cylindrical or slightly flaring lower body, a pronounced inward-sloping shoulder and a marked neck/body angle. (Source: MPRG)
A plate-steel water tank on a steel tower designed to hold 80,000 gallons of water. Designed to Air Ministry drawing number 9526/41.

A large, circular, reinforced-concrete tank supported on concrete staging built to Air Ministry drawing number 1178/25 and designed to hold 30,000 gallons of water. The height of the tower varied according to local site requirements.
A tower serving as a reservoir to deliver water at a required point.
A plate-steel water tower made with two compartments holding 30,000 gallons of water. Designed to Air Ministry drawing number 20/40.

Twin-engined, six-crew, heavy bomber. Conceived as a rival to the Lancaster and Flying Fortress, the HE177 was dogged by mechanical and structural problems. Of a thousand produced, only about two hundred saw action.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around one or more sides of an open cattle yard.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around three sides of an open cattle yard.
A cable railway with ascending and descending cars counterbalanced.
Specify in Description using terms not included in the above
A dam and sluice combination, associated with an aqueduct, for the extraction of water from a river to feed a reservoir or water treatment plant.
An earthen bank indicating the limit of a plantation.
A post box mounted on a lamp post.
A hollow pillar, erected in a public place, containing a receptacle for posting letters.
A post box mounted in, or on, a wall.
A box in which letters are posted or deposited for dispatch.
A vessel (often small obsolete cruisers or pleasure steamers) equipped with batteries of anti aircraft guns as its main armament.
A building licensed for the sale of beer.
A house or shelter for the storage and/or launching of boats.
A vertical timber set on a collar or tie-beam extending to the apex of a pitched roof.
Submerged obstacles to stop the landing of Seaplanes

Highly successful, two-seat, biplane fighter and reconnaissance aircraft with both forward and rear facing guns. Designed to replace the BE2, it entered service with the RFC in mid-1917 and remained in service until 1932.
One of the allotropes of carbon, commonly used in pencils.
A heated stone, brick or iron chamber used for drying corn.
A drawing used to convey information about the arrangement and size of features in a defined location under study.
A stone block set into a wall to support a truss or beam.
A large vessel, sometimes large enough to accomodate several gallons, often made of leather and richly decorated, for storing and serving liquor.
A projecting structure in the roof of a mill containing a winch, allowing loads to be lifted clear of the building's wall and protecting the winch from the weather.
A boundary post for the payment of tax or duty.
A road, sometimes raised as a causeway, which serves as an approach road to a building or bridge.

skos:Concept.skos:definition: Defined as exactly 0.9144 metres by the International yard and pound agreement of 1959

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A purpose-built residence for an artist, containing a studio.
A hand held tool for marking or graving.
A laundry attached to a hospital.
A cube of material used to make up a mosaic.
An umbrella-shaped pavilion, Indian in origin, constructed over a funerary site. Can also refer to a funerary monument or cenotaph constructed in this style.
A sepulchral monument erected to commemorate a person or persons buried elsewhere.

A type of transportable aircraft hangar patented by Miskins and Sons in 1939. The arched hangar was constructed of steel or wooden ribs and generally clad in steel sheets. The hangar did not require any foundations and could be anchored by iron stakes.
A dam and sluice combination, associated with an aqueduct, for the extraction of water from a river to feed a reservoir or water treatment plant.
Single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer. Spruce and plywood in construction, entered service in 1939, continuing to serve as a trainer, and also a target tug, until 1950.
A joint in which the end is shaped like a dovetail.
A joint in which the dovetailed member is proud of the receiving member and is not finished flush with it.
A multi-level structure designed to simulate tall buildings to allow firefighters to practice firefighting and rescue techniques
A civic building housing fire engines and a permanent fire-fighting force.
Several strands of string twisted together to form a strong thin rope, or thick string, though it has been used in the past as synonomous with rope particularly for ropes on ships.
A form of whip or lash, often used for self mortification.
A kind of scourge.
A jar with a profile that slopes inwards from base to rim. Particularly shallow examples have been term Peat Pots; this is a term with a restricted distribution in northern England. (Source: MPRG)
A handled tool with two or more prongs used for digging, cultivation etc.
A large, flattish basket used in winnowing the chaff from the grain.
A two-seat, reconnaissance biplane developed from the FK2 with a more powerful, but heavier, engine. Primarily used for training in the UK.
Outer cases for ammunition shells, e.g. Howitzer shells; not "live" ammunition, i.e. either at the first stage of manufacture, or having been expended.
A mirror designed to be held by hand.
An object which has been carved. Use more specific term where known.
An object showing signs of being worked. Use more specific term where known.
An object placed to mark the site of a grave.
A place where boats are built and stored.
Use for the remains of any part of a human.
A building in which purified charcoal was produced by distillation of wood in sealed cast-iron retorts heated in fire-boxes. Tarry by-products were sometimes recovered by condensation flues.
A building in which wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
A site where wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
A mine used for the extraction of tungsten bearing ore. Use with other mineral ores extracted and MINE, eg. TIN MINE.
A fortified wall surrounding a town or city.
A monument where the evidence that defines the type of the monument derives from the nature of surface markings. Examples include graffitti on quarry walls.
A receptacle for the storage of water.
A covered tank in which rainwater is stored for use when required.
A free standing small turf and timber fortlet, situated every Roman mile along Hadrian's Wall.

Troop and general transport glider. Almost entirely wooden in construction, many were manufactured by the furniture industry. Mk I featured a a door-ramp on the port side whilst the Mk II was fitted with a hinged nose.
A place of worship for followers of Hinduism.
A distinctive magistrates court established by legislation in 1980, dealing with civil family proceedings.
The vertical recessed face of a pediment, often decorated with sculpture.
Single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer used in secondary flying training schools. Serving from 1939-50, was also used as a target tug for gunnery practice.

Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as an F-shaped plan around two cattle yards. Cattle housing and stabling typically extend as three ranges from the longer main range which includes a barn or mixing house.
A surgery where patients who pay for medical treatments are seen and treated.
A room or office at a general practitioners' or veterinary practice, where patients or animals are seen and medicine dispensed.
A plant for bottling manufactured goods, as opposed to a BOTTLE WORKS where bottles were made.

A prefabricated structure of reinforced concrete posts and beams with infillings of pre stressed concrete planks and felted slabs. Initially used for military barracks in WWII and later for civilian housing. Manufactured by the Orlit Company.

A convex, usually round, piece of metal or other material mounted at the centre of a shield. Originally serving a practical purpose in deflecting blows and providing a mounting for the grip, it later developed into an ornamental feature.
A carved or moulded decorative projection adorning an object or, in the case of architectural features, the termination of a moulding or the intersection of ribs or beams.
A device on a boat's gunwale serving as a fulcrum for an oar and keeping it in place.
Dried produce especially, hay, straw etc. used to feed cattle.
Cattle fodder or fertilizer resulting from the extracting of oil from seeds.
A nineteenth century plan where two or four wings of a house are constructed at an angle to the core, usually at approximately 45 degrees to the wall of the core building.
Worked or unworked block/boulder/cobble, on which grain was ground by to-and-fro motion, resulting in a deep smooth elongated hollowed area.
A purpose built indoor cricket facility for training and playing matches
A microlith retouched to a triangular shape. They can be sub-divided into scalene and isosceles triangles. (Source: SARC)
An elevated table or podium on which to place, or sacrifice, offerings to a god or gods.
An object which has been rejected eg due to being misshapen, spoilt etc.

Fleet Air Arm fighter and torpedo-bomber, designed for operation from aircraft carriers. All-metal in construction, it entered service in 1944 and was rendered obsolete after the war by the advent of the jet aircraft.
A small bottle for liquids.
An inn temporarily used for the performance of plays and other public entertainment.
A building used primarily for the performing of plays.
A place where tin ore is washed using a stream as the water source.
One of a pair of large circular stones used for grinding corn in a mill.
A bowl adapted by having a pedestal base. (Source: MPRG)
A building with first aid facilities to deal with accidents and other medical emergencies.
A structure comprising two upright spars, joined at the top to form a triangle, with a hoisting tackle suspended from the apex. Used to lift cargo or other weights.
An oil obtained by the distillation of wood and used as a solvent and paint thinner and in some medical preparations.

Four-engine, seven-crew heavy bomber. Entered service with RAF Bomber Command in 1940, becoming one of the twin sources of bomber strength along with the Lancaster. Also used for transport and glider tug duties.

A Neolithic burial monument comprising a rectangular or trapezoidal stony mound which contains either a passage at one end with or without lateral chambers, or one or more smaller chambers entered from the side of the mound.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a mound of stones. Use more precise term where known.

A prefabricated cargo vessel produced in large numbers by North American shipyards during World War II to replace shipping losses caused by German submarines and replacing the earlier 'LIBERTY' ships.
A capital warship lightly armoured but with the same gun armament and stem turbine propulsion as a DREADNOUGHT BATTLESHIP.
An inn temporarily used for the performance of plays and other public entertainment.
A site used for the production and/or working of metallic lead.
An urn containing a cremation burial.
A portable stand by set house built to Air Ministry drawing number 3527/43.
A factory in which logs are converted to timber by running them through a series of saws.
A cheap restaurant.
An outbuilding where a horse-drawn carriage is kept.

A signalling structure used on WWII airfields, comprising a concrete square base with a kerbed border into which concrete signal symbols could be placed to advise pilots in the air of current airfield state e.g. directions of landing and airfield circuit.
A technique that uses the emission of gamma rays of specific energies to identify the presence and concentration of certain radioactive isotopes in a sample
A factory or works used for the production of turpentine, wood alcohol and similar chemicals by the distillation of pulped wood.
A building in a quarry consisting of a series of loading bays in which stone is loaded onto wagons.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the extraction of stone. Includes preparation processes.
An outdoor theatre for the staging of dramatic productions.
A purpose-built area of hard material of indeterminate use.

Rectangular slabs of concrete with a sloping top usually with sides of 5 feet by 3 feet and 3 feet high which when placed in rows were intended to form a substantial barrier to enemy armoured divisions in the event of invasion.
A bridge carrying a road over land or water.
A mechanically operated display board used in greyhound racing, which showed the state of the Tote, or cumulative betting on individual greyhounds.
A covered walkway attached to a building.
A non perforated stone used as a hammer in making stone tools.
A hammerstone but with broad groove worked around much or all of centre to enable fixing to a handle; usually associated with mining/metalworking.

A building used by the Royal Observer Corps as a headquarters and reporting centre. It may also fulfil an observation and nuclear fallout monitoring role. Use term to describe headquarters for plotting and monitoring nuclear fallout.
Planks or boards manufactured from softwood timber.
British single-engine, two-seat night fighter. Originally intended as a day fighter, but withdrawn and converted in August 1940, this was the first fighter to incorporate a power-driven gun turret.
Boulton Paul Aircraft, Ltd., formed in 1934 to take over the Aircraft Department of Boulton & Paul, Ltd.

A coin which has been struck in relief on one side, usually the obverse side face down on the anvil die, and incuse on the other side, due to a previously struck coin sticking to the upper or punch die.
A garden building, usually in the Gothic or classical style. The term can be applied to many types of garden building with an interior space in which to stand or sit. Use specific type where known.
An 18th century garden building, designed in the style of a classical Ionic temple, used for standing or sitting in.
An apparatus for weighing, usually consists of a beam on a pivot with a means of supporting the object to be weighed on one side and weights on the other.
A balance with unequal arms where the contents of a pan on the short arm are weighed by a weight or weights attached to the long arm.
A flat heavy slightly curved blade.
The limit line of a parish.
A long, wooden, metal or stone vessel holding drinking water for horses.
The seal of a papal document
A mobile piece of equipment used by the Royal Observer Corps to track the movements of enemy aircraft.
A single acting, non-rotative beam engine worked by atmospheric pressure.
A plan type, usually for a church, having a rectangular core with one apsidal end wall.
An open area of prepared ground used for practising putting with golf clubs.
A series of recessed, ornamental panels decorating a ceiling.
A house in a terrace built on top of another, with access at high and low level to either side.
An Egyptian container for holding the entrails of a mummy.
A jug with a body profile resembling two cones joined together at their widest points, producing a distinct carination. (Source: MPRG)
A reservoir or tank used to hold a supply of water for fire-fighting purposes in the event of the main supply being damaged or cut off.
Worked pieces of stone. Use more specific type of stone where known.
Carved stones used for marking a grave.
Products manufactured from stone.
For the collection of money by charities, churches, etc.
Defined as species introduced after the last glaciation, e.g. sycamore, sweet chestnut, etc. Specify in Description whether currently managed, neglected, unmanaged or management not determined.
Coarse jute sacking
A factory complex consisting of PRINTING SHOPS, COLOUR HOUSES, DYE HOUSES, etc, in which patterns are printed onto calico.
A factory or complex containing machinery for the manufacture of printed materials.

A long, narrow, irregularly constructed and generally unstructured mound of stones. Normally a by-product of field clearance for agricultural purposes, though prehistoric examples may include burials and other deposits.
An irregularly constructed, generally unstructured, mound of stones. Often, but not necessarily, circular. Normally a by product of field clearance for agricultural purposes.
A group of cairns occurring within close proximity to each other. Use for instances where the majority are clearance cairns. Also index specific types where known.
The residence of health workers. Includes single dwellings of doctors, nurses etc. but not multiple dwellings eg.NURSES HOSTEL
A vertical timber in a truss, descending from the ridge, and projecting below the lower transverse timber, normally used with scissor beams.
Two-seat, single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer. Square-winged and fitted with dual controls, this popular trainer was used by British Commonwealth, as well as American and Canadian, air forces.
A vessel with a single mast, fore and aft rigged.
A key usually with a long stem with bit, stem and terminal in line.
A pillbox which varies from standard designs.
A weapon, usually blunt, used to strike an opponent.
A long staff, occasionally bound with metal, used as a weapon.
A railway which runs beneath the surface of the ground, eg. the London Underground Railway.
A building or site used for the manufacture of swords.
A windmill with a rotating cap containing the windshaft, and a stationary body in the form of a tower.
Stones used to edge a pavement or raised path.
An area of privately owned land attached to, and incorporating, a country house and associated buildings.
Northumberland
Northumberland

A hospital ward block, completely open on the south side apart from a low railing and sun blind. It was thought beneficial for the recovery of wounded soldiers as well as those with diseases of the chest.
An object which fastens cross ways.

Standard dwelling of the non-ruling classes of Japan until the mid twentieth century. Minkas are timber-framed houses with mud-plastered panels and thatched roofs. The design varies from region to region. Minkas served as home as well as workplace.
A complete written work including books and anthologies.
Post-World War Two, single-engine, high-wing utility transport. Manufactured by De Havilland Canada, was also produced in a seaplane version. Known as the U6A from 1962.
A factory used to make packaging equipment.
A bar fixed across a frame at an angle to stiffen it.
A rod around which fibre is wound for spinning
For the disposal of town refuse. Some 19th century plants were linked to a power station. Later ones incorporate INCINERATORS, recycling facilities, etc.
A central point for the deposit, collection and recycling of waste materials.
Material consisting of at least 90% organic matter by dry weight. Formed from plant material under damp, wet or acid conditions where the rate of accumulation is greater than the rate of decay.
A communal sleeping room in medieval houses for male servants.
A type of factory building, often single-storey, designed so that windows incorporated into the vertical faces of its saw-tooth roof can allow the maximum amount of natural light into its interior.

Single-engine, single-seat, long range fighter originally designed in 1940 to a British requirement. Outstanding low-level speed and range resulted in its assignment to the ground support (Army co-operation) role.
A device for hoisting, or operating pumps, using water displacement as a lifting and balancing medium.
A German coastal minelaying submarine in use during the First World War.

A prefabricated structure of a steel frame clad in corrugated iron. Semi-circular in section they were used as accommodation for the armed forces and, during WWII, as emergency housing for bombed out civilians. Also used for storage.
A bell mounted on an anchored vessel, buoy, headland, rock etc and rung as a warning to mariners in foggy weather.
The hair from the coat of goats and sheep, made into yarn and used in the manufacture of woollen cloth.
Goods, particularly cloth and garments, manufactured from wool.
A report which represents an initial synthesis of the data collected from an excavation ahead of the production of a full publication report.
A site where canvas, coarse, unbleached cloth, made from hemp or flax, was manufactured.
Mill for grinding bark usually for use in the tanning industry. Use with power type(s), eg. WATERMILL where known.
Photographic image produced on transparent medium suitable for use in projection equipment. Use specific term where known.
Photographic transparency on an acetate base material.
A structure associated with forges, watermills, water-powered factories, etc.
A waterwheel where the inflow of water strikes the paddles or floatboards well below the axis of the wheel, ie. the water more or less passes under it.
Three-masted fishing lugger built in and operating out of Yorkshire on the North Sea fisheries; so named as it was crewed by five joint owners, plus two or three paid hands.
A vessel with a lug sail rig. A lug is a four sided sail set on a lug or yard. Modified from square-rigged vessels from the late 17th century. Became a popular fishing boat rig in the 19th century.
Debris resulting from the manufacture of tools and other artifacts from bone.
Waste products ensuing from the casting process.
The debris resulting from metal working processes.
The debris resulting from the production of glass.
waste resulting from the working of wood or associated with a carpenter's workshop.
The remains of a manufacturing process.
Waste resulting from the processes associated with the making of shoes.
A machine for the final reduction in cross sectional area of a cotton sliver into a fine roving preparatory to spinning high counts of yarn.
A flat bottomed drinking vessel with no handle or stem.
A piece of land used to grow vegetables to be sold at markets.
A crane for lowering loaded coal waggons onto a ship.

An enclosed feature, usually sub-terranean, constructed to contain water for public or private recreation and sporting activities. Often part of a larger SPORTS CENTRE. Use OUTDOOR SWIMMING POOL for unenclosed pools.
A large, manmade pool, usually lined with tiles, rubber or similar. Can be placed in the open air, eg. a LIDO, or built as part of a covered sports centre.

An unenclosed feature, usually sub-terranean, constructed to contain water for public or private recreation and sporting avtivities. Sometimes part of a LIDO complex. Use INDOOR SWIMMING POOL for pools with a covering structure.
A container with a perforated bottom through which material is shaken or poured.
A site or factory where waste slag from ironworking if further processed for use in manufacturing.
A mill used for the preparation of raw fleece etc, for spinning by a coarse form of carding.
A weekend retreat for Royal parties and others, when hunting in the Royal forests, or as a viewing station for the chase.
A factory where linoleum is manufactured.
A works, including an extractive site, producing a clay of high plasticity and firmness, used as a basic raw material for porcelain.
A building or workshop where fine furniture, often veneered, is made.
A stall where a cobbler mends shoes.
A site where the manufacture of glass bottles takes place.
A building used, as a meeting place and administration block, by an organization run for the benefit of students at a school, college or university.
A furnace for holding hot steel ingots to equalize their temperature before they are hot-rolled in a steel-making or rolling mill complex.
17th century Dutch vessel built for naval or East India service, with a relatively flat bottom and narrow hull; sometimes rendered into English as `fly-boat'.
A joint in which a dovetailed timber's surface is proud of the receiving member on one side.
Remains of any part of a nut including the nutshell. The definition of nut as used here is any woody fruit or seed.
Remains of any part of a hazel (Corylus avellana L.) nut.
Soft, loose-textured, woollen or man-made fabric.
Woven or felted fabric used in the manufacture of garments, tablecloths, towels etc.
A type of cotton cloth of a pale yellow colour.
Cloth that has been woven in fixed lengths for sale.
Fine cotton fabric of a delicate weave.
West Yorkshire
A building, usually open to the public, containing a number of areas for bathing. In the case of such a complex containing baths for swimming, also index with INDOOR or OUTDOOR SWIMMING POOL.
A building where people could bathe in salt water. Salt water was believed to have medicinal properties.
A tunnel used to test scale model propellers and hulls to consider the impact of caviation on wake, propulsion, vibration and noise.
A flask with a rounded, almost spherical shape. (Source: MPRG)
A small eating and drinking establishment or refreshment bar.
A small eating and drinking establishment or refreshment bar at a railway station for the use of passengers.
A camp for the temporary accommodation of uprooted civilians or foreign ex-service personnel, who had fought for the British forces during WWII (e.g.Polish).
A clasp on a cope.
A modern small factory or workshop, often in the form of a prefabricated shed.
A factory where putty, used as a means of securing windows and for setting plumbing fixtures, is produced from a combination of whiting and oil.
A container for holding ink.
A factory used for the production of red lead used in glass manufacture, or white lead used as the pigment in white paint.

A British two-seater army co-operation aircraft manufactured by Hawker Aircraft for the Royal Air Force. A Hart variant biplane that first flew in 1931, becoming a prominent British aircraft in the inter-war period with over 700 units built.
A stone coffin.
A site with one or more defensive earthworks, often at a river crossing incorporating natural features which define parts of the curtilage.
An imprecise term used to describe large Iron Age settlements of town-like proportions.
Used for the laying out and marking of the smaller parts of a ship prior to construction.
A massive structure designed to transfer canal boats between different canal or river navigations, eg. Anderton boat lift.
A structure consisting of a box or platform for carrying goods or passengers from one level to another. Use specific type where known.
A factory manufactoring caravans.
Animal skin that has been tanned or tawed.
An opening in a structure which is arched.
A long handled heavy hammer used by two hands.
A single-engine, photo-reconnaissance fighter designed for operation from aircraft carriers. Later adapted as a night fighter, it entered service in 1943 and remained in production until 1956.
A chain used to inhibit a prisoner's freedom.
An artificial navigable waterway used for the transportation of goods. Nowadays also used for recreational purposes.
A canal that can accommodate ocean-going ships, usually built across an isthmus or to give access to a river port e.g. Manchester ship canal
A kiln in the form of a pit dug into the earth which was used for the the production of white coal prior to the Industrial Revolution.
A monument consisting of an area of land enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the barrier consists of several straight or near straight sections.

A square shaped area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier. Small square enclosures (with sides of less than c.20m) have been interpreted as the remains of square barrows of Iron Age date.
A building or room used for any type of engineering work. Use more specific type where known.
An engineering workshop, often attached to an engine shed, for the running repairs of operational parts, etc.
A building or site used for the production of frameworks of beds.
A microlith retouched to a thomboid shape. (Source: SARC)

An emplacement housing mobile sound locating acoustic dishes/horns for the detection of incoming enemy aircraft and the triangulation of their positions so that they could be targeted by Anti aircraft guns.
A dam and sluice combination, associated with an aqueduct, for the extraction of water from a river to feed a reservoir or water treatment plant.
A dam which can be raised or lowered to regulate the flow of water.
A lockable box for holding money and valuables.

A musket fired by use of a flintlock. A gunflint is held in the lock which on pulling the trigger pushes back the pan cover creating sparks which set off the powder in the pan causing a flame to go through and set off the charge in the barrel.
A pit where domestic waste material is deposited.
A type of temporary transportable aircraft hangar designed in 1936 by N.S. Bellman. It was designed for ease of installation, and was composed of light rolled steel sections.
A building manufacturing bandages.
A factory, mill or warehouse constructed with the minimum amount of combustible materials.
A building constructed with the minimum amount of combustible materials.
House, where destitute Jews converted to Christianity after the expulsion. Latin for "House of Converts".
Uncultivated land lying alongside a thoroughfare.
A site where a periodical gathering of buyers, sellers and entertainers, meet at a time ordained by charter or statute or by ancient custom.
A textile mill where thread undergoes the processes of twisting and doubling to provide material strong enough to be spun and woven.
A small private chapel in either a house or church.
A substantial vertical member, usually a component of a main framework.
A vertical upright on either side of a door.
The second subdivision of the Neolithic, or New Stone Age.
The third and latest subdivision of the Neolithic, or New Stone Age.

The New Stone Age, this period follows on from the Palaeolithic and the Mesolithic and is itself succeeded by the Bronze Age. This period is characterized by the practice of a farming economy and extensive monumental constructions.
The earliest subdivision of the Neolithic, or New Stone Age.
A factory used for the manufacture of serge, a heavy woollen cloth.
The openings between the upright blocks, or merlons, of a battlement.
A stone blade with one edge blunted.
A place in which the artillery is encamped or collected together.
The powdery residue resulting from the combustion of a substance eg. wood and used for various manufacturing processes.
Landing craft designed for carrying military vehicles and used for beach landings and as a ferry.
A jug with more or less straight sides that flare out from a narrow rim or neck to a wider base. (Source: MPRG)
A site used for the manufacture of leather products.
A workshop used for the small-scale production of leather goods.
A chute for conveying salt.
Single-seat carrierborne jet fighter. Originally conceived as an RAF land-fighter, entered Fleet Air Arm service in 1951 and was the first jet fighter to be standardised in first-line squadrons.
A large drainage channel used for improving the land.
A constructed space beneath the surface of the ground.
A construction of unknown function, either extant or implied by archaeological evidence. If known, use more specific type.
A public institution for the care and protection of children without parents.
A group of buildings or works where the evaporation and crystallization of sodium aluminium sulphate solution is performed.
A channel which carried processed alum as liquid from the alum quarry/works to the alum house

A large steelframed military aircraft hangar designed in 1939, intended for aircraft maintenance on operational stations. It includes side annexes for workshops and offices, provided with a large number of windows. The annexes are of brick or concrete.

skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Religious Society Of Friends Burial Ground

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A burial ground for Nonconformists. Use more specific term where known.
A place of burial for members of the Religious Society of Friends, often known as Quakers.
Any metal that does not contain the chemical element Iron (Fe) as a principal component.
A precious metal of lustrous, white colour with great malleability and ductility.
The premises of a coal merchant where coal and other kinds of solid fuel can be bought.
A building in a zoo or wildlife park used to accommodate giraffes.
A mill used for the preparation of raw fleece etc, for spinning by a coarse form of carding.
A factory, where preserves such as jam and marmalade, are manufactured.
Partially decomposed granite used to produce a glaze for porcelain.
A plain moulding of semi-circular section.
Photographic image with normal polarity.
Colour positive print developed using a dry process.
A bridge constructed using rockwork to create a craggy, naturalistic appearance. A feature of 18th century rococo gardens and parks.
A bridge built to enhance or compliment the surrounding landscape. Mainly found on estates or in parkland and usually 18th and 19th century.
A two-seat trainer chosen to replace the Avro 504. 380 entered RAF service with many finding their way onto the civilian market at the end of their careers.
An instrument showing the direction of magnetic north and bearings from it.
A band worn around the head to denote sovereignty.
Bay-leaf shaped decorative ornamentation, usually adorning mouldings or friezes, often depicted in a garland arrangement.
A room set aside within a building where social and other functions such as parties, presentations and meetings can be held.
Paper made for writing or drawing underwater.
Operations restricted to a depth of no more than 25 cms. If possible state depth in Description.

A two-seat, general purpose biplane. The first to be designed specifically for an Army Co-operation role, it entered service in late 1927. Ended its service as a communications and advanced trainer aircraft.
A stable located at a railway station or goods yard. Horses were necessary both for freight and passengers to continue their journey beyond the railway.
A building for miners to change their clothes.
A place where paper, frequently printed in ornamental designs, used for covering the interior walls of buildings, is manufactured.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the production and use of paper.

A building used as a social venue by people interested in, and involved with, the sport of rowing. An area of the building may be used for the storage of canoes, sculls etc. Often situated by a river.
American, four-engined, medium/heavy day bomber. Entered service in 1937. The prototype was nicknamed the Flying Fortress, which later became a registered trademark.
The Boeing Aircraft Company, established 1916. A subsidiary of The Boeing Airplane Company. Notable aircraft produced include the B17 Flying Fortress and the B29 Superfortress.
A building or set of rooms, primarily of the 18th century, in which social gatherings and balls were held.
A building in which apparatus registering the amount of gas consumed is housed.
A school established by a charity.
The residence of a ferrykeeper.

Roman bow brooch, dating from the third to fifth centuries AD, with a P-shaped profile and a characteristic crossbar, often adorned with knobs at its end and on the head. Shown in contemporary illustrations as being worn by high ranking males.
A type of pottery oven in which the air passes from the base of the kiln out through the top.
A sheet of flat film, 105 x 148mm in size, carrying a matrix of micro images.
Photographic image with normal polarity.
Photographic transparency mounted for use in projection equipment.
Use a term from the Archive Format list.
A hospital where elderly people receive medical treatment, but not overnight accommodation.
A half gable or half pediment concealing the lean-to roof of an aisle.
A beacon, firmly embedded on the sea floor, consisting of an iron mast, with ladder steps leading up to the refuge cage considerably above high-water mark, and capable of holding several people.
Dutch galliot-rigged vessel used mostly for river trade in Holland but sometimes also for coasting or short sea-going voyages
A vessel designed or adapted for the task of keeping shipping lanes and ports free from the threat of naval mines. Use specific type where known. of
A vessel designed or adapted to sweep and explode mined areas at sea without prior detection. (See Minehunter for vessels that detect and destroy individual mines).
A wide street, traditionally lined with trees.

Originally ordered as land based dive-bombers, with 950 being delivered to the RAF, none are known to have flown operationally, instead apparently serving as target tugs. Bermuda was the name given to the Brewster SB2A Buccaneer in RAF service.
American, all-metal-construction, fighter. Entered service in 1941. 209 were delivered to RAF/FAA, most of which were used in the Far East.

The Brewster Aeronautical Corporation was founded in 1932, taking over the plant, equipment, designs and goodwill of Brewster & Co., Inc.'s aircraft division. Initially manufacturing seaplane components, later designed and produced complete aircraft.
An instrument for measuring magnetic forces, especially the strength of terrestrial magnetism.
A building where horses are rubbed down after training.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Nitrate, used as a fertilizer or for use in the explosives industry.

Interbellum, twin-engined, five-crew, biplane flying-boat with a characteristic triple tail-fin. Entered service in 1925 and used for general reconnaissance duties. The Mk.I had a wooden fuselage, whilst the Mk.II's was metal in construction.
A bridge made up of many relatively small members joined together in a series of interconnecting triangles.
A specialized form of truss bridge that extends or cantilevers from both sides of the pier, the inner 'arms' usually supporting a central span.

A building, usually associated with, or found within the grounds of, a cemetery and used for the storage of coffins prior to burial. Reception houses were introduced as a result of concerns around the implcations for public health of C19 burial practices.
An oval or circular structure with seats rising in tiers around a central open space. Used for religious ceremonies, entertainment, training and armed combat contests.
A medieval hospital for lepers, usually consisting of a church and individual shelters for the lepers.
Twin-engined, four-crew German seaplane. Entered service in 1932 as a torpedo bomber and naval reconnaisance aircraft, though by World War 2 those still serving were used mainly for air sea rescue.

A transportable hangar designed by Callender Cable and Construction to Air Ministry drawing number 6633/37. A steel box-girder framework with corrugated iron cladding and canvas doors it had a clear door height of 25ft.
Similar in design to the Callender Hangar but with a reduced height of 17ft. Built to Air Ministry drawing number 17346/40.
The horizontal beam on a lock gate.
An underground passageway for cables, pipes and pedestrians to allow passage beneath an over ground obstacle.
A bowl for the washing of hands, often in a religious institution.
A friary belonging to the Franciscan order. Includes houses of both Friars Minor and Friars Observant or Capuchins.
A hall used by the members of a trade union for meetings and social functions.
The course or channel of a river or stream preserved as a geological feature.

Single-engine navigation trainer and communications aircraft. Constructed of tubular steel and duralumin frame, with a duralumin and canvas covering, 500 were delivered to the FAA, serving from 1944-5.

A farmstead with multiple yards which are grouped together and regularly arranged (other than the defined E, F, H, T or Z plans). The yards may relate to one or more buildings or ranges which may be of either loose courtyard or regular courtyard form.
A model village established by the chartists.
A glasshouse used for growing pineapples.
A pulley running on the outside of a belt to improve the effectiveness of a drive.
A building or buildings where soap is manufactured.
Factual information conveyed orally to a recipient. Where this has been transcribed, use an appropriate term from the TEXT hierarchy.
A building where the administrative functions of a Trade Union are carried on.
An airfield with associated hangars and control buildings used for the storage, maintenance and deployment of military aircraft and airships flown by the Royal Naval Air Service.
A factory producing metallic aluminium by an electrolysis process.
A factory for the assembly of bicycles.
A factory for the manufacture of vehicles
A factory used for the manufacture and assembly of lorries.
A factory where cars are manufactured.
A building where motor cycles are assembled.
A factory for the manufacture of military tanks.

Specific English quarryman's term for any limestone abundant in shell fragments. Use this term with care. When only Gritstone is mentioned, unless otherwise specified, assume it to be Gritstone (Sandstone), since this is the most common usage.
Paper products intended for note-taking or correspondence, e.g. blank notebooks, diaries, writing paper, postcards
A small transportable hangar built by the Teesdie Bridge and Engineering Company. Mainly used on RNAS airfields for folding wing aircraft.
A mill used for the production of cardboard and other similar products.
64 Type DFW55373 projector sites arranged in and 8x8 grid or in 4 groups of 16. 30m between each projector, with hardened personnel and ammunition shelters located midway between each

6 Type DFW 55373s placed in a 3X2 rectangular plan. Each projector was separated by 31-34m. Hardened personnel and ammunition shelters located midway between each projector, but ammunition stored outside the perimeter.
64 Type DFW55373 single projector sites arranged in an 8x8 grid or in 4 groups of 16. 30m between each projector, with hardened personnel and ammunition shelters located midway between each

Unspecified Second World War anti-aircraft battery. There were three types of battery. The U2P and U20P had different arrangements of DFW55373 projector sites for the 20-barrelled 3" projectors. The U9P mounted 12-barrelled projectors.

Rocket projector site with a circular or octagonal concrete holdfast, 1.5m across, surrounded by a 4.6m radius octagonal concrete surround. Six such rocket projectors were arranged in a 3 x 2 grid. Personnel shelters placed midway between each site.
6 DFW55373 projector emplacements spaced in a 3x2 rectangular gid, but each spaced 35m apart. No blast protection was provided at the shelters, which were placed between the projector emplacements.
A camping place set aside for the use of caravans.
A free-standing house, not joined to another on either side.
A tall pole topped with a bell used to summon the workforce to their place of work.
