A joint consisting of a projecting tongue fitting into an open housing in a scarf joint or the apex of a rafter.

Single-engine, two-seat, light, biplane, elementary-flying trainer. Adapted from a civilian design, and constructed from tubular steel and spruce with plywood and fabric covering, entered service in 1931 and was available in land-plane or seaplane forms.
A dwelling cut into the rockface of a cliff or hillside, often with a built frontage. Many date from the Medieval period and are still in use in some areas of the country.
A receptacle for spittle, usually used in a public place.
An opening through which missiles or combustible materials could be dropped upon attackers. Usually through the roof of an entrance way or in a projecting parapet.
Use for a combination (alloy) of two or more different metals where copper (Cu) is the principal component.
Factory producing asbestos sheeting and or asbestos fibre.
Solid bars made from pure tin.
A lustrous, malleable metal, which is resistant to corrosion. Tin is used in alloys such as pewter and used in the manufacture of cans for the storage of food.
Sheets of iron or steel coated with tin.
A fortified house of two or three storeys, the lower floor being used to house animals and the upper for domestic use.

The extraction of samples from selected features on a site to identify a characteristic magnetic response from sediments derived from the features in order to predict the response that similar features would produce. Also used to prospect for sites.
A tool that produces a mark on an object through the application of percussive force through the stamp.
The non-diagonal joint at the right-angled meeting of two stone mouldings.
A building or site used for naval communications.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter, also adapted as a night-fighter, fighter-bomber, rocket-projectile fighter and tank-buster. The first monoplane to enter RAF service with 14,000 being produced between 1937 and 1944.
A cluster of piles for mooring a vessel.
A small room off a bedroom, usually in eighteenth century houses, in which a person would have their wig powdered.
Data storage device in disc form that uses lasers to write and access data; can store data in analog or digital form. [AAT]
The face within a pediment, as enclosed by the cornices, or the solid infill of an arch above an impost, sometimes embellished with sculptural or relief ornament.
A twin engine advanced trainer developed by Beech/ Beechcraft , a US firm, used in WWII
Beech Aircraft Corporation, also known as Beechcraft, established 1932
A type of comb for flax or hemp.
A seed or fruit with a hard shell, often edible or used to produce oils.
A chemical works engaged in the production or refining of toluene, a substance extracted from coal tar or specific types of crude oil, and used in the production of explosives during WW1.

Used to record resources dating to, and associated with, the First World War. For other types of resources dating to, but not directly associated with, the war (such as houses, built during this period) use: Early 20th Century.
The first third of the 20th century.
An enclosed observation tower, usually made of brick or concrete and raised on four legs, associated with WW2 bombing ranges.
Non-specific building type associated with an airfield.
A building in which cows are milked.
A bottle used for the storage of medicine.
An area of land consisting of the lord's demesne and of lands from whose holders he may exact certain fees, etc.
A demasted ship used exclusively for the storage of grain.
A demasted old ship used for storing items.
Buildings and plant used for the extraction and purification of arsenic oxide into various forms of pure arsenic.
A shed, often found at a quarry, in which rough stone is shaped or dressed.
Letters and parcels transported on behalf of the dispatchers by the postal services.
Written communiques, often of a military or governmental nature, requiring fast delivery.
A horizontal door within, and usually flush with surface of, a floor, ceiling or roof.
The remains of the fine powdery substance produced by male elements of flowering plants, uniquely identifiable to the species it came from.
A simple type of plant. For most of their lifecycle they exist as haploids (i.e. only one set of genes as opposed to two). Most have clearly differentiated stems and leaves.
Use for large remains such as fruit, seeds, plant parts, buds etc.
The ocean which surrounds the continent of Antarctica, and includes the most southerly regions of the three largest oceans, the Pacific, Atlantic and Indian.
Curved, interlocking roof tile of S-shaped section usually made of clay or concrete.
An establishment dedicated to the study of God and religion.
An old opencast iron ore site, which has been abandoned.
A site where clay is mined from the ground.
A tank within a salt works used for storing brine after is has been pumped from underground. The brine is then fed by gravity into the evaporating pans in the Pan House.
A large wooden structure built alongside the edge of a canal where narrow boats may lie for the loading and unloading of goods.
Ornamental wrought iron screen associated with gate lodges or entrance lodges.

The Glenn L. Martin Company, established in 1909 by Glenn L Martin. Produced the first successful American-designed twin-engined aeroplane, the Martin Twin, which was then converted for use as a passenger aircraft.
American twin-engined medium bomber. Entered service with the US 22nd Bombardment Group at Langley Field in February 1941. Also served with the 14th and 39th RAF squadrons.

Carboniferous sandstone varying in grain size from coarse to fine and in colour from white, yellow, pink to brown. When only Gritstone is mentioned, unless otherwise specified, assume it to be Gritstone (Sandstone), as this is the more common usage.
An isolated barn, cow house or shelter shed with a hayloft. Typically found in areas where farmsteads and fields were sited at a long distance from each other.
A decorative garden, often landscaped, laid out with intricate flower beds and hedges, and often containing ornate sculptures, fountains and garden ornaments.
The part of a house frequented by servants when not performing their duties.
A building or site used for the production of naphtha, a volatile petroleum-derived product used in the manufacture of solvents, cleaning fluids etc.
A house built by a local authority.
Similar in design to the Callender Hangar but with a reduced height of 17ft. Built to Air Ministry drawing number 17346/40.

A transportable hangar designed by Callender Cable and Construction to Air Ministry drawing number 6633/37. A steel box-girder framework with corrugated iron cladding and canvas doors it had a clear door height of 25ft.

Twin-engined air/sea rescue and anti-submarine patrol aircraft. Originally developed from the Wellington and intended as a bomber, entered RAF Coastal Command service in 1943. Fitted with a Leigh Light and ASV radar.
A building or site where the carcasses of whales were butchered and rendered into by products such as oil, fenk and whalebone.
A musical instrument producing sound from a membrane.
An instrument made by inserting a stick through a membrane stretched over a hollow vessel then played by rubbing the stick.
A circular frame with a stretched membrane and small cymbals in the frame.
An instrument made of a hollow cylinder or hemisphere covered at one or both ends and sounded by striking.
Kent
A small dwelling providing living accommodation for a tin miner.
Industrial worker's house which has been purpose built by an employer, as opposed to the workshop houses used by artisans.
A mechanism, either automated or consisting of winches and pulleys, that raises sacks of grain on ropes or chains from one floor of a mill to another, usually through one or a series of trap doors.

Six-crew, medium-range, twin-engined reconnaissance flying-boat. Entered service with 209 Squadron in 1939 but, due to design and operation problems, saw little action and was not produced in large numbers.
A ship used for treating patients or moving them between a battle zone and a safe area.
An alloy of tin, antimony and copper used as a replacement for pewter.
Citrus fruit of a distinctive orange colour.
A report detailing the archaeological and architectural potential of a site or locality.
Garden comprising rockwork features including grottoes, cascades and arches, often in different architectural styles ie. Gothic, Chinese and rustic. In use from the mid C18.
Use for vessels registered in Australia.
Use for vessels believed to come from Australasia but where the precise nationality is not known.
Use for vessels registered in New Zealand.
The entry to a hall through opposed doorways, but without a passage formed by a wall or partition.
A device used to gauge the speed of a vessel at sea.

A unenclosed feature, usually sub-terranean, constructed to contain water for public or private recreation and sporting activities. Sometimes part of a LIDO complex. Use INDOOR SWIMMING POOL for pools within a covering structure.
A bag or case stuffed or padded, designed to be slept on.
Soft items used to make a bed ready to be slept upon.
A small room used as a study for the preservation of papers etc. Generally use for any small room appended to a larger one.
Single-seat fighter-bomber with a single, midships engine and tricycle landing gear. After proving a failure as an air-combat fighter, was used mainly in the ground attack role.
A pond with underwater arches where the poles for masts were stored to prevent them from drying and splitting.
A stone with a concave upper surface on which grain was ground by using a rubbing stone.
A building or room where items of pottery are manufactured. Includes handcrafted and machine made pottery.

Two-seat, twin-engined light/medium bomber celebrated for its speed and versatility. Entering service in 1941, was also adapted for duties as a fighter-bomber, Pathfinder, mine-layer, transport, trainer and photo-reconnaissance aircraft.
A site where scientific and technical instruments such as microscopes are assembled.
A factory manufacturing timepieces, including clocks and watches.
A building, often converted from its original use, for use as a temporary accommodation by members of the Women's Land Army during the First and Second World Wars.
A small eating and drinking establishment or refreshment bar at a railway station for the use of passengers.
An iron bar or ingot of distinctive form with a pinched end previously thought to have been used as a medium of exchange in the Iron Age but is now believed to be a roughout for a sword.
A central area within a building.
A tall multi-storey block of flats, slender with a square plan.
A component of another building, often a house, used for storing nets.
A factory where linoleum is manufactured.
Used for orthographic drawings in the horizontal plane, generally from above generally depicts localised areas.
A small house, usually on the estate of a country house, forming part of a widow's dower and intended as her residence.
A representation in the round of a living being, allegorical personage, eminent person or animal, etc, sculptured, moulded or cast in marble, metal, plaster, etc.
A workshop where wooden brushes are manufactured on a small scale.

Imported Roman brooch with a wide, highly arched flat backed bow, one end rolled forward onto the head to form a hinge for the the pin. Named for the head inscription assumed to be a maker's name. Dated to first half of 1st entury AD.
A type of back to back house built on a hillside, of four storeys and with entrances at different levels.
An instrument for measuring height above sea level.
An area of ground used for the game of quoits.
A book in which visitors to a property, monument or exhibition record their thoughts and impressions on their experience.
A staircase where the vertical members are placed at the ends of flights to support the strings, handrails, trimmers and bearers.
A long barrelled firearm. The barrel is spirally grooved on the interior, which gives the bullet a spinning motion leading to greater accuracy over a longer range.
A device on an airfield for securing aircrafts when parked outside in order to prevent major movement due to the weather or other conditions.
A building containing a range of processes for cleaning and processing metallic ores.
A factory where tapestries were manufactured.
A box containing tinder, any dry inflammable material, usually also contains flint and steel for lighting fires.
Single-engine, single-seat biplane day fighter developed by Siddeley. Variations included an all-metal, fabric-covered Mk.III, which became the RAF's main fighter in the 1920s.
A craft of uncertain function over 30 metres long.

A trench dug through topsoil in an arable field in order to extract underlying clay which was then spread on the field and ploughed in to improve soil fertility. Usually found in peaty soil areas such as the Lincolnshire and Cambridgeshire fenlands.
An item used as part of a manicure.
A small file for manicuring a person's nails with.
A site used for the extraction of metallic zinc by a variety of processes.
A shelter on a firing range from which the wepaons testing can be viewed in safety.
A beaker adapted by having a pedestal base. The upper part of the pedestal is solid and may be thrown as an integral part of the vessel, or added as a separate element.(Source: MPRG)
A wall for growing fruit, dating in England from the mid-18th century, whose curving lines gave added strength, thus doing away with the need for buttressing.
A room for the storage of food and drink.
A sports arena with a steeply banked oval track for bicycle racing. There are outdoor as well as indoor velodromes.
Traditionally the chief residence of a land owner. Now used specifically to describe the residence of the Lord Mayor of London.
The residence of a master ropemaker.
A machine for combing out wool, mohair and alpaca, removing short fibres and any extraneous matter, and laying the long fibres more or less parallel to each other.
An aerial photograph taken at an angle other than 90 degrees to a feature in the landscape.
A WWII British biplane produced by Hawker Aircraft, used for army cooperation duties.
The structure at the top of a draw well.
A horticultural site where trees, shrubs and plants are grown for sale and transplanting elsewhere.
Photographic negative using nitrate process on a film base material.
A chair fixed to the end of a plank which was pivoted to allow the incumbent of the chair to be ducked into water as a punishment.
A complete written work including books and anthologies.
A slender and elegant base usually of Attic type with two tori, two scotiae and two astragals.
The measurement of trapped electrons by exposure to high-frequency electromagnetic radiation. A useful technique for dating tooth enamel, shells, coral and calcite form 5,000-1,000,000 years old.
A group of colleges and associated buildings belonging to a university.

A site, building or structure used for the detection of approaching hostile aircraft, shipping or missiles early enough to allow a counterattack or defensive measures to be taken. Use more specific term.
A complex of buildings using Radar or satellite tracking to monitor and detect enemy missile launches early enough to allow a counterattack or defensive measures to be taken.
A hoisting mechanism powered by electricity.
A stationary hoisting machine consisting of a rotating drum around which a cable, rope or chain is attached.
A site where machine tools, machines designed to remove surplus material from a work piece by accurately guided cutting tools, are manufactured.
A very short brace between post and tiebeam, or post and wall plate.
Card printed with an image, often a photograph on one side, and space for a short message and a postal address on the other.
Controlled investigation, recording and removal of archaeological deposits under threat of destruction from building development. A pre PPG 16 activity, usually under strict time constraints.
A guard or cover put in front of a fire to prevent embers or flames setting fire to a building.
A panel of often decorated wrought-ironwork forming the arch between two gate-piers or standards or above a gate. Also used for an arched support for a lamp-holder between two standards.
An instrument using lenses to magnify the object being viewed.
An ornate version of an eight-voluted Ionic capital known as an angular capital or Scamozzi under which are added two tiers of acanthus leaves.
A detached, sometimes monolithic vertical structural element usually circular, square or polygonal bearing an ornate eight-voluted Ionic Capital.
An order composed of elements of the Ionic and Corinthian orders.
A style of construction following an established set of criteria, based around the conventional use of a type of column.
Bases of this order are often referred to as spira and have a double astragal in the middle.
A lancet arch designed in the composite style.
The horizontal assembly of architrave, frieze and cornice carried upon columns and pilasters in the Composite order; and so containing elements of the Ionic and Corinthian orders.
Small scale enterprise producing bricks but not at the same site as the extraction of clay.
A place of worship for followers of the Wesleyan Association. This group split from the Methodists in 1836 and were separate until joining the Methodist Reform Church in 1857.
A dwelling, located at the entrance, or gates, to an estate or park, etc.
A bridge whose trusses or girders form parapets on either side of the deck.
A pouch for containing tobacco.
A coastal site producing salt by dissolving rocksalt or other impure salt in seawater, then boiling the concentrated brine in a PANHOUSE
A building or complex in which visitors to a prison can meet with the inmates under the supervision of the prison staff.
A house in which a pair of curved timbers form a bowed A-frame which supports the roof independently of the walls.
A CRUCK HOUSE where the cruck blades are truncated and joined by a collar beam, above which is a separate roof construction.
British twin-engined light/medium bomber developed from the model 142 civil transport. Noted for its speed, this three-crew monoplane had an all-metal, stressed skin structure and a 1000lb bomb load.
A building providing accommodation, dining and recreational facilities for commissioned naval officers.
A building providing dining facilities and recreation for commissioned officers.

Single-engine, two-crew multi-role aircraft designed for RAF Army co-operation. Entered RAF service in 1938. Noted for its role dropping agents into Europe, also served as a night-fighter, day ground-attack aircraft and target tug.
Use for the remains of an egg whether from a bird, reptile or amphibian.
A chapel attached to or founded by a college.
A building housing transformers to convert AC electricity supply to DC supply for use by tramcars.
A small sailing vessel armed with guns.
A roomspace within an abode which combines the specific functions of several of the more traditional roomspaces into a singular unified space.
A pot for drinking hot milk curdled with ale and flavoured with spice used as a remedy eg for colds.
A column at the corner of a structure.
A specific form of globular jar with a rounded or very sagging base and an inturned, generally simple, rim. (Source: MPRG)
A jar with a rounded profile merging into a rounded base with no discernible basal angle. (Source: MPRG)
Twin-engined, single-seat fighter-bomber. Flown by USAAF fighter groups from 1942, excelled as a ground-support fighter. Could carry two 1600 lb bombs or rocket projectiles.
A medieval wind instrument.
A flat based stone used in conjunction with a grinding stone
An interment of a human body that displays unusual burial practice such as positioning of the body, decapitation, dismemberment or over-secure burial.
A room in which cloaks, coats, hats etc may be left and often including coathooks, hat boxes and similar fixtures and fittings.

Wood and fabric transport glider, twenty of which were produced with twin Bristol Mercury engines. Fitted with a hinged nose for loading and unloading, this was the largest glider used by the RAF and could accomodate a 7-ton tank.
General Aircraft Limited.
Trees, hedges and shrubs planted in the form of a medieval cathedral sometimes used as a memorial.
A round barrow in which the mound and ditch are separated from each other by a berm. The ditch may be accompanied by an external (or occasionally internal) bank.

Also spelt "oszemundt" and other variants. Low-grade cast iron in the form of balls or spheres, produced in small workshops and exported across the North Sea and Baltic region. Particularly associated with 16th century Sweden.

Component part of a mungo and shoddy mill, where non-wool fibres from shredded material are destroyed by either soaking rags in an acid solution or rotating them in drums in a hot acidic gas followed by heat. The result is an all-wool product.
A mill in which poor quality woollen cloth was made from fibres produced by grinding light woollen rags.

A spatially discrete, though sometimes extensive, scatter of lithic artefacts recovered from the surface, eg. by fieldwalking, rather than from a particular archaeological context. Use particular types where appropriate.

A spatially discrete scatter of mixed artefactual material found on the ground, seabed or riverbed which may have been deposited over time rather than resulting from one particular event. Index particular types where appropriate.
A spatially discrete, though sometimes extensive, scatter of flint artefacts recovered from the surface, eg. by fieldwalking, rather than from a particular archaeological context.
A fort with a star trace plan, designed to increase the angles of fire.
An area of land which retains distinctive large-scale rectilinear land divisions characteristic of Roman agriculture. Generally aligned with the course of a Roman road.
A dockside crane with a solid curving jib made out of rivetted iron plates.
A crane with a projecting arm, usually one that can be raised and lowered.
An excavation from which cobble stone is obtained.
An area of a garden with a semi-circular backdrop formed by an ornamental, architectural structure or a natural feature grown to the required shape eg. a hedge

Single-engine, two-crew multi-role aircraft designed for RAF Army co-operation. Entered RAF service in 1938. Noted for its role dropping agents into Europe, also served as a night-fighter, day ground-attack aircraft and target tug.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 3156/41.
A hospital where patients would bathe daily in the sea or in indoor salt-water swimming baths.
A casement window, carried down to floor level, and opening like two-leafed glazed doors to a garden, veranda or terrace.
A window where the sash is hung vertically and the window opens outwards or inwards.
A structure for the storage of brine prior to processing, by evaporation, to extract salt.
A room or cupboard usually used for the storage of garments.
A recess or cupboard within a church, usually positioned near the altar, used for the storage of sacred vessels.
A recess, often containing shelves and usually fitted with a door or doors, used for the storage of items.
Use a term from the Archive Format list.
A pebble or small cobble with a small circular depression in one or both faces. The depressions, if on both faces, are usually directly opposite. These items may be unfinished pebble hammers.
Recorded interview intended to preserve the recollections of persons whose experiences or memories are representative of historical life.
A sound is a resource whose content is primarily intended to be rendered as audio. [DC] For example recorded speech, sounds or music.
Recording of a complete broadcast radio programme.
A small, often weatherboarded, roadside house in which cab drivers could rest and take refreshments. Late 19th century onwards.
A sweet fluid substance, the nectar of flowers, gathered and worked up for food by insects such as bees.
The residence of a station master.
A settlement showing evidence for one or more hut circles, enclosed by a distinct boundary ditch, wall, earth rampart or similar barrier. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period.

Six-crew, twin-engined medium night-bomber. Entered service in 1938 and was the RAF's principal bomber until 1943, participating in the first bombing raid of the war. Later versions served as torpedo and reconnaissance-bombers, transports and trainers.
A building used for the storage of equipment.
Recovery and removal of grease (lanolin) from raw wool.
A container designed to assist in cooling foodstuffs or liquids. Use specific type where known.
A container used to assist in cooling wine.
American twin-engined medium bomber. Entered service with the US 22nd Bombardment Group at Langley Field in February 1941. Also served with the 14th and 39th RAF squadrons.
An inclined wooden trough which channels grain evenly from the feed hopper into the eye of the stones in a corn mill.
A report detailing the results of an archaeological excavation.
A purpose-built dwelling for the supervisor of a factory, mine or other industrial complex.
The gearwheel on the upright shaft within a windmill from which secondary drives operating other parts of the machinery are powered. are taken

A pit in a road or trackway covered with a grid, usually of metal poles (but can be of wood or stone) with sufficient space between the poles to prevent animals from crossing, without restricting access for vehicles and people.
A shallow pond containing salt water and used for the manufacture of salt through the evaporation process. For metal vessels associated with the DIRECT BOILING and SLEECHING SALT WORKS use SALT PAN.
Hampshire
A waterwheel turned by the force of water falling upon the top of the wheel into buckets placed round the circumference.
The piece of stone or flint remaining after flakes have been produced. This is a by-product of tool manufacture.
A core with more than two distinct platforms usually including one or two striking surfaces and the the traces of former platforms. Usually restricted to flake production. (Source: SARC)
A stone or boulder which lies lengthways on the ground and may be used as a table, altar etc. Use only for isolated stones.
1st World War end-opening aeroplane hangar.
A dump for wasters; pieces of pottery spoiled in the manufacturing process.
An entrance chamber from tide water to basin, with gates at each end and means of pumping up or lowering the level of water to suit.
A recreation ground with usually permanent structure. It usually contains rides such as ghost trains, helter skelter and roller coasters.
A factory or works housing machinery used to produce stockings and socks, using mechanized knitting processes.
A tomb designed in the form of a cist or stone box placed over a burial. Its outward form often reproduces the features of the classical sarcophagus or medieval effigy base.
Solid bars made from steel.
Steel, usually unworked, in the form of bars.
Alloys of iron which have great strength, malleability and which are able to be tempered to different degrees of hardness. Used for the manufacturwe of tools, machinery etc.
Steel which has been formed into sheets.
A place of worship for Roman Catholics.
A structural member that supports a purlin. Use PRINCIPAL RAFTER where the principal is also a common rafter.
A principal that has a short, angled section, resembling a knee-joint, at one end.
A kiln in the form of a pit dug into the earth which was used for the the production of white coal prior to the Industrial Revolution.
Meat precooked and then sealed in cans made from steel, tin or aluminium plate to preserve it.
The meat obtained from cattle.
A fatty substance derived from the fat of animals used in cooking.
The cured flesh of a pig.
The flesh obtained from pigs eaten as food.
The flesh of animals, either raw or cooked, used as food.
A processed used to increase the thickness of the natural oxide layer on the surface of metal parts. The part being treated forms the anode of an electrolytic cell.
A column in which the shaft is interrupted by stone bands.

The interpretation of information on aerial photographs usually resulting in the production of maps and records of archaeological sites and landscapes. Many aerial photographs may be consulted for a single analytical survey.
Any form of fastener used to fasten a girdle together.
An often ornate building housing the source of an ornamental cascade, eg. Chatsworth House.
A large park for keeping deer. In medieval times the prime purpose was for hunting.

Area in a deer park where a single deer was chased by dogs over a set distance, with bets made on the outcome. It usually includes a stand (for viewing) and can also include three distance markers, a finishing post and a ditch behind the last post.

Collective name for the oolitic limestone quarried in the Isle of Purbeck region, geologically classified into two main groups. Firstly, a fine grained whitish variety, Purbeck Portland, secondly a fossil-rich cream/gold to grey variety, Swanage Stone etc
A sculptured group comprising a chariot drawn by four horses.
A place of worship for members of the Russian Orthodox Church, the national church of Russia.

A small tower or bartizan, which was often placed at the angles of a castle, to increase the flanking ability, some only serving as corner buttresses. Also used to describe the small rectangular towers situated between the milecastles along Hadrians Wall.
A building used for the care of the sick. Only to be used where part of a complex, eg. a workhouse. In such cases use with appropriate monument type.
American, four-engined, long range, medium/heavy day bomber. Produced in greater numbers than any other American aircraft during the war.
A large warehouse or store for upholstery.
A small bag or detachable outside pocket.

A monument consisting of a small (generally less than 100m diameter) subcircular enclosure with a narrow approach way consisting of parallel ditches (thus banjo shaped). Believed to be associated with stock management in the Later Prehistoric period.
A site where cementstone nodules are extracted.
The case containing the charge for a firearm.
A wooden hammer.
A written work issued in parts, with the intention of creating a completed sequence.
1st World War end-opening aeroplane hangar.
A mill which contains machinery for separating grain from the chaff.
A concave groove or series of grooves.
A ring worn on a toe.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around two sides of an open cattle yard.
A longitudinal member in a roof, running beneath the collar beams and intended to give stability to the roof.
A purlin that is joined to a principal rafter by a tenon joint.
A horizontal timber set in the plane of a roof's slope and supporting common rafters.
A small two masted craft, with oars as well as sails.
An instrument for measuring or drawing angles, consisting of a quarter circle, graduated to 90 degrees, with a movable arm.
A prepared area of ground, featuring a 'mini' golf course with obstacles, used to undertake the leisure pursuit of miniature golf or 'crazy golf'. Often popular at seaside resorts.
A tool used to polish the surface of an artefact.
A moulding which projects beyond the face of a panel or frame, usually found in panelling or in doors.

A civil passenger transport biplane produced by the Farman Aviation Works from 1919. Instrumental in the creation of early airlines and commercial routes in Europe after World War I. Initially designed in 1918 as a heavy bomber. Some 60 units built.
A building used for the finishing, drying and storage of lace.
A large store for textiles.
A naturally occurring deposit formed by the decomposition and partial carbonisation of vegetable matter in waterlogged conditions.
A Classical convex moulding, often decorated with egg-and-dart or similar motifs.
A small projection designed to allow space for a bed.

A building or buildings ranged around a courtyard on at least three sides. They occur in the Iron Age, as well as being an influential plan type of house from the 15th century onwards. Index with appropriate period.
An object used to retrieve birds used in hawking. Consists of feathers tied to a rope, food is contained in the lure whilst training the birds.
A building or site incorporating equipment used for detecting the presence of enemy aircraft or ships. Radar Stations can also be used to aid aircraft navigation in dark or poor conditions.
A radar station with sets operating on a wavelength of 10cm or less. They were highly accurate radars and gave better sea level coverage than the earlier Chain Home Low stations.
A radar station with sets operating on a wavelength of 1.5m. Chain Home Low Stations were intended for use in locating low-flying aircraft but was also capable of detecting high-flying aircraft.

Part of the WWII air defence radar system, whereby in 1939 a chain of radar stations were established along the south and east coast of Britain. The equipment was based upon apparatus developed for ionospheric research.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Coast Defence Chain Home Low Station
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A radar station with sets operating on a wavelenght of 1.5m established to provide radar plotting of both shipping and aircraft movements.
Timber from trees of the genus Juglans, used for the manufacture of furniture
An ornamental decoration which projects from the surface it is part of.
A thin board forming part of a musical instrument and placed in a position to strengthen or increase its sound.
Lantern slide developed using a wet process.
A distinctive, clerestory-roofed building of five 10ft bays, used for the drying, storage and packing of military parachutes and built to Air Ministry drawing number 17865/39.
A terrace house sharing a common wall with its neighbours.

A house within a row. At first floor level a gallery which runs through the front of the building. Access to the gallery was gained by steps set at intervals along the row. Commonly found in the city of Chester.
A curved roofing tile.
A small, fast boat used for carrying orders between sailing vessels.
A site where clay is extracted from the surface of the ground.
Decorative ornamentation in the form of an upright, stalked trefoil used in Tudor architecture.
Seaside structure, usually consisting of a manmade retaining wall that keeps a relatively large area of the tidal water partitioned off for controlled boating or swimming.

A fishing vessel which tows a dredger to gather oysters. This is an iron wedge shaped contrivance with a small net attached. Towed behind the vessel the iron wedge loosens the oysters and they fall into the net.

A tunnel built alongside a canal tunnel to enable a horse to be unhitched and led through the hillside to meet the barge when it emerged from the tunnel. Mainly built prior to the development of the towpath tunnel.
A free-standing house, not joined to another on either side.
A biplane, reconnaissance aircraft with a crew of 3 or 4 which equipped 3 and 22 squadrons RAF before passing to the Fleet Air Arm. Produced in two variants.
Ore hearth specifically for the refining of silver.
An arrangement of one or more standing stones. Use particularly for isolated recumbent stones, or where original form of monument unclear. Use specific type where known.
A group of, usually three, standing stones forming a square with an open side and often found with a stone circle.
Sites, buildings or structures involved in passive air defence, usually by forcing hostile aircraft to fly high or drop their bombs on the wrong targets. Use more specific term.
A chapel adjacent to, associated with or containing a well.
A textile mill where crepe is manufactured.Crepe is a fine cloth particularly silk or mixture of silk and cotton.
An establishment where deaf people receive education, training and social support.
A site where canvas, coarse, unbleached cloth, made from hemp or flax, was manufactured.
An object used in tablet weaving to control the shed.
A group of planted trees or shrubs, generally of uniform age and of a single species.
Data stored in a format that is meant to be manipulated and read in one or more software systems.
A short principal rafter that that rises from a tiebeam to a collar.
A thick fabric cover used to provide warmth.
An initially worked quern that is still to be finished.
Area of a garden for the cultivation of ferns.
A strong, fortified dwelling, of between two and four storeys. Occupied only in times of trouble built mainly in the border country of the North from the mid 14th to the 17th century.
An underground foot tunnel primarily constructed to allow for the passage of pedestrians beneath an over ground obstacle.
A coastal site producing salt by scraping up salt-impregnated sand and silt, leeching out the salt to produce a concentrated brine, then boiling in 'saltcotes' (small huts containing lead pans)
A substance secreted by some plants which hardens upon drying but is soluble in water.

A roughly circular monument featuring a low, more or less level platform of stones surrounded or retained by a low stone kerb. Some may feature a small central open area, thus resembling a ring cairn.
A stony mound containing or concealing deliberately deposited human remains. Use specific type where known.
A building in which goods or items are stored. Use more specific type where known.
Loading machinery tipping coal into railway wagons usually at a pithead.
A tippler, a machine for loading wagons at a pithead, operated by hydraulic power.
Finishing process for cloth, especially linen, running the cloth between heavy rollers.

Two-seat, twin-engined fighter/fighter-bomber designed as a replacement for the Bf110. Of the 600 or so produced, only 258 reached the Luftwaffe due to serious design faults. The ME210 was superseded by the ME410 Hornisse.
A site available to the public for the pursuit of leisure and recreational activities.
A complex of buildings and earthworks constructed for the storage of bombs and pyrotechnics.
A commercial premises offering advice on destinations and other travel arrangements, and where travellers may purchase flights,make hotel reservations or book package holidays and tours.
A lime kiln where the fuel is not mixed with the limestone but burnt below it.

A streamlined, twin-engined bomber, the DO17 entered service in 1937 with the Condor Legion, having started life as a high-speed mail and passenger transport aircraft, a role for which it was ill-suited due to the narrowness of the fuselage.
An artificial hill constructed in Tudor gardens, especially, to provide a good view.
An artificial mound, generally conical, placed within a garden or park to provide a viewing point to overlook the garden or park. It may also serve as a visual focus in the garden or park layout.
A works where bleach is manufactured.
A place where products are manufactured from wood.
A building or site for the industrial manufacture of locks.
A stone on which plague victims placed vinegar-disinfected money to pay for food left for them by the townspeople.
A factory used for the production of acetate.
A pillow-shaped, flat topped rectangular mound often surrounded by a shallow ditch used to farm rabbits.
Hard white/grey coloured liassic limestone. Quarried on the Devon-Dorset border.
Hard, white/grey coloured liassic limestone. Quarried near Somerton in Somerset.
An artificial steep-sided earthen mound on, or in, which is set the principal tower of a castle.
A curved moulding with a sharp edge running along its centre. So named as its profile resembles the keel of a ship.
A residence of two or three monks of the Benedictine order dependent on an English mother house.
The taking of samples at regular intervals from the surface of a study area in order to retrieve information on the different chemical elements present.
The systematic use of portable X-Ray Fluorescence equipment to retrieve information on the different chemical elements present in the soil.
The systematic collection of samples from a defined study area analysed for phosphate content. Elevated concentrations of phosphate are a generalised signature of human activity.
A large bag made of coarse cloth or thick paper.
A pier of brick, masonry, etc, to which the hinges of a gate are attached.
Large submarine intended to operate with a surface fleet at sea.
A long stone or metal vessel for dogs to drink water from.
A wall, usually perforated to allow free passage of air, supporting the ground-floor joists of a building.
A window which has its head beam decorated with elements of tracery.
This period follows on from the Neolithic and is characterized by the increasing use of Bronzework. It is subdivided in the Early,Middle and Late Bronze Age.
The second subdivision of the Bronze Age.
A grain grinding mill in which the meal is ground into flour between revolving metal rolls.
A factory where collars, for shirts and other garments, are manufactured.
A place where ropes are made.
Buildings and structures associated with the manufacture of rope.
A tiebeam whose central section is omitted to increase head room; its inner ends are held by a slip-braces or struts rising from a dropped tiebeam and can be used in end frames.
A clear area in a church covered by the transepts and crossing.
A jug with a rounded profile and a rounded base, i.e. with no discernible basal angle. (Source: MPRG)
An earth derived pigment.

A forcing house used for various types of fruit which first appeared in the 19th century. Lean-to houses were used for wall-grown fruit and free-standing houses for fruit grown in pots or for trees planted in the ground.
A triangular gable usually above an entablature.
A pediment with a gap at its apex, sometimes filled with an urn or other decorative feature.
Food, usually hay or straw, kept for the feeding of animals.
A craft used to retrieve torpedoes after practice firings.
A timber running obliquely across a series of common rafters.
A building, or group of buildings, deliberately designed for rhinos.
Photographic plate, on glass, developed using a wet process.

A circular pillbox, usually consisting of a concrete pipe with a timber and corrugated iron roof, surrounded and covered by earth and sandbags. Built to a design by Norcon Ltd, a company dealing in concrete pipes.
A place with organized amusements for people on holiday.
Purposely built camp with recreational facilities and individual chalets for accommodation.
A stringed instrument with a fingerboard which has frets on it.
An instrument played mainly by plucking the strings. Use narrower term where known.

An Iron Age round defended house, found mainly in the north and west of Scotland. Brochs have a tapering profile and thick, usually hollow dry stone walls which contain galleries, cells and a stairway, with guard cells at the entrance.
Expanding storage tank for gas, often includes a meter for measuring the amount used.
Storage tank for coal gas and possibly other types of gas .
Use specific type where known, eg picture frame.
A border put around a picture to enhance it and ususally to hold in place the picture and any covering, eg glass.
A place where soup and food is available to the homeless.
A cemetery comprising inhumations or cremations interred in stone cists.
A stone, usually found in a schoolyard, either built into a wall or forming part of a free standing structure, on which pencils can be sharpened. Although increasingly rare examples do survive.
A gulley in the form of a circle for holding vertical posts in the walls of iron age round houses.
A type of engine house creating power by means of compressed air, typically associated with collieries where it is used for raising coal.

A structure over an opening usually formed of wedge-shaped blocks of brick or stone held together by mutual pressure and supported at the sides; they can also be formed from moulded concrete/ cast metal. A component; use for free-standing structure only.
An underground channel with a vaulted roof. Use specific type where known.
A tunnel with strengthened construction, used as an emergency exit from a civil defence building.
Mark 2 or the second variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
An area of ground, set apart for the burial of the dead.
A cemetery containing more than one burial type eg cremations and inhumations.
A group of cairns in close proximity which are predominantly funerary or ritual in nature.

A high status, walled, Roman burial ground containing cremations and/or inhumations in mausolea, tombs, barrows, coffins or cists. Dating from the late 1st to the 4th Century AD. DO NOT USE for cemeteries of later dates which are walled.
A cluster of closely spaced barrows and related monuments (eg. ring ditches). Use with specific barrow-types where known.
A shaft or pit dug in the ground over a supply of spring-water.

A natural spring located within a, usually small, man-made structure, such as a niche or a box. The structure is so placed to accomodate use for a specific non-religious function, such as communal bathing.
A hand held weapon used to throw missiles such as stones or bullets.
A roof design, common to weaving sheds, featuring a sawtooth profile with unequal slopes forming each ridge and lights on its northern side.
A battery equipped and ready to fire salutes
A large vessel with raised or applied cordons running horizontally on the body of the vessel.
A garden incorporating Egyptian architectural features such as sphinxes and tomb-like features, etc.
A large tent which can be used as accommodation for parties and exhibitions.
A buttress placed at the exterior corner of a building, forming a 135 degree angle with the walls it supports.
A small container used for dispensing table salt for seasoning purposes.

Seven/eight-crew, heavy night-bomber. The first four-engine bomber to join the RAF, with a bomb load of 14000 lb, entered service in 1940. Superseded as a bomber by the Lancaster and Halifax, later versions served as transports and tugs.
A building housing a generator.
A textile factory where the process of doubling, the twisting together of two spun yarns, takes place.
A building situated within the estate of a manor or country house.
A laundry situated within the estate of a manor or country house.
A building containing a small stone cylindrical furnace, eg. used for tin smelting in Cornwall.
A wide ditch surrounding a building, usually filled with water. Use for moated sites, not defensive moats. Use with relevant site type where known, eg. MANOR HOUSE, GARDEN, etc.

A tandem two-seat, twin-engined, all-weather, long-range supersonic jet interceptor fighter/fighter-bomber originally developed for the United States Navy by McDonnell Aircraft.It first entered service in 1960 with the U.S. Navy.
McDonnell Douglas was a major American aerospace manufacturer and defense contractor, producing a number of famous commercial and military aircraft.
A window in the form of a three-leafed clover.
A quern where one stone is rotated on another to grind grain.
A post, usually of iron or concrete, used to support a street lamp.
Weight on the end of a graduated line for measuring the depth of water.
American, four-engined, long range, medium/heavy day bomber. Produced in greater numbers than any other American aircraft during the war.

A 19th century establishment for the provision of work for the unemployed poor of a parish; later an institution administered by Guardians of the Poor, in which paupers are lodged and the able-bodied set to work.
An aircraft, usually towed or radio-controlled, designed for use as an air-to-air, or ground-to-air, gunnery target.
A piece of ground, or a building, on which artillery may be fired at targets.
An area of ground on which anti tank guns can be placed for testing purposes and to practice firing at targets.
Single-seat fighter-bomber with a single, midships engine and tricycle landing gear. After proving a failure as an air-combat fighter, was used mainly in the ground attack role.
The land mass comprising, the continents of North and Central America and South America. Use more specific type.
A curfew with a rounded profile merging into a rounded top, with no discernible angle. (Source: MPRG)
A textile factory where the process of doubling, the twisting together of two spun yarns, takes place.
A water-drain connected to a stone bowl within a niche in the south wall of a chapel, used to receive the water in which the priest washed his hands and rinsed the Chalice.
Small stone hearth set up in a shallow pit. Burns vegetation and coppiced twigs to produce potash.

A jar adapted by the addition of a pierced bunghole just above the base. The hole can be simply a hole in the wall of the vessel or made through a circular knob or disc of clay. There may be one or two vertical loop handles. (Source: MPRG)
A pit where calcium oxide (Quicklime) has been hydrated to produce calcium hydroxide, known as slaked lime.
The residence of a prison governor.
A firing step from which standing defenders could fire over the crest of a high parapet.
A cutting, bank or block positioned against the wall of a trench, fort, parapet etc. to allow riflemen to shoot over the crest of the wall or parapet from a standing position.
Use for vessels registered in Austria.
A tank found on hop farms in which creosote was held, heated from below by a fire with a chimney. The ends of hop poles were dipped in the tar to prevent rotting in soil.
Container for the storage of unspecified materials.
A screen separating the choir from other parts of the church.
A fence or barrier made of metal or wooden rails.

A core which has two opposing platforms. One end serving as the main platform for the removal of blades - the other being used to straighten the face of the core and correct knapping errors. Removals are taken from the full circumference. (Source: SARC)
A sharp pointed nail with a large flat head.
A decorative container for serving cream.
A Roman brooch dating from approximately 50 to 150 AD. Derived from the earlier Aesica Brooch, and fitted with a hinged pin, the body widens to a triangular plate below the bow.
Miles M.14 Magister. Single-engine, two-crew training and communications aircraft. Spruce and plywood in construction, with open cockpits and a fixed landing gear, served between 1937 and 1945.
A large site specializing in the manufacture of locomotives.
The dwelling place of a farm worker.
Photographic negative developed on paper.
The residence of a storekeeper of naval ordnance.
British three-seat, single-engine light bomber. All metal in construction, this monoplane had a 1000 lb bomb load.
A centre used by the Territorial Army, the volunteer reserve of the British army.
A document or book written by hand.
Use for vessels registered in Venezuela.
A roof truss used for small spans with a saw-tooth overall shape braced by vertical and diagonal members.
Use for vessels registered in France.
A place where dockyard craftsmen both design and build ships.
Single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer used in secondary flying training schools. Serving from 1939-50, was also used as a target tug for gunnery practice.
Woven material.

An area of a port, dock or harbour, often including buildings for passport control and customs, where passengers and vehicles using ferry services can embark/disembark and where supplies can be taken on board.
An object designed to add curls into hair.

A term for a type of house, with varying definitions according to period. Roman villas were high-status and usually associated with a rural estate, whereas Georgian and later period villas were often semi-detached, town houses.
Specify in Description
A steam driven winding engine house for raising coal to the surface.
Sporting venues and competitions in progress.
Workshop for placing handles on mugs, teapots, etc.
Goods, usually foodstuffs, which have been sealed inside canisters, usually made of tin or steel, to preserve them.
Meat precooked and then sealed in cans made from steel, tin or aluminium plate to preserve it.

A flask holding gunpowder used to prime a firearm, ie to provide a small quantity of gunpowder to be put in the pan which would be lit to set off the main charge in the barrel. The powder would often be a finer grade than that used for the charge.
A tower-like structure of wood or brick with a wooden cap and sails which are driven around by the wind producing power to work the internal machinery. Use with product type where known.

A type of tower mill, either with turbine-type sails able to take wind from any direction, or with sails working with shrouds to direct wind from one direction. The sails directly drove millstones set beneath them.
A fairground ride, often a permanent structure, consisting of a tower with an internal staircase and an external spiral shaped slide.
A type of fairground or seaside amusement, often a permanent structure, where carriages travel at high speeds on an undulating track raised some distance from the ground.
Forms of ride which are designed for entertainment.
A small, usually inexpensive, restaurant with a limited menu of light meals served at counters or tables.
A training ground and fighting arena for knightly sports.
A building used for drilling out the bores of cannon and other military pieces.
A room or part of a church where the vestments, vessels and records are kept.
Mill for fine grinding of tin ore between millstones.
A factory where food is preserved either by freezing, salting or pickling
A building, either purpose-built or modified, used for the co-ordination of the Fire Service.
Building housing machinery used in the production of wooden pulley blocks for the rigging of sailing ships.
A mound used to elevate buildings associated with a fishery e.g. smoke houses, above the level of a flood plain.
A place in which turpentine is produced.
The SI derived unit for the refractive index.
A residence of two or three monks of the Augustinian order dependent on a foreign mother house.
A large, "bottle-shaped", oven of brick construction used in the baking or firing of pottery.
Hard semi-translucent ceramic material made out of kaolin, quartz and feldspar which is biscuit fired at around 1000 degrees Celsius and glaze fired at around 1300 degrees Celsius.
A mill where long-staple hair, often from llamas, is made into yarn.
Four-crew, twin-engined, general reconnaissance flying-boat. Entered service after World War One, becoming the RAF's standard flying-boat until replaced by the Supermarine Southampton in 1925.
A factory where cheese is produced and processed.
An open pit from which coprolites or phosphatic nodules were extracted. Commonly found in the Fens and East Anglia coprolites were ground up and used as fertilizer.
Site or building used for paintballing.
An mill in which manganese was ground to a powder between two horizontal millstones.

A type of prefabricated house erected, to 11 approved designs, as part of the Temporary Housing Programme, between 1944 and 1948. This scheme was devised to relieve the post-war housing shortage at a time when conventional materials were unavailable.
A building combining a pigsty at ground level with a poultry house in a loft over.
An area attached to a house, or part of an estate used for pleasure and recreation.
A patented design of twin-cylinder, inverted vertical steam engine, which can be started irrespective of the position of the crank.
An enclosed piece of land, generally large in area, used for hunting, the cultivation of trees, for grazing sheep and cattle or visual enjoyment. Use more specific type where known.
A small park or enclosure where animals are kept.

Single-engine, testbed monoplane built to Air Ministry Specification 43/37. Only twelve were produced, the first of which tested the Sabre I engine in 1940, and were used throughout the war. The cockpit could seat two observers behind the pilot.

Formed in 1936 as British Marine Aircraft Ltd. to construct civil flying-boats. In 1937, with the arrival of H P Folland, formerly Chief designer for Gloster Aircraft Co., became Folland Aircraft, Ltd..
A raised platform at the end of a hall on which the high table sat, though sometimes used to describe the table itself.
A miniature railway on which targets can be placed to provide moving targets on a firing range.
An area of ground used for the testing of, and practicing with, weapons against fixed and moveable targets.
A workshop or factory where brass articles are made by casting molten material into a mould.
A type of pottery kiln in which air rises up inside the oven to be forced back down and out through the base of the oven.
A beam steam engine, reciprocating or rotative, powered by two steam cylinders side by side.
An aircraft equipped to deploy explosive mines.

Three-seat, twin-engined minelaying, torpedo-bombing and reconnaissance twin-float seaplane. First flown in 1936, in 1938 it set eight world speed records for its class in various range and payload categories.
A commemorative stone inscribed with a dedicatory inscription to a person or event.
A stone commemorating a person or event.
City in Northern Sweden.
A place where gold is worked into articles or products.
A geophysical technique for imaging subsurface structures in cross section from electrical measurements made at the surface, or by electrodes in one or more boreholes.
A pond storing water to supply a HAMMER POND.
A type of updraught intermittent kiln of rectangular plan and battered sides, but with an open top.
A toilet or toilets for public use.
A bolt for fastening metal plates. One end is put through prepared holes and then beaten flat.
A burial ground for military personnel.
A metal or pneumatic rubber rim to a wheel.
Record of an individual context (ie layer or feature) from an archaeological excavation.
A wall containing apertures to allow a weapon to be fired through it.
Use only for historic state of Czechoslovakia, where new state is known index with CZECH REPUBLIC or SLOVAKIA.
An industrial facility concerned with the manufacture of magnesium from magnesium hydroxide derived from sea water. Magnesium was used in the manufacture of aircraft.
A trench cut around a building or structure to prevent the spread of fire.
A temporary brick and timber watch office based on the all-timber 2423/39. Built after 1941 on many Operational Training Unit airfields the design was superseded by 8936/40.
A stringed instrument with a very rounded body.
A workshop where baskets were manufactured.
A railway at a dockyard used for the transportation of goods to and from the dock side.
Building housing switch gear to control electricity supply either to the National Grid, industrial or domestic premises.
The remains of living organisms preserved in stone over a long time period. This may be the internal or external moulds of, usually, the hard parts of an organism (shells, bones, etc.).
Pertaining to or deriving from a living organism. See ANIMAL Class list for narrow terms.
Hard, protective covering made largely of calcium salts secreted by soft bodied invertebrate animals.
Animal skin that has been hardened or treated by a tanning process.
Any of the pieces of hard tissue consisting largely of calcium phosphate that make up the skeleton of a vertebrate animal.
A liquid derived from wood tar through a distillation process. Now used to describe timber preservative derived from coal tar.
Building used for field studies and outdoor pursuits in the countryside and in an urban context.
Personal apparatus for telling the time, worn either as jewellery or purely functional in nature, usually on the wrist or as a suspended fob.
A factory used for the manufacture of ordnance including small arms, ammunition, artillery pieces and armoured fighting vehicles.
Mercantile vessel converted during the First World War for the purposes of examining and boarding enemy vessels.
The space in which a door is placed, allowing passage through.
A progressive development of the DO17, the twin-engined DO217 entered service in 1941. The DO217 saw service as a bomber over the UK and took part in the 'Baedecker' raids of 1942.
An enclosed settlement surrounded by a single or double row of close-set timbers embedded in a foundation trench, without ditches or banks.

A small, defended settlement dating to the Early Iron Age, located on spurs, promontories or hilltops. The defences are marked by single or double trenches which originally held substantial palisades.
A monument featuring a bank or mound constructed primarily of stone. Use specific type where known.
Long alignment of cairns lying between two large cairns; first recognized as a site type on Sourton Tor, Dartmoor.
Traditionally the chief residence of a land owner. Now used specifically to describe the residence of the Lord Mayor of London.
A railway at a dockyard used for the transportation of goods to and from the dock side.
A concrete which is either aerated or made from lightweight aggregate.
A building or school where music is taught.
Planks or boards manufactured from softwood timber.
A circular building for housing and repairing railway locomotives.
A manmade barrier built across a river in order to increase the depth of water.
A sawn piece of timber, thinner than a plank and often rectangular.
A portable object of stone, bone, metal or other material featuring a deliberately engraved or incised design.
The horizontal beam on a lock gate.
Buoyant, light material obtained from the cork tree.
A type of pottery oven in which the air passes from the base of the kiln out through the top.
A two-storey watch office, built to Air Ministry drawing number 1959/34 but with slight design modifications as detailed in drawing number 1960/34.
A device for catching fish, may be a portable or permanent structure, often a fence or row stakes made in a river, harbour, etc
A fence or row of stakes, often with nets attached forming an enclosure within a river or harbour and used for catching, or holding, fish.
A pot for ink usually housed in a hole in a desk.
A hospital block from where patients are discharged after an operation or other treatment.
A stylised, leafy decorative feature reminiscent of, and sometimes referred to as, honeysuckle

A tower or structure, with a powerful light or lights at the top, usually erected at an important or dangerous point on or near the sea-coast for the warning and guidance of mariners, but can also be erected inland for the guidance of travellers.

A lighthouse whose lantern is sufficiently high to be seen at a long range and above low lying cloud or fog. In locations where varying weather conditions occur a High Light is usually accompanied by a LOW LIGHT built alongside or nearby.

A lighthouse whose lantern is sufficiently low to be seen below low lying cloud. In locations where varying weather conditions occur a Low Light is usually accompanied by a HIGH LIGHT built alongside or nearby.
A lighted pillar or LIGHTHOUSE, eg. Dunston Pillar, Lincs., erected in 1751 to guide travellers over the heath.
A refreshment house in a public park or country house garden.

Highly successful, two-seat, biplane fighter and reconnaissance aircraft with both forward and rear facing guns. Designed to replace the BE2, it entered service with the RFC in mid-1917 and remained in service until 1932.
A wooden cylinder or dowel used for pinning planks or timbers together.
A small stone structure, usually at a spring or bog, in which dairy products were kept cool on slate shelves.
A bridge, carrying a footpath or road, usually across marshy or waterlogged ground.
Second World War defence work usually consisting of securinng points for a boom defence, associated gun, and searchlight, emplacements
A block for mounting a horse.

Seven/eight-crew, heavy night-bomber. The first four-engine bomber to join the RAF, with a bomb load of 14000 lb, entered service in 1940. Superseded as a bomber by the Lancaster and Halifax, later versions served as transports and tugs.
A communal room or building attached to flats.
A light plough used to break up the earth. It does not have a mouldboard to turn the earth.
A place where sandstone is excavated.
A place where padlocks and rim locks for doors are made from iron and brass.
An institution for the imprisonment of felons and debtors.
A windbrace that bypasses one purlin to be jointed into the next purlin or principal.
Grains of rock fragment larger than coarse sand and finer than pebbles (diameter 2-4mm).
A house with an aisle on one side only.
A structure providing protection against the weather at tram stops.
A shelter on a firing range from which the wepaons testing can be viewed in safety.
A hot steam bath introduced from the East, in which heavy perspiration is followed by soaping, washing, massage and cooling.
Building used for the display of inscription panels and memorials to those buried in the underlying catacomb.
A multi-purpose, two-storey barn, built on a hillside with entrances at both levels to a first floor threshing barn and ground floor animal housing.
A building for the storage of all stores supplied for naval service other than victualling and armament.
A length of cord usually made from twisting fibres together which increases the strength of the rope.
The pelts of beavers used for the manufacture of fur coats and hats.
A comb or slide used to hold hair in place.
A ring used to hold hair in place.
An object originally created to be worn on the human body or on clothing for ornamentation rather than for protection or as a body covering.
Decorative ornamentation worn in the hair.
A pin used to hold hair in place.
Coiled metal used to give or limit motion.
A bridge, often over a canal or road, allowing access between two parcels of land.
A jar with a rounded profile merging into a rounded base with no discernible basal angle. (Source: MPRG)
A specific form of globular jar with a rounded or very sagging base and an inturned, generally simple, rim. (Source: MPRG)
Squared block of glass, tile, stone or marble used in mosaic.
A measure for liquid holding two pints which is a quarter of a gallon.
A circular kiln or oven used in the manufacture of bricks. Common in Staffordshire in the 18th century.
A place of meeting and worship for followers of the Church Army, a body of trained lay evangelists devoted to evangelism and social work.

Two-crew, twin-engined bomber. Entered production in 1934 and designed for dual use as a high-speed commercial transport. Technical problems hindered its use as a bomber and led to conversion to high-altitude reconnaissance.

Junkers Flugzeug und Motorenwerke, A.G.. Formed in 1910 with Professor Junkers being granted a patent for an all-wing aeroplane. Produced first successful all-metal aeroplane, the Junkers J1, in 1915.

A single-engine dive-bomber, the JU87 was very successful during the invasions of Poland and France but suffered heavy losses during the Battle of Britain. Withdrawn from NW Europe in 1941 for use in the Mediterranean and on the Eastern Front.
A twin-engined development of the JU88, the JU188 had a higher service ceiling and greater maximum speed. JU188s operated over the UK from 1944 onwards as night intruders and reconnaissance aircraft.

A twin-engined, multi-role aircraft built by Junkers. Originally designed as a medium bomber with the speed of a fighter, but its adaptability allowed it to fulfil the roles of night fighter, torpedo-bomber, anti-tank aircraft and photo-reconnaissance.
The grains of various plants from which new plants grown.
Seed of the cotton plant from which edible oil is extracted.
A building used for the storage of rope made from the fibrous stems of the hemp plant.
Transport vessel hired for the enforced removal of convicts to penal colonies abroad(e.g. Virginia, Australia), or for their return to Britain.
Molluscs found in salt or brackish water. Use more specific term where known.
The remains of the shell of an oyster.
The remains of a shell of a mussel.
A power driven machine or device for raising a liquid or forcing it along a pipe, or for compressing a gas.
A pump for removing condensed steam from the condenser of a steam raising plant.
Two masted vessel with a square rig on both masts.
Hindu festival dedicated to Shiva.
Characterisation of organic molecules extracted from fossil or sub-fossil materials, including lipids, DNA etc.

Single-engine, two-crew fighter, also used for convoy escort and reconnaissance. Designed to operate from aircraft carriers. Entered service with the Fleet Air Arm in 1940 and remained in use until 1945.
A turret, tower or look out occupying a prominent position to provide a view, either a separate building, or part of a villa.
A classical order in which the columns or pilasters are applied to a wall.
An airfield with associated hangars and control buildings used for the storage, maintenance and deployment of military aircraft and airships flown by the Royal Naval Air Service.
A landing circle marked out in white used as the airfield symbol.
A landing and taking-off area for military aircraft. Often includes ancilliary structures and buildings for the maintenance and storage of aircraft, etc.
A large tank where particles suspended in water, or other liquids, are allowed to sink to the bottom forming a sediment.
A truss in which spaces between timbers are filled, as between rooms and at the ends of a building.
The part of an object by which it is held when in use, being moved or carried.
A mutiple role hangar for aircraft and general storage, manufactured in the USA as a kit for on-site assembly during WWII and post-war. It comprises a steel box frame and a canvas covering.
A building or room used for the practice and study of dance.
The Percival Aircraft Company was formed in 1932 and re-organized as Percival Aircraft Ltd. in 1937, when the works moved from Gravesend to Luton.
Single-engine, spruce and plywood, fabric-covered training and communications low-wing monoplane. Served from 1939 to 1950.

Feature, typically a ship, boat, aircraft or vehicle, deliberately sunk for recreational and diver educational purposes in inland bodies of water used as dive centres, such as lakes and water-filled quarries, or offshore as artificial reefs.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising an approximately circular stony mound which contains a stone-built chamber, with or without additional lateral chambers.
An outbuilding containing brewing equipment, as opposed to a large commercial BREWERY. Often found in conjunction with public houses, country houses etc.
For example asthma, Cystic Fibrosis, Pneumoconiosis, Bronchieactasis, mycotic and other chronic infections, sleep related breathing disorders and lung transplant.
An abbey or priory belonging to the Tironian order.
A building housing the engines used to power equipment used by a searchlight, anti-aircraft or coastal battery.

Permian limestones which have had their chemical composition naturally altered with the calcium content being replaced by magnesium. Fine grained and varying from yellow/brown to cream in colour, although they weather to a dark grey.
American-built, twin-engined flying-boat designed for maritime patrol and reconnaissance. Entered US Naval service in 1936 as the PBY-1; christened the Catalina by the RAF, who used it from 1939 on.
Documents relating to the administration of planning applications.

A prefabricated structure of a steel frame clad in corrugated iron. Semi-circular in section they were used for storage and as workshops, cinemas etc during WWII. Designed at Romney House, London by the Directorate of Fortifications & Works.
A porch in front of the solid wall of a cloister.
A jar with a roughly cylindrical or slightly flaring lower body and a rounded, inward sloping shoulder. (Source: MPRG)
Castles constructed between 1481 and 1561 for defence using heavy guns.
An artificial water channel for carrying water over long distances. Use also for bridge-like structures that carry the channel or canal across a valley, river or other obstacle.

A bowl with a straight handle projecting horizontally or diagonally upwards from the rim, particularly or completely hollow, but not opening into the vessel. A jar adapted by the addition of one or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
A bowl adapted by the addition of one or more handles. The handles may be vertical or horizontal loops, or straight, or may comprise vertical or horizontal lugs. (Source: MPRG)
A triangular piece of wood used to raise slates next to a wall or similar.
A motor vehicle designed to transport cargo.
A shafthole adze with additional hammer knob, normally polished stone.
A dining hall for the use of seasonal labourers.
A kiln in which stone is burnt as it falls through a heated and slightly inclined steel tube.
A site or establishment for the casting and refining of metallic copper.
A series of links joined together to form something that is flexible and strong. Usually metal, chains have a variety of uses but usually involve joining one item to another.
A house with a pitched roof with a double slope and gables on the side elevations of the building.
A house with a pitched or gabled roof with a double slope and gables on two or more sides.
A movable stucture which enables or prevents entrance to be gained. Usually situated in a wall or similar barrier and supported by gate posts.
A barrier which rotates on an axis and is usually so arranged as to allow a person to pass through an opening only in one direction.
The hot room in a Roman baths.
A simple, one-piece Bow Brooch with a spring of four coils, sometimes less, its chord tucked beneath its head and variations to bow and catchplate. Dating from the first century AD.
The seed of the flax plant used to produce oil and, in LINSEED CAKE, as fodder.
Oil produced from the seed of the flax plant. Used in the production of paints, varnish etc.
An object which when hot is used to smooth fabric.
An ancient Egyptian gem cut in the shape of a scarab beetle and engraved with symbols on its flat side.
An entrance chamber from tide water to basin, with gates at each end and means of pumping up or lowering the level of water to suit.
A school associated with a cathedral or college originally intended to provide a general education for their choristers.
A small ornamental case, usually on a necklace or chain, that holds a picture, keepsake etc.
Prayer hall at burial ground, especially a small walk-in memorial devoted to a deceased Hasidic rabbi.
The residence of a chauffeur or driver
A mill for crushing flint. Crushed flint was used in the manufacture of pottery in order to whiten and strengthen the body of earthenware pottery.

Component part of a Flint Mill where flint is calcined before it is brittle enough to be ground in the mill. Ground, burnt flint is used in the production of earthenware pottery, which whitens and strenghens the body.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of metal boxes or cases.
A jar with roughly vertical body walls which in some cases may be slightly convex. (Source: MPRG)
A piece of stone or timber with a small cup shaped depression in its upper surface, set into the ground to fasten a door, gate, window etc to allow it to open and shut.
A two-seat trainer chosen to replace the Avro 504. 380 entered RAF service with many finding their way onto the civilian market at the end of their careers.
A chapel for a private residence.
A hospital for the reception of women during their confinement.
A school in which the funds were raised through a system of shareholding whereby parents bought shares in the school and thus paid for their children's education.
Aluminium coated by a protective film of oxides created by electrolysis.
A command post used to direct the guns of a coastal battery.
A defensive gun battery positioned to face out to sea to fire on enemy ships and amphibious craft.
A defensive battery positioned facing out to sea enabling the guns to be brought to bear on enemy shipping and amphibious craft.

A conglomerate rock comprising well rounded flint pebbles in a very hard matrix of fine pale coloured sand, bound together by hard natural silica cement. The pebbles are usually coloured ochre or red and have black rims.
An area of land, heavily though not totally covered with trees, set aside for the royal hunt by Norman and Plantagenet kings.
A calciner used in arsenic production from the 1820s to the 1950s featuring a distinctive, slowly rotating hearth.
A type of calcining kiln used in arsenic manufacture.
A site where terracotta, made from weathered clay and grog, was manufactured.
A complex of buildings used for the manufacture of pottery.
A building or site where bodies are burnt, and the ashes collected for burial or dispersal.
Place for the cremation of animals.

The extraction of wood samples for dating analysis. Tree ring dating is the science of dating cultural and environmental events in the past by comparative study of the growth rings in trees and aged wood.
A screen, with a wide central opening, or multiple narrower openings, spanning the lower end of a medieval hall, screening the cross entry and defining the screen, or cross, passage.
Cutting or copy from published work
A building used to pump sewage from the sewers to the filter beds of a sewage works.
A decorative S-shaped moulding, usually placed at the top of a cornice, with a concave lower half and a convex upper half.
Large field or yard used to lay fabrics out ready for bleaching.
A private chapel for a royal court.
A small private chapel in a church or house, either attached or in a separate building.
A factory manufacturing sports equipment.
A factory manufacturing billiard tables.
The blade or sharp-pointed head attached to the end of a spear's shaft.

A spearhead with an elongated hollow cast into the base of the blade to receive the end of the wooden spear shaft. The spearhead was secured to the shaft by pegs set at right angles or by lashings fixed to loops cast at the base of the spearhead.
Partly subterranean operations rooms for the lighting arrays of the various types of bombing decoys in use during the Second World War.

An operations room, built to drawing number 3395/40, to control the lighting arrays of the 'T' type of bombing decoy in use during the Second World War. It was semi-sunken for added protection and then covered in earth
The intersection and space between the nave, chancel and transepts in a cruciform church.

The Gloster Grebe was the Royal Air Force's first post WWI fighter aircraft, entering service in 1923. Designed by Henry Folland, a single-seat, single-engined biplane of fabric-covered wood construction with two Vickers machine guns (133 planes built).
Goods, including machinery, manufactured from iron.
A building where milk is deposited and stored before it is despatched to the consumer.
Photographic print using carbon
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of chlorophyll for medical purposes.
A large-scale site where medicinal drugs are maufactured.
A mill or factory in which raw cotton, wool, nylon or other material is spun into yarn or thread.
Finishing process for cloth, especially linen, running the cloth between heavy rollers.
A medieval hospital for lepers, usually consisting of a church and individual shelters for the lepers.
