A building found in conjunction with a WATERMILL, used for the drying of corn after harvesting, with a slatted drying floor set above a kiln.

A type of aircraft hangar from the closing years of WWI either of steel or wood utilising a type of lattice work roof support known as a Belfast Truss, which features diagonally interlaced pieces of thin pine. The roof appears as a smooth curve.
A framework of crossed or parallel wooden or metal bars placed over an opening to prevent access but allow the passage of air, light, water etc.
A purpose-built fisherman's house, eg. a house with a first floor dwelling and ground floor fish store, or a house with a watch tower for spotting shoals.
An arch of the Tuscan Order.

Interbellum, twin-engined, five-crew, biplane flying-boat with a characteristic triple tail-fin. Entered service in 1925 and used for general reconnaissance duties. The Mk.I had a wooden fuselage, whilst the Mk.II's was metal in construction.

A funeral rite in which the human body is burnt, usually on a pyre, leaving fragmentary charred or completely combusted remains. Often found buried, occasionally in a container associated with grave goods.
Urn containing a cremation. Where component use with wider site type.
The engine housed within the fuselage of an aircraft that powers its flight.
A machine consisting of a number of moving parts designed to produce a specific physical effect, such as the powering of a craft or other device.
A housing estate comprised of housing stock owned and let by a local authority.
A residential district planned as a unit.
A stick used to bring down curses.
An arch built into a wall above another arch or lintel to relieve it of some of the weight of the structure above.
A capital which is decorated with stylized leaves similar to small volutes.

A small prefabricated, reinforced concrete structure manufactured by Messrs Orlit Ltd for the Royal Observer Corps. The first were ordered in 1951, most were redundant by 1955, a few remained in use in eastern England until 1965.
A container for pills or tablets.
A crane located on a quayside used for the loading and unloading of goods and materials to and from vessels.
A crane fixed to a quay, used for the unloading of ships cargoes.

Blocks of solid concrete,in the form of truncated pyramids usually 3 feet square x 2 feet high which could be placed in rows to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion. Pimples were recommended for use on soft ground.
Use broader site type where known
Material, stone or wood, lining the inside of a grave.
An inhumation burial in which the body is covered by a shroud, placed in a coffin of stone, wood or lead and covered with gypsum, plaster or lime. Roman and early Medieval.
A field covered with herbage for the grazing of livestock.
An area of land, often enclosed, used for cultivation or the grazing of livestock.
German three-engined air/sea rescue and transport flying boat. Entered service in 1940 as a replacement for the DO18.
The earliest subdivision of the Mesolithic, or Middle Stone Age.
A chamber attached to the sewer of a building to facilitate the removal of any blockage.
A container used to hold ammunition.
A fereter or repository for relics or any building containing such a repository, or any place or structure where worship is offered or devotions are paid to a saint or deity.
An opening or shrine, usually containing a statue, framed by a pair of pilasters or columns supporting an entablature and pediment.
Collective name for the seeds of various cereal grasses.
A container for holy relics.
The powdery residue left after the combustion of substances, especially wood and paper.
A circular construction at the intersection of two or more roads to aid the passage of vehicles from one road to another.
A place where two or more roads meet.

A curved military aircraft hangar produced in 1939. The frame is steel which is then clad with steel sheeting and reinforced concrete and typically covered with a thin layer of concrete, earth and turf.
A vessel used to carry away mud etc from a dredging machine and discharging it elsewhere.
Fish of the family Clupeidae, common to the North Atlantic. They are caught for food.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of firelighters.
A raised platform for the unloading of coal from waggons or other containers.

An aircraft lifted by gas bags, containing hydrogen or helium, but propelled by engines. Also known as a dirigible balloon, firm and streamlined in shape and incapable of high speeds. Used extensively during World War One.
A rigid frame type of airship pioneered by Count Zeppelin and used by the Germans in WWI for military purposes: do not use asa generic name for airships
An area where the sport of wrestling takes place.
The cover for a garderobe on which a person would sit.
A hospital department for the medical treatment of ear, nose and throat disorders.
A communal wash area, sometimes a dedicated outbuilding, or facility, such as a basin or trough, used by monks.
Use only where evidence is specific, ie. copper/tin alloy. For working of copper based alloys of unknown composition use COPPER WORKING SITE.
Mediaeval-17th century mining method which involved exploiting an exposed surface vein. Rarely associated with waste.
An appliance for holding an object while work is done on it, usually has a pair of jaws.
A float or pontoon supporting a flexible steel roadway as part of a Mulberry Harbour.
A sitting room or lounge in a house intended mainly for use during the morning.
A complex of buildings used for the manufacture of pottery.
A site where terracotta, made from weathered clay and grog, was manufactured.
A site or establishment for the casting and refining of metallic copper.
A building forming part of a complex or larger establishment, such as a workhouse, that serves as an entrance equipped with facilities associated with procedures undergone by new arrivals.
A tool with a sharp tapering end used for piercing materials or as a weapon point.
A bone or antler point with rows of barbs, usually on one side only.
Monument existing as an upstanding earthwork, ditch or artificial watercourse, or as a low stone built feature not covered by the other categories.
Monument visible as remains of former earthworks.
A mug with little or no discernible neck and an even, convex profile from rim to base, which have roughly equal diameters. (Source: MPRG)
A shaped rod which passed through a hole in the door and was used to raise a latch or to slide a bolt.

A platform projecting from the surface of a wall of a building carried on brackets, consoles or columns, usually placed before windows or openings, and protected by a railing or balustrade. It can also be a gallery in an auditorium.
A modern piece imitating an ancient coin, such as a replica sold in a museum.

A sailmaker's thimble used in the sewing of canvas, consisting of a flat thimble in a canvas or leather strip with a thumb hole. The whole is worn across the palm of the hand, which gives it its name.
A small cap for protecting the finger or thumb whilst sewing.
Crystalline allotropic form of carbon used in pencils, as a lubricant etc.
A place where people can recover from illnesses or health problems through controlled eating and programmes of exercise, etc.
Large fish, native to the North Atlantic and adjacents seas which has been fished since the Middle Ages.
Workshop for producing crates, particularly for the packing of pottery.
A tablet, often made of lead, on which curses are written. Sometimes the tablet is transfixed with a nail.
A large concave moulding.
A rectilinear ritual enclosure of Iron Age date
A report that primarily details the results of attempts to assign a date to orgainic material by measuring the amount of carbon 14 it contains.
A report that primarily details the results of attempts to assign a date to materials or deposits using scientific methods such as Palaeomagnetism, Dendrochronology or Radiocarbon Dating.
A report that primarily details the results of attempts to assign a date to wooden structures or objects by the comparative study of the growth rings in trees and aged wood.
A staff with a bent head used by a shepherd. For a crook used by a bishop use crozier.
A large, undergound watercourse.
A processing house where surplus water is removed from gunpowder after incorporating.
A grotto or shrine dedicated to the nymphs, composed of fountains designed to imitate a natural grotto.
Single-engine, two-seat tractor bomber and reconnaissance aircraft. Entered service in 1916 and, during 1917 and 1918, equipped nine RFC squadrons in its reconnaissance role.
A two-seat trainer chosen to replace the Avro 504. 380 entered RAF service with many finding their way onto the civilian market at the end of their careers.
A machine used in the silk industry for applying the final twist to silk threads to make them suitable for weaving into a fabric.
A piece of metal or timber holding two elements together.
A storehouse in 16th and 17th century houses.
An area of land enclosed by one or several boundary ditches. Double index with a term to indicate the shape of the enclosure where known.
An area of land enclosed by two parallel ditches. Use with specific shaped enclosure where known.
A place where coal is mined.

Chance Vought Division of the United Aircraft Corporation. Was reconstituted as a separate division in 1943, after being part of the Vought-Sikorsky division, to concentrate on the production of combat aircraft.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter. Entered service in 1943 as a land-based fighter. Converted to a carrierborne fighter in 1944 for use by US Navy and Fleet Air Arm. Mostly saw action in the Pacific and Far East.
A small tool for boring holes with a cross handle and a screw tip.
A bridge whose upkeep and repair was financed by the exaction of a toll.
The residence of a telegraph keeper, associated with a telegraph station.
A factory or works which has been temporarily turned over to the manufacture of goods for the war effort.
An existing factory that was converted for use as aircraft works in the run up to or during the Second World War.
A modern small factory or workshop, often in the form of a prefabricated shed.
A multi-purpose farm building.
A threshing barn which also houses farm animals and is somethimes used to stotre grain, house carts and other functions.

skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: City Of London Coal Duties Boundary Marker
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A cast-iron or stone boundary post, obelisk or plate found on roads, railways, canals etc around London marking the boundary within which a duty was payable on coal.
An area or wing of a hexagonal plan workhouse or prison from where the supervision of the inmates is carried out.
A long pillow, especially one used as an under pillow.
Use for a craft powered by a rocket engine which uses stored rocket propellant mass for forming its high-speed propulsive jet eg. Flying bombs
Use for craft powered by an engine which provides propulsion by expelling reaction mass, such as jet and rocket engines.
The residence of a cloth cutter.
A stick for digging up roots etc. Sometimes a stone weight is attached.
A Roman Bow Brooch dating from the mid-second to mid-third centuries AD, characterized by the pronounced curvature of the bow, resembling a knee. Usually used by military personnel.
A building or site used for the manufacture of small arms and artillery pieces, etc.
A factory used for the manufacture of ordnance including small arms, ammunition, artillery pieces and armoured fighting vehicles.
A brace extending from a vertical to a higher horizontal timber.
A prominent structure situated on land specifically as a guide to navigation for travellers or as an aid/warning to sailors out at sea.
An abbey or priory of Grandmontine monks.
Buildings associated with the extaction of uranium from its pitchblende or copper ores.
A hotel adjacent to a railway terminus. Railway hotels were often owned by a railway company.
Pit for mixing raw materials with water in the preparation of a clay body.
A textile building where the process of combing, a preparatory process for long wools, takes place.
A canal built as a military obstacle, but also used for the transport of military stores, equipment and personnel.
A container for holding water that has been blessed by a priest and is used for symbolic rituals of purification.
A port, dock or harbour where ferries, hovercraft, ocean liners and cargo vessels can load and unload. May include road and/or rail terminals for transportation to the port.
An area of a port, dock or harbour, often including buildings for passport control and customs, where passengers of ocean liners can embark/disembark and where supplies can be taken on board.
Large, single-engine, eight passenger airliner biplane.
A round barrow featuring a low, wide mound surrounded by a ditch which may be accompanied by an external bank.
A wooden framework with holes for the feet, and occassionally hands, in which the offender was restrained.
Use for any shell of an animal, principally, molluscs, crabs etc.
A type of Ionic diagonal capital where all four sides are the same and with therefore eight volutes.
A box or place of confinement for animals, made wholly or partly of wire, wood or bars of metal, so as to admit air and light.
A garden or park, with ancilliary buildings, in which wild animals are kept and reared for public exhibition.
An enclosure for wild cats such as Lions and Tigers
Including accommodation for animals, birds, reptiles and fish in captivity.
An enclosure, usually within a zoo, designed to represent the natural environment for Lemurs, including shelter.
A factory manufactoring caravans.
Temporary accommodation for war evacuees.
A machine, usually contained in a building called a flour mill which reduces grain into constituent parts or �streams� which include flour. For a Flour Mill buliding use FLOUR MILL in Monument Type.

A flour milling machine which uses one or more pairs of horizontal millstones to grind wheat into flour which millers call a �sudden death� process; within not more than 90 seconds complete wheat grain becomes wholemeal flour.
Principal glider-pilot training glider fitted with tandem seats. Spruce and plywood in construction, the Hotspur served with the Glider Pilot Regiment between 1941 and 1945.

Plain clay tile suspended, loose, from the top edge of a tiling lath or batten so as to overlap two courses below. It is held in place by a small wooden peg wedged into, or passed through, one (or sometimes both) of two holes in the head of the tile.
The courtyard of a castle, ie. the area enclosed by the rampart or curtain. Use with wider site type where known.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of foot disorders and diseases.
An enclosure in which ships are built and repaired, and all sorts of ships' stores are brought together.
A naval base that builds, repairs, docks or converts warships, and is manned by civilian engineers and workers and administered by engineer duty officers.

A vertical vein of metallic ore, usually lead, occuring between walls of rock and cutting through the bedding. Often rakes have been worked from early times leaving deep trenches several km long, with adits leading off and shafts sunk at the side.
A residence of two or three monks of the Order of Tiron dependent on a foreign mother house.
A kiln in which the prolonged heating or roasting of materials to drive off water, volatiles and sulphur so that they may be reduced to a powder, was performed.
A piece of sculpture usually representing the head, shoulders and breast of a person.
A place where sails are manufactured.
A temporary settlement or shanty-town erected by railway construction workers or "navvys".
A small spherical bell for fastening onto the leg of a hawk.
A bell worn by an animal, eg sheep, goats, cows and hawks, to inform the owner of the animal's position.
An all-steel end-opening, hangar with canted sides designed for folded-wing aircraft.
Fabric manufactured from fibrous materials, consolidated by heat and compression so that the fibres become matted together.
A site where tanks and armoured fighting vehicles can be stored.
A storage facility used for the accommodation and dispersal of vehicles. Often used by the military and emergency services.
Four-crew, twin-engined monoplane designed as a torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance aircraft for RAF Coastal Command. Withdrawn from operations in November 1940 and downgraded to a trainer.
An informal encampment, usually near a military establishment, set up as a public protest against that establishment or against some aspect of military policy.
A temporary settlement established as a public protest against an aspect of government policy or more specifically the development of a site.
A cylindrical device using ceramic or metallic balls to grind materials like ores, chemicals, ceramic raw materials and paints
A room or group of rooms usually reserved for use by the monarchy or government.
A site inhabited by a modern order of nuns, founded in 1900 at Lanherne, Cornwall, following Carmelite traditions.
A specialist hospital where the elderly receive medical treatment.
An apparatus around which cables or hawsers are wound for hoisting anchors, lifting weights, etc.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by a double line of ramparts.
An alloy of steel.
A foreshore structure to prevent barges from sinking in the river mud. Made by placing chalk on fascines of brushwood, which is in some cases retained by a timber revetement.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter. Entered service in 1943 as a land-based fighter. Converted to a carrierborne fighter in 1944 for use by US Navy and Fleet Air Arm. Mostly saw action in the Pacific and Far East.

Chance Vought Division of the United Aircraft Corporation. Was reconstituted as a separate division in 1943, after being part of the Vought-Sikorsky division, to concentrate on the production of combat aircraft.
A small area of managed woodland, created to provide cover for deer and other game.
A stone, either in situ or part of a monument, bearing one or more small, roughly hemispherical depressions, generally created by chipping or pecking.
A barge with a lugsail rig commonly found on the River Thames in the late 19th century. Also a general term applied to the family of Deal luggers.
Single-engine, single-seat biplane seaplane built for the 1924 Schneider Cup Race.
A staple foodstuff made with flour, water and usually yeast, which is kneaded and then baked. Can include unleavened (no yeast) varieties.
A steel framed seaplane hangar designed for Royal Navy Air Stations by the admiralty in 1917-1918.
A small, steel shelter designed for use as a firewatchers post during an air raid.
A portable indoor air raid shelter in the form of a steel topped table, often with wire meshing around the sides.
A reinforced concrete structure, usually sited underground, intended to be used by the regional government as an air raid shelter in the event of a nuclear attack.

A commercially manufactured air raid shelter, using prefabricated parabolic concrete panels which could be combined to produce any length of shelter.Usually semi-sunken and covered with earth they were mainly used on RAF sites.
An air raid shelter, designed to be placed in the garden. Made from prefabricated components, they were often semi-sunken and the structure then covered with soil for added protection.
A small, industrially manufactured, air raid shelter, designed to be used inside buildings and to provide cover for nightwatchmen or firewatchers remaining on site during air raids.
A structure, usually of earth and concrete, and usually, although not always, subterranean, designed for protection against explosives.
A fortified structure used to protect civilians and military personnel from enemy bombing.
An instrument for measuring atmospheric pressure by its effects on mercury in a glass tube. It can also be used to measure altitude and depth and is especially used for predicting the weather.
A windmill with a rotating cap containing the windshaft, and a stationary body in the form of a tower.
The Douglas Aircraft Company, Inc., established in 1920, reorganized in 1928. Produced such notable aircraft as the Dakota.
Originally a light day-bomber, the Boston II, re-christened the Havoc, was adapted for night-flying in the fighter-intruder role. Was capable of a top speed in excess of 300 mph.
A decorative band or feature.

An ornamental (carved and/or painted) frieze carved into, or attached to, the planking either side of a vessel's bow carrying the vessel's name and often illustrating some aspect of the name, port/country of origin etc.
A type of carriage house, usually in a churchyard, for storing a hearse.
An outbuilding used for the storage and maintenance of horse-drawn carriages.
A body of wax or tallow, usually formed into a long, thin, cylindrical shape enclosing a wick and burnt to produce light.
A tall stack used to disperse foul air from the bottom of a mine.
A type of calcining kiln used in the processing of iron ore.
A kiln for roasting ore.
Large shallow dish or plate.
The major tower of a fortification, often acting as its last defence.
A fortified keep in the form of a tower, used as a last refuge or defence. If a component of a larger site, use KEEP.
A Norman keep, in the form of a circular or polygonal enclosure surrounded by a wall.
A metallic alloy of iron, carbon and silicon formed by casting in a mould.

A jar adapted by the addition of two handles. Handles may be horizontal or vertical loops or horizontal or curved lugs. Handles are nearly always opposed. Profiles vary and should be double indexed with the appropriate JAR type. (Source: MPRG)
A thin timber, usually sloping on both sides, fixed to the floor between the jambs of a doorway.
An object which perforated the axle cap, passing through the axle and so keeping the wheel in place. Usually made of metal, though can be made of wood or antler.
Steps found at a landing point.
A series of flat-topped structures, usually made of stone or wood, used to facilitate a person's movement from one level to another.
A vault where the bay is divided by diagonal and transverse ribs into four cells or webs.
A vault with a ceiling or undersurface subdivided by ribs into bays or webs.
A building used for the crystallization process in alum making.
A small monastery or nunnery of the Augustinian order dependent on a larger mother house.

A circular or octagonal building at the base of a post mill to provide storage space and to give protection to the superstructure. The roundhouse is not attached to the mill itself. Some roundhouses were later converted for domestic purposes.
Small (<2cm diameter) roundwood often complete with buds or leaf scars.
The Boeing Aircraft Company, established 1916. A subsidiary of The Boeing Airplane Company. Notable aircraft produced include the B17 Flying Fortress and the B29 Superfortress.
A photo- reconnaissance variant of the Boeing Superfortress, used from 1944, initally deployed in the Pacific war, later for Cold war duties over Europe.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 14383/40.
A residue, primarily lead oxide, formed during refining silver
A building or buildings used for the production of paints, varnishes, colours and distemper.
A school for instruction in the art of horsemanship.
A small tower, usually round or polygonal and attached to a structure. When a separate building, treat as a monument.
A small or subordinate tower, normally forming part of a larger structure, housing a spiral or winding stair.
A factory for the assembly of bicycles.
A temporary settlement or encampment erected by construction workers (eg for reservoir construction).
A container used to measure liquids.
A measure for liquid, usually for a quarter of a pint.
A grooved block placed in series, alternating with the metopes, in a Doric frieze.
A tract of land with trees, sometimes acting as a boundary or barrier, usually smaller and less wild than a forest.

A list of English battlefields maintained by English Heritage. Inclusion in the document does not confer any statutory status. It lists and records the details of battlefields to preserve their nature and survival.
A mill where flax fibres were woven into linen cloth.
Part-decomposed vegetable matter formed under waterlogged conditions into a firm, brown deposit resembling soil. Used as a brick for infilling in timber framed walls.
Pertaining to or deriving from a botanical living organism. See VEGETAL Class List for narrow terms.
A bowl adapted by the addition of three or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
A decorative moulding depicting an animal or bird head with a tongue or beak that overlaps the moulding set below it.

An aerial photograph taken from directly above a feature in the landscape, suitable for mapping or survey purposes. For photographs taken from the air at an angle to the subject use OBLIQUE AERIAL PHOTOGRAPH.
A book of hymns.
Generic name for the fine grained, brown coloured carboniferous sandstone, quarried in the Leeds, Bradford and Halifax area.
A small building used as a shelter by a shepherd.
A training college for the instruction of military trainees in the theory and practice of warfare.
A vertical or inclined plane, channel, or passage through which objects are moved from a higher to a lower level by means of gravity.
The bottom storey of a building, often below or partially below ground level.

Used by Ordnance Survey to record high accuracy height above Ordnance Datum Newlyn. Marked by a low concrete pillar, and maybe surrounded by railings, they comprise an underground chamber protecting the reference point, built directly onto stable bedrock.
A flask with a hollow ring-shaped form. (Source: MPRG)
A single-engine, photo-reconnaissance fighter designed for operation from aircraft carriers. Later adapted as a night fighter, it entered service in 1943 and remained in production until 1956.
A combination of obstructions, used either to stop enemy forces or force them off the road.
A roadblock, usually manned by the Home Guard, where the credentials of civilians and military personnel where checked before allowing them to proceed.
A non-vertical kiln where the shaft and burning zone is horizontal to the ground thereby allowing material to be fed in.
An engineering works that produces tufting machinery especially for use in the manufacturing of carpets.
Any form of fastener used to fasten clothing together.
A pan with a perforated bottom for straining or rinsing food.
An inclined plane built to allow tanks to be loaded and unloaded between rolling stock on the railway network and vehicular low loaders.
A place where perfume is sold, as well as manufactured.
An optical instrument for making distant objects appear nearer and larger, often found on the promenade or pleasure pier at a seaside resort or at a site of scenic beauty.
A small box or chest for valuables, especially jewels.
A place where ambulances are serviced and maintained.

A land based installation armed with wire -guided and powered "Brennan torpedoes" which were in operation beween 1890 and 1906. These torpedoes were invented by Louis Philip Brennan. The stations were used to defend the coast from enemy shipping.
A land based establishment armed with torpedoes and used to defend the coast from enemy shipping.
A decorative moulding featuring a repeating star-like motif carved in relief.
The lower surface of a room.
A narrow strip of land where a plough and team could turn. This usually remains higher than the ploughed land.
Place where food or money was handed out to the poor.
The dwelling and workshop of a framework knitter.
A building or group of buildings situated close to the sea used by coastguards to enable them to monitor the coastline.
A bowl divided into two or more compartments by vertical slab partitions. (Source: MPRG)
An area of ground where training in the use of grenades can be carried out.
Ore containing a high proportion of zinc.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the chief engineer of GHQ home forces.
An instrument for measuring and indicating the height of tide.
Daily record of events or appointments.
Permanently moored historic maritime craft preserved and converted into a museum and open to the public.
A horn used to hold loose gun powder for recharging firearms.
A rope, clog or fetter used to limit the movement of animals through the tying of two or more feet together.
A place where social and other functions such as parties, presentations and meetings can be held.
A workshop or factory where brass articles are made by casting molten material into a mould.
A brass manufacturing complex incorporating battery mill furnaces, hammers, etc.

Single-engine, two-crew multi-role aircraft designed for RAF Army co-operation. Entered RAF service in 1938. Noted for its role dropping agents into Europe, also served as a night-fighter, day ground-attack aircraft and target tug.
A plucked string instrument of a specific medieval / early post medieval type.
An attachment to a lamp.
Small ocean going vessel fitted with loading doors in the bow. Used for ferrying tanks or other fighting vehicles to beach landings.
Ammunition manufactured for use in hand held firearms.
A written work being one of several found in a monograph or serial
Two masted merchant vessel, rigged as a brig.

An offshore station, equipped with a fixed electronic radio navigation and positioning system such as Hyperfix. The transmission principle are pulsed and phase comparisons systems. Superceded by Global Positioning System in 1994.
A large vertical stone forming part of a structure. If the structure is roofed, the orthostat will stretch from the floor to the roof as a single slab.
WWII secret bases, sometimes partially underground, intended for use by the British resistance in the eventuality of a foreign invasion.
A bridge whose deck is hung from above by large cables, chains or pinned iron or steel bars hanging from towers.
A freestanding public call box, containing a telephone and usually operated by inserting coins.
A roadside telephone box for use by motorists in need of assistance.

A mineral crystal of thin, tough fibres which can be woven. Used for high temperature insulation or as reinforcement in asbestos cement building board and corrugated roofing. If used to imitate slate, use artificial slate also.
A building, often close to a churchyard, used for the entertainment of poor people on their wedding day.
A mine designed specifically to be dropped from an aircraft, often into the sea.

The main German, medium bomber of the war, the HE111 first saw action during the Spanish Civil War. HE111s took part in the Battle of Britain and from 1944 onwards were used to launch airborne flying bombs against London.
A building or set of rooms where a newspaper is compiled and produced, before being printed. May include facilities for printing.
A stone basin for containing holy water often set in inside walls of a church, especially near the entrance.
A missile fired from a sling.
A deliberately made missile fired from a sling.
A specific form of cauldron, generally of rounded profile made in the Low Countries. (Source: MPRG)
A large pot used for boiling.

An artifically constructed wall with recessed and projecting grips for hands and feet and places to attach ropes. Used for practising rock climbing. If the wall is a free-standing external structure use term for the Thesaurus of Monument Types.
A jug with more or less straight sides that flare out from a narrow rim or neck to a wider base. (Source: MPRG)
A structure used for the lifting of boats and other water craft.
A garment worn on the foot and lower leg.
A building or room within a monastery in which the monks were allowed to warm themselves. The warming house was often the only place where a fire was allowed.
An area within a building (usually the barn or stable) for storing husks from the grain crop (chaff) for animal feed after it has been threshed and winnowed in the barn.
A place where gypsum is extracted.
The bark and wood of trees of the genus Aspidosperma used to produce tannin.
Niche intended for pigeons or other birds to nest in, allowing the squabs and eggs to be harvested. Found inside specially built dovecotes and in the walls of other buildings.
Room in a building or complex, such as a workhouse, in which work is carried out.
The measurement of the ratio of a radioactive potassium (K) isotope and the argon (Ar) gas produced as a by-product of its decay. Useful for dating volcanic material older than 1,000 years.
A factory where preserved food is canned.
A factory where gloves are manufactured.
A hospital department which treats patients without keeping them in overnight or for a longer period.
The Percival Aircraft Company was formed in 1932 and re-organized as Percival Aircraft Ltd. in 1937, when the works moved from Gravesend to Luton.
Single-engine, spruce and plywood, fabric-covered training and communications low-wing monoplane. Served from 1939 to 1950.
A type of kiln, usually built into banking, with a stone lining that was used to produce white coal which was used as fuel in the lead smelting process.

The systematic study of ground surfaces and collection of visible archaeological material. Fieldwalking can be carried out as line-walking, grid collection and transect or quadrant sampling. Any material recovered is logged and stored by sample unit.
A vessel for carrying a cargo of coal in bulk.
A factory where seaplanes are manufactured.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
A purpose-built building with a brick tower constructed on one end, based on drawing number (9294/42). Used for the drying of parachutes.
A purpose-built building with a steel framed tower, based on drawing number (11595/42). Used for the drying of parachutes.
A purpose-built building with a tower used for the drying of parachutes.
A brick tower, based on drawing number (9290/42), usually added to an existing building. Used for the drying of parachutes.
A building where ambulances are housed awaiting emergency calls.
A 1930s British short-haul biplane airliner for 6-8 passengers. It proved an economical and durable craft, despite its relatively primitive plywood construction. Primarily used by the RAF.
An observation tower is a structure used to provide panoramic views of the surrounding area. They are often used as attractions at seaside resorts e.g. Blackpool Tower.
A building in which coal slurry, produced in the coal washing process, is recovered.
A hospital block where patients come for day-care medical treatment.
Buildings and sites associated with the manufacture of cotton.
Use for vessels registered in the Netherlands.
A type of Ionic diagonal capital where all four sides are the same and with therefore eight volutes.
A weight used to hold down thatch.
A three dimensional representation.
A flat, circular object often made from metal, wood, bone or ivory and of unidentified purpose.
An aircraft, either whole or in part. Aircraft often survive as commemorative monuments, gate guardians or crash sites.
A box in which letters are posted or deposited for dispatch.
A hollow pillar, erected in a public place, containing a receptacle for posting letters.
An object from which clothes can be hung.
A chapel dedicated to our Blessed Lady, often placed to the east of the High Altar, sometimes in other positions.
A mill, including a forge and powered hammers where hot metal is shaped by hammering and rolling.
A site where a single large balloon was attached by fine wire cables to the ground to form an aerial obstruction to attacking enemy aircraft.
A building associated with a barrage balloon site and intended to provide shelter for the balloon crew from air attack.
A mooring, usually consisting of a concrete plinth, to which a barrage balloon was attached.
A facility where the exterior of a motor vehicle can be cleaned.
A road, used traditionally for the transportation of a corpse to a place of burial.
Book used to record information or impressions in the field, often as a preparation for more formal reporting at a later date.
A crane mounted on a large metal gantry, used for the lifting of large-scale building materials, etc.
Large semi-subterranean feature often packed with straw for the storage of potatoes and other root crops.
A distilling or brewing house.
A factory for the production of missiles

A device in which a large quantity of low pressure water is made to pump a small proportion of itself to a greater height than its source or to a higher pressure; achieved by using the pressure rise resulting from suddenly interrupting the flow
Light microscopy in which vibration directions of the light are constrained into single planes.
An example from which another object is made.
A hospital where patients can rest and recover after an operation or illness. Medical facilities for treatment are also available.
A pit used to trap game. Often originally covered and consealed, and sometimes with sharpened stakes in the base.
A calcareous, hard substance, the external skeleton of marine polyps, used in the manufacture of jewellery.
Use for cargoes of live animals only.
Animals and products made from the carcasses and hides of dead animals.
Post-World War Two, single-engine, high-wing utility transport. Manufactured by De Havilland Canada, was also produced in a seaplane version. Known as the U6A from 1962.
A medieval house with central open hall and two storey bays, jettied at first floor level, on either side.
A wealden house with only one end being jettied.
Reproductive process for non-photographic media in which the image is created by transferring ink from a plate, block etc.

A sheet or board made from a mixture of thin strips of wood and cement which are bound together through compression within a mould. Woodwool slabs are used for roof or wall cladding, providing fire resistance, and heat and sound insulation.
Twin-engined fighter-bomber. All metal in construction, entered service in 1940. Supported bombing operations and participated in attacks on France, but not widely used due to engine faults.
A naval base that builds, repairs, docks or converts warships, and is manned by civilian engineers and workers and administered by engineer duty officers.
An enclosure in which ships are built and repaired, and all sorts of ships' stores are brought together.
A building or buildings used for the production of whistles.
A jar whose profile resembles two truncated cones joined together at the widest point, forming a carination at the centre of the vessel. (Source: MPRG)

An American turbojet fighter-bomber aircraft. The F-84 was the first production fighter aircraft to utilize in-flight refuelling and the first fighter capable of carrying a nuclear weapon. Designed by Alexander Kartveli, 1946.

The RAF's first jet fighter, flown operationally during 1944-5, with later versions serving for a further ten years after the war. The Meteor's first active operations were in the interception and destruction of V.1. flying bombs.
British three-seat, single-engine light bomber. All metal in construction, this monoplane had a 1000 lb bomb load.

Sites used for the accommodation, welfare and recreation of servicemen, especially those serving in the Royal Air Force. Use only for sites associated with military installations. For non-military sites use DOMESTIC class and its narrower terms.
A camp used to accommodate members of the Womens Land Army who undertook essential agricultural work during the Second World War.
A head of water raised in a conduit system.
A gaming piece for the Viking game of Hnefatafl.
A room used for the ritual cleaning of the body prior to burial
A stone with a rectangular depression into which molten metal, usually tin, was poured to create ingots.
A factory where furniture is manufactured.

Originally designed as a wood and steel bomber-reconnaissance aircraft, subsequent variations served as special transports, glider tugs and paratroop carriers. Featured a tricycle-style undercarriage.
A wing joined to the main body of the building with the roof at right angles to the main roof.
A mineral composed of SiO2. Commonly clear or milky in appearance. A common constituent of rocks and sediments.
An industrial site or building where the machinery is powered by a steam engine.
A small building housing pilot's and locker rooms with flight offices and a watch office. The only known example was built at Tangmere.
A building or site used for the exercise and training of military personnel.
A curb-roof with curved or steeply pitched lower slopes and a hipped or pitched roof above. Named after the French Classical architect F. Mansart.
Hard, fine grained, blue/grey coloured sandstone. Quarried in South Wales and the Bristol area and commonly used, throughout the country, as a stone roofing material (stone slate).
A flask with a rounded, almost spherical shape. (Source: MPRG)
Mark 5 or the fifth variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
A large kitchen garden enclosed by a substantial wall, not usually adjacent to its associated house.
A private garden established primarily for growing vegetables and herbs for domestic consumption.
The measurement of chemical alterations in the amino acids in protein molecules from bones, shells and teeth. Date range can be between 1,000 and several million years.
Angus, Scotland
A circular moulding.
Instruments and their component parts used to produce music or audible signals of all forms.
Use more specific term where available.
Use specific form where known.

An object which serves as a vessel. This class includes containers for which the function is either specific or unknown. Where the function is known, the term is also included within another class, eg churn.
A vessel used as an ornament, often to hold flowers.
A type of bowl designed to be suspended, usually from the roof.
A substance used to affect a human or animal by changing mental or physical states, particularly used in medicine.

A jug with a pierced bunghole just above the base. the bunghole can be made through an applied knob or disc of clay, or simply a hole in the vessel wall. In use, the hole would probably have had a tap or spigot attached. (Source: MPRG)
A large tract of land covered with trees and interspersed with open areas of land. Traditionally forests were owned by the monarchy and had their own laws.
An area of land, heavily though not totally covered with trees, set aside for the royal hunt by Norman and Plantagenet kings.
A truss which does not subdivide a space, as in the centre of a hall of two bays or in an undivided building such as a barn.
A conical container, usually made of earthenware, into which boiling sugar was poured and allowed to crystallize.
A press in which the juice is extracted from grapes in the manufacture of wine.
An outdoor or indoor place where flowers were sold.
A large, flattish basket used in winnowing the chaff from the grain.
A steam generator comprising a pressure vessel, and/or rows of tubes arranged to receive heat from a firegrate.
A general name given to a series of machines which successively reduce the diameter of rovings before the final spinning into yarn.
Single-seat carrierborne jet fighter. Originally conceived as an RAF land-fighter, entered Fleet Air Arm service in 1951 and was the first jet fighter to be standardised in first-line squadrons.
Right angled triangular plate for determining, measuring or setting out set angles.
A monument consisting of parallel banks, normally accompanied by ditches, which appears to mark out an approach to another monument or monuments.
A building or room where food is prepared and cooked.
A factory where pencils are manufactured.
An object used to mark each mile and to indicate distances to locations.
A feature formed by water falling from the roof of a building and creating a linear or curving indentation in the ground.
A small stem powered warship with its hull protected by iron plates. Used to bombard targets onshore, especially in the Crimean War.
Walls composed of clay, earth, straw, lime and sand, mixed with water. Constructed without shutters in layers upon a stone or brick plinth and usually covered with protective limewash.
Cob type construction typical to Buckinghamshire using a local clay with a high chalk content to produce walls of notable inherent stability.
A bell worn by a cow to identify its location.
A container for sand which was used to stop ink from spreading.

A schedule of work set out in sufficient detail for it to be quantifiable, implemented and monitored. Can include contractual details relevant to the commissioning body. A project design may be a research proposal independent of the planning framework
Twin-engined, four-seat medium bomber. A re-engined variant of the Hampden, less than 200 were built but never became operational due to engine unreliability. Some were converted to Hampdens.
A building or structure for the storage of processed minerals, chemicals or agricultural products, etc. Use more specific type where known.
A low-temperature oven for the firing of metallic-based colour onto pottery after glazing.
A place of worship for Particular Baptists, a Calvinistic Baptist denomination who believe in predestination.

A place of worship for Strict Baptists, a sect who broke away from the Particular Baptists and kept up the practice of denying communion to non members after the union of General and Particular Baptists was formed in 1891.
A two storey building with a watch office on the ground floor and a control room above. Originally based on drawing number 12096/4.
A night fighter station watch office based on the standard design dor Bomber Satellite Station watch offices
Single-engine fighter/dive-bomber. The Fleet Air Arm's first operational monoplane, and its first aircraft to shoot down an enemy during the war.
A small piece of metal or other material used to hold objects together.
A metal pin with two arms which is passed through a hole and held in place by the springing apart of the arms.
A small building used as a shelter by a shepherd.
A missile base armed with the Thor Intermediate Range Ballistic Missile. Thor Missiles were deployed in Britain under joint British/US control between 1959 and 1964.
A walk or path lined with lime trees.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
A group of electricity-producing windmills or wind turbines.
A disc >4mm with a central perforation.
An object which has one or more holes through it. Use more specific term where known.
A post set up alongside a canal to mark the miles to and from a place.
A tool for threshing grain.
A room used primarily for storing food and drink.
A building where tallow is produced, ie. solid animal fat that has been separated by heating, usually for making candles.
A railway used for the conveyance of coal and other minerals.
A pumping station used as part of a clean water supply system.

Four-engine, ten-crew, long-range maritime reconnaissance and anti-submarine aircraft. Developed from the Short C-class Empire airliner. All metal in construction, entered RAF Coastal Command service in 1938.

Six-crew, twin-engined medium night-bomber. Entered service in 1938 and was the RAF's principal bomber until 1943, participating in the first bombing raid of the war. Later versions served as torpedo and reconnaissance-bombers, transports and trainers.

An enclosure of Late Neolithic/Early Bronze Age date, related to henges, defined by a circular arrangement of pits, probably none of which originally held posts. More than one circle, concentrically arranged, may be present.
A building where masts are made and stored.
Beech Aircraft Corporation, also known as Beechcraft, established 1932
A twin engine advanced trainer developed by Beech/ Beechcraft , a US firm, used in WWII

An establishment where alcoholic and non alcoholic drinks are served, food may also be served. May be a an individual room within a larger multi purpose building such as a sports pavilion or a theatre.
A site used for the production of dyes from controlled chemical reactions. In use from the mid 19th century onwards.
A site used for the production of dyes from natural ingredients.
The SI derived unit of concentration (of amount of a substance).
Twin-engined, four-crew German seaplane. Entered service in 1932 as a torpedo bomber and naval reconnaisance aircraft, though by World War 2 those still serving were used mainly for air sea rescue.
A metal or wooden framework suspended within an opening in an external wall, fence, hedge etc, to allow ingress or egress.
A vessel in which incense is burnt.
An area off the coast where ships anchor.

Two-seat, twin-engined light/medium bomber celebrated for its speed and versatility. Entering service in 1941, was also adapted for duties as a fighter-bomber, Pathfinder, mine-layer, transport, trainer and photo-reconnaissance aircraft.
A winch powered by a steam engine.
House owned by the church, often used for meetings.
A shed in which delicate plants are reared from seedlings for planting out later.
Powder produced by grinding cacao beans, used as the main ingredient for the drink Cocoa.

Four-engine, ten-crew, long-range maritime reconnaissance and anti-submarine aircraft. Developed from the Short C-class Empire airliner. All metal in construction, entered RAF Coastal Command service in 1938.
An establishment open at night for refreshment and entertainment.
A cylindrical, polygonal, or square element of brick, metal or terracotta fixed on top of a chimney stack to extend the flue and improve the extraction of smoke.
A vertical member dividing a window into two or more lights.
A mullion which divides a window with four or more lights and is larger than the mullions either side of it, often sharing the dimensions of the frame?s members.
A mullion of square section set diagonally.
A container for perfume.
Stone consisting of nearly pure silica, which can be used as a building material or knapped to produce flint objects.
A semi-circular window, often decorated and with its glazing bars radiating like the ribs of an opened fan, set above a door.
A strong, fortified dwelling, of between two and four storeys. Occupied only in times of trouble built mainly in the border country of the North from the mid 14th to the 17th century.
Stonemason's term for any coarse/hard stone that is not easily worked. Index with specific stone type where given. Not to be confused with Kentish Ragstone.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
Three-seat tactical support aircraft. Entering service with the US 9th Air Force in 1944, the Invader had a bomb load of 4,000 lbs and was later used as a conventional medium bomber.
Diesel engined submarine designed for long ocean voyages in search of enemy shipping.
A house constructed with a basic timber framework; between the members are panels which can be infilled with timber, wattle and daub, plaster, brick or other materials.
A house in which a pair of curved timbers form a bowed A-frame which supports the roof independently of the walls.
A timber framed house comprising horizontal and vertical timbers, forming the walls of the building and directly supporting the roof.
A building where people pay to see films and 'moving pictures'.
A rib which spans a vault passing from springer to springer at right angles to the axis of the vault.
A moulding on a flat or vaulted ceiling, suggesting a structure or forming a pattern derived from vaulting..
A twin engined advanced trainer aircraft developed for the military by the US firm of Cessna
Unable to identify actual place from documentary sources alone.
A farm building erected in the 18th and 19th century which were architect-designed rather than built in the local vernacular style.
Thin, rectangular tiles, usually made of wood, used for roofing.
A vessel used for inspecting vessels entering port during wartime.
American A-20 twin-engined, light, day bomber. Some supplied to the RAF and known as the Boston I. Subsequent variations adapted to night flying and re-christened the Havoc.
A place where boats are stored.
A non-metallic element, yellow in colour, used in a variety of processes.
A freestanding public call box, containing a telephone and usually operated by inserting coins.
A roadside telephone box for use by motorists in need of assistance.
A covered shopping street, sometimes with galleries, dating from the late 18th/early 19th century.
An ornamental foliation in panels or tracery so called because it is arranged around five intervals, known as foils or cusps, that describe the outlines of five leaves or petals.
An enclosure used for baiting bulls.
An indoor market used for the sale of antique goods.
A building or area within a brewery where barrels of ale are stored.
A mollusc usually used as a foodstuff.
A wall for growing fruit, dating in England from the mid-18th century, whose curving lines gave added strength, thus doing away with the need for buttressing.
A stone or brick wall either in, or enclosing, a garden.
An ancilliary workshop used for repairs, etc.

A building that houses material that can be used to facilitate the study of a site, landscape or an historical event/period. Such centres are often found in close proximity to the sites and/or landscapes that they seek to encourage the study of.
A machine for applying protective size to yarn intended for warp
A fine grained rock which splits easily into plates. Used for the manufacture of roofing tiles etc.
Thin plates of slate, usually rectangular in shape, used as roofing tiles.
An internal combustion heat engine which uses gas as its fuel, and acts as a prime mover or power source for driving other machinery.
A broad container, usually used for cooking.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Offshore Renewables Protocol for Archaeological Discoveries (ORPAD)

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: An outdoor trail that has keep fit equipment with supporting information plaques intermittently positioned along its route
A building in which textile rags are sorted according to fibre types.
An appliance for producing motion by the stepping of men on movable steps on a revolving cylinder. Used as a form of punishment in prisons.
Usually a cotton spinning factory, although some mills have weaving sheds attached, in which case the end product is completed cloth, not yarn only.
Textile mill producing calico, ie. coarse, unbleached cotton cloth.
Use for vessel registered in Cyprus whether Greek or Turkish.
A representation of the crucifixion of Christ or related scenes as a sculpture in a churchyard, etc.
An educational institution for the training of teachers.
Traditionally the chief residence of a land owner. Now used specifically to describe the residence of the Lord Mayor of London.
A building or site used for the manufacture of weapons, ammunition and military supplies. Use more specific type where known.
A works or factory where shells or projectiles were machined before they were dispatched to a filling factory to be filled with explosives.
A shell-shaped moulded hood over an exterior opening, such as a doorway.
Reformatory established under the Inebriates Acts 1879-1900 for repeat alcohol related offenders
The residence of a priest.
A chronological journal, generally showing appointments, or recording memories and impressions of a days events over a period of time.
A diary used to record the events and activities during an excavation.
A German stoneware form of conical mug. (Source: MPRG)
A mug with more-or-less straight side which flare out from the rim to the wider base. (Source: MPRG)
A vertical, pointed structure usually resembling a pyramid or cone. Use for component of a larger building type where it is now used as a freestanding ornament.

Twin-engined, four-seat torpedo-bomber designed to replace the Vildebeest. Entered service with RAF Coastal Command in 1939. Later versions incorporated a remote-controlled machine gun with periscope sight.

Long-range, four-engine reconnaissance-bomber. Initially produced as a transport, converted and used against Allied convoys in the Channel and the Atlantic. Also served as a VIP transport, one of which was the Immelmann III: Hitler's personal aircraft.
A stone used to instruct a coachman to unhitch a horse, previously taken on to help pull the coach up a steep gradient.
Very light, depositional limestone formed by the precipitation of calcium carbonate rich water (Tufa). The more dense and compact form, Travertine, is formed in a similar way.

Single-engine, single-seat carrierborne fighter: a Spitfire VB fitted with an arrester hook. Modifications on later versions included folding wings, rocket-assisted take-off gear and conversion for photo-reconnaissance duties.
A door with a planked outer face and spaced horizontal members such as battens or ledges on the inner face.
A type of drying house, usually circular with a conical roof.
Written copy of recorded interviews collected to illustrate history from personal experiences.
A building in London belonging to one of four legal societies having exclusive right of admitting persons to practise at the English bar.

Roman-era pottery, principally made in areas from modern-day France and Germany, for food use, with a characteristic glossy red surface and which may be either decorated or plain, and often produced in quantity as an export cargo.
Usually slag, a residue from burning stone, but can be used for vitrified bricks.
A shallow channel to collect rain water, attached to the eaves of a building.
First practical submarine design. The first to use a combination of battery power and internal combustion engines.
A hospital for the treatment of diseases of the nerves and nervous system.
A narrow bridge for people and animals to cross on foot.
Four-crew, twin-engined monoplane designed as a torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance aircraft for RAF Coastal Command. Withdrawn from operations in November 1940 and downgraded to a trainer.
Moving images made available through projection, video or other methods.

A hinged plate of brass, iron or wood inboard of a ship's scuttle or porthole which can be lowered and secured with a butterfly nut to prevent damage to glass in heavy weather or mask internal light from enemy vessels.
An object attached to a window which is removable.
An associated group of manicure implements.
A workshop with equipment for the making and repair of ships' rigging.
A structure which protects an area of ground from the weather.
A simple, lean-to structure, such as those built by the dock companies to provide shelter for dock workers waiting for work.
The Festival of Sacrifice.
Monument visible on the sea, lake or river bed, either totally submerged at all times, or exposed at low tide, low water conditions etc.
A bay in a two storeyed house open to the roof to allow smoke to escape.
American, single-engine fighter designed for operation from US Naval aircraft carriers. Produced between 1940 and 1945, Wildcats provided to the British Fleet Air Arm were renamed Martlets.
A progressive development of the DO17, the twin-engined DO217 entered service in 1941. The DO217 saw service as a bomber over the UK and took part in the 'Baedecker' raids of 1942.
A courtyard in a prison or workhouse for the inmates to take exercise.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of urinary disorders and diseases.
A room in a monastery used by monks or nuns as a day room.

Four-engined heavy bomber, developed by Avro from the twin-engined Manchester. Entered service in 1942 as the RAF's principal night bomber and took part in the 1,000 bomber raids as well as the famous Dam Busters raid.
A building where pins are manufactured.
A report detailing the results of a study of the fabric of a standing building.
An internal door flush with, and decorated to match, the wall it is set in for the purpose of concealment.
A long vertical pillar usually of stone used as a structural support in buildings often artistically sculpted or shaped.
A chapel for a prison, either attached or in a separate building.
A latrine, or privy, situated at the rear of a monastery dormitory.
A latrine.
A room intended for, and usually equipped to aid, the performance of ablutions.
Use for vessels registered in the Faroe (also spelt Faeroe) Islands, e.g. at Torshavn
A defensive or boundary earthwork.
A linear earthwork, usually a bank accompanied by a ditch, which runs across rather than along an area or ridge of higher ground.
A structure extending into the sea for the purpose of preventing further movement of washed up sand and shingle.
A shaft allowing access to an area. Often used as an additional escape route to the main shaft in a mine or as an air shaft.
A shaft designed to allow for the adequate circulation of air through a transport tunnel, for example.
Use only if function unknown, otherwise use specific type.
A passageway, duct or pipe used for the conveyance of heat, gasses, smoke or air.
A building in a military complex (eg. naval dockyard, castle, etc.) for preparing gunpowder.
A wooden rod passed through a spindle whorl. Used to handspin fibre.
A site used for the manufacture of lasts, shoemaker's models of the foot for shaping and repairing footwear. Lasts can be from a variety of materials, such as wood or iron.
Combined physical and mental health difficulties or conditions.
A space in a Buddist building that is used for teaching Dharma/Dhamma - the teachings of Buddha.
A building housing the services of professionals with an expert knowledge of the law such as the offices of solicitors, barristers and lawyers.
Stone used to line a furnace or oven.

Long-range, four-engine reconnaissance-bomber. Initially produced as a transport, converted and used against Allied convoys in the Channel and the Atlantic. Also served as a VIP transport, one of which was the Immelmann III: Hitler's personal aircraft.
A mixed earthy substance consisting principally of clay mixed with calcium carbonate and sand in very variable proportions.
A purpose built apparatus for the testing of helicopters.
A specialist hospital where women receive medical and surgical treatment.
A dam and sluice combination, associated with an aqueduct, for the extraction of water from a river to feed a reservoir or water treatment plant.
A water feature intended to play a trick on a visitor by drenching them unexpectedly. The device would be triggered by the visitors foot or remotely. Italian for 'water jokes'.
A fertilizer containing nitrogen, derived from sodium nitrate.
An engine which uses air or the products of combustion as its working medium.
A container used to assist in cooling water.

A permanent military RAF aircraft hangar type, designed in 1924. It features a steel frame (with longitudinal ridge and valley trusses for the roof) reinforced concrete and brick infilling for the walls. Typically 122 foot span by 249 foot in length.
An aircraft hangar built to Air Ministry design. Mainly constructed on aircraft factory aerodromes.
A room in which commercial or administrative activities are carried out.
A wooden or stone plinth for depositing milk churns on.
A long, narrow mound of earth or stone and of uncertain date and function. Use more appropriate term where possible.
A burial ground for Roman Catholics.
An instrument used to compress a substance into a smoking pipe.
A rescue station serving a number of mines in the immediate area.

American troop and supply-glider constructed from steel tube and fabric-covered wood, with a hinged nose to allow loading and unloading of troops or light vehicles. Also known as the Haig, this was the only US glider to see combat service.
An open area, often paved or cobbled, surrounded by buildings and accessible to the public.
A site equipped for active defensive action against an airborne enemy assault.
An airfield, and associated structures, used by one or more bomber squadrons.
A prepared area, traditionally grass, where tennis is played.

Four-engine, long range heavy bomber. Developed from the Lancaster, and originally designated the Lancaster Mk. IV, it was larger in size, bombload and fuel capacity. Never used operationally in World War Two.
A late 12th Century capital featuring large, unribbed leaves growing outwards from each angle before curving up towards the abacus and turning inwards at the top.
An establishment providing care for the terminally ill.
Fine earthenware with raised patterns of coloured decoration in the form of an enamel or coloured opaque glaze. Use for decorative wall facings.
Designating or pertaining to hard, brittle substances produced by strong heating of clay.
Hard, unglazed, brown, versatile earthenware which can be used as a tile or moulded into statuary. Used in a structural or semi-structural context as a moulded hollow block.

A bridge consisting of a lattice girder spanning the distance between the tops of two towers. Designed to transport vehicles across the gap in a container suspended at road level by ropes under a travelling crane on the girder.
An instrument of torture used to compress one or both thumbs.
Machine, frequently horse powered, for mixing raw clay into brick earth.
A large bath used for Jewish ritual ceremonies.
A room intended to contain a bed.
A private bed sitting room.
An elevated table or podium on which to place or sacrifice offerings to the deities.

Test pits dug by geotechnical engineers or engineering geologists to obtain information on the physical properties of soil, sediments and bedrock around a site to design earthworks and foundations for proposed structures.
Any subsurface investigation conducted to assist with the technical rather than archaeological aspects of a proposed development or extraction scheme.
A site where large sheets of thin metal are manufactured.
A bridge which takes the towpath across the canal.
A channel dug, or built up, to carry away surplus water from a river or waterway to prevent it bursting its banks and flooding.
Manmade constructions used to prevent water flooding the surrounding area. Often taking the form of a bank or wall but may be more elaborate e.g. the Thames Barrier.
An object made up of a wick surrounded by wax or tallow which burns slowly to provide light.
A spirally grooved object used to join two or more materials together.
A report detailing the results of archaeological fieldwork that has been produced in advance of a full synthesis of the collected data.
A building for the storage, repair and maintenance of chains for lighthouses, lightships and lightbouys.

Single-engine, single-seat, long range fighter originally designed in 1940 to a British requirement. Outstanding low-level speed and range resulted in its assignment to the ground support (Army co-operation) role.
American twin-engined medium bomber and ground-attack aircraft that entered service in 1941. A small number were delivered to the RAF under the British designation Mitchell I.

A transonic jet fighter, first introduced by North American Aviation in 1947. Best known as the United States's first swept wing fighter. Total production at 9,860 units. Important fighter aircraft in the Korean War. Retired in 1994 (Bolivia).
North American Aviation, Inc., incorporated in Delaware in 1928.
Two-seat, single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer. Square-winged and fitted with dual controls, this popular trainer was used by British Commonwealth, as well as American and Canadian, air forces.
A room for temporary imprisonment and detention at a Police Station.
A site where large sheets of thin metal are manufactured.
German single-engine, four-seat maritime patrol and reconnaissance flying-boat. In production between 1934 and 1940, the DO18 was replaced by the three engined DO24.
A prefrabicated home sited in parks where a pitch fee is charged. Although technically mobile they usually only make one journey before being permanently installed.
A site used for the production of anaesthetic gas.
Pinion which engages with the spur wheel and drives the millstones in a corn mill.
A pointed instrument for writing, usually on wax tablets.
Blocks of cast iron as it appears when first removed from the smelting furnace.
Long stole worn by Anglican clergy during a service.
A workshop used by a joiner; a craftsman working with wood and producing more ornate work than that of a carpenter.
A nunnery of nuns belonging to the Order of the Servants of the Blessed Virgin Mary or Servites.
A ship acting as a base for smaller vessels and or submarines.

A funerary site, either totally or partially underground, for the depositing of the dead. Often found in cemeteries in the form of a circular or semi-circular sunken area comprising of several galleries with vault entrances built into the side.
An area where builders keep building materials such as brick, stone, planks and cement.
Construction blocks manufactured using clay which is then fired or sun dried.
The limit line of a parish.
An early form of railway for the transportation of freight by wagons on rails on a road.
Three-seat, single engine, high wing braced monoplane designed for civil use and first flown in 1929. Saw military service in World War 2 in an Army co-operation and communications role.
An aircraft used in the assistance of ground-based military operations.
A cross designed to be placed upon an altar.
An object consisting of a vertical member with a transverse member. Usually there is a religious or ritual significance to such an object.

A crane consisting of a lattice girder carried on a lattice tower forming a T-shaped structure. A hoist is carried along the girder by a 'crab', enabling the crane to perform a variety of tasks eg loading/unloading of ships.
A handheld lamp used to send morse code messages ship-to-ship or ship-to-shore.The lamp and its reflector can be covered/uncovered by a trigger operated shutter.
Objects used to transmit a definite message through a visual non written means, includes stamps and matrices to create these.
A substance designed to emit a sweet smell.
A factory for the assembly of bicycles.
A large cross designed to be carried in a procession.
A place where military personnel parade, practice marching, assemble or muster for a march or any other special purpose.

A biplane torpedo-bomber designed to be flown from aircraft carriers. Equipped with foldable wings for ease of storage. Joined Fleet Air Arm service in 1940, intended as a replacement for the Swordfish.
A stall where eels, either raw or cooked, are sold.
A single-engine, two-crew biplane day bomber and general purpose aircraft, developed from the IIIF (some of which were converted into Gordons) and first flown in 1931.
A mill used to process logwood, the inner red wood of a South American tree used widely in dyeing. Imported in the form of logs and cut and ground into dye by a mechanical process.
A container for drinking, with a base and stem but without handles.

A wall within a lead mine surrounding a dressing floor, where waste from mining and smelting is deposited, to protect livestock from entering and consuming contaminated material and becoming poisoned, or 'bellanded'.

A prefabricated structure of standard lightweight timber wall sections bolted together. Externally the walls were clad with plasterboard covered with felt. Designed in 1940 for use as barrack accommodation.
A factory where hemp, the woody stalk of the hemp plant, used for the making of coarse cloth and cordage, was processed.
An arch with jambs that do not stand at an angle of ninety degrees to its face.

A small underground chamber from where it was intended to monitor radioactive fallout in the event of nuclear attack. The majority were built between 1956 and 1964, although construction continued into the early 1970s.
A civil and administrative area incorporating a town of medieval origin.
British two-seat, twin-engined night fighter. Also used for roles such as long-range escort fighter, ground-attack and anti-shipping strike aircraft, bomber, torpedo-carrier and rocket fighter.
A smooth, flammable liquid, produced naturally or from plants or animals, and used for a variety of purposes.
Unrefined oil used in the manufacture of petroleum.

Twin-engined, six-crew, heavy bomber. Conceived as a rival to the Lancaster and Flying Fortress, the HE177 was dogged by mechanical and structural problems. Of a thousand produced, only about two hundred saw action.
A portable beehive, often made of straw.
A receptacle used as a home for bees, traditionally made of thick straw-work in the shape of a dome, but sometimes made of wood.
The top stone of an arch which holds it all in place.
A fishing vessel employed exclusively on the Grand Banks cod fisheries.
A measure for liquid holding two pints which is a quarter of a gallon.
A site containing slipways and associated buildings used specifically for the repair of ships and larger ocean-going craft.
A path for pedestrians only.
A path covered in a layer of water-worn or pounded stones.
A way made for pedestrians, especially one merely made by walking (often not specially constructed).
A rock-like deposit consisting largely of calcium carbonate, formed by the precipitation of calcium carbonate out of calcium-rich water bodies such as springs.
A structure used for the lifting of boats and other water craft.
German three-engined air/sea rescue and transport flying boat. Entered service in 1940 as a replacement for the DO18.
A mill where long-staple hair, often from llamas, is made into yarn.
A square pillar.
A commercial building, or buildings, used for the production of soft drinks.
A building for housing, maintaining and repairing motor cars. Dating to the 1890s.
Use only for buildings which house motor vehicles. Includes garages for vehicle repair. For petrol sales use PETROL STATION.
An area of a port, dock or harbour where cargo vessels can load and unload large storage containers. May include a rail terminal for containers which have been transported to the port by rail.
Argyll and Bute
A factory or complex where chamois leather is produced using fish oils as the tanning agent.
A factory for the manufacture of leather goods, such as shoes, saddles, etc. Use TANNERY for the manufacture of leather.
A bridge in which one leaf may be retracted in a horizontal plane, passing on rollers over or under the adjacent fixed leaf.
A form of frying pan, usually medieval.

A maritime investigation that records depth data which can be used to map submerged topography utilising echo sounders which emit a short acoustic pulse. Depth is calculated by measuring the time taken for the pulse to be reflected back to the transducer.

Defined as species present after the last glaciation e.g. oak, ash, elm, beech, birch, alder, hazel, hornbeam etc. Specify in Description whether currently managed, unmanaged, or management not determined.
An abbey founded in 1415 for nuns of the Bridgettine order.

A horizontal surface separating the base of a rampart or earthwork from an associated ditch or moat. Can also refer to a continuously sloping bank of earth against a wall, as in a fortified city wall.
A container for a pyx which is often a canopied niche in a wall.
Essex
The sculpted head, shoulders and breast of a person.
Use for vessels registered in Argentina.
A castle built on a simple, rectangular plan, usually with a tower at each corner. This design became common in England after 1300.
A natural flow or current of water issuing from a source.
A building or room used for the repair and maintenance of machinery in a large complex, such as a hospital, school or factory.
Wood which is soft or easily cut, particularly the wood of coniferous trees.
A court of criminal, and limited civil, jurisdiction in England and Wales. Established in 1972 to replace the Assize Court, following legislation in 1971.
A building or group of buildings situated close to the sea used by coastguards to enable them to monitor the coastline.

A building within the gunpowder works complex. During the gunpowder production process, the mill cake was broken down, pressed and then corned. The remaining dust was removed from the corned powder by tumbling it in gauze-covered revolving cylinders.

A building within a gunpowder works complex, where the mill cake (pulverised and incorporated ingredients of gunpowder) was broken down. It was crushed or broken down by passing it between pairs of revolving gunmetal rollers in a breaking-down machine.
A site used for the manufacture of gunpowder.
A mill used for the preparation of Barilla, an ash of burnt seaweed that was used for the production of soda.
A structure, partly underground, for the preservation of ice for use during warmer weather.
Unsorted sediment (i.e. containing everything from clay to boulders) laid down directly by a glacier.
Deposits formed as the result of the action of ice masses during glacial periods.
A stone edging on a footway dividing it from a carriageway.
A stick used to beat a drum.
A tool with a curved blade and a short handle. The blade is on both sides of a line extended from the handle. If just on one side use reaping hook.
A capital warship, often steam driven, heavily armoured with armament of large calibre guns deployed in turrets.
A heavily armoured capital ship with an armament composed entirely of large calibre guns and powered by stem turbines. In effect any battleship constructed after 1908.
An instrument with a series of pipes at different pitches, the air being produced by bellows, and pipes selected by keyboard or sliders.
Four-seat, twin-engined medium bomber. Entered service in 1938. After serving Bomber Command from 1939-42, was converted to a torpedo-bomber and mine-layer with RAF Coastal Command.
A material resulting from the smelting of iron ore.
A boat fashioned out of a section of tree trunk.
A college where the applied sciences and the mechanical arts are taught.
A flat stone, often sandstone, used for paving.
Three-seat, single engine, high wing braced monoplane designed for civil use and first flown in 1929. Saw military service in World War 2 in an Army co-operation and communications role.

A chemical works engaged in the manufacture of the coal tar derivative, picric acid, often associated with the textile industry where it was used as a dye, but more commonly with the explosives industry where it was used as the shell filling Lyddite.

Roman, mid-1st century AD two-piece Bow Brooch, derived from the Colchester Brooch, with a winged, transverse head protecting a spring mechanism held by a rear facing hook over the chord, its profile evoking a leaping dolphin.
A room, usually lined with wood panels, that is heated to a hot and steamy temperature using a small stove and intended to be used for relaxation and therapeutic purposes.
An instrument for holding back a part of a body eg an organ.
A large shallow bowl for letting liquids stand.
Fortified wine produced on the island of Madeira.
A spheroid produced predominantly by birds, though also produced by some animals, which encases the young creature providing a place for it to develop.
A site used by a carrier to accommodate his horses and vehicles and store goods awaiting transportation, etc.
A site where wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
A building in which wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
A German coastal minelaying submarine in use during the First World War. The U Boat carried 12 mines but was otherwise unarmed with no deck gun or torpedo tubes.
