A technique which uses the measurement of decay in radioactive lead (Pb) isotopes to determine a date. Useful for sediments and lead-based paints between 1 and 400 years old.
A gauge for measuring the volume of water flowing from a river to machinery using the water for motive power??
A small-scale garden.
A wheel which is turned by a horse in order to provide power. Used in mines, manufacturing and farming.

Also known as the C-47 Skytrain, this twin-engined, military transport was developed from the DC-3 twenty-eight-seat commercial airliner and was the most extensively employed transport of the Second World War.
An old ship hull used as a base for lifting tackle.

A structure consisting of different cells equipped with instrument posts which supported finders. These provided range and bearing of the projected position of the target to guns emplaced in a nearby battery. Errected along the coast in the late 1870s.
A site where products containing sugar or honey, such as cakes, sweets, crystallized fruits or jam, were manufactured.
Principal glider-pilot training glider fitted with tandem seats. Spruce and plywood in construction, the Hotspur served with the Glider Pilot Regiment between 1941 and 1945.
A building in which hoops (for masts) were heated.
A building on a railway system housing levers used to regulate trains on the tracks using signals and to change the points to enable a train to transfer from one track to another.
An establishment or building where the breeding and training of birds of prey takes place.
Record colour in appropriate field.
A sculptured group comprising a chariot drawn by four horses.
Miles M.14 Magister. Single-engine, two-crew training and communications aircraft. Spruce and plywood in construction, with open cockpits and a fixed landing gear, served between 1937 and 1945.
Miles Aircraft, Ltd., originally known as Phillips & Powis Aircraft Ltd.. Formed in 1935 as a public company to take over aircraft manufacture from Phillips & Powis Aircraft (Reading) Ltd.
A cast iron post similar to a lamp post, with revolving top to carry either coloured plates, or an oil lamp with coloured glass at night. Associated with canal or river navigation locks.
A factory where tweed, a twilled woollen fabric with an unfinished surface, is manufactured.
Buildings and sites associated with the printing and publishing industry.
A printer's workshop in the newspaper/publishing industries.
A recess for holding the Holy Sacrament.
A vehicle with two wheels for carrying loads.

Small, light, fast, all-purpose craft designed primarily for inland use. Generally flat-bottomed, often with rocker; sharp bow, sharp or transom stern, lapstrake or carvel planking. Propelled by oars, sails or motor. Used for fishing and leisure.
A factory where packaging products, such as cardboard boxes, are produced.
A round hut, similar to a CHARCOAL BURNERS HUT, associated with forest industry. The bark was later used in the tanning process.
A purpose built tower used for the testing of helicopter rotor blades.

American, four-engine, long range, heavy strategic bomber. Entered service in 1943 and used exclusively against Japanese forces. The B29s Enola Gay and Bock's Car were used to drop atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945.
A site used for the production of dyes from natural ingredients.
A site used for the production of dyes from controlled chemical reactions. In use from the mid 19th century onwards.
A place in which turpentine is produced.
An explosive-proof vaulted chamber used for the storage or ordnance.
A factory for the manufacture of heels for the shoe making trade.

An enclosed structure of brick, stone or metal in which material is heated or burned, or, in a domestic context, food is cooked, through the continuous radiation of heat from its floor, walls or ceiling.
A site where jet is extracted from the surface of the ground.
A fortified building or site with purpose built emplacements for artillery pieces.
A steam-powered machine used for raising ore or water from a mine.
A separate residence for guests, a house on a private estate or a monastery building specifically for receiving visitors.
A bridge built to enhance or compliment the surrounding landscape. Mainly found on estates or in parkland and usually 18th and 19th century.
A bridge constructed using rockwork to create a craggy, naturalistic appearance. A feature of 18th century rococo gardens and parks.
A bridge decorated with shells forming an ornamental feature.
A house by a toll gate or toll bridge where tolls are collected.
A signpost, usually placed at a juntion or crossroads, bearing a number of individual signs radiating outward from the post to indicate locations in several directions.
A post bearing one or more signs indicating the direction, and often the distance, to specified locations or routes.
A biplane, reconnaissance aircraft with a crew of 3 or 4 which equipped 3 and 22 squadrons RAF before passing to the Fleet Air Arm. Produced in two variants.
A window that forms a projection from the body of a building, extending down to ground level, forming a bay in the wall's interior.
A funnel, connected to an opening in the floor of the tun encasing the grindstones in a corn mill, that carries ground meal away to a bin or sack.
Use for the remains of epidermis or outermost layer. Relates to both animals and plants. If describing the actual object use PLANT REMAINS, ANIMAL REMAINS or HUMAN REMAINS.
A site where all the processes for the production of glass and objects made from glass are carried out.
A factory used for the production of thick, flat glass used for shop window panes, etc. Plate glass is produced by rolling and casting rather than traditional blowing.
A mechanical device, used in a corn mill, that separates bran from meal to produce a whiter flour.
A mechanical device, used in a corn mill, that sieves and grades flour or meal and separates oversized particles.
A place where watches and timepieces are manufactured and mended.
Flexible, twisted fibres, joined together, for tying objects.
A timber framed house comprising horizontal and vertical timbers, forming the walls of the building and directly supporting the roof.
A house where the upper storeys rest on projecting floor joists and so create the effect of an overhang.
A house constructed with a basic timber framework; between the members are panels which can be infilled with timber, wattle and daub, plaster, brick or other materials.
A house in which a pair of curved timbers form a bowed A-frame which supports the roof independently of the walls.
A block in the position of a tiebeam.
A small dwelling for the solitary confinement of a pious reclusive religious woman or nun, often attached to the north wall of a church. A squint enabled the occupant to witness the Mass.
Small stone hearth set up in a shallow pit. Burns vegetation and coppiced twigs to produce potash.
A roadside telephone box for use by motorists in need of assistance.
A device patented in 1733 for speeding up the weaving of cloth.
A watchtower used to guard prisons, camps or other facilities.
An apartment for the use of people of high status, often the owner of the building. Also a room adjoining, or close to, a hall and used as a drawing room or venue for private functions.
Articles, usually woven from coarse fibres or made from hard wearing materials (eg. rubber or cork) used to protect the floor or for lying, sitting or kneeling on.
A buttress attached to a corner of a structure, seeming to be a continuation of one of the walls.
A room in a church where vestments and sacred vessels are stored.
A large wooden structure built alongside the edge of a canal where narrow boats may lie for the loading and unloading of goods.
A dockyard crane permanently mounted on a lighter.
Scaffolding erected on a beach and in the surf so as to prevent hostile forces from landing.
A workshop or factory where brass articles are made by casting molten material into a mould.
A brass manufacturing complex incorporating battery mill furnaces, hammers, etc.

A type of stoneware jug dating to the 16th and 17th centuries, popularly known as a Bellarmine jug, shaped in the figure of a bearded man. They were produced in the Cologne region, particularly Frechen.
A commercial bakery or bread factory. If domestic use BAKEHOUSE.
A building or site used for the storage and distribution of food.
A building, or buildings, providing accommodation for an infantry regiment.
A disc-shaped plate brooch.

An Anglo-Saxon disc brooch featuring an upturned rim. Usually decorated with zoomorphic or geometric designs either chip-carved directly on the face or applied to a thin bronze plate affixed to the brooch's floor.
A parterre consisting of an area of turf often with a pattern cut into it.
A parterre consisting of square beds containing ornamental plants often laid out in intricate patterns mimicking embroidery.
A level space in a garden occupied by ornamental flower beds.
A vessel used in 'dry cupping' to form a vacuum over an area of skin.
an instrument or tool used for medical purposes.
A long narrow spoon used to remove cosmetics or medicines from narrow necked containers.
A cylinder containing a piston by which fluid can be ejected or sucked in.
An instrument for letting blood.
A shed used for the maintenance and repair of aircraft.
Range used by the Navy with reinforced observation huts which housed quadrant equipment to record accuracy and damage.
A combination of spear and axe on a long handle.
Originally a fence against which trees and shrubs were grown. Later used to describe a row of trees and shrubs forming a hedge clipped into a green wall.
A central office dealing with financial accounts.

Unspecified defensive structure like a mound of earth, a rampart, an embankment or a wall-like fortification. Also used as an early term for a bastion or blockhouse. Use more specific term where known.
A building housing computers and information technology equippment e.g. for a business, factory or other instituion.
A place from which clay is extracted.
A pit used for the excavation of clay suitable for making bricks.
A site used for all the processes associated with the manufacture of roof, floor or decorative tiles.
A mechanical structure, consisting of a roller or beam on supports, round which a rope or chain is wound, and used for various purposes, eg. raising a bucket from a well, etc.
A factory where lengths of soft, woollen cloth, loosely woven to retain heat, used as a bed covering, were manufactured.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Poor Knights of Christ and the Temple of Solomon, commonly known as the Knights Templars
A garden designed to provide living material for the study of botany and horticulture.
A lancet arch designed in the composite style.
A steam-powered machine used for raising materials such as ore or water from a pit or shaft.
A tool with a handle and curved blade designed to cut through grass sods.
A building used for the dissemination to the public of such items like tourist brochures, travel maps, guide books and other documents, etc.
A two-storey watch office, built to Air Ministry drawing number 1959/34 but with slight design modifications as detailed in drawing number 1960/34.
A bowl with a single loop handle crossing over the top of the vessel from one side of the rim to the other. (Source: MPRG)
A type of spearhead with a triangular blade bevelled at the edges and with a groove(s) following the outline.
The SI derived unit for current density.
Maritime monument identified as a ferrous object lying on the sea bed detected using marine surveying equipment that detects localised anomalies in the Earth's magnetic field.
Four-crew, twin-engined monoplane designed as a torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance aircraft for RAF Coastal Command. Withdrawn from operations in November 1940 and downgraded to a trainer.
An accounts office, especially within an industrial or commercial complex.
A drawing, often made in the field as the basis for later work, or to quickly convey important information.
A three-sided structure for the production and storage of silage.
A post mill in which the drive is taken down to the base of the mill by putting an upright shaft in the hollowed post.
A type of windmill, mainly timber-framed, whose body, containing machinery and carrying the sail, rotates about an upright post.
A twin engine advanced trainer developed by Beech/ Beechcraft , a US firm, used in WWII
A building plan in which the principal fireplace is positioned on the side wall.

Single-engine, two-crew fighter, also used for convoy escort and reconnaissance. Designed to operate from aircraft carriers. Entered service with the Fleet Air Arm in 1940 and remained in use until 1945.
A mill in which strands of yarn are twisted together to produce a strong thread with a uniform thickness.
A building used for the crystallization process in alum making.
A group of buildings or works where the evaporation and crystallization of sodium aluminium sulphate solution is performed.
A large tank used for soaking alumina-bearing shale in water and chemicals, the initial stage in the alum-making process.
A channel which carried processed alum as liquid from the alum quarry/works to the alum house
A stone with the date on it, sometimes of an event, person etc.
A place where vehicles can be filled up with petrol, oil, water, etc.
A long, low-rise building consisting of rows of attached individual suites of rooms used for overnight accommodation by motorists.
A German coastal minelaying submarine in use during the First World War. The U Boat carried 12 mines but was otherwise unarmed with no deck gun or torpedo tubes.
A house with a range at the end of it, at right angles to the main range.
A platform, sometimes floating, for the landing of passengers and goods from vessels.
Record of events.
A post or pillar set up alongside a road to mark the miles from or to a place.
A post set up alongside a canal to mark the miles to and from a place.
Twin-engined fighter-bomber. All metal in construction, entered service in 1940. Supported bombing operations and participated in attacks on France, but not widely used due to engine faults.
A place of worship for followers of the Countess of Huntingdon's Connexion, a Calvinistic Methodist sect founded in the 1740s by Selina Hastings, Countess of Huntingdon.

Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber: Curtiss P40 Warhawk, known to the RAF as the Tomahawk, later renamed Kittyhawk. Serving from 1941 to 1942, control difficulties in dive attacks impeded bombing accuracy, resulting in use for larger targets only.
A mine used for the extraction of any hard dark-coloured rock.
A roof with one side longer than the other, continuing at the same pitch over an extension to a building. Commonly found in New England Colonial architecture.
A lean-to or monopitched roof, or a projecting canopy over a door, window, or stair.
An artificial mound of earth indicating either the former site of a windmill or built as the base of a post windmill.
A private chamber usually in a Royal residence.
A radio station set up to broadcast signals aimed at 'bending' or altering German navigation transmissions.
An attachment to furniture that can be detached.
Soft coverings and associated objects for walls, furniture, floors and windows. Also items such as chairs, beds, and cupboards.
An enclosed area of parkland used almost exclusively for the hunting of deer.
A building used for the treatment of victims of chemical, gas or other forms of contamination.
A wooden or metal structure covering a shipbuilding slip way.
A chemical works engaged in the production or refining of toluene, a substance extracted from coal tar or specific types of crude oil, and used in the production of explosives during WW1.
An abbey or priory for monks of the Benedictine order.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of eye disorders and diseases.
Single-engine, two-seat tractor bomber and reconnaissance aircraft. Entered service in 1916 and, during 1917 and 1918, equipped nine RFC squadrons in its reconnaissance role.
Ground oats used as food, often in the form of porridge.
An upright timber standing on a tiebeam to support a collar or purlin. Once used as an alternative to king post, this term is now restricted to the shorter post ending at collar level.
Use for vessels believed to come from Central America but where the precise nationality is not known.
Use for vessels registered in Panama. Often used as a flag of convenience.
An area of land, roughly shaped like a polygon and enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
A mill where flax fibres were woven into linen cloth.
Extremely hard, fine grained, grey to brown silica rich sandstone. It is often found on the surface of the South Downs and has been used, as found, since prehistoric times.
Dried kernel of coconut
An abbey or a priory of Cistercian nuns.
A covered walk, walled on one side and usually arcaded on the other, surrounding or partly surrounding an open area in a monastery or similar complex of Christian buildings.
A boat roofed over and fitted up as a home for living in permanently or temporarily.
Building housing apparatus for testing chain links.
A site where wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
An unsocketed earthenware or porous concrete pipe laid end to end unjointed so as to drain the ground.
Any building, group of buildings, or site at which tungsten ores have been converted to sodium tungstate by means of the Oxland Process. This was first used at Drakewalls Mine, Cornwall, in 1850.
A large barn used to store the tithe (a tenth part of the annual produce of agriculture etc.) which was paid by the tenants of ecclesiastical lands.
A site where peat (vegetable matter decomposed in water and partly carbonised), used for fuel, is cut.
A building in which an organization or society is instituted to promote literature through lectures, study and research, etc.
Pieces of wood used to form the sides of barrels.
A picture or pattern produced by cementing together small pieces of stone or glass of various colours. May be in the form of a floor.
The impost, or point at which a vault rests upon its support, and from which it seems to spring. Hence the term describes the bottom stone of a vault, which lies on the impost.
A specific type of early medieval pin. Do not use in instances where a pin has become detached from the brooch.
An object marked or shaped by the pressure of another object upon its surface, whether by deliberate process or unintentionally.
An object decorated or otherwise marked by the use of a stamp; for example, a maker's stamp.
A levelled area of ground on which a barn is built. A platform is often the sole surviving evidence for a barn.
An area within a hospital where children are accommodated during the period of their medical or surgical treatment.
Use for deposits formed in caves.

A machine tool for producing large flat surfaces on metal objects. It comprises a large work table which slides backwards and forwards along a substantial guide bed, passing under a stationary bridge containing a fixed tool.
A hilltop enclosure bounded by a single rampart, usually accompanied by a ditch.
A radio-controlled target tug version of the Tiger Moth used for target practice. 380 were built for the RAF.
A brace, parallel to another, in wall framing or arcading, or in trusses between post and tiebeam; also referred to as a duplicate brace.
The third and latest subdivision of the Bronze Age.
A bowl whose form resembles two cones joined together at their widest points, forming a carination.
A place where beehives are kept.
A building with shelves and/or stands for skeps or wooden hives, and flight holes through the walls for bees.
A dark outbuilding or cellar with internal recesses for overwintering skeps of bees.
A building in which cattle are housed overnight, normally tethered in stalls.
A bridge carrying a railway track across a river, valley, road etc.
A small, handled, open vessel, generally with a steep profile, designed to sit partially within a larger vessel and used to warm drinks. (Source: MPRG)

The RAF's first jet fighter, flown operationally during 1944-5, with later versions serving for a further ten years after the war. The Meteor's first active operations were in the interception and destruction of V.1. flying bombs.
A place where meat and fruit, etc, is preserved by salting and/or drying.
A hollow ball for containing aromatic substances eg perfume.
That area between high and low water levels. Specify in Description using; sand, shingle, mud flat, estuarine silt, rock etc.
A place where the popular gambling game of bingo is played.
Buildings where gambling takes place.
A garden building usually in a secluded spot, resembling a hermit's dwelling and built as a resting place, retreat or viewing point.
A type of 18th century public park, with refreshment houses, concert rooms, etc.
A room with apparatus for washing the hands and face, now often combined with a water closet.
British twin-engined light/medium bomber developed from the model 142 civil transport. Noted for its speed, this three-crew monoplane had an all-metal, stressed skin structure and a 1000lb bomb load.
A room usually set aside for the provision of materials used in a household.

Three/four-crew, single-engine, shipboard observation and air/sea rescue amphibian seaplane. Entered RAF service in 1936. Also employed for gunnery spotting, anti-submarine and convoy protection duties.
Covered area for making large engineered constructions such as sections of ships or bridges.
An arch, either pointed or round, which broadens above the springing line, creating a horseshoe shape.
Polished bone used to burnish objects eg pottery.
A site with one or more defensive earthworks, often at a river crossing incorporating natural features which define parts of the curtilage.
An imprecise term used to describe large Iron Age settlements of town-like proportions.
A workshop for the manufacturing of furniture.
Any wall enclosing a building or complex of buildings, eg. prisons, dockyards, factories, etc.

A coin struck, cast or stamped imitating an official coinage issue of contemporary or slightly later time period. The piece may consist of a similar alloy or a base core with plating of varying thickness.
A specific form of cauldron, generally of rounded profile made in the Low Countries. (Source: MPRG)
A large pot used for boiling.
A garment hook having a flat plate, often decorated, with two or more holes for attachment and a hooked projection. The term is often used for early Medieval examples.
Railway constructed specifically for the movement of coal around the pithead of a coal mine.
Any metal prinicipally composed of the chemical element Iron (Fe).

Class of elements and alloys that are characteristically lustrous, ductile, fusible and malleable. These are extracted from ore minerals originally existing in nature and processed before becoming a recognisable metal.
Decorative armour used for parades and display, not for combat.
Area feature visible as an earthwork or cropmark with no known function.
A light, mostly wooden errected structure serving as workshop for the building, storage, repair and maintenance of boats.

American troop and supply-glider constructed from steel tube and fabric-covered wood, with a hinged nose to allow loading and unloading of troops or light vehicles. Also known as the Haig, this was the only US glider to see combat service.

The Waco Aircraft Company, established in 1921. One of the largest pre-war producers of civil aircraft in America, Waco specialised in the production of troop and cargo carrying gliders during World War Two.
A public house licensed for the sale of wine and other alcoholic drinks.
The public house was a 19th century development, distinctive from the earlier BEER HOUSE by its decorative treatment and fittings.
A hospital where people with learning difficulties receive medical treatment.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Hospital For People With Learning Difficulties

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: Nowadays a hospital where patients suffering from psychiatric disorders receive medical care and treatment. Traditionally they were often places where psychiatric patients were kept confined away from society receiving minimal medical care or attention.
A factory used to make packaging.
A spoon used to dispense communion wine.
A market for the sale of cheeses.

Structures, traditonally consisting of a long shank with two arms at one end and a ring to attach to cable at the other, used to hold a ship in one place by mooring it to the bottom of the sea. Usually made of stone or metal.
A low, wide, circular ring or bank of stones surrounding an open, roughly circular area which is (or was initially) free of cairn material. The inner and outer faces of the bank may be kerbed.
An abbey or priory of Augustinian canons.

A type of warehouse found in naval victualling yards, used for the storage of rum, a ration of which was given on a daily basis to members of the Royal Navy, up until the 1980s, when this practice ceased.
For the production of clay tobacco pipes.
A gun emplacement which conforms to Department of Fortification and Works drawing number 55422.
Cargo vessel specially constructed to carry bulk items such as grain. Does not include liquid cargoes.
A carving, often a bust or full-length figure, originally found above a ship's cutwater. Use as an external feature only.
A round barrow featuring a small mound separated from a ditch of much greater diameter by a wide berm. The ditch may be accompanied by an external (or occasionally internal) bank.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
A factory used for the manufacture of serge, a heavy woollen cloth.
Buildings, sites and structures associated with the manufacture of lace.
A building where lace was laid out to dry.
A workshop where baskets were manufactured.
A two-storey watch office similar in design to drawing number 1959/34 but constructed completely from concrete. A large, almost square, ground plan with a central observation tower.
A processing house containing equipment for sieving caked gunpowder to produce graded granules.
An internal combustion engine which uses a mixture of air and petrol as fuel, the combustion of which is by an electric spark.
Submerged obstacles to stop the landing of Seaplanes
Shallow ditches and/or poles erected across open land to obstruct the landing of enemy aircraft and gliders.
Originally a large tract of wooded country, owned by the Monarchy, for the purpose of hunting. The royal parks of London, eg. Greenwich, are all open to the public and have been for centuries.
A bench with a back, usually in a church.
An overshoe with a thick sole or set on an iron ring to raise the wearer's foot out of the mud and so protect normal shoes.
Cottage provided for guests to a country house.
The spanning of an opening without the use of a lintel.
A strong alloy of steel.
A small object designed to hold together the two ends of a cuff.
A bent piece of metal or bone, often with a barb, which is tied to a line and used to catch fish.
A jug with straight vertical sides and roughly equal rim and base diameters. (Source: MPRG)
Three-seat tactical support aircraft. Entering service with the US 9th Air Force in 1944, the Invader had a bomb load of 4,000 lbs and was later used as a conventional medium bomber.
A type of sword often used by infantry.
Transect or area-based arrangements of drilled auger-holes used to describe deposits and collect samples.
A house, the inhabitant of which keeps an official register e.g. a registrar's house near a cemetery would keep an official record of deaths and burials.
Steel coated in zinc, giving good protection against weathering.
A load carrying horizontal structural member.
Decorative mounts on horse harness
An aircraft hangar built to Air Ministry design number 454/43. Mainly constructed on aircraft factory aerodromes
The approximate location at which stray finds of artefacts were found. Index with object name.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
A torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance biplane in service with the Fleet Air Arm 1935-1938. Rendered obsolete after 1938 by the Swordfish and withdrawn from service.

The English Electric Company Limited. Formed in 1918, but didn't move into aircraft production until 1938, at the Government's request. Continued to develop aircraft after the war and in 1948 produced the `Canberra', Britain's first jet-propelled bomber.

Twin-engined jet-fighter. The first British aircraft to exceed Mach 1 in level flight, later to exceed Mach 2. Entered service in 1960. After 13 years was superseded in its primary defence role by the Phantom, though remained in RAF service until 1988.
A mixture of lime or more recently cement with sand and water used for bonding stones or bricks.
A container used to catch blood during bleeding.
A pumping station for draining a mine or colliery.
Single-engine aircraft designed as a dive-bomber. Found to be inadequate in this role, a number of those delivered to the RAF were used as target tugs. Entered service in 1941.

Twin-engined jet-fighter. The first British aircraft to exceed Mach 1 in level flight, later to exceed Mach 2. Entered service in 1960. After 13 years was superseded in its primary defence role by the Phantom, though remained in RAF service until 1988.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of eye and ear disorders and diseases.
A terrace or row of dwellings, with a NAIL SHOP attached to each house.
Single-seat fighter-bomber with a single, midships engine and tricycle landing gear. After proving a failure as an air-combat fighter, was used mainly in the ground attack role.
A short piece of track lying parallel to the main railway line enabling trains and trucks to pass one another. Sidings can also be used to park trains which are not in use.
Oared sailing vessel developed in the 15th century, the larger English version with secondary oars coming into use in the 16th century. Not to be confused with GALEAS.
A long handled weapon which has a long blade in line with the shaft, sharpened on both sides and ending in a point.
Four-seat, twin-engined medium bomber. Entered service in 1938. After serving Bomber Command from 1939-42, was converted to a torpedo-bomber and mine-layer with RAF Coastal Command.
Three-seat, single engine, high wing braced monoplane designed for civil use and first flown in 1929. Saw military service in World War 2 in an Army co-operation and communications role.
An aircraft used in the assistance of ground-based military operations.

Area or zone of sea where a battle, skirmish or action was fought between naval ships or warships and privateers. Not to be used for enemy action upon mercantile ships or a sudden strike by mine/torpedo against an enemy warship.
A tray used for separating the grain from husks and straw.
A dredger which can act as its own hopper and can thus transport the mud which it picks up to dump it at the desired place.
A small, handled axe.
A structure found on lighthouses, piers, etc, capable of emitting a loud noise to warn shipping in foggy weather.
A building or site from which a lookout can be kept.
Roughly spherical, > 5 µm, soot particles produced from the incomplete combustion of fossil fuels. Used as an indicator of industrialisation, and can also be used as a dating tool.
Power generation by releasing stored water through a turbine driving a generator.
The DH5 was an attempt to give a tractor-type fighter a good forward view. However it suffered from unpleasant flying characteristics and, as a result, had a short service career.

A type of large permanent military aircraft hangar with a curved steel frame and storage annexes on its side used in World War II. It was intended for storage purposes on Aircraft Storage Unit stations.

An American turbojet fighter-bomber aircraft. The F-84 was the first production fighter aircraft to utilize in-flight refuelling and the first fighter capable of carrying a nuclear weapon. Designed by Alexander Kartveli, 1946.
A steam powered winding gear used at a colliery or other mine.
Wood of a coniferous tree native to Scotland and Scandinavia.
A rescue tug equipped to care for survivors from torpedoed vessels and also available for towing to port ships damaged by enemy action.
A vessel used for carrying mines between warships and supply depots.
A stand by set house built to Air Ministry drawing number 4238/44.
A path in a garden.
A hospital devoted to the curing or correcting of physical deformities.
A simple, pointed implement for piercing.

A strategic food store, directly operated by, or on behalf of, the government. The stores were used to store a variety of foodstuffs. They were in operation from the end of the Second World War until the early 1990's.
A base of the Roman Doric order with a torus, an astragal and a fillet.
A building, often located in a park, where players can change and store equipment and from where spectators can watch the game.
An area of ground immediately surrounding a cathedral.
A vertical timber resting on a hammer beam and forming a triangle between it and a principal.
Photographic format.
A laithe with an attached house.
An Anglo-Saxon fortified town or other defended site, not necessarily urban.
A group of trees planted as part of a designed landscape.
A type of public building common in the 18th and 19th century, serving as an educational and/or learned society institute.
A hospital building of uncertain function. Use more specific type if known.
A building or room used for holding, viewing, identifying or examining dead bodies prior to burial or cremation.
Potassium Carbonate obtained from the ashes of burnt plant matter and used as a fertilizer.

A streamlined, twin-engined bomber, the DO17 entered service in 1937 with the Condor Legion, having started life as a high-speed mail and passenger transport aircraft, a role for which it was ill-suited due to the narrowness of the fuselage.
A box in which one or more games are stored.
An ornamental wand or rod carried as a symbol of authority

A subsidiary enclosure externally attached to an enclosure of known or unknown date and function. The annexe is generally smaller than, and secondary to, the main enclosure. Use more specific site type where known. Do not use for Roman military sites.
A prominent structure situated on land specifically as a guide to navigation for travellers or as an aid/warning to sailors out at sea.
A building used for the testing of steel.
A hut, usually built as part of a complex on a military base or airfield and used for the recreation of military personnel.
A container, usually glass, used for storing medicinal substances.
A mechanism used to turn a trolleybus around.

A small, metal, crescent-shaped object, often highly decorated, worn across the upper part of the chest by military personnel as a badge of rank and as a symbolic representation of the former piece of armour (see GORGET (ARMOUR).
A specialist hospital for the medical treatment of patients suffering from epilepsy. Originally epilepsy was seen as a mental illness.
A precious metal characterised by its yellow colour and resistance to tarnishing.
A covered gateway, at the entrance to a churchyard, where during a funeral a coffin could be set down until the vicar arrived.

Areas within the urban environment with their surfaces open to the sky, that have been consciously acquired or publicly regulated to serve urban shaping function, in addition others may provide recreational opportunities.
An area, often consisting of widened streets or a town square, where booths and stalls may be erected for public sales.
An area of agriculturally used land, which is divided into small, elongated, rectangular fields running parallel to each other.
The SI derived unit for density or mass density.
An area or wing of a hexagonal plan workhouse or prison from where the supervision of the inmates is carried out.
A refuse heap.
A refuse heap of discarded shells.
An opening or cavity through which a stream or natural watercourse disappears underground.
A body which has been interred in boggy or marshy ground or other similarly waterlogged environment. Interment may have been deliberate or accidental.
A small gable above a hipped roof. Also used ornamentally, such as on a buttress or over a niche.
A pond located at or near a swannery.
A mechanical device consisting of a system of signal lights operating in sequence, placed at road intersections and pedestrian crossings to regulate traffic.
A small hole filled or vacated by a stake, normally driven into the ground.
A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of meat.
A stone (including standing stones, natural boulders and rock outcrops) decorated with carved motifs.

Roman mid-first to third century AD S or reverse-S shaped brooch. Often enamelled, with its central section expanded for decoration, the brooch depicted stylised creatures derived from Celtic art. The pin was looped over the neck of the brooch.
A house joined to another to form one building.
A mine countermeasure vessel built to detect and destroy individual naval mines. (See Minesweeper for vessels that sweep and explode mined areas at sea without prior detection).
An artificial steep-sided earthen mound on, or in, which is set the principal tower of a castle.
An alloy where the predominant component metal is copper.
The choir and sanctuary in the liturgical eastern part of a church appropriated for those who officiate during services.
Railway engines designed to travel under its own power and to draw railway carriages and rolling stock.
A cup with sides falring outwards from the base towards the rim, usually with a single handle.

Type of furnace used in the glass industry to pre-heat glass in crucibles, prior to the main melt. This may have been a separtate structure, or may have been part of the main furnace. All periods from the Roman onwards.
Small fish, common in European waters, caught for food.
A decorative style on a block or band from which an arch springs.
A building where people congregate to undertake sustained mental contemplation or religious or spiritual reflection.
Use for vessels registered in Sweden.
A 1930s British short-haul biplane airliner for 6-8 passengers. It proved an economical and durable craft, despite its relatively primitive plywood construction. Primarily used by the RAF.
A mill used for the manufacture of twilled dress material of worsted with or without a mixture of cotton or silk.
German city spanning the river Rhine.
A high-humped, narrow, cobbled bridge used by trains of packhorses, often located in upland areas where the bulk of goods were carried by horses.
A high tower, attached to or detached from a building such as a church, with a belfry stage containing bells.
A brace running from a vertical to a lower horizontal timber.
A raised lawn in a garden or park.
A flat, and usually level area of mown and cultivated grass, attached to a house.
The Consolidated Aircraft Corporation. In 1943 merged with Vultee Aircraft, Inc. to form the Consolidated Vultee Aircraft Corporation.
American-built, twin-engined flying-boat designed for maritime patrol and reconnaissance. Entered US Naval service in 1936 as the PBY-1; christened the Catalina by the RAF, who used it from 1939 on.
A press used to extract the juice from apples, which was then used to make cider.

A British two-seater army co-operation aircraft manufactured by Hawker Aircraft for the Royal Air Force. A Hart variant biplane that first flew in 1931, becoming a prominent British aircraft in the inter-war period with over 700 units built.
An impulse water turbine comprising a wheel with hemispherical cups arranged around the circumference using high water pressure to revolve the wheel.

A prime mover in which a central wheel with curved vanes, enclosed in a chamber, receives water directed onto the curved vanes by a ring of fixed guide vanes, causing the wheel to rotate about its axis.
Area of land set aside and managed for the preservation of flora, fauna, their natural habitats and physical features.
Fine grained limestone, yellow or yellow/white in colour. Imported from France, mainly for ecclesiastical use.
A structure found on lighthouses, piers, etc, capable of emitting a loud noise to warn shipping in foggy weather.
An apparatus worked by hand or mechanically for weaving yarn into textile.
Hillslope forts with wide spaced ramparts.
A site where copper ore is extracted directly from the surface of the ground.

An unenclosed feature, usually sub-terranean, constructed to contain water for public or private recreation and sporting avtivities. Sometimes part of a LIDO complex. Use INDOOR SWIMMING POOL for pools with a covering structure.

Manmade structure for bathing or swimming that is located on the beachfront and filled by tidal waters. Similar to a LIDO, with the main difference being the extent of the built up complex around the pool.
A workshop containing machinery used to press textiles.
Not subdivided
Wax used to seal letters, envelopes, documents, etc.
A meeting hall, sometimes equivalent to a GUILDHALL, but also associated with some early mining industries.
A small brewery, often situated in a public house, producing limited quantities of beer, for consumption locally and/or on the premises.
Four-crew, twin-engined monoplane designed as a torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance aircraft for RAF Coastal Command. Withdrawn from operations in November 1940 and downgraded to a trainer.
An entablature consiting of an architrave, usually a frieze and cornice.
A ship used to process whales into saleable products.
A form of lock on a river, which increased the depth upstream and had a gated opening.
A narrow container, especially one in which food or water for animals is put.
A large, rectangular open space at the centre of a Roman town, incorporating public spaces and a market area.
An arch which is half an ellipse.
A building in which a view is projected onto a wall by means of a lens.
A group of buildings and machines, usually situated close to the pithead, enabling the rapid, mechanized loading of goods wagons with coal.
A lid for a well. Well covers are often ornate and can be made of various materials.
A building or compound housing a permanent establishment of members of a religious organization to do missionary work.
A place where gold ore is extracted.
A water pond in which lilies are grown.

Six-crew, medium-range, twin-engined reconnaissance flying-boat. Entered service with 209 Squadron in 1939 but, due to design and operation problems, saw little action and was not produced in large numbers.
Single-engine, single-seat biplane day fighter developed by Siddeley. Variations included an all-metal, fabric-covered Mk.III, which became the RAF's main fighter in the 1920s.
A site, usually including hardstandings and associated buildings, used for the storage of military vehicles.
The band or block from which the springing of an arch occurs.
A decorative style on a block or band from which an arch springs.
A highly-prized, hard, white, fine-grained dentine constituting the main part of the teeth of walruses, hippopotami and elephants. Used in the manufacture of ornaments and piano keys.
The large, pointed teeth, made of ivory, which are specially developed to protrude from the mouth of elephants.
A prepared area of ground, often enclosed, used for the game of basketball.
Accommodation and facilities for aircrew away from the main RAF airfield.
A piece of material that has been inlaid, or prepared and shaped for inlaying, in an object, decorative feature or other setting.
The area of a town or city, such as a harbour or dockyard, alongside a body of water.
A canal built as a military obstacle, but also used for the transport of military stores, equipment and personnel.
A building used for meetings and other events by Scouts Associations.

A building used for storing Sulphur, a highly inflammable chemical element used in the manufacture of matches, gunpowder and sulphuric acid. It is also used in bleaching, for vulcanizing rubber and as a disinfectant.
Three-seat tactical support aircraft. Entering service with the US 9th Air Force in 1944, the Invader had a bomb load of 4,000 lbs and was later used as a conventional medium bomber.
A large room within a hospital set aside for emergency patients.
An establishment where patients can rest and recover after an operation or illness.
A column of the Tuscan Order featuring a plain, unfluted shaft.
An aircraft maintenance workshop deriving from the use of weather proofing varnish to aircraft canvas called "dope" in order to keep the canvas taut and airtight. From 1912 onwards.
A crane mounted on wheels and/or rails, used for the unloading of ships' cargoes.
A round hut, similar to a CHARCOAL BURNERS HUT, associated with forest industry. The bark was later used in the tanning process.
A wall between two towers or pavilions, usually surrounding a building, and often forming a major part of the defences.
A plant community which includes low shrubs e.g. heathers, bilberry, gorse also the presence of bracken.
An abbey of Franciscan nuns also known as Minoresses or Poor Clares.
A bridge which takes a towing path over a branch canal, basin, etc.
A chapel where the followers of the Anglican tradition worship.
A refuse heap.
A refuse heap of discarded shells.
A community of Protestant followers of Hussite doctrines, first founded by Moravian emigrants in Saxony, Germany.
An abbey or priory of Dominican nuns.
A mine in which access is gained by a straight entrance driven on a constant downward slope. Use with product(s) extracted and MINE where known, eg. COAL MINE.
A vault whose bay is divided by diagonal and transverse ribs into six compartments or cells.
Ornamental wrought iron screen associated with gate lodges or entrance lodges.

A pistol fired by use of a flintlock.A gunflint is held in the lock which on pulling the trigger pushes back the pan cover creating sparks which set off the powder in the pan causing a flame to go through and set off the charge in the barrel.
A form of handgun.
A round or polygonal building containing a wheel turned by an ox to provide power.
A pit which appears to have been dug for, or which contains, objects apparently deposited for reasons other than storage, disposal or extraction. Index with principal object types.
A factory or works principally engaged in the manufacture of blasing or explosive gelatine.
Steam-powered torpedo boat developed in the early 20th century, and used in the First World War, a development of the torpedo boat destroyer, and distinct from the motor torpedo boat of WWII.
A jar for the storage of ointment.
A site where iron is smelted or iron goods made.
A signalling station which used a series of shutters to indicate various messages.
A decorated screen behind an altar.
A hollow, cylindrical structure or tube made of clay, lead, steel, wood etc. through which gas, oil, water or other liquids can be conveyed.
An exterior, vertical pipe that carries rainwater from a roof's guttering, usually to a drain.
A building or room where beer is decanted from conditioning tanks, into casks or barrels.
One of several stones used to raise a farm building, such as a granary, above the ground surface.
Engineering workshop intended either for final adjustments of new machinery or the fitting of replacement parts to machinery under repair.
A gun battery used to signal warnings to ships during bad weather.
A German stoneware form of conical mug. (Source: MPRG)
Domesticated animals, derived from the wild boar, kept as a source of ham, bacon and pork products.
Use for stationary railway carriage being used for a purpose it wasn't originally intended for - office, shelter, etc.
A public house licensed for the sale of wine and other alcoholic drinks.
A system of overhead cables from which cars or containers are suspended (usually driven electrically).
Views achieved from an aircraft or other high location.

A rectangular arena, rounded at one end designed for chariot racing. The racetrack circled a central barrier (spina) constructed between two turning posts (metae). The only known example found in Britain, so far, is in Colchester.
A building where animals are deliberately fattened before being killed for their meat.
A side scraper with a short concavity retouched into an edge. This may be achieved by a single blow. (Source: SARC)
An establishment where wine is produced.
A pipe, usually of reinforced concrete or metal, which delivers pressurized water from a dam to hydraulic turbines.
A tower with one or more horizontal platforms extending out over deep water for use in diving competitions.
A site where vinegar is manufactured from soured beer, wine or cider.
Plan showing a horizontal section, size and arrangement of rooms within a building, may include location of doors, windows and other features.
A horizontal stone placed across a grave.
A barracks including stables and associated buildings housing a cavalry regiment.
A piece of material, usually glass, which has been ground into shape to enhance vision or protect the eyes.
An enclosed area of land of varying size and shape which shows traces of defence.
A base of the Tuscan Order, featuring a square plinth supporting a large torus with a fillet above.

Single-engine, two-crew fighter, also used for convoy escort and reconnaissance. Designed to operate from aircraft carriers. Entered service with the Fleet Air Arm in 1940 and remained in use until 1945.
A building used for the storage of artillery pieces.
A planked or battened door, with large nails or pegs with projecting heads keeping it intact.
A market where goods are bought and sold in bulk, rather than by retail.
A place where students live, sometimes on a college campus.
A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of beer.

An apparatus, featuring an ascending and descending platform or compartment, for carrying people or objects from one level or floor to another. This term can include the shaft or well in which such an apparatus operates.
A basket for the storage and transport of fishing equipment. For the storage and transport of fish use creel.
A chamber built into the side of a covered reservoir to enable the water level to be inspected.
A factory or works principally engaged in the manufacture of the mining explosive sabulite.
A type of bridge which completely encloses the traffic using it.
A loose cloak.
A dwelling-house with outbuildings and land assigned to its use.
A dispersed farmstead where buildings are arranged around scattered yards which can be loose or regular in their form.
Naturally occurring glacial rock fragments (diameter 64-256mm) larger than pebble and smaller than boulder.
A bridge used for carrying liquids, usually water, although sometimes oil, in a pipeline over a river. Mid 19th century onwards.
A waterwheel turned by the weight of water discharged into buckets placed around its circumference from an outlet positioned above it.
A wheel turned by water to generate mechanical power.
A projection from the bottom of a church stall designed to provide some support for a person standing in long services.
A fastener used within a cavity wall to hold the two sides together.
An establishment for the preparation and selling of food to be consumed off the premises.
When a secondary mineral, use term for product type, eg. LEAD MINE.
A factory manufacturing electrical equipment, such as engines, transformers and generators for use in industry.
A roller used in the fulling process to felt cloth.
A residence of two or three monks of the Cistercian order dependent on a foreign mother house.
A room or group of rooms in a building.
A building, department or shop where postal business is carried on.
A building temporarily requisitioned for use as an auxiliary hospital administered by members of the Voluntary Aid Detachment during the First World War.
An industrial building, plant or site where crude substances, such as sugar, metal, oil etc., are purified or refined.
A site where sugar beet was processed before being washed and dried to form granulated sugar.
A bowl adapted by the addition of one or more handles. The handles may be vertical or horizontal loops, or straight, or may comprise vertical or horizontal lugs. (Source: MPRG)
A bowl adapted by the addition of a single handle
1st World War end-opening aeroplane hangar.
A garden with real or supposed Swiss features, including buildings and plantings.
A bowstring truss with the space between its members filled by a lattice of crossing diagonal rods.
An arched, or bow-shaped, segmental timber truss with its ends tied together by a straight or cambered member.

A distinctive form of jar being a flat-based, straight-sided or slightly rounded jar with two opposed, upright, rounded, tongue-shaped lugs raised from above the rim and bridged by added, internal struts used to suspend the pot over a fire. (Source: MPRG)
A small brush used fro cleaning teeth.
A cylindrical container, usually bulging outward in the middle and usually held together by metal hoops.
Four-crew, twin-engined monoplane designed as a torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance aircraft for RAF Coastal Command. Withdrawn from operations in November 1940 and downgraded to a trainer.
The architectural element made of brick, tile, stone or certain woods which surrounds a fireplace to provide aesthetic and safety benefits.
A building or site where bloom iron or cast iron is forged into wrought iron.
A building used for the decarburizing of pig iron to produce wrought iron.
A site where copper or copper based alloys are produced by smelting copper ore.
A mound or structure on which targets are placed for archery practice or competition.
A mound or structure on which an archery, musketry or artillery target is erected. Use specific type where known.

Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber: Curtiss P40 Warhawk, known to the RAF as the Tomahawk, later renamed Kittyhawk. Serving from 1941 to 1942, control difficulties in dive attacks impeded bombing accuracy, resulting in use for larger targets only.
A triangular piece of wood, usually of ebony, to which the lower ends of the strings of a musical instrument are fastened.
A container to hold a liquid in honour of a deity.
A series of cages in which hens are confined for intensive egg laying.
A strong, sweet fortified wine made in Portugal.
A roof consisting of a series of rafters and arch braces set closely together to give the appearance of a continuous, uninterrupted arch or curved plate.
An abandoned settlement, usually of the Medieval period, often visible only as earthworks or on aerial photographs.
A factory manufacturing insulation material for electrical cables.

A slender, cylindrical object. Use specific types of rod where possible. Where it is a rod of material which is part of a production process, eg a glass rod, use rod and enter the material in an object material field.
A hole dug in the ground to act as a, usually temporary, communal toilet facility.
The second subdivision of the Iron Age.

A type of military building associated with military airfields, where air crews were briefed for missions. The room could be a seperate building or part of an operations block and are built of varying types of temporary brick or nissen hut constructions.
A ring worn around the neck.
An anti tank wall constructed specifically to be used for training purposes.
The Curtiss-Wright Corporation, Airplane Division, established in 1910. Notable aircraft produced include the Kittyhawk.

Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber: Curtiss P40 Warhawk, known to the RAF as the Tomahawk, later renamed Kittyhawk. Serving from 1941 to 1942, control difficulties in dive attacks impeded bombing accuracy, resulting in use for larger targets only.
Visual, descriptive and analytical record of a building, usually interior and exterior. Equivalent to Historic England Level 3.

A hexagonal pillbox, with an internal anti-ricochet wall and loopholes for fives light machine guns and one rifle. Originally designed to have 15in bulletproof walls many were built with 42in thick shellproof walls. Designed by DFW branch 3.
A collection of items presented in a protective folder.
A factory built for the production of breakfast cereals.
A large medal.
A first-floor chamber, often serving as a parlour, bedchamber or private room, in a medieval house. Also a loft, rood-loft or garret.
The SI derived unit of luminance.
A bead or group of beads used in prayer.
A water-powered forge or wire mill which manufactured metal wire combs for use in the textile industry.

An entablature often of great magnificence with bead and reel between fasciae of the architrave, frieze ornamented with continuous sculpture and cornice, with ornate coffers and richly carved modillions.
The horizontal assembly of architrave, frieze and cornice carried upon columns and pilasters in the Composite order; and so containing elements of the Ionic and Corinthian orders.
An entablature of the Tuscan Order consisting of a plain architrave, frieze and cornice without decoration or enrichments..
In the Classical Orders, the horizontal assembly of architrave, frieze and cornice carried upon columns and pilasters.
An entablature consiting of an architrave, usually a frieze and cornice.
An entablature with a plain architrave or principal beam over which are the frieze and cornice.
A truss in which two pairs of arch braces form a continuous curve from the wall-heads or below to meet in the centre of the collar.
A large fork with wide spaces between its tines, used to throw grain etc into a breeze to separate grain from chaff.
A basin of water used by priests for ritual ablutions.

A floating breakwater in the form of a hollow cruciform tube 200 ft long by 25 ft high. Bombardons were designed to reduce the height of waves and formed the outer breakwater of the Mulberry harbours.
A trough or gutter for conveying liquids such as water or molten metal. It can be cut in the surface or formed of wood or other materials.
A pit dug in the ground used to store meat, grain and other foodstuffs. A common feature of Iron Age farms.
A pit where grain is stored.
A house or hut for a nightwatchman; including parish watch houses in churchyards and private watch houses, eg. in dockyards, factories, etc.
Smooth rendering applied to the exterior of buildings which may be incised to suggest coursed masonry. Made of lime and sand or brick dust, and more recently, cement.
A three masted fully rigged warship armed with 24 to 38 guns on a single gundeck.
A stable used for riding horses or those used to pull coaches, gigs, etc.
Photographic print using albumen.
An instrument for measuring time.

The main German, medium bomber of the war, the HE111 first saw action during the Spanish Civil War. HE111s took part in the Battle of Britain and from 1944 onwards were used to launch airborne flying bombs against London.
A single-seat fighter which began service with the RFC's fighter squadron in 1916. Some short-term success in dealing with new Fokkers but was withdrawn from service in mid-1917.
British single-engine, two-seat night fighter. Originally intended as a day fighter, but withdrawn and converted in August 1940, this was the first fighter to incorporate a power-driven gun turret.
A small dome on top of a larger dome, roof etc.
A hangar used for the storage of barrage balloons.
A factory used for the production of red lead used in glass manufacture, or white lead used as the pigment in white paint.
A dark blue powder, obtained from plants or synthetically manufactured, used as a dye.
A building in which pack animals could shelter.
A substantial bank and ditch forming a major boundary between two adjacent landholdings. Most date from the late Bronze Age and Iron Age.
A multiple, parallel arrangement of linear earthwork ditches, usually accompanied by banks, and often of considerable territorial extent. Usually of later prehistoric or Roman date.
A roof truss supported by arcade posts in an aisled building.
A building from which the firing of torpedoes can be controlled and evaluated.
A designated area of water in which the perfromance of torpedoes can be evaluated.

A factory or group of buildings engaged in the manufacture of acetone. A variety of processes may be used to manufacture acetone including the use of destructive distallation of wood and fermentation technology.
A long thin piece of wood,
A separate residence for guests, a house on a private estate or a monastery building specifically for receiving visitors.
Dried or partially dried plums eaten as fruit.
A fortified keep in the form of a tower, used as a last refuge or defence. If a component of a larger site, use KEEP.
The major tower of a fortification, often acting as its last defence.
A building within a transport terminal, often associated with the registration and clearing of incoming and outgoing passengers or freight.
Powder mixed with water and applied as a paste for binding stones and bricks or for forming floors, walls etc.
A place where watches and timepieces are manufactured and mended.

A mill used for the production of mortar; a combination of sand, lime and water, used to make the joints between courses of bricks in buildings. In more recent times cement has replaced lime to create a quicker drying mortar.
Originally, a house of higher social status in a town or port, often with a storage cellar.
Purpose-built housing for railway workers.
An establishment used for the manufacture of jacquards and dobbys, which are textile loom components that control the weaving of complicated or figured patterns.
Sweet red peppers.
The inner rafter of a compound rafter.
A doubled rafter, separated by cleats, spacers or distance pieces.
The central division of a church, extending from the west end to the chancel or transepts.
A mine used for the extraction of the mineral Witherite. When secondary mineral, use with term for product, eg. LEAD MINE.
Flat bottomed vessel used for coasting on the River Humber.

Highly successful, two-seat, biplane fighter and reconnaissance aircraft with both forward and rear facing guns. Designed to replace the BE2, it entered service with the RFC in mid-1917 and remained in service until 1932.
A fence that indicates the limit of an area or a piece of land.
A construction of wood or metal used to enclose an area of land, a building, etc.
A window with three openings, the central light being arched and wider than those flanking it.
A site, including hangars, moorings and ancillary buildings, used for the storage, maintenance, take off and landing of airships.
A model village built by a utopian society or group of artists.
A searchlight battery, which points out to sea, used to locate enemy shipping

An important two-seat, tractor biplane, initially used by the RFC in a reconnaissance role and by the RNAS as a bomber. Later converted to a single-seat Home Defence fighter and ultimately used as a trainer.
A council-owned block of flats.
Long poles or spars, usually set vertically, on sailing boats and ships to support the sails.
American, four-engined, medium/heavy day bomber. Entered service in 1937. The prototype was nicknamed the Flying Fortress, which later became a registered trademark.
An establishment where tea and other non-alcoholic refreshments and light meals are served.
A market consisting of stalls erected in the street and selling a variety of goods.
A textile mill where thread undergoes the processes of twisting and doubling to provide material strong enough to be spun and woven.
A pole projecting to the rear of a post mill to allow the sails to be moved into the wind.
A textile mill where felt is produced.
An extension to a building, though sometimes contemporary with it, housed under a lean-to roof.
Each of a pair of long narrow pieces of wood, usually pointed and turned up at the front, fastened under the feet for travel on snow.
A shopping complex, usually indoors, comprised of a number of separate retail outlets surrounding an open space. Often on more than one level.
A storage area usually for naval weapons and stores.
A depression in the ground caused by the explosion of a mine or bombshell.
Use for vessels registered in Hungary.
A joint which has a splay interrupted by a step

A small, defended settlement dating to the Early Iron Age, located on spurs, promontories or hilltops. The defences are marked by single or double trenches which originally held substantial palisades.
A substantial area of ground surrounded by slight univallate earthwork often interpreted as stock enclosures or as sites where agricultural produce was stored.

A piece of wire or similarly flexible material shaped to form a clip for fastening papers together; invented by the Norwegian Johann Vaaler in 1899. The familiar double-oval 'Gem' clip was developed by Gem Manufacturing Ltd. in England the same year.

Single-engine, single-seat carrierborne fighter: a Spitfire VB fitted with an arrester hook. Modifications on later versions included folding wings, rocket-assisted take-off gear and conversion for photo-reconnaissance duties.
A light, often suspended from a lamp-post, to illuminate a street or road.
A street lamp in which the light is produced by the burning of coal gas. More recently natural gas has been used.
Manmade feature to contain water for the purpose of floating miniature boats in it. Different to BOATING LAKE as lake can be naturally occuring park feature and can be used for full sized boats.
A place in which turpentine is produced.
A curfew with straight sides flaring outwards from the top. (Source: MPRG)
Hard, compact, unprocessed, fibrous cellulose substance. The roots, trunks and branches of trees and shrubs consist of this tissue.
Material comprising entrie or partial transverse sections of stems. Bark may be present or not. Can include complete sections of tree trunk but generally comprises smaller (<20cm diameter) material.
Small (<2cm diameter) roundwood often complete with buds or leaf scars.
A closed chamber used for heating or baking objects.
A factory or works housing machinery used to produce stockings and socks, using mechanized knitting processes.
A piece of wood or iron to secure ropes, etc to or on.
The residence of a lock-keeper.
A specific form of cauldron, generally of rounded profile made in the Low Countries. (Source: MPRG)
A large pot used for boiling.
Single-engine fighter/dive-bomber. The Fleet Air Arm's first operational monoplane, and its first aircraft to shoot down an enemy during the war.
A thin strip of material used for binding.
A site where fluorspar or fluoride of calcium, often used as a flux by copper-ore smelters, is extracted from an open cast mine.
A flexible, transparent sheet of film bearing a number of reduced images.
A roofed structure, open on one side, usually attached to a building, providing a seating area and its occupants with an uninterrupted exterior view.
A building associated with rope manufacture, especially in naval dockyards.
A purlin that rests against the lower surface of a principal rafter and is supported by a queen post, collar or raking strut.
An apparatus for burning refuse to ashes.
A wall mounted, hydraulically operated crane or winch, sometimes used to operate lifts.
Buildings and works around a mine shaft with an artificial embankment on which the winding gear etc, is located.
A factory, incorporating power driven machinery from the late 18th century, where cloth was manufactured from threads interlaced at right angles to each other in a loom.
A factory where security safes are manufactured.
Large mammals, domesticated for riding and as draught animals.
Hard, protective covering made largely of calcium salts secreted by soft bodied invertebrate animals.
An object for touching or pricking an animal's sides to increase control of it, usually used with horses.
A type of spur with the goad in the form of a rotating disc.
A type of spur which ends in a point, blunt or sharp, which is used to aid control of an animal eg a horse.
An engineering site where railway carriages are manufactured.
A tube for conveying the voice from one room or building to another.
A polygonal or circular stone forming part of the shaft of a column.
A buttress which encases the corner between two walls.

A shaft which appears to have been dug for, or which contains objects apparently deposited for, reasons other than storage, disposal or extraction (eg. of stone, water, etc). Index with principal object types.
American, single-engine fighter designed for operation from US Naval aircraft carriers. Produced between 1940 and 1945, Wildcats provided to the British Fleet Air Arm were renamed Martlets.
Structured descriptions of an archive or collection used to assist retrieval and management, or presentation to the public.
Structured list of information about items of interest to a research project, for example monuments of a particular type.
A factory or works used for the forging and sharpening of a variety of tools including scythes, spades, etc.
A factory used for the manufacture of scythes.
Four-seat, twin-engined medium bomber. Entered service in 1938. After serving Bomber Command from 1939-42, was converted to a torpedo-bomber and mine-layer with RAF Coastal Command.

Accommodation used as an alternative to the workhouse following several Poor Law Acts. Modelled on continental examples and first erected at the end of the 1860s, it is based on the idea of a "village" of small houses accommodating a small group.
A workshop with equipment for the making and repair of ships' rigging.
A heavy substance, usually gravel, sand or lead, placed in the bilge of a ship or boat to provide stability.

A central tower with a single-storey wing either side. The tower contained the watch office on the ground floor, observation room on the second with each wing containing an office for the Chief Flying Instructor or the officer commanding and their aides.
A control tower designed for use on Very Heavy Bomber Station Airfields. Designed to Air Ministry drawing number 294/45 they were the first to be have a Visual Control Room
skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Very Heavy Bomber Station Control Tower (294/45)

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A high building at an airport from which air traffic is controlled by radio.
The first standardized design for a building for the duty pilot. It took the form of a small bungalow with a bay window on the front elevation.
A plan form in which pavilions lead off from a spiral corridor.
A shallow pond, often located near an ICEHOUSE, built to provide ice during the winter.
A mine for the extraction of iron ore.
A building or area where stone is stored for industrial or agricultural use.
A carved stone female figure often found on castles and churches.

A. V. Roe & Co., Ltd. formed in 1909. A subsidiary of the Hawker Siddeley Aircraft Co., Ltd. from 1935, having formerly been a member of the Siddeley group. Produced such notable aircraft as the Lancaster, the York and the Anson.
A two-seat trainer chosen to replace the Avro 504. 380 entered RAF service with many finding their way onto the civilian market at the end of their careers.
A tripod used to support pots over a fire.
A solid material which is combustible distilled from petroleum.
An engineering workshop, often attached to an engine shed, for the running repairs of operational parts, etc.
Type of survey involving the drilling of deep and narrow shafts in the ground used to describe deposits, understand stratigraphy and collect cores amples.
Single-engine aircraft designed as a dive-bomber. Found to be inadequate in this role, a number of those delivered to the RAF were used as target tugs. Entered service in 1941.
A building found in conjunction with a WATERMILL, used for the drying of corn after harvesting, with a slatted drying floor set above a kiln.

A building, often with underground rooms, used to receive all reports of aircraft locations, to assimilate and assess this information in order to provide the most accurate possible picture to the Operations Room of a fighter or bomber Group.
A pit which shows evidence for having been used for cooking. Often contains charcoal, burnt bone fragments etc.
Small, marine crustaceans are used as food.
American, all-metal-construction, fighter. Entered service in 1941. 209 were delivered to RAF/FAA, most of which were used in the Far East.
A place of worship for followers of Sikhism.
The main hall of worship within a Sikh Temple.
A small stone blade with one edge blunted.
A metal thread.
A channel, usually placed upstream of a mill, that carries water from a river or other water source to a waterwheel.
A building used to house apes and monkeys.
Part of a large church, east of the nave, appropriated for singers and clergy.
A trap designed and used to catch fish.
A religious cloth often used to cover coffins.
A type of clothier's house, consisting of TOPSHOP and dwelling, used for hand-weaving of textiles.
An object supported by a crosspiece on a post, used by knights as a target in tilting.
An unsocketed earthenware or porous concrete pipe laid end to end unjointed so as to drain the ground.
A building or site producing nitrogen-rich fertilizer.
Triangular concrete pyramids with 6 feet long sides and 5 feet high, intended to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion. Thought to be confined geogaphically to Southern Command.

Single-engine, two-seat, light, biplane, elementary-flying trainer. Adapted from a civilian design, and constructed from tubular steel and spruce with plywood and fabric covering, entered service in 1931 and was available in land-plane or seaplane forms.
?what does this mean?
A triangular or wedge-shaped timber cocking-piece attached to the upper face of a rafter near its foot in order to reduce the slope above the eaves. Such eaves are referred to as being sprocketed.
A passageway or lane between buildings.
A permanent Roman fort enclosed by a number of ditches and ramparts, used to house a garrison of auxiliaries.
A written extract taken from a published newspaper.
A written work for publication, being one of several found in a serial, monograph or magazine.
A site used for the extraction of peat.

Highly successful, two-seat, biplane fighter and reconnaissance aircraft with both forward and rear facing guns. Designed to replace the BE2, it entered service with the RFC in mid-1917 and remained in service until 1932.
An area or defined space believed to have been used for trades and/or manufacturing activity. Only use when evidence for more specific site type is lacking.
A scroll containing prayers.

Four-engined heavy bomber, developed by Avro from the twin-engined Manchester. Entered service in 1942 as the RAF's principal night bomber and took part in the 1,000 bomber raids as well as the famous Dam Busters raid.
A workshop or foundry where iron articles are made by casting molten material into moulds.
A place where a yearly or half-yearly court of record is held by lords of certain manors.
A site or building used for the storage and maintenance of both land and sea vehicles and from which terrestrial or maritime operations could be carried out.
A building or room in which images of outside objects are projected on to a screen from a long-focus lens using natural light.
The residence and office of an archdeacon.
Works for the extrusion of aluminium and for creating aluminium products.
A detached vertical structure acting as support to a superstructure. Where a pillar is a separate monument, use a monument type thesaurus.
A small, steel shelter designed for use as a firewatchers post during an air raid.
A highly defensible gateway, usually of stone with two or more storeys, built into the defensive walls of a town or city.

Rocket projector site with a circular or octagonal concrete holdfast, 1.5m across, surrounded by a 4.6m radius octagonal concrete surround. Six such rocket projectors were arranged in a 3 x 2 grid. Personnel shelters placed midway between each site.
6 DFW55373 projector emplacements spaced in a 3x2 rectangular gid, but each spaced 35m apart. No blast protection was provided at the shelters, which were placed between the projector emplacements.
A device for converting one voltage of alternating current to another voltage.
Short-range naval weapon with a low muzzle velocity.
A heavy artillery piece consisting of a metal tube mounted on a gun carriage.
A counter balance designed to support the excess weight of a mineshaft's wooden beams.
Mud, which has often been dredged from the beds of rivers.
The DH5 was an attempt to give a tractor-type fighter a good forward view. However it suffered from unpleasant flying characteristics and, as a result, had a short service career.
A prepared area of grass on which the game of football is played.
A small, narrow boat with pointed ends propelled by paddling.
A form of silica, similar to quartz. Commonly black or white in colour and used for tool manufacture. Flints heated in antiquity may be dated using thermoluminescence.
A round bottomed container to be held in the palm of the hand.
A plan of a building which consists of two or more cells where the chimney is placed on the axis of the building between two rooms and midway between the lateral walls.
A monument erected as a permanent reminder of a military victory. The design usually includes images of the spoils of the battle.
A pond used as a water supply for the operation of a furnace or blast furnace.
The area that contains the ambulatory, apse and chapels. Usually found in larger churches, monasteries and cathedrals.

A large twin-engined airliner produced by the Dutch aircraft manufacturer Fokker in the 1920s. First flight March 1927. Designed by Reinhold Platz. Mixed construction, fuselage/ tail in steel covered with plywood, canvas and duralumin (11 units built).

Dutch aircraft manufacturer named after its founder, Anthony Fokker. Set up in 1912 in Schwerin, Germany, moving to the Netherlands in 1919. The world's largest aircraft manufacturer in the late 1920s.

Any notification, update or amendment relating to the scheduling of a monument. Usually includes description and a map showing the limit of the scheduling. It confers a statutory status and receipt is an acknowledgement of the scheduling.
Covered area for making large engineered constructions such as sections of ships or bridges.
Use for vessels registered in Spain.
A fine grained earth which becomes more plastic when water is added and can be moulded and dried to make bricks, tile, pottery, etc.
Collective name for any stone that has become impregnated with iron oxide. Index with specific stone type where given.
A small structure used to support strings on an instrument pushing them away from the body of the instrument.
A pond or pool with arms covered with nets into which wild birds, are lured and then caught. Monument type includes water feeder channels.
A burial ground for followers of the Eastern Orthodox church.
A house with an aisle on one side only.

Single-engine, single-seat carrierborne fighter: a Spitfire VB fitted with an arrester hook. Modifications on later versions included folding wings, rocket-assisted take-off gear and conversion for photo-reconnaissance duties.
A 17th century garden in the Dutch style: usually flat and compact, with an emphasis on small canals, hedges, topiary, lead statuary and flowering shrubs and bulbs.
