A geometrical planting of trees in the form of the number 5 as represented on a dice.
Large warship with no armour and a high speed. Used for reconnaisance and raids on enemy merchant shipping.
Large warship equipped with turret mounted guns. Intended for independent action for trade protection, reconaissance and fire support for amphibious operations.
Shelly, gold/brown, coloured liassic limestone containing large quantities of crystalline calcite.
A small pumping station.
A room or building where a pump is worked.
Specify in Description using: path, road, track, bridge, lay-by etc.
A microlith retouched to a trapezium shape. (Source: SARC)
A small vessel with a cabin as an integral part of its construction.

A type of motorboat that provides accommodation for crew and passengers within the crafts cabin. Cabin Cruisers are usually between 25 feet and 45 feet long in length and are not to be confused with cruise ships which are substantially larger.
Photographic negative on polyester base material.
Support or 'mother ship' used for the repair, maintenance and refuelling of submarines, specifically 20th century submarines.
A building used by teachers for in-service training.
A large, "bottle-shaped", oven of brick construction used in the baking or firing of pottery.

The investigation of heritage assets along thematic lines, usually to inform the production of a thematic study. Such studies bring specialist insights to bear on the particular area of study, but may not address other aspects of the site's significance.
A tunnel built to allow internees (in a camp, prison etc.) to escape.
Four-engined, five to seven crew, heavy bomber biplane. Entered service in 1918.
Building used for children to play in.
A building in which the lay sisters resided. Lay sisters were not nuns and as such weren't bound by any vows. They could leave the convent and even marry if they wished.
A steam engine working at a fixed location.
Civil building in Cornwall and Devon for assay and sale of tin ingots.

A pit lined with the bony cores of animal horns. Thought to date from the 17th/18th centuries and believed to have been used in the tanning industry although some may have been used for casting cannon.
Small vernacular building used by fishermen for the preparing of nets and storage of equipment.
A school where young children, usually under the age of seven, are taught.
A small crane fixed to the wall of a warehouse or similar building.
A lighted pillar or LIGHTHOUSE, eg. Dunston Pillar, Lincs., erected in 1751 to guide travellers over the heath.
A carved bust, figure or representation usually fixed to the bow of a ship.
Oven for roasting coal to drive off chemical constituents and reduce it to almost pure carbon, ie. coke.
A rectangular pillbox with an enclosed square plan section for three light machine guns and an adjacent open area housing a mounting for a light anti-aircraft weapon. Designed by DFW branch 3.
A progressive development of the DO17, the twin-engined DO217 entered service in 1941. The DO217 saw service as a bomber over the UK and took part in the 'Baedecker' raids of 1942.
A stand, either fixed or free-standing, usually with a sloping surface from which a bible, book or notes can be read, found in a church or lecture theatre.

A sheet formed from wood which has been separated into its fibrous elements and reconstituted under pressure. The natural fibres produce resins which act as adhesive, but often additional adhesives are used.
A building in which pottery ware is made by shaping plastic clay on a spinning turntable, known as a potter's wheel or throwing wheel.

A reinforced concrete structure, which may be sited above ground or semi-sunken, from where it was intended to conduct the business of government from, in the event of nuclear war. Date specific to the early-mid 1950's.
A flat blade used to beat the weft against the newly woven cloth in weaving.
An aisled timber or masonry hall, serving as the chief administrative public meeting centre and law courts for a Roman town. Usually located alongside the forum.
A site with one or more defensive earthworks, often at a river crossing incorporating natural features which define parts of the curtilage.
A bell-shaped pit used in early coal mining. Use with functional type if known, eg. COAL WORKINGS.
A type of Roman lodging house, frequently sited near the town gate.
A long seat, usually made of stone or wood, with or without a back.
A small, heavy object used for keeping loose papers in place.
A hospital block where pregnant women are accommodated and receive medical treatment before and after child birth.

Fleet Air Arm fighter and torpedo-bomber, designed for operation from aircraft carriers. All-metal in construction, it entered service in 1944 and was rendered obsolete after the war by the advent of the jet aircraft.
A large building used for the storage of finished cloth.
Accommodation in a monastery for new monks.
A hillfort enclosure with defences composed of more than one bank and ditch.
A vault shaped trellis on which climbing plants are trained.
A framework used as a support upon which fruit-trees or climbing plants are trained.
A place where manganese ore is extracted. Use with other ores extracted and MINE where relevant.
A small, single storey building used as the Pilots' room on fighter stations and as the watch office on bomber stations.
A mill for the removal by mechanical means of the dried wood and seeds of the flax and cotton plants after retting. The resulting 'tow' is then spun into linen and cotton respectively.
Use for vessels registered in Switzerland.
An order in which the columns rise more than one storey in height from the ground or plinth.
An earthen mound, usually within an ornamental garden, on which a tree was planted.
A building where sugar is stored.
A vertical structure usually made of stone, brick, timber, etc.
A separate hospital building, or block of an asylum, where new arrivals were segregated from old inmates for a defined period. This system was developed from the mid-19th century onwards.
The cleaning and sorting of horse hair mainly for use in the upholstery trade.
Draught animals produced by mating asses and horses.
Any material consisting of glass filaments woven into textiles, paper or board.
A vessel to contain the wafers used in the Eucharist.
Mark 11 or the eleventh variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
A figurative or decorative object made of corn, used as a charm for luck or to ward off evil spirits.
For example chronic liver disease, inflammatory bowel disease, weight loss, liver transplant and other related illnesses.
Preservation of material by toxic effect of corrosion products in the immediate vicinity, or within, the material.
The top of a cornice in an entablature.
An aircraft hangar designed to Air Ministry specifications (drawing number 2243/41). Constructed from prefabricated A-frames and clad in corrugated iron.

A mound of fire-cracked stones, normally accompanied by a trough or pit which may have been lined with wood, stone or clay. Assumed to be locations where heated stones were used to boil water primarily for cooking purposes.
Includes dissertations
A closely mown piece of ground used for the game of lawn bowling.
A garden created within woodland where imported species such as camellias, magnolias and rhododendrons are grown.
An all-steel end-opening, hangar with canted sides designed for folded-wing aircraft.
A radar station with sets operating on a wavelength of 10cm or less. They were highly accurate radars and gave better sea level coverage than the earlier Chain Home Low stations.

skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Religious Society Of Friends Meeting House
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A place of worship for members of the Religious Society of Friends, often known as Quakers. The Religious Society of Friends is a denomination founded by George Fox in c.1650 who believed in passivist principles and a rejection of the sacrament.
Moray, Scotland

A transonic jet fighter, first introduced by North American Aviation in 1947. Best known as the United States's first swept wing fighter. Total production at 9,860 units. Important fighter aircraft in the Korean War. Retired in 1994 (Bolivia).
American, all-metal-construction, fighter. Entered service in 1941. 209 were delivered to RAF/FAA, most of which were used in the Far East.

The Brewster Aeronautical Corporation was founded in 1932, taking over the plant, equipment, designs and goodwill of Brewster & Co., Inc.'s aircraft division. Initially manufacturing seaplane components, later designed and produced complete aircraft.

Originally ordered as land based dive-bombers, with 950 being delivered to the RAF, none are known to have flown operationally, instead apparently serving as target tugs. Bermuda was the name given to the Brewster SB2A Buccaneer in RAF service.
A case in which a pipe would be held to protect it.
A factory for the production of plastics by chemical processes.
A lime kiln built into a low hillside or slope to facilitate top loading of the limestone.
The residence of a clothier.
A factory where musical instruments are manufactured.
A building where violins are manufactured and the art of violin making is taught.
A stringed instrument usually with a triangular frame.
A cornice along the sloping edge of a pediment or gable.
Photographic transparency mounted for use in projection equipment.
A factory used for the manufacture of ordnance including small arms, ammunition, artillery pieces and armoured fighting vehicles.
A building or site used for the manufacture of small arms and artillery pieces, etc.
An outfall from a canal, river or reservoir.
A dam constructed on the reaches of a canal or river designed to retain the water and to regulate its flow.

Cones of solid concrete usually 3 feet 6 inches in diameter x 2 feet high which, when placed in rows or groups were intended to form a substantial barrier to enemy armoured divisions in the event of invasion.
A mixture of coals that have been formed into briquettes or blocks. This fuel took its name from the fact that it was under patent in the late nineteenth century.
When secondary product use with major product and MINE, eg. COPPER MINE.
Matting manufactured using the fibres from the outer husks of coconuts.
A long shaft topped by an axe head. Differs from a battleaxe by the length of the shaft.
A road/carriage way giving access from the main road to the house, stables.
Single-seat carrierborne jet fighter. Originally conceived as an RAF land-fighter, entered Fleet Air Arm service in 1951 and was the first jet fighter to be standardised in first-line squadrons.
A tool used to sharpen another tool or object.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of eye and ear disorders and diseases.
An establishment dedicated to the study of theology and religious training.
Large, single-engine, eight passenger airliner biplane.
Use for any thread-like material.
Use where the intervening arcade is closed but timber-framed.
A house with no row of posts between the central space and the aisles.
The principal Roman Catholic church in a diocese in which the cathedra or bishop's throne is to be found.

An excavation technique that involves the machine stripping the topsoil/subsoil from the area to be excavated, plotting observed features onto a site plan and then partially or fully excavating those features.
Polished stone balls interpreted as ritual objects in the Scottish Iron Age.
A mill used for the manufacture of narrow strips of woven fabric used in the closing or fixing of garments, or for binding the edges of fabric goods.
A building in which wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.

A device, usually cast iron and often decorative in design, placed upon, embedded in or built into a doostep facilitating the removal of mud, dirt, manure etc. from footwear before entering a building.
Object produced commonly by firing clay, but can include coarser material to temper it.
A decorative moulding cosisting of two ogee-forms with joined faces.
Large piston used to operate lifting bridges, lock gates, etc.
An enclosure of stakes driven into the ground, sometimes for defensive purposes.
The residence and office of an archdeacon.
A body suspended so as to be free to swing, especially one regulating the work of a clock.
A form of compass, sometimes with a screw for setting to small intervals.
A small vessel used to attack other vessels and setting themselves and then the enemy alight.
A common type of lock in the form of a chamber with gates on either side.
A factory, mill or warehouse constructed with the minimum amount of combustible materials.
Use for the remains of a cargo which have been accidentally lost at sea, or purposefully dumped, and which consist the only physical evidence of a vessel.
Waste material or dross separated from metals during smelting or refining.
A weight made to be hung from a steelyard.
A covered arcade, often attached to a building, open on one or more sides.
A type of bridge which completely encloses the traffic using it.
A balance measuring weight by the tension of a spring.
A building combining a cow-house with crop storage space.
A heavy grating, often made of wood or iron, usually lowered vertically as a defensive barrier at the entrance to a gatehouse or barbican.
A church, usually found in East Anglia, of early Medieval and/or Medieval date with attached or detached round tower.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of all types of wax.
An observation post, usually well concealed, intended for use by the Auxiliary Units (or British Resistance Organisation), in the event of an invasion, to watch enemy movements without being seen.
A site containing slipways and associated buildings used specifically for the repair of ships and larger ocean-going craft.
An engaged column, that is one attached to a wall.
A room in a monastery from which alms were distributed; or the residence of an almoner.
A hangar used for the storage of barrage balloons.
A law court builidng established during the 1970's accommodating offices and courtrooms fro the Crown and County Courts.
A compound steam engine with provision for bleeding off some steam after it has passed through the high pressure cylinder and before it enters the low pressure cylinder.
A joint which has a splay with a short perpendicular section at each end.
Aggregate, cement and mortar combined with structural elements of iron or steel mesh or rod reinforcement to form stonelike masses for load bearing, structural building work.
Container with arched handle used for carrying liquids, foodstuffs etc.
A hooked blade used to cut crops. All the blade is to one side of the handle rather than being on both sides as in a sickle.
Early form of photographic print.
A torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance biplane in service with the Fleet Air Arm 1935-1938. Rendered obsolete after 1938 by the Swordfish and withdrawn from service.
Mineral ore comprising mainly aluminium ore and mined for aluminium extraction.
A covered chalice used for the Eucharist.
A jettied house where the overhanging upper storey runs along the entire length of one side.
A flake of stone struck from the core where the length is less than twice the width.
A flake that has had small flakes removed to blunt, sharpen, refine the outline or prepare the edge of the tool.
Small fragments of waterworn stone used in the construction industry.
A tall, hollow pipe, usually cast-iron, resembling a lamp-post. Used to ventilate sewer systems.
An artificial pond or pool constructed for the purpose of watering livestock, particularly in prehistory.
Holders for one or more candles, usually of metal or pewter.
A section of a window between mullions; thus for example a three-light window.
The vertical side of a window, archway, doorway or fireplace.
A building occupied by the corps responsible for police and disciplinary duties in the armed forces.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Perchlorate, a product used in the explosives industry.
The residence of a vicar, parson or rector.
The official residence of the chief officer of the municipal corporation of a city or borough in England.

A monument consisting of a small (generally less than 100m diameter) subcircular enclosure with a narrow approach way consisting of parallel ditches (thus banjo shaped). Believed to be associated with stock management in the Later Prehistoric period.
A building where distillation, a chemical process used in the production of a range of different chemicals, took place.
A bowl divided into two or more compartments by vertical slab partitions. (Source: MPRG)

Single-engine, single-seat fighter, also adapted as a night-fighter, fighter-bomber, rocket-projectile fighter and tank-buster. The first monoplane to enter RAF service with 14,000 being produced between 1937 and 1944.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Gilbertine order.
A painting executed directly onto a wall.
A small cargo vessel used on the West coast of Scotland.
Mark 12 or the twelfth variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
A container, usually rectangular and having a removable or hinged lid.
A stone or brick wall enclosing a park.
The space enclosed between the gates and side-walls of a lock.
The official residence of the chief officer of the municipal corporation of a city or borough in England.
An earth based plaster the mixture of which may contain clay, dung, straw, lime putty, sand or horsehair.
A two panelled altar decoration that can be closed.
An often ornate wrought-iron bracket used to hang lamps outside public houses, shops, hotels and restaurants, etc.
A house with no row of posts between the central space and the aisles.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged around three sides of a yard which is open to one side.
A latrine built into, or projecting beyond, the wall of a medieval castle featuring a stone or wooden seat situated above a pit or the castle moat.
A pond used for the punishment, by ducking in water, of offenders.
Storage vessel, usually a two handled narrow necked jar.
Glass fragments collected for re-melting. This includes not only worked fragments, but pieces broken from blowing irons and pontils, (moyles). All periods from the Roman onwards.
A rib placed at an angle to support timbers.
A set of marks found on the wall of a building, thought to be a form of sundial.
A small semicircular moulding.
A reinforced wall designed to reflect the blast from an explosion. Often found associated with powder magazines, pillboxes and air raid shelters.
A building housing material used to explain the significance of a site or landscape to the public e. g. an archaeological site or nature reserve.
An establishment from which food is distributed to the public during wartime or similar states of emergency.
West Yorkshire
A hospital where people with learning disabilities receive medical treatment.
Fibres obtained from plants and used in the manufacture of ropes, sacking, canvas etc.
A tile used within a floor.
A vessel equipped with water tanks and pumps for fighting fires at sea or on the shore line.
A tug equipped with water tanks and pumps for fighting fires at sea or on the shore line.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of firelighters.
An area within a hospital concerned with the care and medical treatment of expectant mothers.
A half-pier, corbel or other architectural element, usually situated at the end of an arcade, attached to a wall to support an arch.
Use for vessels registered in the United States of America.
A piece of machinery on which a railway engine, carriage or wagon can be rotated at a railway terminal.
A rural school serving a number of villages, built in Cambridgeshire in the 1930s.
A site, in which salt is obtained by boiling and evaporating salt brine or seawater in large pans. Often the only surviving evidence are the mounds formed from the waste produced by the process.
A building containing a number of areas for bathing, some of which are naturally heated by thermal springs.
Stones placed in the bed of a stream or on wet ground, to enable crossing on foot.
A pit where calcium oxide (Quicklime) has been hydrated to produce calcium hydroxide, known as slaked lime.
A hole occupied by a timber post or the void remaining after its removal, usually with packing.
The space occupied by or left where a post has been.
A building or structural plan with a U shape.
A long, narrow, rectangular plot of land used for the manufacture of rope. Usually walled, it may include small buildings and awnings at each end. Often attached to a warehouse.
A piece of animal bone roughly shaped with grooves in which pins are laid and held whilst being sharpened.
A decorative piece connected to the altar.
A system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used to simulate an airfield and thus confuse enemy aircraft into bombing these counterfeit targets.

A decoy site designed to replicate the layout of an RAF satellite airfield, complete with dummy aircraft, simulated runways and simple structures intended to fool enemy aircraft during daylight raids.
A hydraulic machine used to magnify the stroke of a hydraulic piston. The pulleys and chains of a crane or other device are attached to the jigger.
A place where photographs are displayed for sale.
The exercise hall of a Roman baths complex.
A factory in which is ink is prepared from pigments and additives.
A child's bed, usually with rockers.
A building, usually associated with a port or dock, where seamen could get a meal and a cheap room. Often established by religious groups for the moral betterment of seamen.
A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of wine.
A strap from the reins to the girth of a horse, preventing it from raising its head too high.
A metal mouth piece used to control an animal, usually used on a horse.
Attachments that form part of the bridle.
A projection from the inner angle of a building around a court or with advancing wings, usually containing a staircase and often crowned above the roof line with an ogee dome.
A flat bottomed vessel for receiving mud and other material from a dredger.
A flat object which is broad and rounded at one end and tapers to a handle at the other.
A stable located at a railway station or goods yard. Horses were necessary both for freight and passengers to continue their journey beyond the railway.
A container for incense.
A bowl used to contain and burn incense.
A position or place that allows a wide or favourable overall view of a scene or situation.

Special concrete loading ramps nicknamed 'hards' had been constructed along river banks, beaches and inlets to enable organised embarkation onto various types of landing craft to take place, irrespective of tides.
A mound in excess of 150 metres in diameter, of Late Neolithic date and presumed ritual function, eg. Silbury Hill.

Traditionally an amber-coloured globe lamp atop a tall black and white pole, acting as a signal to road users that there is a pedestrian crossing. Modern beacons may also include an outer ring of flashing LED lights.
A factory where lace is manufactured.
A place where calcite is extracted using both quarrying and deeper mining techniques. Calcite/limestone is used for making glass, paper, photography, statues, building, and animal food.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber and ground-attack aircraft. Entered service with the Luftwaffe in mid-1941. Approximately 20,000 were constructed between 1941 and the end of the war.
A brace halved to the inside of studs, and so not visible from outside.
A workshop in which carded wool was passed through heated combs to straighten and separate the long and short fibres prior to spinning. Associated with the worsted branch of the textile industry.
A process using an electron microscope in which the surface of the specimen is scanned by a beam of electrons which are reflected to form an image. Very high magnification is possible.
A clock with special mechanisms and dials to display astonomical information.
A semi-automatic loom developed in Lancashire. Although it is self-acting, it has to be stopped to recharge empty shuttles.

Airspeed (1934) Ltd. registered in 1934 when associated with shipbuilders Swan, Hunter and Wigham Richardson Ltd.. Acquired by de Havilland in 1940, maintaining own identity and changing name to Airspeed Ltd. in 1944.

A British six-seat single-engined light aircraft, built by Airspeed Limited. First flew in 1933, saw some use as an airliner. The first British type with a retractable undercarriage. Designed by Hessell Tiltman (co-founder). 16 Couriers built.
A path across a road, usually marked as a crossing for pedestrians.
A path across a road marked with black and white stripes where pedestrians may cross.
Purpose-built structure with thick walls used to store clay before transportation.
A gun emplacement which conforms to Department of Fortification and Works drawing number 55491.
A pavilion at the end of a PLEASURE PIER.
Fused ash from furnaces used as aggregate.
A small shield.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of kidney disorders and diseases.
A vessel composed of three or more separate compartments, joined together and pierced to allow liquid to flow from one to another. There may be one or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
A jar whose profile resembles two truncated cones joined together at the widest point, forming a carination at the centre of the vessel. (Source: MPRG)

In fortification, a detached triangular outwork consisting of two battered faces forming a salient angle. Usually positioned in the ditch in front of a rampart and between two bastions. Term mainly for military architecture from 15th century and later.
A collared urn with a heavy rim or collar on top of a straight-sided or slightly bowed body narrowing to a small flat base. Decoration may extend for a short way below the collar, but this is rare.

Four-engine, seven-crew heavy bomber. Entered service with RAF Bomber Command in 1940, becoming one of the twin sources of bomber strength along with the Lancaster. Also used for transport and glider tug duties.
Alcoholic drink distilled from wine or fermented fruit juice.
A building containing the colliery showers. Also often containing first aid and mine rescue facilities.
A garden specifically planted with sweet smelling, fragrant plants.
A residence of two or three monks of the Cistercian order dependent on an English mother house.
A long handled fork with two or three long curved tines for tossing straw or hay.
A purse, sometimes of bronze, usually worn on the forearm.
A small bag or pouch for carrying money, especially coins.
A thin, rectangular panel, sometimes enriched with sculptural relief, placed between the triglyphs in a Doric Order frieze.
Ore hearth specifically for the refining of silver.
A two pronged spear for catching eels.

Composed of a wide variety of substances and materials such as whole or broken bricks, cobblestones, flints, pebbles and sand which are set into hydraulic lime. Used most often to form external walls and is commonly found in the Brighton/Lewes region.
A hillfort enclosure with defences composed of more than one bank and ditch.
A non-profit making restaurant administered by a Local Food Committee which provided customers with good quality and wholesome food which could be purchased without ration coupons.
A place where refreshments or meals may be obtained.
A decorative motif representing a palm leaf. Often painted, incised or applied in relief, can occur singly or as a repeating pattern.
A hall associated with a church, used for holding functions, meetings and for conducting parish business.
An area for the testing of rockets and guided missiles. Includes all structures associated with both the firing and testing of rockets and missiles.
A building used for the testing of aircraft and aircraft engines.
A structure with semaphore arms and/or coloured lights used as a means of warning on railway systems.
A layer underneath the topsoil containing rubble or fragments of building material, e.g. mortar, tile, flint.
An archaeological unit of soil in a horizontal plane which may seal features or be cut through by other features.

A single-engine dive-bomber, the JU87 was very successful during the invasions of Poland and France but suffered heavy losses during the Battle of Britain. Withdrawn from NW Europe in 1941 for use in the Mediterranean and on the Eastern Front.
A wall enclosing a precinct.
A building where civilians are enlisted to join the military forces.

A prefabricated structure consisting of trough shaped asbestos sheets bolted together to form a seven sided building in section with end walls of rendered brick. Manufactured from 1942 by the Universal Asbestos Company for use as airfield accommodation.
A scaled drawing based on measurements taken from life.
The principal house of a manor or village.
A device to limit the amount of liquid coming from a pipe or hole.
An item used to fasten a cloak either to another garment or to itself.
A balance engine used to replenish the water levels of a river by transferring water from a reservoir or other supply.
An area normally below a stage or dais occupied by an orchestra or musical group for performances and entertainment.
A building or part of a building used for the storage of shoes or boots.
A building or structure in which processed cloth is dried.
A rod, often of antler, with a hole through it and decorated.
A rustic building of picturesque design, often associated with a model farm, country house or estate. Although ornamental in design they are intended to be functional.
A public house licensed for the sale of wine and other alcoholic drinks.
A factory where explosives and the components of munitions of all types are brought together for assembly.

A pillbox design, assigned a drawing number by DFW branch 3. Although originally believed to be a distinct type, FW3/45 has recently been found to be a design for modifications to existing types. Double index with specific type where known.
Use for vessels registered in Italy.
A bridge which is fortified at one or both ends.

Four-engine, seven-crew heavy bomber. Entered service with RAF Bomber Command in 1940, becoming one of the twin sources of bomber strength along with the Lancaster. Also used for transport and glider tug duties.
A purpose-built triangulation pillar used for the metrical survey of Britain carried out by the Ordnance Survey.
A purpose-built triangulation point used for the metrical survey of Britain carried out by the Ordnance Survey.
The beans, or powder resulting from grinding the beans, of shrubs of the genus Coffea. The powder is used to make the drink Coffee.
Monument visible as a below ground man-made structure. Use for tunnels, mineworking, cellars, shelters.
Photographic print using albumen.
An embankment or cutting on a railway system, surfaced at a uniform gradient, up or down which materials were hauled by rope.
Oil used to lubricate moving parts, particularly in machinery.
Tyne and Wear
A factory built as a pattern for improved design.
A pier where passsengers can embark and disembark and goods can be transferred to and from vessels.
Starshaped cairn with three radial arms of equal length, a monument unique to upland Northumberland. (Late Neolithic or early Bronze Age).
A cairn erected to mark a particular spot in the landscape. Can be used for various reasons.
A gate leading to water, either a river or the sea. Used as a means of supplying castles, for example, with goods brought by water transport.
A building or complex producing umbrellas, parasols and canes.
A bowl with concave body walls. Wide-mouthed, narrow-based examples, particularly those in larger sizes, have been termed Pans or Pancheons. (Source: MPRG)
A part of the chancel of a church where the altar is situated.
A writing material prepared from the pithy stem of an aquatic plant.
A building containing a bier; a movable stand on which a corpse, often in a coffin, is placed prior to burial.

Single-engine, single-seat carrierborne fighter: a Spitfire VB fitted with an arrester hook. Modifications on later versions included folding wings, rocket-assisted take-off gear and conversion for photo-reconnaissance duties.

A long narrow rectangular earthwork enclosure of Neolithic date, usually defined by a bank and ditch and presumed to be of ceremonial function. Known examples range in length from less than 100m to c.10km.
A container to hold and or pour a liquid in honour of a deity.
An aperture cut obliquely in a wall, usually of a chancel, affording a view between the high altar and the aisles or side chapels.
A bowl adapted by the addition of a single handle
A kiln in which the prolonged heating or roasting of materials to drive off water, volatiles and sulphur so that they may be reduced to a powder, was performed.
Accommodation for the warrener(s) usually located within the boundary of the Rabbit Warren. They also provided a place to store nets, traps and other necessary equipment.
A complex of buildings used for the manufacture of radio valves or similar electronic components.
A place where specific skills are taught on short courses.
An alloy of tin, antimony and copper used as a replacement for pewter.
A sloping timber in a staircase holding the ends of treads and risers.
An object fixed to the door or floor to limit the amount a door can open.

Originally designed as a wood and steel bomber-reconnaissance aircraft, subsequent variations served as special transports, glider tugs and paratroop carriers. Featured a tricycle-style undercarriage.
A twin engined advanced trainer aircraft developed for the military by the US firm of Cessna

Single-seat, single-engine biplane fighter. In operational service from 1939 to 1941, this was the last, and believed to be the best, biplane to be flown in the RAF. All-metal in construction with fabric and aluminium covering.
A centre providing emotional and practical support to those living with life-threatening illnesses.
A compact steam engine of moderate power in which the steam cylinder was placed vertically on a table with the crosshead and guides mounted immediately above.
A principal that has been reduced to the same thickness as a common rafter where the roof has clasped purlins.
A wooden panel, mounted on the wall of a church, bearing the Achievement of Arms of an individual whose funeral has taken place there.
A factory or group of buildings used for the production of plated goods. Plating is the process whereby one metal object is coated with a thin layer of another metal.
A building associated with a barrage balloon site and intended to provide shelter for the balloon crew from air attack.
A site where a single large balloon was attached by fine wire cables to the ground to form an aerial obstruction to attacking enemy aircraft.
A mooring, usually consisting of a concrete plinth, to which a barrage balloon was attached.
A small one masted craft, often using oars as well as sails.
A twin engine advanced trainer developed by Beech/ Beechcraft , a US firm, used in WWII
A hall in a village used for meetings and other functions.
A works used for the production of parchment from animal skin.
Any type of jug with decoration representing the form of a human face or figure. The shape of the vessel often forms the outline of the human face or figure. (Source: MPRG)
A walkway around the parapets of a castle or the roof of a church.
An alignment of posts or postholes of unknown function
A river canalized for shipping.
A single-engine, heavy, long range, three to five-crew day bomber. Served only with 99 Squadron RAF, 1924-5.
Machinery and parts for the manufacture or assembly of military tanks, i.e. armoured vehicles.
Tracked, armoured fighting vehicles designed for front-line combat.
A support for an arch, lintel, beam etc.
A rectangular pier projecting slightly from the face of the wall it buttresses.

Long-range, four-engine reconnaissance-bomber. Initially produced as a transport, converted and used against Allied convoys in the Channel and the Atlantic. Also served as a VIP transport, one of which was the Immelmann III: Hitler's personal aircraft.
A modification of WATCH OFFICE (12779/41) where the original large windows were removed and smaller frames fitted, the gap being filled with straight-joint brickwork.
Equipment used to perform circumcision.
A knife that is used for circumcision.
A plate used during circumcision.
A pair of scissors used in circumcision.
A works site making and/or maintaining drive belts for industrial power.
A graving tool used for engraving objects. Prehistoric versions are usually made of flint or other stone, later versions usually of metal.
In Roman architecture either 1. A block of buildings enclosed by four streets or 2. A large tenement house or apartment block.
A works where cotton waste is stored or processed.
A Mark 2A aircraft which has undergone slight modifications to enhance performance or armament.
East Friesian Islands, Germany
Germany
American, four-engined, medium/heavy day bomber. Entered service in 1937. The prototype was nicknamed the Flying Fortress, which later became a registered trademark.
A double lock placed between tidal water and a canal, etc..
An aisle within a chancel providing access to, and around, the High Altar and surrounding cells.

The side compartment of a building, usually a church, hall or barn, separated from the main body of the building by an arcade; or a passage allowing access to rows of seats in an auditorium or church.
An aisle divided into chapels. This term is sometimes applied to the screens dividing the aisle, or the chapels themselves.
A narrow aisle that pierces an internal buttress.
A term used to describe a vaulted roof where the vault goes from either the newel of a staircase to a wall or from one wall to another where the walls are circular in plan.
The period covering the reign of Edward VII. Do not use for the reigns of Edwards I-VI.

Twin-engined monoplane that served the RAF as an advanced trainer and flying ambulance. Mk. I featured a gun turret and served for gunnery and bombing-crew training. Subsequent versions used for pilot, radio and navigation training.
Form of dam, usually associated with ponds supplying water for blast furnaces.
A wall in a flower or kitchen garden, containing conduits or pipes for heating the wall.
Underground chambers and stone passages of Iron Age date found in South West England.
A law court exercising summary criminal jurisdiction, preliminary hearings and some civil jurisdiction. Formally established by name following legislation of 1949.
Single masted east coast trading vessel, ketch rigged or single masted.
A training establishment for gunnery personnel.
A stone or brick structure that projects into, or out of, a room and contains the flue.
A club or cafe where popular music is played for dancing.
A coke-filled tower used for the dissolving and neutralising of acid produced by alkali-making processes.
Two masted ship with fore and aft sails and two or more masts.
A gate used to seal the entrance to a dock to prevent water escaping from a wet dock or entering a dry dock.
Glass to control or reduce the effects of the sun, includes both reflective and absorpative types of glass.
Transparent, hard substance made by fusing soda-silica which solidifies from a molten state.
Vehicles owned or used by the armed forces. Includes tanks, armoured vehicles as well as civilian vehicles in use by the military eg. ambulances.

Inshore craft used for carrying troops and military equipment used either for beach landings or as a ferry; as cargo smaller landing craft could be carried aboard larger craft in the D-Day operations, for example.
A solid ball fired from cannons, size and weight would depend on the calibre of the cannon.
A long wooden shafted weapon tipped with a metal point.
A method of determining peat degradation; quantified as the percentage light transmission value of the extracted humic acids, measured at a specific wavelength.
A warehouse used for the storage of fruit and/or vegetables.
A vehicle or aircraft placed at the entrance to a site as a symbolic guardian.
A passenger vessel equipped to carry a large number of emigrants usually with large third class decks and plenty of cargo space.
A piston mounted horizontally supplying power via a valve gear directly to a crankshaft or flywheel.
A pole with a blade used for rowing or steering a boat by leverage against the water.

A site which is known, or believed to be, where an aircraft crashed. It is an offence to interfere with the wreckage of crashed military aircraft without a licence (Protection of Military Remains Act 1986). Index with AIRCRAFT TYPE where known.
A maze used for the act of penitence.

A transonic jet fighter, first introduced by North American Aviation in 1947. Best known as the United States's first swept wing fighter. Total production at 9,860 units. Important fighter aircraft in the Korean War. Retired in 1994 (Bolivia).
A rail used to suspend objects from.
A coastal battery designed for use in short range engagements with enemy vessels, minelayers, blockships ad torpedo craft.
A building providing accommodation, dining facilities and recreation for non commissioned officers.
A military dining room where members of the armed forces eat and take recreation.
A sugar factory.
A low, hemispherical cairn surrounded by a freestanding, continuous circle of boulders.
Post-World War Two, single-engine, high-wing utility transport. Manufactured by De Havilland Canada, was also produced in a seaplane version. Known as the U6A from 1962.
An enclosure, usually private, used for burial. Often found within a cemetery.
An instrument strung with metal pieces which sound when shaken.
Use for vessels registered in Scotland.

Interbellum, twin-engined, five-crew, biplane flying-boat with a characteristic triple tail-fin. Entered service in 1925 and used for general reconnaissance duties. The Mk.I had a wooden fuselage, whilst the Mk.II's was metal in construction.
A building or site used for the storage of goods or equipment.
The barrel of a feather, usually goose, used as a pen.
A horizontal timber positioned at the bottom of a framed wall into which posts and studs are tenoned.
The place where a house stood or had once stood, often adjoining a garth or croft.
A fishing boat using nets which are free to move with the tides and currents.
A type of concrete bridge, developed in the 20th century, that consists of reinforced concrete deck slabs that sit on the supporting bridge piers and/or abutments.
Mountings, often decorative, attached to a book.
Objects used or associated with the transmission of ideas and information through the written medium.
A room decorated, and furnished, in the style of the Chinese.
Range used by the Navy with reinforced observation huts which housed quadrant equipment to record accuracy and damage.
A vertical shaft, usually with an internal ladder, allowing access to a sewer or underground counduit for inspection and maintenance.
A housing for racing pigeons usually situated in allotments of back yards.
A darkened room or workshop used by photographers to process prints from glass plates or photographic film.
A passage, usually horizontal, leading into a mine to allow for access or drainage.

Accommodation used as an alternative to the workhouse following several Poor Law Acts. Modelled on continental examples and first erected at the end of the 1860s, it is based on the idea of a "village" of small houses accommodating a small group.
A shaped piece of iron perforated for nails and used on horses.

A recess in a stone or brick wall, usually bounding a garden or orchard, set two to three feet from the ground and facing south to south-east to catch the morning sun, in which a bee skep/beehive is placed. Often found in groupings of three to six.
The residence of a keeper of a royal park etc.
A hospital department, open 24 hours a day, for the immediate reception and treatment of emergency cases.
River principally lying between the states of Maryland and Virginia, USA, with its outlet to the sea in Chesapeake Bay.
Ore containing a high proportion of tin.
A CRUCK HOUSE where the cruck blades are truncated and joined by a collar beam, above which is a separate roof construction.

A nineteenth century stone calciner, similar to a lime kiln, used for extracting arsenic from mined ores, consisting of a solid structure with a central shaft and a drawing-hole at the base for calciner waste.
Threads prepared for use in a manufacturing process such as spinning, weaving etc.
A shallow place in a river or other stretch of water, where people, animals and vehicles may cross.
A complex maze incorporating tall hedges. A popular feature of 16th and 17th century gardens.
A small gateway cut through the curtain wall or its flanking towers. Used primarily as an outlet for counter-attacking forces.
A structure sited within the grounds of a fire station used for drying hoses.
The residence of a ford keeper.
An arcade providing shelter for perishable market goods which also provides protection from the elements for the occupants of the adjoining properties.
A designed for the carriage of livestock usually cattle or sheep.

Monument visible, usually from the air, due to the fill of features being of a different colour than the surrounding subsoil. Soilmarks show up well in ploughed fields or areas where the topsoil has been stripped. Term derived from AN32 Glossary
A factory where shirts are manufactured.
A brewing or baking house attached to a vernacular building, 16/17th century.
Site associated with the testing of nuclear material or its containers.
Usually a rural hospital with up to 25 beds. Can include small pre-Cranleigh institutions, eg: dispensaries with in-patients.
A building or structural plan shaped like a T.
A frame set with teeth used to drag over ploughed fields to break down the earth clods etc.
Building housing apparatus for testing chain links.
A flaky or spheroidal byproduct of the iron forging process, composed of either iron oxide or magnetite.
A road block formed by placing curved rails, "hairpins", in sockets in the road surface.
A site where iron is smelted or iron goods made.
A small carved or sculpted figure.
The line of a flat rod system transmitting power from an engine or waterwheel.

A stone core made on a large thick flake and characterized by a distinctive, unworked or slightly-shaped handle section. The platform is plain and microblades are detached mainly form the front section of the core. (Source: SARC)
A small, ornate structure in which candles were placed either during masses for the dead or to indicate the position of the cemetery at night .

Impressed civil, twin-engined airliner converted to a military transport. Thirty were ordered for military use, though only eleven were actually built. Entered service in 1940, with the last being scrapped in 1950.
A barrel-making workshop or factory, found in conjunction with a number of industries.
A piece of written or printed matter providing a record of events, agreements, ownership or identification.
A papal document.
A place where watches and timepieces are manufactured and mended.

A large, movable barrier, usually an iron or wooden grating with pointed bars along its bottom edge, with its sides set in vertical grooves above a castle's gateway enabling it to be dropped to bar entry.
A movable barrier, usually external, within an opening in a wall, fence, hedge or similar.
A small narrow rectilinear enclosure with high hedges boundaries for the cultivation and shelter of flowers, particularly Daffodils and Narcissi.
Urban road or open space with typical activity, traffic and pedestrians. Double indexing may be appropriate with e.g. TRADE AND COMMERCE or CONSTRUCTION.
A building where matches are manufactured.
A building, structure or site used for the storage of charcoal.
A road or way for riding on horseback within a park or estate.
Term used by the RAF to describe an open walled structure built of concrete, brick or sandbags which enclosed one or more machine-guns mounted on pintels for light anti-aircraft and ground defence.
A barbed spear head used to catch marine life, usually has a rope or line attached to it.
A residential home for children with physical or learning disabilities, sensory impairment and/or mental health issues but who do not necessarily need medical attention.
A single-engine, heavy, long range, three to five-crew day bomber. Served only with 99 Squadron RAF, 1924-5.
An enclosure within a bailey which contained a keep and sometimes took the place of a motte.
A building where patients or inmates of a hospital or workhouse were disinfected and their clothes washed or burnt to prevent the spread of infectious diseases or other ailments.
A track of two parallel ruts deliberately cut in the ground or living rock for the guidance of two-wheeled carts when the way was obscured by darkness or water.
A pathway, not necessarily designed as such, beaten down by the feet of travellers.
A kiln used for the slow burning of vegetable matter to produce potassium carbonate.

Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as two linked ranges to create an L-shape. They can comprise a barn and an attached shelter shed to a cattle yard or an interlinked cattle housing and fodder range.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Hospital For Fistula And Rectal Diseases
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of fistular and rectal disorders and diseases.
A building incorporating a model representation of the planetary system projected onto the ceiling.
A commercial building, or buildings, used for the production of soft drinks.
A modification of WATCH OFFICE (12779/41) where the original large windows were removed and smaller frames fitted, the gap being filled with straight-joint brickwork.
Photographic negative on film. Use for all acetate material types.
A mill used for the manufacture of narrow strips of woven fabric used in the closing or fixing of garments, or for binding the edges of fabric goods.
Mud walled building found on the Solway Plain.

Twin-engined jet-fighter. The first British aircraft to exceed Mach 1 in level flight, later to exceed Mach 2. Entered service in 1960. After 13 years was superseded in its primary defence role by the Phantom, though remained in RAF service until 1988.

The English Electric Company Limited. Formed in 1918, but didn't move into aircraft production until 1938, at the Government's request. Continued to develop aircraft after the war and in 1948 produced the `Canberra', Britain's first jet-propelled bomber.
Workshop for producing crates, particularly for the packing of pottery.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of ear disorders and diseases.
A tube to produce drops of liquid.

Single-seat, single-engine biplane fighter. In operational service from 1939 to 1941, this was the last, and believed to be the best, biplane to be flown in the RAF. All-metal in construction with fabric and aluminium covering.
A Romano-British brooch type, appearing at the end of the first century AD and developing during the second, characterized by a flat plate to which the pin and catchplate are attached at the back.
An enamelled plate brooch, dating from the second and third centuries AD, depicting an animal often with religious significance, such as hares, birds, fish and horses, sometimes with rider.
The residence of a clothier.
A small building used as a shelter by a shepherd.
A protective covering to a drain.
A vertical stone mullion or shaft situated in the centre of a wide doorway to support its lintel or tympanum.

Systematic recording of building facades that produces a seamless mosaic of digital images by identifying control points and defining limits to each image. The rectified mosaic can then be introduced into a CAD environment.

A transonic jet fighter, first introduced by North American Aviation in 1947. Best known as the United States's first swept wing fighter. Total production at 9,860 units. Important fighter aircraft in the Korean War. Retired in 1994 (Bolivia).
Germany
A road or track specifically used by drovers or herders to drive their animals to market.
A powder made from charcoal, sulphur and potassium nitrate and used as an explosive in fireworks, flintlock guns etc.
Temporary accommodation for war evacuees.

Four-engine, ten-crew, long-range maritime reconnaissance and anti-submarine aircraft. Developed from the Short C-class Empire airliner. All metal in construction, entered RAF Coastal Command service in 1938.
A brush used in writing.
A form of Neolithic long barrow comprising an oval, rather than rectangular or trapezoidal mound.
An island, partly or wholly artificial, built up by dumping timber, earth and stones onto a lake or river bed. Often revetted with timber piles or palisade.
An excavation open to the sky, caused by the extraction of coal, stone or similar. Use with product type where known.
A bridge which is fortified at one or both ends.
A decorative ornamentation of interlaced bands in the form of a plait.
Lantern slide developed using a dry process.

A German aircraft manufacturer of the 1930s and 1940s, pre-war the company were noted for making sailplanes and sports planes; during the Second World War they made military aircraft including flying bombs.

The Fi 103 is the more technical nomenclature for the Second World War German V1 flying bomb, produced by Fieseler. Multiple index together with Fieseler and flying bomb for maximum chance of retrieval for users.
A factory manufacturing insulation material for electrical cables.
Covered area for making large engineered constructions such as sections of ships or bridges.
A factory where nails are manufactured.
Four-crew, twin-engined, general reconnaissance flying-boat. Entered service after World War One, becoming the RAF's standard flying-boat until replaced by the Supermarine Southampton in 1925.
Marine Aircraft Experimental Establishment, RAF Felixstowe. Developed seaplanes and flying boats until World War Two, when the establishment moved to Helensburg, Scotland.
A mill where flax is processed to make linen, thread and yarn.
A tool for threshing grain.
A single edged sword.

Six-crew, twin-engined medium night-bomber. Entered service in 1938 and was the RAF's principal bomber until 1943, participating in the first bombing raid of the war. Later versions served as torpedo and reconnaissance-bombers, transports and trainers.
Worked or unworked block/boulder/cobble, on which grain was ground by to-and-fro motion, resulting in a deep smooth elongated hollowed area.
East Friesland, Lower Saxony, Germany
A barn in which a central space is separated from a side aisle by posts and braces.
A low lying area of land that is usually waterlogged at all times and is flooded in wet weather.
A building used for the education of, and as a residence for, chantry priests.
A communal residence of secular priests and/or other clerics sometimes with the condition of learning and education attached.

Measures the remanent magnetisation direction of magnetic minerals. Useful for dating fired structures, in-situ since their last firing, and for sediments settling from non turbulent water bodies. In the UK, calibration data extends back to 1000BC.
A house plan with a hall and a single wing.
A wall plate used by insurance companies to identify insured property.
A steam engine in which the cylinder, crosshead and crankshaft lie in a horizontal line, as opposed to vertical designs.
A lake, often artifical, in a park or open space, used for the recreational rowing and sailing of boats.
A large body of water surrounded by land.
Establishments responsible for the research into and the design, development and manufacture of nuclear warheads.
A building or room used for the storage of pottery moulds.
A stone used for sharpening edged tools, knives etc.
An offshoot of the Wesleyan movement founded in 1838 by John Banyard at Rochford, Essex. In 1956 it changed name to the Union of Evangelical Churches. There are 17 chapels in Essex and London.
A rectangular sheet of roofing material created by a man made process (eg. asbestos cement slate) and made to look like, and used in the same way as, natural slate.
Use for vessels registered in India.
Flat bottomed vessel used for loading colliers in the north east, similar to a lighter.
A department devoted to the curing or correcting of physical deformities.
Principal glider-pilot training glider fitted with tandem seats. Spruce and plywood in construction, the Hotspur served with the Glider Pilot Regiment between 1941 and 1945.
Corrosive, dense, oily acid, usually in aqueous solution, used in the chemical industry.
Corrosive chemical compounds, usually liquids, which are neutralized by alkalis.
An ornament made of thin plates of gold or silver, with repousse ornament.
A supended ornament.
A hollow, concave formation or place, which has sometimes been dug out.
A roof in which pairs of rafters are fixed to the ridge piece and the wall plates without any collars or tiebeams.
A system of lights, controlled fires or dummy constructions, used to simulate a railway yard or sidings and thus confuse enemy aircraft into bombing these counterfeit targets.
A prepared slope with rails on which boats can be transferred from one canal to another at a higher or lower level. The boats can either be floated in a caisson or carried in a cradle or sling.
A workshop or factory where brass articles are made by casting molten material into a mould.
A brass manufacturing complex incorporating battery mill furnaces, hammers, etc.
A container for drinking, with a base and stem but without handles.
Use for miniaturized monument type. Index with actual monument type where possible.
The residence of the supervisor of an inclined plane.
A garden house situated to provide a commanding view.

Four-engine, ten-crew, long-range maritime reconnaissance and anti-submarine aircraft. Developed from the Short C-class Empire airliner. All metal in construction, entered RAF Coastal Command service in 1938.
A pit dug for the extraction of brine.
A cigar shaped implement used to release knots and tangles in weaving.
An area used for the breeding and rearing of rabbits.
A factory manufactoring caravans.
A gun emplacement which conforms to Department of Fortification and Works drawing number 55414.
Building or structure housing a buddle.

A stone building with external access to the domestic accommodation via a permanent stair. The ground floor is normally used as a byre in rural contexts, but in an urban setting it may be intended for one of a number of other non domestic uses.
A usually south-facing wall used for the cultivation of fruit plants.
A wall for growing fruit, dating in England from the mid-18th century, whose curving lines gave added strength, thus doing away with the need for buttressing.
Wind or water-powered mill for land drainage in fens or marshlands.
A reverberatory furnace used for forging wrought iron from pig iron using coal as fuel.
A building in which hoops (for masts) were heated.
A hall in a village used for meetings and other functions.
A column of the Tuscan Order featuring a plain, unfluted shaft.
A structure indicated by the presence of post holes and of uncertain interpretation.
A structure, building or room within a building, used by a local authority for the continuance of local government in the event of a military or civil emergency.
A short trench used to protect troops or to provide defensive fire from, often dug for practice purposes.
That portion of the Pacific which stretches from the equator to Antarctica.
A point where water issues naturally from the rock or soil onto the ground or into a body of surface water.
A pipe or channel to carry water outwards from a gutter or behind a parapet. If decorated with grotesque heads it is called a gargoyle.
An attic workshop for textile manufacture, usually weaving.

skos:Concept.skos:definition: One tenth of a nautical mile. Equal to 100 fathoms under the strict definition.

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A concrete structure, based on drawing number (11008/41), intended to be the headquarters for the coordination of an airfield's defences. Constructed partially underground it was considered less vulnerable than the (3329/41).

A structure, based on drawing number (3329/41), intended to be the headquarters for the coordination of an airfield's defences. Constructed above ground this design was found to be vulnerable and was superceded by the (11008/41).
A concrete structure designed to be the headquarters for the coordination of an airfield's defences. Constructed partially underground it was only intended to be occupied during an attack.
A fine white clay used specifically for the manufacture of clay tobacco pipes and for whitening leather.
Fine grained earth which becomes more plastic when water is added. Mainly used in the manufacture of bricks, pottery and other ceramics.
A photographic reproduction of written or printed material produced by using toner particles under heat and pressure to fuse a copy onto blank paper.
Traditionally, the hall of a crafts, trade, or merchants' guild. Nowadays, often used to describe a TOWN HALL.
An engine house which used air pressure to power trains on the experimental atmospheric railways of the 1840s.
A vessel used to put down and pick up moorings on the sea bed for large vessels.
Decorative ornamentation of a flower or leaf.
A training establishment for gunnery personnel.
A sailing vessel, generally with three masts, square rigged on the fore and main mast.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter manufactured by Messerschmitt. First used as part of Germany's Condor legion during the Spanish Civil War, the 'one-o-nine' was the Luftwaffe's most widely used fighter seeing service throughout World War II.
A bungalow joined to another to form one building.
A one-storey house.
A bar or rod, usually of metal, used to push another object into place eg to push coals within a fire.
A manufacturing complex incorporating furnaces, calciner and condenser flues. Use SMELTERY for more modern type of plant.
A site used for the production and/or working of metallic iron.
An ornamental wand or rod carried as a symbol of authority
A kiln for roasting ore.
A type of calcining kiln used in the processing of iron ore.

A chemical works engaged in the manufacture of the coal tar derivative, picric acid, often associated with the textile industry where it was used as a dye, but more commonly with the explosives industry where it was used as the shell filling Lyddite.
A pit used for the containment of clay whilst it is mixed to the right consistency for brickmaking.

A French airliner which entered service in 1920. A conventional biplane design with enclosed cabin for four passengers and open cockpit for the pilot. Fitted with an early audible guidance system. Withdrawn from service in 1921.
A camp where people who fled from danger or problem whithin their country or across international borders and who are in need of international protection are temporarily placed.
A room in a public house, hotel, club etc. containing a bar from which alcoholic drinks are served.
Single-engine aircraft designed as a dive-bomber. Found to be inadequate in this role, a number of those delivered to the RAF were used as target tugs. Entered service in 1941.
Pipes manufactured from copper used for a variety of purposes, especially plumbing.
A jar for the storage of ointment.
A multi-level structure designed to simulate tall buildings to allow firefighters to practice firefighting and rescue techniques
An undefined structure used in the training of people in a certain skill.
A large tank used for training divers.
The residence of a priest.
A house or centre used for meditation, contemplation and/or prayer.
A depression in the ground caused by the impact of a falling object, such as a crashed aircraft.
A drawing which depicts to scale a feature within the landscape. For drawings of selected features of a site use SCALE DRAWING..
A large tank where particles suspended in water, or other liquids, are allowed to sink to the bottom forming a sediment.
A court of summary jurisdiction established, following legislation, in 1908 for the trial of offenders below the age of legal reponsibility.
A place where canal boats are built and maintained.

Single-seat, single-engine biplane fighter. In operational service from 1939 to 1941, this was the last, and believed to be the best, biplane to be flown in the RAF. All-metal in construction with fabric and aluminium covering.
An area of a building or complex specifically housing the kitchens, sculleries and services.
Microscopic animal remains. Use more specific term if known.
A component of another building, often a house, used for storing nets.
Two-seat, single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer. Square-winged and fitted with dual controls, this popular trainer was used by British Commonwealth, as well as American and Canadian, air forces.
Fish of any kind preserved by salting, for example salted cod such as bacalhau or bacalao.
Mackerel which has been salted to preserve it.
Medium grained, intrusive, black or dark green coloured, igneous rock.
The residence of a canal worker.
A stone slab, raised on stone or wooden piers, used for the display of fresh fish. Usually found in market places.
A building where radium is used in the treatment of cancer.
A series of steps designed to enable fish to ascend a fall of water or a dam.
A plan type of a hall with two wings and a central porch.
Traditional roof covering consisting of materials such as reed, straw or heather layered and fastened together onto roof to form a run off to prevent water penetration.
A place where boats or ships are built or repaired.
A strung object used to produce sound usually from a string instrument eg a violin bow.
A place where silverware is manufactured.
A workshop used for the manufacture of items of jewellery and/or timepieces from precious metals and precious or semi-precious stones.
A school where theological subjects are taught.
A wooden, stone or iron post for securing things to or for preventing vehicular access to pedestrianized areas.
An abbey or priory of Cistercian monks.
A factory complex consisting of PRINTING SHOPS, COLOUR HOUSES, DYE HOUSES, etc, in which patterns are printed onto calico.
A factory or complex containing machinery for the manufacture of printed materials.

Combination of organic and inorganic material cohered to form a hard solid wall or covering. Use for structures created by the excavation and piling up of earth, such as ice houses. Earth may be used in combination with other materials.

skos:Concept.skos:definition: Used for measuring distances at sea. Until the adoption of the international definition of 1852 metres in 1970, the British nautical (Admiralty) mile was defined as 6080 feet.

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A single-seat, pusher prop, escort and patrol-fighter. Used in the UK in a Home Defence role until superseded in 1917.
A grain grinding mill in which the meal is ground into flour between revolving metal rolls.
An internal combustion engine powered by the combustion of vapourized oil.
A plant used for the manufacture of tubes and tubing, from wrought iron or steel.

Wood and fabric transport glider, twenty of which were produced with twin Bristol Mercury engines. Fitted with a hinged nose for loading and unloading, this was the largest glider used by the RAF and could accomodate a 7-ton tank.
A structured set of data taken from a larger work to assist in location of particular subject matter.
Cards, often printed with forms, for the recording and sorting of information in a structured manner.
The most common form of joint between two timbers meeting at right angles or at an oblique angle, the mortice being a socket cut in one timber to receive the tenon projection of the other.
A manor house, which was granted a royal licence to crenellate.
Thick, black liquid distilled from bituminous coal, and containing many organic chemicals.
A settlement site enclosed within a timber palisade.
Twin-engined, four-seat medium bomber. A re-engined variant of the Hampden, less than 200 were built but never became operational due to engine unreliability. Some were converted to Hampdens.
An ornamental bracket on either side of a doorway supporting a cornice.
Twin-engined, four-crew bomber. Wooden framed, with linen covering, entered service in 1924, equipping several RAF squadrons.

Soil marks and other features of natural origin, including periglacial frost wedging, solifluction deposits, abandoned water courses, etc, recorded to avoid future confusion with features of human origin.
A site used for the small scale extraction and working of surface boulders.

A conglomerate rock comprising well rounded flint pebbles in a very hard matrix of fine pale coloured sand, bound together by hard natural silica cement. The pebbles are usually coloured ochre or red and have black rims.

Developed as a long range, heavy day-fighter, the ME110 found its niche as a night fighter. It saw service over Southern and Eastern England during the Battle of Britain but lost out in the daytime to the faster British fighters.
Single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer. Spruce and plywood in construction, entered service in 1939, continuing to serve as a trainer, and also a target tug, until 1950.
An official residence of a bishop used during the summer months.
A dwelling house forming part of a Chartist Land Colony.

Six-crew, twin-engined medium night-bomber. Entered service in 1938 and was the RAF's principal bomber until 1943, participating in the first bombing raid of the war. Later versions served as torpedo and reconnaissance-bombers, transports and trainers.
A stone, usually inscribed, laid during a ceremony to commemorate the founding of a new building
An open grating of wrought iron, bronze, wood etc., forming a screen to a door, window or other opening, or used as a divider.
The field or area of ground on which a battle or skirmish was fought.
Sites, buildings, structures, features & areas of land commemorating an historical event, person or animal.

Area or zone of sea where a battle, skirmish or action was fought between naval ships or warships and privateers. Not to be used for enemy action upon mercantile ships or a sudden strike by mine/torpedo against an enemy warship.
An early steam engine using steam at atmospheric pressure. Chiefly employed in mine pumping. sometimes known as a vacuum engine.
64 Type DFW55373 projector sites arranged in and 8x8 grid or in 4 groups of 16. 30m between each projector, with hardened personnel and ammunition shelters located midway between each
A room for children to play in.

A glass sphere in a metal frame standing on a small pillar. A card is placed behind the sphere which focuses any sunlight, marking the card and thus indicating how many hours of sunlight there was on that day.
A structure consisting of combustible material, typically wood, on which a body is placed and then cremated, sometimes with accompanying grave goods. Use only when evidence of structure exists.
A cleansing or separating machine used in a corn mill for removing smut from grain before it is ground.
An alcoholic spirit distilled from malted barley or barley and maize or rye.
A form of lock on a river, which increased the depth upstream and had a gated opening.
A flake produced from a carefully prepared core.
Use with other minerals extracted and MINE where relevant, eg. ZINC MINE.
A large wooden gate, positioned at either end of a canal or river lock, equipped with sluices to let water through.
Line used with hooks attached to it in order to catch fish.
A jug form characterized by the addition of three applied feet. The feet are usually short and stubby. Double index with the appropriate profile type. (Source: MPRG)
A type of concrete bridge, developed in the 20th century, that consists of reinforced concrete deck slabs that sit on the supporting bridge piers and/or abutments.
A structure used for the transmission and interception of radio signals. Usually composed of a number of different elements such as aerials, receiving equipment and supporting pylons.
An aircraft used for towing gliders aloft.
An aircraft used for towing another aircraft or object, such as a glider or target.
A light, ornamental building or structure built to incorporate, or in association with, a mineral spring.
Decorative motif in the form of an ox skull.

Accommodation given rent-free along with or as part of a corrody, which is a provision of an annual allowance of food and money by a religious house to an individual, usually in return for service or by purchase. Term used until mid 16th century AD.
A building or site used for the manufacture of swords.
A factory complex consisting of PRINTING SHOPS, COLOUR HOUSES, DYE HOUSES, etc, in which patterns are printed onto calico.
An area of ground indicating the site of a horse or man-powered winding mechanism.
The passage, area, lobby, room or vestibule into which a building's main entrance opens.
Single-engined fighter, developed from the Camel. Entered service in 1918 and became the RAF's first mainstay peacetime fighter.
A sundial capable of giving an accurate reading of standard time to the minute.
A works or factory principally engaged in the manufacture of dynamite
An enclosed field for horses.
A straight sided drinking vessel, usually with a wide mouth and without handles.
A beaker with convex body walls. (Source: MPRG)
A purpose-built dwelling for the manager of a factory, works, textile mill, etc, often found within the complex itself.
A horse-powered apparatus, for the crushing of commodities such as ore or cider apples, consisting of a stone wheel running over a circular iron or stone bed.
A weapon with a long shaft and a three pronged head.
Fish of the Salmonidae family, caught for food.
Salmon which has been pickled in vinegar or brine to preserve it.
A fighter version of the SKUA fitted with a four-gun turret. The majority were converted to target tugs for use by the RAF and Fleet Air Arm.
A hydraulically-powered crane constructed from open box girders.
A file of computer information stored on a computer connected to the internet coded so that it can be accessed over the internet using browser software.
A WWII British biplane produced by Hawker Aircraft, used for army cooperation duties.
The young of the sheep.
Medium-sized animals domesticated for their wool, skin, meat and milk.
Dried leaves from the plant Camellia sinensis, which is used to make a drink by infusing the leaves in boiling water.

A gate, made of wood, used as a livestock barrier by continuing a fence line across a river or stream. The gate usually consists of a series of droppers, that can float up and down depending on water levels, attached to a length of cable or wooden pole.
A flint tool for piercing holes.

American, single-engine fighter designed for operation from US Naval aircraft carriers. The Hellcat was a more powerful version of the Wildcat, a total of 1000 being provided to the Fleet Air Arm under Lend-Lease.
A complex of buildings where barytes is processed for industrial use.
A factory which produces artificial imitations of mineral water, such as soda water.
An aircraft designed for the testing of engines or other aircraft components.
A walk bordered by trees or clipped hedges in a garden or park. Made of gravel, sand or turf, it is different from a path or avenue.
Waste material from a kiln
A rectangular recess along the edge of a timber to receive a shutter, door or window.
A building in which oxen are accommodated.

The Gloster Grebe was the Royal Air Force's first post WWI fighter aircraft, entering service in 1923. Designed by Henry Folland, a single-seat, single-engined biplane of fabric-covered wood construction with two Vickers machine guns (133 planes built).
Large covered spaces where the steel plate used for ship construction was cut and marked out, prior to being craned onto the hull, etc.
Pit for soaking animal hides as part of the tanning process.

A building used for the preparatory processes in which long and short staple flax fibres were separated by passing through combs. Flax dressing or 'heckling' shops may be located both on and off mill sites.
A factory where nails are manufactured.
A small bag or detachable outside pocket.
A room where letters and parcels are sorted prior to dispatch

Blocks of solid concrete,in the form of truncated pyramids usually 3 feet square x 2 feet high which could be placed in rows to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion. Pimples were recommended for use on soft ground.
A structure, or building, forming a supplementary and subsidiary part of a main complex.

A rectangular chamber of brick or stone with heavy wooden gates at either end equipped with sluices to let water in and out, thereby enabling a canal boat to be lowered or raised to a different level.
An area within a building used for the storage of cheese.
An enclosure used for the cultivation of fruit trees.
A turret on the side of a house providing views across the surrounding countryside.
A blunt headed instrument used for striking objects.
A place where boats or ships are built or repaired.
A deliberate miniaturised replica of an object.

A complex of buildings at a seaport, comprising of a terminal building, landing pier and hangars, used for the embarkation of passengwers and/or freight on flying boat services during the 1930's-50's.
A defensive position, often constructed from sandbags, designed to protect a group of infantry.
A two-storey watch office similar in design to drawing number 1959/34 but constructed completely from concrete. A large, almost square, ground plan with a central observation tower.
An establishment for the storage of food for use during wartime or similar states of emergency.
A gate on a toll road where travellers had to pay a toll to the toll-keeper.
A bobbin where thread is wound around it, used for example in spinning and weaving
A laithe with an attached house.
A building or cage in which parrots are bred and kept.
A large bed surrounded by an earthwork and filled with composing vegetable matter and animal waste. This was used to produce Nitre, a constituent of gunpowder.
A thin, flat rectangular piece of slate, or similar material, used as a roofing tile.
A specialist school for the teaching of blind people.
A market building, pre-19th century, incorporating other function rooms, eg. theatres, courtrooms, schoolrooms.

Four-engine, ten-crew, long-range maritime reconnaissance and anti-submarine aircraft. Developed from the Short C-class Empire airliner. All metal in construction, entered RAF Coastal Command service in 1938.

A two-seat, general purpose biplane. The first to be designed specifically for an Army Co-operation role, it entered service in late 1927. Ended its service as a communications and advanced trainer aircraft.
A container within which a body is placed for burial, usually made of lead or wood.
A factory where floorcloths are manufactured.
Steel in the form of rails eg. for use in the construction of railways.
The entrance to a tramway tunnel.
A site where traditional public shows, in which the display of exotic animals, combined with feats of agility and comedy, were held.
