Traditionally, the hall of a crafts, trade, or merchants' guild. Nowadays, often used to describe a TOWN HALL.
A pair of scissors used in circumcision.
A metal, shankless bit, with a ring on either side used to control an animal (usually a horse) by exerting direct pressure on the tongue, lips and the side of the mouth.
A garden consisting primarily of rocks and rock plants.
A closely mown lawn used for the game of croquet.
An area of hardstanding for parking aircraft, in a state of readiness, usually around the perimeter of an airfield.
A green coloured gemstone. A variety of the mineral beryl coloured green by trace amounts of chromium and sometimes vanadium.
Prior to 1822 a vessel used by the customs department involved with the prevention of smuggling.
A single masted cutter built specifically for the prevention of smuggling and the enforcement of customs regulations.
A stringed musical instrument, usually played with a bow.
A stringed instrument usually played with a bow.
An instrument played mainly by bowing the strings. Use narrower terms where known.
A container, in the form of an urn, for keeping the ashes of the dead after cremation.
A settlement whose plan suggests the aggregation of several formerly distinct settlement nuclei into a single settlement.

A family of jet fighters capable of vertical/short takeoff and landing. A subsonic aircraft, later designs adapted for use from aircraft carriers. Built between 1967-2003. Used by the RAF and the Royal Navy.
A light, ornamental building or structure built to incorporate, or in association with, a mineral spring.
An enclosed container to hold coals or logs of a fire.
Use for deposits formed as a result of construction activities undertaken by humans or animals.
A joint in which one timber is applied to the surface of the other.
A place where silverware is manufactured.
A tray on which an offering is made.
A concrete, concave wall 200 feet in length used as an acoustic listening device to detect approaching enemy aircraft.
A fixed basin, containing Holy Water, positioned near the entrance of a church, usually placed within a niche, on a wall or pier, or freestanding upon a pedestal.

A place of worship for Wesleyan Methodists. This was the original Methodist church from which the other denominations seceded. In 1932 they joined the United Methodists and the Primitive Methodists to form the Methodist church.
Dating to the reign of James I of England (VI of Scotland).
Dating to the reign of the Stuart kings of England (including the Commonwealth inter-regnum)
A pumping station used as part of a clean water supply system.
Any of the pieces of hard tissue consisting largely of calcium phosphate that make up the skeleton of a vertebrate animal.
A form of bone, which grows on the heads of members of the deer family and is shed annually. Antler can be used by man for a variety of purposes
The body of a church or chapel as opposed to galleries.

A place of worship and meeting hall for members of the Salvation Army, an evangelical sect founded by William Booth in Nottingham in 1865 and derived from Wesleyan Methodism. They rejected the sacraments and adopted a quasi-military rhetoric and style.
A plinth or pedestal, usually of concrete, to which an anti aircraft or coastal battery gun was fitted. Holdfasts are often the only evidence for a weapon which survive.

An operations room, built to drawing number 3395/40, to control the lighting arrays of the 'T' type of bombing decoy in use during the Second World War. It was semi-sunken for added protection and then covered in earth

Seven/eight-crew, heavy night-bomber. The first four-engine bomber to join the RAF, with a bomb load of 14000 lb, entered service in 1940. Superseded as a bomber by the Lancaster and Halifax, later versions served as transports and tugs.
A small building used as a shelter by a constable of the watch responsible for patrolling the streets at night to safeguard life and property.
A case or container for an amulet.
Fish of the family Clupeidae, common to the North Atlantic. They are caught for food.
Character of operations not determined.
Anglo-Saxon two-piece bow brooch, dating from the 8th to 9th centuries AD, so named for the distinctive bow shaped like the arching body of a caterpillar.

A jar with a profile that flares outwards from base to rim, but usually with a constriction at the neck. Squat examples, with a height less than the minimum diameter, could be classified as bowls. (Source: MPRG)
A narrow bridge for people and animals to cross on foot.
Flat bottomed vessel used as a platform for a pile driver.
An engineering works that produces machinery specially for use in textile making.
Use wider site type where known. Only use term where no other part of original building survives.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter manufactured by Messerschmitt. First used as part of Germany's Condor legion during the Spanish Civil War, the 'one-o-nine' was the Luftwaffe's most widely used fighter seeing service throughout World War II.
A building or buildings where electronic components or devices are designed, developed, manufactured and assembled.
A building housing a board organized to protect the interests of commerce.
A hospital where people with learning difficulties receive medical treatment.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Hospital For People With Learning Difficulties

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A priory of Gilbertine double order of nuns and canons.
A term for a drinking vessel, although its use often implies a recognised quantity.
A factory or plant for the manufacture of ice using mechanized refrigeration techniques.
A vehicle used to transport passengers. Cars usually have four wheels and an internal combustion engine.
A car adapted for ease of use by people with disabilities.
A vertical iron bar fixed within a window opening to support a leaded light.
Equine mammal used primarily as a beast of burden.
The hole through which the fuel for a fire is put to start and maintain the fire.

An establishment where alcoholic and non alcoholic drinks are served, food may also be served. May be a an individual room within a larger multi purpose building such as a sports pavilion or a theatre.
A workshop for printing textiles in a CALICO PRINTING WORKS.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up the chief engineer of Scottish Command
Originally a light day-bomber, the Boston II, re-christened the Havoc, was adapted for night-flying in the fighter-intruder role. Was capable of a top speed in excess of 300 mph.
In which the density of trees is significantly less marked than in woodland; if parkland is currently cultivated then classify land accordingly.

Accommodation given rent-free along with or as part of a corrody, which is a provision of an annual allowance of food and money by a religious house to an individual, usually in return for service or by purchase. Term used until mid 16th century AD.
An unbleached cloth of hemp, flax or other coarse yarn.

An important two-seat, tractor biplane, initially used by the RFC in a reconnaissance role and by the RNAS as a bomber. Later converted to a single-seat Home Defence fighter and ultimately used as a trainer.
A large vessel, sometimes large enough to accomodate several gallons, often made of leather and richly decorated, for storing and serving liquor.
A WWII British biplane produced by Hawker Aircraft, used for army cooperation duties.
A watch office designed for bomber satellite station comprising a long, temporary brick hut with a watch office, operations room and crew briefing room.

A detached building without an operations block and crew briefing room designed on modern lines similar to, but smaller than WATCH OFFICE (12779/41). Began appearing on new stations from September 1941.
A hole dug in the ground to act as a, usually temporary, communal toilet facility.
Chronic kidney disease, diabetes, thyroid illnesses.
Accommodation designed for the elderly, disabled, etc, as individual units.
A Swiss-styled house, usually with steeply pitched and projecting roof.
A building, in a garden, park or open space, either housing a fountain or the machinery which powers one.
An arch at the liturgical east of the nave, carrying a gabled wall above, separating nave from chancel.
A factory used for the production of red lead used in glass manufacture, or white lead used as the pigment in white paint.
Large concrete letters representing the ground-to-air airfield code. It has been used to show pilots in WWII the name of the airfield they were above e.g. DW for Dunkeswell.
A single-seat, biplane fighter. One of the last open cockpit types to see widespread service with the RAF, equipping 10 squadrons and, at one point, 70% of the Home Defence fighter force.
A light, soft, moderately-strong wood obtained from trees of the genus Picea.
A stone commemorating the date of a specific event.
A castle erected without permission, ie. without a royal licence to crenellate.
1st World War end-opening aeroplane hangar.

Early to mid-1st century AD Bow Brooch with a P-shaped profile, a cylindrical or semi-cylindrical spring cover and a round or lozenge-shaped centre plate with a short bow above and a flat leg below, both of which are reeded like the Langton Down Brooch.
Traditionally a mineral that could be used for striking fire but now a term commonly used to refer to various sulphides, especially iron disulphide.
A mould in which a sword is cast.
A two edged broadsword.
A truss with braces crossing and fixed to each other, thus tying a pair of rafters together.
The area or platform at the top of a staircase.

A nineteenth century stone calciner, similar to a lime kiln, used for extracting arsenic from mined ores, consisting of a solid structure with a central shaft and a drawing-hole at the base for calciner waste.
A small house in which leeches were bred for medical purposes.
A ship or brig peculiar to the Mediterranean.
Citrus fruit, usually green.
A method of grinding cereals where one stone is rotated on another by hand.
Term includes Salting etc
Mill for fine grinding of tin ore between millstones.
A building that housed humans and cattle under one roof, with a shared entrance providing access to the cattle housing (usually downslope) and the dwelling area.
A church, sometimes circular in plan, founded by the Poor Knights of Christ and the Temple of Solomon, commonly known as the Knights Templar.
A structure providing protection against the weather at bus stops.

A single engine, jet propelled twin boom aircraft which came into service in 1945 in a variety of roles including night fighter, trainer, the carrier-borne Sea Vampire, and the MK5 version, a fighter bomber. Produced by De Havilland.
A place of worship for Primitive Methodists, a group who were formed in Staffordshire and influenced by American evangelical ideas and who left the Methodists in 1811.
A factory where floorcloths are manufactured.

Twin-engined jet-fighter. The first British aircraft to exceed Mach 1 in level flight, later to exceed Mach 2. Entered service in 1960. After 13 years was superseded in its primary defence role by the Phantom, though remained in RAF service until 1988.
A short hooded cloak.

A designated area within a town or village with fixed defences such as pillboxes, anti tank ditches and gun emplacements, designed to threaten the flanks of an enemy force which had broken through a stop line.

A building where fish are stored. Often taking the form of a single storey building with one room, but also may provide living accommodation for a fisherman above. Found mainly in the South West of England.
A circular stylised ornament, essentially a patera with floral enrichment, associated with classical architecture and occurring on the soffits of coffers, and as the fleuron of the Corinthian abacus.
A staircase for the use of servants, tradesmen or individuals not permitted to use the main part of a building or establishment.
A thin flat board or plate usually with a raised edge on which things can be carried.
A layer of impervious material, such as lead or bitumen, usually placed between a wall and a roofline to exclude water.Impervious material to exclude water.
Solid masonry placed to counteract the lateral thrust of a vault or arch.
Supplies including food, drink and equipment necessary for a journey.

A World War One German three-crew, twin-engined, long range heavy bomber biplane manufactured by Gothaer Waggonfabrik A.G.. Entering service in 1917, this aircraft incorporated a ventral tunnel allowing the gunner to shoot downwards and to the rear.
An area where birds are protected and bred.
The area of water retained above a mill dam for driving a mill.

A British six-seat single-engined light aircraft, built by Airspeed Limited. First flew in 1933, saw some use as an airliner. The first British type with a retractable undercarriage. Designed by Hessell Tiltman (co-founder). 16 Couriers built.
French coasting vessel

Any structural component, usually of wood, which is believed to have derived from a vessel. Double index with the appropriate type of structural component eg. BEAM or if known the original term from the MARITIME FIXTURES AND FITTINGS thesaurus.
A laundry built in conjunction with a PUBLIC BATHS.
A building where clothes are washed.
A fighter version of the SKUA fitted with a four-gun turret. The majority were converted to target tugs for use by the RAF and Fleet Air Arm.
Twin-engined fighter-bomber. All metal in construction, entered service in 1940. Supported bombing operations and participated in attacks on France, but not widely used due to engine faults.
A device, monogram or symbol incised in stonework by a mason as a means of identifying his work. Particularly common in Romanesque and Gothic buildings.
A standardized rectangular steel container used for the transportation of goods by road rail and sea.
A structure, into which a cart can be drawn, to enable it to be loaded from above.
Underground passage with storage chambers found in South West England.
A wooden or metal object used to provide a rhythm by striking another object.
A two-seat, reconnaissance biplane developed from the FK2 with a more powerful, but heavier, engine. Primarily used for training in the UK.
A works engaged principally in the manufacture of ammonal explosives.
A small edge blown instrument with no finger holes, producing one note.

A freelance boat used off the south and east coasts of England to provide passing ships with pilots, supplies, new anchors and other gear. Some helped sailing ships and barges get underway. Generally lug-rigged. Also used for fishing. Half decked.
A power house built to Air Ministry drawing number 207/17 and comprising four rooms; a driver's room, workshop and store, battery room and engine room containing 2 generator sets.
A windmill with a stationary timber body which contains the grinding machinery, and which supports a rotating cap in which the sails rotate.
A place where wheels and wheeled vehicles were manufactured, originally from wood.
A place for recreation with electronic game machines and gambling machines.
A piece of cast metal obtained from a mould in a form suitable for storage.
Large blocks of timber used to support railway tracks.
Manufactured objects and devices used to apply a force to an object or perform a particular mechanical function.
Tools and equipment used for agricultural purposes.
A garden of regular, linear or geometrical design, often associated with the traditional Italian, French and Dutch styles.
A bayonet designed to fit over the muzzle of a musket or rifle, allowing the gun still to be fired.
A bridge carrying a tramway.

Wood and fabric transport glider, twenty of which were produced with twin Bristol Mercury engines. Fitted with a hinged nose for loading and unloading, this was the largest glider used by the RAF and could accomodate a 7-ton tank.
A technique used to date obsidian (volcanic glass) of all ages and is thus not commonly used in the UK.

A curved dam usually built of concrete and designed with the curve upstream so that the force of the water compresses the structure and strengthens it as it pushes it into its foundations. Arch dams are best suited to narrow gorges
A mug with roughly vertical body walls. (Source: MPRG)
The position of a fire in a wood-fuelled furnace. All periods from the Iron Age to the 17th century.
A column that is attached to or partly sunk into a wall or pier.
An ore, such as stibnite, containing a high proportion of antimony.
A windmill with a stationary timber body which contains the grinding machinery, and which supports a rotating cap in which the sails rotate.
A factory used to make packaging equipment.
A collection of associated artefacts recovered from a single site.
Gold fashioned into coins for use as currency.
A type of pottery oven in which the air passes from the base of the kiln out through the top.

A large twin-engined airliner produced by the Dutch aircraft manufacturer Fokker in the 1920s. First flight March 1927. Designed by Reinhold Platz. Mixed construction, fuselage/ tail in steel covered with plywood, canvas and duralumin (11 units built).

Dutch aircraft manufacturer named after its founder, Anthony Fokker. Set up in 1912 in Schwerin, Germany, moving to the Netherlands in 1919. The world's largest aircraft manufacturer in the late 1920s.
The dwelling and workshop of a framework knitter.
A spoil heap consisting mainly of slag, pieces of refuse material separated from a metal during the smelting process.
A conical or flat-topped tip of waste discarded from a mine or similar site.
A barge with a lugsail rig commonly found on the River Thames in the late 19th century. Also a general term applied to the family of Deal luggers.
A military base used for training service personnel.
A horizontal iron bar set in a window opening to which a leaded light is fixed.
A bollard made from, or in the form of, a cannon barrel.
A covered area used for the drying of animal hides.
A beam steam engine originating in Cornwall, first used for raising water from mines.
An axehead of flint or other stone commonly used for Neolithic types.
Mascarene Islands, Africa; dependent territory as a departement of France.
British two-seat, twin-engined night fighter. Also used for roles such as long-range escort fighter, ground-attack and anti-shipping strike aircraft, bomber, torpedo-carrier and rocket fighter.
Single-engine, spruce and plywood, fabric-covered training and communications low-wing monoplane. Served from 1939 to 1950.
A pair of SHEER LEGS mounted on shore or on a SHEER HULK, used as a crane to hoist a mast and lower it into place on a ship.
A factory built for the production of breakfast cereals.
A table made of stone, found in streets, parks, etc.
A water pump situated at the side of a road or track for use by travellers and their animals.

The RAF's first jet fighter, flown operationally during 1944-5, with later versions serving for a further ten years after the war. The Meteor's first active operations were in the interception and destruction of V.1. flying bombs.
A large one handled drinking vessel, sometimes fitted with a hinged lid.
A covered stall at a market or fair, etc.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of candles.
A place where hats are made and sold.
Mill for grinding bark usually for use in the tanning industry. Use with power type(s), eg. WATERMILL where known.
A place where abrasive mediums such as sand-paper and grinding wheels are manufactured.
American, four-engined, long range, medium/heavy day bomber. Produced in greater numbers than any other American aircraft during the war.
1st World War end-opening aeroplane hangar.
A building where matches are manufactured.
A soft, marshy garden, often peat-based where water- and peat-loving plants are grown.
A wickerwork basket for holding fish or catching lobsters.
Rock fragment (diameter 4-64mm) larger than gravel and smaller than cobble, combined with other material e.g. flint, for decorative effect.
A small dwelling providing living accommodation for a tin miner.
Use for vessels registered in Estonia.
An instrument for measuring the angular distance of objects, and particularly used for navigation by noting the position of the stars.
Buildings used in the production of animal food.
Factory for the production of Pet Food.
A stand by set house designed to drawing number 13244/41 and comprising of 4 rooms; a fuel storage room, a transformer chamber, a switchgear chamber and the main engine room with 2 diesel engines.
An arboretum devoted mainly to the growing of conifers.
A building used for the collection and storage of electricity using large lead-acid batteries (accumulators).

A chemical works engaged in the manufacture of the coal tar derivative, picric acid, often associated with the textile industry where it was used as a dye, but more commonly with the explosives industry where it was used as the shell filling Lyddite.
Granular material consisting of small eroded fragments of rock or mineral grains, finer than gravel used as an ingredient in mortar and other traditional building materials.
A pit or enclosed area used for cockfighting.
A projectile fired from a bow.
A strap or series of straps and or bars worn over the mouth of an animal to prevent it biting.
A bridge in which one leaf may be retracted in a horizontal plane, passing on rollers over or under the adjacent fixed leaf.
Warships constructed of iron plate or with wooden hulls covered by iron plates. Used as a generic name for the first examples of armour plated warships.
A warship constructed of iron plate with its main armament mounted in a revolving turret on deck.
An often stately and ornate entrance to a canal tunnel.
The west end of a church made up of a tower, entrance hall and upper room, usually with an altar.
The outer boundary of an airfield.

The capture of imagery using an orbiting satellite. The type of imagery is very varied including visible light photography, infrared and multi spectral photography as well as imagery derived from radar and lidar data.
A rounded or convex moulding, such as an ovolo or torus.
A room in a school devoted to the formal instruction of pupils.
A room where a class of pupils is taught.
A deposit that has been burnt and not subsequently disturbed. Refer to Archaeological Science thesaurus for terminology relating to those redeposited from their original location.
A two-seat trainer chosen to replace the Avro 504. 380 entered RAF service with many finding their way onto the civilian market at the end of their careers.
An indoor play area for the game of badminton.
Trees planted in an ornamental circle. For earthwork surrounding trees use TREE ENCLOSURE RING.
A bowl used for divination.
A buttress shaped like an arch and springing from a pier in arched form to the wall.
A site where cement is manufactured for the building industry.
A beaker adapted by having a pedestal base. The upper part of the pedestal is solid and may be thrown as an integral part of the vessel, or added as a separate element.(Source: MPRG)
A factory manufacturing timepieces, including clocks and watches.

An American turbojet fighter-bomber aircraft. The F-84 was the first production fighter aircraft to utilize in-flight refuelling and the first fighter capable of carrying a nuclear weapon. Designed by Alexander Kartveli, 1946.
A biplane, reconnaissance aircraft with a crew of 3 or 4 which equipped 3 and 22 squadrons RAF before passing to the Fleet Air Arm. Produced in two variants.

A site where a cable was fired into the air, with parachutes attached to either end, to present an aerial obstruction to bring down, through contact, fouling and general drag, or obstruct the passage of an aircraft. Usually found as one of a group.

An instrument for determining, measuring or setting out right angles, usually consisting of two pieces or arms set at right angles to each other, but sometimes with the arms hinged or pivoted to measure any angle.
A garden in which flower beds are the primary focal point.
A garden, often geometrical in layout, or area for the cultivation of roses.
A box in which letters are deposited on delivery.
A settlement where previous house sites are now unoccupied, but often visible as earthworks, crop or soil marks.
A small galley or Dutch trading vessel similar to a barge in construction.
A pool of water, and ancillary buildings, designed to accommodate penguins.
An Ionic base with a lower disc with horizontal fluting or reeding, above which is a torus, also reeded.
A room or rooms containing fitness equipment such as running machines and weights.
Any vessel designed for speed or endurance racing.
Solid masonry slabs (tiles) of terracotta which are usually used as a cladding by bedding in concrete. Faience also refers to decorative glazed units.
A stone which has a socket for an unknown function. Use specific term where known.
A vessel for collecting tears.
An inscribed tablet.
A factory where shirts are manufactured.
Mill for producing a smooth surface and edges on newly sawn timber.
Also use with other metal ores extracted and MINE where relevant.
A machine that uses liquid pressure to exert a large force on two platens so that items placed between them are pressed to a shape, compressed, or forced together.
A short, horizontal brace set between a tiebeam and a wall plate to strengthen the structure.
A firm beach or foreshore used for landing and loading of ships and other vessels. In more recent times hards have been reinforced with concrete.
A works where bleach is manufactured.
A large approximately triangular stone at the foot of a gable, cut to have a horizontal bed and a top conforming, wholly or in part, to the slope of the gable.

Two-seat, twin-engined light/medium bomber celebrated for its speed and versatility. Entering service in 1941, was also adapted for duties as a fighter-bomber, Pathfinder, mine-layer, transport, trainer and photo-reconnaissance aircraft.

Areas of past and current land improvement, involving operations capable of disturbing the archaeology, e.g. land drainage, land reclaimation, cultivation including areas of ridge and furrow but not Celtic Fields.
An aircraft hangar designed by T. Bedford Consulting Engineers usually erected on aircraft factory sites rather than operational airfields.
Aircraft hangars designed by T. Bedford Consulting Engineers to meet the requirement to repair damaged heavy bombers in situ on their airfields.

A large type of military repair hangar mainly used on WWII bomber bases, constructed using steel stanchions and clad in corrugated iron. B 1 hangars were part of a series of prefabricated buildings intended to supplement existing hangars on bases.
A coastal battery containing one or more artillery pieces for to defend the coast against hostile motor torpedo boats.
A surface interpreted as a buried cultivation layer, for example an agriculturally cultivated field.
A bowl comprising three or more equally spaced lobes. There may be one or more moulded animals or other figures inside the base and two or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
A column base featuring a hollow, concave - or scotia - moulding between two tori, which are projecting, convex mouldings.
A building or structure from which observation is kept of the approach of danger.
A prepared area of grass on which the game of rugby is played.

Underwater investigation of the seabed, using side-looking sonar device that emits fan shaped acoustic pulses down toward the seafloor. The intensity of the acoustic reflections from the sea floor are recorded as an image of the seabed.
A kiln for drying hops in a brewery or maltings complex, as distinct from the OASTHOUSES found on farms.
A container made of interwoven strips of pliable materials, such as cane or reed, often carried by a handle.
A plucked string instrument in which the strings pass over the soundbox and parallel to the sides of the instrument.
An object used to hold offerings to a deity.
Canal docks where the freeboard of a boat was marked. By placing increasing ton weights at 4 points around the boat, its displacement could be marked for toll purposes.
A place where oysters are bred for consumption.
Articles of value particularly those made with precious metals and precious stones, usually worn for adornment.
A chapel within a parish church containing an altar and one or more tombs.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter-bomber developed from the Typhoon and the abandoned Tornado. Entered service in 1944 with its greatest success being in destroying V.1. flying bombs. One of the fastest World War 2 aircraft, with a top speed of 436 mph.
A roofed, lightweight structure, usually attached to a house, provdiing access from and to the garden.
Triangular concrete pyramids with 6 feet long sides and 5 feet high, intended to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion. Thought to be confined geogaphically to Southern Command.
A factory where worsted, a well-twisted woollen yarn made from long staple wool and used in the manufacture of suits and other garments, was produced.
American twin-engined medium bomber and ground-attack aircraft that entered service in 1941. A small number were delivered to the RAF under the British designation Mitchell I.
The limit line of an area pertaining to a medieval manor.

A biplane torpedo-bomber designed to be flown from aircraft carriers. Equipped with foldable wings for ease of storage. Joined Fleet Air Arm service in 1940, intended as a replacement for the Swordfish.

A British two-seater army co-operation aircraft manufactured by Hawker Aircraft for the Royal Air Force. A Hart variant biplane that first flew in 1931, becoming a prominent British aircraft in the inter-war period with over 700 units built.
A suburb of a town, especially Roman or Medieval, situtated or extending beyond its formal limits, usually demarked by defences.
Seats or benches covered in turf, built against a wall, tree or fountain, were a common feature of medieval enclosed gardens.
A pair of principal rafters with a tiebeam, usually with a collar.

Impressed civil, twin-engined airliner converted to a military transport. Thirty were ordered for military use, though only eleven were actually built. Entered service in 1940, with the last being scrapped in 1950.
Line, cord or thread, especially that used for tying up parcels, etc. Also use for "twine", i.e. twisted thread, for the same purpose, and medieval equivalents, e.g. "packthread".
Small vessel built or adapted to lay and recover anti submarine nets in harbours and anchorages.
The festival for the first day after Ramadan.
A factory where carpets are manufactured.
A shortened common rafter that runs between ridge and a valley rafter, or between eaves and a hip rafter.
An establishment in which prostitution is practiced.
A small vessel attached to a larger vessel (usually a warship) for general harbour duties such as taking crewmen ashore or fetching supplies.
A type of small boat that was often carried, or towed by a larger vessel and used as a ship's boat. Dinghies can also be used recreationally as independent sailing vessels.
A device with a handle and cutting edge to help remove skin from vegetables and fruit.
A prominent structure situated on land specifically as a guide to navigation for travellers or as an aid/warning to sailors out at sea.
A water-filled hole used for the disposal of aggregate originally used as ballast in ships.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber and ground-attack aircraft. Entered service with the Luftwaffe in mid-1941. Approximately 20,000 were constructed between 1941 and the end of the war.
A place where products are manufactured from wood.
A crane, usually used in engineering workshops, that can be moved from place to place, often by means of rails.
A crane, usually used in engineering workshops that can be moved from place to place by means of overhead rails..
American-built, twin-engined flying-boat designed for maritime patrol and reconnaissance. Entered US Naval service in 1936 as the PBY-1; christened the Catalina by the RAF, who used it from 1939 on.
A pedestrianized shopping street, or a more complex arrangement of shopping 'squares' and walkways.
An area of flattened or compacted ground used for charcoal burning.
A knife designed to be used for pruning plants.
An area in a church, sometimes defined by screens, containing a shrine. Also a shrine, usually portable, containing religious relics.

Airspeed (1934) Ltd. registered in 1934 when associated with shipbuilders Swan, Hunter and Wigham Richardson Ltd.. Acquired by de Havilland in 1940, maintaining own identity and changing name to Airspeed Ltd. in 1944.

Troop and general transport glider. Almost entirely wooden in construction, many were manufactured by the furniture industry. Mk I featured a a door-ramp on the port side whilst the Mk II was fitted with a hinged nose.

A British six-seat single-engined light aircraft, built by Airspeed Limited. First flew in 1933, saw some use as an airliner. The first British type with a retractable undercarriage. Designed by Hessell Tiltman (co-founder). 16 Couriers built.

Twin-engined monoplane that served the RAF as an advanced trainer and flying ambulance. Mk. I featured a gun turret and served for gunnery and bombing-crew training. Subsequent versions used for pilot, radio and navigation training.
Iron Age or Roman coastal site producing salt by boiling of seawater in fired clay pans, resulting in characteristic mounds of 'BRIQUETAGE' (see Archaeological Objects Thesaurus).
Twin-engined, single-seat fighter-bomber. Flown by USAAF fighter groups from 1942, excelled as a ground-support fighter. Could carry two 1600 lb bombs or rocket projectiles.

The Lockheed Aircraft Corporation. Founded in 1916 by Allen and Malcolm Loughead. In 1926 the company moved to Burbank and changed its name to The Lockheed Aircraft Company, and was then incorporated in 1932.

Twin-engined maritime-reconnaissance bomber adapted from pre-war American airliners, the A-28 and A-29, evident from the row of portholes along its fuselage. Entered service with RAF Coastal Command just before the outbreak of World War Two.

Area in a deer park where a single deer was chased by dogs over a set distance, with bets made on the outcome. It usually includes a stand (for viewing) and can also include three distance markers, a finishing post and a ditch behind the last post.
A navigational device.

A classical ornamentation featuring foliage, fruits and, unlike Arabesque, human and animal figures, sometimes fantastic or mythological in nature. The term may have originated from the fact that many examples of such ornamentation were found in grottoes.
Senegal
Long parallel soil ridges less than 5 metres across separated by furrows, formed by using a heavy plough capable of turning the soil.
Hard, durable, dark grey stone, the purest native form of silica, which can either be used decoratively or as a main material. Predominantly found in East Anglia and the South East.
An Italian cornice consisting of a bed moulding, a row of plain block corbels or modillions, and a corona or cornice.
A building or structure where electricity is generated.
A bridge crossing under railway property.
A column set on a pedestal and decorated with the bows of warships to celebrate naval victories. Originally a Roman form, it was revived in 17th and 18th century decoration.
A building where carpets and other floor furnishings were woven.
An opening within a structure to allow air and light in and or to allow a sight outside or inside.
Vertical screens made of wood or steel framing mounted on concrete blocks were built to protect airships from cross winds when entering or leaving the airship sheds.
A ridged roof that slopes on all four sides.
Open sided barn for the storage of wood produced by the periodic cutting of small trees.
A jettied house where the upper storey only overhangs the end elevation of the building.

Blocks of solid concrete, in the shape of a round bottomed cone usually 2 feet 6 inches across x 2 feet 9 inches high. Buoys were mainly used in road blocks intended to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion.
A usually large school providing courses for children of all abilities, between the ages of eleven and sixteen.
A protective structure, often made of sandbags with reinforcement, designed to protect aircraft at airfields from enemy attack.
The residence of health workers. Includes single dwellings of doctors, nurses etc. but not multiple dwellings eg.NURSES HOSTEL
Watch Office with operations room designed to Air Ministry drawing number (13079/41)
A building, originally used as a shelter for the duty pilot or officer on watch on an airfield, incorporating an operations room.
A bridge carrying a road over land or water.
A wooden bar sliding from a long channel at one side of a doorway into a socket in the other jamb so as to bar the door.
One of a number of tiles cemented together to form pillars supporting the floor above a hypocaust.

A twin-engined, multi-role aircraft built by Junkers. Originally designed as a medium bomber with the speed of a fighter, but its adaptability allowed it to fulfil the roles of night fighter, torpedo-bomber, anti-tank aircraft and photo-reconnaissance.
A small, usually inexpensive, restaurant with a limited menu of light meals served at counters or tables.
A peat-based garden where various types of heather are grown.
A building or room, where business and/or administrative activities to do with the canals was conducted.
An object representing the sun, made of bronze or gold usually dating from the European Bronze Age.
Grain from a cereal of the genus hordeum, often used in the manufacture of alcoholic spirits.
A building or site conducting research into communication techniques for use in the Royal Navy.

A site, usually with docks and control buildings, used for the storage, maintenance and deployment of military vessels or the administration of the Royal Navy. May also include accommodation buildings for personnel.

A core used to produce flakes from a single plain platform. The base of the core, or 'keel', is often formed by alternate removal from a process resembling cresting. Often one end has a relatively unmodified section. (Source: SARC)
A site where cobalt is mined
A folding circular cover on a stick held in the hand for protection against rain.
An object lying on the sea bed detected by marine survey equipment that emits and receives high frequency sound waves.
An object projecting out of the sea bed detected by marine survey equipment that emits and receives high frequency sound waves projected sideways from a boat or towed array.
A moulded object.
Transport version of the four-engined Lancaster bomber. Serving from 1943 to 1951, and all metal in construction, this aircraft was used extensively during the Berlin airlift.
The building attached to a cathedral or collegiate church where the dean, prebendaries or monks and canons met for the transaction of business.

Seven/eight-crew, heavy night-bomber. The first four-engine bomber to join the RAF, with a bomb load of 14000 lb, entered service in 1940. Superseded as a bomber by the Lancaster and Halifax, later versions served as transports and tugs.
A hall in which public assemblies and meetings can be held.
A site where barytes (barium sulphate) is mined. Barytes is also commonly worked from the waste tips of lead mines.
A circular plan with a series of cells around a central core, often used for prisons.
An expansion period stand by set house designed to drawing number 974/35 and containing a single generator set and switch board. Constructed with brick cavity walls.

A two-storey, structure with a brick ground floor and a reinforced concrete upper floor with balcony and large windows to the watch office and control room. This became the most common building design for air traffic control in the Second World War.
A container for holding water that has been blessed by a priest and is used for symbolic rituals of purification.
US Navy version of the four-engined, six-crew B24 heavy bomber. Modified for long-range reconnaissance duty and used as a patrol-bomber against shipping and submarines.
A stone screen, usually found in a monastic or collegiate church, that separates the choir from the nave.
A small outlying farm building, especially common in southern England, used to store ash (which was used as a fertilizer).
A farm on which liquid sewage was regularly used for irrigation as a means of sewage disposal.
A pit containing the waste product form iron working.
A set of small pincers used for gripping and plucking.
An establishment where musical performances take place.

The measurement of the light emitted from sedimentary minerals, mineral inclusions in bricks, burnt flint or unburnt calcite when they are heated. The signal relates to their prior exposure to radioactivity. Used to date samples up to 500,000 years old.
A badge, usually of lead alloy, distributed at various religious shrines of the medieval period and worn on clothing as proof of a pilgrimage and as a talisman.
A horizontal beam over an opening to support a wall.
The top layer of earth consisting of humus and rock particles.
Sedimentary clay with smectite mineral properties, originally used for the cleansing ["fulling"] of cloth; in the 20th century it was used for a wider range of industrial applications.

Dutch coaster of the late 17th to late 19th centuries with a square hull and 2 masts, generally having a heavy keel and round stern and bilges, although later examples were built on more refined lines.
Small cargo vessel used for short coastal voyages carrying a variety of cargoes.
Seed of the cotton plant from which edible oil is extracted.
A district, suburb or quarter of a town or village adjacent to a fort, with the lowest legal status accorded to a built up area.
A small doll controlled by the operators hand either directly or with strings.
A factory that manufactures watches.
A bowl with a single loop handle crossing over the top of the vessel from one side of the rim to the other. (Source: MPRG)
The office or headquarters of a local police force, or of a police district.
A type of late 19th century tenement block for tenants of a higher social status - usually reflected in the more ornate facades.
Small pieces of wood, tipped with a chemical composition which ignites when rubbed against a rough or, if safety matches, prepared surface. Normally contained within a small box.
A form of round barrow intermediate between the Bell Barrow and the Disc Barrow. Only use where it is not possible to determine specific type.
A large wooden gate, positioned at either end of a canal or river lock, equipped with sluices to let water through.
A compound consisting of potassium and silica, used in various processes.
Originally gold coins issued in Florence, but later used for various coins issued on the continent. In modern Britain, the two shilling piece.
A linear groove worn into the surface of a road or thoroughfare by the continuous passage of wheeled vehicles. Usually expected to occur in pairs.
Areas of indeterminate function.
A length of straight, curved or angled earthwork or cropmark of uncertain date or function.
A sulphuric acid compound.
A type of large steel framed aircraft hangar introduced by the Royal Air Force in its Expansion Period with a number of designs between 1934 and 1939, to accomodate heavy bombers.
A section of road that provides a passage beneath another road or railway.
A laithe with an attached house.
An abbey or priory of Savigniac monks. Order merged with Cistercians c1147.
A sewer or irrigation channel designed to avoid blockage.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of children.
An area, often a village, with fixed defences such as pillboxes, anti tank ditches and gun emplacements, designed to stop the advance of an enemy force and to hold out for an agreed period of time.
A factory or complex where chamois leather is produced using fish oils as the tanning agent.
A factory for the manufacture of leather goods, such as shoes, saddles, etc. Use TANNERY for the manufacture of leather.
An area of hardstanding on which ammunition is stored.
An installation used for the storage of ammunition.
A gaming piece used specifically to play chess.
A rough table usually for working upon.

An aircraft designed to land on water. They can be divided into 2 types: Flying boats (designed with a hull allowing the aircraft to land directly on water) and Floatplanes (where the undercarriage was replaced by fixed floats).
A factory where ribbons are manufactured.
Festival of Lots
In which coniferous and deciduous are present in roughly equal proportions. Specify in Description whether currently managed, neglected, unmanaged or management not determined.
A specific German Stoneware form of rounded mug. (Source: MPRG)
A mug with a rounded body profile below a deep neck. There may be a marked junction between the neck and the body. The neck may be inward-sloping, upright or everted. (Source: MPRG)
The establishment of an undertaker who is responsible for the management of the ceremony connected with the burial or cremation of a dead body.
A command post used to direct the guns of an anti aircraft battery.
An enclosed encampment, often featuring temporary or semi-permanent structures, used for the detention of prisoners of war, refugees or other civilians detained on political or social grounds.
An Egyptian religious statuette.
A workshop in which saggars - fire clay boxes to protect ware from direct action of flame and gases during firing - were manufactured.
A truss comprising principal rafters and wall-posts secured by knee-braces or sling-braces, but lacking tiebeams.

A distinctive form of terrace found in the northeast consisting of a long, two storey terrace indistinguishable from a conventional house externally, save that each unit has two front doors, one leading to a separate dwelling or dwellings upstairs.
A building used to dry teazle heads in. Teazles were used to raise the nap on cloth in teazle shops.
General Aircraft Limited.
Principal glider-pilot training glider fitted with tandem seats. Spruce and plywood in construction, the Hotspur served with the Glider Pilot Regiment between 1941 and 1945.
A place where furs are made into finished products.
A contrivance of interlocking parts used to fasten objects together.
A rope, cord etc used to hold or secure animals.
A house consisting of a single storey open hall with a two storey domestic range attached to both ends forming an H shape.
An assessment of a known wreck or underwater archaeologcial site through diving.
A mine for the extraction of iron ore.
Lenses worn in a frame designed to improve or protect the vision of the wearer.
Use for deposits formed in lakes or ponds.
Fine-grained, non-humified, organic mud formed under water. Principally composed of plant material, typically of faecal origin.
A place where photographs are taken of people or things on a commercial basis.

A small three-masted lateen-rigged vessel used exclusively in the Mediterranean from the 16th to the 19th century. Its hull was similar in form to that of a polacre but with an extended bow and stern.
Dairy produce obtained by churning cream and used in cookery as a source of fat.

A pointed arch which, on a plan, is shown to be constructed around four arcs: two centred below and two centred upon the springing line, which is the level at which the vertical sides of the arch begin to curve.
A place where shoes and boots are mended.
An unroofed structure, found on military airfields, protected by brick walls and earth banks for shelter during air raids.
A room or group of rooms for healing the sick. Where it is a monument use the Thesaurus of Monument Types.
A court, usually with only 2 walls, used for playing pelota and its variants.
A camp kitchen, usually associated with the military.
A heavy, metallic element, which is liquid at room temperature. Used in thermometers and medicinal preparations.
A large disc of stone revolving on an axis, used for grinding, sharpening and polishing.

Single-engine, two or three-crew pre-World War 2 biplane fighter and general purpose aircraft. First flown in 1931, the Seal was a Naval variant on the Fairey Gordon and a forerunner of the Swordfish.

A single engine two seat cabin monoplane tourer, first flown in 1933 as a successor to the Puss Moth. Impressed into military sevice in WWII by the RAF and the Fleet Air Arm as a liaison and communications aircraft, also used by training units.
A medicinal or mineral spring often with an associated building.
A wooden stake fence, often associated with deer hunting.

Originally obtained by burning limestone to produce quicklime. Now a fine grey powder made from a mixture of limestone and clay used with water and sand to make mortar or with water, sand and aggregate to make concrete.
A form of cement originally named since it was said to be like Portland Stone in appearance.
A press used to extract the juice from apples, which was then used to make cider.
A building in which the fibres of new woollen cloth were raised by brushing with teazle heads.

A jug form which usually has a short, narrow neck and rim and an applied spout. The spout is usually tubular and free standing, or attached to the rim/neck, rising from just above the high shoulder or girth. (Source: MPRG)
A type of chain shot characterized by a number of chains attached to the main shot, causing maximum damage. Sometimes known as a Spider shot.
A structure used for music, dance, ceremonial or civic events.
A round barrow featuring a mound surrounded by a ditch, with no intervening berm. The ditch may be accompanied by an external bank.
A crane for lowering loaded coal waggons onto a ship.

Single-engine, single-seat, long range fighter originally designed in 1940 to a British requirement. Outstanding low-level speed and range resulted in its assignment to the ground support (Army co-operation) role.
An area of land, usually enclosed, set aside for the breeding of hares.
A mill used for the mechanized processing of silk.
A tank used for the storage of water, usually found as part of an institution like a workhouse or hospital complex

The main German, medium bomber of the war, the HE111 first saw action during the Spanish Civil War. HE111s took part in the Battle of Britain and from 1944 onwards were used to launch airborne flying bombs against London.
Use for the remains of any part of a reptile.
A textile mill where felt is produced.
A fortified house of two or three storeys, the lower floor being used to house animals and the upper for domestic use.
A building or site used for the production of anchors.
Grinding mill for producing dyes and pigments from natural materials.
A Mark 5A aircraft which has undergone further modifications to enhance performance or armament.
A place of worship for Unitarians, a movement which does not believe in the Trinity but only in the Unity of Christ. Christ was to them just an exalted human teacher.
A termination, either in the form of a decorative feature or a right-angle applied to the end of the moulding, of a label, dripstone or string course.
A housing, normally of triangular section, in a post to take the end of a prop, to hold the post upright during construction.

A place a worship situated at the end of, or built onto, the structure of a bridge. Often associated with bridge maintenance through the collection of donations, they may be endowed as a chantry for the celebration of Masses for the soul of the founder.
A room for storing guns.
A small rake used to move the embers of a fire.
American A-20 twin-engined, light, day bomber. Some supplied to the RAF and known as the Boston I. Subsequent variations adapted to night flying and re-christened the Havoc.

A German coastal minelaying submarine in use during the First World War. In addition to 18 mines, the U BOAT also carried 7 torpedoes in 3 tubes (2 bow/1 stern) and and 88mm or 105mm deck gun. A very successful design, UCIIs sank more than 1800 vessels.
A brush for applying paint.
A burial site for animals.
Daily record of events or appointments.
A wooden, or wooden soled, shoe.
A type of pottery kiln in which air rises up inside the oven to be forced back down and out through the base of the oven.
A finishing process for cloth involving the pounding of the cloth with heavy weights.
An abbey of the Bridgettine double order of nuns and religious men.
A large, "bottle-shaped", oven of brick construction used in the baking or firing of pottery.

A jet-powered tailless delta wing high-altitude strategic bomber plane, operated by the RAF from 1956 until 1984. Typically armed with nuclear weapons but capable of conventional bombing missions. Used as a nuclear deterrent in the Cold War.
A pen or enclosure used for containing sheep.

A single engine, jet propelled twin boom aircraft which came into service in 1945 in a variety of roles including night fighter, trainer, the carrier-borne Sea Vampire, and the MK5 version, a fighter bomber. Produced by De Havilland.
A metal receptacle used for burning coals, charcoal etc to provide heat.
A coupled timber built end-opening First World War aircraft hangar.
An observation tower located on or near to a bombing range.
A building with a regulated moderate temperature for the cultivation of plants.
A modern building in which the load is carried by a reinforced concrete framework. Use for reinforced concrete buildings.

The earliest side-opening standard type of aircraft hangar designed in 1913 and used in WWI. Originally constructed from wooden trusses and struts, one example has steel frames. It comprised a single or coupled shed with rear workshops.
skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Royal Flying Corps Side Opening Aircraft Hangar

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: The earliest side-opening standard type of aircraft hangar designed in 1913 and used in WWI. Originally constructed from wooden trusses and struts, some examples have steel frames. It comprised a single or coupled shed with rear workshops.
A building providing lodgings for police constables.
A dome shaped building, housing training apparatus, including a projector, for training ground gunners in the art of airfield defence. (WWII).
An abbey or priory of Premonstratensian canons.
An establishment where tickets/reservations for events, journeys or entrance to a site can be purchased.
Iron in the form of rails eg. for use in the construction of railways.
A tower in a semaphore communication system. Often a three-storey building on a hill in line-of-sight, signal towers provided working and living space, usually for two crewmen with their families.
A structure for visually communicating the exact time to ships in anchorage. A ball slides down a mast at the top of the tower, usually at noon or one o'clock exactly.
The residence of a bridge keeper.
Hard, corrosive alloy of copper and tin.
A garden deliberately planted with white plants and shrubs.

Single-engine, testbed monoplane built to Air Ministry Specification 43/37. Only twelve were produced, the first of which tested the Sabre I engine in 1940, and were used throughout the war. The cockpit could seat two observers behind the pilot.

A two-seat, single-engine bomber. Fast, versatile and well armed, but with a fuel tank poorly placed between pilot and gunner, was considered to be the best day bomber of the First World War. Later entered civil service.
Single-engine, three-crew torpedo-spotter, reconnaissance and anti-submarine biplane. Entered Naval service in 1936, designed for operation from aircraft carriers and equipped with folding wings.
Use for a craft powered by a steam engine that uses three expansion stages of progressively lower pressure, to extract further energy from the steam.
A jug with little or no discernible neck and an even, convex profile form rim to base, which are roughly equal in diameter. (Source: MPRG)
A short timber laid across the top of a masonry wall to carry a wall plate or the foot of a common rafter.
A government office used for the collecting of excise tax/duty.
A cup adapted by the addition of a pedestal base. (Source: MPRG)
A metal bar to strengthen the heel and or sole of a piece of footwear.
A mineral containing high quantities of Copper.
Container with a handle, spout and narrow neck.
A mechanically operated lift used to transfer rolling stock from one level of track to another.
A large communal room within a college complex used for functions, assemblies, examinations etc.
A large room within a school or college used and appropriately furnished for the sitting of examinations by students..

Single-engine, single-seat interceptor fighter developed from the race-winning Schneider Trophy seaplanes. One of the most famous of all combat aircraft, entered RAF service in 1938 and was still in use in the 1950s.
A truss with a transverse timber like a hammer-beam, but braced to a principal or collar without a hammer-post.
A place where ambulances are serviced and maintained.
A place where pigs are reared.
A turbine driven by gas flow or the gas from combustion.
A rotary prime mover. Turbines may be steam, water or gas operated.
A sea within a sea, the Adriatic consists of that part of the Mediterranean which separates Italy from the Balkans and Greece.
Rock containing a high proportion of calcium phosphate.
A concave glass dish used to hold material for observation or experimentation; so named for its resemblance to the disc covering the face of a watch.

Blocks of concrete with four protruding arms so that, whichever way up the caltrop is placed, one arm will always point upward. Used in imitation of the iron caltrops thrown on the ground to impede cavalry.

Canadian-built, single-engine, high-wing transport and communications aircraft converted from a civilian model. Metal-framed with fabric covering, saw service in 1944-5. Was capable of being equipped with wheels, floats or skis.
A non-specialist hospital dealing in general medical and surgical treatment.
A cutting tool where the plane of the blade is at right angles to the shaft.

Observations made by antiquarians (Those who studied sites and landscapes prior to archaeology and architectural history becoming established disciplines in the 19th century) and reported through publication or from unpublished manuscripts.
An area in a town where traffic is prohibited, often containing shops.
Chamber built into underside of a structure to exercise demolition.
A piece of furniture intended to hold drinks, side dishes etc.
An instrument composed of several pipes in which air is made to vibrate by blowing across the top edge.
A reading desk usually placed near the west end of the choir.
A two storied open fronted structure comprising a cattle or cart shelter on the ground floor with a hayloft above. Most common in South West England.

Component part of a Flint Mill where flint is calcined before it is brittle enough to be ground in the mill. Ground, burnt flint is used in the production of earthenware pottery, which whitens and strenghens the body.
A mill for crushing flint. Crushed flint was used in the manufacture of pottery in order to whiten and strengthen the body of earthenware pottery.
A gable with curved sides and an identifiable pediment.
A building or site where aircraft can be stored and maintained.

Fleet Air Arm fighter and torpedo-bomber, designed for operation from aircraft carriers. All-metal in construction, it entered service in 1944 and was rendered obsolete after the war by the advent of the jet aircraft.
A gripping tool consisting of two hinged arms, usually with serrated jaws.
The subsoil traces of prehistoric cultivation, presumed to have been caused by the use of an ard to till the soil.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter, also adapted as a night-fighter, fighter-bomber, rocket-projectile fighter and tank-buster. The first monoplane to enter RAF service with 14,000 being produced between 1937 and 1944.
A three dimensional representation of a figure, whether animal or human, produced by carving, casting sculpting or similar.
The junction of two timbers at right angles, with chamfers or mouldings meeting on a diagonal line, where one timber is cut to fit around the chamfer or moulding of the other timber.
Twin-engined monoplane originally designed as a reconnaissance aircraft, but also widely used as a trainer. Entered RAF service in 1936.
The space enclosed between the gates and side-walls of a lock.

Two-crew, twin-engined bomber. Entered production in 1934 and designed for dual use as a high-speed commercial transport. Technical problems hindered its use as a bomber and led to conversion to high-altitude reconnaissance.
A factory manufacturing fireplaces.
A wide ditch surrounding a building, usually filled with water. Use for moated sites, not defensive moats. Use with relevant site type where known, eg. MANOR HOUSE, GARDEN, etc.
A roughly square mound of stones which may also contain or conceal a burial.
A container for cooking.
A tool for pounding or grinding.
A formal garden consisting of lawns, walks and borders belonging to a college or university, eg. Oxford or Cambridge.
A passage between two rooms in a house or leading from the door to the hall.
Three-crew, single-engine carrierborne torpedo-bomber. Entered service in 1942, first seeing action during the Battle of Midway. Served with the US Navy until 1956.
A room in which a judge sits to hear cases and undertake other official proceedings which are not of a sufficient importance to be brought into court.
A tall, polygonal structure with ornamental roofs at each storey which is associated with Buddhist temples; the style was adapted for secular eyecatchers and pavilions in the 18th century in England.
A boat, ship or other vessel either whole or in part. Watercraft often survive as commemorative monuments or have been reused as floating restaurants, museums, hotels etc.
Form of ore crushing machinery associated with tin mines often wooden and water-powered.
A workshop or factory where bells are made by casting molten metal into moulds.
A natural or man-made earth mound on which a gallows was erected.
Programmes of research or investigation which seek to identify the significance of a heritage asset, often to inform proposals for change
A fortified river or river bank forming part of the anti invasion infrastructure.
A box or cupboard enclosing the fuses for the electrical circuits within a building.
A building housing a flight simulator designed to air ministry drawing number 4188/42.
Glass which has been coloured and decorated by painting.

A small stone core with a conical form and a single core platform which may or may not be prepared. Microblades are removed form the circumference of the platform. The end opposite the platform usually tapers to a point. (Source: SARC)
A medieval high status farmstead, acting as the centre of the estate, directly controlled by the lord and used for the benefit of his household and dependents.

An important two-seat, tractor biplane, initially used by the RFC in a reconnaissance role and by the RNAS as a bomber. Later converted to a single-seat Home Defence fighter and ultimately used as a trainer.
A building used for broadcasting radio programmes for public entertainment. Often includes recording studios, transmitters and offices. Use RADIO STATION for non-broadcasting uses eg. Military.
Series of wire mesh screens used for grading lumps of coal according to size.

A building or buildings ranged around a courtyard on at least three sides. They occur in the Iron Age, as well as being an influential plan type of house from the 15th century onwards. Index with appropriate period.
An outward projection from a defensive wall allowing the defenders to attack the flanks of any force attacking the wall.
A model village built by a utopian society or group of artists.
Twin-engined monoplane originally designed as a reconnaissance aircraft, but also widely used as a trainer. Entered RAF service in 1936.
A steam engine in which steam flows in one direction only at each stroke, as opposed to the commoner contra-flow engines.
Use for vessel registered in Cyprus whether Greek or Turkish.

A club often with a dance floor or small stage and featuring entertainment generally of an improvisational, satirical, or topical nature which can be watched by the clientele whilst they drink and dine.
A holding on a smaller-scale than an ordinary farm.
Equipment including diving suits, wet suits, oxygen tanks etc. used to enable people to undertake underwater activities.
Mill for grinding bark usually for use in the tanning industry. Use with power type(s), eg. WATERMILL where known.
A barn with steam powered threshing.
A net used in fishing to catch or land fish.
An area of ground which has been cleared of plants and other obstruction.
A closely mown lawn used for the game of croquet.
A small house or cottage at the entrance to a cemetery, usually occupied by a caretaker or gardener, etc.
An early form of castle consisting of a flat-top steep-sided earthen mound, supporting a wooden tower, and a bailey.
Sodium carbonate, usually derived from common salt, used for a variety of purposes including the manufacture of glass and soap.
A ship used for treating patients or moving them between a battle zone and a safe area.
A heavy bladed knife.
Small coastal vessel.
A building housing equipment for the process of distillation.
A room designed or suitable for dancing.
A device for containing food whilst cooking it by the action of steam.
An instrument for taking measurements and describing circles, with two straight arms connected at one end by a movable joint.
An open roofed structure on which climbing plants are grown in order to provide a shaded walkway or seating area.
Machinery for raising and lowering men and materials to and from the surface of a mine.
A building equipped with facilities for bathing, and occasionally public baths.
A bowl for the ritual washing of hands.
A three-storey RNAS control tower, incorporating meteorological office on the ground floor and an air watch office on the second floor.
A complete cross-frame from ground level to ridge in a box-framed building.

A type of prefabricated house erected, to 11 approved designs, as part of the Temporary Housing Programme, between 1944 and 1948. This scheme was devised to relieve the post-war housing shortage at a time when conventional materials were unavailable.
A house built using experimental building techniques and materials.
Miles M.14 Magister. Single-engine, two-crew training and communications aircraft. Spruce and plywood in construction, with open cockpits and a fixed landing gear, served between 1937 and 1945.
A hut provided as accommodation for hop pickers and may also be know as a Hop Pickers' Hut
A building or complex where soft skins are produced by tanning with alum.
A mill, on two or more levels.
A hospital department where heat, light, sound, electricity, etc, is administered to patients suffering from muscular or skeletal disorders.
A utensil used to pour a liquid in honour of a deity.
A polished reflective surface.
A stationary winding steam engine positioned at the top of a railway incline for hauling up trains and locomotives.
Northern quarryman's name for any fine grained, dark grey/black to green coloured igneous rock. Index with specific stone type where given.
A semaphore signalling tower on a railway.
A stone ring built to enclose and sometimes revet a burial mound or cairn.
View across roofs, generally in an urban context, showing details of roof and chimney construction.
A temporary, usually roofed, wooden structure placed on the ramparts or walls of a castle to improve the defenders field of fire along the length of a wall.
A mill or works where needles were manufactured.
A channel or casing containing and protecting wiring, piping etc.
A weight used with letter scales for weighing letters or parcels and establishing the required postal rate.
A building in which engineered metal products are finished and polished.
The slab or place on which a fire is made.
A place for strolling, public walks, etc. Usually associated with coastal resorts.
A site with accommodation buildings and ancillary facilities for Royal Air Force personnel.

A design of beam steam engine introduced circa 1800 in which, instead of a single overhead rocking beam, there are two beams positioned alongside the cylinder, one either side, giving a lower overall height.
A large wooden structure built alongside the edge of a river where boats may lie for the loading and unloading of goods and passengers.
A large pit formed by, and for, the extraction of iron ore.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of women and children.

Any form of arms or ammunition whether from a formal organized military context or as a general cargo. Use specific terms - e.g. swords, bombs, where known; otherwise use this term primarily in contexts where the arms are unspecified or ancient.
Part of textile mills.
A factory used for the manufacture and assembly of lorries.
Durable wood from the cedar tree.
A tool with a scoop end for digging up roots etc.
A small containment for drugs which can be ingested.
Site with important historical association.
A container, usually square or rectangular, used in metal processing for separating metals one from another, usually silver from gold.
A military side-opening aircraft hangar originally designed for seaplanes and used RNAS bases from 1916. Steel framed with asbestos or corrugated iron cladding.
Photographic negative on glass developed using a dry process.
The wood, stone or brick framework, lining a doorway, from which the door is hung.
A manufacturing site producing weaving shuttles for the textile industry.
A mill in which barytes concentrates were ground to fine white powder, normally by use of flat millstones similar to those of a corn mill.

A four-storey RNAS control tower. The first floor contained offices for the commander flying and meteorological offices and the upper two floors, in the form of a central tower, provided offices for air traffic control.
Stiff hairs used in the manufacture of brushes.
Hair taken from animals and used in a variety of manufacturing processes.
Hair from the Angora goat

A French airliner produced in 1925. A four-engined biplane developed from the Bleriot 115 and 135 but larger than these. Two were built for Air Union (the Paris-London route). Both crashed with fatalaties in 1926 (Kent).
A vessel for policing fishing grounds and fishing vessels.
A factory where hemp, the woody stalk of the hemp plant, used for the making of coarse cloth and cordage, was processed.
A fragment of the rim of a vessel, or hollow object, usually of ceramic or glass. If known, use specific vessel type.

A single engine, jet propelled twin boom aircraft which came into service in 1945 in a variety of roles including night fighter, trainer, the carrier-borne Sea Vampire, and the MK5 version, a fighter bomber. Produced by De Havilland.
A hospital department for the identification and treatment of skin tissue disorders.
A building housing one end of an underwater telegraph cable.
A purpose-built trench used to test chemical warfare weapons.
A high status Iron Age grave in which a two or four wheeled vehicle accompanies a frequently richly furnished inhumation burial. A barrow may overlie the grave.
A building housing a Russian-style steam bath or banya.
A building housing a Finnish-style steam bath.
A row of houses whose facade in plan follows the concave arc of a circle or ellipse, eg. The Royal Crescent, Bath.
Any wall enclosing a building or complex of buildings, eg. prisons, dockyards, factories, etc.

A waterwheel where the incoming supply of water is introduced at the top of the wheel and drops onto the paddles, or buckets, of the wheel which rotates in the reverse direction to that of the incoming flow.
An establishment for the preparation and selling of food to be consumed off the premises.
The stalks of cereals separated from the grain br threshing and used as fodder, basket manufacture, thatch etc.
A tread-wheel by which a crane was formerly worked.
A mineral of the composition Zr[SiO4]. Commonly brown or yellow in colour. May contain high levels of uranium and thorium. Can be used for dating using luminescence or fission track methods.
A stone-lined pit in which seaweed was burnt. The calcined ashes were used in the manufacture of soap and glass, amongst other things.
A natural or man-made earth mound on which a gallows was erected.
A room, or part of a kitchen, for the cleaning and storage of kitchen utensils.
Used for boiling sections of willow for basket making, etc.

Source from which stone utilized for the manufacture of non-flint artefacts, including axes, was obtained. Applied only to sources exploited during the Neolithic and earlier Bronze Age. Do not use for flint mining or knapping sites.
The corner upright bar of a polygonal sash.
A vessel with a specially adapted mouthpiece, to assist in feeding young animals and humans.
A roof consisting entirely of common rafters, without the use of principals, in pairs but not connected by collar-beams.
Clay used in the manufacture of fire bricks.

Four-engine, long range heavy bomber. Developed from the Lancaster, and originally designated the Lancaster Mk. IV, it was larger in size, bombload and fuel capacity. Never used operationally in World War Two.
A hearth used for the reheating of metal slag to extract further metal.
A workshop where tapestries were made.
Buildings and plant used for the extraction and purification of arsenic oxide into various forms of pure arsenic.
A friary belonging to the Crutched Friars also known as Crosiers or Fratres.
A purpose-built, or modified, building where organizations and associations meet for presentations and consultation.
A long, narrow ditch designed to carry water away from a waterlogged area.
Redcar and Cleveland
A works, including an extractive site, producing a clay of high plasticity and firmness, used as a basic raw material for porcelain.
A small pin or stud worn in the lapel, often decorative.
A container for holding votive offerings.

A rectangular chamber of brick or stone with heavy wooden gates at either end equipped with sluices to let water in and out, thereby enabling a canal boat to be lowered or raised to a different level.
A rafter set outside a gable to carry the roof beyond the wall face.
a hard metal used in a lot of alloys.
A building used as a social venue by people interested in, and involved with, the sport of hunting.
Weight used with any kind of balance.
British multi-purpose, single-engined monoplane that served as a torpedo-bomber, dive-bomber, reconnaissance aircraft and in other roles. Equipped with folding wings for use aboard aircraft carriers.

Impressed civil, twin-engined airliner converted to a military transport. Thirty were ordered for military use, though only eleven were actually built. Entered service in 1940, with the last being scrapped in 1950.
An indoor or outdoor market where fruit and vegetables are sold.

A type of stoneware jug dating to the 16th and 17th centuries, popularly known as a Bellarmine jug, shaped in the figure of a bearded man. They were produced in the Cologne region, particularly Frechen.
A building providing lodgings for police constables.

Twin-engined, seven-crew, coastal reconnaissance, biplane flying-boat. Designed to the same specification as the Saro London, entered service in 1937. Also serving in an anti-submarine role, was replaced by the Consolidated Canso (Catalina) in 1943.
Containers used to serve food and drink. Use appropriate term.
A soil, which may be buried or exposed, that has developed in a past landscape.
A distinctive, clerestory-roofed building of three 10ft and two 12ft bays, used for the drying, storage and packing of military parachutes and built to Air Ministry drawing number 10825/42.
A grouping of retail warehouses and supermarkets with associated car parking.
A pressure vessel used to store gasses at above atmospheric pressure.
A turf-covered mound in a curvilinear E-shape, and hard-standing to take an aircraft. There were usually an access point to an air raid shelter at the rear. In use during WW2
An area of hardstanding, surrounded on three sides by a protective wall or bank, used for parking aircraft, in a state of readiness, usually around the perimeter of an airfield.
A gateway with one or more chambers over the entrance arch; the flanking towers housing stairs and additional rooms. Use with wider site type where known.
A long metal or stone vessel for cattle to drink water from.
Mark 1 or the first production variation of an aircraft.
Clay used in the manufacture of fine ceramics especially porcelain.
A coupled timber built end-opening First World War aircraft hangar.
A sandglass that runs for an hour.
A reversible device for measuring time by the transfer of sand from upper to lower glass bulb.
Data suitable for processing using database management software.
Small engineering works specialising in the production of items such as ploughs and threshing machinery.
A building housing the acoustic detection equipment for a sound mirror
A structure for adding coal to railway locomotives usually by gravity from a higher level.

A two-seat, single-engine bomber. Fast, versatile and well armed, but with a fuel tank poorly placed between pilot and gunner, was considered to be the best day bomber of the First World War. Later entered civil service.
An establishment used for gambling.
A dark, viscous substance obtained, from the distillation of wood tar or turpentine, and used as a sealant for caulking the seams of a ship or boat.
A double lock placed between tidal water and a canal, etc..
A site where slate is quarried from the ground.
A building, usually in a rural setting, with a range of facilities for the use of members.
A piece of metal, usually in the form of a disc, struck or cast with an inscription or device to commemorate an event, or awarded as a mark of distinction.

A monument previously consisting of a built structure, but which has been demolished, such that only a ground plan and foundations or similar are thought to remain. Where all below ground traces have also been removed use DESTROYED MONUMENT.
A very long trough laid between the rails of a railway track to allow a suitably equiped steam engine to scoop up water whilst in motion.
A hammer designed to fight with, often has a hammer side and a spiked side.

For example mood disorders, agoraphobia, anxiety, bipolar disorder, chronic depression, eating disorders, dissociative identity disorder, multiple personality disorder, obsessive-compulsive or paranoid personality disorder and schizophrenia.
A device for catching eagles, falcons and hawks.
An object used to catch animals.
A structure in which pottery tiles were baked.
A place where shoes and boots are mended.
A court established in England and Wales by Parliament in 1846 to decide minor civil disputes.
An early form of lead furnace, set upon a hilltop or crest to utilize winds in smelting.
A passenger vessel equipped with recreational facilities for long voyages for pleasure and sight seeing.
A series of flat-topped structures, usually wooden or stone, on which a person places their feet when ascending or descending, facilitating movement from one level to another.
The horizontal surface of a step or stair.
An apparatus around which cables or hawsers are wound for hoisting anchors, lifting weights, etc.
