The residence of an employee with the duty of maintaining a section of a railway or road.

A building which has been moved from its original site either through active human intervention or natural processes such as erosion. For structures or objects such as gravestones use MOVED STRUCTURE.
A place where meat and fruit, etc, is preserved by salting and/or drying.
A floatable concrete vessel, numbers of which made up the main breakwater of the Mulberry Harbours used to secure beachheads during the allied invasion of Europe in June 1944.
A building used to accommodate hippopotami.
An arch where vertical piers raise the springing line.
A tool used to produce designs in plaster on the outside of buildings.
A kiln used to reduce the shells of shellfish to calcium carbonate.
The heraldic bearings or shield of a person, family or corporation.
A short timber supporting end of joists or rafters to facilitate an opening, such as a door or dormer.
A microlith retouched to a half moon or crescent shape. (Source: SARC)
A large, powerful, hand-drawn bow, usually 6 ft (1.8m) in length and traditionally made of wood.
A weapon for shooting arrows.
A small ornamental building in a garden, usually one-storeyed and consisting of one room. Use a more specific term where known.
A large jug, usually rounded with a narrow neck, used for holding liquids.
German three-engined air/sea rescue and transport flying boat. Entered service in 1940 as a replacement for the DO18.
A conspicuous object, such as a beacon, used by mariners to aid navigation at sea.
An unlit, highly visible and distinctive feature on the coast that can be used by mariners for navigation during daylight only.
A large container with lip and handle usually for milk.
A vessel used to produce butter from milk through agitation.
The large wooden framework that supports the grinding wheels in a corn mill.
Circular structure, normally indicated by one or more rings of post holes and/or a circular gulley, and usually interpreted as being of domestic function.

A section of the water channel of a river, shut off above and below by lock gates provided with sluices to let water in and out and thus raise or lower boats from one level to another. Often found situated next to a weir.
A room for baking.
Articles, particularly drinking vessels, manufactured from glass.
An aircraft hangar designed to Air Ministry specification (drawing number 6910/43). Similar in design to the ROBINS AIRCRAFT HANGAR but larger.
A heavy framework of parallel beams used to support a ship in dock.
A layer of remains left by a single culture, from which the culture can be dated or identified.
An office used by a qualified pilot, expert in ship-handling and with local knowledge, who assists the captain or master to take a vessel in or out of a harbour or through narrow waters.

A place of worship for Bible Christians, a group who split from the Wesleyan Methodists to form their own church in the South West of England. They were amalgamated into the United Methodist Church in 1907.
A site, usually including hardstandings and associated buildings, where ambulances can be parked and stored.
Easily formed metal alloy composed of copper and zinc.
A room for servants, particularly where they would eat.
Photographic transparency on nitrate base material.
A case which holds and protects a mirror.
A kiln used to reduce the shells of shellfish to calcium carbonate.
A pair of common rafters with a collar.
Single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer. Spruce and plywood in construction, entered service in 1939, continuing to serve as a trainer, and also a target tug, until 1950.
A farmstead where the house and working buildings are attached and in-line. Can include Bastles, Longhouses and Laithe houses.
A kiln in which stone is burnt as it falls through a heated and slightly inclined steel tube.
A building on a river or canal in which the water levels are controlled.
Based on a typical 18ft span, 40ft long temporary brick hut but with two bay windows in the front elevation, one for the watch office and one for the chief instructor.

Four-engine, seven-crew heavy bomber. Entered service with RAF Bomber Command in 1940, becoming one of the twin sources of bomber strength along with the Lancaster. Also used for transport and glider tug duties.
A band worn around the leg to hold up a sock or stocking.
A prepared area used for the game of netball.

An American turbojet fighter-bomber aircraft. The F-84 was the first production fighter aircraft to utilize in-flight refuelling and the first fighter capable of carrying a nuclear weapon. Designed by Alexander Kartveli, 1946.

A mask worn over the face to protect the wearer from inhaling airborne pollutants and toxic gases. The mask forms a sealed cover over the nose and mouth, but may also cover the eyes and other vulnerable soft tissues of the face.
A machine used in the worsted industry for cleaning woollen slivers after gilling and cording.
A small workshop, employing up to 10 men, working on hand-operated carding engines and hand jennies, spinning yarn for handloom weavers.
A device to extract juice, usually from fruit.
A set of two or more pins joined together by a chain.
A pin worn to hold two or more pieces of material together, often when being worn as clothing.
A structure used for the drying of food using an indirect source of heat.
A structure used for the roasting or drying of chicory.

Six-crew, twin-engined medium night-bomber. Entered service in 1938 and was the RAF's principal bomber until 1943, participating in the first bombing raid of the war. Later versions served as torpedo and reconnaissance-bombers, transports and trainers.

A structure comprising of two walls of stone or wood with nets or fish traps attached. Located in coastal waters, on shelving coastlines or in river estuaries they form large enclosures with a V or L shaped plan. The narrow point on the seaward side.
An outdoor meeting place.

Single-engine, two or three-crew pre-World War 2 biplane fighter and general purpose aircraft. First flown in 1931, the Seal was a Naval variant on the Fairey Gordon and a forerunner of the Swordfish.
The place where a house stood or had once stood, often adjoining a garth or croft.
Horse powered ore crusher, consisting of a stone wheel running over a circular iron or stone bed.
A cleansing agent, manufactured by reacting natural oils and fats with a strong alkali. Nowadays, formed into bars with added colouring and perfume.
Beams of wood, iron, steel etc., used in the construction industry.
An engine in which a vertical piston rod supplies energy via a crankshaft directly to the flywheel suspended above the cylinder.
A design of vertical steam engine patented in 1802.
Small fishing craft used mainly for fishing, cutter or ketch rigged.
A room in a house, hotel, business premises etc. where guests or visitors are received.
A lake, often artifical, in a park or open space, used for the recreational rowing and sailing of boats.
For the production of clay tobacco pipes.

Low-grade cast iron in the form of balls or spheres, produced in small workshops and exported across the North Sea and Baltic region. Particularly associated with 16th century Sweden. Also spelt "oszemundt" and other variants.
A building or structure with a six-sided plan.
A quoin, usually of stone, with a concave rebate at one corner forming the surface against which the rounded edge of a canal lock gate turns, making a kind of hinge.
A stone or brick used on a corner to reinforce it and also as decoration.
A stand or tray for ink bottles and or pens

Wood and fabric transport glider, twenty of which were produced with twin Bristol Mercury engines. Fitted with a hinged nose for loading and unloading, this was the largest glider used by the RAF and could accomodate a 7-ton tank.
A spiked stick, the spiked tip frequently of metal, used to urge livestock forward.
Twin-engined fighter-bomber. All metal in construction, entered service in 1940. Supported bombing operations and participated in attacks on France, but not widely used due to engine faults.
American, single-engine fighter designed for operation from US Naval aircraft carriers. Produced between 1940 and 1945, Wildcats provided to the British Fleet Air Arm were renamed Martlets.
A bridle joint which is invisible from all sides of the timber.
An inhumation burial in which the corpse is laid on a wooden bed, often surrounded by a collection of grave-goods. Anglo-Saxon rite of 7th century AD.
A factory which produces artificial imitations of mineral water, such as soda water.
A native hardwood of the Beech family with hard and durable characteristics which traditionally made it appropriate for structural work.
A room within a building or complex, such as a workhouse, used for purifying objects with smoke.

Traditionally an amber-coloured globe lamp atop a tall black and white pole, acting as a signal to road users that there is a pedestrian crossing. Modern beacons may also include an outer ring of flashing LED lights.
A drinking vessel, made of glass, designed expressly to be used for the consumption of wine.

A room provided for the use of people waiting for a service, such as a train or bus service, or to see an individual such as a doctor or a dentist. When a dedicated structure, see Thesaurus of Monument Types.
A circular pillbox designed by the Croft Granite, Brick and Concrete Company, with six loopholes. With no roof or door access was gained through the roof.
A building or complex where cork is treated and processed to be used in various products.
A site where unprocessed wood is used to manufacture goods.
A building or complex where corks and stoppers are made for use in bottling.
A dam with a watertight upstream side, which may be flat or curved, supported by a series of buttresses on the downstream side.
Rammed earth or clay of a low moisture content used to make floors or walls, or found between shuttering.
A bowl with convex body walls. (Source: MPRG)
A protected parachute store similar in design to the 6351/37 except constructed wholly from reinforced concrete.
A missile base armed with the Bristol Bloodhound surface-to-air missile. Bloodhounds were deployed to defend the launch sites of Thor Intermediate Range Ballistic Missiles.
A pointed two-edged surgical knife.
A hall built as part of a complex and used for the recreation of the workers or inhabitants. Usually associated with model estates, factories, flats etc.
A building used to accommodate elephants at a zoo or wildlife park.
A large piece of material used on a bed for sleeping on or under.
The partially enclosed western part of a chapel, leading to the chapel proper.
A metal structure supporting high powered lights.
A massive hammer of wood, stone or iron.
A system of trenches dug by troops for practice purposes.

Twin-engined, medium bomber with a 1200 mile range and a bomb load in excess of 10,000 lb. Entered service in 1940, but engine faults resulted in retirement in 1942 with its design later modified into the acclaimed four-engine Lancaster bomber.
The stem of the plant Zingiber officinale, with a characterisitc hot and peppery taste, used in cookery and medicine.
A house, enclosure or large cage for the keeping and breeding of birds.

Armoured military vehicle with its own firepower, which operates on tracks for troop mobility over rough terrain. Some may be adapted, or purpose-built, to be amphibious, and may then be double-indexed as AMPHIBIOUS VEHICLE.
A heated room or building used to dry yarn after it has been washed.
Use a term from the Archive Format list.
A gatehouse bridging a canal.
A house having four rooms of equal height on each of two floors; in larger houses there are often two parallel and equal roofs.
A factory manufacturing bearings, including ball bearings for use in precision equipment.
A vessel with heating apparatus beneath it, for cooking or keeping food warm at the table.
A low bank on the edge of a defensive ditch on the side away from the main rampart.
A building, usually part of a hospital complex, in which contaminated clothes, bedding and utensils are disinfected.
A method of floor construction in which sections of joists run at right-angles to one another.
A partition or wall behind an altar, often separating the choir and altar from the ambulatory and east chapel.
An instrument for writing or drawing with ink.
A device for receiving and sending radio-transmitted signals into the atmosphere.
A factory where biscuits are manufactured.
A base of the Tuscan Order, featuring a square plinth supporting a large torus with a fillet above.
A bag containing food hung around a horse's head.
An unhewn piece of felled tree, or similar rough mass of wood.
A dredger that works by the use of suction.
A factory that manufactures toys.
A factory where hemp, the woody stalk of the hemp plant, used for the making of coarse cloth and cordage, was processed.

The measuring of annual tree-ring growth shown by most tree species in temperated regions. Regional chronoliges are required to date any particular piece of wood, the longest of which, for Germany, works for the present to approximately 14,000 yrs ago.
A county judicial building where the Quarter Session and the Assizes for the County were held.

Cones of solid concrete usually 3 feet 6 inches in diameter x 2 feet high which, when placed in rows or groups were intended to form a substantial barrier to enemy armoured divisions in the event of invasion.

Use for the remains of internal parasites of vertebrates, including humans, such as flukes, tapeworm, including their calcified cysts, etc. Eggs of the nematodes Ascaris sp. (maw-worm) and Trichuris sp. (whipworm) are commonly reported.
A jug with a constriction between the upper and lower body sections. (Source: MPRG)
A plan of a building where the entrance is in the gable wall.
A house of friars of the Augustinian order. Also known as Austin Friars

A British six-seat single-engined light aircraft, built by Airspeed Limited. First flew in 1933, saw some use as an airliner. The first British type with a retractable undercarriage. Designed by Hessell Tiltman (co-founder). 16 Couriers built.
Generally understood to mean aircraft whose normal loaded weight is less than 2750kg (6060 lb).

A stone axe in which the surface is fully covered by negative removals. Core axes may be made on flakes and have part of the flake's original surface but this cannot be part of the edge otherwise use FLAKED AXE. (Source: SARC)
A building used for the crystallization process in alum making.
Old ship converted to a floating coal store.
A precious metal, lustrous white in colour. Used for the manufacture of coins and other valuable items.
A large store where wool is stored.
Small two or three masted ship used as trading vessels in the medieval mediterranean.

A jug that incorporates a practical joke or conundrum into its construction. A combination of cut-outs in the body and hollow handles and tubes render conventional use impossible. The puzzle being to work out how to empty it. (Source: MPRG)
The dwelling and workshop of a framework knitter.
Sorting offices constructed during the Second World War designed to rapidly move goods from the vulnerable docks and ports via the rail network.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.

Twin-engined, six-crew, heavy bomber. Conceived as a rival to the Lancaster and Flying Fortress, the HE177 was dogged by mechanical and structural problems. Of a thousand produced, only about two hundred saw action.
A complex of buildings and earthworks constructed for the storage of bombs and pyrotechnics.
Generally understood to mean aircraft whose normal loaded weight is less than 2750kg (6060 lb).

A British six-seat single-engined light aircraft, built by Airspeed Limited. First flew in 1933, saw some use as an airliner. The first British type with a retractable undercarriage. Designed by Hessell Tiltman (co-founder). 16 Couriers built.
A factory used for the production of red lead used in glass manufacture, or white lead used as the pigment in white paint.
A large space in an underground tunnel, usually wider than the tunnel itself, used for storage, etc.
A flat arch or lintel with quadrants on the corbels rising from the jambs.

A sunken, circular, concrete pillbox used on airfields. They remained flush with the surface to permit the free movement of aircraft but, if attack threatened, could be raised hydraulically or by a counterbalance, and manned to give covering fire.

A jug form which usually has a short, narrow neck and rim and an applied spout. The spout is usually tubular and free standing, or attached to the rim/neck, rising from just above the high shoulder or girth. (Source: MPRG)
A device to catch and hold one object to another, eg a door to a doorpost.
A cheap restaurant.
A group of planted trees or shrubs, generally of uniform age and of a single species.
A timber framed house comprising horizontal and vertical timbers, forming the walls of the building and directly supporting the roof.
A temporary hostel built for industrial or transport workers; for example, railway workers' hostels were provided for engine drivers.
A straight brace from rafter to collar in a common rafter truss.
Frozen water. Prior to the invention of the refrigerator, ice was used to preserve food.
A building used for meetings and worship by a religious community trying to propogate its faith in an area.
A building, usually associated with a port or dock, where seamen could get a meal and a cheap room. Often established by religious groups for the moral betterment of seamen.
A garden where woodland and meadow flowers grow in an apparently natural way.
A pair of uprights supporting a crosspiece. Often very decorative, fire dogs were probably used as a spit or to hold pots over the fire.
A building where threads of different qualities and colours are mixed together.
A cast iron hammer used for shingling iron or making heavy forgings.
A single-engine, heavy, long range, three to five-crew day bomber. Served only with 99 Squadron RAF, 1924-5.
A structure housing machinery for crushing coal. Usually found at the pithead of a colliery or coal mine.

Four-engine, ten-crew, long-range maritime reconnaissance and anti-submarine aircraft. Developed from the Short C-class Empire airliner. All metal in construction, entered RAF Coastal Command service in 1938.
An arch whose height is equal to its span.

6 Type DFW 55373s placed in a 3X2 rectangular plan. Each projector was separated by 31-34m. Hardened personnel and ammunition shelters located midway between each projector, but ammunition stored outside the perimeter.
An establishment used to serve ice cream to the general public.
An airfield, and associated structures, used by one or more fighter squadrons.
A pit dug into the ground or a simple construction made of stone, brick or metal. Designed to contain a fire and prevent it from spreading, but can also be used to heat stone for breaking.
Mark 16 or the sixteenth variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter. Entered service in 1943 as a land-based fighter. Converted to a carrierborne fighter in 1944 for use by US Navy and Fleet Air Arm. Mostly saw action in the Pacific and Far East.
A pavilion used for exhibitions, e.g. the exhibition pavilions at the Great Empire Exhibition, Wembley, 1925.
A vessel, usually made of stone, which contains the consecrated water for baptism. Use a broader monument type if possible.
Fragments of metal broken up and set aside for reprocessing.
A hut consisting of a frame of reinforced concrete posts into which panels could be slotted. Designed by the British Concrete Federation (BCF) during WWII.

A hut consisting of a frame of reinforced concrete posts into which panels of either pre cast concrete or corrugated asbestos could be slotted. Designed by the British Concrete Federation during WWII.
Day of Atonement.

Monument visible as substantial above ground remains, retaining evidence of architecture and materials, with walls partially or completely intact but with roof and interior walls substantially or completely destroyed.
A water-filled hole used for the disposal of aggregate originally used as ballast in ships.
Cluster of dwellings of medieval or later date (Scots)
A machine used for the purification of water, usually for drinking purposes.
The channel of water that provides a current of water to drive a millwheel.
Water channel leading to water wheel.
A building used for storing tree bark.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Nitrate, used as a fertilizer or for use in the explosives industry.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter manufactured by Messerschmitt. First used as part of Germany's Condor legion during the Spanish Civil War, the 'one-o-nine' was the Luftwaffe's most widely used fighter seeing service throughout World War II.
An object used in the preparation of a body following death. It was used to plug the orifices of the body.
Four-engined, five to seven crew, heavy bomber biplane. Entered service in 1918.
A system of communication used in a house to summon servants or on board ship to transmit orders to the engine room.
Includes crests, hatchments and supporters.
A stemmed cup used for holding the wine during communion.
A garden maintained for the study and cultivation of plants for medicinal purposes.
An enclosed, defensible passageway, equipped with gun ports, extending into or traversing a dry ditch.
The limit line of a county.
A glazed opening in a roof or ceiling.
A rectangular shaped area of land enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
Use for vessels registered in Cuba.

A cathedral in which the chapter was composed of canons who lived in their own houses and were not governed by a monastic rule. Nine such cathedrals existed in England between the 11th and 16th centuries.
A building or part of a building used for the storage of stationery materials.
A reinforced concrete structure, often sited underground, used as a shelter from the threat of nuclear attack.
A vessel used to transport bombs and depth charges from the shore to flying boats during the Second World War.
A chapel within a parish church or other religious building for use by the lord of the manor and his family
Rolled iron or steel formed into rails.
A building or structure in which bricks are made.
An embanked shute, often stone paved, allowing carts to tip their loads of coal from the road into a storage area.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Full Shielded Self Propelled Mounting System

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: ?what does this mean?
Sites used for the production of drugs and other medical products.
A distillery for the manufacture of perfumes from herbs.
A place where lead ore is extracted from an open cast mine.
A section of a psychiatric hospital or psychiatric ward set aside for children and/or adolescents with mental illness.
A vertical pillar or post, often shaped.
A works where bleach is manufactured.
A large stone used by cattle to rub up against and so scratch themselves.
A small enclosure built onto the perimeter of a Roman fortress or fort.
A factory where preserved food is canned.
Central two-storeyed tower surmounted by an octagonal glazed control room giving a 360 degree view. Flanked by single-storey wings.
A handheld serrated device for grooming horses.
A handloom weavers workshop where the weaver received yarn from a clothier and manufactured a woven piece of cloth from it.
A building where carpets and other floor furnishings were woven.
The flat end of a barrel.
A place where swans are bred and reared.
A bay window, supported by corbelling, cills or brackets, projecting from an upper storey of a building.

A prefabricated structure consisting of sectional timber framed units that were bolted together. The structure was clad with weatherboarding and had a felted roof. They were used as temporary accommodation on airfields. Also see 'Type A'
A pit used for the containment of clay whilst it is mixed to the right consistency for brickmaking.
A place for sharpening metal objects like tools and weapons.
A small building housing a mechanism used for winding a cable.
A bottle for the confinement of evil spirits.

A British six-seat single-engined light aircraft, built by Airspeed Limited. First flew in 1933, saw some use as an airliner. The first British type with a retractable undercarriage. Designed by Hessell Tiltman (co-founder). 16 Couriers built.
A crane in which, during any alteration of radius, an automatic device causes the load to move horizontally.

Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber: Curtiss P40 Warhawk, known to the RAF as the Tomahawk, later renamed Kittyhawk. Serving from 1941 to 1942, control difficulties in dive attacks impeded bombing accuracy, resulting in use for larger targets only.
The Curtiss-Wright Corporation, Airplane Division, established in 1910. Notable aircraft produced include the Kittyhawk.
A narrow flake which is the by-product of making a burin.
A settlement located on or near to the shores of a lake. Buildings associated with lake villages are usually raised on piles to prevent them from being flooded.

A bridge consisting of a lattice girder spanning the distance between the tops of two towers. Designed to transport vehicles across the gap in a container suspended at road level by ropes under a travelling crane on the girder.
A hydraulic machine used to drive a pillar crane.
House owned by the church, often used for meetings.
A tool for splitting and chopping.

A steel aircraft hangar evolved from the German "Lamellendach", a segmental roof design of the 1920s using a diamond shaped web of pressed steel producing a hangar with a shallow curving profile. Used for both military and civil purposes.
A mill manufacturing bobbins for the textile industry.
An arch formed around two arcs whose radii are each equal to the span of the arch.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of all types of wax.
A two post structure with cross beam for hanging criminals.
A Norman keep, in the form of a circular or polygonal enclosure surrounded by a wall.

A jar adapted by the addition of a pierced bunghole just above the base. The hole can be simply a hole in the wall of the vessel or made through a circular knob or disc of clay. There may be one or two vertical loop handles. (Source: MPRG)
A long spear with a double barb where one barb is longer than the other.
A plan with four foils radiating out from a central point.
Part of an instrument that is used to modify or limit the sound of a note.
The structure across the lower end of a medieval hall containing the spere, its supporting posts and tie-beam.

A flour mill which uses one or more pairs of horizontal millstones to grind wheat into flour which millers call a ï¿½sudden deathï¿½ process; within not more than 90 seconds complete wheat grain becomes wholemeal flour.
A tract of land with trees, sometimes acting as a boundary or barrier, usually smaller and less wild than a forest.
A building or site where boat sails are manufactured from processed cloth.
A factory where fish are processed into food products.
A large building used for the storage of grain.
Powder made from particles of stone used in mining to make the coal dust in the air less combustible.
Fairground attraction containing a number of ghoulish displays designed to scare visitors.
A grave or sepulchre including a monument.
A rotating, domed, steel turret set over a circular pit used as a gun emplacement.
A HORSE GIN used for domestic cider manufacture, especially on farms.

All physical evidence for a monument has certainly been completely destroyed (allowing no future reinvestigation) by activity implying substantial ground disturbance. Eg quarrying, road cutting, or natural disaster, erosion, acts of God etc.
A factory manufacturing bearings, including ball bearings for use in precision equipment.
A lid with a shallow conical profile and an integral knob. (Source: MPRG)
Use for vessels registered in Brazil.
A holistic approach to urban character, using GIS to map areas of urban character and historical development, as a tool for managing future change in ways that are appropriate and sustainable.
A large building where iron is stored.

Twin-engined, four-seat torpedo-bomber designed to replace the Vildebeest. Entered service with RAF Coastal Command in 1939. Later versions incorporated a remote-controlled machine gun with periscope sight.
A clip used to attach pieces of harness together.
A place where members of the British Legion meet.
Method used for the recovering of material by floating large whole earth samples, usually between 40-60 litres per context (or 100% if context contains less than this).
A house, enclosure or large cage for the keeping and breeding of birds.
A stemmed cup used for holding the wine during communion.
A library for use of the public.
A structure providing protection against the weather, situated on railway platforms.
An architrave surrounding a door, window or niche interrupted by large blocks of stone, and often by a massive keystone set under a pediment. Named after the architect James Gibbs (1682-1754).
A coloured, glass-like substance (opaque or partially opaque) that is fused to the surface of metal or glass or pottery for decorative or protective purposes.
A wheel driven by wind or steam for the lifting of water.
A lid resembling an inverted dish with a flat top and an integral or added knob or loop handle. (Source: MPRG)
A leather strap for sharpening a razor.
A transportable hangar designed by A & J Main of Glasgow.

skos:Concept.skos:altLabel: Infra Red Line Scan Aerial Photography
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A specific type of Infrared photography that uses an airborne scanning infrared sensor to record differential spectrums of features both extant and buried.
A farmstead where the farmhouse and working buildings are attached and in-line. They can comprise the extension of linear farmsteads.
A timber, horse-powered device consisting of a large, rotating drum around which a rope would be wound, hoisting material from a quarry pit, mine shaft etc..

Long-range, four-engine reconnaissance-bomber. Initially produced as a transport, converted and used against Allied convoys in the Channel and the Atlantic. Also served as a VIP transport, one of which was the Immelmann III: Hitler's personal aircraft.
Rendering material containing lime and sand spread on walls as a pliable mixture before drying to a hard surface.
The cleaning and sorting of horse hair mainly for use in the upholstery trade.
A building in which silk was dried.
German single-engine, four-seat maritime patrol and reconnaissance flying-boat. In production between 1934 and 1940, the DO18 was replaced by the three engined DO24.
A flat surface designed to hold objects. For a set of shelves use shelving.
A room for storing and maintaining the equipment used in riding, eg saddles, bridles, reins etc.
A comb used to comb fibre before spinning.
A bridge carrying a tramway.
A secondary rib usually springing from the junction of two other ribs, or one that rises between a main diagonal and transverse rib, from the springing to the ridge rib.
A room in which domestic appliances and facilities for cleaning are stored.
A structure consisting of a vertical mast and a horizontal boom operated by cables on a separate engine or motor. Used for hoisting and moving heavy loads or objects.
A cast of a person's face taken after death.
A microlith retouched to a half moon or crescent shape. (Source: SARC)
The staff or crook of a bishop or abbot.
Usually a L or T-shaped tumbler lock key which allowed the bolt to be pulled across by a cord.
A building containing machinery for operating sluices.
A form of temporary horseshoe, of Roman date, used when unshod animals were brought onto metalled roads. Usually consists of flat plate, winged sides and hooked heel.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter, also adapted as a night-fighter, fighter-bomber, rocket-projectile fighter and tank-buster. The first monoplane to enter RAF service with 14,000 being produced between 1937 and 1944.
A device fitted and locked onto the head of a woman as a form of punishment, featuring a metal plate that fits into the mouth to impede speech..
Place where ships and boats are dismantled.
A building plan consisting of three rooms placed in a straight row.
Movable stand for carrying a body to its grave.
A place where an anti-corrosion coating of zinc is added to iron and steel products to prevent them from rusting.
A staff of office or authority.
Scaffolding erected on a beach and in the surf so as to prevent hostile forces from landing.
A column whose shaft is interrupted by square blocks.
Finishing process for cloth, especially linen, running the cloth between heavy rollers.
A hospital department where research and treatment into the causes and nature of diseases or abnormal bodily conditions is carried out.
A microlith retouched to a point, usually with oblique retouch. They are synonymous with 'obliquely blunted points' of the English Mesolithic. (Source: SARC)
An object used to pick the teeth with.

A World War One German three-crew, twin-engined, long range heavy bomber biplane manufactured by Gothaer Waggonfabrik A.G.. Entering service in 1917, this aircraft incorporated a ventral tunnel allowing the gunner to shoot downwards and to the rear.
Single-engine, single-seat fighter-bomber. Designed to replace the Hurricane as an interceptor, excelled as a rocket-projectile-firing ground-attack fighter. Entered RAF service in 1941.
A long pointed weapon used to catch fish by stabbing.
A fishing spear with two heads to grip fish between.
A bowl comprising three or more equally spaced lobes. There may be one or more moulded animals or other figures inside the base and two or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
Tyne and Wear
A site where clay is both extracted and fired to produce bricks.
A machine consisting of a continuously moving band of fabric, rubber, or metal used for transporting people or objects from one place to another.
Netherlands

A large hilltop or hillslope enclosure in South West England, located close to rock outcrops, and surrounded by one or more circuits of stone built walls. All are prehistoric; some are definitely Neolithic.
Garden area next to public house used for the comsumption of alcoholic beverages.
A pumping station used as part of a clean water supply system.
Pond, created specifically for providing power to water-powered forges, blast furnaces, helve or other hammers.
A container used to catch blood during bleeding.
A furnace used for melting metals for casting or for heating shot.

A section of the water channel of a river, shut off above and below by lock gates provided with sluices to let water in and out and thus raise or lower boats from one level to another. Often found situated next to a weir.
A moveable covering, usually to a window, made up of a frame containing slats set at an angle. Allows air to circulate but limits light entering.
Factory for making Chenille a yarn produced by placing short lengths of yarn (the pile) between two core yarns (the core) these are then heated to set the pile in place.
A plan in which the building is two rooms deep but has no central corridor.
A tower which rises above the space at the intersection of the nave, chancel and transepts of a church. Usually pierced by windows to provide light directly to the area below.
A place where dockyard craftsmen both design and build ships.
A small structure comprising of a 'shelf' of wood or metal sitting on pillars and erected for the benefit of porters to allow them to rest their burdens.
A factory or plant for the manufacture of ice using mechanized refrigeration techniques.
A purpose-built terrace of shops.
Cargoes transported in sacks or bags, usually wheat, corn, flour, fruit, or coal. To be used only where the cargo is said to be "sacks" or "bags" of goods. Use specific term where known.
A bowl whose form resembles two cones joined together at their widest points, forming a carination.
Large, three-engined, long range reconnaissance flying boat. Wooden hull and frame construction, with linen covering. Entered service in 1930.

A blade attached to a shoe to glide on ice. It can be made of bone, and examples are known from at least as early as the Bronze Age. Metal blades have progressively replaced bone skates since the sixteenth century.
A part of a musical instrument played by the feet.
A place where people recovering from illnesses or accidents are helped to recover their physical and/or mental capabilities.
An automata or water device which surprises the unwary onlooker with water. A feature of 16th and 17th century gardens.

A timber building based around a sunken hollow, the floor of which may have been suspended above the hollow to counteract dampness. Grubenhauser are believed to date from the 5th to 8th centuries AD but may be earlier. Use Grubenhauser as plural.
A monument consisting of an area enclosed by a ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier, where the barrier follows an almost rectangular course.
A piece of pointed wood, usually to be driven into the ground.
A hydraulic machine used to magnify the stroke of a hydraulic piston. The pulleys and chains of a crane or other device are attached to the jigger.
A report detailing the results of a field survey. Usually restricted to a survey of a small or specific area or site.
A unifacially worked early stone tool.
A small warship engaged in patrolling coastal waters.
A large building, situated by or near a dock, canal, road or railway and used for the temporary storage of goods or merchandise awaiting transportation.
A large store for the temporary accommodation of goods awaiting transportation to or from the sea.
Cylindrical, self-propelled missiles which travel underwater and explode on impact.

skos:Concept.skos:definition: The rod is also called pole or perch and equal to 5 1⁄2 yards

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: The residence or official premises of a consul, the official appointed by a state to protect its citizens and commercial interests in a foreign state.
A site where artefacts are manufactured from jet.
A wedge shaped brick used to construct arches.
The wedge-shaped block placed at the crown of an arch to consolidate the structure. Sometimes employed as a decorative feature.
A wealden house with only one end being jettied.
That area below low water level and inside territorial waters; the term maritime includes saline waters within tidal environments.
Series of rooms in a workhouse complex where children were housed and looked after.
An area of a port, dock or harbour where a container vessel docks to take on or unload its containers.
The residence of a drover.

A relative dating technique for assessing bones from the same deposit. Often used to check for contemporaneity of bones selected for radiocarbon dating or to check for hoaxes such as the Piltdown Man.

A jet-powered tailless delta wing high-altitude strategic bomber plane, operated by the RAF from 1956 until 1984. Typically armed with nuclear weapons but capable of conventional bombing missions. Used as a nuclear deterrent in the Cold War.
The official residence of a dean.
A forester's cottage.
A jug with a maximum diameter in the lower half of the vessel and with no discernible shoulder. (Source: MPRG)
A field or piece of ground used for the playing of games and other activities.
An engine used for directly winding up coal from deep mines, first used in the 18th century.
A winch powered by a small steam engine used to drag barges, boats and other vehicles up an inclined plane.
An extra sole on a shoe.
Bricks capable of withstanding heat without burning. Used to line fireplaces, kilns etc.
An establishment for the testing of eyesight, making up of optical prescriptions and the sale of spectacles.
Thin sheets of material used for a variety of purposes such as writing on, painting on, or printing on.
A vessel comprising two or more dishes, generally of small size, joined together. There may be one or more handles of varying forms. (Source: MPRG)
A stoppered bottle, for serving drinks.
Photographic print on glass, using a wet process.
A stone placed over or at the head or foot of a grave, or at the entrance to a tomb.
A staircase, usually rising through more than one storey, with a space at its centre around which the stair is carried by strings and newels.
A garden which consists of rocks and rock-loving plants that require little water.
A tree named after a person or event associated with it, e.g. Byron's Oak at Newstead.
A place where wheels and wheeled vehicles were manufactured, originally from wood.

A vault composed of concave cones, inverted and overlaid with ribs that rise from the springing of the vault and diverge equally in different directions, producing an effect like the ribs of an opened fan.
A factory or works used for the production of turpentine, wood alcohol and similar chemicals by the distillation of pulped wood.
A lock at the point where two waterways join together.
A structure consecrated for devotional purposes.
A water point with a device to regulate the flow of water.
A point in a village providing water for drinking and washing.
Loose notes
An establishment or works where the distilling of spirits is carried out.
A place where metal knives and edge cutting tools were manufactured.

A prefabricated structure of a steel frame clad in corrugated iron. Semi-circular in section they were used as accommodation for the armed forces and, during WWII, as emergency housing for bombed out civilians. Also used for storage.
A rigid holder for a bladed weapon.
A sign, situated near a road or bridge, indicating a toll.

A jug form which usually has a short, narrow neck and rim and an applied spout. The spout is usually tubular and free standing, or attached to the rim/neck, rising from just above the high shoulder or girth. (Source: MPRG)
A structure with semaphore arms and/or coloured lights used as a means of warning on railway systems.

A type of dish specifically designed to catch the juices from roasting meat. The dish may be oval, semi-circular, rectangular or wedge-shaped. Usually has one or two handles located on one long side and a lip at one or both short sides. (Source: MPRG)
A church, usually found in East Anglia, of early Medieval and/or Medieval date with attached or detached round tower.
American twin-engined medium bomber. Entered service with the US 22nd Bombardment Group at Langley Field in February 1941. Also served with the 14th and 39th RAF squadrons.
An open sided building known to have been used for sheltering cattle.
A Roman cremation burial in which the human cremated remains are placed inside or adjacent to a wooden casket, frequently decorated with lion-headed mounts and studs.
A box with one transparent side within which a picture, jewel etc can be displayed.
A factory where carpets are manufactured.
A chapel where Roman Catholics worship.
A residential home for older people or people with physical and/or mental disabilities who need care provided by registered nurses.
A privately-funded home for the care of the elderly.
A tool used to remove shavings from an object.
British multi-purpose, single-engined monoplane that served as a torpedo-bomber, dive-bomber, reconnaissance aircraft and in other roles. Equipped with folding wings for use aboard aircraft carriers.
A circular or oval window or panel. Also the circular opening at the top of a dome.

This is a pit used in the glass industry for the production of cylinder glass. The only surviving examle in England is at the Hartley Wood Glasworks, Sunderland. It is a feature of 19th century and later glassworks
A vessel to contain the wafers used in the Eucharist.
A notional line of resistance defined by anti tank obstacles, pillboxes and gun emplacements.

An underground structure from which operations covering the whole, or part, of the country could be directed in the event of a nuclear attack. Usually equipped with air filtration equipment and supplies for several months.

A building used by the society, fraternity or order organized under this name with initiatory rites, mystic signs of recognition and various degrees of dignity or honour, for social or benevolent purposes.
Northumberland
A market where fish is sold.
A two-seat, reconnaissance biplane developed from the FK2 with a more powerful, but heavier, engine. Primarily used for training in the UK.
A bowl with straight sides which are at an approximate right angle to the base, i.e. a roughly cylindrical shape. (Source: MPRG)
A machine for cleansing flax, hemp or cotton and forming the fibres into a continuous wide lap or sheet in preparation for carding.
Open sided barn for the storage of wood produced by the periodic cutting of small trees.
An English seventeenth century house plan consisting of a rectangular block two rooms deep, the rooms sometimes separated by a passage.
A fishing vessel that catches fish by using a Seining net, that is a large net that is made to hang in the water by attaching weights along the bottom edge and counteracting floats along the top.
Fragments of wrought or cast iron broken up for reprocessing.
A local civil court first established during the 17th Century by local Acts of Parliament to deal with minor cases of debt. Based on a model established during the reign of Henry VII.
A place where ceramic tiles are manufactured.

A system of excavation, developed by Mortimer Wheeler, whereby a site was uncovered by means of a grid of square trenches with baulks between them to aid the recording of the stratification of all four sides of each trench.
Small tower projecting from a castle wall, or other fortified wall. Allows defenders to fire along the length of the wall.
A dam with a watertight upstream side, which may be flat or curved, supported by a series of buttresses on the downstream side.
A small convex moulding, often decorated with beads and reels.
A stone, situated alongside a road, providing directions to travellers.

Generally rectangular structure normally used for burial purposes, and formed from stone slabs set on edge, and covered by one or more horizontal slabs or capstones. Cists may be built on the surface or sunk into the ground.
A grave lined with slabs of stone or slate and covered by a large slab of stone. Commonly found on the Isle of Man.
An intricately designed garden in which ground coves, low shrubs or coloured earths are arranged in interlacing patterns resembling knots
A building or range of buildings used for the cleaning, crushing and loading of freshly mined coal.
A jug with a rounded profile and a rounded base, i.e. with no discernible basal angle. (Source: MPRG)
A shallow dish or plate used to serve main meals off or to serve sweetmeats, these usually being painted with devices and riddles.
An earthwork used as a boundary marker.
A quarry for the extraction of Serpentine, a major metamorphic mineral which is easily polished and easily carved. A major variety, lizardite, is found in Cornwall.

Single-engine, single-seat, long range fighter originally designed in 1940 to a British requirement. Outstanding low-level speed and range resulted in its assignment to the ground support (Army co-operation) role.
A malleable water repellant substance created by animals or as a coating to parts of plants.
An inclined timber running from a rafter to the inner face of a wall, forming a triangle.
Short vertical timbers which go from the rafters to the inner plate on a thick wall.

Originally ordered as land based dive-bombers, with 950 being delivered to the RAF, none are known to have flown operationally, instead apparently serving as target tugs. Bermuda was the name given to the Brewster SB2A Buccaneer in RAF service.
Small fragments of granite.
A room that is underground or partially underground. Primarily used for storage.

Twin-engined, medium bomber with a 1200 mile range and a bomb load in excess of 10,000 lb. Entered service in 1940, but engine faults resulted in retirement in 1942 with its design later modified into the acclaimed four-engine Lancaster bomber.
A managed small wood or thicket of underwood grown to be periodically cut to encourage new growth providing smaller timber.
A coastal site producing salt by solar evaporation of seawater in a series of PONDS, followed by boiling of the concentrated brine in a PANHOUSE
Single-engined fighter, developed from the Camel. Entered service in 1918 and became the RAF's first mainstay peacetime fighter.
A kiln used for extracting salt through the evaporation of salt water.
Soft, pear-shaped fruits of the Ficus carica tree. They can be eaten fresh or dried.

The material that does not float during the floatation of samples as a means of recovering charred plant remains from an archaeological context. Also, the material remaining following wet or dry sieving of course sieved samples.
An area within a hospital where patients receiving privately-funded medical and surgical treatment are accommodated. Often includes separate rooms.
A flag or military symbolic representation on a pole.
A rail or balustrade that separates the altar from the rest of the church.
Solid bars made from pure Copper metal.
A reddish metal used in alloys, coins and the construction and electronics industries.
A self propelled vessel for deepening harbours using a continuous chain of buckets
A timber set on the back of a cruck blade to carry a purlin.
A dockyard crane permanently mounted on a lighter.
A part of a building or complex where administrative duties are undertaken.
A pier made up of several shafts against it. The shafts can be attached or detached.
Scissor like object used for cutting, clipping, shearing etc.
A finishing process for cloth involving the pounding of the cloth with heavy weights.
Celebrates worship of the Hindu goddess Durga.
A circle of wooden stakes or stake holes in the ground.
An alignment of stakes or stakeholes of unknown function
A bridge on which dwellings or commercial premises have been built.
A kind of primary school kept by elderly women.
A small anti submarine escort vessel built in World War II
Single-seat, single-engine fighter biplane renowned for its high performance and manoeuvrability. Entered service in 1917.
A signal station incorporating equipment for visually conveying coded communications.
A factory where glue is produced.
Non bituminous coal
A heated iron used to label, burn or mark animals, slaves, criminals etc.
The residence of a ford keeper.
An earthen bank that indicates the limit of an area or a piece of land.
A monastic cattle ranch with associated buildings, paddocks and pastures.
The SI derived unit for acceleration
American, all-metal-construction, fighter. Entered service in 1941. 209 were delivered to RAF/FAA, most of which were used in the Far East.
An arrangement of railway tracks, stations and other buildings that together form a railway transport system.
Portable device that generate stable and consistent flame by combining flammable liquids or pressurised gases with a spark.
A plastic covered tunnel designed to protect vulnerable plants from the weather and allow vegetables to be grown out of season
A place of worship for followers of the Orthodox Catholic Church. Use only where the specific denomination is unknown.
A non residential building providing recreational, social and other facilities, especially for the elderly and those with special needs.
Horizontal masonry or timber work at the entrance to a dock.
A coastal battery used for delivering fire at long distance thus forcing a warship threatening or bombarding shore installations to withdraw out of range.
A metal pillar with a flashable lamp on top containing an emergency telephone for use by members of the public and by officers of the local police force.
A specialist hospital where water treatment is given to patients suffering from muscular-skeletal complaints, etc.
A wall with niches in a CREMATORIUM to display the urns containing ashes. Use only when related to funerary site.

For example arthritis, club foot, back pain, amputations and loss of certain functions. Major dysfunction of a joint, reconstructive surgery, disorder of the spine, amputations, fractures of extremities and growth impairments.
The residence of a person entrusted with the management of a great house or castle.
Material burnt at high temperature (above 700 degrees Celsius) leaving only the mineral component.
A defensive bank and ditch, circular or oval in plan, surrounding one or more buildings.

A propulsion system for ships which need a maximum speed that is considerably faster than their cruise speed, particularly warships. It consists of diesel engines for cruising and gas turbines for high-speed transits.
Internal combustion engine powered by diesel fuel.

Originally designed as a wood and steel bomber-reconnaissance aircraft, subsequent variations served as special transports, glider tugs and paratroop carriers. Featured a tricycle-style undercarriage.

A jar adapted by the addition of three or more vertical loop handles. They may be equally spaced, or confined to one section of the circumference. Profile vary and should be double indexed with the appropriate JAR type. (Source: MPRG)
A type of ferry that is designed to carry wheeled vehicles that can be driven on to and off the vessel.
A tunnel running under a river or through a hill along which vehicles may travel.
A walk, common in 18th century gardens, providing a view across the surrounding countryside.
An enclosure used for the cultivation of fruit trees.
A workshop where wooden brushes are manufactured on a small scale.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter manufactured by Messerschmitt. First used as part of Germany's Condor legion during the Spanish Civil War, the 'one-o-nine' was the Luftwaffe's most widely used fighter seeing service throughout World War II.
A military storage aircraft hangar built in the late 1930s. It comprises a semicircular concrete structure with reinforced concrete columns, featuring a curved roof and straight walls.
Photographic print on self-developing photographic paper in a format developed by Polaroid in the 1970's
A large jug, usually rounded with a narrow neck, used for holding liquids.
A place of worship for Christadelphians, a fundamentalist sect founded in America in the late 1840s who rejected the trinity and awaited the second coming of Christ.
A supported, roof structure covering all, or part, of a railway platform.
Coarse hard sandstone often coloured with iron oxide creating its characteristic brown shades.
A container with a perforated bottom through which material is shaken or poured.
A small cargo boat found on the River Severn in England, with a mast which could be taken down to allow the boat to pass under low bridges.
A room within a building or complex used for storing clothing.
Wind-blown silt.
Bells used either as a percussion instrument or for other purposes such as calling attention, marking time periods etc.
British two-seat, twin-engined night fighter. Also used for roles such as long-range escort fighter, ground-attack and anti-shipping strike aircraft, bomber, torpedo-carrier and rocket fighter.
A place devoted to the cultivation and exhibition of rare trees.
Thin plates of slate, usually rectangular in shape, used as roofing tiles.
A mat used on the floor as a covering.
Use for vessels registered in Iceland.
A large drain or conduit for carrying away wastes.
The outlet or mouth of a sewer where it dispenses into the sea, lake, etc.
A lintel over a window.
A deposit formed by wave and tidal action on an estuarine or marine beach.
A landing and taking off area for civil aircraft, usually with surfaced runways and aircraft maintenance and passenger facilities.
A site, including an airfield and customs house, where air passengers embark and disembark.
A container to receive milk during the milking process.
Fine grained, acidic, light-grey/white/ brown/red-coloured igneous rock.
A room for holding receptions particularly balls.
A render including an aggregate of gravel or stone chipping thrown rather than trowelled onto an external wall.
The receptacle at the top of a rain-water pipe which gathers the water from one or more outlets or gutters on the roof.
Photographic transparency on nitrate base material.
A bowl used to wash in.

Fleet Air Arm fighter and torpedo-bomber, designed for operation from aircraft carriers. All-metal in construction, it entered service in 1944 and was rendered obsolete after the war by the advent of the jet aircraft.
A plant used to sterilize water for use in public bathing establishments, not to be confused with desaliation or purification units for drinking water.
A zinc smelting furnace patented by William Champion of Bristol in 1738 for the reduction of zinc from zinc oxide by means of condensing.
An agricultural implement with sharp blades for cutting or turning over the earth.
A small dwelling providing living accommodation for a tin miner.
A microlith retouched to a trapezium shape. (Source: SARC)
A building or room, purpose built for the teaching, rehearsing and playing of music.
An establishment where books, periodicals, music, etc, are produced from original manuscripts and distributed to booksellers, dealers and the public.
An institution for the imprisonment and training of 16-21 year olds first established officially in 1908. Replaced by Youth Custody Centres in 1982.
A structure, partly underground, for the preservation of ice for use during warmer weather.
Essex
A vessel with a specially adapted mouthpiece, to assist in feeding young animals and humans.
An animal skin prepared as a writing or painting surface.
A bowl-shaped cavity or depression created in the subsoil by the long term presence and growth of tree roots or when a large tree is blown over or has its stump pulled out.
A factory that manufactures watches.
A protective earthern mound.
An area or series of tiles applied, usually to an interior floor or wall's surface, for practical or decorative effect.
A photographic print of a polychrome image (composed of colours other than, but not exclusive of, black, white or grey tones).
Very tough transparent sheeting often used for security glazing.
A prefabricated structure of a light timber frame with external weather boarded walls and a timber felt covered roof. They were used as barrack blocks during WWII. Manufactured by Magnet Limited.

American troop and supply-glider constructed from steel tube and fabric-covered wood, with a hinged nose to allow loading and unloading of troops or light vehicles. Also known as the Haig, this was the only US glider to see combat service.
A stepped, roadside platform, usually of stone on which a sedan chair was placed to allow the porters to lift the chair without having to bend.
A dedicated or consecrated offering.
A vessel comprising of two or more bowls, generally of small size, joined together. There may be one or more handles of varying forms. (Source: MPRG)
A tile which covers the ridge of a roof.
A crane, located in an engineering workshop or similar establishment, which can be moved on rails and thus used anywhere within the workshop.
A crane suspended from running rails in the roof of an engineering workshop or similar establishment.

Twin-engined bomber. The Whitley was the first 'heavy' bomber to be built in quantity for the RAF and made the first bombing attack on Germany in May 1940. It was later used for convoy protection and reconnaissance.
An impression made in soft ground by a passing animal or human. The soft ground may have subsequently hardened.
A kiln used for the slow burning of vegetable matter to produce potassium carbonate.
A swimming pool restricted to the use of females only.

A French airliner produced in 1925. A four-engined biplane developed from the Bleriot 115 and 135 but larger than these. Two were built for Air Union (the Paris-London route). Both crashed with fatalaties in 1926 (Kent).

A French aircraft manufacturer founded by Louis Bleriot and Gabriel Voisin, both aviators and inventors, in 1903, dissolved in 1906. After World War I Bleriot founded Bleriot Aeronautique developing commercial aircraft.
A framed canopy suspended above the dais or high table at the upper end of a hall.
A monument commemorating an animal.

A flour milling machine which uses horizontal steel rollers and dressing machines � seives and purifiers � to gradually reduce wheat grains into constituent parts or �streams� which millers call a �gradual reduction� process.
A maritime monument where the vessel remains are buried in the sea bed.
A place for sharpening metal objects like tools and weapons.
An instrument in the form of a pair of pincers used to grip and pull objects, usually used in surgery.
Working area for rag sorting and grading.
A factory where explosives and the components of munitions of all types are brought together for assembly.
A rotative beam steam engine patented in 1790.
A district, suburb or quarter of a town or village adjacent to a fort, with the lowest legal status accorded to a built up area.
Open yard for keeping cattle in during winter. Used from the mid-14th century in drier, Eastern, arable counties.
A radar station with sets operating on a wavelength of 1.5m. Chain Home Low Stations were intended for use in locating low-flying aircraft but was also capable of detecting high-flying aircraft.
A bowl with straight sides which are at an approximate right angle to the base, i.e. a roughly cylindrical shape. (Source: MPRG)
A pediment with a gap at the centre of its base.

Single-engine, single-seat carrierborne fighter: a Spitfire VB fitted with an arrester hook. Modifications on later versions included folding wings, rocket-assisted take-off gear and conversion for photo-reconnaissance duties.
Thinner and narrower than a horse shoe these are also rarer as donkeys tend to be shod less often than horses.
A town for citizens of Roman or Latin status with a constitution governed by charter, which if possessing only Latin rights could be promoted to the status of a colonia.
An arched half-rib applied to the lateral wall surface in a vaulted bay, its function, rather than structural, being to complete the pattern of the vault's main ribs.
A hearth, normally placed clear of the walls, without a chimney stack or hood above.
The area directly in front of a fireplace or the floor of a firecplace itself.
A heating apparatus in which coals or embers are placed in the pedestal or base below a container in which food or liquid could be held and kept warm.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the chief engineer of GHQ home forces.
A mill used to process logwood, the inner red wood of a South American tree used widely in dyeing. Imported in the form of logs and cut and ground into dye by a mechanical process.
A stage in a church tower where bell ringers stand.
An Ionic base with a lower disc with horizontal fluting or reeding, above which is a torus, also reeded.
A fuel derived by dry distillation from coal.
A narrow bridge for people and animals to cross on foot.
A house of friars, originally hermits from Mount Carmel. Also known as ' white friars'.

Roman, mid to late 1st century, hinged Bow Brooch, related to the Aucissa Brooch, with side knobs on the upper bow, the curvature of which is confined to the brooch's top half, the lower half being straight. Frequently tinned to give a silver appearance.
A site where coal is processed.
Single-engine, single-seat fighter-bomber. Designed to replace the Hurricane as an interceptor, excelled as a rocket-projectile-firing ground-attack fighter. Entered RAF service in 1941.
A dial for showing the hours of the night by the moon.
A column that is equidistant, with intercolumniations, even at the corners, with two or more triglyphs over each intercolumniation.
Basic, black coloured, fine grained, igneous rock.
A machine that presses apples to extract juice for the production of cider.
A place of worship for followers of the Methodist New Connexion, a movement founded in 1791 when Alexander Kilham led the first group to split from the Methodists.
A factory where biscuits are manufactured.
A microlith retouched to a rectangular shape. (Source: SARC)
A small concrete turret placed on top of a standard 4 ft. diameter concrete pipe sunk into the ground. Intended for use in defending road junctions, airfields and beach exits.
The part of a musical instrument in which notes resonate and increase the sound of the instrument.
A bowl used to wash in.
A giant figure of a man, animal or symbol carved on chalk hillsides mainly in southern England.
A building, usually part of a complex, where medical treatment and hospital facilities are provided.
Small submarine with a two or three man crew. Used for special missions such as sinking warships in heavily defended harbours.
A factory making laminate flooring.
A horizontal member of a wall frame between posts or studs, also the horizontal member in panelling, a panelled door or a window.
Lancashire

A Neolithic burial monument comprising a rectangular or trapezoidal stony mound which contains either a passage at one end with or without lateral chambers, or one or more smaller chambers entered from the side of the mound.

A rectangular or trapezoidal non-megalithic stony mound of Neolithic date, with human remains in cists rather than a large chamber. Mound construction and associated features vary considerably in type and complexity.
A building or site where boat sails are manufactured from processed cloth.
A vessel used to produce butter from milk through agitation.
A large container with lip and handle usually for milk.
A building housing the services of professionals with an expert knowledge of the law such as the offices of solicitors, barristers and lawyers.
An outer wall of a castle or similar fortification.
An oven used in the coal industry for the recovery of gas, tar and other by-products of the coking process. Late 19th century-20th century.
An open balcony or gallery extending along the outside of a building, providing principal rooms with shade by means of a roof or canopy supported by posts or light columns.
A workshop where tapestries were made.

An area of a port, dock or harbour, often including buildings for passport control and customs, where passengers and vehicles using hovercraft services can embark/disembark and where supplies can be taken on board.
A building or complex, often associated with a historic site or place of interest, containing interpretation panels and information for visitors to the site or area.
A type of textile mill found in Lancashire in the 19th century. Small businesses paid the owner rent for space for their machines, and power from the mill engine or waterwheel.
A place where metal-cutting hand files were made.

Traditionally a building or site where stage coaches were built. Nowadays the term is applied to buildings used for the manufacturing of the body work and furnishings of motor vehicles and railway carriages.
Upright stones engraved on the edges with a Celtic script consisting of lines or notches.
A steam motor in which rotory motion is produced by steam impinging directly upon a series of vanes upon the circumference of a revolving cylinder or disc.
A propulsion system for ships using a combination of steam turbines and gas turbines to power the shafts.

Originally an area planted with evergreens or winter-flowering plants for winter display, they can also be large glasshouses built for public entertainment where the original purpose of displaying plants has either disappeared or been minimalised.
Clasp for fastening together two loose ends.
Goods, usually foodstuffs, preserved in glass bottles, jars, etc. Examples are bottled fruit, pickled onions, jam, honey.
A basin or harbour, which is open to the tides. Vessels can only enter and leave at high tide and are stranded at low tide.
A staff to support a lame or legless person.
A factory or group of buildings used for the production of plated goods. Plating is the process whereby one metal object is coated with a thin layer of another metal.

Any boat used to transfer crew from shore to an offlying vessel. May also carry the catch from a fishing boat to shore. Used as special boats by the Royal National Lifeboat Institution for conveying crew from the beach to a moored lifeboat.
A harbour constructed from floating pontoons or caissons connected end to end.
A sheltered port for ships.

American, four-engine, long range, heavy strategic bomber. Entered service in 1943 and used exclusively against Japanese forces. The B29s Enola Gay and Bock's Car were used to drop atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945.
A wooden frame with holes, through which the head and hands of an offender were thrust, in which state they would be exposed to public ridicule and assault.
A building, usually within the grounds of a school and often containing dormitories, used by pupils who board.
An establishment where the theory and practice of medicine is taught.
A quern where one stone is rotated on another to grind grain.
A stud used for fastening an item usually used for clothing.
Factory for the production of safety fuses used in the ignition of gunpowder for blasting.
A works where cotton waste is stored or processed.
A container with a human face appliqued onto it, often used as a funerary vessel.
A site, usually including hardstandings and associated buildings, where ambulances can be parked and stored.
A post box mounted in, or on, a wall.
A place where processed cloth is cut for use as garments or soft furnishings, etc.
A pilotless aircraft armed with explosives and fuelled to stall over its intended target.
A house for drying wool after fulling and dying.
A thick heavy weapon used to strike the opponent.
A processing house where surplus water is removed from gunpowder after incorporating.
Pentecost.
An area within a building open to the public where light meals and drinks can be purchased and consumed.
A parcel of land.
Housing provided for refugees. Similar to refugee camp but with the reuse of existing buildings rather than a temporary camp.

Use for a craft where a type of steam engine where the steam is first expanded in a high-pressure cylinder, then having given up heat and losing pressure, it exhausts directly into one or more larger volume low-pressure cylinders.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a circular or sub-circular earthen mound. See RELIGIOUS, RITUAL AND FUNERARY Class List for context.
Medium grained, hard, white/grey coloured stone consisting of quartz and often silica, produced by the metamorphosis of sandstone.
A wind-powered pump for land drainage.
A bridge whose deck is hung from above by large cables, chains or pinned iron or steel bars hanging from towers.
A school established by the National Society which was founded in 1811 to promote the education of the poor.
Large, single-engine, eight passenger airliner biplane.
The recording and analysis of the fabric of a structure or bnuilding
A building used for housing, and protecting from the weather, carts, waggons and farm implements, often open-fronted.
Remains of arthropods characterized as having a body divided into two segements and four pairs of legs, such as spiders, scorpions, ticks and mites.
Use for ticks and true mites. Related to spiders, mites are widely present in archaeological deposits but are rarely studies in detail as they can prove difficult to identify.
A thin vegetable based sheet used for writing, drawing, printing etc.
A close fitting cap covering the sides, back and top of the head.
A scale or index of a sextant, astrolabe or similar instrument.
Four-crew, twin-engined monoplane designed as a torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance aircraft for RAF Coastal Command. Withdrawn from operations in November 1940 and downgraded to a trainer.
A mowing implement with a large curved blade and a long handle.
Sheets of iron or steel bent into a series of ridges and hollows to give added strength and rigidity.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of metal boxes or cases.
A container used with an alembic as part of the distilling process.
A container holding a set quantity used specifically for measuring grains or cereal.
A pond or pool with arms covered with nets into which wild birds, are lured and then caught. Monument type includes water feeder channels.
A container used to hold ammunition.
A hand held utensil with two or more prongs to hold food.
A stable associated with a horse-drawn tramway system.
A site where the manufacture of glass bottles takes place.
A stone used to cover a grave.
A vessel with a lid, handle and spout used particularly for boiling water.
Principal glider-pilot training glider fitted with tandem seats. Spruce and plywood in construction, the Hotspur served with the Glider Pilot Regiment between 1941 and 1945.
A barrier, usually of wood or chain, stretched across the entrance to a harbour, port or anchorage, to control entry and/or limit the effect of the weather on the wave action.
A measuring rule not graduated in feet.
Pieces of material, usually decorated, used as standards, for signalling or for decoration. Often used as a symbol of a particular nation eg. the Union Flag of Great Britain.
Where several minerals produced, use with other products and MINE, eg. ARSENIC MINE.
A decoy site designed to simulate permitted lighting, such as locomotives, furnaces and tramwire flashes, to lure attacking night bombers away from legitimate targets.
A hotel where no alcohol is available.

A type of military aircraft hangar of the Cold War, hardened and therefore protected against the effects of nuclear weapons. It comprises a semi-circular structure built of corrugated-steel supporting a reinforced-concrete skin. Three NATO designs.
The interpretation of visualisations derived from Airborne Laser Scanning, or LiDAR, data usually resulting in the identification of archaeological features and landscapes.
A single-seat, pusher prop, escort and patrol-fighter. Used in the UK in a Home Defence role until superseded in 1917.
A place of law to which debtors were taken for the recovery of monies by their creditors.
Twin blades each with a sharpened edge connected together by a pivot which cut when opened and closed on an object.

A modern building system in which both steel and concrete are utilized together to carry the load in ways that neither material predominates over the other. There are many varieties e. g. a steel frame surrounding a concrete core.
Circular enclosure featuring an enclosing bank with no accompanying ditch. Use specific type where known.
Linear or curvilinear construction of earth, turf and stone, often, but not always accompanied by a ditch. Use specific type where known.
A building appropriated by a school for the purpose of teaching pupils.
A factory where seaplanes are manufactured.
A twin-engined development of the JU88, the JU188 had a higher service ceiling and greater maximum speed. JU188s operated over the UK from 1944 onwards as night intruders and reconnaissance aircraft.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Partial Shielded Self Propelled Mounting System

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A short stabbing weapon.
A metal fastener used to hold a tile or stone against a spacer and driven into a wall thus forming a flue between the wall and the tile or stone. Also used to hold timber together.
A factory for processing rubber or manufacturing rubber goods, such as tyres.
A broad container, usually used for cooking.
Programmes of investigation which assess and record the condition of heritage assets.
A written work issued at regular intervals and numbered consecutively.
Series of machines for mechanically slaking lime. 20th century.
A vehicle on runners for carrying loads or passengers, especially over snow. Could be drawn by horses, dogs, reindeer and/or pushed or pulled by people.
A fine, soft fibre produced by silkworms and used to make thread for textiles. Also the cloth made from this thread.
A small vessel propelled on water by an engine, oars or sails.
A boat fashioned out of a section of tree trunk.
A small works used for the production of agricultural tools such as hay rakes.
A system of artificial or natural drains and ditches used to drain off surplus water.
A container for ointments or perfume.
A building or workshop where fine furniture, often veneered, is made.
A gate or valve that controls the flow of water from a reservoir, harbour, etc..
An independent school for children up to the age of 11 or 13 in which pupils are prepared for entry into a public school.

A building used for the preparatory processes in which long and short staple flax fibres were separated by passing through combs. Flax dressing or 'heckling' shops may be located both on and off mill sites.
A strip of cultivated land situated against the exterior of a walled garden's perimeter, so placed to maximise usable wall space.

A British medium-range biplane airliner designed and built by Handley Page in 1921. A twin-engined variant of the Handley Page W series (W8, W9), retired in 1931. Built for Imperial Airways (4 units built).
A structure used for the storage of coal.
A building for the storage, repair and maintenance of chains for lighthouses, lightships and lightbouys.
A tool used for digging where the blade is at right angles to the handle.
Loss of speech and other forms of speech disorder.
A large, "bottle-shaped", oven of brick construction used in the baking or firing of pottery.
A kiln principally used in brick making which gives a continuous operation.
A drinking vessel, made of glass, designed expressly to be used for the consumption of wine.
An object used to burn incense in.
A screen that separates a tomb or a chapel from the main body of a church.
A mechanism, either automated or consisting of winches and pulleys, that raises sacks of grain on ropes or chains from one floor of a mill to another, usually through one or a series of trap doors.
A residence used during short visits by an official and attendants of the Knights Hospitallers for administrative purposes on their estates.
The highest judicial court where appeals can be heard and whose rulings are not subject to further review by another court.
Glass that has been coloured by fusing glass with a metallic oxide film or by burning pigment into the surface.
A simple form of stone slab bridge, particularly associated with South West England.
A bridge in which the load is carried by a single beam, or beams, spanning the space between two supports.

Four-engine, long range heavy bomber. Developed from the Lancaster, and originally designated the Lancaster Mk. IV, it was larger in size, bombload and fuel capacity. Never used operationally in World War Two.

An earthwork feature used by hunters to trap deer comprising a steep ditch into which the deer are chased with an enclosure to hold them at one end, known from the Isle of Rum and a debateable example in Cumbria.
A path, barred to vehicles, reserved for riding horses.
A place of worship for followers of Emmanuel Swedenborg who believed he was the medium through which the New Jerusalem would be founded on earth. The church was formed in 1787.

A capital with two rows of eight acanthus leaves rising above an astragal;from between the leaves of the upper row rise eight stalks,each surmounted by a calyx from which emerge volutes carryingthe corners of the concave sided abacus and central ornaments
