A hole in the ground which has been created by driving or hammering an upright stake into the ground. As a feature of some archaeological sites they may often represent the only surviving evidence for the former presence of an above-ground structure.

A structure to which a net filled with mail bags is attached. Situated next to railway lines, it allows mail to be collected by a train without it stopping, the bag being 'caught' by the train as it passed. Can also be used to 'catch' mail.
A channel which carried processed alum as liquid from the alum quarry/works to the alum house

A shelter for doves or pigeons, often containing nesting boxes, either free-standing or built into other structures (barns, towers etc.). If a dedicated, free-standing structure, index with MONUMENT TYPE: DOVECOTE.
Three-crew, single-engine carrierborne torpedo-bomber. Entered service in 1942, first seeing action during the Battle of Midway. Served with the US Navy until 1956.
A room containing copper or steel vessels in which hops are added to the basic beer mixture.
A house or shelter for the storage and/or launching of boats.
A fob can consist of a chain and or a ring.
A wall, usually of reinforced concrete, designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle
A purlin that sits in a trench cut in the back of a principal rafter.
An enclosure used for corralling deer.

An earthwork feature used by hunters to trap deer comprising a steep ditch into which the deer are chased with an enclosure to hold them at one end, known from the Isle of Rum and a debateable example in Cumbria.
An apparatus around which cables or hawsers are wound for hoisting anchors, lifting weights, etc.
A jug with little or no discernible neck and an even, convex profile form rim to base, which are roughly equal in diameter. (Source: MPRG)

Single-engine navigation trainer and communications aircraft. Constructed of tubular steel and duralumin frame, with a duralumin and canvas covering, 500 were delivered to the FAA, serving from 1944-5.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around four sides of an open cattle yard.

Single-engine, two-seat, light, biplane, elementary-flying trainer. Adapted from a civilian design, and constructed from tubular steel and spruce with plywood and fabric covering, entered service in 1931 and was available in land-plane or seaplane forms.
Use for vessels registered in Germany or any of the states prior to unification.
A brass plaque, usually on the ground rather than a wall fixture, commemorating a person or event.
A circular band, usually metal, worn on the finger for ornamentation.
A factory or site where wooden clogs are manufactured.

A jar adapted by the addition of one straight handle, attached to either rim or body, and usually with a lip at right angles to the handle. The body is generally rounded, with a short neck and an everted rim. (Source: MPRG)
A jar adapted by the addition of a straight handle and three feet. Profiles vary and should be double indexed with the appropriate JAR type. (Source: MPRG)
A type of light fixture affixed to a wall in such a way that it uses only the wall for support, and the light is usually directed upwards.
Single-engine aircraft designed as a dive-bomber. Found to be inadequate in this role, a number of those delivered to the RAF were used as target tugs. Entered service in 1941.
A burial in which the body is placed in, or covered by a boat, which is then covered with earth. Use with barrow type where relevant.
The latex of plants tacky in its normal state and elastic after treatment. Used for a variety of purposes.
A roof with a slope of less than ten degrees to the horizontal.
A site used for the manufacture of lasts, shoemaker's models of the foot for shaping and repairing footwear. Lasts can be from a variety of materials, such as wood or iron.
A site where iron or steel bolts, and often their accompanying nuts, are manufactured. Sometimes referred to as NUT AND BOLT WORKS.
A high-humped, narrow, cobbled bridge used by trains of packhorses, often located in upland areas where the bulk of goods were carried by horses.
A curved blade used by the Romans and Greeks to scrape the body after bathing.
Soft, very fine grained, dark coloured, sedimentary rock which splits easily.

A device or engine powered by one or more horses or donkeys walking around a circular track and harnessed so as to turn a large toothed wheel, either in the same plane or above, which turned smaller wheels operating machinery.
Normally an unpowered vessel, moored in places where the construction of a lighthouse is impractical.
Four-engined, five to seven crew, heavy bomber biplane. Entered service in 1918.
A place from where rescue missions are co-ordinated and casualties treated after an accident, offensive action or disaster.

Single-engine, two or three-crew pre-World War 2 biplane fighter and general purpose aircraft. First flown in 1931, the Seal was a Naval variant on the Fairey Gordon and a forerunner of the Swordfish.
A factory where worsted, a well-twisted woollen yarn made from long staple wool and used in the manufacture of suits and other garments, was produced.
A site where tanks and armoured fighting vehicles can be stored.
A container for holding votive offerings.

Single-engine, single-seat interceptor fighter developed from the race-winning Schneider Trophy seaplanes. One of the most famous of all combat aircraft, entered RAF service in 1938 and was still in use in the 1950s.
The cutting part of an auger.
Various seaweeds which are burnt to obtain the salts contained in their ashes, which are used in the manufacture of soap and glass.
A building plan that features a hall lying between, and at right-angles to, two projecting wings.
A bungalow joined to another to form one building.
A one-storey house.
A workshop used for the manufacture of clay tobacco pipes.
Roman coastal forts fortified with large walls and a ditch, introduced to cope with raids from across the English Channel and North Sea.
20th century plant for separating minerals using variations in water-repellent properties under controlled chemical conditions. Survives as ruins of buildings or tanks.
Use for vessels registered in Malta.
A flake that has had small flakes removed to blunt, sharpen, refine the outline or prepare the edge of the tool.
A flake of stone struck from the core where the length is less than twice the width.
A tertiary vault rib, usually employed for decorative purposes, that links one intersection of the main ribs to another.

A series of parallel railway sidings on which goods wagons originating from different locations can be sorted or re-sorted into new trains before being despatched to their next destination or sorting points.
A raised platform or walkway connecting two buildings or a ship with the quay, etc.
A flat, horizontal piece of timber or masonry projecting from or recessed into a wall to hold objects.
A steam engine that uses the same steam successively to drive pistons in high and then low pressure cylinders.
Scale drawing showing the horizontal extent, height and arrangement of an excavated layer or feature on an archaeological site.
A mechanical device consisting of a system of signal lights operating in sequence, placed at road intersections and pedestrian crossings to regulate traffic.
A building or structure from which observation is kept of the approach of danger.
Non-pavilion type of attached ward block.
A pumping station used in the production of hydraulic power, eg. in warehouse complexes, goods depots on railways, etc.
A small building used by a gatekeeper.

Manmade structure for bathing or swimming that is located on the beachfront and filled by tidal waters. Similar to a LIDO, with the main difference being the extent of the built up complex around the pool.
A storage rack for sections of steel plate used in the construction of ships.
A piece of wood scored across with notches for the items of an account and then split into halves of which each party kept one.
A channel that returns water that has been used to turn a waterwheel back to the river or source from which it came.
A path running by the side of a canal or navigable river for use in towing vessels.
The residence and office of a chaplain.
A site where iron or steel bolts, and often their accompanying nuts, are manufactured. Sometimes referred to as NUT AND BOLT WORKS.
A screen of wood or stone, used to divide the nave from the choir.
A screen dividing one part of a church from another.
A large building, situated at a railway terminus, used for the temporary storage of goods or merchandise awaiting transportation to or from a railway.
A frame used to lift unco-operative horses off the ground during shoeing.
Lead which has been rolled into a sheet and often used as a roof covering.
A common type of lock in the form of a chamber with gates on either side.
A lime kiln built into a low hillside or slope to facilitate top loading of the limestone.
A vessel used for storing and issuing gunpowder, usually moored well away from the dockyard.
A site where chalk is extracted from the ground.
A decorative piece descending vertically from the bottom of a newel on a staircase, or from the junction of barge boards at the apex of a gable.

A family of jet fighters capable of vertical/short takeoff and landing. A subsonic aircraft, later designs adapted for use from aircraft carriers. Built between 1967-2003. Used by the RAF and the Royal Navy.
A factory or works used for the production of turpentine, wood alcohol and similar chemicals by the distillation of pulped wood.
A room or building in which riding tackle is stored.
A smooth bore weapon usually for firing shot as opposed to bullets.
A dam constructed on the reaches of a canal or river designed to retain the water and to regulate its flow.
An outfall from a canal, river or reservoir.
A factory where tweed, a twilled woollen fabric with an unfinished surface, is manufactured.
A picturesque garden building decorated with tree roots, often serving as a HERMITAGE or ARBOUR.

Wooden rods or stakes which can be interlaced with twigs or branches to make walls or fences, or more commonly, to form the basis of panels in traditional timber framed buildings which are then covered with daub.
A window that is lower than others in the chancel side wall.
A factory for the production of plastics by chemical processes.
Originally a metallic alloy of copper and tin or zinc, now used solely for an alloy of copper and zinc.
American, four-engined, medium/heavy day bomber. Entered service in 1937. The prototype was nicknamed the Flying Fortress, which later became a registered trademark.
A metal stud hammered into the sole of footwear to provide grip.
An establishment where wagering and the placing of bets takes place.
An arch of the Tuscan Order.
Tyne and Wear

A freelance boat used off the south and east coasts of England to provide passing ships with pilots, supplies, new anchors and other gear. Some helped sailing ships and barges get underway. Generally lug-rigged. Also used for fishing. Half decked.
A workshop or factory where brass articles are made by casting molten material into a mould.
A high pole, painted with spiral stripes of different colours and decked with flowers, erected on an open space, often the village green, for merrymakers to dance around on May Day.
A capital which is circular and has several mouldings but no foliage.
The residence of a herder.
A Neolithic burial monument comprising a stone-built chamber within a circular or sub-circular earthen mound. See RELIGIOUS, RITUAL AND FUNERARY Class List for context.
Block, often made of concrete, to secure smaller maritime craft. Many were made during the Second Wold War to secure craft which were to be used in the D-Day landings.
A window with a frame for holding the glass, capable of being raised and lowered in vertical grooves.

Twin-engined bomber. The Whitley was the first 'heavy' bomber to be built in quantity for the RAF and made the first bombing attack on Germany in May 1940. It was later used for convoy protection and reconnaissance.
A garden devoted to the growth of vegetables.
Wind or water-powered mill for land drainage in fens or marshlands.
A stick for agitating milk in a butter churn.
A cord manufactured by twisting strands of material, such as flax, cotton, nylon etc., together to form a strong line.
Post-World War Two, single-engine, high-wing utility transport. Manufactured by De Havilland Canada, was also produced in a seaplane version. Known as the U6A from 1962.
The junction of two timbers at right angles which involves chamfers or mouldings meeting on a diagonal line and where the timbers meet on the 45 degree line of the chamfer or moulding junction.
A decorative feature of a shield for armorial bearings.
A large free-standing arch erected to commemorate a triumph or victory.
A material made from extremely fine fibres of glass and is used as a reinforcing agent for many polymer products.

An area of land incorporating bodies of water, either natural or manmade for use in water sports activities such as canoeing, rowing and sailing. Usually includes a leisure complex with facilities for the users.
An open floor surface for dancing.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber and ground-attack aircraft. Entered service with the Luftwaffe in mid-1941. Approximately 20,000 were constructed between 1941 and the end of the war.
A projection left on a stone block to allow it to be hoisted into position.

American, four-engine, long range, heavy strategic bomber. Entered service in 1943 and used exclusively against Japanese forces. The B29s Enola Gay and Bock's Car were used to drop atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945.
A greenhouse for the growing of figs.
An office for the administration of town or country estates.
A place where saltpetre, the chief component of gunpowder, is kept.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of chlorophyll for medical purposes.
A large-scale site where medicinal drugs are maufactured.

An earthwork feature used by hunters to trap deer comprising a steep ditch into which the deer are chased with an enclosure to hold them at one end, known from the Isle of Rum and a debateable example in Cumbria.
A square, hewn or worked, high class freestone which can be 'freely' cut and is laid in horizontal courses with vertical joints.
The residence of a prison governor.
A factory where cheese is produced and processed.
A rotating circular platform operated by machinery to turn a steam locomotive around.
A monument consisting of parallel lines of standing stones, which appears to mark out an approach to another monument or monuments.
Not subdivided
Photographic negative developed on waxed paper.
A works or factory where shells or projectiles were machined before they were dispatched to a filling factory to be filled with explosives.
A building or site where phosphorous-based fertilizers are produced by controlled chemical reactions.
The rectangular pit in which the lower part of a waterwheel revolves.
A steam engine in which the pistons are long relative to their diameters, and there are no piston rods and crossheads.
Part of textile mills.
Hut for use at Level Crossings that were not adjacent to Signal Boxes.
A fighter version of the SKUA fitted with a four-gun turret. The majority were converted to target tugs for use by the RAF and Fleet Air Arm.
A jar with roughly vertical body walls which in some cases may be slightly convex. (Source: MPRG)
A decorative tile incorporated into the front of a tile stove.
An item with both secular and religious signifigance.
An area speciallly developed to accommodate commercial buildings.
An area including buildings dedicated to scientific research for commercial purposes. Often associated with, or operated by, a university or higher education institution.
A mill used for the production of cardboard and other similar products.
A small pair of shears with crossed blades, usually used for pruning.
A site where the process of combing, the preparatory process for long wools, takes place.
An artificial mound created by the disposal of aggregate originally used as ballast in ships.
A building used as a meeting place by a synod, an assembly of the clergy.
Use for objects made from coal or for stray finds of coal where the association with a wreck site is not proven and thus cannot be stated as either cargo or bunkers.
18th-19th century stone-lined pit which held the balance bob for a pump-rod or flat-rod system. It includes examples where the surviving feature is a pillar for the bearing, rather than the pit.
A large portable container used for carrying items such as clothes, papers etc.
Victoria, Australia
Material used for construction, commonly fired in its manufacture.
A drinking vessel, usually curved in shape, fashioned out of animal tusk or horn and sometimes with bands of decoration.
A sparkling, white wine traditionally from the Champagne region of France. Now used, loosely, to refer to any sparkling white wine.
A drinking vessel with two or more handles.
A recording of voice, music or other sounds.
A piece of fabric with a design, used as an emblem for military or naval purposes, signalling, decoration, display, propaganda etc.

Troop and general transport glider. Almost entirely wooden in construction, many were manufactured by the furniture industry. Mk I featured a a door-ramp on the port side whilst the Mk II was fitted with a hinged nose.
A pad on which a post rests to support part of a structure.
A camp where people who fled from danger or problem whithin their country or across international borders and who are in need of international protection are temporarily placed.
A site where clay pipes used for drainage are manufactured.

Three-seat, twin-engined minelaying, torpedo-bombing and reconnaissance twin-float seaplane. First flown in 1936, in 1938 it set eight world speed records for its class in various range and payload categories.
An area of ground belonging to a church, often used as a burial ground.
A purpose-built dwelling for the supervisor of a factory, mine or other industrial complex.
A place where patients have X-Rays taken to highlight an illness or irregularity.
A post mill in which the drive is taken down to the base of the mill by putting an upright shaft in the hollowed post.
A type of windmill, mainly timber-framed, whose body, containing machinery and carrying the sail, rotates about an upright post.

A type of warehouse found in naval victualling yards, used for the storage of rum, a ration of which was given on a daily basis to members of the Royal Navy, up until the 1980s, when this practice ceased.

A fishing vessel which tows a dredger to gather oysters. This is an iron wedge shaped contrivance with a small net attached. Towed behind the vessel the iron wedge loosens the oysters and they fall into the net.
Principal glider-pilot training glider fitted with tandem seats. Spruce and plywood in construction, the Hotspur served with the Glider Pilot Regiment between 1941 and 1945.
A building or room where nets are made
A ring with separated, often ornamented, terminals.
A vessel comprising two or more dishes, generally of small size, joined together. There may be one or more handles of varying forms. (Source: MPRG)
Deciduous wood from the native elm tree, commonly used for framing or cladding of lesser timber framed structures due to its poorer weathering qualities as compared to oak.
Sandy, rough blue to green/grey coloured limestone. Quarried in Kent and widely used throughout the South East.
A device allowing a variable amount of air through in a single direction which varies the note produced.
The consecrated ground immediately surrounding a tomb or grave.
A room within a church or cathedral in which holy relics were kept.

A rectangular chamber of brick or stone with heavy wooden gates at either end equipped with sluices to let water in and out, thereby enabling a canal boat to be lowered or raised to a different level.
Passover.
A small, single-masted merchant vessel, designed for maximum hold capacity and not for sailing ability.
Use for vessels registered in Lithuania.
The site of the formal burial of cremated bone, sometimes 'urned' in a vessel or casket of glass, wood or, more commonly, ceramic.
A mug with more-or-less straight side which flare out from the rim to the wider base. (Source: MPRG)
A German stoneware form of conical mug. (Source: MPRG)
Grain, especially barley, prepared for brewing, distilling or vinegar making.
A terrace of BACK TO EARTH HOUSES.
A block of metal with a device cut into it, used to impress a coin blank.
A ticket booth in a theatre or cinema.
Power station using domestic refuse as its principal fuel.
A linear earthwork, usually a bank accompanied by a ditch, which runs across rather than along an area or ridge of higher ground.
A defensive or boundary earthwork.

A design of steam engine in which either three cylinders, in the case of vertical engines, or four cylinders on horizontal engines, permit steam to be expanded three times as it passes through the installation.
Originally designed as a trainer but relegated to use by the RNAS in a Maritime Reconnaissance and anti-submarine role when the Avro 504 became the standard trainer.
A single-engine, photo-reconnaissance fighter designed for operation from aircraft carriers. Later adapted as a night fighter, it entered service in 1943 and remained in production until 1956.
A residential home for children with physical and/or learning disabilities, sensory impairment and/or mental health issues who need medical intervention and/or care provided by registered nurses.
Buildings and structures associated with a private aviation club undertaken as a leisure pursuit. Usually situated on or near an airfield.
Kent
A small house or a portion of a house used as a self-contained apartment.
A vessel used to carry a pilot to a ship.
An iron bar or rod running through the core of a windmill's windshaft that causes the opening and shutting of the vanes on patent sails.

Component part of a mungo and shoddy mill, where non-wool fibres from shredded material are destroyed by either soaking rags in an acid solution or rotating them in drums in a hot acidic gas followed by heat. The result is an all-wool product.
A mill in which poor quality woollen cloth was made from fibres produced by grinding light woollen rags.
A decorative feature in the form of small pyramids in a continuous line.
A factory where ribbons are manufactured.
A place of meeting and worship for Open Brethren, a non exclusive fundamentalist puritan sect which was created when the Brethren split in 1847.
A vault used for the storage of cider.
Essex
A factory, mill or warehouse constructed with the minimum amount of combustible materials.
A medieval plan with the hall situated at one end of the main range.
A building where tallow is produced, ie. solid animal fat that has been separated by heating, usually for making candles.
A mill used for the mechanized processing of silk.
A factory making flame retardant materials.
An engraved object which when struck imparts the image engraved onto the leather.
North Yorkshire
An oval window placed with its long axis horizontal. The term is often applied to similar round windows.
A technique in which the date is deduced from the presence of fauna and/or flora considered to be characteristic of a given peirod of time or that gives and indication of a probable date.
A road used primarily, but not exclusively, for the rapid transport of military vehicles, equipment and personnel.
A large cauldron used in the making of a preservative from the bark of spruce, fir or other conifers. The preservative was used to treat nets, sails and other fishing gear.
A mine used for the extraction on tin bearing ore.
Written or typed correspondence, usually between two or more parties.
A single storey mill used in the textile industry.

Single-engine, single-seat, long range fighter originally designed in 1940 to a British requirement. Outstanding low-level speed and range resulted in its assignment to the ground support (Army co-operation) role.
A mound or structure on which an archery, musketry or artillery target is erected. Use specific type where known.
A mound or structure on which targets are placed for archery practice or competition.
A compact design of steam engine which eliminates a connecting rod by having the piston rod directly attached to the crank.

A single-engine dive-bomber, the JU87 was very successful during the invasions of Poland and France but suffered heavy losses during the Battle of Britain. Withdrawn from NW Europe in 1941 for use in the Mediterranean and on the Eastern Front.
Two or more adjacent locks where the upper gates of one lock serve as the lower gates of the next.
A 1930s British short-haul biplane airliner for 6-8 passengers. It proved an economical and durable craft, despite its relatively primitive plywood construction. Primarily used by the RAF.
Engine driving a continuous wire rope for the haulage of tubs in a mine and at the heapstead.
Natural feature or area deliberately enhanced to construct a monument, eg rock carving, cave, rock shelter.
A lime kiln in which coal is burnt, as distinct from a flame-free kiln in which wood or peat is used.
An object fashioned in the image of a penis.
A storey of lesser height than those above and below it.
A small arched hangar built by the Canadian company Fromson of Byfleet to drawing number 3971/43. Used only as storage sheds on RNASs.
Similar in design to the FROMSON HANGAR but designed to drawing number 3752/43 and used for storing aircraft with small wingspans.
Engineering workshop intended either for final adjustments of new machinery or the fitting of replacement parts to machinery under repair.
A bowl with concave body walls. Wide-mouthed, narrow-based examples, particularly those in larger sizes, have been termed Pans or Pancheons. (Source: MPRG)
A complex of purpose-built or adapted buildings used for the maintenance, storage, assembly and control of sea mines and minefields.
Documents written on sheets of paper or similar, collected together and bound between protective covers.
If managed at all, then only to a low intensity, e.g. mowing, spraying etc., involving operations which are not archaeologically damaging.

A large twin-engined airliner produced by the Dutch aircraft manufacturer Fokker in the 1920s. First flight March 1927. Designed by Reinhold Platz. Mixed construction, fuselage/ tail in steel covered with plywood, canvas and duralumin (11 units built).

Dutch aircraft manufacturer named after its founder, Anthony Fokker. Set up in 1912 in Schwerin, Germany, moving to the Netherlands in 1919. The world's largest aircraft manufacturer in the late 1920s.
An early washing machine used in bleaching works for washing calico and other textiles.
A house or centre used for meditation, contemplation and/or prayer.
A house joined to another to form one building.
An area of land, roughly shaped like a trapezoid and enclosed by a boundary ditch, bank, wall, palisade or similar barrier.
A small, walled fortlet, situated every Roman mile along the length of Hadrian's Wall to defend a gateway allowing the passage of people and as a garrison to accommodate patrol troops.
A small shaped container designed to bathe the eye.

A streamlined, twin-engined bomber, the DO17 entered service in 1937 with the Condor Legion, having started life as a high-speed mail and passenger transport aircraft, a role for which it was ill-suited due to the narrowness of the fuselage.
A radar station with sets operating on a wavelenght of 1.5m established to provide radar plotting of both shipping and aircraft movements.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Coast Defence Chain Home Low Station

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: The warm room in a Roman baths.
A water tank, often raised on stilts, used to supply water to steam trains.
A site used for the production of dyes from natural ingredients.
A site used for the production of dyes from controlled chemical reactions. In use from the mid 19th century onwards.
A strap passing underneath the animal to hold saddle in place.
A slate tablet, often framed in wood, for writing purposes. Use a materials thesaurus to record the material type slate.
A kiln for drying hops in a brewery or maltings complex, as distinct from the OASTHOUSES found on farms.
A coastal site producing salt by solar evaporation of seawater in a series of PONDS, without any boiling stage
Use for the remains of any part of an amphibian.
A dish comprising three or more lobes, usually equally spaced. There may be one or more animal or other figures inside the base and two or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
A bag containing food hung around a horse's head.
A sewer or irrigation channel designed to avoid blockage.
A site where iron is smelted or iron goods made.
A specialist school for the teaching of deaf people.
NB currently Includes ISOMETRIC though this has a separate term.
A cultivated plantation of watercress, usually situated near springs or small running streams.

Three-seat, twin-engined minelaying, torpedo-bombing and reconnaissance twin-float seaplane. First flown in 1936, in 1938 it set eight world speed records for its class in various range and payload categories.
A photo- reconnaissance variant of the Boeing Superfortress, used from 1944, initally deployed in the Pacific war, later for Cold war duties over Europe.
A core part of a town or city that has or had a particular set of characteristics; for example an area of high status residences or an area where a particular industry/trade was centred.
A site where aircraft are stored, dismantled and processed for the recovery of serviceable parts.
A house with a pitched roof with a double slope and gables on the front and rear elevations of the building.
A bridge carrying a tramway.
A site where iron or steel bolts, and often their accompanying nuts, are manufactured. Sometimes referred to as NUT AND BOLT WORKS.

Twin-engined, medium bomber with a 1200 mile range and a bomb load in excess of 10,000 lb. Entered service in 1940, but engine faults resulted in retirement in 1942 with its design later modified into the acclaimed four-engine Lancaster bomber.
A site used for the production of dyes from controlled chemical reactions. In use from the mid 19th century onwards.
Based on a typical 18ft span, 40ft long temporary brick hut but with two bay windows in the front elevation, one for the watch office and one for the chief instructor.
Mill for fine grinding of tin ore between millstones.
Use for a tusk or tooth of a mammal large enough to be carved or used to make objects such as those of mammoths, elephants, walruses and whales.
Use for teeth, hard structures found in the jaws of vertebrates used principally for chewing and eating.

Impressed civil, twin-engined airliner converted to a military transport. Thirty were ordered for military use, though only eleven were actually built. Entered service in 1940, with the last being scrapped in 1950.

skos:Concept.skos:definition: The British Admiralty in practice used a fathom of 6 feet. This was despite its being 1⁄1000 of a nautical mile (i.e. 6.08 feet) until the adoption of the international nautical mile.

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A lodging house for apprentices learning a trade or profession. This accommodation was often provided in lieu of wages.
A container for ointments or perfume.
A settlement site enclosed within a timber palisade.
A building where advice, counselling and medical treatment is available.
A place of worship for Calvinistic Methodists, Welsh Methodists who split from the established church in 1811.

A garden or park, with ancilliary buildings, in which young and domesticated animals are kept for public exhibition, especially for children. Children are given the opportunity to come into close contact and handle animals.
Hard, transparent, brittle substance manufactured by fusing soda or potash with other ingredients. Used for glazing windows and in the manufacture of drinking vessels.
An establishment with automatic washing machines available for public use.
A temporary overnight camp enclosed by a shallow ditch and palisade, constructed by Roman troops on campaigns or manoeuvres.
Component: Use wider site type where known.
A hospital department where surgical and medical dental treatment takes place.

A small tower or bartizan, which was often placed at the angles of a castle, to increase the flanking ability, some only serving as corner buttresses. Also used to describe the small rectangular towers situated between the milecastles along Hadrians Wall.
A pier which supports a gate.
A solid support of masonry to sustain vertical pressure and frequently each of the pillars from which an arch springs.
A type of Roman lodging house, frequently sited near the town gate.
A cross with the image of Christ upon it.
Container with a handle, spout and narrow neck.
A chalet designed in the Swiss style, eg. Kenwood, London.
A purpose built theatre with a central open yard, dating to the Elizabethan period. Famous examples include The Globe and the Swan.
A bishop's court for ecclesiastical causes and offences, formerly having wider jurisdiction in matters of moral discipline.
A coastal gun/watch tower built as part of the anti-invasion defences during the Napoleonic Wars.
A long bed planted with perennial flowers and plants.
A naval dockyard building used for the manufacture of flags.
Building with underfloor kiln used for drying China Clay slurry prior to packing and transportation. Central feature of China Clay Works.
A target range used for rifle and small arms practice and recreational purposes.
A bridge decorated with shells forming an ornamental feature.

Troop and general transport glider. Almost entirely wooden in construction, many were manufactured by the furniture industry. Mk I featured a a door-ramp on the port side whilst the Mk II was fitted with a hinged nose.
A chain used to inhibit a slave's freedom.
A place where weapons are kept.
A movable bridge lifted at one end by chains or ropes either to stop traffic passing over it or to let traffic pass under it.
A very small spoon used to provide liquid to mix with ink on an ink stone.
A two masted craft which is square rigged on the foremast and fore and aft rigged on the main mast.
Thin flexible sheets made from the pulp of wood or other fibrous matter.
A building where motor cycles are assembled.
The part of a rib or arch visible below the general surface of the vault.
A covering of metal, stone or pottery set on a chimney breast above a fire to prevent smoke entering the room and instead directing it up the chimney.
A farm on the estate of a manor.
A building in which works of art are displayed, permanently or temporarily.
A place of worship for the followers of Buddha.
An image used to convey information, often as part of a larger publication or exhibition.
A window usually spanning the full width of the north side of a roof allowing the maximum amount of direct and indirect light to enter.
A telescope which is mounted so as to allow the observation of only those objects in the sky which are passing over a local meridian, an event known as transit.
An optical instrument for making distant objects appear nearer and larger, usually found at an observatory, through which astronomical or meteorological phenomena may be observed.
A dish comprising three or more lobes, usually equally spaced. There may be one or more animal or other figures inside the base and two or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
Building housing the machinery for the shredding and grinding of wood in running water and pressing of the resulting fibres into a pulp.
A cargo vessel designed to carry goods packed in large containers that can be loaded directly onto trains or lorries.
A mill used for the preparation and production of Calamine.
A room or small building kept at low temperatures for the storage of perishable items, particularly food.
A mixing or grinding vessel.
A large tank used for soaking alumina-bearing shale in water and chemicals, the initial stage in the alum-making process.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of chlorophyll for medical purposes.
A large-scale site where medicinal drugs are maufactured.
A floatable concrete vessel, numbers of which made up the main breakwater of the Mulberry Harbours used to secure beachheads during the allied invasion of Europe in June 1944.
A mineral of copper, iron and sulphur and is the main ore of copper.

A six oared rowing boat which originated in Cornwall in the 18th century. Originally used as a pilot vessel, useage adapted to include cargo vessel and lifeboat. Today gigs are used in sporting events.
A dam with a watertight upstream side, which may be flat or curved, supported by a series of buttresses on the downstream side.
A building with malt kilns for the malting of grains and with other similar equipment for brewing work.
The SI derived unit of speed or velocity
Small stones which have been rounded usually by the action of sea water.
A kiln used for the production of any of the soda group of alkalis by the heating of plant remains or salt.
A house in which a member of the Royal Court lives.
A circular flask with one or two flattened faces. (Source: MPRG)
A water channel leading from a water wheel.
A jar used to store medicines, drugs or the constituent parts of medicines and drugs.
A building, administered by the Navy, Army and Air Force Institutes, providing retail and leisure services to members of the armed forces.
A factory where knitted fabrics are manufacterd using knitting machines.
A factory engaged in the manufacture of small arms ammunition, especially the metal components and filling with the explosive propellant.
A stone channel sunk into the ground, employed from the mid-19th century, to carry away gases produced during smelting.
A bank, often faced with stone, with a hedge planted on top.
A refractory lined furnace in which an electric arc is struck between the electrode and the metal to be melted.
A temporary brick building, based on drawing number (2901/43), used for the repair, packing and storage of inflatable liferafts.
A bowl with no noticeable base angle, so that the walls and base form a continuous rounded curve (Source: MPRG)
Large, single-engine, eight passenger airliner biplane.
A type of mace with bolster shaped stone or metal head on a wooden or metal shaft. Where the use is thought to be ceremonial, double index with ceremonial object.
A microlith retouched to a point, usually with oblique retouch. They are synonymous with 'obliquely blunted points' of the English Mesolithic. (Source: SARC)

An enclosed feature, usually sub-terranean, constructed to contain water for public or private recreation and sporting activities. Often a component of a larger SPORTS CENTRE. Use OUTDOOR SWIMMING POOL for unenclosed pools.
A drinking bowl, often wooden.
A room containing a toilet, water closet etc..
A box with a perforated top used for perfume.
A place where vehicles can be filled up with petrol, oil, water, etc.
A fountain erected specifically to supply drinking water.
A nodule of iron pyrites used to create fire in combination with tinder and flint or another nodule of iron pyrites.
A channel carrying overflow water past a dam. Early 19th century onwards.
A centre where treatment and rehabilitation training is given to patients recovering from injuries or accidents.
The consecrated ground immediately surrounding a tomb or grave.
Mark 10 or the tenth variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
An apartment or suite of rooms usually occupying the top floor of a building.

Two-seat, twin-engined fighter/fighter-bomber designed as a replacement for the Bf110. Of the 600 or so produced, only 258 reached the Luftwaffe due to serious design faults. The ME210 was superseded by the ME410 Hornisse.
Use for vessels registered in Japan.
A building containing a number of single roomed cells used for detaining prisoners.
A flattened rectangular version of a column of one of the classical orders.

A pilaster terminating the side walls of a temple whose capital and base differ from those of its associated columns. Such an arrangement, where the columns do not project beyond the faces of the antae, is said to be 'in antis'.
A mine yielding rock salt.
A temporary castle built to house and protect troops beseiging another castle or town.
A sheet of flat film, 105 x 148mm in size, carrying a matrix of micro images.
Use for vessels registered in Portugal.
Two-wheeled vehicles for personal transport with pedals for propulsion by the rider.
A building where an officer of a county, district or municipality acting as a representative of the Crown holds inquests, including deaths through violence or accident and treasure trove.
Casing for electrical connections: an enclosed and protected box inside which electrical circuits are interconnected or branched for distribution.
Hard, often coloured, can be transparent. Found on its own as crystals and veins but also as a major constituent of all three geological rock types.
A calciner dating from the early 17th to early 20th centuries, usually made of brick and without moving parts, consisting of a reverberatory furnace, and used for the extraction of arsenic.
A frame to a structure formed by precast concrete beams placed in pairs.
A HORSE GIN used for domestic cider manufacture, especially on farms.
A place where two or more railway lines meet.

A human constructed underwater structure, usually built to promote marine life in areas with a generally featureless eas bed but have also been built to control erosion, block ship passage, or improve surfing.
An alloy of tin, antimony and copper used as a replacement for pewter.

A unit of weight in the avoirdupois system equal to 2,240 pounds (1,016.05 kg) in Britain (the long ton) and 2,000 pounds (907.18 kg) in the United States (the short ton). As a unit of volume it is equivalent to 100 cubic feet (the register ton) or 40 cubic feet (the freight or measurement ton)

A hexagonal pillbox with an interanl anti-ricochet wall. The rear wall was lengthened to take two rifle loopholes in addition to the five light machine gun. Both 15in and 42in thick walls are common. Designed by DFW branch 3.
Data suitable for processing using computer aided design (CAD) packages.
Unable to identify actual place from documentary sources alone.
A depression in the ground caused by the explosion of a mortar shell.
A barn which is constructed with a timber framework; between the members are panels which are infilled with timber, wattle and daub, plaster, brickwork, stone or other materials.
A barn in which a pair of curved timbers form a bowed A-frame which supports the roof independently of the walls.
A receptacle used as a home for bees, traditionally made of thick straw work in the shape of a dome,but sometimes made of wood.
A hard sharp point used to cut a design into metal.

A large shallow pan, usually metal, in which seawater or brine is evaporated for the extraction of salt. The name is also often applied to the exterior pits or ponds used for the same purpose (see Thesaurus of Monument Types).
A place where architectural ornaments such as stone vases and urns are manufactured.
An alignment of trees planted as part of a designed landscape. For a belt lining a road use TREE AVENUE.
A building housing material used to explain the significance of a site or landscape to the public e. g. an archaeological site or nature reserve.
A wooden stake fence, often associated with deer hunting.
A room, within a building or institution, equipped for conducting scientific experiments or research.
Merchandise wrapped in canvas and tightly bound with cords or hoops to form bales.
Equipment or tool used to compress an object into a desired form, a flatter appearance etc.
A residue left as the result of the burning of material.
Volcanic ash.
The point or tine of a fork.
An apparatus designed with a large vaned wheel rotated by the wind in order to generate electricity.
A chemical works engaged in the production or refining of toluene, a substance extracted from coal tar or specific types of crude oil, and used in the production of explosives during WW1.
A shallow, usually circular, dish on which food is served or eaten from.
Use for the remains of any part of a bird.
A lid with a carinated conical profile and straight vertical sides, surmounted by a conical top with and integral knob. (Source: MPRG)
A jug with a roughly cylindrical or slightly flaring lower body, a pronounced inward-sloping shoulder and a marked neck/body angle. (Source: MPRG)

World War II-era British merchant ships used in convoys as an emergency stop-gap until sufficient escort carriers became available. They were equipped with a rocket-propelled catapult launching a single Hawker Sea Hurricane plane.
A place of worship for members of the Church of Scotland which has been Presbyterian since 1690. It is the national Church of Scotland and is free and endowed.
A building or works in which carriages were built. Use RAILWAY CARRIAGE WORKS for sites making railway carriages.
A joint in which one timber is reduced in thickness.
A decorative moulding shaped to resemble a length of cable or twisted rope.

A sculpture, drawing, or other representation of a face surrounded by or made from leaves and branches or vines. Green Men are frequently found on carvings in both secular and church buildings, and are though to represent pagan fertility deities.
A temporary airfield in use during the build-up to D-Day. They consisted of a natural earth or grass surface reinforced with wire mesh.
A large container used for washing the body.
A hospital for the reception of women during their confinement.
A projecting vertical window in the sloping roof of a house.
A pillbox constructed for use in training exercises forming part of a simulated defensive position

Staircase whose moving steps are driven mechanically whilst remaining permanently in a horizontal plane allowing users or objects to be moved effortlessly from one level to another, within or outside a building.
A college associated with, or forming part of, a university.
Buildings and plant used for the extraction and purification of arsenic oxide into various forms of pure arsenic.

A system of defensive works such as anti-tank obstacles, ditches and pillboxes, designed to stop the advance of an enemy. Defence lines were constructed across and around strategic areas of ground and sites such as industrial towns.
An early form of powered forging hammer, featuring a cast-iron hammer head fixed to a pivoted wooden arm, introduced circa 1500 and used primarily in the iron industry.
A depot or warehouse for the storage, distribution and repair of shoe making machines.
A wooden framework with holes for the head and hands, in which the offender stood.
A device used to trap or kill animals considered to be pests, eg. rats.
Originally, the inner sanctuary of a Greek temple from where the oracle was delivered. Now used for any private chamber or sanctuary.
A jettied house where the upper storey only overhangs the end elevation of the building.
Blocks carved out of granite and used as a building material.
A place for strolling, public walks, etc. Usually associated with coastal resorts.
A composite instrument in which air is forced through one or more drones and chanter from an inflated bag or bladder.

Periodic visits being made to a site by an archaeologist to record archaeological deposits and recover finds that have come to light since the previous visit. An archaeological presence is not maintained during groundwork as it is with a watching brief.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
British, single-engined, light day bomber biplane. Built in 1923, this was the RAF's first interbellum designed day bomber.
An inscribed marker stone found on Hadrian's Wall.
The first driven gearwheel on the vertical shaft within a corn mill which meshes with the brake wheel in a windmill, or the pit wheel in a watermill.
A principal member in a cruck truss.
A small light vessel with a schooner rig often used for fishing.
Residential area built to house athletes and their coaches at the Olympic Games. The buildings are generally reused as public housing after the contest.
A residential home for older people or people with physical and/or mental disabilities who need care provided by registered nurses.
A privately-funded home for the care of the elderly.
A technique that uses the emission of alpha particles of specific energies to identify the presence and concentration of certain radioactive isotopes in a sample
A round or polygonal building containing a HORSE ENGINE. Commonly found on farms next to the threshing barn, where it is used to power the machinery.
Twin-engined monoplane originally designed as a reconnaissance aircraft, but also widely used as a trainer. Entered RAF service in 1936.
A tool for creating holes in the ground in which to plant seeds or plants.
A flexible container with an opening at one end.
A short chain or chains attached to a woman's belt for carrying keys etc.
A factory manufacturing electrical equipment, such as engines, transformers and generators for use in industry.
A factory used to manufacture fibreglass.

A prefabricated structure of lightweight timber wall sections bolted together. Externally the walls were clad with plasterboard covered with felt. Designed for use as officers accomodation during WWII.
A long, low-rise building consisting of rows of attached individual suites of rooms used for overnight accommodation by motorists.
A temporary kiln, in which the pots are stacked and baked in a pit underneath a bonfire.
A building or site used for the production of frameworks of beds.
A machine for creating bails of straw.

A decorative emblem stating the name of a village or town and depicting aspects of the place's history of culture. Most signs are mounted on a post and usually errected in a central position near the church or village green.
An encircling ornament for the head, usually denoting sovereignty.
A shop where fish and chips are sold.
A joint in which the end of one timber is cut in V- form and rests on the edge of another timber, frequently found between common rafters and wall plates.
A type of dagger, usually used by civilians in the medieval period, with a H shaped hilt.
A single storey building designed so that windows incorporated into the saw tooth roof catch the available light.
A shallow artificial pond, usually found on the coast, in which sea water is allowed to evaporate leaving behind the salt.
A cross connected to a reliquary or containing a relic itself.
An object used to create a blast of air.
A bowl adapted by the addition of three or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
A piece of stone, usually shaped, of uncertain origin or use.
An educational establishment for the training of police cadets.
The outer curve of an arch or vault.

A waterwheel in which the incoming water is directed onto the periphery at approximately the same level as the axle, the water being kept in contact with the floats, or buckets, by breastwork of masonry, timber or iron.
A garden created to commemorate a person or event.
A factory where cheese is produced and processed.
A small yard attached to the rear of a house or other building.
Shed for grinding rags, eg. for use in mungo and shoddy mills.
A German coastal minelaying submarine in use during the First World War.
A bridge that crosses over a railway.
A three panelled altar decoration that can be closed.
Three storey house with a topshop; machinery powered by shafting through the upper floor.
Twin-engined monoplane originally designed as a reconnaissance aircraft, but also widely used as a trainer. Entered RAF service in 1936.
A crane powered by a treadwheel and used for lifting and lowering, dating from the Roman period. Also used in later periods to assist on building sites, at mines and in ports.
A place set apart to contain books for reading, study or reference.
A tower used to store grain in.

Also known as the C-47 Skytrain, this twin-engined, military transport was developed from the DC-3 twenty-eight-seat commercial airliner and was the most extensively employed transport of the Second World War.
A small, single storey building used as the Pilots' room on fighter stations and as the watch office on bomber stations.
A building used to house railway carriages.
A small dish, often with a handle, for soup, porridge etc.
A small, handled axe.
A crane consisting of a vertical tower or similar structure from which projects a movable boom, or jib, fitted with a mechanical hoist.
A specialised form of crane, usually employed on a dockside, featuring a curving, solid jib.

A British two-seater army co-operation aircraft manufactured by Hawker Aircraft for the Royal Air Force. A Hart variant biplane that first flew in 1931, becoming a prominent British aircraft in the inter-war period with over 700 units built.
Originally partially covered baths shaped somewhat like a slipper, now usually a number of single baths of the modern domestic style installed for hire at public baths.
A large, watertight enclosure in which the water is maintained at the high-tide level so that vessels remain constantly afloat in them.
A wool combing machine for very fine wools.

Four-engined heavy bomber, developed by Avro from the twin-engined Manchester. Entered service in 1942 as the RAF's principal night bomber and took part in the 1,000 bomber raids as well as the famous Dam Busters raid.
An ornate version of an eight-voluted Ionic capital known as an angular capital or Scamozzi under which are added two tiers of acanthus leaves.
A sulphuric acid compound.
A waste product from smelting metal.
The third and last subdivision of the Palaeolithic or Old Stone Age; characterized by the development of projectile points made from bony materials and the development of fine blade flint tools.

A section of the water channel of a river, shut off above and below by lock gates provided with sluices to let water in and out and thus raise or lower boats from one level to another. Often found situated next to a weir.
A factory engaged in the manufacture of small arms ammunition, especially the metal components and filling with the explosive propellant.
A man made ditch designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle. Ditches were often reveted with concrete or wood.
A small flake or blade with a series of notches along the edge.
Fittings for animal harness.
A kitchen set up, specifically during World War Two, to serve food to members of the public, especially families whose homes had succumbed to enemy bombing.
A calciner used in arsenic production from the 1820s to the 1950s featuring a distinctive, slowly rotating hearth.
The cold room in a Roman baths.
Breast ornament
A white, caustic solid obtained by heating limestone and used in the preparation of mortar and cement.
A small store building at a railway station for the storage of equipment and other stores associated with the railway.
A jug with a body profile resembling two cones joined together at their widest points, producing a distinct carination. (Source: MPRG)

A calciner commonly used between 1870 and circa 1900 for extracting arsenic from mined ores and featuring a slightly inclined rotating iron tube with a firebox at the bottom and an ore feed at the top.
A large building, situated by or near a canal, used for the temporary storage of goods or merchandise awaiting transportation to or from the canal.
A chamber usually used for sleeping.
A WWII British biplane produced by Hawker Aircraft, used for army cooperation duties.
An early power loom in which the shedding actions of the machine were controlled by tappets, or wipers, which received their motion from a rotating cam shaft positioned at one side of the loom.

Double-handled storage jars characterised by a long neck and long body used as food and wine containers and for carrying such goods as cargo, found on shipwrecks from Classical antiquity (Greek/Roman).
A non-vertical kiln where the shaft and burning zone is horizontal to the ground thereby allowing material to be fed in.
A building that housed humans and cattle under one roof, with a shared entrance providing access to the cattle housing (usually downslope) and the dwelling area.
Building or buildings used for the production of Gas Masks. Consider double-indexing with the term WAR PRODUCTION FACTORY if appropriate.
An object used to catch fish. The line is tied in the middle of the fish gorge which then lodges in the throat after the fish has swallowed it.
The horizontal piece of timber or stone forming the bottom of a window, doorway or other opening, usually and properly designed to throw off water.
A factory producing drabbet, a type of linen cloth.
A site where the process of combing, the preparatory process for long wools, takes place.
A pump driven by steam power generated by solid fuels.
A building or area where processes like bleaching, dressing, etc, are conducted under one roof.
All-weather fighter/interceptor first flow in 1951, introduced into service in 1956 and retired from the RAF in 1968.
A factory built as a pattern for improved design.
An arch built by corbelling or cantilevering in from both sides with horizontal joints.
A circular, metal or wooden cover, covering a hole in the pavement where domestic coal deliveries were dropped into a store below.
Place for the Home Guard to store equipment and amunition, either structural or subterranean during the defence of Britain.
Building for testing the condition and strength of textiles.
A specific type of hand held hollowed wooden clapper, known in Europe from medieval times onwards.

Blocks of solid concrete, in the shape of a round bottomed cone usually 2 feet 6 inches across x 2 feet 9 inches high. Buoys were mainly used in road blocks intended to impede enemy movement in the event of invasion.

Troop and general transport glider. Almost entirely wooden in construction, many were manufactured by the furniture industry. Mk I featured a a door-ramp on the port side whilst the Mk II was fitted with a hinged nose.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 17658/40.
A channel, usually placed upstream of a mill, that carries water from a river or other water source to a waterwheel.
Pond for storing cut lengths of timber to prevent them becoming seasoned.
A building or structure to house railway wagons.
An area for the testing of rockets and guided missiles. Includes all structures associated with both the firing and testing of rockets and missiles.
Wood which is used as fuel for fires.
Three-seat tactical support aircraft. Entering service with the US 9th Air Force in 1944, the Invader had a bomb load of 4,000 lbs and was later used as a conventional medium bomber.
A building where the bones of the dead were stored.

An important two-seat, tractor biplane, initially used by the RFC in a reconnaissance role and by the RNAS as a bomber. Later converted to a single-seat Home Defence fighter and ultimately used as a trainer.
The residence of a lacemaker.
The residence of a chauffeur or driver
A hard metallic element used in steels and magnetic alloys. Compounds containing manganese are used in glass-making and other industrial processes.
A strut which is at an angle between the principal rafter and tiebeam.
A school attended by children between the ages of eleven and sixteen offering a vocationally orientated curriculum.
A round bottomed container to be held in the palm of the hand.
Purpose-built lodgings for assize court judges. Early 19th century.
A raised step, usually made of concrete, on which supporters stand to watch a game of football.
A bridge crossing under railway property.
A flatbed lorry with a concrete defensive position fitted on the back enabling the "pillbox" to be driven to where it was most needed in the event of an airborne force landing on the airfield.
A bowl used in magical ceremonies.
A building, usually part of a textile mill complex, where warp yarn is sized prior to weaving. Sizing is the application of a starch solution to warp threads to add strength and protection.

The light emitted from sedimentary minerals or mineral inclusions in bricks when stimulated in the laboratory by light of a different wavelength. Used to date samples up to 250,000 years old; especially appropriate for geological sediments.
A plain, narrow moulding or area, sometimes projecting, separating two decorated mouldings or features such as the vertical grooves on a fluted column.
Flint which has been burnt. It is not necessarily worked.
A steep bank or slope. In fortifications, the bank or wall immediately in front of and below the rampart.
A lime kiln in which coal is burnt, as distinct from a flame-free kiln in which wood or peat is used.
A rescue tug equipped to care for survivors from torpedoed vessels and also available for towing to port ships damaged by enemy action.
The top stone in a gable end.
A building used for the shelter and protection of deer, especially in winter.
A threshing barn, usually timber framed which is raised on staddle stones.
A barn usually containing a single, central threshing floor.
An area of land which has been drained or cleared for habitation and/or cultivation.
Use for vessels registered in Croatia.
The third and latest subdivision of the Iron Age.
The main dwelling-house of a farm, it can be either detached from or attached to the working buildings.
A surface made up of small pieces of hard material such as stone or tile, often in a decorative pattern.
The lower, horizontal surface of a room on which people walk. Can also mean a storey of a building.
Remains of wheat (Triticum sp.) grain (caryopyses). These grains are sometimes itemised separately.
A road block formed by placing curved rails, "hairpins", in sockets in the road surface.
Weights used on a type of vertical loom to hold the warp threads taut.
A garden designed in the style of the elaborate gardens of the Renaissance, eg. formal, geometrical layouts of lawn and paths, stone steps, balustrades and statuary and fountains.
A concept dating in England from the second half of the 18th century, when hardy North American plants were relatively easy to obtain.
A road block formed by placing rails or girders in an upright position in sockets in the road surface, forming a moveable barrier.
An all timber constructed watch office with meterological section. Similar in design to 2328/39 and 5845/39. There were only two known examples built in the UK at Wick and St.Eval.
A Mark 2B aircraft with which has undergone further modifications to enhance performance or armament.
A shed for storing fishing bait.
A protected building or site used for the safe storage of chemical weapons
A large, flat dish.
Goods stowed in barrels and therefore indicating that the barrels were in use as containers with goods stored therein, rather than as cargo in their own right.
A farmstead where mostly detached buildings have developed around one side of an open cattle yard.
A mill for the manufacture of low grade cloth made from ground-up heavy woollen rags.

Component part of a mungo and shoddy mill, where non-wool fibres from shredded material are destroyed by either soaking rags in an acid solution or rotating them in drums in a hot acidic gas followed by heat. The result is an all-wool product.
A hotel where no alcohol is available.
A place where architectural ornaments such as stone vases and urns are manufactured.
A kiln principally used in brick making which gives a continuous operation.

A chemical works engaged in the manufacture of the coal tar derivative, picric acid, often associated with the textile industry where it was used as a dye, but more commonly with the explosives industry where it was used as the shell filling Lyddite.
A building where reptiles are accommodated at a zoo or wildlife park.
A torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance biplane in service with the Fleet Air Arm 1935-1938. Rendered obsolete after 1938 by the Swordfish and withdrawn from service.
A mechanical component or device that can change the direction of motion of a pump rod from the vertical to the horizontal plane and vice versa.
The hair from the coat of goats and sheep, made into yarn and used in the manufacture of woollen cloth.
Goods, particularly cloth and garments, manufactured from wool.
Timber or stone built structure, traces of which are found within some long and round barrows, in which human remains were interred prior to mound construction.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber. Fitted with eight fixed forward-firing machine guns in the wings, plus two 1000lb bombs or six rocket projectiles.
A 1930s British short-haul biplane airliner for 6-8 passengers. It proved an economical and durable craft, despite its relatively primitive plywood construction. Primarily used by the RAF.
A radio-controlled target tug version of the Tiger Moth used for target practice. 380 were built for the RAF.

Six-crew, medium-range, twin-engined reconnaissance flying-boat. Entered service with 209 Squadron in 1939 but, due to design and operation problems, saw little action and was not produced in large numbers.
A house with a pitched roof with a double slope and gables on the front and rear elevations of the building.
A climbing plant (Rubia tinctorum) which was formerly cultivated for the reddish-purple dye obtained from the roots.
A storehouse using mechanical means of controlling temperature rather than ice or insulation.
A site which has been bombed but where there is no crater, eg. bombed buildings.
Debris derived from the demolition of buildings or other structures. If unsure of whether debris is resulting from construction or demolition, index with both terms.
Use for vessels registered in Russia.
A heated room within a monastery where monks could warm themselves.
Photographic negative on film. Use for all acetate material types.
A temporary kitchen set up in the field providing food for troops. Use with MILITARY CAMP if existence of this is known.
A shore establishment for the teaching of maritime theory and practical skills.
A craft designed for use on canals and inland waterways. Usually 70ft long x 7ft wide though can be longer and broader.
Originally designed as a light bomber but diverted for use as a high speed target tug to replace out-dated biplanes.
A factory where gloves are manufactured.
A bowl comprising three or more equally spaced lobes. There may be one or more moulded animals or other figures inside the base and two or more handles. (Source: MPRG)

A tandem two-seat, twin-engined, all-weather, long-range supersonic jet interceptor fighter/fighter-bomber originally developed for the United States Navy by McDonnell Aircraft.It first entered service in 1960 with the U.S. Navy.
An instrument designed to measure temperature.
A storeroom for valuable goods, such as wine, oil and spices.
An ornamental tablet of brass. Use a materials thesaurus where brass is a material.
The earliest subdivision of the Bronze Age.
A fortified wall surrounding a town or city.
A factory principally engaged in the manufacture of the propellant explosive cordite.
A building used as the headquarters for the Home Guard during the Second World War.
A pan with a long handle which would be filled with coals and drawn over sheets to warm a bed.
An object which encloses a light source but allows light out through holes, glass etc.
A twin engine advanced trainer developed by Beech/ Beechcraft , a US firm, used in WWII
A designated area, usually sited at a strategic crossroads, with fixed defences such as pillboxes, anti tank ditches and gun emplacements, designed to act as a rallying point for defenders.
Photographic format.
Paste or cake of the fruit of the cacao-tree, sweetened with other substances and used to make beverages or confectionery.
A defensive embankment with three or more ditches.
A protective earthen mound, often the main defence of a fortification.
Wool, textile, or synthetic floor covering material.
An arch which has a larger radius on the front face of a wall than on the back.

A jug with a pierced bunghole just above the base. the bunghole can be made through an applied knob or disc of clay, or simply a hole in the vessel wall. In use, the hole would probably have had a tap or spigot attached. (Source: MPRG)
An engine in which the oscillating motion of the beam is translated via gearing to a rotative motion.
A steam engine with a horizontal beam connecting the piston and crank.
An instrument used for making a loud sound for information or warning.
A pedestrian passageway, often elevated, connecting two buildings or sections within a building.
The undressing room in a bath house or similar.
A site used for the extraction of metallic zinc by a variety of processes.

A pit in which lye is used to clean hides/bones/etc. generally as part of the tanning process to remove excess fat, flesh, hair, etc. from the raw hide. The residue from these pits formed a crude soap which could be used for various cleaning purposes.
A building used for storing tree bark.

Fish which have been caught and kept alive. Fish were kept alive on ships in earlier centuries to ensure they reached their destination as fresh as possible. In more recent times exotic fish have been kept alive to sell as pets.
A metal binding or ring fastened around the top of a pile to stop splitting.
Conelike spikes of the hop plant used in the brewing industry to give a bitter flavour to beer and malt liquors.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter-bomber developed from the Typhoon and the abandoned Tornado. Entered service in 1944 with its greatest success being in destroying V.1. flying bombs. One of the fastest World War 2 aircraft, with a top speed of 436 mph.
A medieval court established for the administration of forest law.
A court of summary jurisdiction formally recognized by statute in 1848. Renamed Magistrates Court, following legislation, in 1949.
A building housing court rooms and associated offices and cells, in which the Quarter Sessions were held.

A single engine two seat cabin monoplane tourer, first flown in 1933 as a successor to the Puss Moth. Impressed into military sevice in WWII by the RAF and the Fleet Air Arm as a liaison and communications aircraft, also used by training units.
British single-engine, two-seat night fighter. Originally intended as a day fighter, but withdrawn and converted in August 1940, this was the first fighter to incorporate a power-driven gun turret.
American, single-engine fighter designed for operation from US Naval aircraft carriers. Produced between 1940 and 1945, Wildcats provided to the British Fleet Air Arm were renamed Martlets.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter-bomber developed from the Typhoon and the abandoned Tornado. Entered service in 1944 with its greatest success being in destroying V.1. flying bombs. One of the fastest World War 2 aircraft, with a top speed of 436 mph.
The residence of a lifeboatman.
A machine used to raise and lower miners to and from the pit bottom.
A factory where cars are manufactured.
A temporary settlement or shanty-town erected by railway construction workers or "navvys".
A tool used for digging the ground.
A type of buddle used as an ore-cleaning device for seperating metallic ore from waste material by washing the dirty ore in a continuous flow of water.
A single-engine, photo-reconnaissance fighter designed for operation from aircraft carriers. Later adapted as a night fighter, it entered service in 1943 and remained in production until 1956.
Single-engine, two-seat tractor bomber and reconnaissance aircraft. Entered service in 1916 and, during 1917 and 1918, equipped nine RFC squadrons in its reconnaissance role.
A building or room within a granary used to dry grain. Often consisting of an oven with a refractory-brick drying floor above, on which the grain was placed.
A four-armed metal coupling, positioned at the centre of a windmill's sails, connected to the front of the striking rod and the shutter bars of all the sails, causing the shutters to open and close.
Specify in Description using: river, stream, estuary above tidal (saline) influence etc.
A building housing an engine, usually with an attendant boiler house and chimney. Used for winding from a pit.
Dried or partially dried grapes eaten as a fruit.
German three-engined air/sea rescue and transport flying boat. Entered service in 1940 as a replacement for the DO18.
An area within a hospital where patients with contagious diseases are isolated from the rest of the hospital.
A wall and area of ground where the game of fives is played.

A jar with a profile that flares outwards from base to rim, but usually with a constriction at the neck. Squat examples, with a height less than the minimum diameter, could be classified as bowls. (Source: MPRG)
An partly-worked millstone that is still to be finished.
A mill used for the preparation of raw fleece etc, for spinning by a coarse form of carding.

Series of rooms in a workhouse, prison or hospital, often including porter's lodge, baths, clothes store, washrooms, casual cells, rooms etc, for receiving inmates/patients. Use term in Monument Type Thesaurus if it is a freestanding building.
Technique using electromagnetic fields to map subsurface electrical conductivity anomalies. Can be used as a high-sensitivity metal detector.
A concave sided jar made in tin-glazed earthenware. (Source: MPRG)
A jar with vertical concave body walls. (Source: MPRG)
A small workshop, employing up to 10 men, working on hand-operated carding engines and hand jennies, spinning yarn for handloom weavers.
A timber frame placed in the bell chamber of a church tower or belfry designed to hold the bells.
American A-20 twin-engined, light, day bomber. Some supplied to the RAF and known as the Boston I. Subsequent variations adapted to night flying and re-christened the Havoc.
Photographic negative on glass developed using a dry process.
A small, defensive settlement, usually consisting of one dwelling and ancillary buildings, surrounded by a palisade.
A flanking tower, or projection from the main walls of a defensive work from which a garrison can defend the ground in front or on the flank.
Animal skins which have been treated by tanning or similar.
The limit line of a county.
A building containing pans in which salt water or brine was boiled to produce salt.

Controlled intrusive fieldwork which examines, records and interprets archaeological deposits, features and structures and, as appropriate, retrieves artefacts and ecofact remains within a specified underwater area.
Dried flower buds, used as a pungent aromatic spice.
A structure, often movable, used as a platform for the display of a traders goods in a market.
A sculpted female figure carrying a basket on her head.
A building used for a variety of administrative purposes, usually at a military base.
The main dwelling-house of a farm, it can be either detached from or attached to the working buildings.
A structure which allows aircraft fitted with radar equipment to 'home' in on an airfield in the dark or in poor visibility, and land safely. Radar beacons can also be used as navigation aids.
A factory or building where furniture is upholstered.
A building used for the daily administration of that branch of the RAF dealing with training pilots.
A workshop or factory where statues are made by casting molten material into moulds.
An artificial mound, generally conical, placed within a garden or park to provide a viewing point to overlook the garden or park. It may also serve as a visual focus in the garden or park layout.
An artificial hill constructed in Tudor gardens, especially, to provide a good view.
A radio-controlled target tug version of the Tiger Moth used for target practice. 380 were built for the RAF.

A purpose-built facility providing an area for wheeled sports, such as skateboarding, skating and BMX cycling, equipped with ramps and other structures and obstacles for the performance of tricks and manoeuvres.
A steam engine with a horizontal beam connecting the piston and crank.
An engine in which the oscillating motion of the beam is translated via gearing to a rotative motion.
A roof, circular in plan, usually semicircular in section, over a circular, square or polygonal base.
A farm or group of buildings where Silkworms are bred. The Silkworm when changing into a pupa spins a cocoon made of silken filaments, these are then unwound and used to manufacture silk thread.
A tall, narrow window with a pointed arched head.
In use as a building.

An underground hideout containing radio equipment to be used by the Special Duties sections of the Auxiliary Units to co-ordinate information collected by the outstations for relaying to headquarters.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Auxiliary Unit Special Duties Control Station

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A temporary kiln, in which the pots are stacked and baked in a pit underneath a bonfire.
A loft for the drying of thread or cloth.
Photographic negative developed on waxed paper.
A building, or part of a church, used for baptismal rites, usually containing a font.
A purpose-built hall (usually 19th century) which was available for public hire and could be used for a variety of activities, eg. lectures, meetings, balls and concerts.
A small hole for a lace, cord or hook to be passed through.
Comparison of different proportions of natural occurring isotopes of lead (Pb), strontium (Sr), oxygen (O), carbon (C) and nitrogen (N).
A long narrow spoon used to remove cosmetics or medicines from narrow necked containers.
Fast arterial road with separate carriageways limited to motor vehicles

In the glass industry, material spilled or raked from the top of the crucible during melting:important for assessing the methods of glassmaking and a common find on furnace sites. Roman period onwards.
A hand operated machine for winding cotton and linen thread into balls - invented in 1802.
Term for ore store/ore hopper, used particularly in Yorkshire and Derbyshire.
A US aircraft manufacturer. The Cessna Aircraft Co Inc was established in 1927
A twin engined advanced trainer aircraft developed for the military by the US firm of Cessna
A long, narrow mound of earth or stone and of uncertain date and function. Use more appropriate term where possible.
The hard, heavy wood obtained from plants of the genus Guaiacum.
A small cup for holding a boiled egg upright while it is being eaten.
A place of burial for members of the French Protestant Church.
A site used for the sport of badger baiting using fighting dogs.
A stable where horses are kept at livery, or are let out for hire.
Ordnance, expended or otherwise, weapons, armour, personal effects, transport wreckage, or ship wreckage, left behind on the site of a terrestrial or naval battle.
A container for incense.
A room or building used for the making of films, television or radio programmes and musical recordings (CDs, LPs, etc).

Three-seat, twin-engined minelaying, torpedo-bombing and reconnaissance twin-float seaplane. First flown in 1936, in 1938 it set eight world speed records for its class in various range and payload categories.
A hospital where people would pay a subscription in order to recieve treatment when ill.
A county judicial building where the Quarter Session and the Assizes for the County were held.
