American, four-engined, medium/heavy day bomber. Entered service in 1937. The prototype was nicknamed the Flying Fortress, which later became a registered trademark.
A lock where the gates rise vertically. Rarely found on canals but common on navgable rivers in the Fens, particularly the river Nene.
A market appointed for the sale of wool.
A structure used for execution by hanging. Usually two uprights and a cross-piece, from which the offender is suspended by the neck.
Use for vessels registered in Russia.
A radio-controlled target tug version of the Tiger Moth used for target practice. 380 were built for the RAF.
An isolated building, circular in plan, generally consisting of one apartment with a domed roof, eg. Mausoleum at Castle Howard, Yorkshire.
A sharp, pointed metal object.
A type of spike, often on candlesticks.
A yard or enclosure attached to a farmhouse, usually surrounded by other farm buildings.
A crude, stone built structure, often roofless, used by tin miners to store equipment.
A cruck, forming the main upright of a wall but whose blades are truncated by a transverse member.
The premises of a police officer for a parish or township who was appointed to act as a conservator of the peace within the district.
Decorative ornamentation of a key pattern
A single-seat, biplane fighter. One of the last open cockpit types to see widespread service with the RAF, equipping 10 squadrons and, at one point, 70% of the Home Defence fighter force.
A building housing a whim, a machine worked by a horse, used for raising ores, etc, from a mine.
A decorative moulding featuring a series of small, projecting, dome-like shapes each resembling a halved nutmeg.
A vessel for keeping the ashes of the dead after cremation.
A vane usually combined with crossed rods to show the four compass points. Used to indicate the direction of the wind.
A wall in a flower or kitchen garden, containing conduits or pipes for heating the wall.
A terrace of houses built on a slope giving the roofline a stepped appearance.
A small round dish on which a drinking vessel is set.
A crane in which, during any alteration of radius, an automatic device causes the load to move horizontally.
When secondary product use with major product and MINE, eg. COPPER MINE.
A plant where freshly mined coal was washed down and any dust removed before loading for transport away from the colliery.
Two-seat, single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer. Square-winged and fitted with dual controls, this popular trainer was used by British Commonwealth, as well as American and Canadian, air forces.
The point or block from which an arch or vault starts. The block generally has a horizontal base and sloped top.

Structural board comprising a core of thin layers of wood bonded together, which is faced on one or both sides with a sheet of metal, usually galvanised steel or aluminium. Mainly used for external wall cladding.
One of a pair of straight or curved members set at an angle on the tie-beam and framed into a principal rafter, often supporting a purlin.
A wall between two towers or pavilions, usually surrounding a building, and often forming a major part of the defences.
A system of individually enclosed fields.
A place of worship for members of the Methodist Reform Church. This group was the result of a secession from the Methodists in 1849. They remained until joining with the Wesleyan Association in 1857.
A boarding or day school for children who had committed minor crimes or who lived in circumstances where they were likely to commit crime.
A horizontal, stationary steam engine with two cylinders in line, one behind the other, the steam passing through each cylinder in turn.
A hiding place for a (Roman Catholic) priest.
A gun designed to be held in one hand. It has a short barrel length compared to long guns.
A factory where brushes are manufactured. Use for all types of brush.
A farm where stallions and mares are kept for breeding.
A wall connecting two pavilions, bastions, towers etc..
Use with wider site type where known.
A semi-permanent ahed designed to Air Ministry specification 1136/27 as a quick and cheap hangar for stations overseas
A large, flat dish.
A graduated vessel or instrument for gauging or measuring the force or quantity of a fluctuating object, such as rainfall, tide, wind etc.
An establishment where chocolate was available as a beverage.

A two-seat, general purpose biplane. The first to be designed specifically for an Army Co-operation role, it entered service in late 1927. Ended its service as a communications and advanced trainer aircraft.
A building containing a number of areas for bathing, some of which are naturally heated by thermal springs.
A report detailing the results of an archaeological evaluation
A hiding place for stores, often underground, used by smugglers.
An alloy which is composed predominantly of tin (c.85-99 percent).
Twin-engined fighter-bomber. All metal in construction, entered service in 1940. Supported bombing operations and participated in attacks on France, but not widely used due to engine faults.
A factory for the manufacture of military tanks.

Highly successful, two-seat, biplane fighter and reconnaissance aircraft with both forward and rear facing guns. Designed to replace the BE2, it entered service with the RFC in mid-1917 and remained in service until 1932.
A house in which a passage runs across the building, usually adjacent to a hall, between front and back entrance doors.

An open area of water, usually artificial and enclosed by dock gates or locks, lined with wharves and warehouses, where barges, narrow boats and other canal vessels can load and unload goods and supplies.
The area at the end of an axle or shaft around which a wheel, bearing etc. pivots or rotates.
Mill incorporating water-powered hammers for beating brass sheet, etc. into vessels, pots, etc.
A signal usually mounted on a gantry, be it mechanical or electronic, to provide guidance to traindrivers on access to sections of track.
A processed used to increase the thickness of the natural oxide layer on the surface of metal parts. The part being treated forms the anode of an electrolytic cell.
A photographic frame of developed colour film which can be used to print a photographic image.
Single-engine, single-seat fighter-bomber. Designed to replace the Hurricane as an interceptor, excelled as a rocket-projectile-firing ground-attack fighter. Entered RAF service in 1941.
A distinguishing emblem or mark, often worn to signify membership, achievement, employment etc.
The channel of water that provides a current of water to drive a millwheel.
Water channel leading to water wheel.
A long stick or rod used as an aid in walking, climbing etc. Where it is a weapon use quarterstaff or staff weapon. Where there is another use, use the appropriate term eg surveying staff.
A band or bracelet worn around the arm.
A place where the homeless are accommodated, permanently or temporarily.
A capital with an abacus, ovolo, neck and astragal.
A place where jockeys are accomodated.
Ash and partially fused residues from a coal fired furnace or fire.
A factory where fish are processed into food products.
A weight used for the measurement of wool.
British 'M' class submarine modified to carry and launch a small sea plane.
British, single-engined, light day bomber biplane. Built in 1923, this was the RAF's first interbellum designed day bomber.
A bowl used in the marriage ceremony.
Lantern slide developed using a wet process.
Lantern slide developed using a dry process.
Use for deposits formed as a result of the modification of soils by humans for agricultural purposes.
An educational building where examinations are held.
A factory for the production of plastics by chemical processes.
A supply of water used to keep canals that were vulnerable to water shortage topped up.
A fort with projecting bastions, which came into use from the 16th century onwards.
A hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of military personnel and/or their families.

1st or 2nd century Bow Brooch derived from the Colchester. It typically has a pin hinged on a bar held in a cylindrical crossbar, the bow tapering and commonly decorated. Developed examples often have a headloop and enamelled panels.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Perchlorate, a product used in the explosives industry.
A metal reinforcer worn on the sole or heel of a boot.
A place of worship for Sandemanians, a movement founded by John Glass after his expulsion from the Church of Scotland in 1728. It was spread to England by his son-in-law, Robert Sandeman.
A place where processed cloth is cut for use as garments or soft furnishings, etc.
A wedge shaped stone or brick forming part of an arch or vault, with its radiating sides coinciding with the radii of that arch.
A round or polygonal building containing a HORSE ENGINE. Commonly found on farms next to the threshing barn, where it is used to power the machinery.
A place where the creative arts are taught to students.
A vessel comprising of two or more bowls, generally of small size, joined together. There may be one or more handles of varying forms. (Source: MPRG)
A decorative fitting of mid to late 11th century date, mainly of copper alloy, often traingular or trapezoidal in shape. Mounted at the junction of the stirrup and stirrup strap.
A road or way along a ridge of downs or low range of hills.
A Mark 6B aircraft which has undergone further modifications to enhance performance or armament.

An enclosed structure, usually glass fronted, designed to contain, and facilitate the viewing of, objects or notices. May be built into the fabric of a room, affixed to an exterior or exterior wall or free standing.
A circular bank of stones and turf, sometimes accompanied by a ditch, surrounding a natural outcrop of rock, usually a tor, or an earthfast boulder.
A figure, representation or image, which is itself regarded as sacred.
A mechanically operated lift used to transfer rolling stock from one level of track to another.
A road vehicle designed to carry many passengers.
A pit filled with rubble, etc., into which rain or waste water flows in order to disperse into the surrounding soil.
A building or site used for the manufacture of swords.
Wooden panelling, especially interior wall panelling that rises only to dado height.
Photographic negative developed on paper.
A moulding on an entablature that is between the frieze and the corona.

Two-seat, twin-engined fighter/fighter-bomber designed as a replacement for the Bf110. Of the 600 or so produced, only 258 reached the Luftwaffe due to serious design faults. The ME210 was superseded by the ME410 Hornisse.

An American turbojet fighter-bomber aircraft. The F-84 was the first production fighter aircraft to utilize in-flight refuelling and the first fighter capable of carrying a nuclear weapon. Designed by Alexander Kartveli, 1946.
A water channel leading from a water wheel.
A building containing celestial telescopes in which astronomical or meteorological phenomena may be observed.
A funerary vehicle used to carry a coffin from a church or funeral home to a cemetery.
Stone which has been crushed for use in the construction industry.

A brick-built building with four windows on the north-facing wall with a pitched roof and with a dormer roof light on both sides, intended for drying, storing and packing parachutes.The 2355/25 was the first design for a purpose-built parachute store.
A ditch constructed to surround a town for defensive purposes.
A small moulding on the top of the architrave in the Doric order.
Bed coverings, usually of woollen or similar natural or artificial fabrics.
The blue dyestuff prepared from the leaves of the plant Isatis tinctoria, and sometimes used to discribe the plant itself. Later superseded by indigo.
One of a pair of inclined struts that meet at the bottom to form a V shape.

Approximately circular or oval setting of spaced post holes indicating the former presence of a free-standing arrangement of upright timber posts. Often regarded as a wooden equivalent of the better known stone circles.
A large, fortified permanent Roman military base, made of timber and stone, surrounded by a rampart and ditches.
Small port on River Trent, North Lincs.

A type of clinker built wooden boat or ship held together with tendons of flexible wood such as roots and willow branches. Sewn boat construction techniques were used in many parts of the world prior to the development of metal fasteners.
A small warship mounting between 20 and 28 nine-pounder guns on a single deck.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Sixth Rate Ship Of The Line

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: Not subdivided
A container in which needles are held.
The lowest part, or base, of a structure, sometimes built into the ground, on which the weight of the whole rests.
A semi-permanent ahed designed to Air Ministry specification 1136/27 as a quick and cheap hangar for stations overseas
Place for people who underwent regular blood letting.
A free-standing building with enough space to hang and dry nets.

Area in a deer park where a single deer was chased by dogs over a set distance, with bets made on the outcome. It usually includes a stand (for viewing) and can also include three distance markers, a finishing post and a ditch behind the last post.
A large park for keeping deer. In medieval times the prime purpose was for hunting.
An apartment, usually with a north-light, used by artists.
The primary mechanism within an engine or device that transmits motion, especially rotary motion, to wheels, cogs, turntables etc.
An electricity-producing power station fired by oil.
A cottage for workers on a country house estate.

An airfield building housing a turret gunnery trainer used to teach air gunners how to report the correct position of enemy aircraft by practising shooting against projected moving images of enemy aircraft displayed on a target screen (WWII).
An unconsolidated geological deposit sometimes iused as a bonding material in stone walls.

A well or spring, possessing religious or otherwise ritualistic significance, around which a structure, such as a niche, wall or shelter, has been constructed. In the case of the water source being a natural spring, double-index with SPRING.
Sailing vessel generally with three masts square rigged on the foremast only.
Four-crew, twin-engined, general reconnaissance flying-boat. Entered service after World War One, becoming the RAF's standard flying-boat until replaced by the Supermarine Southampton in 1925.
A purlin that is joined to the back of a principal rafter.
Operations in excess of 25 cms. If possible state depth in Description.
An object that has been cut off.
A pit where bears were housed for baiting and entertainment purposes. If not used for baiting use BEAR ENCLOSURE.
A small building used by the keeper of a castle, park, etc.
A photographic slide of a colour (polychromatic) image.
Boulders of unprocessed granite.
Transport version of the four-engined Lancaster bomber. Serving from 1943 to 1951, and all metal in construction, this aircraft was used extensively during the Berlin airlift.
A building or site where lead is obtained from ore.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of metal boxes or cases.
Specialist hospital treating patients with physical disabilities.
An establishment where the theory and practice of medicine is taught.
A terraced field usually found on hillsides. Comprising a flat strip of land, called the tread, and a steep, scarped lynchet or edge, called the riser.
Photographic negative developed on waxed paper.
A concrete, circular concave dish 20 feet in diameter used as an acoustic listening device to detect approaching enemy aircraft.
The edible seed of the palm tree.
A workshop used for completing the shape of a product or part by turning on a lathe or wheel.
A building containing the colliery showers. Also often containing first aid and mine rescue facilities.
A hole dug to provide a firm base for an upright post, often with stone packing. Use broader monument type where known.
A tower, normally forming part of a larger structure, housing a staircase.
A burial ground for victims of the plague.
A hall, apartment or large room, designed or used primarily for festive or state functions.
Regularly cultivated and re-seeded grassland (but not including temporary grassland within arable rotation - this would be classified under Cultivated Land).

Small, light, fast, all-purpose craft designed primarily for inland use. Generally flat-bottomed, often with rocker; sharp bow, sharp or transom stern, lapstrake or carvel planking. Propelled by oars, sails or motor. Used for fishing and leisure.
An establishment for the testing of eyesight, making up of optical prescriptions and the sale of spectacles.
Single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer used in secondary flying training schools. Serving from 1939-50, was also used as a target tug for gunnery practice.
A site with one or more defensive earthworks, often at a river crossing incorporating natural features which define parts of the curtilage.

A covering of thin copper plates secured, on top of a layer of tar and horsehair, to the bottom of wooden ships to protect the hull against weeds, barnacles and especially Teredo navalis, a wood-boring worm prevalent in tropical seas.
A pit used for the excavation of clay suitable for making bricks.
A place from which clay is extracted.
Mascarene Islands, Africa; dependent territory as a departement of France.

A tower situated above the rampart walkway and in between the angle towers along a defensive structure, such as a castle wall. They were used as lookout towers, roofed strongpoints or platforms from which missiles could be discharged or artillery fired.
Specify in Description using: golf course, playing fields etc.
A cairn featuring a mound of small diameter (normally less than 6m), which is surrounded by a kerb of stones which are considerably taller than the mound.
A hook on harness to help attach items.

A steel pipe driven into the ground at a shallow, oblique angle and packed with explosives. They were intended to be detonated on the approach of a hostile amroured vehicle or tank in order to create an obstacle directly in its path.

A building used by the society, fraternity or order organized under this name with initiatory rites, mystic signs of recognition and various degrees of dignity or honour, for social or benevolent purposes.
A Very High Frequency device to allow aircraft to pinpoint their position as an aid to naviagation. Built as part of the Rotor programme.
A stone placed over or at the head or foot of a grave, or at the entrance to a tomb.
A tool used in making wooden hurdles.
The equivalent of a colonnade but using pilasters.

A device used to slow the fall of a person or an object from a great height. When open it consists of a large umberella like sheet with wires or ropes converging from the edge to a harness attached to the lower end.
A public music or dancing establishment often with facilities for gambling.
A bridge, usually resting on raised arches, carrying a railway across low-lying land or water.
American twin-engined medium bomber. Entered service with the US 22nd Bombardment Group at Langley Field in February 1941. Also served with the 14th and 39th RAF squadrons.

The Glenn L. Martin Company, established in 1909 by Glenn L Martin. Produced the first successful American-designed twin-engined aeroplane, the Martin Twin, which was then converted for use as a passenger aircraft.
A mill or factory in which raw cotton, wool, nylon or other material is spun into yarn or thread.
An image created manually using paint or pigments, to record, illustrate or convey impressions.
A small cutting hook on a long handle.
A decoy site designed to simulate a burning urban area during a bombing raid in order to lure enemy bombers away from legitimate targets.
A building for the weighing or testing of metals, eg. at a mine site.
A friary belonging to the Friars of the Sack also known as Friars of Penance or Penitentia.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Friary Of Friars Of The Sack

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: American A-20 twin-engined, light, day bomber. Some supplied to the RAF and known as the Boston I. Subsequent variations adapted to night flying and re-christened the Havoc.

Any form of arms or ammunition whether from a formal organized military context or as a general cargo. Use specific terms - e.g. swords, bombs, where known; otherwise use this term primarily in contexts where the arms are unspecified or ancient.
A receptacle to hold water used in baptism usually found in a baptistery or nave of a church.
A structure, usually sunk into the ground, for the purpose of allowing total bodily immersion as part of a baptismal ceremony.
A small piece of metal used to mend ceramic, glass or metal plates and vessels.

An institution created with the merging of Gaols and Houses of Correction in 1865. Nowadays term used for a prison to which people are sent whilst remanded in custody before trial or direct from court after conviction.
A capital of the Tuscan Order featuring a square abacus.
A cemetery for baptist followers.
A priory of double order of Fontevrault nuns and brethren.

An anti aircraft battery armed with 3 inch rockets with a ceiling of 22,000 feet. Both single and multiple launchers were designed. Single launchers being used to defend vulnerable points such as coastal batteries with multiple launchers defending town.
A plan featuring a lobby entry, situated at one end of a side wall, which provides access to one room only.
An artificial mound of earth indicating either the former site of a windmill or built as the base of a post windmill.
A cruck blade, sometimes jointed, set in the centre of a gable wall, usually of a cruck-framed building.
Large covered spaces where the steel plate used for ship construction was cut and marked out, prior to being craned onto the hull, etc.
A crane located on a quayside used for the loading and unloading of goods and materials to and from vessels.
A crane fixed to a quay, used for the unloading of ships cargoes.
The cleaning and sorting of horse hair mainly for use in the upholstery trade.
A commercial building used for the production of detailed, often technical, drawings.
A tablet with a handle fitted to the back of it.
Mark 3 or the third variant of an aircraft with its associated modifications.
A place where products are manufactured from wood.
A joist which rests on top of a beam.
A communal residence of secular vicars whose duties included the education of choristers attached to cathedrals and collegiate churches.

A prefabricated structure consisting of six curved asbestos cement sheets that were bolted together, without a frame, creating a hut semi-circular in section. Used on airfields during WWII and manufactured from 1942 by the Turner Asbestos Company.
A place where sand is extracted from surface workings.
A stable, on two or more levels.
An earth derived pigment.
A space used for the storage of chemicals.
A bowl adapted by the addition of three or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
A rafter set diagonally where two sloping rooves meet.
A dam constructed across a stream to raise its water-level and make it available to power a mill wheel.
Scissor like tool, usually larger than scissors, used for cutting, pruning or trimming.
A specialist hospital treating patients with chest disorders and diseases, can be pre sanatoria.

A tandem two-seat, twin-engined, all-weather, long-range supersonic jet interceptor fighter/fighter-bomber originally developed for the United States Navy by McDonnell Aircraft.It first entered service in 1960 with the U.S. Navy.
An unidentified feature on the seabed recorded by fishermen as an obstruction to trawling.
Floatable vessel used as a floodgate in docks.
A horizontal member dividing a window into two or more lights.
A raised floor along the side of a line at a railway station, for convenience in entering and alighting from a train.
A plan featuring three foils or lobes radiating outwards from a central point.
Specify in Description.
A decorated, hanging sign, bearing the name and also often a pictorial representation of the inn or public house to which it is attached.
A bridge that incorporates a span that moves upwards vertically to provide a passageway for navigation.
A piece of ground, or a building, on which artillery may be fired at targets.
An area of ground on which anti tank guns can be placed for testing purposes and to practice firing at targets.
A place where stained glass is manufactured, traditionally for church windows.
Use for vessels registered in Georgia.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
The Grumman Aircraft Engineering Corporation founded by Leroy R Grumman and incorporated in 1929.
Three-crew, single-engine carrierborne torpedo-bomber. Entered service in 1942, first seeing action during the Battle of Midway. Served with the US Navy until 1956.
A WWII structure designed to project sheets of flame across an area such as a beach, the sea or a road, to hinder attacking forces.
A passage that runs axially across the end of a hall with a screen between it and the hall and doorways to service rooms on the other side.
A centre for the teaching of crafts.

Interbellum, twin-engined, five-crew, biplane flying-boat with a characteristic triple tail-fin. Entered service in 1925 and used for general reconnaissance duties. The Mk.I had a wooden fuselage, whilst the Mk.II's was metal in construction.
A scientific laboratory where marine life is studied and researched.
A grass, used in paper making, native to Spain and North Africa.
A pilaster without base or capital.
A place where letters and parcels are sorted before being distributed. Usually found at a large general post office.
A garden building on an estate used by fishing parties.
A specialist hospital for the medical treatment of skin diseases.
To mark the end of a turnpike road.

American, single-engine fighter designed for operation from US Naval aircraft carriers. The Hellcat was a more powerful version of the Wildcat, a total of 1000 being provided to the Fleet Air Arm under Lend-Lease.
Transparent, hard substance made by fusing soda-silica which solidifies from a molten state.
Four-engined, five to seven crew, heavy bomber biplane. Entered service in 1918.
French Banker, fishing vessel for the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, generally three-masted or of brig type, from the late 19th and 20th centuries.
Second World War allied patrol-bomber built by Lockheed Vega, a Lockheed subsidiary. This aircraft was a military development of the Lodestar, USAF designation B-34.
The area where the act of Offertory, where bread and wine are placed upon the altar, takes place.
An arcaded upper aisle, wall passage or blind arcade, usually occurring in large Romanesque or Gothic churches, above the aisle and below the clerestory.
An engineering works that produces machinery specially for use in textile making.
Three-seat, single engine, high wing braced monoplane designed for civil use and first flown in 1929. Saw military service in World War 2 in an Army co-operation and communications role.
A Roman mixing vessel with a gritted inner surface.
A hospital for the treatment of diseases of the nerves and nervous system.
A stone found on route to a churchyard on which the coffin is rested during transportation.
A structure, often within a CHURCHYARD or LYCH GATE, on which a coffin could rest prior to burial.
An apparatus for weighing people, animals or things.
Artificial water channel, usually leading to a mill.
An arch associated with the portion of the stage between the curtain and the orchestra.
An educational establishment where the art of garden cultivation is taught.
A piece of iron cut from blooms and lengths of bar, probably for transportation, which were then reworked.
Use specific form where known.
A works where crude oil is distilled into its fractions or cuts.
A container for keeping the ashes of the dead after cremation.
An area of ground on which a house is built. A platform is often the sole surviving evidence for a house.
A stone-lined pit in which seaweed was burnt. The calcined ashes were used in the manufacture of soap and glass, amongst other things.
A public house offering lodgings to the passengers, and stabling for the horses of stage coaches.
A building used to store navigational buoys.
A gable with sides shaped like a flight of steps.
Large, brown, hard-shelled seeds of the palm tree Cocos nucifera, the flesh and liquid contained within the shell can be eaten.
A wooden commode containing earth, which was used to cover and absorb human waste. An alternative, and rival, to the water closet.

Twin-engine, three-crew, long-range heavy bomber biplane. Entered service in 1917. Of wooden construction with a fabric covering, the Vimy was fitted with a skid under the nose of its fuselage to prevent tipping forward upon landing.
A place where the science of historical and comparative language is taught.
A lid with a shallow domed profile and a central knob. (Source: MPRG)
Depicting the nature and arrangement of strets and buildings within a built-up or urban area. For views within a singel street use STREET SCENE.
A tray used for separating the grain from husks and straw.

A section of a building distinguished from the rest either architecturally or as a separate structure joined to the main building, often intended for entertainment, specialised functions or ornamental purposes.
A military base for the training of SOE operatives in the skills and techniques required to survive in enemy-occupied territory.
A military camp providing training facilities.
A large, rectangular pillbox based on the FW3/28 with the addition of a small infantry chamber to one side of the main gun chamber.
Unenclosed wasteland, forest and pasture used in common by the community.
A glasshouse for the cultivation of ferns.
A place where gold is worked into articles or products.
A large wooden structure built alongside the edge of a canal where narrow boats may lie for the loading and unloading of goods.
A bowl with no noticeable base angle, so that the walls and base form a continuous rounded curve (Source: MPRG)
A workshop used for the manufacture of clay tobacco pipes.
A large jug or pitcher with a wide mouth.
A hooked blade used to cut crops. All the blade is to one side of the handle rather than being on both sides as in a sickle.
A shaped piece of wood that makes up a barrel, key etc.
Cloth finishing process using machinery to raise the nap of the cloth before shearing.
East Friesian Islands, Germany
A framework, often made of steel, supporting a crane or similar structure, or for supporting a platform or stage.
A grave or sepulchre including a monument.
The main vertical axle running through the centre of a mill.
A set of clippers for finger or toe nails.
A colourless, thick sweet liquid used in the manufacture of chemicals.
A street market.

A form of Neolithic burial monument primarily found in Cornwall and the Scilly Isles. It comprises a round cairn, usually with a retaining wall or kerb, and an entrance leading directly into a chamber.
A building used as a social venue by people interested in, and involved with, the sport of sailing. Often situated by a MARINA.
Poles of timber, metal etc. used as masts, booms or yards on a vessel.
A school where the applied sciences and the mechanical arts are taught.
The residence of an engineer.
Single-seat carrierborne jet fighter. Originally conceived as an RAF land-fighter, entered Fleet Air Arm service in 1951 and was the first jet fighter to be standardised in first-line squadrons.
A steam whistle or siren used for signalling purposes.
A signal station incorporating equipment for visually conveying coded communications.
Buildings in London formerly used as hostels for law students.
The residence of a lock-keeper.
A steep bank or slope. In fortifications, the bank or wall immediately in front of and below the rampart.
The dried leaves of the plants, Nicotiana tabacum or Nicotiana rustica, which are smoked (in pipes, cigars or cigarettes), chewed or taken as snuff for their relaxing properties.
A factory where matresses are made.
A structure used for drying yarn in open fields.
Building housing the machinery for the shredding and grinding of wood in running water and pressing of the resulting fibres into a pulp.
Sulphate of Barium
A factory where linoleum is manufactured.
A site where the manufacture of glass bottles takes place.

Twin-engine, three-crew, long-range heavy bomber biplane. Entered service in 1917. Of wooden construction with a fabric covering, the Vimy was fitted with a skid under the nose of its fuselage to prevent tipping forward upon landing.
A building housing machinery.
A Mark 1B aircraft which has undergone further modification to enhance performance or armament.
A prepared core from which a single flake or blade has been produced. The technique was primarily used in the Palaeolithic and Neolithic.
A beaker with a construction above the base to form a waisted profile. (Source: MPRG)
A flat, horizontal strip, block or moulding, sometimes decorated, on a facade or interrupting an architectural feature such as a column.
A two-seat, reconnaissance biplane developed from the FK2 with a more powerful, but heavier, engine. Primarily used for training in the UK.
Bridge for carrying pipes between buildings or working areas.
Character and / or management not determined.
A dispersed farmstead where the farm buildings and farmhouse are loosely grouped together within the boundary of the farmstead.
A house occupied by an employee of a waterworks. Usually found in association with a pumping station or waterworks.
A drill bit used in metal and wood working.
A platform or other structure for the use of a band of musicians.
A pulley block and metal ring used to guide a line or rope and cause it to run easily without chafing.
A building where artefacts, scientific specimens, antiquities and similar objects of interest could be examined through microscopes by members of the public.
A bishop's court for ecclesiastical causes and offences, formerly having wider jurisdiction in matters of moral discipline.
A piece of fabric for wiping the nose, face or hands.
An instrument for measuring and indicating the height of tide.
A WWII British biplane produced by Hawker Aircraft, used for army cooperation duties.
Twin-engined monoplane originally designed as a reconnaissance aircraft, but also widely used as a trainer. Entered RAF service in 1936.
Three-seat, single engine, high wing braced monoplane designed for civil use and first flown in 1929. Saw military service in World War 2 in an Army co-operation and communications role.
A point in a village providing water for drinking and washing.
Single-engined fighter, developed from the Camel. Entered service in 1918 and became the RAF's first mainstay peacetime fighter.
A shed for storing fishing bait.
Heart failure and various heart conditions.
A container to provide a set amount of gun powder.

The Gloster Grebe was the Royal Air Force's first post WWI fighter aircraft, entering service in 1923. Designed by Henry Folland, a single-seat, single-engined biplane of fabric-covered wood construction with two Vickers machine guns (133 planes built).
A tool used for weeding and breaking up the ground prior to planting.
Three-seat tactical support aircraft. Entering service with the US 9th Air Force in 1944, the Invader had a bomb load of 4,000 lbs and was later used as a conventional medium bomber.
64 Type DFW55373 single projector sites arranged in an 8x8 grid or in 4 groups of 16. 30m between each projector, with hardened personnel and ammunition shelters located midway between each
A two or three wheeled motor vehicle.

A jet-powered tailless delta wing high-altitude strategic bomber plane, operated by the RAF from 1956 until 1984. Typically armed with nuclear weapons but capable of conventional bombing missions. Used as a nuclear deterrent in the Cold War.
Use for complexes where services (eg. restaurants, shops) are provided in addition to facilities for buying petrol.
A mill for beating and cleaning cloth, using soap or fullers earth.
A portable beehive, often made of straw.
Use for an aircraft propelled by a jet engine, which provides forward thrust by pulling in air, heating and compressing it, then expelling it along with exhaust gases.
One of a line of blocks on the floor of a building slip on which the keel of the ship to be constructed is laid. Also used in dry docks to rest a ship when a dock is pumped dry.
Fairground attraction designed to create optical illusions to give a sense of unbalance and unease.
A place where silverware is manufactured.
A room set aside for the purpose of reading, such as in a library or a club.
A large building, situated at a railway terminus, used for the temporary storage of goods or merchandise awaiting transportation to or from a railway.
A door adorned with panels, usually arranged in pairs.
A type of updraught intermittent kiln of rectangular plan and battered sides, but with an open top.
Monument thought to be archaeological or historical but proved to be natural.
The residence of a lacemaker.
A booth, cubicle or recess, often enclosed, in which a priest, usually screened from view, hears confessions.
Use for blocks in Emergency Medical Scheme hospitals (WWII).
Photographic film responsive to infrared radiation. Used to record temperature variations in the subject, indicative of hidden archaeological or architectural features.
A factory for the assembly of components. Usually associated with the manufacture of vehicles: cars, lorries, etc.
The central part of a road between the pavements or the verges.
A section of roadway attached at one end to a harbour or dockside and ending at a landing stage, rising and falling with the tide, for the loading and unloading of vehicles and pedestrians.
A half gable or half pediment concealing the lean-to roof of an aisle.
A sheet of flat film, 105 x 148mm in size, carrying a matrix of micro images.
A garden incorporating fountains and pools in which aquatic and other water-loving plants are grown.
A building or buildings used for the production of paints, varnishes, colours and distemper.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of fistular and rectal disorders and diseases.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Hospital For Fistula And Rectal Diseases

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A small tank or cistern, often lead or cast-iron and sometimes ornamented, that collects rainwater from a gutter or channel prior to it being discharged.
A building for the manufacture of condensed milk.
Flat stones used to create flat surfaces, e.g. pavements.
A device used in the production of hard cheeses that exerts pressure upon fresh curds in order to remove and drain away excess whey.
A place where stained glass is manufactured, traditionally for church windows.
A bridge with two or more decks allowing it to carry various modes of transport at the same time.
German three-engined air/sea rescue and transport flying boat. Entered service in 1940 as a replacement for the DO18.
A building used to pump sewage from the sewers to the filter beds of a sewage works.
A handled tool with two or more prongs used for digging, cultivation etc.
A mowing implement with a large curved blade and a long handle.
A structure used to test the aerodynamics of aircraft or vehicles.
A pedestrianized shopping street, or a more complex arrangement of shopping 'squares' and walkways.
A type of large steel framed aircraft hangar introduced by the Royal Air Force in its Expansion Period with a number of designs between 1934 and 1939, to accomodate heavy bombers.
Medium hard, green/black coloured. Found in many igneous and metamorphic rocks.
Originally designed as a light bomber but diverted for use as a high speed target tug to replace out-dated biplanes.

A single engine two seat cabin monoplane tourer, first flown in 1933 as a successor to the Puss Moth. Impressed into military sevice in WWII by the RAF and the Fleet Air Arm as a liaison and communications aircraft, also used by training units.
A small brick structure attached to a house for keeping fish prior to cooking.
A device with a funnel-shaped entrance designed for catching eels.
A sign, situated near a road or bridge, indicating a toll.
A meeting hall of the Temperance Society.

Any animal other than livestock (animals carried as food); animals used for transport (horses; mules); and domestic pets. Such animals may be exported as specimens, for zoos, menageries, and circuses, or as unusual pets (e.g. elephants, monkeys).
An embankment or cutting on a railway system, surfaced at a uniform gradient, up or down which materials were hauled by rope.
British three-seat, single-engine light bomber. All metal in construction, this monoplane had a 1000 lb bomb load.
A window in a spire, often in the form of a dormer.
A brush or perforated ball on a handle used to sprinkle holy water.
An institution for the imprisonment of vagrants and misdemeanants.
A place where a yearly or half-yearly court of record is held by lords of certain manors.
A base embellished with horizontal reeds and other mouldings.
An object made to hurl a spear further and faster than possible by hand.

A rectangular chamber of brick or stone with heavy wooden gates at either end equipped with sluices to let water in and out, thereby enabling a canal boat to be lowered or raised to a different level.
A hut, usually containing lead pans, in which salt water is boiled to produce salt.
A bracelet holding charms or being itself a charm.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of ear, nose and throat disorders and diseases.
A works where cotton waste is stored or processed.
A lock at the point where two waterways join together.
A steam engine working an underground cable haulage system in a late 19th century coal mine.
The residence of a well keeper.
A mill used for the sizing and drying of warp threads before they were wound onto warp beams as part of the power-weaving process.
A building or structure in which processed cloth is dried.
An 18th century garden with a Chinese layout and ornaments.
A round, oval or rectangular straight-sided dish, divided into two or more units or compartments of varying sizes by vertical slab partitions. (Source: MPRG)
A standard latine block on RAF airfields.

A circular bank in which trees have been planted for ornamental purposes or to create an enclosure. May exist purely as a bank which has been formed over the stumps of the trees which had been planted to form the enclosure.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of ear disorders and diseases.
Part of the glass making process, the frit is broken up into a crucible and heated to create glass.
A rod used to measure the imperial measurements of a pole or a perch.
A type of calcining kiln used in the processing of iron ore.
Originally, a house of higher social status in a town or port, often with a storage cellar.
A small spoon used with incense.
An old ship hull used as a base for lifting tackle.
Ornamental plasterwork applied to the exterior of a building, especially timber-framed houses of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries..
A factory where lace is manufactured.
Protective eyewear.
A large structure, usually associated with power stations, in which hot water undergoes a process of cooling before being re-used .
Pieces of timber shaped for use in the construction of buildings, barrels etc.
A site where limestone is extracted.
A site for the sale or hire of agricultural machinery.
A joint in which both timbers are reduced in thickness.
Developed from the DH4, featured the pilot and gunner cockpits in closer proximity, but suffered from engine reliability problems. Also known as the Ninak, saw service from 1918 to 1931.

Name given to a workhouse after 1929. The Local Government Act of 1929 abolished Poor Law Unions and Guardians, and control passed to public assistance authorities run by county boroughs and county councils. Lasted until 1948 when poor laws were repealed.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Fourth Rate Ship Of The Line
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A ship of the line mounting between 46 and 64 guns
A building adjoining a cricket pitch with facilities for players and spectators.
Large, three-engined, long range reconnaissance flying boat. Wooden hull and frame construction, with linen covering. Entered service in 1930.
A working tunnel or gallery in a mine used for the extraction of ironstone.
An enclosure containing a dock, boat yard, warehouse, etc, in which canal vessels are built and repaired, and all sorts of stores and merchandise for transportation brought together.
Use for vessels registered in the former Czechoslovakia between 1918 and 1992. See also CZECH and SLOVAK.
A house used to accommodate camels, often found at a zoo or wildlife park.
A road whose upkeep and repair was financed by the exaction of a toll.

Twin-engined, four-seat torpedo-bomber designed to replace the Vildebeest. Entered service with RAF Coastal Command in 1939. Later versions incorporated a remote-controlled machine gun with periscope sight.
A steam engine which produces rotary motion.
A bowl used in the marriage ceremony.
Single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer used in secondary flying training schools. Serving from 1939-50, was also used as a target tug for gunnery practice.

Monument either never or no longer visible above ground surface, but whose presence is indicated by proven below ground stratigraphy revealed by deliberate investigation, including geophysical survey, or other surface disturbance.
A tall, metal structure erected as a support for electric power cables.
A gate which allows water to pass into a dock, etc, at flood tide, and by which it is retained during the ebb tide.
A side-opening steel framed shed. A smaller version of the SEAPLANE SHED (TYPE F) they were built from 1916 on RNAS seaplane bases
A table of months and days in the year.
The part of an organ or similar instrument into which air is pushed then is emitted through the pipes.
Any church of the Anglican Communion.
A block for mounting a horse.
A long slim candle used for igniting objects.
Northern Hemisphere
A horse-powered winding engine used at mining sites.
People who leave their native country to settle in another, often for financial or religious reasons.
Loading machinery tipping coal into railway wagons, usually at a pithead.
An hydraulically powered machine that tips coal into railway wagons, usually situated at a pithead.
A wall-mounted moulding defining the upper edge of the dado, intended to protect the wall's surface from damage caused by chairs being pushed against it.
Any member that connects two bodies, such as the sloping sides of a roof, to prevent them pulling apart.
A place where graphite is extracted.
An external structure used to sit on.
A civilian settlement outside a Roman fort.
A light anti aircraft position, usually open-walled and built of concrete, brick or sandbags used to emplace one or more machine guns mounted on pintels.

A British medium-range biplane airliner designed and built by Handley Page in 1921. A twin-engined variant of the Handley Page W series (W8, W9), retired in 1931. Built for Imperial Airways (4 units built).

An enclosed feature, usually sub-terranean, constructed to contain water for public or private recreation and sporting activities. Often part of a larger SPORTS CENTRE. Use OUTDOOR SWIMMING POOL for unenclosed pools.
A platform on which corpses are placed and allowed to decompose in the open air, so as to leave only the bones for subsequent burial.
A departmental building within a college or university where a particular subject is taught and administered.
A stone used for divination.
A site where lime (calcium carbonate) is made.
A chapel for the use of travellers and pilgrims.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter-bomber developed from the Typhoon and the abandoned Tornado. Entered service in 1944 with its greatest success being in destroying V.1. flying bombs. One of the fastest World War 2 aircraft, with a top speed of 436 mph.
A furnace used for smelting or re-heating of iron, either for casting or for further working.
A motor in which rotary motion is produced by steam power.
A horizontal, riven board, tapered in section, used for external cladding.
Any of the pieces of hard tissue consisting largely of calcium phosphate that make up the skeleton of a vertebrate animal.
A type of pottery kiln in which air rises up inside the oven to be forced back down and out through the base of the oven.
A barracks comprising eight barrack blocks accessed via a central corridor. With four blocks on either side of the corridor the whole structure resembled a spider in plan.

A maritime coring technique which uses vibration to facilitate ground penetration. With the force of gravity, and sometimes a piston, it can penetrate much deeper layers although the vibration provokes a slight mixing of the sediments.

An astonomical instrument, and navigational aid, in the form of one eighth of a circle and used to measure the angular altitude of heavenly bodies. Invented in 1731 and used into the 19th Century, it was superceded by the sextant.

A type of stoneware jug dating to the 16th and 17th centuries, popularly known as a Bellarmine jug, shaped in the figure of a bearded man. They were produced in the Cologne region, particularly Frechen.
Narrow strips of wood used in the building industry.
A handled tool with a broad blade with slightly raised sides used for scooping or shovelling.
A small piece of timber occupying the angle between two other timbers.
Subsidiary settlement of lay brothers attached to some Carthusian monasteries.
The masonry beneath a lock gate, sometimes projecting several feet from the gate.
A bay in a two storeyed house open to the roof to allow smoke to escape.
A machine for further attenuating a sliver of cotton after it has been through a draw frame.
A rock carving, especially a prehistoric one.
A place of residence and worship for Anglican monks.

A metal, often decorative, hinge constructed with a single large strap attached to the surface of the moving part wiht a loop in the end which fits over a pintle attached to the adjacent stationary frame.
The residence of a canal worker.
A factory where lace is manufactured.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Second Rate Ship Of The Line
skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A ship of the line mounting between 90 and 98 guns on three gun decks
A pond with underwater arches where the poles for masts were stored to prevent them from drying and splitting.
A workshop used for the small-scale production of leather goods.
A mound kerbed with wooden stakes or boulders.
A site where small electrical goods such as radios, lamps and heaters are manufactured.
A factory where tapestries were manufactured.
A structure in which pottery tiles were baked.
A porch with columns and pediments.
A works used for the production of parchment from animal skin.
A hearth for roasting metallic ore, usually non ferrous, before smelting.
A lock where the gates rise vertically. Rarely found on canals but common on navgable rivers in the Fens, particularly the river Nene.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter biplane renowned for its high performance and manoeuvrability. Entered service in 1917.
A cargo vessel constructed in the U.S.A. during World War II from prefabricated sections by welding.
A hard copy of digital data that has been printed onto paper.
A ditch that indicates the limit of an area or a piece of land.

A stone core which is irregular in shape. It can have numerous usuable or abandoned striking platforms. It is the most common core type and it is often the last attempt of a knapper to extract the final usable flakes form the core. (Source: SARC)

A twin-engined, multi-role aircraft built by Junkers. Originally designed as a medium bomber with the speed of a fighter, but its adaptability allowed it to fulfil the roles of night fighter, torpedo-bomber, anti-tank aircraft and photo-reconnaissance.
A transverse ceiling beam set below wall-plate level in order to increase head room within the roof space; it carries knee principals, or the struts or braces of an interrupted tiebeam truss.
A piece of furniture containing a chamber pot or wash basin.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of ear, nose and throat disorders and diseases.
A small narrow pointed missile that is thrown or shot.
A raised platform, especially in a theatre or auditorium, for the use of performers or speakers etc.
Use for vessels registered in Latvia.
A vertical structure used to draw off smoke from a fire.
A circular range of houses dating from the 18th century, eg. John Wood's Circus at Bath.
A circular kiln or oven used in the manufacture of bricks. Common in Staffordshire in the 18th century.

Twin-engined, four-seat torpedo-bomber designed to replace the Vildebeest. Entered service with RAF Coastal Command in 1939. Later versions incorporated a remote-controlled machine gun with periscope sight.
A hall built for the use of people living within a parish boundary.
One of a pair of posts, placed symmetrically on a tie beam, supporting a collar purlin or plate.
A long graduated staff used in surveying to help measure distance or height.
The blue dyestuff prepared from the leaves of the plant Isatis tinctoria, and sometimes used to discribe the plant itself. Later superseded by indigo.
Paper applied to walls.
A bridge that incorporates a span that moves upwards vertically to provide a passageway for navigation.
Three storey house with a topshop; machinery powered by shafting through the upper floor.
A room over the vestry of a church, often thought to have been where anchorets lived.
An often secluded garden set below the level of surrounding ground, usually surrounded with terraces.
A house, the inhabitant of which keeps an official register e.g. a registrar's house near a cemetery would keep an official record of deaths and burials.
A pit dug to protect a small group of infantry men.
A convex, finger-like moulding, usually applied in a series to form a pattern of ridges.
Arado Flugzeugwerke. Formed in 1931 in Germany when the aircraft manufacturer Albatros Flugzeugwerke was declared bankrupt and part of it merged with Arado Handells-Gessellschaft.
Single engine, two-crew shipboard reconnaissance and patrol seaplane. Entered service in 1939, this was the last combat floatplane built in Europe.
A building used to dry wool in.
A section of roadway attached at one end to a harbour or dockside and ending at a landing stage, rising and falling with the tide, for the loading and unloading of vehicles and pedestrians.
Factory making slippers.
A movable bridge that swings or rotates around a central pier, or one that is pivoted only at one end, to provide a passageway for navigation.

A jug with a pierced bunghole just above the base. the bunghole can be made through an applied knob or disc of clay, or simply a hole in the vessel wall. In use, the hole would probably have had a tap or spigot attached. (Source: MPRG)
A simple, one-roomed structural plan.
A steel framed seaplane hangar designed for Royal Navy Air Stations by the admiralty in 1917-1918.
An elevated area or platform in a synagogue where the person reading aloud from the Torah stands.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 14383/40.
A small bar raised or lowered by a latchlifter which is used to fasten gates or doors etc.
A yard intended for the purpose of taking exercise, for example within the grounds of a prison.
A passageway or corridor beteen two areas which is covered.
A place of worship for Christian Scientists, a sect founded in the mid-19th century in America who believe that God is the only reality and can bring healing to humanity.
An earthen mound, usually within an ornamental garden, on which a tree was planted.
A container for drinking, with a base and stem but without handles.
Single engine, two-crew shipboard reconnaissance and patrol seaplane. Entered service in 1939, this was the last combat floatplane built in Europe.
A bridge, usually resting on raised arches, carrying a road across low-lying land or water.
An informal garden attached to a cottage where flowers, vegetables and fruit trees are grown.
A garden containing trees or shrubs pruned and trained into various geometric, zoomorphic or fantastic shapes.
Material consisting of fragments of stone, sand, gravel, slag etc. used in the manufacture of concrete.
A small container for holding oil, vinegar, salt etc for use at the table.
A maritime monument where the hull structure and fabric of a vessel remain wholly or mainly intact.
Early form of photographic print.
A temporary castle built to house and protect troops beseiging another castle or town.
An edging of stone forming the kerb of a path.
A bridge, carrying a footpath or road, usually across marshy or waterlogged ground.
A place of worship at the site of a mortuary.

A British six-seat single-engined light aircraft, built by Airspeed Limited. First flew in 1933, saw some use as an airliner. The first British type with a retractable undercarriage. Designed by Hessell Tiltman (co-founder). 16 Couriers built.
An individual section of panelling. Can form fences, ceilings, an outer layer to a wall etc.
An establishment where chocolate was available as a beverage.
A hospital where more 'natural' means of treatment are used rather than conventional methods.
A house built by a local authority.
A village laid out systematically with spacious and garden-like surroundings.
A seat of state, often highly decorative, used by monarchs, bishops, etc.
A commercial bakery or bread factory. If domestic use BAKEHOUSE.

Two-seat, twin-engined fighter/fighter-bomber designed as a replacement for the Bf110. Of the 600 or so produced, only 258 reached the Luftwaffe due to serious design faults. The ME210 was superseded by the ME410 Hornisse.
A site where merchandise and goods are temporarily stored before or after transportation by rail.

Wood and fabric transport glider, twenty of which were produced with twin Bristol Mercury engines. Fitted with a hinged nose for loading and unloading, this was the largest glider used by the RAF and could accomodate a 7-ton tank.
The residence of a lacemaker.
A large Mediterranean cargo or transport vessel of the 15th to 17th century, usually less than 400 tons.

Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber: Curtiss P40 Warhawk, known to the RAF as the Tomahawk, later renamed Kittyhawk. Serving from 1941 to 1942, control difficulties in dive attacks impeded bombing accuracy, resulting in use for larger targets only.

A stone building with external access to the domestic accommodation via a permanent stair. The ground floor is normally used as a byre in rural contexts, but in an urban setting it may be intended for one of a number of other non domestic uses.
Four-engined, five to seven crew, heavy bomber biplane. Entered service in 1918.
A hot steam bath introduced from the East, in which heavy perspiration is followed by soaping, washing, massage and cooling.
A bit which scoops out material.
An office for the payment of wages, especially in industrial or commercial complexes.
Traditionally any food preserved by boiling with sugar, salting, pickling etc. Nowadays used specifically for fruit which has been preserved with sugar.
A mould in which bullets or musket balls are cast.
A chemical works engaged in the production of the coal tar derivative phenol, a chemical used for the manufacture of explosives during WWI.
A crude, stone-built shelter for persons involved in lime production and the processing of lime burning.
A storehouse associated with rope manufacture (eg. in naval dockyards).
A building housing a gas engine, used as a power source for driving other machinery.
A projecting spout to throw water from a gutter away from the wall, frequently decorated with grotesque figures to spew out evil away from the House of God.

Clothes which are distinctive in cut, colour and fabric and worn by members of the armed forces, emergency services or civilian organizations to help to distinguish their members form other organizations.
A circular ornament worn on the head.
A pillbox built to a design by the commander of the Royal Engineers for the Colchester Garrison.
An area of ground used for children to play on, often attached to a school.

A British two-seater army co-operation aircraft manufactured by Hawker Aircraft for the Royal Air Force. A Hart variant biplane that first flew in 1931, becoming a prominent British aircraft in the inter-war period with over 700 units built.
A meeting hall of the verderers, who were the officers appointed to maintain the King's forests.

Structural elements (parts of hull etc.) or fixtures and fittings (masts, etc.) lost during a naval engagement without incurring the actual loss of a ship. May also be used as a monument type for expended ammunition (e.g. shells, cannonballs).
A portable timepiece capable of being worn on the wrist or carried in a pocket.
A mobile crane.
A mobile crane usually found on a marine or inland quay.
A mug with straight sides flaring outwards from the base towards the rim. (Source: MPRG)

Three/four-crew, single-engine, shipboard observation and air/sea rescue amphibian seaplane. Entered RAF service in 1936. Also employed for gunnery spotting, anti-submarine and convoy protection duties.

A technique that measures the amount of time it takes pulses of electromagnetic energy sent into the ground, from a transmitter, to reflect back from the interfaces between layers and other subsurface features in order to produce a subsurface profile.
Factory making slippers.
A jar with one or more lips added on the outside of the vessel wall over a hole pierced through the wall. The lips do not usually rise above rim level. (Source: MPRG)
An arch whose purpose is to arrest or prevent structural movement in a building.
An area of a building functioning as a hospital.
A multi-purpose farm building in an outlaying area of a farm.
Photographic print using carbon
A circular window with tracery or shafts radiating from the centre.
A projecting wall or structure, such as a parapet or battlement, supported by a series of corbels.
An aircraft hangar designed by T. Bedford Consulting Engineers usually erected on aircraft factory sites rather than operational airfields.
A Roman sanctuary, devoted to the Graeco-Roman cult of Mithras.
A wing of a house used specifically for the storage of household materials and victuals.
A drinking vessel, usually curved in shape, fashioned out of animal tusk or horn and sometimes with bands of decoration.

A dating technique for the founding of individual populations based on the assumption of steady rates of mutation in mitochondrial DNA. Sometimes used to produce dates for stratigraphic layers containing fossil specimens of populations.
A strip of material, leather etc used to hold two sides of an object together.
A vessel for maintaining the buoys, hawsers and netting of a boom defence.

A jug that incorporates a practical joke or conundrum into its construction. A combination of cut-outs in the body and hollow handles and tubes render conventional use impossible. The puzzle being to work out how to empty it. (Source: MPRG)

The rarest of the recognized types of round barrow, consisting of a flat, wide circular mound, which may be surrounded by a ditch. They occur widely across southern England with a marked concentration in East and West Sussex.
Coiled substance, usually metal or plastic, used to absorb shocks or in timepieces since it can stretch and return to its original shape.
A workshop in which textile fibres were spun into yarn by hand.
The residence of a keeper of a royal park etc.
A court in front of a church, usually open.
A textile factory where the process of doubling, the twisting together of two spun yarns, takes place.
An ancilliary building, usually to provide gas for lighting a particular building (eg. railway stations, factories, etc) as opposed to public GAS WORKS.
A single-span aircraft hangar designed by Boulton & Paul of London and Norwich (drawing number 4178/44). Mainly used on aircraft factory sites and at Armament Training Schools.

An area of a port, dock or harbour, often including buildings for passport control and customs, where passengers and vehicles using ferry services can embark/disembark and where supplies can be taken on board.
A house built using experimental building techniques and materials.

Canadian-built, single-engine, high-wing transport and communications aircraft converted from a civilian model. Metal-framed with fabric covering, saw service in 1944-5. Was capable of being equipped with wheels, floats or skis.
A small timber one-roomed dwelling where holiday makers could rest after a day spent sunbathing, swimming and playing on the beach.
Descriptive of inhabitants of, and cultural artefacts belonging to, Vietnam.

An investigative method using an infrared camera to detect temperature differences in the ground. The thermal camera does not record the actual temperature of the object in question. Instead the camera records the infrared radiation emitted by the object.
A post set up, to which offenders were tied to be whipped.
A refreshment house in a public park or country house garden.

Baggage, plate, money, clothes and other personal belongings of all kinds. Use only where the vessel is a cargo vessel conveying the goods of a person of consequence, e.g. a noble or diplomat, rather than for a general passenger vessel.
Use for cargoes which are not specified.

A steam engine in which the spent steam leaving the cylinder passes to a condenser instead of being exhausted to the atmosphere. The condenser creates a partial vacuum which increases the pressure drop across the engine, so raising its efficiency.
An artificial fall of water often taking the form of a water staircase.
A factory where fruit and seed oil is produced by an oil machine.
A cup with a marked change of angle in the body wall, generally at the point of maximum girth. (Source: MPRG)
A projection on which an object is fastened or which can pass through eyelets to fasten.
Complete and parial hearing loss.
A building or buildings used for the production of pens.
A natural or man-made gap in vegetation or other combustible material that acts as a barrier to slow or stop the progress of a fire.
A bridge which takes a towing path over a branch canal, basin, etc.
A cruck with its feet sitting on a ceiling beam on the first floor.
A mine from which potash is obtained. Potash is a deposit of potassium carbonate: the only example of a potash mine in the country is at Boulby in Cleveland.
A college founded for the education and betterment of the working classes. Lectures usually being held after the end of the working day.
A small area of managed woodland, created to provide cover for foxes.
An abbey or priory of Gilbertine Nuns.
A hollow or rectangular block which acts as a flue allowing the passage of gases or heat.

An underwater technique used to create 3D terrain models and to record objects on the seabed through the comparative analysis of reflections from high frequency sound waves emitted in multiple beams allowing large swathes of the seabed to be surveyed.
A two-storey watch office, built to Air Ministry drawing number 1959/34. It became the standard design for watch offices with a large, almost square, ground plan with a central observation tower.
Site or building constructed or adapted for indoor and/or outdoor leisure and sport activities, for example archery, team-building and "outward-bound" activities based on military training.
A factory or complex of buildings where creosote oil is produced. Creosote oil is distilled from coal tar and used as a wood preservative.

Transport vessel used for the repatriation of wounded troops, particularly during the First World War. Loosely described as "hospital ships", these ships were distinct from hospital ships proper by being defensively armed.
A place where the game of squash is played.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 18441/40.
A column of the Ionic Order, set upon a base and characterized by its slender form.
The residence of a piermaster.
A prepared piece of ground on which the game of Petanque is played.
Single-engine fighter/dive-bomber. The Fleet Air Arm's first operational monoplane, and its first aircraft to shoot down an enemy during the war.
An early type of steam engine, similar to a Cornish Engine, designed by Edward Bull.
A bridge that crosses over a railway.
A lift powered by an hydraulic system.
A site where small electrical goods such as radios, lamps and heaters are manufactured.

A British six-seat single-engined light aircraft, built by Airspeed Limited. First flew in 1933, saw some use as an airliner. The first British type with a retractable undercarriage. Designed by Hessell Tiltman (co-founder). 16 Couriers built.
Decorative ornamentation in the form of a ball enclosed within petals.
Circular spoil heap surrounding a wide central depression, the entrance to a mine shaft.
A box used for divination.
A trench, usually linking two or more rows of trenches, enabling the conveyance of messages or equipment safely from one trench to another.
Oil obtained from the liver of the cod, providing a rich source of vitamins A and D.
For the storage and recharging of battery-powered miners lamps.
A room frequently in a military building where sentries guard and protect the premises.
A site where Celestine or Celestite (a SrSO4), originally used in sugar beet refinement, is extracted from an open cast mine.
A fighter satellite station watch office built to Air Ministry design drawing number 18441/40.
An enclosure within a bailey which contained a keep and sometimes took the place of a motte.
A device controlling the passage of liquids or gases.
A site containing a forge for the manufacture of cutlery.
A large, "bottle-shaped", oven of brick construction used in the baking or firing of pottery.
An elementary steam engine working on the atmospheric principle; often used downstream of an overshot waterwheel.
The deliberate deposit of a body in the ground, usually located in a special area set aside for the purpose of burial, such as a graveyard or cemetery.
A military base used for training service personnel.
Use for the historic region of Flanders only
American twin-engined medium bomber and ground-attack aircraft that entered service in 1941. A small number were delivered to the RAF under the British designation Mitchell I.
A pronged iron hook used in cookery.
A Mark 1E aircraft which has undergone further modifications to enhance performance or armament.
A device with two flat plates and a mechanism used to force the plates together, to help solidify milk products in cheese making.
A piece of military ordnance, of sufficient size to require mounting and used for firing projectiles, traditionally cannon balls but more recently high explosive shells.
A high-humped, narrow, cobbled bridge used by trains of packhorses, often located in upland areas where the bulk of goods were carried by horses.
An institution for the detention of prisoners, surrounded by a wall and/or fence as a barrier to escape. The level of security depends on the category of inmate detained.
Three-masted fishing lugger built in and operating out of Yorkshire on the North Sea fisheries; so named as it was crewed by five joint owners, plus two or three paid hands.
A brace, running from a post to a principal, stiffening an interrupted tiebeam.
A manufacturing complex where the hides of animals are turned into leather, consisting of buildings for fleecing and drying, as well as treatment pits.
A prefabricated structure of reinforced concrete posts supporting a pitched roof frame with an infilling of sawdust concrete panels. Produced by Maycrete Ltd during WWII.
Use for vessels registered in Turkey or the Ottoman Empire.
A container for keeping the ashes of the dead after cremation.
A school for parentless children.
Usually made of iron, this bound the end of an axle and was perforated to allow a linch pin to pass through the axle and keep the wheel in place.

A factory used for the production of artificial limbs. They were often located within the precincts of a hospital, to enable fittings to take place and help the amputee to get used to wearing the limb.
A small work shop for nail manufacture, most commonly situated at the back of a nailer's dwelling.
A truss of slighter construction between principal trusses in an elaborate roof.
A room for private work, reading etc.
A room set aside for the purpose of reading, such as in a library or a club.
A suite of rooms.
A jug with a sinuous profile where the rim, girth and base are of roughly equal diameter, and the neck and lower body are narrower.(Source: MPRG)

Twin-engined jet-fighter. The first British aircraft to exceed Mach 1 in level flight, later to exceed Mach 2. Entered service in 1960. After 13 years was superseded in its primary defence role by the Phantom, though remained in RAF service until 1988.
WW2 LAA battery consisting of two or four 40m guns or Bofors guns. Associated structures included tented accommodation, ammunition shelters, a 100 gallon water tank, latrines, wash-house and kitchen.

Three/four-crew, single-engine, shipboard observation and air/sea rescue amphibian seaplane. Entered RAF service in 1936. Also employed for gunnery spotting, anti-submarine and convoy protection duties.
Photographic negative on glass developed using a dry process.
A building offering accommodation to people who are visiting a town or locality renowned for its mineral springs.
The main gearwheel in a water mill, sharing the same shaft as the exterior waterwheel but placed within the mill.

A transonic jet fighter, first introduced by North American Aviation in 1947. Best known as the United States's first swept wing fighter. Total production at 9,860 units. Important fighter aircraft in the Korean War. Retired in 1994 (Bolivia).
A bowl with concave body walls. Wide-mouthed, narrow-based examples, particularly those in larger sizes, have been termed Pans or Pancheons. (Source: MPRG)

An apparatus, featuring an ascending and descending platform or compartment, for carrying people or objects from one level or floor to another. This term can include the shaft or well in which such an apparatus operates.

Soft, often white, but may be transparent. Dolomite can be found on its own, but may also occur as a replacement mineral found in some rocks, particularly limestone, formed after action by magnesium-rich fluids.
Two buttresses which meet at a right angle at the corner of the structure they are supporting.
A piece of cladding in the form of a length of timber fixed horizontally to the building.
A device on an airfield for securing aircrafts when parked outside in order to prevent major movement due to the weather or other conditions.
A pier made up of several columns clustered together. They can be attached through their whole length or only at top and bottom.
A large strong case or box used to contain objects for storage or transport.
A wedge shaped stone used in an arch.
A large, luxuriously appointed hotel.
Purpose-built housing for railway workers.
A hard, durable wood obtained from trees of the genus Ulmus.
A decorative ball usually used to ornament a bench end, canopy, gable, pinnacle or spire.
A type of textile mill found in Lancashire in the 19th century. Small businesses paid the owner rent for space for their machines, and power from the mill engine or waterwheel.
Vertical or horizontal levels driven into a hill slope to assess the viability of mineral resources but never fully exploited.
A mechanized gate or barrier at a level crossing used to prevent road vehicles crossing a railway line when a train is approaching.
A stone placed across a grave.
A structure used for the roasting or drying of chicory.
British multi-purpose, single-engined monoplane that served as a torpedo-bomber, dive-bomber, reconnaissance aircraft and in other roles. Equipped with folding wings for use aboard aircraft carriers.
A horizontal timber that joins the collars of a series of roof trusses.
A missile consisting of a number of weights joined together by cord. The bolas entangles the legs of a target causing it to fall.
The residence of a verger, typically a layperson who assists in the ordering of religious services within the Anglican church.
A strong container, usually metal, secured for storing money or valuables.

A device used to slow the fall of a person or an object from a great height. When open it consists of a large umberella like sheet with wires or ropes converging from the edge to a harness attached to the lower end.
A factory where furniture is manufactured.
An ornamental, commemorative tablet. Use with materials field when indexing.
The residence of a signalman.
A small disc or flat ring of metal, wood or leather.
A tool used to notch, line cut or scratch into a surface.

Twin-engined, six-crew, heavy bomber. Conceived as a rival to the Lancaster and Flying Fortress, the HE177 was dogged by mechanical and structural problems. Of a thousand produced, only about two hundred saw action.
Production of smokeless domestic fuel by roasting anthracite in a type of kiln.
A large house dating from the 16th century onwards, built as a symbol of the wealth and status of the owner but not intended to be defensible unlike the castles and manor houses it replaced.
A hospital department for the medical and surgical treatment of teeth disorders.
A buttress set away from the structure it supports, joined to it by an arch.

Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as an E-shaped plan around two cattle yards. Cattle housing and stabling typically extend as three ranges from the longer main range which includes a barn or mixing house.

A prefabricated structure of reinforced concrete posts supporting a pitched roof frame with an infilling of concrete panels. Produced by during WWII as barrack accommodation and as emergency housing. Similar in style to Maycrete huts.
A hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of patients with cancer or related illnesses.
A detached fort covering a strategic point.
A structure, often built undergound, used for defence and co-ordination of military activity.
A tool for perforating or stamping, used in conjunction with a hammer.
A building for the crushing of stones and minerals.
Machinery and parts for the manufacture or assembly of military tanks, i.e. armoured vehicles.
A building housing a set of bellows used to provide the blast of air to a blast furnace or similar installation.
A building or site from which a lookout can be kept.
An iron frame placed over a coffin or at the entrance to a grave to act as a deterrent against resurrectionists.
The residence of a glover.
A Byzantine bell-type capital, ornamented with carving resembling wicker-work or basket-weave.
Developed from the DH4, featured the pilot and gunner cockpits in closer proximity, but suffered from engine reliability problems. Also known as the Ninak, saw service from 1918 to 1931.
Visual and descriptive record of a building, drawing on the full range of sources and including consideration of significance. Equivalent to Historic England Level 4.
