A device, usually wooden, or fabric on a timber frame, designed to catch, and be driven by, the wind in order to power a windmill. For maritime uses see the Thesaurus of Maritime Archaeology.

A two-storey, all-concrete construction with a watch office and additional rooms given over to the meteorological section, including a forecast room and met store. A concrete parapet all around the roof differentiates it from 5845/39.
A square, wooden drinking vessel.
Mill for fine grinding of tin ore between millstones.
A building used for the crystallization process in alum making.
An article, but published as a separate item.
Debris consisting of excess construction material used in the building of a nearby site or structure. If unsure of whether debris is from construction or demolition, index with both terms.
Small vernacular building used by fishermen for the preparing of nets and storage of equipment.
A ring containing a scarab shape.
Large granite stone used as the base stone of a stamping mill against which ore was crushed. Contains distinctive striations from the crushing process.
A railway yard with associated buildings used for the maintenance and storage of locomotive engines and rolling stock.
A house with an aisle on one side only.
A large room or building at a school used for assembly and other activities.
Single-engine, two-seat tractor bomber and reconnaissance aircraft. Entered service in 1916 and, during 1917 and 1918, equipped nine RFC squadrons in its reconnaissance role.
Traditionally, the hall of a crafts, trade, or merchants' guild. Nowadays, often used to describe a TOWN HALL.
A device with a spirally twisted shaft, pointed end and handle for removing corks from bottles.
a wooden, metal or stone post used to tether a horse, or other animals.
An object with a ceremonial or symbolic function. Multiple index with specific object where possible, eg for a ceremonial battleaxe index as ceremonial object and battleaxe.
The application of a chemical test to a material, usually as a rapid approximation.
A building in which works of art are displayed for sale.
A Mark 3 aircraft which has undergone slight modifications to enhance performance or armament.
A separate compartment for livestock in which they are free to move about.

A subrectangular earthen enclosure defined by a ditch, usually with an internal bank, assumed to have been used for the primary exposure or burial of human remains in the Neolithic period prior to secondary burial elsewhere.
A place where fish are processed after being caught.
A Prehistoric monument type in South West England in which a natural boulder is surrounded by a man-made kerb of stones.
Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Germany
A machine tool for producing flat surfaces and slots on small work pieces by cutting away surplus material.

Three-seat, twin-engined minelaying, torpedo-bombing and reconnaissance twin-float seaplane. First flown in 1936, in 1938 it set eight world speed records for its class in various range and payload categories.

A type of temporary military hutting used throughout WWII constructed of brick in 'stretcher bond' 4.5 inches thick with a light steel truss roof usually covered with corrugated asbestos sheeting. Used for accommodation, as gyms, training huts etc.
A building housing a winching mechanism.
A place where metal knives and edge cutting tools were manufactured.
Four-crew, twin-engined monoplane designed as a torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance aircraft for RAF Coastal Command. Withdrawn from operations in November 1940 and downgraded to a trainer.
A light anti aircraft position, usually open-walled and built of concrete, brick or sandbags used to emplace one or more machine guns mounted on pintels.
A crane used for the refueling of coal-powered vessels.
Photographic print on glass, using a wet process.
A container used in the distilling process to catch the distilled liquid.
An establishment where offenders who have committed the most serious crimes, e.g. serial killers, are confined.
Photographic print using albumen.
A Roman mixing vessel with a gritted inner surface.
A range of buildings used to house abandoned or stray dogs.
A stone on which flax stems were beaten with wooden mallets, a process known as beetling.
Outgrowths of bone borne by most members of the deer family (Cervidae). They are shed and re-grow each year.

Single-engine navigation trainer and communications aircraft. Constructed of tubular steel and duralumin frame, with a duralumin and canvas covering, 500 were delivered to the FAA, serving from 1944-5.
The residence of a lightkeeper.
An instrument for measuring the angle of slopes, usually in inches per yard, consisting of a weighted graduated wheel with movable sights.
A small semi circular scraper current in the Bronze Age.
Soft sandstone stained by iron oxide often used in the Surrey area.
Scotland
An open area of water, usually artificial and enclosed by dock gates or locks, lined with wharves, warehouses and berths to enable vessels to load and unload.
A circle made out of stones, which is used for making wheels.
A small shovel used with incense.
A plan in which the chimney stack backs onto the cross passage between a building's two entrances.
Single engine, two-crew shipboard reconnaissance and patrol seaplane. Entered service in 1939, this was the last combat floatplane built in Europe.

A stone building with external access to the domestic accommodation via a permanent stair. The ground floor is normally used as a byre in rural contexts, but in an urban setting it may be intended for one of a number of other non domestic uses.
A curved sword designed to cut with used by cavalry.
A pier where passsengers can embark and disembark and goods can be transferred to and from vessels.
Buildings and structures associated with the acquisition of electronic signals for the purpose of intelligence gathering.
Timber framed construction where a box of horizontal and vertical members is created to support the roof.
A decorative container for serving cream.
For example chronic heart failure, high blood pressure, congenital heart disease, heart transplants, rheumatic fever and other related illnesses.
A stone on which plague victims placed vinegar-disinfected money to pay for food left for them by the townspeople.
A tower in which shot is made from molten lead poured through sieves at top and falling into water at bottom.
An open grating of wrought iron, bronze, wood etc., forming a screen to a door, window or other opening, or used as a divider.
An open grating of wrought iron, bronze or wood, forming a screen to a door, window or other opening, or used as a divider.
A floating bridge, generally temporary, whose decks are supported on low flat-bottomed or hollow floats.

Area or zone of sea where a battle, skirmish or action was fought between naval ships or warships and privateers. Not to be used for enemy action upon mercantile ships or a sudden strike by mine/torpedo against an enemy warship.
A small building built over the end of a water conduit or spring.
A liquid used to provide a protective or decorative cover to a surface.
Use for hair, fur etc: filaments growing out of the outermost layer of mammalian skin.
American, four-engined, long range, medium/heavy day bomber. Produced in greater numbers than any other American aircraft during the war.
A tool, usually metal, with roughened surfaces in the form of very small teeth.
A barn used to store hops.
The edible seed of the palm tree.

A small rectangular or sub circular area or areas bounded by an earthwork, ditch or similar boundary, where one side is formed by an existing linear boundary, forming a pattern reminiscent of clothes hanging from a washing line.
A command post used to direct the guns of a coastal battery.
A collection of objects deliberately grouped together and hidden.
British, single-engined, light day bomber biplane. Built in 1923, this was the RAF's first interbellum designed day bomber.
A mill which is powered by a turbine.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of children.
A passage or road closed to traffic at one end.
A canopy or building to cover the platforms in a railway station.
A small window placed to cast light upon a fireplace.
The use of oxygen (O) isotope ratios in ice or ocean sediment cores to date global environmental change.
A specialist hospital for the medical treatment of skin diseases.
A road which has had mines placed within its structure to enable it to be destroyed in the event of an invasion.
A casement, usually wooden, in a mill enclosing the grindstones and preventing the loss of ground material before it is channelled into sacks.
A ramp or incline between differing levels constructed to allow carriages access.
A piece of bone used for divination.
A chemical works engaged in the production or refining of toluene, a substance extracted from coal tar or specific types of crude oil, and used in the production of explosives during WW1.
Product of boiled blubber
A short timber linking two pieces of timber.
A progressive development of the DO17, the twin-engined DO217 entered service in 1941. The DO217 saw service as a bomber over the UK and took part in the 'Baedecker' raids of 1942.
A small, Iron Age/Romano-British enclosed settlement found in South West England.
A lock at the end of one company's canal where it joins another company's canal.
A container for ointments or perfume.
A building containing soft play equipment for children.
A pump used to transfer petrol from a storage tank into cars, lorries and other road vehicles.

An area of a port, dock or harbour, often including buildings for passport control and customs, where passengers and vehicles using hovercraft services can embark/disembark and where supplies can be taken on board.
A buttress that is set slightly away from a corner. Usually one of a pair.
A long straight timber, halved across other roof timbers, especially running from a wall post or aisle post across the tiebeam to the opposing rafter.
A non-conformist minister's house.
A small, defensive settlement, usually consisting of one dwelling and ancillary buildings, surrounded by a palisade.
American, single-engine fighter designed for operation from US Naval aircraft carriers. Produced between 1940 and 1945, Wildcats provided to the British Fleet Air Arm were renamed Martlets.
A cheap eating establishment traditionally serving jellied eels, pies and mash.
A room or building where clothing and other fabrics are washed, mangled, steamed and ironed.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter manufactured by Messerschmitt. First used as part of Germany's Condor legion during the Spanish Civil War, the 'one-o-nine' was the Luftwaffe's most widely used fighter seeing service throughout World War II.
A site used for the extraction of metallic zinc by a variety of processes.
A room set aside for the initial treatment of injuries sustained for example in public amenities such as lidos.

A large steelframed military aircraft hangar designed in 1939, intended for aircraft maintenance on operational stations. It includes side annexes for workshops and offices, provided with a large number of windows. The annexes are of brick or concrete.
Glaucoma, diabetes, cataracts, retinal detachment and other related conditions.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber. Fitted with eight fixed forward-firing machine guns in the wings, plus two 1000lb bombs or six rocket projectiles.
Developed from the DH4, featured the pilot and gunner cockpits in closer proximity, but suffered from engine reliability problems. Also known as the Ninak, saw service from 1918 to 1931.
A place of accommodation for a stablehand.
A large container for holding or storing liquids.
Fertile soil composed mainly of humus, sand and clay.

A form of cup which incorporates a joke or conundrum, where cut-outs or holes in the body make conventional use impossible. The puzzle is how to drink from it without getting wet; usually achieved by sucking through a hollow rim or handle. (Source: MPRG)
A type of foundation in the form of a post sunk into the ground to support a building platform.
A sculptured likeness, portrait or image, often found on a tomb or other memorial.

Name given to a workhouse after 1929. The Local Government Act of 1929 abolished Poor Law Unions and Guardians, and control passed to public assistance authorities run by county boroughs and county councils. Lasted until 1948 when poor laws were repealed.
The part of the chancel, between the altar rail and the eastern wall, containing the high altar.
A decorative pattern, as used in tracery or a Gothic arch, featuring six lobes, or foils, separated by cusps.
A stepped, roadside platform, usually of stone on which a sedan chair was placed to allow the porters to lift the chair without having to bend.
One of a set of windows placed vertically and linked either decoratively or by aprons extending to the lintel below.
Dating from the 15th century, it is a hard alloy of iron and carbon, melted and shaped into various moulded forms.
A garden that has been specifically created to be accessible to both disabled and non-disabled visitors. They may contain scented and edible plants and features designed to make sound etc.
A building over a well housing machinery for raising the water. Often consisting of a DONKEY WHEEL or HORSE GIN.
A transverse vestibule at the west end of a church.
Pieces of undressed stone, waste fragments of stone or fragments of slate.
The seed of the flax plant pressed into cakes and used as cattle fodder.
A gun battery used to signal warnings to ships during bad weather.
A large, undergound watercourse.
A jug with a body profile resembling two cones joined together at their widest points, producing a distinct carination. (Source: MPRG)
Establishments responsible for the research into and the design, development and manufacture of chemical weapons
Photographic print using carbon
A Saxon quoin consisting of alternating horizontally and vertically laid stones.
Manmade structure that contains water that is heated to a high temperature and sometimes has bubbling air jets. Meant to be used for therapeudic purposes.
A drinking bowl, often wooden.
Cloth finishing process using machinery to raise the nap of the cloth before shearing.
A pond used for the rearing, breeding, sorting and storing of fish.
In the glass industry this is bench-like structure within the melting-furnace on which crucibles are placed.
A trinket worn as a protection against evil.
A place on which a fire is made.
A light weight umbrella used as a sun shade.
Three storey house with a topshop; machinery powered by shafting through the upper floor.
A treasury, often the bursar's room in a college or university.
Two or more tablets of wood attached by a string or leather thong, with a raised border one side of which was filled with wax to write upon. Thin wooden tablets with ink writing are also known.

A small notebook formed from two tablets usually made of wood, bone, ivory or metal. They were given as commemorative gift by a consul on his installation and often decorated with the image of the consul.
A bowl with a single loop handle crossing over the top of the vessel from one side of the rim to the other. (Source: MPRG)
A factory, where preserves such as jam and marmalade, are manufactured.

A curved military aircraft hangar produced in 1939. The frame is steel which is then clad with steel sheeting and reinforced concrete and typically covered with a thin layer of concrete, earth and turf.
An ornate public house that developed in the 1830s after the passing of a law to encourage the drinking of beer in alehouses licensed for the sale of beer only.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
A cereal, yellow in colour, the grains of which are embedded in a core known as the cob.
A post, usually carrying a tiebeam, which forms part of a wall in a timber framed building.

Lightweight building block traditionally made with coke breeze from gas works combined with sand and cement. Use this term generally to denote a light, modern concrete building block with man made characteristics.
A school where handicrafts are taught.
A pair of SHEER LEGS mounted on shore or on a SHEER HULK, used as a crane to hoist a mast and lower it into place on a ship.
A fence made of pales.
An area of common grassland in a village used for grazing cattle, recreational purposes, etc.
A complex of buildings producing power derived from nuclear energy.
A man-made trough or valley through a hill, carrying at its base a railway.
A pond located at or near a swannery.
A principal with a curved lower end that continues down the wall for a short distance.
An industrial manufacturing complex producing bricks.
An abbey or priory of Gilbertine monks.
A building used to smoke fish or meat.
A field system with one prevailing axis of orientation, in which most field boundaries are either aligned with this axis or run at right angles to it.
A gentry house in a town or city, either detached or in a terrace.
A section of stone or brickwork employed in a timber-framed building to fill the spaces between uprights or studs.
A building in which newly made bricks are laid out to dry.

A high status building of the medieval period, consisting of a hall and attached room at first floor level with rooms below possibly for storage or living accommodation for a lower status family. The first floor was accessed by an external staircase.

American, single-engine fighter designed for operation from US Naval aircraft carriers. The Hellcat was a more powerful version of the Wildcat, a total of 1000 being provided to the Fleet Air Arm under Lend-Lease.
A site where large sheets of thin metal are manufactured.
A vertical structure usually with an Attic base or spira with slender and elegant design, with a capital decorated with acanthus leaves and an entablature rich in carved ornament.

A signalling structure used on WWII airfields, comprising a concrete square base with a kerbed border into which concrete signal symbols could be placed to advise pilots in the air of current airfield state e.g. directions of landing and airfield circuit.
A pattern cut out in wood or metal to help shape something accurately or to reproduce shapes.
A small transportable hangar built by the Teesdie Bridge and Engineering Company. Mainly used on RNAS airfields for folding wing aircraft.
A flat-topped, often elongated, construction at which customers are served by staff in a commercial establishment such as a bank, shop, inn etc.
A counter from which beverages are served in a bar room.
Photographic negative developed on paper.
A Neolithic monument comprising an irregularly circular enclosing ditch, interrupted by frequent causeways, and often accompanied by an internal bank, also causewayed.
A place of worship for military personnel.
A vessel, usually made of stone, which contains the consecrated water for baptism.
Tropical giant grass with hollow stem used structurally or as a covering material.
A building providing shelter for sheep and storage for fodder and shepherding equipment.
A core part of a town or city that has or had a particular set of characteristics; for example an area of high status residences or an area where a particular industry/trade was centred.
A mill used for the preparation and production of Calamine.
A room intended to contain a bath and often other toilet facilities.
A playing piece for the medieval game of table.
Hard wood, reddish-brown in colour with a fine-grain often used in the manufacture of furniture.
Single-engine fighter/dive-bomber. The Fleet Air Arm's first operational monoplane, and its first aircraft to shoot down an enemy during the war.
A pit or tank containing chemicals for the preserving of animal hide.

Also known as the C-47 Skytrain, this twin-engined, military transport was developed from the DC-3 twenty-eight-seat commercial airliner and was the most extensively employed transport of the Second World War.
A crane deriving its power from steam generated from solid fuels.
A decorative moulding in a diamond shape.
1st World War end-opening aeroplane hangar.
A vessel comprising of two or more bowls, generally of small size, joined together. There may be one or more handles of varying forms. (Source: MPRG)
A structure providing protection from the elements to passengers waiting to board a ferry service at a dock, riverside, harbour or quay.
A steam engine that uses the same steam successively to drive pistons in high and then low pressure cylinders.
An underground, or partially underground, vault or crypt beneath a church or other building.
A steep-sided pit formed by, and for, the extraction of gravel.
A gable supporting a roof, placed at right-angles to the main part of the roof.
Workshop used in the the production of tripe.
An inclined ramp of earth, stone or brick used to deliver fuel to the firing hole of a kiln. Mediaeval and later.
A one or two storey reinforced concrete structure, usually associated with two T shaped radio masts. Term is specific to army anti-aircraft control centres operational between 1950-55.
Tool used in dentistry either for examination or surgery.
A small hand operated rotary drill used by dentists.
A component of a salt works housing iron pans where the brine was evaporated above a furnace and flue. Such houses were lightly built in order to allow the heat and steam to escape.
A chamber built into a wall in a defensive structure.
Photographic colour print developed using wet process.
An engine powered by high pressure water, originally used in mine drainage.
A large building used for the storage of leather goods or processed animal skins.
A lock at the point where two waterways join together.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter, also adapted as a night-fighter, fighter-bomber, rocket-projectile fighter and tank-buster. The first monoplane to enter RAF service with 14,000 being produced between 1937 and 1944.
A report that primarily details the results of a survey that was conducted using remote sensing techniques such as resistivity and magnetometry.
A chapel built on, or at the end of, a causeway.
A framed fireplace hood built on a bressumer and extending from one outer wall to the other or to a spere.
An elevator used to raise locomotives.
A factory or site where wooden clogs are manufactured.
A small eating and drinking establishment or refreshment bar.
A small eating and drinking establishment or refreshment bar at a railway station for the use of passengers.
A short timber set on top of two cruck blades.
A building used to accommodate donkeys.

A solid concrete or stone base on which a machine (often an engine and therefore called the engine bed, forming part of an engine house) was mounted to power an industrial process. Dates from the 19th century.
A workshop forming part of a domestic dwelling.
A special type of barn, lacking a threshing floor, usually with open walls, intended for the dry and well ventilated storage of hay only.
A settlement used for trading.
A positive black and white image on film which can be projected onto a screen when light is shone through it.
A coastal battery used for delivering fire at long distance thus forcing a warship threatening or bombarding shore installations to withdraw out of range.
A case in which a comb was carried.
Single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer used in secondary flying training schools. Serving from 1939-50, was also used as a target tug for gunnery practice.
A protected parachute store built with permanent brick cavity walls and a roof of reinforced concrete slabs in two heights separated by lantern lights.
Large mammals of the genus Bos, domesticated to provide milk, beef and materials eg. leather. Use only for live animals.
Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged around all four sides of the yard.

Two-seat, twin-engined light/medium bomber celebrated for its speed and versatility. Entering service in 1941, was also adapted for duties as a fighter-bomber, Pathfinder, mine-layer, transport, trainer and photo-reconnaissance aircraft.
A bridge carrying a railway track across a river, valley, road etc.
A structure used for the roasting or drying of chicory.
All-weather fighter/interceptor first flow in 1951, introduced into service in 1956 and retired from the RAF in 1968.
A brewery building where malt is mixed with hot water to form wort.
A tower, containing a gate, built into the walls of a town, castle or similar fortification.
The round, firm fleshed fruit of the apple (Malus Domestica) tree. Grown in numerous varieties throughout the world.
Gun emplacement for static or mobile light anti aircraft artillery.
An aircraft used to facilitate communications, for example in a military context.

A single engine two seat cabin monoplane tourer, first flown in 1933 as a successor to the Puss Moth. Impressed into military sevice in WWII by the RAF and the Fleet Air Arm as a liaison and communications aircraft, also used by training units.
Three-seat, single engine, high wing braced monoplane designed for civil use and first flown in 1929. Saw military service in World War 2 in an Army co-operation and communications role.
A box to contain the dowry which is a gift or endowment given to or on behalf of the wife.
A room in which disused items, such as furniture, are stored.

A place of worship for the sect known as 'Cokelers', formed circa 1850 by John Sirgood. Most aspects of Dependent belief are fairly orthodox within the Arminian traditions of Protestant dissent. Chapels can be found in Sussex, Surrey, London and Kent.
Twin-engined, four-crew German seaplane. Entered service in 1932 as a torpedo bomber and naval reconnaisance aircraft, though by World War 2 those still serving were used mainly for air sea rescue.
A monumental burial place, usually for a single person or family.
An earthen bank indicating the limit of a wood or coppice
A building used for the storage of picked fruit.
A space usually in front of a church entrance but can include the space surrounding a church.

Style of early Bronze Age pot found widely in north-western Europe with a deep, largely plain, outwardly flared body above which is sharp carination, usually decorated and sometimes with an applied cordon, and an inwardly angled neck.
A place of worship for the followers of Jainism
A village cemetery where cinerary urns were buried in large numbers during the Bronze Age.
A bridge that crosses over a railway.
A tug equipped with water tanks and pumps for fighting fires at sea or on the shore line.
A simple flat-topped lid resembling an inverted dish but with no central knob or handle. (Source: MPRG)

Also known as the C-47 Skytrain, this twin-engined, military transport was developed from the DC-3 twenty-eight-seat commercial airliner and was the most extensively employed transport of the Second World War.
A friary belonging to the Pied Friars also known as Friars of Blessed Mary or St Mary de Arens.
The residence and office of an ambassador.
A substantial structure supporting or surrounding a gate. May be ornate or monumental, and have associated structures such as lodges, tollbooths, guard houses etc.
A dredger with a grab hung on ropes or chains giving it unlimited depth of excavation. they can lift solids or pieces of wreckages and can work close to ships or to a dock wall.
Animal skin that has been hardened or treated by a tanning process.
Plant for the processing of uranium ores, such as pitchblende. Uranium is the principal extract, but radium may also be recovered as a by-product
A school founded in or before the 16th century, for teaching Latin, later becoming a secondary school teaching languages, history, science, etc.
A close fitting skull cap, usually worn under a helmet.
A place where a product is given any finishing processes before being despatched to the user.
Collection of artefacts recovered during archaeological investigation of a site.
A channel for taking a rapidly flowing stream of water away from a canal lock, or away from the canal itself.
The dwelling of a blacksmith, nailer, sword cutler, etc, often adjacent to, or containing, a BLACKSMITHS WORKSHOP.
A musket fired by a piece of burning match being held in the lock which, when the trigger was pulled, would contact with powder in the pan to set off the charge.

A square pillbox with loopholes for four light machine guns with 18 in thick walls. Probably designed by DFW branch 3 although it may have been adapted from an external source as Southern Command correspondence refers to the type as 'Stento'.

Long-range, four-engine reconnaissance-bomber. Initially produced as a transport, converted and used against Allied convoys in the Channel and the Atlantic. Also served as a VIP transport, one of which was the Immelmann III: Hitler's personal aircraft.
A kiln principally used in brick making which gives a continuous operation.
Single-seat, single-engine fighter-bomber and ground-attack aircraft. Entered service with the Luftwaffe in mid-1941. Approximately 20,000 were constructed between 1941 and the end of the war.
A vessel used for the laying and removal of buoys and other navigational markers.
A workshop for combining flax or hemp as a preparatory stage of rope making.
A piece of forest land converted into arable.
The foremost church within a parish.
A type of cushion capital with the lunette on each face cut into a series of truncated cones to form a scallop shell-like decoration.
A cube-shaped capital with its lower corners rounded to facilitate the transition from the circular shaft below to the square abacus it supports.
A kiln for drying hops in a brewery or maltings complex, as distinct from the OASTHOUSES found on farms.
A building or site used to produce alkaline chemicals by controlled reactions.
A movable bridge lifted at one end by chains or ropes either to stop traffic passing over it or to let traffic pass under it.
A small two masted craft, with oars as well as sails.
A hospital for the treatment of venereal disease.
A place in which brewing and sometimes baking took place.
The residence of an admiral of a port.
A pipe through which water is conducted.
A plant, Salsola soda, burnt to produce alkali.
A short timber connecting a cruck's timber, or blade, to a wall plate.
Preparations for beautifying or enhancing the body, face, hair or skin, e.g. creams, and coloured "make-up" items, e.g. rouge, lipstick, etc.

Single-engine, single-seat interceptor fighter developed from the race-winning Schneider Trophy seaplanes. One of the most famous of all combat aircraft, entered RAF service in 1938 and was still in use in the 1950s.
A twisted fibre which is immersed in wax, grease or oil except for one end which is lit.
A decorative moulding depicting an animal or bird head, similar to a beak head moulding but with a shorter, cone-like tongue or beak overlapping the moulding set beneath it.
A works or factory where nitroglycerine is manufactured.
A chemical works engaged in the production of Ammonium Perchlorate, a product used in the explosives industry.
A shoe of soft leather.
A semaphore signalling tower on a railway.
A bag stuffed with soft material used to support the head whilst sleeping.

Ammunition from any period found to have been expended (cannonballs, shells, bullets) which may indicate the possible site of a battle or action on land or at sea. Index where appropriate with Battlefield Debris as a Monument Type.

A structure, based on drawing number (3329/41), intended to be the headquarters for the coordination of an airfield's defences. Constructed above ground this design was found to be vulnerable and was superceded by the (11008/41).
A bridge supported by large beams or girders, originally of wood or iron, now usually of steel or reinforced concrete.
French warship broadly equivalent to the English 4th to 6th Rates, with as few as 4 to as many as 50 guns.
A naturally occuring deposit of calcareous tufa ('shell marl') sometimes found in alluvial deposits.
A preparation made from the evaporated juice of the rhizome of the plant Glycyrrhiza glabra, used medicinally and as a sweet, usually in the form of a black, chewy substance.
A horizontal brace linking tiebeam and wall plate, or adjacent wall plates at the corner of a hipped roof.
A government employment agency for those out of work offering advice on jobs, training and retraining.

A lighthouse whose lantern is sufficiently high to be seen at a long range and above low lying cloud or fog. In locations where varying weather conditions occur a High Light is usually accompanied by a LOW LIGHT built alongside or nearby.
A large container or reservoir for liquids or gases.
Cut or uncut stones, usually intended to be set into jewellery, and including precious gems, e.g. diamonds, sapphires, or semi-precious materials, e.g. quartz, agate, amber.
Salts or organic derivatives of phosphoric acid, especially compounds of Calcium or Iron found in cereals and minerals.
A church established by a religious community to propogate its faith.
Use for vessels registered in China.
A building or buildings where soap is manufactured.
Tyne and Wear
Moray, Scotland
The Islamic New Year.
The residence of a signalman.
A boiling vessel used in the direct boiling process, or the sleeching process, used for the manufacture of salt. For evaporating features associated with SOLAR and PARTIAL SOLAR sites use SALT POND.
A building for the storage of ammunition and other military stores.
A small works used for the production of agricultural tools such as hay rakes.
A mug with roughly vertical body walls. (Source: MPRG)

A square pillbox with walls up to 48in thick, designed to emplace a 2 pounder anti-tank gun. A large opening in the back allowed the gun to be wheeled into position at the large embrasure in the front wall. Designed by DFW branch 3.
1st World War end-opening aeroplane hangar.
A residence of two or three monks of the Premonstratensian order dependent on an English mother house.
A deposit that forms the ground surface (when the evidence is collected), particularly a hard surface such as a floor or road.
A room in which servants slept.
A block in the position of a tiebeam.
City and port on the Mediterranean coast.
A mill used for the manufacture of twilled dress material of worsted with or without a mixture of cotton or silk.
Hard, coarse grained, green to pink coloured igneous rock. Commonly used as a polished cladding.

A bowl with a straight handle projecting horizontally or diagonally upwards from the rim, particularly or completely hollow, but not opening into the vessel. A jar adapted by the addition of one or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
Material, especially rock, worn smooth by the passage of water.
A jar adapted by the addition of a single handle. Profiles vary and should be double indexed with the appropriate JAR type. (Source: MPRG)
A Neolithic burial monument comprising an approximately circular stony mound which contains a stone-built chamber, with or without additional lateral chambers.
A place where ceramic tiles are manufactured.
A pot for drinking hot milk curdled with ale and flavoured with spice used as a remedy eg for colds.
A small metal ring through which a nail or rivet is passed and fixed.
A strut which is part of a pair which support the collar and are supported by the tiebeam.
Large open hearth furnace often located inside a brick cone for use in steelmaking.

Twin-engined air/sea rescue and anti-submarine patrol aircraft. Originally developed from the Wellington and intended as a bomber, entered RAF Coastal Command service in 1943. Fitted with a Leigh Light and ASV radar.

Long-range, four-engine reconnaissance-bomber. Initially produced as a transport, converted and used against Allied convoys in the Channel and the Atlantic. Also served as a VIP transport, one of which was the Immelmann III: Hitler's personal aircraft.
A small cup for holding a boiled egg upright while it is being eaten.
A pillar, rod, pin, or plate of a sundial, showing time by its shadow.
A medieval court for tin miners in Devon and Cornwall.

Twin-engined monoplane that served the RAF as an advanced trainer and flying ambulance. Mk. I featured a gun turret and served for gunnery and bombing-crew training. Subsequent versions used for pilot, radio and navigation training.
Baths containing water impregnated with mineral substances in which patients bathe for medicinal purposes.
A substantial monument attached to a wall and often standing on the floor.
A shore establishment for the teaching of maritime theory and practical skills.
A dock with gates which open for access for some hours before and after high water.
Wood from non-coniferous trees, eg. oak, known for their hardness.
A dish with straight or convex sides that turn inwards, forming an acute basal angle. (Source: MPRG)
A separate residence for guests, a house on a private estate or a monastery building specifically for receiving visitors.
A pond used for the punishment, by ducking in water, of offenders.
A conical brick structure in which glass articles were made.
A wall, usually of reinforced concrete, designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle
Material that has been penetrated or disrupted by the roots or rhizomes of plants.
An aircraft hangar designed to Air Ministry specification (drawing number 6910/43). Similar in design to the ROBINS AIRCRAFT HANGAR but larger.
Large, single-engine, eight passenger airliner biplane.
A twin engined advanced trainer aircraft developed for the military by the US firm of Cessna
A strong durable wood originating in India and south-east Asia.
A place where railway engines are kept.
Sulphates, used in medicine and to colour inks.
A long handled hook used for pulling a boat to a place eg another boat, or pushing off from a place.
A platform, usually in concrete, on which radar equipment was mounted to assist the targetting of artillery guns. The platform is often the only evidence surviving in the landscape.
A soft, heavy, malleable metal, often obtained from the mineral galena. Traditionally used in the construction industry for roofing and plumbing.
Solid bars made from pure lead.
An earthwork used as a boundary marker.
A purpose-built residence for an artist, containing a studio.
A works engaged principally in the manufacture of the explosive bellite.
A trough or gutter for conveying liquids such as water or molten metal. It can be cut in the surface or formed of wood or other materials.
A board indicating the name of the railway station.
A small, open air bowl-shaped furnace, in which the flames are fanned by bellows. Used for both ferrous and non-ferrous smelting.
A specialist hospital where women receive medical and surgical treatment.
Small revolving wooden chalets that could be turned with their backs to the prevailing wind so that hospital patients could recline in them on long chairs in all weathers.
The residence of the supervisor of an inclined plane.
A room equipped with apparatus to facilitate physical exercise, gymnastics or indoor sports.
Fish eggs, e.g. from cod or, for example, caviar.
A system of stones or wooden obstacles placed close together to impede the advance of enemy forces. Do not use for HILLFORT sites.
An article, but published as a separate item.

Highly successful, two-seat, biplane fighter and reconnaissance aircraft with both forward and rear facing guns. Designed to replace the BE2, it entered service with the RFC in mid-1917 and remained in service until 1932.
A flat, circular plate, usually made of iron, on which food items are baked.
A settlement showing evidence for one or more hut circles, enclosed by a distinct boundary ditch, wall, earth rampart or similar barrier. Characteristic of the later prehistoric period.
Photographic plate, on glass, developed using a wet process.
A place of worship for members of the Serbian Orthodox Church, the national church of Serbia.
Originally a light day-bomber, the Boston II, re-christened the Havoc, was adapted for night-flying in the fighter-intruder role. Was capable of a top speed in excess of 300 mph.
An inclined ramp of earth, stone or brick used to deliver fuel to the firing hole of a kiln. Mediaeval and later.
A shallow pond, often artificial, fed by the condensation of water from the air, occuring on high land which has no other adequate water supply.
A close fitting garment, usually stiffened by boning or similar and tightly laced to shape and support the wearer's figure.
Developed from the ill-fated ME210, the ME410 Hornisse entered service in May 1943. Although underpowered as a day fighter the ME410 saw service over the UK as a night fighter from 1943-45.

A nineteenth century stone calciner, similar to a lime kiln, used for extracting arsenic from mined ores, consisting of a solid structure with a central shaft and a drawing-hole at the base for calciner waste.

Four-engine, long range heavy bomber. Developed from the Lancaster, and originally designated the Lancaster Mk. IV, it was larger in size, bombload and fuel capacity. Never used operationally in World War Two.
A plan in which the front entrance opens into a lobby opposite to an axial chimney stack.
A projecting spout to throw water from a gutter away from the wall, frequently decorated with grotesque figures to spew out evil away from the House of God.
For chemical processes making nylon, rayon, etc.
A dome shaped structure, with an aperture open to the sky, used to house a telescope.
A flag or object depicting a symbolic representation carried as part of a religious ceremony.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
A coastal battery constructed at short notice usually mounting a variety of artillery pieces.
Sedimentary clay with smectite mineral properties, originally used for the cleansing ["fulling"] of cloth; in the 20th century it was used for a wider range of industrial applications.
A capital with a half figure projecting from each corner
A sheet or cloth used to lay the corpse out in for burial.
A Swiss-styled house, usually with steeply pitched and projecting roof.
An establishment serving coffee and other refreshments and inexpensive foods. Between the 17th and 18th centuries they were also meeting places for political discussions.
Place where tanned leather is dressed and coloured.
Use only for the historic region of North America. For modern places use NORTH CAROLINA or SOUTH CAROLINA.
A thin flat slab used to mix cosmetics on.
A workshop used for the manufacture of statues, either cast or carved.
A pier used to raise a structure or building above ground floor level so that there is open space beneath the structure
An object constructed to allow birds to bathe in it.
An automatic power loom invented by James H Northrop in 1894.
A stone on which a monarch traditionally sat during the coronation ceremony.
The part of footwear that touches the ground.
A small circular enclosure defined by a turf or earthern bank.
A workshop or factory where bronze articles are made by casting molten metal into moulds.
A crane powered by a steam engine.
A spandrel which supports a dome and aids the transition between the dome and its square or octagonal base.

A maritime technique similar in theory to sub bottom profilers, however for 3D seismic surveys the receiver array is more complex involving multiple receivers so that a volume of sediment is studied rather than a single 2D line.

An information gathering exercise to facilitate an understanding of the potential environmental impact of a development proposal; includes the collation of specialist reports from a variety of disciplines.
A prime mover which is rotated by the reaction from forcing a moving fluid to change direction.
A picture or pattern produced by either by cementing together small pieces of stone or glass of various colours or by painting directly onto a wall.
A training college for chefs and other catering students.
A garden seat covered in clipped, camomile plants which release a fragrant smell when sat upon.
Use type of instrument where known.
A factory where chocolate products are produced.
A group of related buildings, primarily with a domestic function, which is arranged along a principle axis such as a main road or routeway.
A chapel attached to, or inside, a church, endowed for the celebration of Masses for the soul of the founder.
The vertical face of a step.

Building block (often a temporary brick structure or Nissen hut) comprising office accommodation for flight commanders and flight sergeants as well as pilots' rest rooms, storerooms and locker rooms. Some flight offices have central corridors.
A two-seat, reconnaissance biplane developed from the FK2 with a more powerful, but heavier, engine. Primarily used for training in the UK.
A type of warehouse, usually one-storeyed.
A workshop used for the decoration of fired pottery or ceramics. Usually part of a larger complex.
A factory in which is ink is prepared from pigments and additives.
A carved, convex block, often richly decorated, at the intersections of vault-ribs, beam-junctions or terminations of mouldings.

A late 17th - early 18th century house with a central chimney and fireplaces and a central door on the front; this door opened closely against the fireplaces, leaving a small lobby for access to the rooms.
A factory or works used for the production of turpentine, wood alcohol and similar chemicals by the distillation of pulped wood.
An upright framing member, or mullion, that separates two panels, such as in a panelled door or a window.
A room for detention and imprisonment within a prison.

An establishment where alcoholic and non alcoholic drinks are served, food may also be served. May be a an individual room within a larger multi purpose building such as a sports pavilion or a theatre.
A calciner dating from the early 17th to early 20th centuries, usually made of brick and without moving parts, consisting of a reverberatory furnace, and used for the extraction of arsenic.
A mill in which strands of yarn are twisted together to produce a strong thread with a uniform thickness.
Scenes viewed at night.
A circular concrete platform onto which aircraft would be taxied allowing the ground crew to calibrate, check and adjust the accuracy of the aircrafts compass, usually by rotating the platform.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Bridgettine order.
A factory used for the manufacture and assembly of lorries.
An associated group of toilet articles.
A building offering accommodation to people who are visiting a town or locality renowned for its mineral springs.
Block, often made of concrete, to secure smaller maritime craft. Many were made during the Second Wold War to secure craft which were to be used in the D-Day landings.
The remains of a vessel which has either sunk or suffered structural damage to the extent where it can no longer function.
A tunnel running under a river or a hillside through which a railway line runs.
A tunnel carrying a railway beneath the surface of the ground.
A rustic garden building made of wood with moss pressed between the wall slats. The mosses could be of different types, forming a mossery.
A single or pair of figures or plates attached to a joist or bar either at the time of construction or later and built into the wall to provide support.
An object which contains or is inscribed with spells against disease, witchcraft etc, or providing luck to the wearer.
Small fragments of wood or bark.
Use only where evidence is specific, ie. copper/tin alloy. For working of copper based alloys of unknown composition use COPPER WORKING SITE.

A bowl with a straight handle projecting horizontally or diagonally upwards from the rim, particularly or completely hollow, but not opening into the vessel. A jar adapted by the addition of one or more handles. (Source: MPRG)
An instrument for measuring angles, usually in the form of a graduated semi-circle.
A roof featuring a covering of straw, reeds, rushes etc. used extensively during the medieval period but also popular in rural or rustic architecture.
A room which contains, wholly or partly, a staircase.
Engineering workshop used for the final assembly of vehicles or structures from parts produced elsewhere in an engineering works.
A dedicated room for housing the organ feeder bellows, can be an underground chamber or a free-standing building.

Originally obtained by burning limestone to produce quicklime. Now a fine grey powder made from a mixture of limestone and clay used with water and sand to make mortar or with water, sand and aggregate to make concrete.
The material which floats during the floatation of samples as a means of recovering charred plant remains from an archaeological context.
A well concealed structure, usually constructed underground, intended for use by members of the British Resistance Organization in the event of invasion.
US Navy version of the four-engined, six-crew B24 heavy bomber. Modified for long-range reconnaissance duty and used as a patrol-bomber against shipping and submarines.
A thin, flexible material made from the pulp of wood or other fibrous matter which is then pressed and dried to form sheets.
A building or site used for the production of naphtha, a volatile petroleum-derived product used in the manufacture of solvents, cleaning fluids etc.
Bag filled with soft stuffing used to support the body.

Extremely thin foil made out of ethyltetraflouroethylene, a modified copolymer which is extruded into a thin film and which is related to Teflon. It has a very high level of light transmission in visible and ultra violet range. Used instead of glass.
A craft with two masts.It is usually cutter rigged on the foremast and has a small mizzen mast.
A flatbed lorry with a concrete defensive position fitted on the back enabling the "pillbox" to be driven to where it was most needed in the event of an airborne force landing on the airfield.
A large, usually metal, container used for the storage of liquid fuels.
A workshop where tapestries were made.
A building that housed humans and cattle under one roof, with a shared entrance providing access to the cattle housing (usually downslope) and the dwelling area.
A large Mediterranean cargo or transport vessel of the 15th to 17th century, usually less than 400 tons.
A bridge whose deck is directly supported from pylons by straight cables without vertical suspenders.
A joint between two timbers meeting end to end.
A site where canvas, coarse, unbleached cloth, made from hemp or flax, was manufactured.
A farmstead where the main range of working buildings are attached in-line and form a long row often facing a series of yards.
A flour milling machine using both stones and rollers to produce flour and, perhaps mainly from the stones, animal feed from grains other than wheat.

A multi-storey, fortified hall house with one of the crosswings being raised in the form of a crenellated tower. Permanently occupied, they date from the mid 14th to the 17th century and are found mainly in the border counties of the North of England.
An odourless, tasteless powder obtained from cereals and potatoes, used for stiffening fabric.

A French airliner which entered service in 1920. A conventional biplane design with enclosed cabin for four passengers and open cockpit for the pilot. Fitted with an early audible guidance system. Withdrawn from service in 1921.
Thin round flexible disc with magnetic surfaces for storing and retrieving data. [AAT]
Platform, usually stone-built, which holds the winding gear of a mine shaft.
A priory of Premonstratensian canonesses.
A narrow timber board or moulding lining the base of an interior wall as a finish between it and and the floor.
Posts with hooks attached to allow drying new cloth to be stretched out between them.
A centre in which the public donate blood that will be used for the care of patients in hospitals.
A residential home for adults with learning difficulties and/or physical disabilities.
A pedestrian passageway, often elevated, connecting two buildings or sections within a building.
A container used as a lavatory.
A container in which weapons are put for storage and or transportation.
A marker, of stone, wood or metal, used to delineate the limits of a stretch of highway, river or canal subject to a toll charge.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter. Entered service in 1943 as a land-based fighter. Converted to a carrierborne fighter in 1944 for use by US Navy and Fleet Air Arm. Mostly saw action in the Pacific and Far East.
A covered way or passage especially in a cathedral or monastic church, leading east from the cloisters between transept and chapter house.
A barrier, usually of wood or chain, stretched across the entrance to a harbour, port or anchorage, to control entry and/or limit the effect of the weather on the wave action.
A pure starch obtained from the tubers of the plant Maranta arundinacea used in cookery as a thickening agent.
A terrace or row of dwellings, with a NAIL SHOP attached to each house.
A channel or pipeline that feeds water to a waterwheel.
A structure used to dry turf on. Turves were used as a fuel and as a roofing material.
A truss with two curved kerb-principals, which are the short principal rafters rising froma tiebeam to a collar, placed either side of a crown strut.
The residence of a herder.
A technique for the dating of damage tracks in volcanic materials caused by the fissioning of decaying radioactive uranium (U) isotopes. Useful in samples more than 50,000 years old.

A term for any vessel powered principally by sail and oars, or oars alone, used especially for war. As a broad term it may refer to Roman galleys, or more specifically to an Anglo-Saxon or Norse warship of the Viking Age.
Timber sawn into long, flat, pieces used for flooring etc. in buildings.
A storehouse in 16th and 17th century houses.
A chapel for followers of Benjamin Ingham after he left the Moravians prior to joining the Sandamanians.
A place where inmates of a workhouse or prison carried out stone breaking.
Use for vessels registered in Ukraine
A well with a superstructure, either partially or wholly enclosed with an access door, designed to protect the water source.
A pointed tool used to pierce holes, usually in textiles.
A base on which pews or benches can be placed.
A vessel for keeping the ashes of the dead after cremation.
Metal shaped blade that flares out to a curved cutting edge, with a side loop to further assist hafting.
A coastal battery containing one or more artillery pieces for to defend the coast against hostile motor torpedo boats.
Originally a light day-bomber, the Boston II, re-christened the Havoc, was adapted for night-flying in the fighter-intruder role. Was capable of a top speed in excess of 300 mph.

An underground hideout containing radio equipment to be used by the Special Duties sections of the Auxiliary Units to recieve coded information from the out-stations in the surrounding area for relaying to headquarters via direct phone line.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Auxiliary Unit Special Duties Zero Station

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: An establishment serving coffee and other refreshments and inexpensive foods. Between the 17th and 18th centuries they were also meeting places for political discussions.
Stone used as a building material which has been finished, or dressed, before use.
A magnetic tape used to record moving images and sound. Use for both cassette and reel tapes.
A by-product usually from the smelting process.
A lawn planted with camomile plants which when walked upon release a fragrant smell.
An area on post-war military airfields for parking aircraft on quick reaction alert to allow immediate access to the runway. Abbreviation ORP.
A group of buildings containing machinery for the production in bulk of butter or related dairy products.
Hook used to support cloth on a tenter frame after fulling to dry the cloth.
A decorative moulding in the form of a chain.
A low-temperature oven for the firing of metallic-based colour onto pottery after glazing.
A factory complex consisting of PRINTING SHOPS, COLOUR HOUSES, DYE HOUSES, etc, in which patterns are printed onto calico.
A concave moulding where the profile is a quarter of a circle.
A report detailing the results of an archaeological event were the ground surface has been studied and any visible archaeological material collected.
A flour mill using both stones and rollers to produce flour and, perhaps mainly from the stones, animal feed from grains other than wheat.
A fire station built for use by the Auxiliary Fire Service, established in 1938 to supplement existing local brigades.
A machine for beating out or separating grain from corn.
A bridge for carrying a road or railway over another.
The place where metallic ores were crushed and washed to remove waste, forming a concentrate which could be used in a smelter.

skos:Concept.skos:definition: Although the proper term is square rod, for centuries this unit has been called a pole or perch or, more properly, square pole or square perch.

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: 3-D physical entity conveying information, e.g. a model, artefact or architectural feature.
The residence and office of a chaplain.

Single-engine, single-seat carrierborne fighter: a Spitfire VB fitted with an arrester hook. Modifications on later versions included folding wings, rocket-assisted take-off gear and conversion for photo-reconnaissance duties.

A formal programme of observation and investigation conducted during any operation carried out for non-archaeological reasons that may damage archaeological deposits. This will be within a specified area or site on land, inter-tidal zone or underwater.
Colour positive print developed using a dry process.
Large inshore craft with a retractable loading ramp in the bow. Used to carry tanks ashore for a beach landing or as a tank ferry.
a wooden, metal or stone post used to tether a horse, or other animals.
A site or building used for the manufacture of goods made from pewter, an alloy of tin and lead.
A fighter version of the SKUA fitted with a four-gun turret. The majority were converted to target tugs for use by the RAF and Fleet Air Arm.
Twin-engined fighter-bomber. All metal in construction, entered service in 1940. Supported bombing operations and participated in attacks on France, but not widely used due to engine faults.

American, four-engine, long range, heavy strategic bomber. Entered service in 1943 and used exclusively against Japanese forces. The B29s Enola Gay and Bock's Car were used to drop atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945.
Single lap regular shaped roof covering which can have one or more water channels. Typically made of clay or concrete. The name does not denote a relationship with the Roman period.
Twin-engined, single-seat fighter-bomber. Flown by USAAF fighter groups from 1942, excelled as a ground-support fighter. Could carry two 1600 lb bombs or rocket projectiles.
A basket for the storage and transport of fishing equipment. For the storage and transport of fish use creel.
Building housing machinery used in the production of wooden pulley blocks for the rigging of sailing ships.
A share or portion of land, allotted to a person, often used for growing, vegetables, fruit, etc.
Use for material that has been burnt at high temperature in a good air supply such that only the silica component remains.
A moulding on the neck of a column.
A building or group of buildings used for the making, processing, storing and selling of milk and other dairy products.
A park for the use of the public for entertainment and relaxation.
The main axle projecting through the front of a windmill on which the sails are mounted.
One of a set used in pharmacy to measure volume or weight for dispensing.
A building or site where phosphorous-based fertilizers are produced by controlled chemical reactions.
A place used for the milking of cows.
A cruck truss whose blades are composed of two pieces of timber joined near the wall head in a variety of ways.
An establishment where patients can rest and recover after an operation or illness.
A friary of the Order of the Friar servants of the Blessed Virgin Mary or Servites. The Servite Fathers came to England in 1864.
Equipment enabling a horse to be ridden or driven, eg. saddles, bridles, harnesses, stirrups etc.
Residence of a leading land-holding family within the district.
Room, usually part of another building, for storing and preparing roots and other animal feed.
A detached external pier by which an arch or vault is prevented from spreading.
A roll of paper or parchment, especially with writing upon it.
Workshop for the manufacture of master parts from working drawings which are then used as patterns for mass manufacture.
A hard material formed by firing clay. For pottery, use POTTERY.
A way, path or road through a cutting.
Use for vessels registered in Finland.

Three-seat, twin-engined minelaying, torpedo-bombing and reconnaissance twin-float seaplane. First flown in 1936, in 1938 it set eight world speed records for its class in various range and payload categories.
A building used for the safe storage and public display of jewellery, eg. the Jewel House at the Tower of London.

A hut consisting of a frame of reinforced concrete posts into which concrete panels were slotted. Designed by the British Concrete Federation during WWII to be resistant to bomb blasts & used for military accommodation, child nurseries and clinics etc.
Hut along the coast, which provided shelter for lookouts known as "huers", who kept watch for the pilchard shoals that passed by the coast. Built of stone or wood. Particular common to Cornwall.
Tabelware manufactured from china clay.
A small square or lozenge-shaped pane of glass as used in a leaded light.
Machinery for raising and lowering men and equipment to and from the surface of a mine.
A vessel used to carry supplies to warships.
A hall associated with a church, used for holding functions, meetings and for conducting parish business.
A building containing the colliery showers. Also often containing first aid and mine rescue facilities.
Originally designed as a light bomber but diverted for use as a high speed target tug to replace out-dated biplanes.
Twin-engined, four-seat medium bomber. A re-engined variant of the Hampden, less than 200 were built but never became operational due to engine unreliability. Some were converted to Hampdens.
Includes excavation, research and general notes.
A centre where patients suffering from venereal and associated diseases receive treatment.

A prefabricated structure of cant sided lightweight timber wall sections bolted together. Externally the walls were clad with plasterboard covered with felt. Designed for use as barrack accommodation during WWII.
Decorative ornamentation of a formalized lily.
A gun emplacment which conforms to Department of Fortification and Works drawing number 55503
A loft for the storage of hay.
The metal ornamental bedding and surround in which a gem or stone is mounted.
A site where metal springs are manufactured.
Long narrow pieces of wood used for a variety of purposes.
A defensive construction situated in the sea, designed to protect the land from seabourne attack. The term applies mainly to those monuments built from around 1860 onwards.
A decorative structure of wood stone or metal, incorporating a shelf, surrounding the opening of a fireplace.
A site including a pitch, stands and other ancillary buildings associated with the game of football.
An enclosure for pigs that includes a covered pen and yard.
A pick with a point at one end and a cutting blade at the other end.
A long handled shallow pan used for frying.
Principal glider-pilot training glider fitted with tandem seats. Spruce and plywood in construction, the Hotspur served with the Glider Pilot Regiment between 1941 and 1945.
Large, single-engine, eight passenger airliner biplane.
A building in which wrought iron or steel chains were manufactured.
A factory where carpets are manufactured.
Purpose built or modified structure or building used for scenery in a television program.
The original pattern/type of an object.
Tile nailed externally to a wall and usually laid in mortar designed to present a brick-like appearance.
A storage rack for sections of steel plate used in the construction of ships.
A WWII British biplane produced by Hawker Aircraft, used for army cooperation duties.
A factory engaged in the manufacture of small arms ammunition, especially the metal components and filling with the explosive propellant.
A 19th century glasshouse built specifically for the fostering of camellias.
A mill used for the sizing and drying of warp threads before they were wound onto warp beams as part of the power-weaving process.
A terrace consisting of a double row of houses sharing a common back wall, characteristic of industrial cities in the North of England.

A World War One German three-crew, twin-engined, long range heavy bomber biplane manufactured by Gothaer Waggonfabrik A.G.. Entering service in 1917, this aircraft incorporated a ventral tunnel allowing the gunner to shoot downwards and to the rear.
A passage constructed within the thickness of a wall.
A manmade chamber cut into a rockface.
The removal of fragile or complex remains from an investigation as a block of earth for excavation under laboratory conditions. Typical examples are grave goods and cremation burials.
Military weapon with long shaft and bill style head. For agricultural style bills use bill hook.

Three-seat, twin-engined minelaying, torpedo-bombing and reconnaissance twin-float seaplane. First flown in 1936, in 1938 it set eight world speed records for its class in various range and payload categories.
A factory where furniture is manufactured.
Platform or structure used for viewing performances.
Mechanical reproductive process using photographic, electrostatic and dry powder techniques.
A structure consisting of a vertical mast and a horizontal boom operated by cables on a separate engine or motor. Used for hoisting and moving heavy loads or objects.
A single storey building designed so that windows incorporated into the saw tooth roof catch the available light.
A motor in which rotary motion is produced by steam power.

A map-based understanding of coastal and marine historic character; its GIS and linked texts extend Historic Landscape Characterisation principles to give a common framework of baseline information for the sustainable management of change from land to sea
A site where lime (calcium carbonate) is made.
A workshop for the manufacturing of furniture.
A weapon which is a blade fixed to a long handle.
Hampshire
A triangular sectioned rod probably used for making sparks.
People who are considered to be the property of someone else and who are bound to obedience.

Developed as a long range, heavy day-fighter, the ME110 found its niche as a night fighter. It saw service over Southern and Eastern England during the Battle of Britain but lost out in the daytime to the faster British fighters.
Containers filled with high explosive, which can be fired from artillery pieces, thrown, dropped by aircraft or placed by hand and detonated in various ways.

A French airliner produced in 1925. A four-engined biplane developed from the Bleriot 115 and 135 but larger than these. Two were built for Air Union (the Paris-London route). Both crashed with fatalaties in 1926 (Kent).
A factory where hats are manufactured.
A tool with a curved blade and a short handle. The blade is on both sides of a line extended from the handle. If just on one side use reaping hook.
A chemical works producing mordants for the dying industry.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the Air Ministry. Usually found on or near airfields.
An office, particularly at a seaport, at which customs are collected.
A schedule of work in sufficient detail for it to be quantifiable, implemented and monitored.

Technically a quick setting hydraulic cement or lime,but term has been adapted to denote cement made from burning lumps of marl found in London clay,a technique adopted for C19th building work. Name not intended to denote a relationship with Roman period
A mine used for the extraction of zinc bearing ore. Use with other metal ores extracted and MINE where necessary, eg. LEAD MINE.
A prefabricated timber structure similar to Sectional hutting that was used by the Air Ministry for accommodation at airfields during WWII. Manufactured by Gerrard and Sons from 1939 to 1941.
Single-engine, single-seat biplane seaplane built for the 1924 Schneider Cup Race.
A mine used for the extraction of tungsten bearing ore. Use with other mineral ores extracted and MINE, eg. TIN MINE.
A well with an unusually high mineral content that combined with extensive periods of evaporation may give objects a stony exterior. Once believed to have been caused by magic or witchcraft.
A long, slender, flexible tube for inserting into a body cavity for the introduction or withdrawal of fluids.
A lock, often containing a fish ladder, which allows fish to swim upstream bypassing a weir or other obstacle.

The hobby of using a metal detector to hunt for buried coins or artefacts; alternatively the use of a metal detector to locate metal artefacts on an archaeological excavation that otherwise would go unnoticed.
The residence of an engineer.
A wheeled device supporting a windmill's fantail that moves around a trackway thus turning the windmill into the wind.
A dish adapted by the addition of a pedestal base. (Source: MPRG)
Artificial water channel, usually leading to a mill.
A jug with a sinuous profile where the rim, girth and base are of roughly equal diameter, and the neck and lower body are narrower.(Source: MPRG)
A building material used for coating walls and ceilings. Plaster can refer to gypsum plaster (also known as plaster of Paris), lime plaster, or cement plaster.
A type of WATERMILL, powered by retaining seawater at high tide and then releasing it at low tide via the water wheel.
An underground foot tunnel primarily constructed to allow for the passage of pedestrians beneath an over ground obstacle.
A form of stopper used to regulate the flow of liquid, often used in a barrel.
A building, group of buildings or installation in which scientific experiments are carried out.
A building housing the instrumentation necessary for the observation and measurement of tremors generated by earthquakes.
A site used for the production of sodium bicarbonate, soda ash or caustic soda.
A miniature railway on which targets can be placed to provide moving targets on a firing range.
An area of ground used for the testing of, and practicing with, weapons against fixed and moveable targets.
Use for vessels registered in Antigua.
A target range used for rifle and small arms practice and recreational purposes.
Coastal base for the docking, launch and maintenance of submarines.
A container for dried foodstuffs.
A commonly coppiced wood from the genus Corylus.
A bowl with a sharp change of angle in the vessel wall, generally at the point of maximum diameter. the carination may be in the upper or lower half of the vessel. (Source: MPRG)

Wood and fabric transport glider, twenty of which were produced with twin Bristol Mercury engines. Fitted with a hinged nose for loading and unloading, this was the largest glider used by the RAF and could accomodate a 7-ton tank.
A place where hats are made and sold.
Potassium nitrate
A roof with four sloping sides, rising from four gables, joining at the apex like a pyramid.
A meeting hall of the verderers, who were the officers appointed to maintain the King's forests.
A device, monogram or symbol incised in stonework by a mason as a means of identifying his work. Particularly common in Romanesque and Gothic buildings.
A straight road lined with trees along either side, also straight lines of trees found in parkland usually leading to a landscape feature.
A workshop used for the manufacture of statues, either cast or carved.

Used to identify and measure various sediment layers that exist below the seabed. A sound source emits a signal vertically downwards and a receiver monitors the return signal that has been reflected off the seafloor and sub seabed sediment layers.
The plan on which a circular building is constructed.
A house which has been altered to increase its defensive characteristics.
An indoor or outdoor market where butter was sold.
A small, walled fortlet, situated every Roman mile along the length of Hadrian's Wall to defend a gateway allowing the passage of people and as a garrison to accommodate patrol troops.
A building where carpets and other floor furnishings were woven.
A single line, or two or more roughly parallel lines, of standing stones set at intervals along a common axis or series of axes.
A rustic building of picturesque design, often associated with a model farm, country house or estate. Although ornamental in design they are intended to be functional.
A large board, often attached to the side of a building, on which advertisements can be displayed. Use for external structures only.
A platform or other structure for the use of a band of musicians.
A rustic building of picturesque design.
A candlestick in which a simple socket is set in the centre of a drip tray or saucer. There may be a vertical loop handle linking the socket to the rim of the saucer. (Source: MPRG)
A purpose-built factory for more than one occupier (eg. for several different workshops).
A short, broad bladed oar used without a rowlock.
A sculpture on top of a tomb etc.

A type of aircraft hangar from the closing years of WWI either of steel or wood utilising a type of lattice work roof support known as a Belfast Truss, which features diagonally interlaced pieces of thin pine. The roof appears as a smooth curve.
An object used to stop a candle burning.
A bottle used for the storage of medicine.
A house or range of buildings where domestic dogs and cats can be kept for a period.
A sailing vessel, generally with three masts, square rigged on the fore and main mast.
Production of steel by reheating wrought iron in charcoal filled containers.
A chamfer that has been hollowed out to form a concave shape. This is also known as a chamfret.

An establishment where alcoholic and non alcoholic drinks are served, food may also be served. May be a an individual room within a larger multi purpose building such as a sports pavilion or a theatre.
A preparation made from the evaporated juice of the rhizome of the plant Glycyrrhiza glabra, used medicinally and as a sweet, usually in the form of a black, chewy substance.
Carriages, locomotives and other vehicles used on a railway.

A prefabricated structure of cellular hollow plywood 'aero' beams and columns clad with timber framed units of flat asbestos facing sheets and a felt roof. Designed as airfield accommodation that could be reused as post WWII emergency housing.
Garden or open-air enclosure, usually connected to commercial premises, where tea and other refreshments are served to the public.
A flat level structure, can be part of a series, used to allow a person to move from one level to another, or can occur singularly on a threshold.
A site or establishment for the casting and refining of metallic copper.

The site of a deserted settlement in cases where there is evidence that it has deliberately been relocated in a single planned action, eg. to remove a settlement from an enclosed park, or to create a model community, as opposed to gradual abandonment.
A place where silica or silicate, the most common mineral component of rock, is extracted from the ground.
A flat, level area of ground within a garden. Often raised and accessed by steps.
A site where iron oxide and iron sulphates, used as brown pigments, are excavated.

Single lap roof covering made of clay. Half cylinder in profile although one end is slightly wider than the other. A Spanish tile roof covering comprises under-tiles and over-tiles, the two have the same shape, but the under-tile is slightly larger.

The monitoring of the excavation of a hole made by a non-archaeologically trained person. Any archaeological evidence that comes to light is recorded by the archaeologist during the course of the work although he/she cannot suspend the groundwork.
The vertical lining of a doorway, window or other opening.
Dried grass used as fodder.
The outward curve at the top or bottom of a column where it joins the base or capital.
A medallion, as on a brooch or ring, with a stone which is often semi precious with a device carved in relief.
A vessel used to carry supplies and equipment needed by recreational or deep sea divers.

A single-engine dive-bomber, the JU87 was very successful during the invasions of Poland and France but suffered heavy losses during the Battle of Britain. Withdrawn from NW Europe in 1941 for use in the Mediterranean and on the Eastern Front.
A smooth bore weapon usually for firing shot as opposed to bullets.
A tower used as a watch tower by the coastguard. Often, though not always, built as part of a Coastguard Station.
Site where steel is produced from molten pig iron using a Bessemer Converter, a development from the cementation and crucible steel-making techniques .
A light, buoyant material obtained from the cork oak. Cork is used in floats and as stoppers for bottles.
A gate which allows water to pass into a dock, etc, at flood tide, and by which it is retained during the ebb tide.
A pillbox built to a design drawn up by the chief engineer of South-Eastern Command.
A farmstead, often of linear plan, where the working buildings are placed opposite and parallel to the house and attached working buildings with a relatively narrow space between.

Wood and fabric transport glider, twenty of which were produced with twin Bristol Mercury engines. Fitted with a hinged nose for loading and unloading, this was the largest glider used by the RAF and could accomodate a 7-ton tank.
17th/18th century lightly armed privateer, usually either a 'Dunkirker' or Dutch.
A protective covering applied to the top of a wall, chimney, gable etc., usually curved, sloping or ridged to prevent rainwater settling.
A garden building on an estate used by fishing parties.
A large scale works for cloth finishing processes.
Block for the treatment of separate diseases.
A mill used for the manufacture of twilled dress material of worsted with or without a mixture of cotton or silk.
A simple form of stone slab bridge, particularly associated with South West England.
A balance for weighing coins.
A hotel adjacent to a railway terminus. Railway hotels were often owned by a railway company.
Wooden or ferro-concrete tower for cooling waste, hot water from a power station. The water cascades from the top of the tower to a pond in the bottom.
A stone used to crush objects.
Any type of jug with decoration representing the form of a human face or figure. The shape of the vessel often forms the outline of the human face or figure. (Source: MPRG)

An enclosure defined by a single bank and entrance. They occur on every type of ground, although they favour sheltered, valley side locations. Smaller and usually less well defended than hillforts they are thought to be settlements of Iron Age date.

Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as two linked ranges to create an L-shape. They can comprise a barn and an attached shelter shed to a cattle yard or an interlinked cattle housing and fodder range.
