Composed of sand, stones or other aggregate and cement mixed with water which sets in a hard mass. The material is usually associated with modern building but was developed by Romans where cement was obtained from quicklime.
A biplane, reconnaissance aircraft with a crew of 3 or 4 which equipped 3 and 22 squadrons RAF before passing to the Fleet Air Arm. Produced in two variants.
A building in which photographers, taken for aerial reconnaissance purposes, are analysed and interpreted to provide intelligence on enemy activities.
A single-seat, biplane fighter. One of the last open cockpit types to see widespread service with the RAF, equipping 10 squadrons and, at one point, 70% of the Home Defence fighter force.
Twin-engined, four-crew German seaplane. Entered service in 1932 as a torpedo bomber and naval reconnaisance aircraft, though by World War 2 those still serving were used mainly for air sea rescue.
A military storage aircraft hangar designed in 1937. It has a curved profile and is constructed from steel ribs supporting a concrete skin. The roof is covered with earth and turf.
A room where fittings such as saddles and harnesses for horses are usually kept.
A place where boats are built and stored.
The unarticulated remains of the body of a human being. If articulated use inhumation.
Developed from the DH4, featured the pilot and gunner cockpits in closer proximity, but suffered from engine reliability problems. Also known as the Ninak, saw service from 1918 to 1931.
A fighter-bomber designed to deploy its bombs during the latter stage of a diving manoeuvre, thus increasing the accuracy of its targetting.
An outlying farm or estate belonging to the Premonstratensian order.
A piece of furniture containing shelves, cupboards or drawers for storage or display.
A silicate mineral used since the Bronze Age as gemstones and abrasives. Found in many colours including red, orange, yellow, green, purple, brown, blue, black, pink and colourless.
American, four-engined, medium/heavy day bomber. Entered service in 1937. The prototype was nicknamed the Flying Fortress, which later became a registered trademark.
A twin engined advanced trainer aircraft developed for the military by the US firm of Cessna
A US aircraft manufacturer. The Cessna Aircraft Co Inc was established in 1927
An umbrella-shaped pavilion, Indian in origin, constructed over a funerary site. Can also refer to a funerary monument or cenotaph constructed in this style.
American, all-metal-construction, fighter. Entered service in 1941. 209 were delivered to RAF/FAA, most of which were used in the Far East.
An early design of pump featuring a series of pistons, or sometimes bundles of rags, passing through a barrel on a continuous chain, forcing water upwards.
A place where paper, frequently printed in ornamental designs, used for covering the interior walls of buildings, is manufactured.
An underground hideout containing radio equipment to be used by the Auxiliary Units to relay information gained from the various out-stations back to headquarters.
A building, within a gas works, housing a gas purifier.
A jettied house where the overhanging upper storey runs along the entire length of one side.
A colonnade all around the exterior of a building or an interior space such as a courtyard.
A stone heated in a fire then dropped into a liquid to heat it.
A command centre used to co-ordinate information received from Royal Observer Corps observation and monitoring posts.
Sorting offices constructed during the Second World War designed to rapidly move goods from the vulnerable docks and ports via the rail network.

Articles intended for personal adornment, usually to be strung on items of jewellery or sewn onto clothing. They may be made out of worked raw materials (eg. shells) or be manufactured goods, for example glass beads.

Four-engined heavy bomber, developed by Avro from the twin-engined Manchester. Entered service in 1942 as the RAF's principal night bomber and took part in the 1,000 bomber raids as well as the famous Dam Busters raid.
Used where an existing building is designated as the residence of an official.
The commonest type of roof with sloping sides meeting at a ridge and with a gable at each end.
Use for vessels registered in the Philippines.
A building where merchandise and goods are temporarily stored before or after transportation by rail.

A residence of two or three monks of the Savigniac order dependent on a foreign mother house. The order was originally founded by monks in Savigny, Normandy, in 1105 and first established in Britain in 1123 at Tulket, Preston.
A building or buildings used for the manufacture of shoe and leather polish, etc.
A site or establishment for the casting and refining of metallic copper.
An underground chamber, store room or passage.
A piece of metal in front of a fire to stop embers rolling onto the carpet.
An uncommon form of a regular courtyard farmstead where the buildings are arranged in a Z-shaped form.
Demasted old ship used as a floating prison.

A jar adapted by the addition of two handles. Handles may be horizontal or vertical loops or horizontal or curved lugs. Handles are nearly always opposed. Profiles vary and should be double indexed with the appropriate JAR type. (Source: MPRG)
Supplies owned by, or for the use of, the government.
A narrow aisle that pierces an internal buttress.

In the glass industry, a furnace of Lorraine Type, comprising a central rectangular melting furnace with ancillary structures at each corner, adjacent to the fires. Post-Mediaeval until superceded by coal-fired furnaces.
A garden building, octagonal in plan, designed in the style of a classical temple, used for standing or sitting in.
A broad design of sword used for cutting and slashing.

A two-piece Bow Brooch dating from the early to mid-first century AD in Britain, originating in Gaul. Featuring a wide flat reeded bow, this and the Thistle Brroch were the first to conceal the spring mechanism with a cylindrical or semi-cylindrical hood.
Photographic image produced using an ink-jet printer.
Areas used for potato-growing.
Record colour in appropriate field.
Field or area of ground where washed new cloth is stretched out to dry.
A grain, obtained from the grass Oryza sativa, eaten as a staple in many parts of the world.

An upright, or originally upright, stone featuring a hole which is often large enough in diameter for a person to pass through, eg. Men an Tol, Cornwall. Do not use for perforated portable stone artefacts.
A horizontal member supporting the posts in a timber framed structure.

A building containing a series of seats for use by the clergy during services. The seats are usually placed in the church and as such this is a very rare monument type, being purpose-built. An example being St. Germoe's Chair in Germoe, Cornwall.
Single-engine, single-seat biplane day fighter developed by Siddeley. Variations included an all-metal, fabric-covered Mk.III, which became the RAF's main fighter in the 1920s.
A fragment of the body of a vessel, or hollow object, usually of ceramic or glass. If known, use specific vessel type.
The lower, or inner, curve of an arch
A viscous, bituminous pitch which can be used for surfacing roads.
A dwelling built on marshy, boggy or waterlogged land using timber piles driven vertically into the ground to raise the floor above the ground to prevent flooding.

Regular courtyard farmsteads where the buildings are arranged as an F-shaped plan around two cattle yards. Cattle housing and stabling typically extend as three ranges from the longer main range which includes a barn or mixing house.
A place of worship for followers of the Pentecost (ie. emphasising the gifts of the Holy Spirit).
Small stone hearth set up in a shallow pit. Burns vegetation and coppiced twigs to produce potash.
A factory where seaplanes are manufactured.
West Yorkshire
A spiny evergreen shrub of the pea family which can be utilized as a roof covering in areas of its predominance, eg. heathland.
A building where masts are made and stored.
A room where weapons and armour are stored.
A jar used to store medicines, drugs or the constituent parts of medicines and drugs.
A factory manufacturing fireplaces.
Used where an existing building is designated as the residence of an official.
A mill for the processing of rice for use in food products.
An axe used by the Saxons and Franks for throwing.
A structure used for the production of hydraulic power. A head of water was raised at the top of the tower by means of pumps. Used for powering machinery.
A pillbox in which the roof is detached from the walls and supported by a central pillar, thus leaving an embrasure allowing a 360 degree field of fire.
Use for deposits representing material discarded or remaining as a result of a process or processes.
A building adjoining a cricket pitch with facilities for players and spectators.
Associated group of drawing implements.
A window cut through a single slab of timber or stone.

The Fi 103 is the more technical nomenclature for the Second World War German V1 flying bomb, produced by Fieseler. Multiple index together with Fieseler and flying bomb for maximum chance of retrieval for users.
A large stone laid horizontally to form the roof of a chamber.
A torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance biplane in service with the Fleet Air Arm 1935-1938. Rendered obsolete after 1938 by the Swordfish and withdrawn from service.
An area within a large fireplace where it is possible to sit.
A cottage erected over a short period of time, by people who had no legal right to the land. Squatters were often tolerated by the landlord as they provided cheap labour.
The wood of the evergreen coniferous tree characterized by single needle-like leaves and errect cones.
A recess within a wall or room.
A diagram or drawing made by projection onto a horizontal plane, often of a building.
A flat bottomed ditch flanked by mounds running to the south of Hadrian's Wall for much of its length, marking the boundary of the military zone.
In use for small scale horticulture.
An inner defensive area within a castle.
The rotating top section of a tower or smock mill.
A hearth constructed specifically for the manufacture of pitch.
Two intersecting beams set on the ground to support a post, usually for a post mill.
Fixed equipment, such as slides, swings and climbing frames for children to play on. Often found in playgrounds, parks and school grounds.
Hut along the coast, which provided shelter for lookouts known as "huers", who kept watch for the pilchard shoals that passed by the coast. Built of stone or wood. Particular common to Cornwall.
A place of worship for followers of the teachings of Martin Luther.
A building where jazz music is performed. Often situated in small venues to afford the intimacy of the musicians performing in close proximity to the audience.
A type of direct-acting, twin cylinder steam driven water pump.

Based on the previous all-timber design 2423/39 and the temporary brick and timber design 518/40, the 8936/40 was built with pre-cast concrete slabs replacing the timber floors and staircases with only the balcony and watch office roof in timber.

A large octagonal pillbox, with a projecting entrance, equipped with loopholes for eight light machine guns and a light anti-aircraft mounting sited in a central well which was accessed from inside the pillbox. Designed by DFW branch 3.
Grounds, usually associated with a country house, laid out so as to produce the effect of natural scenery.
An oven used in the coal industry for the recovery of gas, tar and other by-products of the coking process. Late 19th century-20th century.
A shaped stone, which could be hand held, used in combination with a saddle quern to grind or rub grain.
A building used to manufacture Producer Gas. Producer Gas is a mix of gases formed by passing compressed air through hot coke.
A keystone decorated with a relief sculpture, usually a cartouche
A planned administrative capital for local government which provided amenities for the Roman and peregrine (non-Roman) inhabitants of the town.
A cover consisting of a plate for covering over or closing in a chamber or receptacle.
A public recreational complex centred around an open-air swimming pool. Use SWIMMING POOL as a component of LIDO.
The entire playing area and associated buildings upon which the game of cricket is played.
A mill where mustard is produced.
Application of earth based plaster to a backing of lath or wattle used in internal or external walls. Composite mixture which may include clay soil, dung, straw, lime putty, sand or horsehair.
Coastal area above high water levele. Specify in Description using: sand, sand dune, shingle etc.
A square, wooden drinking vessel.
A photo- reconnaissance variant of the Boeing Superfortress, used from 1944, initally deployed in the Pacific war, later for Cold war duties over Europe.
A small settlement, usually consisting of one dwelling with ancillary buildings.
A sign, often mounted on a post next to a roadside, giving directions or other instructions.
A railway worked by the propulsive force of compressed air or by the formation of a vacuum.
A bowl with convex body walls. (Source: MPRG)
Wood from the elm tree.
Detached block comprising one or more storeys of wards.

A place of worship for the Knights of the Order of the Hospital of St John of Jerusalem, a military order dedicated to the provision of hospitality for pilgrims, to the care of the sick and to the protection of the Holy Land.
A crane mounted on wheels and/or rails, used for the unloading of ships' cargoes.
A building where ambulances are housed awaiting emergency calls.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
A structure, often sunk into the ground, for the purpose of allowing total bodily immersion in mineral sprinwater or similarly beneficial substances.
A dedicated room for housing the organ feeder bellows, can be an underground chamber or a free-standing building.
A barge with a crane or sheer legs used for moving and maintaining mooring buoys.

An airfield building housing a turret gunnery trainer used to teach air gunners how to report the correct position of enemy aircraft by practising shooting against projected moving images of enemy aircraft displayed on a target screen (WWII).
A building used for the testing of steel.

Twin-engined jet-fighter. The first British aircraft to exceed Mach 1 in level flight, later to exceed Mach 2. Entered service in 1960. After 13 years was superseded in its primary defence role by the Phantom, though remained in RAF service until 1988.
A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of beer.
A building or site used to produce alkaline chemicals by controlled reactions.
The fat removed from the carcass of a whale or seal and used in the manufacture of cosmetics and as a fuel for tallow lamps.
A fighter version of the SKUA fitted with a four-gun turret. The majority were converted to target tugs for use by the RAF and Fleet Air Arm.
A low, wide, open container.
A column that is equidistant, with intercolumniations, even at the corners, with two or more triglyphs over each intercolumniation.
An atrium or open court, surrounded by porticoes, at the west end of a church.
A factory making laminate flooring.
A building housing washing facilities and toilets. The term occurs mainly in a military context.

A type of military aircraft hangar of the Cold War, hardened and therefore protected against the effects of nuclear weapons. It comprises a semi-circular structure built of corrugated-steel supporting a reinforced-concrete skin. Three NATO designs.
A fortified tower designed to house a number of artillery pieces and a small garrison. Artillery towers first appear in England in the 16th century.
A plate, usually of wood or metal, used to indicate the limit of an area or piece of land.
A diagonal or arched member placed across rafters to stiffen and support a roof structure.

skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Isla Grande De Tierra Del Fuego

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A place where tobacco is made into cigarettes, cigars, etc.
A form of dagger.
A building in which potatoes can sprout and germinate.
Single-engine, three-crew torpedo-spotter, reconnaissance and anti-submarine biplane. Entered Naval service in 1936, designed for operation from aircraft carriers and equipped with folding wings.
Type of survey involving the drilling of deep and narrow shafts in the ground used to describe deposits, understand stratigraphy and collect cores amples.
A jug form characterized by the addition of three applied feet. The feet are usually short and stubby. Double index with the appropriate profile type. (Source: MPRG)
A site where products containing sugar or honey, such as cakes, sweets, crystallized fruits or jam, were manufactured.
A building that housed humans and cattle under one roof, with a shared entrance providing access to the cattle housing (usually downslope) and the dwelling area.
A sculpted cross, or a cross incised into stone or trees, to mark a parish boundary.
A structure, part of a structure or area constructed from plain bricks.
For example Asbestosis, ME/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome, HIV, Lupus, Lyme Disease, MS, Overactive Thyroid Disease, Pancreatitis and other related illnesses.
A furnace used for the smelting or reheating of lead.
A container, usually glass, used for storing medicinal substances.
Single-engine, advanced-pilot trainer. Spruce and plywood in construction, entered service in 1939, continuing to serve as a trainer, and also a target tug, until 1950.
A single storey mill used in the textile industry.
Systematically positioned hole, or holes, utilised in all studies that aim to sample the nature of the topsoil and subsurface deposits.
An improved water frame spinning machine which differed from the water frame in mechanical details, being larger and operating at a much faster speed.
An object used to grip together objects.
A female figure used instead of a column, usually supporting an entablature.
Fibres of wood reduced chemically or mechanically to pulp for use in the manufacture of paper.
A cleansing house associated with Jewish burial ceremonies
A stable found at a coaching inn where horses are housed.
A bookbinding workshop.
Roman coastal forts fortified with large walls and a ditch, introduced to cope with raids from across the English Channel and North Sea.

A powerful machine comprising a pair of heated cylinders revolving inside a chamber, and used for converting raw rubber into a soft plastic mass by being 'chewed' between knives or teeth projecting from the cylinders.
Factory for making Chenille a yarn produced by placing short lengths of yarn (the pile) between two core yarns (the core) these are then heated to set the pile in place.
A mill in which strands of yarn are twisted together to produce a strong thread with a uniform thickness.
A factory where musical organs are manufactured.
American-built, twin-engined flying-boat designed for maritime patrol and reconnaissance. Entered US Naval service in 1936 as the PBY-1; christened the Catalina by the RAF, who used it from 1939 on.
A place where metal-cutting hand files were made.
A semi metal, poisonous element used in a variety of industrial processes and in some medicinal preparations.
A channel that returns water that has been used to turn a waterwheel back to the river or source from which it came.

Usually dating from the early 20th century these cabinets, sited alongside public highways, were used for the distribution of electricity for street lighting control and later for domestic use. In Wolverhampton these boxes also serviced the tram system.
A building used for the finishing, drying and storage of lace.
One of the rolls forming the sides of an ionic capital, joining the volutes of the front and rear faces.
A furnace composed of two fire brick boxes: the fire was in the lower box and the upper box held the crucibles. Used in the manufacture of steel.
A tall, hollow pipe, usually cast-iron, resembling a lamp-post. Used to ventilate sewer systems.
A chapel in a church for penitents.
A cylinder containing a piston by which fluid can be ejected or sucked in.

A two-seat, single-engine bomber. Fast, versatile and well armed, but with a fuel tank poorly placed between pilot and gunner, was considered to be the best day bomber of the First World War. Later entered civil service.
A loft or gallery supported on a covered, vaulted structure and projecting over the rood screen proper, occassionally used by minstrels or singers.
A drawing, generally on a transparent sheet, which can be placed on top of another image to combine information from both.
A dam and sluice combination, associated with an aqueduct, for the extraction of water from a river to feed a reservoir or water treatment plant.

A biplane torpedo-bomber designed to be flown from aircraft carriers. Equipped with foldable wings for ease of storage. Joined Fleet Air Arm service in 1940, intended as a replacement for the Swordfish.
A deciduous conifer native to Britain and Europe supplying durable and waterproof timber suitable for shipbuilding features such as masts.
A place where metal knives and edge cutting tools were manufactured.
A short timber connecting a cruck blade to a wall above the point at which the blade diverges from it.
A large board found at sporting events, erected so as to be seen by the spectators, on which the score of a game is kept.

A building used for the preparatory processes in which long and short staple flax fibres were separated by passing through combs. Flax dressing or 'heckling' shops may be located both on and off mill sites.
A golf course, clubhouse and ancilliary buildings.
A form of limonite, found in wet ground, from which iron can be extracted.
A works site making and/or maintaining drive belts for industrial power.

A hydrated aluminium phosphate mineral sometimes used as a semi-precious stone, and for carvings and ornamental use. Named after Variscia, the historical name of the Vogtland in Germany. Mainly green in colour.

Single-engine, single-seat interceptor fighter developed from the race-winning Schneider Trophy seaplanes. One of the most famous of all combat aircraft, entered RAF service in 1938 and was still in use in the 1950s.
A club founded to provide education, relaxation, and recreation for working men.

An establishment used for the manufacture of reeds and healds, which are components of a textile loom with related functions, in that they move and control the threads, and similar wire-based construction.
A site where the process of combing, the preparatory process for long wools, takes place.
An often highly elaborate water fountain, usually found in parks, gardens or urban spaces.
A building in which wool or cotton were beaten to clean and separate the fibres.
A jettied house where the upper storey only overhangs the end elevation of the building.
A bottle for the storage and transportation of milk.
A factory where brushes are manufactured. Use for all types of brush.

American, four-engine, long range, heavy strategic bomber. Entered service in 1943 and used exclusively against Japanese forces. The B29s Enola Gay and Bock's Car were used to drop atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945.

A French airliner produced in 1925. A four-engined biplane developed from the Bleriot 115 and 135 but larger than these. Two were built for Air Union (the Paris-London route). Both crashed with fatalaties in 1926 (Kent).

Troop and general transport glider. Almost entirely wooden in construction, many were manufactured by the furniture industry. Mk I featured a a door-ramp on the port side whilst the Mk II was fitted with a hinged nose.

Purpose-built structure, other than a bollard, to prevent vehicle or pedestrian access to a road or site, for example concrete blocks to obstruct vehicles accessing beaches on the north-east coast for illegal sea-coaling.
A building housing a variety of facilities, such as theatres, galleries, concert halls, etc.
A searchlight battery, which points out to sea, used to locate enemy shipping
Characteristic waste flakes struck off in the manufacture of adzes.
A building used to house railway engines.
A hollow moulding, often enriched, similar to a scotia or cavetto, used in Gothic jambs and cornices.
An anti-personnel device consisting of a 40 gallon fuel drum placed on top of an explosive charge and detonator. When detonated the barrel would explode sending burning fuel over the intended target.
An open sided building known to have been used for sheltering cattle.
A chapel situated within the demesnes of a manor. Can be a separate building or an integral part of a manor house.
A spike for separating the strands of a rope.
An artificial, sometimes temporary, platform on which helicopters can take off and land.
A double-span aircraft hangar designed by Boulton & Paul of London and Norwich. Mainly used on aircraft factory sites and at Armament Training Schools.
Any piece of timber that makes up the body of a maritime vessel, e.g. frame, decks, masts.

Four-engined heavy bomber, developed by Avro from the twin-engined Manchester. Entered service in 1942 as the RAF's principal night bomber and took part in the 1,000 bomber raids as well as the famous Dam Busters raid.
A specialist hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of heart disorders and diseases.
A stand by set house built to Air Ministry drawing number 1039/41.
A book containing prayers.
A bridge over a canal.

Four-engine, seven-crew heavy bomber. Entered service with RAF Bomber Command in 1940, becoming one of the twin sources of bomber strength along with the Lancaster. Also used for transport and glider tug duties.
An object designed to add curls to a wig.
A plan in which the staircase is placed at the centre of the building.
A cereal used to make spirits, beer and coarse bread.
A steam engine driving a reciprocating air pump to provide air for a blast furnace.
Use for deposits formed by the action of the sea or under marine conditions.
A bowl divided into two or more compartments by vertical slab partitions. (Source: MPRG)
A priory of the female Order of Knights Hospitallers.

A type of waterwheel where the incoming supply of water leaves a launder near the top of the wheel, and drops onto the paddles or buckets of the wheel which rotates in the reverse direction to that of the incoming flow.
Use for vessels registered in Poland.
A jug with a maximum diameter in the lower half of the vessel and with no discernible shoulder. (Source: MPRG)
A gun using an explosive propellant to fire sharpened metal shafts, usually fired through water.
A garden or collection of potted plants on the flat roof of a house or other building.
An axe used by the Saxons and Franks for throwing.
An entrance large enough for carriages and vehicles leading through a building or wall into an inner courtyard.

A technique utilised in maritime recording; a remote operated vehicle (ROV) is a tethered underwater robot. ROVs have been used to locate and inspect a number of historic shipwrecks in depths beyond the reach of human divers.
A tray for separating grain from chaff.
A building or site used to assess the mechanical state of a vehicle.

Twin-engined bomber. The Whitley was the first 'heavy' bomber to be built in quantity for the RAF and made the first bombing attack on Germany in May 1940. It was later used for convoy protection and reconnaissance.

A form used to record the details of a feature identified by archaeological investigation, generally including location, depth, colour, texture, inclusions and stratigraphic relationship to other contexts.
A factory built for the production of breakfast cereals.
Any object which bears an inscription.

Twin-engined monoplane that served the RAF as an advanced trainer and flying ambulance. Mk. I featured a gun turret and served for gunnery and bombing-crew training. Subsequent versions used for pilot, radio and navigation training.
A hard silica rich rock, black or brown coloured, commonly found in nodular form.
A burial ground for followers of the Islamic faith.

A panel, board or device bearing an inscription, symbol or image, usually describing a function, name, location, instruction, or otherwise distinguishing the object or structure on which it is placed.
A diagonally set modillion placed at a cornice's external corner.
Northern Hemisphere

American troop and supply-glider constructed from steel tube and fabric-covered wood, with a hinged nose to allow loading and unloading of troops or light vehicles. Also known as the Haig, this was the only US glider to see combat service.
A bridge whose trusses or girders form parapets on either side of the deck.
Metal cylinder for producing charcoal using the retort method
A staircase that rises through only one storey and has treads and risers framed into square studs, one of them often on one side of a door-frame; it usually occupies a rectangular space.

A large rectangle roof tile with an upstand on one side, a roll in the centre and another roll on the other side, which fits over the upstand of the adjacent tile. The name does not denote a relationship with the Roman period.
A large metal pylon structure used to tether airships.
A detached subordinate building. Use specific type where known, eg. DAIRY.
A building for housing deer overnight.

A building or part of a building, sometimes attached to a religious community, where religious activities such as worshipping, meetings, teaching about the faith and conferences take place. It can also provide accommodation.
A fencing sword often used for recreational purposes.
A twin-engined development of the JU88, the JU188 had a higher service ceiling and greater maximum speed. JU188s operated over the UK from 1944 onwards as night intruders and reconnaissance aircraft.
A small open boat, usually a very light craft propelled by a paddle.
Layer of grass with earth and matted roots cut from the ground and used for earth buildings and as a covering material.
A written work issued at regular intervals, numbered consecutively with no intended or planned end point.
A factory producing drabbet, a type of linen cloth.
A simple, wind-driven water pump, also known as a windpump.
A house occupied by an employee of a waterworks. Usually found in association with a pumping station or waterworks.
A factory or site where wooden clogs are manufactured.
A small slab in a Doric cornice.
Four-crew, twin-engined monoplane designed as a torpedo-bomber and reconnaissance aircraft for RAF Coastal Command. Withdrawn from operations in November 1940 and downgraded to a trainer.
A pan for cooking fish.
To be used for the frame elements only, not for the bedding.
A herbaceous plant grown for its fibre and marijuana, a drug derivative. The fibres are used in the manufacture of rope.
American, single-engine fighter designed for operation from US Naval aircraft carriers. Produced between 1940 and 1945, Wildcats provided to the British Fleet Air Arm were renamed Martlets.
A piece of furniture with one or more doors concealing storage space.
A factory or building where furniture is upholstered.
Twin-engined monoplane originally designed as a reconnaissance aircraft, but also widely used as a trainer. Entered RAF service in 1936.
American A-20 twin-engined, light, day bomber. Some supplied to the RAF and known as the Boston I. Subsequent variations adapted to night flying and re-christened the Havoc.
A long bed containing rose plants.
A small tool with a shovel blade and a pick blade set at right angles to the handle.
A type of coal preparation plant for the sizing, sorting and washing of coal.
A building plan in which the rooms are symmetrically placed.
A building or part of a building used for the storage of furniture or furniture related materials.
A shaft cut to facilitate the extraction of salt from halite deposits by pumping water into the deposit and pumping out brine from which the salt is later extracted.
An object in the sea bed detected by marine survey equipment that shows the contours of the sea bed beneath a vessel.
A building where distillation, a chemical process used in the production of a range of different chemicals, took place.
A vessel used for the transport of troops, either during wartime or for garrison duties in peacetime.
Machines for automatically feeding fuel onto the fire of steam boilers and other furnace plant, introduced at the beginning of the 19th century.
A kiln in which Iron ores were heated before smelting in order to drive off the impurities such as sulphur.
A room equipped for the care of babies and young children.
A steam-powered factory.
Shelter on military airfield to provide night time accommodation for airmen during WWII.
A building or site used for the maintenance and repair of motor vehicles.
A small auxiliary engine to help start up a large steam engine - invented 1866.
A crude shelter for persons engaged in the production of pure carbon by the controlled burning of wood and other organic materials.
A building in which engineered metal products are finished and polished.
A board fixed at the gable end to purlins, often decorated.
An alcoholic drink made from fermented apple juice.
A wall cladding consisting of slates hung in overlapping rows.
A shelter in a public park.
Model village built as a holiday resort.
The burnt remains of a corpse.
An aircraft engaged in rescuing persons in danger at sea.

An enclosure defined by a single bank and entrance. They occur on every type of ground, although they favour sheltered, valley side locations. Smaller and usually less well defended than hillforts they are thought to be settlements of Iron Age date.
A workshop with a forge for the melting and working of white metal, ie. low-melting alloys. Also used for a smith specializing in decorative or finely finished wrought iron work.

A fishing vessel which tows a dredger to gather oysters. This is an iron wedge shaped contrivance with a small net attached. Towed behind the vessel the iron wedge loosens the oysters and they fall into the net.
A jar with a profile that slopes inwards from base to rim. Particularly shallow examples have been term Peat Pots; this is a term with a restricted distribution in northern England. (Source: MPRG)
A factory which produces artificial imitations of mineral water, such as soda water.
A large container used for the process of cleansing and thickening cloth by beating and washing.
A long rope with a noose at one end for catching animals.
A mould in which an axehead is cast.
A factory where hats are manufactured.
Large shallow dish or plate.
A horizontal timber usually at the bottom of a timber framed wall into which posts and studs are tenoned.
A plan of a structure which has eight sides.
A mechanism used for lifting and lowering weights, operated by hand.
The meeting hall of a secular or ethical society.
A vessel in which incense is burnt.
A container used as a lavatory by bedridden people.
A jar with one or more lips added on the outside of the vessel wall over a hole pierced through the wall. The lips do not usually rise above rim level. (Source: MPRG)
A lightweight prefabricated structure of corrugated galvanized steel having a semicircular cross section. The design was based on the Nissen hut developed by the British during the First World War.

A device, monogram or symbol usually carved on stone or woodwork near a buildingï¿½s entrance points, particularly doorways, windows and fireplaces, to protect inhabitants and visitors from witches and evil spirits.
A building designed to house a lifeboat, usually with a stone ramp to launch the boat into the sea.
A building specifically built to house life saving apparatus used when conditions prevented the lifeboat from deploying.
Seaside structure, usually consisting of a manmade retaining wall that keeps a relatively large area of the tidal water partitioned off for controlled boating or swimming.
An object designed to bring bad luck, divine wrath, disease etc upon the bearer or target of the curse.

Twin-engined, seven-crew, coastal reconnaissance, biplane flying-boat. Designed to the same specification as the Saro London, entered service in 1937. Also serving in an anti-submarine role, was replaced by the Consolidated Canso (Catalina) in 1943.
Single-engine, single-seat biplane day fighter developed by Siddeley. Variations included an all-metal, fabric-covered Mk.III, which became the RAF's main fighter in the 1920s.
A single-storey structure, usually situated against the exterior of a walled garden's south facing wall, used for storage and often accomodation.
The residence and small-scale workshop of a hosier.
A gentry house in a town or city, either detached or in a terrace.
A factory making flame retardant materials.
A clay tube with a small bowl at the end used for smoking tobacco.
Single-seat fighter-bomber with a single, midships engine and tricycle landing gear. After proving a failure as an air-combat fighter, was used mainly in the ground attack role.
A room used in a church to store vestments and for the clergy to dress in.
Scaffolding intended to impede the advance of enemy armoured divisions. Often found in association with "one way" anti tank ditches.
A small dye works, often associated with a CALICO PRINTING WORKS.
Oil obtained from the rendered blubber of whales, used as a fuel in old oil lamps.
A stone or metal post that indicates the limit of an area or piece of land.
A spa building to which water was pumped from springs or wells; usually also serving a social function as an ASSEMBLY ROOM, eg. as at Bath.
A residential home for children with physical or learning disabilities, sensory impairment and/or mental health issues but who do not necessarily need medical attention.
Single-engine fighter/dive-bomber. The Fleet Air Arm's first operational monoplane, and its first aircraft to shoot down an enemy during the war.

A concrete structure, based on drawing number (11008/41), intended to be the headquarters for the coordination of an airfield's defences. Constructed partially underground it was considered less vulnerable than the (3329/41).
A musket with a snaphance lock. This lock consisted of a flint and steel but the pan cover was separate to the steel unlike the flintlock.
A factory where fish are processed into food products.
A container for kohl, a powder usually made of antimony, used as eye shadow.
A round, oval or rectangular straight-sided dish, divided into two or more units or compartments of varying sizes by vertical slab partitions. (Source: MPRG)

skos:Concept.skos:definition: 1/12000 of a foot or 25.4 μm. Also known as mil

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A tool used to smooth wood. It has a flat surface with an adjustable blade protruding through it.
A building used to store coal.

A tandem two-seat, twin-engined, all-weather, long-range supersonic jet interceptor fighter/fighter-bomber originally developed for the United States Navy by McDonnell Aircraft.It first entered service in 1960 with the U.S. Navy.
Reheating of iron from a finery, for rolling or slitting.

A reinforced concrete structure, usually sited underground, from where it was intended to conduct the business of government in the event of nuclear war. Date specific from mid 1980's to early 1990's.
A tool used for weeding and breaking up the ground prior to planting.
An engine house used to pump water to the top of an ACCUMULATOR TOWER.
An indoor court where the ancient and complex sport of real tennis is played, eg. the court at Hampton Court Palace.
American twin-engined medium bomber and ground-attack aircraft that entered service in 1941. A small number were delivered to the RAF under the British designation Mitchell I.
A grave or sepulchre enlosed or covered by a memorial.
A shallow draft vessel used to carry a crane.
A three-storey RNAS control tower, incorporating meteorological office on the ground floor and an air watch office on the second floor.

Four-engine, long range heavy bomber. Developed from the Lancaster, and originally designated the Lancaster Mk. IV, it was larger in size, bombload and fuel capacity. Never used operationally in World War Two.
A drainage structure that extends across and beneath roadways, canals or embankments.

A jar with a single handle attached to the rim edge and looped over the top of the vessel. There may be a lip. Profiles can vary and should be double indexed with the appropriate JAR type. (Source: MPRG)
A strong, durable alloy of iron and carbon.
Smoke generators (also known as smoke pots) were used to create a smoke screen to provide defensive cover for strategic targets
Casual scribbles or pictographs on ancient walls, stones or other surfaces. In more recent times applied to humourous, satiric or obscene writings or drawings executed anonymously in public places.

Headquarters buildings on military airfields for administrative purposes housing offices, lecture rooms and in some cases a library and a meteorological office. On smaller airfields it is called Station Offices. Abbreviation SQH.
The bony outgrowths found on the heads of mammals used for display or combat used for a variety of purposes.
Use for congenital (present at birth) abnormalities (absent/extra or morphologically unusual features) present in an individual or population.
An 18th century garden building, designed in the form of a classical Doric temple, used for standing or sitting in.
A body of water placed in such a way as to reflect a building or landscape feature.
Building housing apparatus for testing chain links.
A large stopper, often of cork.
A flexible container, usually leather, for the storage and transportation of wine.
A small-scale railway, often for the transportation of children at a place of recreation.
An upright post set on a tiebeam or collar and used to support a ridge piece.
A short timber set across the top of a wall to take the foot of a rafter and an ashlar piece.
A building used for the daily administration of that branch of the RAF dealing with training pilots.
A mill for grinding corn. Use with power type where known.
The entrance to a tramway tunnel.
An object of Bronze Age date, usually of gold, with an unknown function.
A type of helmet with a hinged visor.
A common plan form of large medieval and sub medieval houses, with a hall range flanked by two wings; also found with only one wing.
A door divided horizontally into two parts, independently hinged.
A house or range of buildings in which dogs are kept, eg. hunting hounds.

A monument within a church or cathedral representing one of the stations of the cross. Usually images or pictures of successive incidents of the Passion, they are intended to be visited for meditation and prayer.

Single-engine, single-seat fighter-bomber developed from the Typhoon and the abandoned Tornado. Entered service in 1944 with its greatest success being in destroying V.1. flying bombs. One of the fastest World War 2 aircraft, with a top speed of 436 mph.
A mill used for the production of wadding, as opposed to yarn or cloth. Often associated with steam or water power.
A factory where jute (plant fibres), was used to make products such as hessian, sacking, cordage and backing materials for carpet and linoleum.
An object which does not provide light but supports or is attached to lighting equipment.
17th to early 19th century muzzle-loaded long guns.
A post box mounted on a lamp post.
A trench in the form of a flattened 'W' with a flat concrete roof covered in turf, supported on concrete pillars. The name derives from the resemblance to a child's drawing of a seagull in flight.
A mill, including a forge and powered hammers where hot metal is shaped by hammering and rolling.
A grooved ring holding a gem or semi-precious stone.
Multicellular marine alga, which grows on the seashore, in salt marshes, in brackish water or submerged in the ocean.
The principal Anglican church in a diocese in which the cathedra or bishop's throne is to be found.
An abbey or priory of the Trinitarian brethren also named Maturins.
A strong, fortified dwelling, of between two and four storeys. Occupied only in times of trouble built mainly in the border country of the North from the mid 14th to the 17th century.
Explosive devices, usually of metal, placed in the ground or floating in water with the purpose of endangering enemy personnel or shipping.
A hospital where people with learning difficulties receive medical treatment.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Hospital For People With Learning Difficulties

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: A building or subterranean structure used for the storage of meat.
The residence of a glover.

A capital with two rows of eight acanthus leaves rising above an astragal;from between the leaves of the upper row rise eight stalks,each surmounted by a calyx from which emerge volutes carryingthe corners of the concave sided abacus and central ornaments
Building housing a form of early steam engine using steam at atmospheric pressure. Chiefly employed in mine pumping.
An open metalwork structure supporting either a fabrication shed or the runners for an overhead crane.
A man-made ridge to carry a railway across a declivity or area subject to flooding.
An holistic approach to landscape, using GIS, which maps diversity of landscape character as a means to managing future change in ways that are appropriate and sustainable.
A small crane fixed to the wall of a warehouse or similar building.

A hole in a wall in which cross timbers, known as putlogs, were placed to allow scaffolding to be erected. Putlog holes are often left unfilled and are often the only evidence for the use of scaffolding.
A swimmin pool restricted to the use of men only.
A building or site where boat sails are manufactured from processed cloth.
Grains of cereal used as food.
A covering for the foot not enclosing the ankle.
Loose fibres obtained by unpicking old ropes. Mainly used to caulk seams in wooden vessels.
A workshop or factory unit where small or light goods are manufacture without the need for large-scale industrial machinery.
A building or large scale site for the manufacture and/or storage of weapons, ammunition and equipment.
A residential home for children with physical or learning disabilities, sensory impairment and/or mental health issues but who do not necessarily need medical attention.
A staircase normally used by servants and tradesmen.
A factory where pianos are manufactured.
An engraved stamp used to impress an image onto another object.
A medicinal or mineral spring often with an associated building.
A building of varying designs intended for directing military aviation operations. Normally associated with military airfields.
A hospital where Air Force personnel and their families receive medical and surgical treatment.
Large cargo vessel specially built and equipped for handling large quantities of ore.
A term for a drinking vessel, although its use often implies a recognised quantity.
Paper currency. Bank notes may be of any denomination or value and of any nationality.

A monument comprising an irregularly circular enclosing ditch, interrupted by several causeways, surrounding a central circular area used for funerary activities, often concealed originally beneath an earthen mound. Index with barrow type where known.
In a truss, a rafter used to stiffen the principal rafter by doubling it.
A beaker with a construction above the base to form a waisted profile. (Source: MPRG)
Used for vessels registered in Malaysia.
Instruments for measuring and displaying time. Often manufactured as a piece of furniture e.g.a grandfather clock.

A very long, narrow, roofed building, often two-storeyed, used for the manufacture of rope. Often attached to warehousing, an engine house or offices. Can be included within the complex of a textile mill.
A tool of flint or other stone, usually worked bifacially, and thought to be a fairly general purpose tool.
An area used for the training of personnel in civil defence procedures.

An offshore station, equipped with a fixed electronic radio navigation and positioning system such as Hyperfix. The transmission principle are pulsed and phase comparisons systems. Superceded by Global Positioning System in 1994.
A powder made by grinding the edible part of various grains, and used as a foodstuff.

American, single-engine fighter designed for operation from US Naval aircraft carriers. The Hellcat was a more powerful version of the Wildcat, a total of 1000 being provided to the Fleet Air Arm under Lend-Lease.
A massive structure, usually of stone, serving as a pier or breakwater, or joining two places separated by water.
A small, usually hinged, box made of copper alloy which protected a seal.
A building for the storage and drying of hops, often including a hop drying kiln. Usually built as part of a farm.
An abbey or priory of Cluniac nuns.
A part of an arch between the apex and the springer.
A small turret that projects from the top of a tower or parapet.

A short-term storage centre of goods or special parts to facilitate the rapid processing of orders and supply of goods to customers; unlike a warehouse, the emphasis is on the moving of goods rather than on a long-term storage.
A bowl used for divination.
A mine used for the extraction of zinc bearing ore. Use with other metal ores extracted and MINE where necessary, eg. LEAD MINE.

An area of managed countryside designated for visitors to enjoy recreations, such as walking specified parks and trails, in a rural environment. Often provides public facilities such as parking, toilets, cafes and visitor information.
Factory for the production of safety fuses used in the ignition of gunpowder for blasting.

Type of leaf-shaped socketed spearhead with two small holes or loops on either side at the base of the blade. Possibly meant to assist in securing the metal spearhead to the wooden shaft, or to tie streamers of some kind to the top of the spear.
A branched, hanging light fitting, often ornate in design, provifding illumination from a number of candles or lightbulbs.
A light, ornamental building or structure situated close to the sea.

Composite substance of plaster formed by gypsum, sand and lime and coloured with pigments, fixed under heat and highly polished. Used to imitate marble and popular in the 17th and 18th centuries for architectural features.
A type of thermoplastic polymer which is versatile and cheap, often referred to as PVC. This includes plasticized PVC and unplasticized PVC (uPVC).
Soft mineral, colour varying from black/purple to yellow/green. Commonly found as a mineral vein.

A sunken, circular, concrete pillbox used on airfields. They remained flush with the surface to permit the free movement of aircraft but, if attack threatened, could be raised hydraulically or by a counterbalance, and manned to give covering fire.

Court where sessions were held periodically in each county in England, for the purpose of administering civil and criminal justice. Presided over by itinerant judges acting under certain special commissions. Abolished 1971 and in 1972 replaced by Crown C.
The gate of a sluice which can be opened or shut to let out or retain the water.
A manmade barrier built across a river in order to increase the depth of water.
The use of ash and tephra deposits characteristic of single known-date volcanic eruptions to date stratigraphic sequences.
A brittle silvery metallic element used in the manufacture of many alloys.
A bridge on which dwellings or commercial premises have been built.
A factory containing machinery for processing clay for the manufacture of bricks, tiles or pottery.
A freestanding pole, stake etc often used to support a superstructure.
Solid bars or ingots of silver.
A ship of the line mounting between 64 and 80 guns typically built with two gun decks.
skos:Concept.skos:prefLabel: Third Rate Ship Of The Line

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: The area of water retained above a mill dam for driving a mill.
Vickers-Armstrongs Ltd.. In 1938 took over Vickers (Aviation) Ltd., which itself had taken control of Supermarine Aviation Works Ltd. in 1928.

A late 17th - early 18th century house with a central chimney and fireplaces and a central door on the front; this door opened closely against the fireplaces, leaving a small lobby for access to the rooms.
Areas of land that have been designated as national property where habitation and commercial activities are restricted to preserve their outstanding landscapes.
East Lothian, Scotland
The under surface of an arch, lintel or projecting architectural feature.
A narrow hand loom.
A specific German Stoneware form of rounded mug. (Source: MPRG)
A factory where paper is made. Use with power type where known.
A thin masonry facing or cladding employed to conceal the surface or structure behind it.
A building or site used to produce alkaline chemicals by controlled reactions.
A form of pilaster without base or capital.
A tool with a curved blade used for pruning.
A flat, circular plate, usually made of iron, on which food items are baked.
Single-engine, single-seat biplane day fighter developed by Siddeley. Variations included an all-metal, fabric-covered Mk.III, which became the RAF's main fighter in the 1920s.
A book containing information about a place that has been produced for the use of visitors or tourists.
A large bag made of coarse cloth or thick paper.
A tug equipped with water tanks and pumps for fighting fires at sea or on the shore line.
A dredger with a grab hung on ropes or chains giving it unlimited depth of excavation. they can lift solids or pieces of wreckages and can work close to ships or to a dock wall.
A hostel owned by a Christian association which provides cheap accommodation for young people.
Reinforced concrete blocks, walls or ditches designed to obstruct the progress of a tank or armoured vehicle.
A single ditched 3-sided rectilinear enclosure.

A concrete hut produced by the Ministry of Works as a cheaper alternative to the BCF Hut as any suitable wall cladding could be employed in its construction. Usually used to form barrack blocks on airfields from 1944 onwards.
A fixed seat, often enclosed, usually found within an ecclesiastical building and frequently arranged in series to accommodate a congregation, choir or clergy.
A building, usually circular, or containing circular rooms, for the exhibition of panorama paintings.
A building or structure of unknown function found on a railway. Use more specific type where known
A tomb or memorial, resembling an altar, often with a recumbent effigy on top.
A chemical works engaged in the production of the coal tar derivative phenol, a chemical used for the manufacture of explosives during WWI.

A British medium-range biplane airliner designed and built by Handley Page in 1921. A twin-engined variant of the Handley Page W series (W8, W9), retired in 1931. Built for Imperial Airways (4 units built).
A continuous row of WEALDEN HOUSES.
A ship in government use, used to carry naval or military stores.
An item that cannot be identified. Use more specific term, if possible.
Niche intended for pigeons or other birds to nest in, allowing the squabs and eggs to be harvested. Found inside specially built dovecotes and in the walls of other buildings.
A mechanical structure, consisting of a roller or beam on supports, round which a rope or chain is wound, and used for various purposes, eg. raising a bucket from a well, etc.
A wash room. Use with wider site type where known.
British single-engine, two-seat night fighter. Originally intended as a day fighter, but withdrawn and converted in August 1940, this was the first fighter to incorporate a power-driven gun turret.
Small mobile steam engine.
A structure used for the roasting or drying of chicory.
A small semi circular scraper current in the Bronze Age.
A building, similar to a cart shed, but used to house traps, gigs and coaches.
A fertilizer derived from nitrogen; also known as nitrate of ammonia.
Specify in Description using: private, public, formal etc.

An educational institution, introduced in the 1960s. Distinguished from universities by traditionally training technicians in business, industry and commerce for an immediate local area, and offering more part-time classes, etc.
A flag bearing a device, often carried on two poles or hanging from a cross piece. Usually used in processions.
A mill where flax is processed to make linen, thread and yarn.
A mechanism used to turn a tram around.
A sea within a sea, the Aegean consists of that part of the Mediterranean bordered by Greece and Turkey.
The fragmentary or substantial remains of a vehicle or aircraft. Where recovered from excavation double index with SUB SURFACE DEPOSIT.
A tower at the mouth of the harbour to defend the end of the harbour boom.
A factory or works principally engaged in the manufacture of the explosive Gelignite.
A share or portion of land, allotted to a person, often used for growing, vegetables, fruit, etc.
A building where distillation, a chemical process used in the production of a range of different chemicals, took place.
A place where tobacco is made into cigarettes, cigars, etc.
A long-handled implement designed to allow the user to scratch their own back.
The outlet or mouth of a sewer where it dispenses into the sea, lake, etc.
The residence of a station master.

Single-seat, single-engine biplane fighter. In operational service from 1939 to 1941, this was the last, and believed to be the best, biplane to be flown in the RAF. All-metal in construction with fabric and aluminium covering.
Particulars of a property for sale.
Single-engine, single-seat fighter-bomber. Designed to replace the Hurricane as an interceptor, excelled as a rocket-projectile-firing ground-attack fighter. Entered RAF service in 1941.
German three-engined air/sea rescue and transport flying boat. Entered service in 1940 as a replacement for the DO18.
A building containing presses for the compaction of mill cake gunpowder as part of the gunpowder manufacturing process.
A pestle used specifically for grinding cosmetics.
German port of the western bank of the mouth of the River Weser.
Underground chambers and stone passages of Iron Age date found in South West England.
A fighter version of the SKUA fitted with a four-gun turret. The majority were converted to target tugs for use by the RAF and Fleet Air Arm.
A residential home for children with physical and/or learning disabilities, sensory impairment and/or mental health issues who need medical intervention and/or care provided by registered nurses.
A spire, or spirelet surmounting a roof, especially over the crossing of a French Gothic Cathedral.
Site where steel is produced from molten pig iron using a Bessemer Converter, a development from the cementation and crucible steel-making techniques .
Four-crew, twin-engined, general reconnaissance flying-boat. Entered service after World War One, becoming the RAF's standard flying-boat until replaced by the Supermarine Southampton in 1925.

Originally designed as a wood and steel bomber-reconnaissance aircraft, subsequent variations served as special transports, glider tugs and paratroop carriers. Featured a tricycle-style undercarriage.
A shallow outdoor pool, usually rectangular in shape filled with water which when frozen was used for the sport of Curling.
Usually a servants' dining room.
A mill for shredding cloth, for use in flock paper, etc.
An object for cleaning a pipe used for smoking.
A kiln used for the production of any of the soda group of alkalis by the heating of plant remains or salt.

The recovery of material from samples collected during field investigations, usually taken by specialists with a particular area of expertise. Normally processed in the laboratory. Also use for the processing of samples subsequent to investigation.
Any instrument for plucking or strumming a string eg a small piece of wood or plastic used to strum a guitar.

A complex of buildings used as a headquarters and training base for Royal Navy personnel. Even though they are buildings on land shore establishments are deemed to be shipsand are designated 'HMS' eg. HMS Dolphin in Portsmouth.
Single-engine, three-crew torpedo-spotter, reconnaissance and anti-submarine biplane. Entered Naval service in 1936, designed for operation from aircraft carriers and equipped with folding wings.

An entablature often of great magnificence with bead and reel between fasciae of the architrave, frieze ornamented with continuous sculpture and cornice, with ornate coffers and richly carved modillions.

Two-seat, twin-engined light/medium bomber celebrated for its speed and versatility. Entering service in 1941, was also adapted for duties as a fighter-bomber, Pathfinder, mine-layer, transport, trainer and photo-reconnaissance aircraft.

A programme of assessment of the known or potential archaeological resource within a specified area or site on land, inter-tidal zone or underwater by the consultation and collation of existing written, graphic, photographic and electronic data.
The SI derived unit of magnetic field strength.
A truss with transverse timbers, like a tie-beam from which the middle section has been removed, supported on braces and carrying hammer-posts and braces that carry the open structure of the roof.
A place where gold is worked into articles or products.
Office used by a Piermaster.
A piece of grassland, often near a river, permanently covered with grass which is mown for use as hay.
A channel dug, or built up, to carry away surplus water from a river or waterway to prevent it bursting its banks and flooding.
A classroom constructed from prefabricated sections.

Twin-engined maritime-reconnaissance bomber adapted from pre-war American airliners, the A-28 and A-29, evident from the row of portholes along its fuselage. Entered service with RAF Coastal Command just before the outbreak of World War Two.
An aisle within a chancel providing access to, and around, the High Altar and surrounding cells.
A thin, rectangular panel, sometimes enriched with sculptural relief, placed between the triglyphs in a Doric Order frieze.
A small type of seat, usually without a back, set on legs.
Photographic print on self-developing photographic paper in a format developed by Polaroid in the 1970's
An inclined wooden trough which channels grain evenly from the feed hopper into the eye of the stones in a corn mill.
An open area within a bank where financial transactions take place.
A drinking vessel with two or more handles.
A water-powered forge or wire mill which manufactured metal wire combs for use in the textile industry.

One in a chain of stations with semaphore shutters and telescopes which could relay messages according to a planned code. Used from the 1790s by the British Admiralty to speed up communications from London to the ports of Deal, Portsmouth and Plymouth.

An operations room, built to drawing number 367/41, to control the lighting arrays of the DREM type of bombing decoy in use during the Second World War. Unlike earlier designs it was surface built and then covered in earth to protect against flooding.
A bowl with no noticeable base angle, so that the walls and base form a continuous rounded curve (Source: MPRG)
A measure for liquid, usually for a quarter of a pint.
A thin flat board or plate usually with a raised edge on which things can be carried.
A flour mill using both stones and rollers to produce flour and, perhaps mainly from the stones, animal feed from grains other than wheat.
Any carbonate material produced by biological activity, for instance operculae of snails.
A white powder used to colour medicines, paints etc.
A device with a sharpened surface used to grate objects such, as vegetables or cheese, into smaller pieces.

For example, spinal tumor, stroke, Alzheimers, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Cerebral Palsy, Chronic Fatigue, Dementia, Distal Muscular Dystrophy, Huntingtons Disease, Multiple Sclerosis, Narcolepsy and Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder.
A building where matches are manufactured.
Intended for personal decoration, objects made of precious, semi-precious or imitation metals and gemstones.
A maritime monument where the remains of a vessel are scattered over a wide area.

A stand by set house built with a steel-framed pitched roof. Built to drawing number 8760/42 it was intended to supersede all earlier designs and was cheaper to produce. Both the transformer and fuel tanks were located outside the main building.
Large, three-engined, long range reconnaissance flying boat. Wooden hull and frame construction, with linen covering. Entered service in 1930.
A house with no row of posts between the central space and the aisles.
A bowl adapted by having a pedestal base. (Source: MPRG)
A large tank or cask for storing or holding goods, whether liquid, such as chemicals or fermenting beer, or dry, often during a production process.
A post to which the offender is tied to be whipped.
Edible fruit of the vine, which may be either red or white.
A container in which substances are heated to high temperatures.
Generic term for fast sailing ships with schooner rig and fine hull lines.
An adjustable, horizontal beam, supporting the vertical stone spindle in a water or windmill, which allows the gap between the grinding stones to be varied.
A mound in excess of 150 metres in diameter, of Late Neolithic date and presumed ritual function, eg. Silbury Hill.
A parlour in a monastery.
A fortified tower found at the angle of a castle wall.
An area of land used for producing renewable energy, which can comprise a solar farm, wind turbines or biomass facility
An underfloor heating system.
A mill in which textile rags were ground, either to enable the fibres to be respun or to use the pulp in the manufacture of paper.
Ornamental garden building constructed within the branches of trees.
Material preserved due to very low humidity which inhibits decay by micro-organisms.
An earthwork or structure on a rifle range used to mark a set distance from the rifle butts (usually at 50 or 100 yard intervals).
A dwelling for the keeper of a canal wharf.
A modern fodder store on a farm.
Miles M.14 Magister. Single-engine, two-crew training and communications aircraft. Spruce and plywood in construction, with open cockpits and a fixed landing gear, served between 1937 and 1945.
The ground immediately surrounding a place, particularly a religious building.
The smallest piece of timber (2-5cms) across used in building, employed on rafters to support the roof covering or in a partition as a base for plaster or external render and wall covering.

Device for extracting juice from apples, usually crab apples, for use in cooking and medicine. Consists of a stone base carved with channels in the upper surface which was used with an upper weight, often secured with a wooden beam wedged into position.
A vault created by the intersection of two other vaults set at right angles to each other and of equal size.
Watch Office with operations room designed to Air Ministry drawing number (7345/41
A fast, armed vessel, small in size, often used for despatches and mail.
An educational establishment where agricultural theory and practice is taught.
A shrine often including representations of a god or gods or other holy relics which could be carried by worshippers whilst travelling.
An area of ground in which horses can be exercised.
A factory concerned with the commercial manufacture of cider, as opposed to domestic production.
A pillar housing a transformer to convert AC electricity supply, for use by electrified transport systems or for domestic purposes.
A meeting hall of the Temperance Society.
British twin-engined light/medium bomber developed from the model 142 civil transport. Noted for its speed, this three-crew monoplane had an all-metal, stressed skin structure and a 1000lb bomb load.
The hull of a dismantled ship used as a prison.
A timber placed horizontally in a cob or stone wall to support the foot of a post or cruck blade.
Use with form of extraction where known. Also use MINE and other ores extracted where relevant, eg. SILVER MINE.
A Cornish Medieval amphitheatre used for the performance of mystery plays and sports.
A pit or tank where the chemicals used in tanning are washed from the animal hides.
Head wear of a bride.
A pen for holding sheep waiting to be washed.
A small craft of wickerwork covered with waterproof material.
A factory used for the industrial manufacture of firelighters.
A cup offered as a prize in a contest.
A cloth woven from flax.
A step or ramp in the bank of a canal to enable horses to climb out of the water.
An open flat gound where the sport of shooting with bow and arrows is pursued. The ground can be equipped with targets mounted on butts and various fixed distance marker.
A place where two artificial waterways meet each other.
A wall containing apertures to allow a weapon to be fired through it.
A building for the storage and drying of hops, often including a hop drying kiln. Usually built as part of a farm.
A chimney placed at an angle with the walls so that there is an obtuse angle with each wall.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
A German coastal attack submarine in use during the First World War.
A castle built on a simple, rectangular plan, usually with a tower at each corner. This design became common in England after 1300.
A joint in which the side, or face, of a timber has been squarely cut away to fit into a corresponding cut-away in the side of another member.
A vertical piece of wood fixed on corners of walls to help the fixing of plaster and to protect against damage to the plaster.
A hospital for the care of patients with incurable illnesses.
The DH5 was an attempt to give a tractor-type fighter a good forward view. However it suffered from unpleasant flying characteristics and, as a result, had a short service career.
A place where hops are stored.
The residence of a master shipwright.
A small opening built into a stone wall or hedge to allow small animals through.
For example tumors, leukemia, bone/ breast/ colon/ prostate cancer, Hodgings Lymphoma/ Disease, oral/ throat cancer, melanoma, ovarian and pancreatic cancer and other related illnesses.
A door made up of vertical planks on the outer face and horizontal planks on the inner face.

Twin-engined, medium bomber with a 1200 mile range and a bomb load in excess of 10,000 lb. Entered service in 1940, but engine faults resulted in retirement in 1942 with its design later modified into the acclaimed four-engine Lancaster bomber.
Stone used for grinding or polishing during the manufacture of lithic implements
A maritime fitting for spacing rigging elements and preventing entanglement.
Bone like material which grows in a branch-like fashion on the heads of male deer and reindeers in general.

An artificially constructed wall with recessed and projecting grips for hands and feet and places to attach ropes. Used for practising rock climbing. If the wall is situated within a sports centre use term from Components thesaurus.
A grand staircase where the lower flight splits into two upper flights.
Coarse grained, dark coloured, igneous rock.
Instruments for determining position at sea, e.g. compasses, sextants.

Originally an area planted with evergreens or winter-flowering plants for winter display, they can also be large glasshouses built for public entertainment where the original purpose of displaying plants has either disappeared or been minimalised.
Scaffolding intended to impede the advance of enemy armoured divisions. Often found in association with "one way" anti tank ditches.
A hut used by a person who makes items from wood. Often found in a woodland setting.
A hand-operated loom on which figured cloth could be woven, also known as a drawing engine.
An artificial lake, often made by damming a stream. A common feature of landscape parks.
A workshop used for the production of pottery moulds.
A short or long term residential home for people not requiring medical intervention or nursing care, usually for older people.
A dining hall, usually in a monastery or college.
A child's bed, usually without rockers.
Auxiliary or support vessel used for the repair of naval craft.
Use for vessels registered in Northern Ireland.
A metal pin, often with a screw thread and used in conjunction with a nut.
A vessel containing a religious oil or unguent.
Hard, unglazed, brown, versatile earthenware which can be used as a tile or moulded into statuary.

Twin-engined air/sea rescue and anti-submarine patrol aircraft. Originally developed from the Wellington and intended as a bomber, entered RAF Coastal Command service in 1943. Fitted with a Leigh Light and ASV radar.
Specialised fermenting vessel consisting of a two-storey system consisting of a shallow chamber approximately 2m high above which is a walled deck.
A group of buildings containing machinery for the production in bulk of butter or related dairy products.
A light covering for the foot, usually worn indoors.

Single-engine, two or three-crew pre-World War 2 biplane fighter and general purpose aircraft. First flown in 1931, the Seal was a Naval variant on the Fairey Gordon and a forerunner of the Swordfish.
A three masted vessel with a square rig on the fore and main masts and lateen rig on the mizzen mast.
The area of the Basilica, especially in the early church, in which the altar resides.
A stone missile fired from a ballista, larger in diameter than ballista shot.
A small mobile steam engine.
A container, usually round and deep.
An engine in which a vertical piston rod supplies energy via a crankshaft directly to the flywheel suspended above the cylinder. Extensively used as mine winding engines.
Goods manufactured from processed cotton.
An uncommon form of a regular courtyard farmstead where the buildings are arranged in a Z-shaped form.
A stick inscribed with a prayer or prayers for use in praying.
Mechanism for turning around vehicles in a confined space.
A hospital for the medical and surgical treatment of sailors and/or their families. For Royal Naval seamen use ROYAL NAVAL HOSPITAL.
A commemorative monument to victims of the plague.

Canadian-built, single-engine, high-wing transport and communications aircraft converted from a civilian model. Metal-framed with fabric covering, saw service in 1944-5. Was capable of being equipped with wheels, floats or skis.
A soft, powder used in the manufacture of bread and foodstuffs, obtained by grinding wheat or other grain.
A building or site from which a watch can be kept to prevent the illegal import/export of goods.
An area of a carriageway, usually delimited by road markings, for the sole use of bicycles.
Geologist's term for any dark coloured, slightly metamorphosed igneous rock. Index with specific stone type where given.
A square or cylindrical pipe at the top of a chimney which helps the draught of air.

Twin-engined bomber. The Whitley was the first 'heavy' bomber to be built in quantity for the RAF and made the first bombing attack on Germany in May 1940. It was later used for convoy protection and reconnaissance.
A building or structure used for the storage of sugar.
A structure, part of a structure or area consisting of plain masonry.
A capital of the Tuscan Order featuring a square abacus.
The horizontal timber running the length of a roof and positioned at its apex.
Any vessel in use by the West India Company.
Dating to the reign of Queen Victoria.
A small protective fortification, such as an earthwork.
The second subdivision of the Palaeolithic or Old Stone Age. Characterized by the fine flake tools of the Mousterian tradition and economically by a hunter gatherer society.
A ball of chalk found on Neolithic sites.
A site where canvas, coarse, unbleached cloth, made from hemp or flax, was manufactured.
A workshop for combining flax or hemp as a preparatory stage of rope making.
A raised structure from which a priest can preach.
A container used to hold and or pour a liquid in honour of a deity.
Term applied to a pit trap itself and also a walled enclosure containing one or more pit traps.
A temporary settlement or encampment erected by construction workers (eg for reservoir construction).
A CRUCK HOUSE where the cruck blades are truncated and joined by a collar beam, above which is a separate roof construction.

Originally ordered as land based dive-bombers, with 950 being delivered to the RAF, none are known to have flown operationally, instead apparently serving as target tugs. Bermuda was the name given to the Brewster SB2A Buccaneer in RAF service.
A dish with straight or convex sides that turn inwards, forming an acute basal angle. (Source: MPRG)
A furnace for smelting ore in which the fuel and ore are mixed.
Three-crew, single-engine carrierborne torpedo-bomber. Entered service in 1942, first seeing action during the Battle of Midway. Served with the US Navy until 1956.
An object which contains or is inscribed with spells against disease, witchcraft etc, or providing luck to the wearer.

A French airliner which entered service in 1920. A conventional biplane design with enclosed cabin for four passengers and open cockpit for the pilot. Fitted with an early audible guidance system. Withdrawn from service in 1921.
A large, watertight enclosure in which the water is maintained at the high-tide level so that vessels remain constantly afloat in them.
A mill in which textile rags were ground, either to enable the fibres to be respun or to use the pulp in the manufacture of paper.
A shelter, sometimes camouflaged, for the observation of birds and animals at close quarters.
A blank for a knife that has not been hammered out.
A sliding metal bar, often fixed to a door or similar, which moves through staples so that its end fixes into another staple or hole which is attached to a fixed object, eg a door frame.
Mass produced iron framed shed usually clad in metal sheeting.
A window either in the shape of a four leaf clover or circular with four foils enclosed.
A large scale works for cloth finishing processes.
A tear shaped container.
A tool for cleaning a person's nails.
An oval or circular structure with seats rising in tiers around a central open space. Used for religious ceremonies, entertainment, training and armed combat contests.

Any one of the cargo vessels of that name belonging to the different Baltic nations, in use from the mid 18th to the early 20th century. Usually ketch-rigged. Not to be confused with the oared GALEASS.

A steel aircraft hangar evolved from the German "Lamellendach", a segmental roof design of the 1920s using a diamond shaped web of pressed steel producing a hangar with a shallow curving profile. Used for both military and civil purposes.
Solid spherical objects, manufactured from stone or metal, fired from cannon.
Includes excavation, research and general notes.
A building used for a variety of administrative purposes, usually at a military base.
The extraction of a limited quantity of wood for scientific analysis.
Container with a handle, spout and narrow neck.

Alabaster is a name applied to varieties of two distinct minerals: gypsum and calcite. The finer kinds of alabaster are employed as an ornamental stone, especially for internal decoration as it's softness allows it to be carved into elaborate forms.

Single-engine, two-crew multi-role aircraft designed for RAF Army co-operation. Entered RAF service in 1938. Noted for its role dropping agents into Europe, also served as a night-fighter, day ground-attack aircraft and target tug.
Small furnace, used to create an upward draught of air in mine workings.
