A shaped and or carved stone.
Cubes of solid concrete, usually with sides of 3 feet 6 inches or 5 feet which when placed in rows were intended to form a substantial barrier to enemy armoured divisions in the event of invasion.
A representation of a winged boy who represents Cupid or Love.
A large scale works for cloth finishing processes.
Iron, usually unworked, in the form of bars.
A furnace used for the refining of precious metals. eg. the separation of silver from argentiferous lead.
Photographic colour print developed using wet process.
Developed from the ill-fated ME210, the ME410 Hornisse entered service in May 1943. Although underpowered as a day fighter the ME410 saw service over the UK as a night fighter from 1943-45.
A large bottle, generally protected by a basket or box, usually used for containing corrosive liquids, etc.
A multihulled craft consisting of two hulls, or vakas, which are usually joined together by a frame or other structure, formed of akas. Catamarans can be sail or engine powered.
Machine, frequently horse powered, for mixing raw clay into brick earth.
The support from which a lamp was hung.

Twin-engined maritime-reconnaissance bomber adapted from pre-war American airliners, the A-28 and A-29, evident from the row of portholes along its fuselage. Entered service with RAF Coastal Command just before the outbreak of World War Two.
A jar that contains an offering.
A column, in the form of a female figure, used to support an entablature.
The post at the centre of a winding staircase from which the steps radiate; or the post, supporting the handrail and string, at the angle of a square staircase.
A tread-wheel by which a crane was formerly worked.
A place where the homeless are accommodated, permanently or temporarily.
A route across a river, or lake. Use only for small inland ferries and index with LANDING POINT/STAGE/STEPS or PIER where known.
A stone used to instruct a coachman to take an extra trace horse to assist on roads of a steep gradient.

An extra processing unit which can be used in conjunction with single beam echo sounders to determine the roughness and hardness of the seafloor. Mainly used for marine biology, but has been used in archaeology.
A factory, or group of buildings, containing apparatus used to extract specific properties, e.g flavour or scent, from natural ingredients.
A road junction where two (or occasionally more) roads cross each other.
A textile mill where crepe is manufactured.Crepe is a fine cloth particularly silk or mixture of silk and cotton.
A building or site used for the production of acids by a range of chemical processes.
A room in which public or private auctions are held.
A rod or spindle, either fixed or rotating, on which a wheel or group of wheels is fixed.
A plasterer's tool for smoothing the surface of plaster.
A lighted pillar or LIGHTHOUSE, eg. Dunston Pillar, Lincs., erected in 1751 to guide travellers over the heath.
A cereal of the genus Triticum, which can be ground to manufacture flour for bread and pasta.
Two discs at the end of a short shank, used to fasten shirt fronts, collars etc.

A two-seat, general purpose biplane. The first to be designed specifically for an Army Co-operation role, it entered service in late 1927. Ended its service as a communications and advanced trainer aircraft.
Transport version of the four-engined Lancaster bomber. Serving from 1943 to 1951, and all metal in construction, this aircraft was used extensively during the Berlin airlift.
A component of salt works containing flues and drying areas where salt blocks are dried before being crushed and bagged.
A factory in which varnish is manufactured.
A bowl adapted by the addition of a short tubular spout applied just below the rim.
Porous black residue of partly burnt wood, bones etc. used as fuel or, in the form of charcoal pencils, as a tool for drawing.
A major warship equipped with a clear flat deck to provide a landing and taking off place for aircraft.
A building or complex producing umbrellas, parasols and canes.
Report prepared by a specialist in a particular field, often as a contribution to a wider project.
The retrieval of material from deposits by hand, normally large objects visible with the naked eye, eg. Mammal remains and marine molluscs.
A single storey mill used in the textile industry.
Traditionally, pieces of unleavened cake or bread usually small in size and dry, crisp and hard.
American twin-engined medium bomber and ground-attack aircraft that entered service in 1941. A small number were delivered to the RAF under the British designation Mitchell I.
Any vessel propelled by sail or power and used for pleasure and not plying for hire.
